strings.IBR_THENEWORDER_DESC: Spain and Portugal's shrewd policies kept them out of the Second World War, however the new Europe that was birthed from the rubble was no kinder to them. Amid continental economic woes and German aggression, for the first time in centuries Iberia was united into a single state. Jointly ruled by Caudillos Franco and Salazar, the Union seemingly holds true to its mission of Iberian security in the face of the Reich on its doorstep. However the strain of keeping the Union together grows each day. The Union stands at a crossroads, staring down either an Iberian decade or total chaos.

strings.IBR_colombia.2.d:
CONFIDENTIAL

TO: DR. ANTÓNIO OLIVEIRA SALAZAR, GENERALÍSIMO FRANCISCO FRANCO, MINISTRY OF FOREIGN AFFAIRS

INVOLVEMENT IN COLOMBIAN WAR COMMENCING

The time has come. Recent developments in Colombia have colluded to provide us a window into involving ourselves in the war. Already, there have been talks with our chosen side's leadership to begin arranging steady lines of communication. We have pledged or are preparing to pledge diplomatic, logistic, humanitarian, and military support. Now it is only a specifics before we are fully involved in the conflict, with our options for just how we go about backing a side laid out before us. Expect further reports as our presence evolves and solidifies.
strings.IBR_colombia.3.d:
CONFIDENTIAL

TO: DR. ANTÓNIO OLIVEIRA SALAZAR, GENERALÍSIMO FRANCISCO FRANCO, MINISTRY OF DEFENSE

COLOMBIA - VICTORY ON THE BORDER

We've received good news from our allies and agents in Colombia. The bloody skirmishes along the border have relatively ceased. Although casualties were high, our allies prevailed and managed to overpower the enemy lines in a series of increasingly one sided battles. With the enemy's main force broken, Iberian volunteers and local troops set to work rooting out partisans and establishing garrisons to occupy the towns in the area. Although partisans remain an issue, it is negligible enough that we can say for sure that our side has won out in the region.

That being said, the conflict continues to escalate still, the enemy is rearming, and the partisans in the area will not give up so easily. Soon we will have to take action to hold on to our tenuous advantage in Colombia.
strings.IBR_colombia.3.a: At least we have sure footing.
strings.IBR_colombia.4.d:
CONFIDENTIAL

TO: DR. ANTÓNIO OLIVEIRA SALAZAR, GENERALÍSIMO FRANCISCO FRANCO, MINISTRY OF DEFENSE

COLOMBIA - DEFEAT ON THE BORDER

Our agents in Colombia have confirmed the loss of key territories along the disputed borders of the three agitators. The enemy was able to overpower both our allies and our own volunteers, exacting heavier and heavier casualties until morale and supply forced us out of the area. Although a significant partisan presence has remained behind to cause trouble for the foe, who have managed to establish garrisons in there, their presence is not enough to truly dispute enemy control. We must face the fact that the enemy has won this fight and now fully occupies the border territories.

The situation continues to escalate regardless. We are at a significant disadvantage, but we should not let that stop us from preparing for a more intense conflict. With this in mind, we should be ready to take action decisively and effectively if or when the time comes.
strings.IBR_colombia.5.desc:
Cartagena traced its history back to the conquistador Pedro de Heredia, who travelled the West Indies in the early 16th century and founded the city with two hundred men. Between the rivers Magdalena and Sinú the city was strategically important for the Spanish Empire in the Americas, and it grew flush with Spanish capital. Three centuries later, Spanish capital returned to Cartagena with the conclusion of La Violencia.

Perhaps it is unfair to suggest it is solely Spanish capital here. There are Portuguese contractors too, such as Atílio Salgado, a specialist in infrastructure who walked along Central Caribbean Road with a notebook, recording road widths, the poor quality of the gravel and the damage it sustained in the battle to capture the city. But most of the Iberians who came to Cartagena were Spanish. Sergio Díaz held secret meetings with the new mayor, seeking favourable terms for his construction company. At the port, Oier Tarragona oversaw the first merchant ships from across the Atlantic docking, bearing peninsular supplies and ready to receive Colombian treasures. Biel Francisco Gallego stepped off one of the ships, suitcase in hand, ready to enter this newly-opened market.

And in the streets of Cartagena, a young diplomat goes walking through the bustling crowd, ecstatic with their newfound freedom and an end to the violence that plagued this country for years. José Manuel Peralta held in his hand a large manila folder, inside which was a report from the Iberian embassy. It talks of the new government preparing elections, the hopeful mood in the streets, the eagerness for Colombia to return to the world; it speaks also of the government's appreciation for Iberia, and the assets their liberalisation has opened up. He entered the post office and handed the envelope to a clerk; FOR URGENT DELIVERY is stamped on the front, underneath which is the address of the Iberian Union's foreign ministry. Peralta returns to Cartagena with a light heart, eager to embrace the city he would come to think of as a home away from home.
strings.IBR_colombia.5.a: A peaceful land is a stable land; a stable land is good for business.
strings.IBR_colombia.6.desc:
The report sat on Franco's desk unopened. There was no point in reading it, he knew what it said. The situation in Colombia had been deteriorating for weeks, this report was just the final pronouncement. He would spare himself the gory details.

The phone on his desk rang. This did not surprise him either, and he knew exactly who it was. Picking up the receiver, he was met with a slew of Portuguese profanity from his fellow caudillo. He set the phone down on his desk to let Salazar get it out of his system. And it's not like he didn't deserve it. He was the one who had convinced Salazar that this adventure in Colombia would be worth it. He was the one who had spoken of reclaiming old glories, of Iberia once again having a place in the New World. But those days were gone, and this was the proof.

With a sigh, he picked up the phone.

“I agree, Antonio. It was my mistake. We need to cut our losses and pull out everything.”
strings.IBR_colombia.7.desc:
It was late into the night when the cargo ship bearing the defeated cruised into the harbour, emerging from the fog at a languid pace. They had all been woken up by the call of “landfall,” and they were all gathered around the edge of the ship to look upon their homeland, but there was no jubilation to be found in returning home. They all felt empty, confused and tired.

They had lost, and the men who sent them to this defeat were gone. They departed with the knowledge that they had failed Iberia - but on the voyage back home, they wondered what they were fighting for anyway. What was there in Colombia that was worth sending Iberians to die? Their comrades died for a cause they could no longer recall; all the survivors had were their lives, irreparably scarred by this failure.

In the distance, the lights of the harbour glittered. The air was pleasantly cold and dry, welcome relief from the Colombian jungles. No longer would they suffer the oppressive wet heat; no longer would they suffer communist or republican bullets and blades; and no longer would they suffer the dreams of old men in Madrid.

Each man carried a testimony of regret, failure and betrayal they would not only carry in their hearts, but testify to all Iberia. They would tell it in the family home, fathers recalling sanitised versions of the war for their children. They would tell it in the inns and pubs of Iberia, drunken wretches crying into their cups for lost comrades at three in the morning. Some would even tell it in the courts as men considered what compensation they could receive for their sacrifice.
strings.IBR_colombia.7.a: Perhaps they would even tell it on another battlefield, closer to home.
strings.IBR_colombia.8.desc:
Twenty rich men gathered in the vast conference room, in the largest hotel in Bogotá that had not been bombed. Across the room from them was an auctioneer, a government representative and a map of New Granada. They had overlaid lot numbers on the map: the positions of rich estates, fertile valleys and fields most suitable to growing Colombia's finest crop.

In the estates, a colonel enjoys the first day of his retirement. He intended to grow fat on the lucre he had won from the civil war - half of which he had stolen from Jewish families marked traitors to the state by Alzate. The estate was a beautiful colonial holdover, atop a great hill underneath which were vast fields, and a little town that had grown around a small lake. But he did not own it all, not truly. He knew he was but the representative of another man, who let him play landlord for a reasonable fee. “Sold, to the gentleman from Sapporo, for three million.”

A group of farmers were held up by the roadside. Patted down, humiliated, struck in the stomach with the butt of a rifle. New Granadan soldiers raided their caravan, took the crops they had wanted to send to market. Their commander thought himself fair, and left behind a bill with El Duce's face on them. Dejected, the farmers trekked back to their fields, only to find more men bearing a deed to the land, and an order to kick out the squatters. “Sold, to the gentleman from Milan, for four million.”

The village tried to put the war behind them, but the scars remained. When they closed their eyes they still saw the militias descending upon the valley like an avalanche. When they left, seven were dead. The soldiers called them Marxist saboteurs - their only crime was being a village in URC territory. But they were poor, and thought themselves below the attention of anyone else, until a strange man had come and taken samples of their soil. Then came a hundred speculators from distant lands. “Sold, to the gentleman from Barcelona, for five million.”
strings.IBR_colombia.8.a: Sold, to the richest men from the Old World, for a few thousand lives.
strings.IBR_CountryInfo_Content_desc.1:
Not since 1640 has Madrid and Lisbon been united underneath one flag. Yet, fate is a fickle mistress, and not one that takes kindly to those who disobey it. During the Second World War, despite Franco's sympathies towards Berlin, Portugal and Spain remained neutral, albeit not without Spain seizing Gibraltar from the clutches of the dying British Empire. However, as Hitler tamed Europe, so he would try his hand in Africa. With what scattered units they accrued in the Dark Continent, Germany struck the Portuguese colonies of Angola and Mozambique.

Fearing that the unquestioned master of Europe would turn against them once more, meetings were established for a mutual guarantee of sovereignty for the two nations. Eventually, despite Portugal's historical reluctance, a new state was birthed by necessity. The Iberian Union.
strings.IBR_CountryInfo_Content.2: The Dawn of a New Age
strings.IBR_CountryInfo_Content_desc.2:
By the 1950s, the coalition formed between Prime Minister Salazar and Caudillo Franco began to solidify itself, as confidence began to creep into the new Iberian regime. Institutions manifested, and then settled. Interests and costs merged. Although it required rigorous work, the young state began to define itself over the decade, undertaking an economic transition from autarky to dirigisme in search of greater prosperity. Declining substantial ties to both America and the Reich, the Iberian Union sought to eke out its own place on the world stage.

All would have appeared well in the halls of Iberian power, if not for the Golpe d'Albufeira. Led by Humberto Delgado, conspirators aimed to break apart the Iberian Union and return Portugal to her independence - by any means necessary. Once discovered, it achieved little more than securing the power of the Conservatives with a range of repressions, fomenting lingering distrust between the Portuguese and Spanish factions of the Union.
strings.IBR_CountryInfo_Content_desc.3:
Despite the youth of the new nation, the issues that plagued its two parent nations lingered, their shadows stretching out across the Union. As the 1950's progressed it found its economic policies failing to meet expectations, a slow malaise setting in despite all efforts to combat it. The dominant Conservatives struggled to find an answer, each measure disappointing. Power coalesced into factions vying to influence the nation's revitalization efforts, seeking the ears of the meticulous Salazar or the watchful Franco.

But the Caudillos age. Each month passes by with a new notice of their frailty. With no succession plans and a divided political apparatus, only two unifying beliefs hold universally in the halls of power: commitment to the Caudillos, and commitment to moving past them. All recognize that Iberia stands upon a flashpoint, its very soul stands to be settled as the Union stands likely to outlive its founders - or so are the beliefs in Lisbon and Madrid.
strings.IBR_CountryInfo_Content_desc.4:
The Empire creaks, buckling amongst the rising sea of rebellion and foreign encroachment. The Union maintains a vigil on its territories, desperate to retain its colonial legacies. From Guinea-Bissau to Equatorial Guinea, agitation for independence simmers. Many of the Union's sub-Saharan territories find themselves in a desperate cycle of reliance on greater military presence as voracious resource extraction and settler initiatives continue.

Morocco is the jewel in the crown, the colonial prize of the end of the Second World War, but the jewel is losing its shine. Hassan II's patience is not infinite, and the Kingdom's protectorate status leads to frequent clashes between him and Madrid. For now, he regulates the nationalists in Moroccan politics, but they organize ever more boldly. Iberia weighs its options, aware of the untenable status quo but ever knowing that should the King lose his loyalty or his control, the dogs of war may yet overtake Iberia's latest African conquest.
strings.IBR_CountryInfo_Content_desc.5:
While cultivating Mediterranean ties has been an objective of Iberia over the last decade, her true attention has lain to the West and the South. Across Latin America, Iberian diplomats enjoy increasingly close relationships, much to the chagrin of Mexico City. Particular effort has been put into relations with the Dominican Republic and factions within Colombia, to whom Iberia has taken pains to appear as a confidant, supporter and friend; the notion of a Hispanic power bloc tantalizing minds in Madrid.

In South America, the Union enjoys a neutral position in the ongoing tensions between Brazil and Argentina; enjoying the friendship of both. In Africa, Iberian diplomats, missionaries and expeditions continue continent wide, praising the Iberian civilizing mission and affirming its commitments both to the European empires and the colonials they oversee. Legitimacy is the nectar Iberia craves within the dark continent, to keep its rightful territories as the darkness creeps closer.

strings.IBR_Army_Engineers_desc: The Iberian Government has begun to send some of their army engineer specialists to our country to help boost our weak industrial output. This will help us churn out more vital weaponary.
strings.IBR_Air_Sorties_desc: The Iberian Air Force is conducting heavy operations in our skies. Factories and infrastructure are being bombed to dust, and our troops report heavy losses: with no way to fight against an enemy of such magnitude, we can do nothing but endure.
strings.IBR_sabotage_effort_desc:
The outbreak of war with the Iberian puppet has resulted in the Iberian secret service being unleashed against us. A wave of sabotage has swept our country as their agents set to work stealing state secrets, sabotaging military operations, and assassinating officials.

This is proving detrimental to the war effort, not only because of the direct consequences of the sabotage but also because of the paranoia gripping our government as our own agents struggle to prevent further damage.
strings.IBR_military_advisors_desc: Our friends in Iberia have seen fit to dispatch military advisors to aid our armed forces in the current conflict. With their support we shall see a significant improvement in the overall performance of our soldiers, as well as learning important lessons about modern warfare which will improve the efficiency of our armed forces in the future.
strings.IBR_PP_invasion_desc:
Our agents in Havana have passed on alarming reports that the Cuban government has begun training the “Caribbean Legion,” a group of mercenaries preparing to invade the Dominican Republic and overthrow Trujillo's regime. Whispers of increased resistance in the D.R. itself further demonstrate that our friend's once firm grip on control is no longer there. It's obvious that this effort has been orchestrated by the Americans.

If we want to maintain any sort of future influence in the Caribbean, we must make sure that Trujillo survives and that the Legion is crushed.

strings.IBR_ffr_reclamation_desc:
We have promised aid to the French. They have paid their side of the bargain and it is now our turn to pay our fair share. From Bilbao to Barcelona we are ready to cross the border and go all in on backing the Free French. Our troops will begin pouring across the border into France as we engage in combat in continental Europe for the first time since the civil war.

If all goes to plan, we will have a stable ally between us and the German menace to our east. Such an opportunity would be great to give the Germans a taste of their own medicine and scare them with a hostile state on their borders for decades to come.

strings.IBR_CCW_desc: Colombia is our most important strategic partner in Latin America ever since the 40s and the primary means through which Iberian influence can spread into the continent, both to honor our partnership and to ensure they do not fall victim to the influence of radicals, but also to affirm our Union as a true and respectable power on the Continent, we must ensure this Civil War is won by the right government.

strings.IBR_wac_desc_1:
The foothold of Europe in West Africa is under threat! Under the guise of 'anti-colonialism', the Pan-African Liberation Front - little more than Japanese stooges playing up racial politics - is marching upon our French allies, as well as any fellow Africans who have spurned their home-grown version of imperialism.

It is our duty - and in our best interests - to stand against nativists and Marxists.

We have escalated the war by {WAC_escalation}%.

Our ties with Free France are at {IBR_FFR_aid_var}%.
strings.IBR_wac_desc_2:
The foothold of Europe in West Africa is under threat! The French and their allies - old friends of ours - are beset on all sides by enemies of freedom. To the west and north: opportunists and the misguided, striking at the French for all manner of petty reasons. To the east: Japan's hypocritical puppets, the Pan-African Liberation Front.

We have escalated the war by {WAC_escalation}%.

Our ties with Free France are at {IBR_FFR_aid_var}%.

We'll offer social security, subsidies, and other measures in order to attract veterans and volunteers into this elite troop.
strings.IBR_swell_foreign_legion_WA_tt: The French Foreign Legion will expand!
strings.IBR_EC_establish_smokescreen_operations_: Assasination attempts. Bombings. Pipeline sabotage. A slow-burn infiltration of Caracas. Get DFS and DIGEPOL on the trail of every conceivable threat except a military blitz on the capital.
strings.IBR_EC_reach_out_old_friends_desc: Pérez Jiménez, Venezuelan caudillo turned Madrid exile, will only be too happy to tell us which officers are most dissatisfied with the present leftist government.
strings.IBR_EC_call_on_hispanic_sentiments_desc: Much of the populace is against the godless leftism now in Caracas, and looks to the Patria as a better model. We will offer it to them - all they need to do is get out of the jeeps' way.
strings.IBR_EC_procurement_in_colombia_desc: La Violencia makes guns and ammo a bargain just across the Venezuelan border.
strings.IBR_EC_bribe_garrison_officers_desc: Most soldiers know Venezuela's government is a threat to the nation. Others can be reminded by bolivar himself. The banknote, not the Liberator.
strings.IBR_EC_cover_our_tracks_desc: Make sure we're not followed into the next barracks. And kill the maid that saw us enter into the last one.
strings.IBR_EC_mislead_rival_agencies_desc: The Venezuelans and Mexicans are using our operatives' activities to hunt for the coupists. Let's send them on a wild goose chase near Guyana.
strings.IBR_EC_anti_guerilla_operations_desc: An effort to wipe out FALN communists is the perfect excuse for our build-up. Not that we need an excuse.
strings.IBR_EC_from_the_skies_desc: Planes let us supply Castro León's forces over the immensely rugged terrain of the Andes. Shame about all the attention they draw.
strings.IBR_EC_fuel_the_monsters_desc: Moncada Vidal and his Bolivarianist radicals are brutal, wild, and loud. As conspiracy turns to coup, give them everything they need to get it done.
strings.IBR_EC_emphasize_hispanic_unity_desc: Many Venezuelan officers hold deep regard for the overthrow of our illegitimate Republic. As absolute loyalty to Franco was necessary for our victory, absolute loyalty to Castro León is to theirs.
strings.IBR_EC_eradicate_guerillas_en_route_desc: It's a long drive to Caracas, and FALN cells lurk along the way. Put bullets in their heads now, so there's no need to slow down later.
strings.IBR_EC_extract_assets_desc: It's all failed. Grab those pesetas and let's get the hell out of here!
strings.IBR_misleading_rival_agencies_tt: While this decision is active, we will be unable to take any other decisions.
strings.IBR_misleading_rival_agencies_active_tt: If Misleading Rival Agencies is active, we cannot take other decisions.
strings.IBR_EC_promote_hispanism_effect_tt: If the coup succeeds, Venezuela will be more likely to align with our government.
strings.IBR_CN_desc_1:
From the heights of El Hatillo to the banks of the Guaire, they speak of Villalba's old foes, the followers of former dictator Pérez Jiménez, slinking in alleyways. Of officers disenchanted with the military's waning influence. Of an opportunity to seize a foothold in the Caribbean.

These whispers are not yet shouts of anger at the walls of Miraflores. Counterrevolutionary forces are still scattered and weak. But we must use this fleeting moment to build our ties - with dissidents, smugglers, and exiles. So that when Villalba shows weakness, as he inevitably will, they will send him to join his old friend Rómulo Betancourt in hell.
strings.IBR_CN_desc_2:
From the heights of El Hatillo to the banks of the Guaire, they speak of Bolivarianist brutes, skulking in barely concealed rage. Of officers disenchanted with the military's waning influence. Of an opportunity to seize a foothold in the Caribbean.

These whispers are not yet shouts of anger at the walls of Miraflores. Counterrevolutionary forces are still scattered and weak. But we must use this fleeting moment to build our ties - with dissidents, smugglers, and exiles. So that when Caldera betrays his country, as he inevitably will, they will be ready to plunge the dagger into his back.
strings.IBR_CN_fakemission_tt: They'll face the fate of mortal greed.
strings.IBR_CN_regroup_perezjimenezistas_desc: Former Venezuelan Caudillo Marcos Pérez Jiménez maintains a considerable number of loyalists in the military. We'll stop by his residence in Madrid and prepare some correspondence to officers willing to join our network.
strings.IBR_CN_incite_national_sentiment_desc: Caldera is far too cozy with the Canadians and Americans, a disgrace to the legacy of the Libertador! At least, that's what the rumors we'll spread through Fort Tiuna will say.
strings.IBR_CN_coordinate_with_rightist_legislat: The revolutionary triumvirate of COPEI, URD, and AD ignore the few rightist legislators as they bicker. Nevertheless, these wealthy and well-connected citizens will be valuable pieces of our network.
strings.IBR_CN_hide_stockpiles_in_el_avila_desc: The forested mountain park of El Ávila is the perfect place for dead-drops and caches for our agents. Let's seed a few amidst the wildflowers.
strings.IBR_CN_tempt_officers_with_vice_desc: Venezuela's soldiery are disciplined and orderly. But even a good Christian's tongue can loosen after a taste of Baruta's nightlife.
strings.IBR_CN_expand_network_into_miranda_desc: The growing slums inside Petare create a populous enclave in eastern Caracas. A little diversification and deals with local gangs could open new avenues for our network.
strings.IBR_CN_form_traditionalist_circles_desc: Santa Rosalía bless El Hatillo. High above Caracas, we can intermingle with the religious and the country club set, both alienated from Venezuela's revolutionary politics.
strings.IBR_CN_smuggle_an_exile_back_desc: Adherents to the New National Ideal sought refuge in Iberia after Venezuela's rightful government was overthrown. With DIGEPOL in disarray, it's time to bring one influential figure home.
strings.IBR_CN_pump_guns_and_money_desc: We need to show our network that distant Iberia can fulfill their ambitions. Nothing is more convincing than crates of loaded guns and pesetas.
strings.IBR_CN_pressure_from_the_pulpit_desc: A limited, but useful, number of righteous clerics aligned with Francoist thinking stand against Venezuela's revolutionary parties - even COPEI's 'Social Christian' heresies. Let's use one to expand our flock.
strings.IBR_CN_plant_explosives_at_politicians_h: Actions speak louder than words. And the loudest demonstration of DIGEPOL's failures is a bomb.
strings.IBR_pull_on_the_lever_of_tensions: Pull on the Lever of Tensions
strings.IBR_pull_on_the_lever_of_tensions_desc: Currently available resources will be utilised to intensify the protests. The effects of this decision depend on the amount of existing routes.
strings.IBR_get_to_know_bad_people_desc: New resources will be utilised to permanently flame up the island. The more £GFX_fervor_texticon Fervor there is, the less effective this decision is.
strings.IBR_KingstonRiots_OpeningRoute: We are already opening a route
strings.IBR_SalvadoranCoup_TheOldPartiasFavor_de:
-------------
Every time this decision is taken its £political_power_texticon  cost increases by 5. Meanwhile, its cost in $$M is directly proportional to the value of Military Preparedness.
-------------
El Salvador's weak government has allowed Castrist filth to permeate the armed forces. By directing them toward leftist conspirators, we keep true Salvadoran patriots safe.
strings.IBR_SalvadoranCoup_ArmsForTheWorthy_desc:
-------------
Every time this decision is taken its £GFX_weapon_icon  cost increases by 100.
Its power is higher if Castrists are Dominant.
-------------
The logistics of arming Salvadoran patriots from Iberia is fiendish. We will work to rearm certain... enterprising merchants in the region that supply the Hispanists weapons.
strings.IBR_SalvadoranCoup_DesordenFromORDEN_des: Medrano, head of El Salvador's National Guard and its intelligence agency, ORDEN, is a known admirer of Iberian governance. If he were to 'release' a few tortured civilians for public view, the totterring Rivera government would receive another push.
strings.IBR_SalvadoranCoup_HomemadeNationalMarty:
-------------
This decision damages El Salvador's Stability and War Support in proportion to Hispanists' Dominance.
-------------
There are so few righteous men willing to lay down their lives for El Salvador. Others can be convinced with a few credible threats to their families.
ERROR: UNKNOWN EFFECT. PLEASE FULLFIL DECISION'S PREREQUISITES TO CONTINUE.
strings.IBR_SalvadoranCoup_GiftsAndFavors_desc:
-------------
Every time this decision is taken its£GFX_green_dollar_sign cost increases by 5M.
If its cost exceeds $15M, it will be more powerful.
-------------
Many Salvadoran officials have too much to lose in a coup to be turned by gifts within our means. Their personal secretaries however...
strings.IBR_SalvadoranCoup_GiftsAndFavors_modifi: The Government's Efforts to Combat the Plot will be less effective at decreasing Military Preparedness and Civilian Anger.
strings.IBR_SalvadoranCoup_UnderTheTableBargaini:
-------------
Every time this decision is taken its£GFX_green_dollar_sign cost increases by 5M.
If Hispanists are Dominant, Military Preparedness increases but the Day of {els_getflag} Reckoning accelerates.
If Castrists are Dominant, the effects are reversed.
-------------
Corruption worms throughout the Rivera administration, as its predecessors. We can lean on a hardline coffee oligarch to bring their clique alongside.
Adds 15 days from the Day of {els_getflag} Reckoning.
Removes 15 days from the Day of {els_getflag} Reckoning.
strings.IBR_SalvadoranCoup_SpreadingAnInferno_de:
-------------
This decision increases Military Preparedness by 20% of Civilian Anger, and increases the Popularity of the Dominant faction.
-------------
Santa Ana, San Miguel are smoldering. By unleashing rabid troops backing the coup against the governments' loyalists, we can set them alight!
strings.IBR_TMW_desc:
Following unsuccessful incursions into the rebel Moroccan government, Iberian military heads have outlined a clear, decisive plan for reclaiming her most crucial Maghrebian posts. The plan calls for a quick, decisive strike in order to recapture the ports of Melilla and Ceuta and hold off the Moroccan onslaught, and international attention.

Although not the main objective, Iberia could seize the rest of the Rif region should the opportunity arise, and give a greater command over the strait. However, such aggressive actions may begin to draw attention to the war and risk further retaliation from the Casablanca government. The war strikes a critical point for Iberia: either a full retreat from the Maghreb or an honorable hold - and possible expansion, of her remaining power.
strings.IBR_The_Shedding_Of_Doubt_desc: We have limited time to complete all of our operations in Morocco, and by the countdown's end, we will have to withdraw from Morocco and make do with what we have gained.
strings.IBR_A_Matter_Of_Pride_desc: The enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla are Iberian, and we will not tolerate their illegal Moroccan occupation. It should be in our best interest to secure them as soon as possible.
strings.IBR_The_Pyrrhic_Solution_desc: We have managed to make limited gains in Morocco, notably the enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla. Even though we don't control the Rif, this is an acceptable outcome.
strings.IBR_The_Return_To_1912_desc: We have managed to secure our previous holdings in Morocco, notably the enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla, along with the Rif. This closely resembles our 1912 borders, making this a more than acceptable outcome.
strings.IBR_TMW_wrapped_up_tt: We have finished our operations in Morocco
strings.IBR_reach_foreign_elites_2_VEN: Reach Out to More Foreign Elites
strings.IBR_FFR_aid_negotiations_tt: Our past involvement in the West African War will affect our negotiating power.
strings.IBR_FWI_referendum_acquire_albrand_backi: Médard Albrand is a political power of the Guadeloupe plantocracy, friendly with the Americans but devoted first and foremost to his class' interests. If we can sway him against the Confederation, we will deal it a mighty blow.
strings.IBR_FWI_referendum_faciliate_the_fraud_d: Albrand's connections have allowed us to isolate and work isolated plantations where some 99% of the vote can be secured against the Confederation.
strings.IBR_FWI_referendum_faciliate_the_fraud_t: Our relations with Albrand will greatly influence the effect of this decision.
strings.IBR_FWI_referendum_collaborate_with_guil: A vehement anti-American populist on Guadeloupe, Raymond Guilliod could assemble a powerful anti-Confederation coalition. A multi-racial and cross-class one that might alienate some of our more natural allies on the islands...
strings.IBR_FWI_referendum_court_martinique_cons: The various leftist currents on Martinique have respectable citizens considering the Confederation as a possible defense. By propping up Edmond Valcin as an alternative, we can secure new backing.
strings.IBR_FWI_referendum_recycle_separatist_pr: With less than two months before the referendum, we do not have the luxury of nuance. Grab some of the separatist garbage in the archives, translate it to French, and slap Guadeloupe or Martinique on it somewhere.
strings.IBR_FWI_referendum_guide_the_flock_desc: Priests across the Antilles have good reason to be suspect of the godless Americans. A few missives and they will steer their parish against the Confederation.
strings.IBR_FWI_referendum_convince_the_planteur: The Antilles is dominated by planters, many of whom are rightfully outraged by the American's failed urbanization initiatives. Hold a few dinner parties and their natural opposition to the Confederation will bloom.
strings.IBR_FWI_referendum_frighten_the_beke_des: The few white denizens of the Antilles are pillars of their communities. A few acts of sabotage will convince them that the Confederation cannot keep them safe from the black communists that surround them.
strings.IBR_FWI_referendum_frighten_the_beke_tt: This decision will become more powerful if the French West Indies are unstable.
strings.IBR_FWI_referendum_the_tried_and_true_de: There is a world of commerce for the Antilles once they break the Americans' hold. We'll offer a few prominent planters a taste of what awaits.
strings.IBR_FWI_referendum_involve_our_french_al: The Free French offer a valuable counterpoint to U.S. dominance and look to grow their own influence in the Antilles. We'll offer transportation to Basse-Terre.
strings.IBR_FWI_referendum_involve_our_dominican: Involve Our Allies in the Dominican Republic
Our Dominican allies will lend their voices to the referendum campaign, tilting another Caribbean domino in our direction.
strings.IBR_FWI_referendum_increase_albrand_back: This will closen our relations with Albrand
strings.IBR_FWI_referendum_decrease_albrand_back: This will strain our relations with Albrand

strings.IBR_AP_ROUTE: £GFX_TNO_game_rule_flag_IBR_CONGRESS   Iberian Federation - Fate of Alianza Popular
strings.IBR_DIVORCE_FATE: £TNO_game_rule_flag_IBR  £TNO_game_rule_flag_SPA  £TNO_game_rule_flag_POR   Iberian Union - Fate of the Iberian Divorce
strings.IBR_collapsing_military_desc:
Mass desertions plague the Iberian Armed Forces. Thousands of soldiers abandon the centralized Iberian military to instead fight for the regional armies of their homelands. Besides the desertions, which are crippling in their own right, the Armed Forces has also found themselves caught within an irreconcilable rift between reformist and hardline officers.

The two camps of officers have effectively shattered the chain of command, and now act completely independent of each other. In the streets of Madrid, Barcelona, and Bilbao, and countless other cities across the nation, chaos and banditry caused by these rogue units have become the new norm.

Inside El Pardo, the Caudillo of Spain sits alone. He is powerless to stop the tragedy.
strings.IBR_Torn_Apart_desc:
In the wake of the Basque declaration of independence, Portugal has come to realize that the Iberian Union is not long for this world. Not wishing to be dragged into the inferno alongside the Spanish, the Portuguese government instead chose to abandon the Union and try to save themselves.

Portugal's departure predictably threw all sectors of the government and military into disarray. The economy had already been experiencing malaise ever since the 50s, and had fully destabilized due to the growing protests across the country. Now, the final nail has been driven into the coffin, and complete economic collapse has arrived.
strings.IBR_last_days_nation_desc:
The first Iberian Union, which spanned from 1580 to 1640, was born out of pure chance. Portugal's only viable heir just so happened to already be the King of Spain. Thus two mighty empires merged into a single personal union, creating a prosperous nation that only collapsed due to revolts.

The second Iberian Union was born not out of chance, but out of necessity. This union was supposed to allow the two nations to prosper, but alas, it was not to be.

Hope is dead, and over its grave lay yellow and fearful flowers. Violence has come to Iberia, born not from some external army, but instead its own people. The Iberian government has finally given up fighting for unity, and instead can only watch as the nation burns down around them.

strings.IBR_iberian_labour_charter_desc: Inspired by Fascist Italy's Carta del Lavoro, the Iberian Labor Charter represents an amalgamation of pre-Unification labor codes from Portugal and Spain. From the outset, the laws have been a mix of Fascist and Catholic Corporatism, but as the Caudillo system has shifted toward a more market-oriented economy, amendments have been made to move these laws away from corporatist elements. It has often been said that a good compromise pleases no one, and, in the eyes of the Caudillos, this arrangement has been near-perfect: neither employer nor employee is truly satisfied with the situation, keeping both under the thumb of the government.
strings.IBR_non_united_colonies_desc: Closer to a policy than a law; among the many agreements reached during negotiations over Iberian Unification, it was agreed that Portugal and Spain would govern their respective colonies without the other's interference. Portugal's colonies are still managed under the old Portuguese Colonial Act, while Spain's are governed by the various laws that stood in place before Unification. The Union does not possess any ministry to govern these overseas colonies, but rather a state secretary who serves as a rubber stamp, signing off on whichever side of the Union wishes to govern their colonies.
strings.IBR_organic_bases_of_the_creation_of_the: Organic Bases of the Creation of the Union

The assorted and numerous agreements signed between Portugal and Spain in order to bring about Unification. These deals delineate how both governments can merge into one while leaving many institutions on both sides untouched, resulting in the “Pyramid System:” the closer a body or institution is to the top, the more centralized it is, and the further away from the top one goes, the more unchanged it will be from the pre-Union days. Through this way, the unique identities and needs of the Union's participants are preserved while ensuring cohesive governance.
strings.IBR_prestige_foreign_policy_desc: The end of the Second World War proved that treaties, pacts, and other diplomatic agreements have limits on how far they can go to protect a nation. If Iberia is to flourish in this new world order, she must prove that she is as much of a diplomatic and military force as any other world power. Focused on Latin America and the African regions that border their colonies, the Union has adopted a flexible foreign policy, willing to work with anyone —whether local or global players —so long as the Caudillos see them as worthy of their assistance. In summary, the Iberian Union's foreign policy is guided by aligning nations with Iberia or by assisting established allies.
strings.IBR_iberian_council_law_adv_desc: The Iberian Council is an advisory body of 16 men chosen by the Caudillos. The Council has no actual power, with its duties being to review and suggest changes to laws sent to them by the Caudillos. While a seemingly simple institution, the Council has many unwritten rules mostly revolving around giving each faction of Iberia fair representation in the body. A balanced Council can bring harmony to the otherwise chaotic politics of the nation. An unbalanced Council can tear the country apart even more.
strings.IBR_iberian_council_law_leg_desc:
Created by the Caudillos to quell the democratic unrest, the Iberian Council is an attempt to create a legislative branch of the Iberian government. Meant to give the veneer of choice to Iberians, the council members are elected in accordance with the principles of “organic democracy,” with 450 members being elected every four years by various groups across the peninsula.

While the Council has the initiative to propose laws, these are all laws from the government that the Council discusses. Following a standard legislature process, the laws are debated and changed by the Council. All laws are passed, but not without Council changes. Full of factionalism and nepotism, the Council rarely helps the citizens of Iberia, and instead bickers among itself.
strings.IBR_iberian_charter_desc: Theoretically one of the most important laws of Iberia, the charter dictates the rights and obligations of Iberia's citizens. As expected of the Caudillos, the rights of the people are few and can be suspended in case of “any extreme or notable threats to national security,” a purposefully vague situation as to strengthen the dictatorship. Similarly, the obligations of citizens is to be subservient and dutiful to their Caudillos and their government.
strings.IBR_organic_law_of_the_state_desc: With the nations having gone without a constitution for so long, the Organic Law of the State puts pen to paper the law of the union. Officially recognizing the Caudillos as Co-Heads of State, with the future after their death uncertain. This pseudo-constitution, while flimsy, is a necessary part for the legitimization of the Iberian government.
strings.IBR_fundamental_statute_of_the_iberian_u: Fundamental Statute of the Iberian Union

All States require a bedrock upon which to define itself clearly, and from that be allowed the capability to make sound legislation with which to govern itself. This question has dogged Iberia for years, however with great effort the web of pretenses, precedents and understandings will be defined, previous legislation relating to these matters being streamlined into a new fundamental statute for the State.

This single, supreme law shall establish the fundamental responsibilities of the State and its character, from the citizen to the nations within the Union. No more should Iberia rest upon hastily arranged supports but a single, robust foundation capable of outliving the generation who birthed it.
strings.IBR_law_of_political_reform_desc:
Renewal requires that space be made for it, lest it trip over the State it wants to aid. Further, renewal is made more complicated by webs of responsibilities that now stand to be revised.

This law formally suspends all previous laws relevant to the fundamental identity of the State, simply defining a liberal democratic legislature and mandating a national election regulated under noted liberally democratic requirements such as universal suffrage. The Government formed will carry the responsibility of creating a new constitution to formalise a sound foundation for the State, to be approved via popular referendum.
strings.IBR_provisional_estatue_on_the_fundament: Provisional Estatute on the Fundamental Laws

In light of recent developments, a legal definition of Iberia is both vitally important but equally difficult to outline within our legal structure due to contradicting legislation. This hasty law aims to serve as a stop gap to bridge the gap while sounder legislation is drafted.

The Law of Political Reform will be suspended, however its effects are not all unilaterally reversed. The changes in legislature and the requirement for a new Constitution and accompanying referendum will be struck down while the Government will be granted power to reactivate articles of Laws suspended by the Law by decree, if proven necessary, on an emergency basis until new legislation redefines relevant Laws.
strings.IBR_iberian_constitution_desc:
Often the question has been debated, in offices of state or kitchen tables. What is Iberia? A Caudillo's playground? A complicated mess of responsibilities between Portugal and Spain? A body to empower the Iberian citizen? Numerous suggestions have been emphatically argued, but with the constitution the matter should be laid to rest.

Outlining rights both political and personal, establishing the politics of the new Iberia and highlighting the new, democratic reality of the peninsula, the State's identity should no longer be in question. This constitution envisions every Iberian as equal, and the State as the servant of the Iberians.
strings.IBR_pro_ofn_foreign_policy_desc:
There is one immutable fact in international politics; times change. Why should Iberia be the exception?

Iberia will always seek to place Iberia first within her considerations, however it now sees itself as part of a fraternity of nations with mutual goals. Iberia shall be stronger through the OFN and the OFN shall be stronger with Iberia, the ideals of national autonomy and rejection of those who seek to subvert independent nations guiding both of us into the day. A partnership is mutually advantageous and gives us new platforms and levers of support. Let the Iberian Flag be seen worldwide as a symbol committed to the freedom of nations.“
strings.IBR_pro_pakt_foreign_policy_desc:
There is one immutable fact in international politics; times change. Why should Iberia be the exception?

Iberia will always seek to place Iberia first within her considerations, however it now sees itself standing side by side with those committed to the achievement of national strength. It is through discipline that determination is found, and with that determination bonds can be forged across nations that leave both with renewed power, over themselves and those that would seek to undermine civilisation. Ourselves and the Pakt only stand to gain together, so let our flag become a symbol; a symbol of stability and strength worldwide.
strings.IBR_committee_on_the_african_territories:
Africa continues to be a contentious issue across the nation, Iberian commitments to the continent through its colonies warring with the increasing unrulyness of the landmass.

As such, a committee shall be appointed to discuss the future of Iberia's presence within the continent, as well as establishing our diplomatic approach to its ever changing reality. We will call upon representatives drawn from both Iberia itself and the colonies, Iberians and Natives together. Through such a committee, with all voices appropriately heard, Iberia's African future should be illuminated.
strings.IBR_the_moreria_plan_1_desc:
Adriano Moriera's plan is comprehensive, and may represent the best chance at stabilising the relationship between Iberia and the colonies of the strategies yet presented.

In addition to Iberia's constitutional vote, each colony shall have a referendum to approve the creation of new autonomous administrations to replace the legacy systems currently operated under. This shall be paired with a large welfare package for each colony, to be administered by a fresh generation of civil servants. Current civil servants on the continent will be, unless necessary for their role or found to have exceptional qualification, rotated out of their current African positions and returned to Iberia. This new generation, with a new methodology, should be able to guide our territories through this transition period.
strings.IBR_the_moreria_plan_2_desc:
Adriano Moreira's plan is striking, presenting perhaps the most promising way to maintain Iberia's position on the continent in the face of its present malaise.

The colonies shall have their regions delineated firmly, with new councils created to oversee their administration in affairs of local policy. All individuals with political rights will be eligible to stand for a seat upon those councils, as well as vote in their elections, so long as they register and are found to have no ties to any organisations with militant rhetoric or paramilitary associations. Governors will be replaced, with new men selected specifically for their interest and qualification to oversee local infrastructure projects tailored to each region by the Plan.
strings.IBR_Francisco_Franco_hog_desc:
Caudillo of Iberia
Despotism
--------------
Francisco Franco Bahamonde is to be considered an ecumenical figure of reaction; a synthesis and deferment of the ideological contradictions within the victorious nationalist faction of the late thirties Spanish Civil War. Perhaps, that is what Franco is above all: A Victor. And for Franco, the spoils of his victories are power and power alone.

A coarse man from an upper-class family, Franco's rule is not any rigid ideological program but varied policy brought forward by assorted factions, judged according to his prejudices and predilections, these typical to a man of his political and social origins. A Carlist, a fascist, a falangist; he is none of these. Men from such groupings have served his ascendance, but he is beyond such confines.

His treatment of Salazar, his greatest benefactor in Spain's reconquest, is surprisingly gracious, especially given Portugal's weakened position. Perhaps this is recompense for his assistance in the Spanish Civil War. Perhaps it is deference to his elder colleague. Whatever his reasons, their partnership bears much potential; Franco is military, and Salazar civilian. After all, under the twin guidance of such eminences, what less could rise than new power?
strings.IBR_Francisco_Franco_Post_Salazar_hog_de:
Caudillo of Iberia
Despotism
--------------
Francisco Franco Bahamonde is to be considered an ecumenical figure of reaction; a synthesis and deferment of the ideological contradictions within the victorious nationalist faction of the late thirties Spanish Civil War. Perhaps, that is what Franco is above all: A Victor. And for Franco, the spoils of his victories are power and power alone.

A coarse man from an upper-class family, Franco's rule is not any rigid ideological program but varied policy brought forward by assorted factions, judged according to his prejudices and predilections, these typical to a man of his political and social origins. A Carlist, a fascist, a falangist; he is none of these. Men from such groupings have served his ascendance, but he is beyond such confines.

But a new foe has increasingly shown its hand to the Spanish Caudillo, a foe that he struggles to match: time. Every day, the memories of the Civil War and the early days of the Union fade. Time has taken his fellow Caudillo, Salazar, his confidant and friend. Every morning, time saps a little bit more of him while Iberia continues to find its destiny. Franco refuses to stand idly by, even in this late hour, but there is an entropic truth that he cannot deny. At the very top of Iberia's society, he increasingly feels alone and so very, very tired.
strings.IBR_Antonio_Salazar_hog_desc:
Caudillo of Iberia
Civilian Dictatorship
--------------
António de Oliveira Salazar, with his patient didacticism, would have made for an excellent priest, perhaps even an excellent Bishop. Yet, aged 19, Salazar discerned out of seminary life. He made for an excellent professor; 10 years as finance chair at the University of Coimbra. Possessing little and leading a life of study, he was happy to dwell there until fate would call him elsewhere.

He joined the undertakers of the first republic as the dictatorship's finance minister, a position he had been offered many times. His rise to leadership resulted not from any coup or seizure of power, in truth, all the oft given reasons for the retention and exercise of power seem little more than obscene rationalizations when contrasted with the force of circumstance that led Salazar to rule Portugal, as he would find himself the only indispensable part of any subsequent government.

The financial salvation in the late 20s, quick recovery from recession in the early 30s, and rapidly increasing literacy in both decades, allowed Salazar to withstand the upheaval following the loss of much of its remaining empire. Bolstered by increased ties with a Spanish regime he helped bring to power, Salazar, now in his 70s, remains committed to a Portugal defined by the values of God, family, and fatherland.
strings.IBR_Marcelo_Caetano_hog_desc:
Caudillo of Iberia
Civilian Dictatorship
--------------
Born on the 17th of August 1906, to the uneducated in Portuguese politics, Marcelo José das Neves Alves Caetano may appear an unlikely choice for Caudillo. Despite once serving in a range of roles, from Chief of the Mocidade Portuguesa youth organization to Minister for the Colonies, by the early 1960s, he seemed neutralized. Denied a formal political role and often at odds with António Salazar, many would have written him off as a lawyer unable to read the political winds of the day.

Such a judgment could not be more wrong.

Caetano represents the face of a huge network of technocratic reformists within the Portuguese political sphere. A network that, even despite his lack of formal political engagement, has made him informally tremendously active. Further, dalliances with Monarchism in his youth have instilled within him a reverence for institutions.

Caetano sees beyond an Iberia held together by men of exceptional governmental capacity. He envisions an Iberia ruled by procedures; the Estado Novo as a living system and an example for all Iberia. The liberal corrupters will be crushed, the backwards reactionaries sidelined; through him, a new nation will be born.
strings.IBR_Fernando_Maria_Castiella_for_desc:
Minister of Foreign Affairs
National Catholicism
--------------
Born in Bilbao in 1907, Fernando María Castiella has seen the world change. His youth saw a world dominated by British and French Empires, his beloved Spain disregarded as a decaying nation adrift with instability and cultural rot. He made it his mission to overcome this, driven by his patriotism and traditional Catholicism, to see a strong Spain; and now a strong Iberia.

The means to this are varied. To the Germans, he will reminisce of his wartime experiences in Russia to break the ice. With the Italians, a shared distrust of the German behemoth. To the Americans, a desire for prosperity. A pragmatist with little time for ideology limiting him, he cares little for politics - only for Iberia's interests.
strings.IBR_Jose_Ferreira_Dias_eco_desc:
Minister of Economy
Civilian Dictatorship
--------------
Born in Lisbon in 1900, José Ferreira Dias had enjoyed a prolific career as an engineer, enjoying positions at the Instituto Superior Técnico, Junta de Electrificação Nacional, and the Portuguese Government all by 1940. Committed to Portuguese electrification, he had been a part of many projects to develop the nation.

However, it wouldn't be until 1958 he would be invited by Salazar to oversee the Iberian economy, bolster several planned projects and legislate, however constant infighting has dashed such plans upon rocks. Where once there was a dream of a prosperous Iberia, now José can do little more than manage the myriad economic factions and keep the Iberian economy afloat, powerless to break it free.
strings.IBR_Luis_Teixeira_eco_desc:
Minister of Economy
Civilian Dictatorship
--------------
Born in Campelo in 1927, Luís Maria Teixeira Pinto's life has been committed to understanding economies. In institutions from Lisbon, Paris, and Rome he has studied, and he watched the economic malaise of Germany in the 1950s with great interest. Published and direct, politics matters little to him; the numbers do.

Inheriting a sluggish economy, a Mediterranean in turmoil and a miasma of competing economic factions, Luís seeks to cut through it to the heart of the matter. Technocrats propose self-indulgent reforms, corporatists are constrained by their own borders, but all have some good points mired in the dogma. He will take only their best, break them free and use them to revitalise Iberia.
strings.IBR_Jose_Correia_Oliveira_eco_desc:
Minister of Economy
Civilian Dictatorship
--------------
José Gonçalo Correia de Oliveira was promoted from Minister of Trade to the position of Minister of Economy after his predecessor, Luís Maria Teixeira, was deemed to be too hostile in his interactions with the nation's businessmen. Correia de Oliveira is one of Salazar's closest allies, and has been intimately entangled with the development of the Iberian economy since the Union's very beginning.

Given Iberia's relatively optimistic economic outlook upon his ascension, Correia de Oliveira has turned his attention to the most formidable of tasks on his plate: the further integration of the Portuguese and Spanish economies, as the two halves of the Union still remain quite divided in practice. As a staunch believer in integrationism, he hopes to eventually extend this policy towards all of the Union's colonies, without exception.
strings.IBR_Antonio_Barroso_Sanchez_sec_desc:
Minister of the Army
Despotism
--------------
Scion of politicians and appropriately named officers, not to mention hero of the Crusade and ally of Franco's, Antonio Barroso y Sánchez-Guerra was a natural choice to lead the Iberian Army, as he has since 1957, following a long career in High Command.

A man with an eye for the future, Sánchez-Guerra has intended to forge a modernized military for years, but the African conflicts have stymied his best efforts. When unoccupied by affairs in Morocco, he has focused on personnel reform and equipment modernization. Regardless, his retirement looms, and it appears that the old General's peacetime ambitions will remain unfulfilled, reform a task to be left for his successor as the 60s unravel.
strings.IBR_Pablo_Martin_Alonso_sec_desc:
Minister of the Army
Despotism
--------------
Minister of the Army Pablo Martín Alonso is only a few years younger than his predecessor, Sánchez-Guerra, retired on account of age. Another confidant and fierce loyalist to Franco, Alonso distinguishes himself by way of his domineering, almost despotic personality, being found directly ordering troop formations more often than at the headquarters of High Command.

His authoritarian, overseeing style is oriented towards equipping the serviceman, training him, and improving his living conditions—to the detriment of the bigger picture, some say. The approach may have merits, but it remains to be seen if Iberia's military will find itself ready for war under his constant supervision.
strings.IBR_Camilo_Menendez_Tolosa_sec_desc:
Minister of the Army
Despotism
--------------
The death of Pablo Martín Alonso has propelled Camilo Menéndez Tolosa into heading the Army, and with him a readjustment of military priorities. Tolosa is committed to continuing the modernization efforts of the past decade, but with a technocratic bend—both political and practical.

Tolosa believes that the most pressing security concern has become African anti-colonial bands, a threat left to fester despite past attempts at reining it in. Rather than chasing ever-scarcer Peninsular militias, the minister will focus his tenure on procuring and unleashing the arms of a modern fighting force for the defense of Iberia's empire.
strings.IBR_Antonio_Castro_Fernandes_eco_desc:
Minister of Economy
Corporate Statism
--------------
With the Iberian Union deciding upon a more distinctly Falangist direction for its economy, no candidate was more fitting for the task than António Júlio de Castro Fernandes, one of the few openly fascist members of the high circles of Portuguese politics.

However, while he does genuinely idolize Mussolini and his ideals, Fernandes is still an example of a fascist who sacrificed some of his ideals to remain influential in politics. As such, his reorganization is staffed with like-minded fellow, defanged fascists and old backers of Portugues integralism. His main goal is to make the Union's economy fully corporatist. Given the nation's current conditions, such a risky and far-reaching policy could spell doom if done without care and precision.
strings.IBR_Mariano_Navarro_Rubio_eco_desc:
Minister of Economy
National Catholicism
--------------
After much deliberation, the Iberian Union has approved the Economic Stabilization Program, and Mariano Navarro Rubio has been placed at its helm as Minister of Economy. Navarro is a member of the technocratic faction in politics, composed of those who seek to create a more robust and liberal-influenced economic model for Iberia.

The top priorities on Navarro's agenda are to restaff the economic ministries with technocrats and young professionals trained both at home and abroad, the removal of corporatism's last vestiges within the economy, and to curb the economic imbalances of the past. It is the belief of the technocrats that if they are given the proper support in their modernizations, Iberia's economy could see unprecedented growth in the next few years.
strings.IBR_Juan_Castanon_Mena_sec_desc:
Minister of the Army
Despotism
--------------
Juan Castañón de Mena has, at Tolosa's retirement, leveraged his position as the military's arch-technocrat towards a sweeping reform as Minister of the Army. As with his predecessors, he's a career man and Franco ally, but his tenacity and perceived wisdom signals a renewed era of modernization.

De Mena is no liberal, being a member of the Opus Dei, but his technocratic convictions promote less ideological, more professional officers, and a military that supports their businesslike operational efficiency. The hope is that an old man's vigor can ensure Iberia's army is not left behind in the 60s, much less the 50s, during the approaching decade.
strings.IBR_Fernando_Herrero_Tejedor_hog_desc:
President of the Government
Conservatism
--------------
Were it not for history's habit of upending orders, Fernando Herrero Tejedor would have been an 'Español cualquiera', or any old Spaniard. The son of a military officer, he fought in the Civil War, going onto law school and to positions within the FET y de las JONS. In the 1950s, he became the Civil Governor of Ávila, and then he was an 'Español cualquiera' no more.

Around him he saw nothing but stagnation, so he threw his lot with the reformists, watching his words so as to not step out of line. He pushed the weight of progress through the sands of Iberian politics: When the Council was being formed, he was a quiet advocate for and force behind its power, given his ties within FET-JONS and Opus Dei. When Caetano attempted to anchor Iberia with a constitution that was merely a political pause button, he was the force behind its rejection. Now, Fernando has succeeded not in a revolution, but a chance for Iberia to choose its own destiny.
strings.IBR_Jose_Maria_Areilza_for_desc:
Minister of Foreign Affairs
Liberal Conservatism
--------------
José María de Areilza, Count of Motrico, would prefer to be advocating for a kind of democratic monarchism that now lies dead in post-war Europe. Instead, as Minister of Foreign Affairs since the transitional cabinet, his primary responsibilities involve assuaging the concerns of those who killed it, in Germania, and those never very amenable, in Washington.

Iberia is undergoing profound transformation, and without a careful balancing act, her sphere could easily fall under threat. An ambition towards the government's presidency is buttressed by the task of forming a big-tent coalition to advocate centrism in the elections, as well as his diplomatic duties. It's clear Areilza will play a part in the country's future, but it remains to be seen how.
strings.IBR_Enrique_Fuentes_Quintana_eco_desc:
Vice-President for Economic Affairs
Moderate Technocracy
--------------
Enrique Fuentes Quintana has held a long career in the economic areas of the Iberian government. Holding great respect for the works and ideas of Keynes, Fuentes hails from a group of falangist economists, some of the nation's first generation of true economic professionals. They sought the creation of a welfare state with a large and robust public sector.

Given the current transitional pains within the Union, and Fuentes possessing some key contacts within reformist circles, he was tapped to become Vice-President of Economic Affairs in order to transform Iberia economy during its transition into a democracy. Politically independent, Fuentes and his reforms aren't tied down by any factional ties or party politics.
strings.IBR_Fernando_de_Santiago: Fernando de Santiago y Díaz de Mendívil
strings.IBR_Fernando_de_Santiago_sec_desc:
Minister of Defense
Conservatism
--------------
Fernando de Santiago y Díaz de Mendívil, appointed Minister of the Army in both the pre-election cabinet and People's Alliance government, maintains good rapport with reform-minded generals, his conservative Francoism's commitment tempered by youth and a certain adaptability. Santiago serves as a buffeted rock for the military and society's old “culture”, accepting reforms that he finds agreeable while attempting to hold back the waves.
strings.IBR_Torcuato_Fernandez_Miranda_hog_desc:
Vice-President of the Government
Liberal Conservatism
--------------
Torcuato Fernández-Miranda has been a man of several hats: political science professor, education bureaucrat, Nationalist lieutenant, and public servant. Reformist may prove his most impactful role as Vice-President of the Government, but how much influence his temperate stance will have remains to be seen.

At present, his position is broad enough to have vague responsibilities, and so he's served as a catch-all advisor to the cabinet, a moderate voice in the Democratic Center's coalition. Having made clear that his role will be contained within the constitutional legislature period, some have speculated that Fernández-Miranda won't accomplish much, but his contacts even among reformist circles affords him weight to throw around, if he chooses to do so.
strings.IBR_Joao_Freitas_Cruz_for_desc:
Minister of Foreign Affairs
Liberal Conservatism
--------------
João de Freitas Cruz is a career diplomat, scion of the Foreign Affairs Ministry, and now its head within the Democratic Center's cabinet. The government has tasked him with maintaining a stable neutrality for Iberia, but inching towards the OFN as possible. This alone risks invoking the Reich's rage if conducted without a deliberate rhythm, and that's before the further goal of deepening ties with Latin America comes into play.

A 'liberal, democratic Hispanism for the next century' is at the core of this campaign of delicate statecraft, taking what was learned in Franco's day and painting it with a brighter brush to suit the changing political winds. It remains to be seen if this ideology has a future, and indeed if Iberia does outside Europe, but Freitas Cruz may be just the man for the job.
strings.IBR_Manuel_Gutierrez_Mellado_sec_desc:
Minister of Defense
National Conservatism
--------------
Manuel Gutiérrez Mellado, the Democratic Center government's Minister of Defense, has dedicated his tenure to that title alone. Though a staunch personal conservative, like most military commanders, Mellado believes the military has no place in civilian politics. Drawing on knowledge from a long career in the High Command and courses abroad, he is committed to forging a modern military for a democratic Spain.
strings.IBR_Joao_Pereira_Campos_hog_desc:
Vice-President of the Government
National Conservatism
--------------
The União Nacional's reconstruction into Acção Nacional Popular, and thus it being a competitive force in the elections, owes much to João Mota Pereira de Campos, a relatively young jurist who has sought to tie the remnants of Salazar's government to Portugal's future.

Now Vice-President of the Government, Pereira has maintained his dominance over the ANP yet tellingly sticks to the backrooms, avoiding media scrutiny given his shaky allegiance to democracy. His 'neoregimentalist' bloc would rather change little about Iberia's politics, yet these goals put them on a collision course with a broad spectrum of reform-minded liberals. The old ways persist like a tumor at the highest levels through the likes of Pereira, posing a profound threat if allowed to fester.
strings.IBR_Andre_Goncalves_Pereira_for_desc:
Minister of Foreign Affairs
National Conservatism
--------------
André Gonçalves Pereira is a man of domestic law, but his being tapped for Minister of Foreign Affairs isn't without precedent. Representing the Iberian state in judicial posts abroad, with some work in international law, Pereira was further an attractive candidate for the People's Alliance on account of lacking ANP ties.

Neutrality is the Alliance's Iberia primary foreign outlook, balancing a measured approach to the OFN with Pakt economic ties, all the while working to safeguard Iberian influence in Latin America. The region is ever unstable, and Pereira's foreign office is willing to tolerate token moderation from its unsavory regimes, as befits their 'neutrality' on the ever-contentious issue of Hispanic and European authoritarianism.
strings.IBR_Laureano_Lopez_Rodo_eco_desc:
Vice-President for Economic Affairs
National Conservatism
--------------
A lawyer, scion of both the venerable Universities of Barcelona and Madrid, as well as the Opus Dei, Laureano López Rodó is a peculiar fit to lead the Spanish technocrats. His economic career had been marginal until recently, staying outside of the state ministries while refining the liberal ideas that he, now appointed, seeks to put in practice.

His group, the so-called “Gang of Eight” has joined together into a so-called People's Alliance, but their diverse composition's very nature is already leading to factionalism that could hamper specific reforms. Rodó is committed to a technocratic, market-based economy as Vice-President for Economic Affairs, but it remains to be seen if his theories will be a force of rejuvenation—or out the revolving door in short order.

--------------
Had the conditions been any different, the Iberian Union would be prosperous beyond belief, as the combined forces of Spain and Portugal came together to economically conquer the Mediterranean. Unfortunately, the circumstances do not allow for such blessed dreams to become reality.

While the economy struggles to breathe, suffocated by a mile and a half of red tape, the system in place exists in constant conflict with itself, as our bizarre mix of capitalism, corporatism, and high-state participation acts in constant opposition with the economy's attempts at growth.
strings.IBR_Iberian_Economic_Miracle_desc:
The Present State of the Iberian Economy is: {ibr_economy_state}, incurring the following effects:
GDP Growth: [?IBR_gdp_growth_nightmare_variable|=|+%%]

--------------
Long mired in economic stagnation due to its conflicting and ill-designed mix of capitalism, corporatism, and state intervention, Iberia failed to achieve its growth potential.

Until now. Recent reforms and investments have at last provided Iberia a coherent economic vision. Business and consumer confidence is reviving, and it seems like a new factory or hotel opens its doors each week.

strings.IBR_plus_ultra_base:
For centuries Spain and Portugal possessed the greatest colonial empires on Earth. Controlling all of Central and South America, the Philippines, vast amounts of land in Africa, and with enclaves even into Asia proper, the old hegemonies are now but a sad remnant of their former greatness. Iberia's last grasps on Imperial Ambitions are their two Guinean colonies, the small islands off Africa's West Coast, and their holdings in the Maghreb.

None know prosperity, nor, since their founding, profitability, yet they endure nonetheless, choking what little life the Iberian Economy possesses. Indeed, these rump holdings are but the shadows of an empire, for the concept has since been redefined. Time will tell if Iberia can adapt, or if these last heirlooms of a bygone era will simply fade away.
strings.IBR_plus_ultra_alg:
For centuries Spain and Portugal possessed the greatest colonial empires on Earth. Controlling all of Central and South America, the Philippines, vast amounts of land in Africa, and with enclaves even into Asia proper, the old hegemonies are now but a sad remnant of their former greatness. Iberia's last grasps on Imperial Ambitions are their two Guinean colonies, the small islands off Africa's West Coast, and their holdings in the Maghreb.

None know prosperity, nor, since their founding, profitability, yet they endure nonetheless, choking what little life the Iberian Economy possesses. Indeed, these rump holdings only contribute to the pride of men who'd never have to pay the price they incurred themselves. Iberia's solution was, of course, to add more to the pile, more for their pride... What better way to achieve that than to co-opt the largest and least stable colony in all of Africa?
strings.IBR_colonial_algeria_warning: Be warned, while booting the Italians from Algeria may be more than achievable, the costs of administering the colony ourselves may bring down the Iberian Economy.

strings.IBR_Council_Dissolved_desc: By the orders of the influential Caudillos, the Iberian Council is to be dissolved. However, this news comes as a surprise to many, who've seen the council as a way to bridge the gap between the various peoples of Iberia, give equal representation for all parties, and successfully approve or disapprove of laws, all while avoiding the messy legislative and bureaucratic problems of the prior system. Many politicians have voiced their concerns and many are in favor of reestablishing it, but the Caudillos assure that measures are being implemented to smoothly transition. They estimate that in a few week's time, the outrage will have petered out and normality will ensue once more.
strings.IBR_Betray_Old_Guard_desc:
Throughout their climbs to power, Salazar and Franco have had to rely on many political groups, from falangists to technocrats. With the unification of Spain and Portugal, these groups have persisted, still competing for power and influence over the regime.

While opportunistic, these groups can be useful to the Caudillos, when incentivized correctly. However, without a strong hand, the groups can take a toll on the nation, pushing and pulling the government toward their own agendas.
strings.IBR_Disorderly_Federal_Army_desc:
The Iberian military is an ancient beast. Many of its officers, Spanish or Portuguese, have served from long before the time of Second World War, and in their hubris have learned little from it, nor displayed a shred of willingess to change that.

Hope remains, but only in the form of the impending days the rusted swords of yore will be replaced by young minds sharpened in academies abroad.
strings.IBR_Disorderly_Federal_Army_2_desc: After a long drought of young officers, the young men have finally returned from abroad. This new generation has replaced the old guard and are ready to implement their new ideas. These innovations take time however, and it may be years before the military is fully modernized.
strings.IBR_Crippled_Sovereignty: The Two Halves of the Whole
strings.IBR_Crippled_Sovereignty_desc:
The creation of Iberia involved negotiations between the two sides, with both trying to conserve as much of the old regimes as possible. This means that at the national level things have more or less coalesced but at the regional and local levels things are pretty much run as they were before Iberia, meaning that the government has to keep in mind the two systems that still exist.

“The modern Iberian Union was not, unlike its historical predecessor, born out of a personal union between the two countries' monarchies. Rather, it was a negotiated affair between two highly conservative and nationalist governments that wished to change as little as possible within their respective governments' day-to-day operations. While this ensured a smooth and stable transition, the differences between national and regional administrations in the two constituent countries have left an administrative hurdle that is difficult to navigate.”
strings.IBR_Crippled_Sovereignty_notsomuch_desc: As our Union has existed for quite some time now, and many laws have been approved and put into effect, the system used in the Union's national governance has slowly been adopted from the regional down to the most local of levels in both constituent countries. Of course, some administrative peculiarities are bound to exist still and will cause a few issues, but as administrators become accustomed to navigating these systems and our governance becomes more streamlined, the obstacles in our path become increasingly easier to surmount.
strings.IBR_liberalisation_desc: As the democratization process is underway, the Iberian political structure is being liberalized, as the government's end goals include changing the system to that of a democratic one.
strings.IBR_Mediterranean_Tech_Exchange_desc: In order to facilitate faster military development, a technological exchange program has been established. Countries surrounding the Mediterranean Sea will be participating, trading equipment such as simple firearms to more advanced mechanized vehicles with one another. With this program, every nation involved can hopefully create new material to equip their armies with.
strings.IBR_Dissolving_Iberian_Union_desc:
In order to avoid the possibility of a major crisis, the Iberian government has decided that the Iberian nation as many know it will be dissolved permanently. Many have said their grievances and some even protest, but the executive decision has already been approved. That being said, the administration will ensure the dissolution will be seamless and efficient. Once complete, the peninsula shall be divided into two, with Spain in the East, and Portugal in the West.

The Union that held out for two decades is now finally coming to an end.
strings.IBR_Severing_Economic_Ties_desc: As part of the Iberian dissolution efforts, the economic ties binding Spain and Portugal together will be severed. This is done in order to prevent another economic crisis in the foreseeable future.
strings.IBR_Severing_Military_Ties_desc: As part of the Iberian dissolution efforts, the Federal Armed Forces containing both Portguese and Spanish troops will be abolished, and that the old Portuguese and Spanish Armed Forces shall be recreated as fully independent organizations in their respective countries.
strings.IBR_Dissolved_Federal_Government_desc: The final part of the Iberian dissolution is the abolishment of the federal government itself. The old administration is finally being dissolved, and the many bureaucrats and ministers who've held positions are receiving accommodations to compensate. While the last step has been made, the only thing holding back the official split of Iberia is the lack of recognition of the federal government's closure from both Spain and Portugal.
strings.IBR_State_Exemplary_desc:
Current stability is at: [?ROOT.IBRIberiaStability|Y0%%]

The Iberian Union and its people can rejoice, for they are the shining example of national stability in Europe, or perhaps even the whole world. Thanks to the efforts of the government, even the most pessimistic naysayers can agree that the Iberian Peninsula stands firmly united.
strings.IBR_State_Strong: State of the Union - Extremely Stable
strings.IBR_State_Strong_desc:
