Now, Guiné prospers, more profitable than it was any other year post-abolition.
strings.IBR_starting.13.a: Slavery was begun by Iberians. But has it really ended?
strings.IBR_starting.14.d:
The choice was between ten years in prison or five years in the cashew orchards. Food was expensive these days, and Umaro wasn't about to let his family starve, even if it meant stealing. Alas, the rice-seller alerted an officer whom Umaro had not seen, and as Umaro tried to flee, 20 kilograms of stolen rice weighed him down.

His wife and children had to join him in the orchard. If they refused, how would they eat? Little Harouna, all of four years old, gathered cashew fruits that had fallen to the ground alongside his seven-year-old sister, Duwa. Umaro and his wife, Jainaba, sat at the shelling station hammering the cashew shells to expose the nuts within. Dust entered Jainaba's lungs, and she struggled to breathe as particles of toxic resin lodged themselves in her windpipe. Umaro's left hand was blistered from the resin; his glove was partly torn and he needed to work another 40 hours to “purchase” a new one.

The lodging was paltry at best. Blankets sprawled over a concrete floor, each man, woman, and child, packed side by side. Bathing consisted of stripping naked in a line outdoors and being sprayed down with hoses. The food was even worse. A bowl of rice twice a day. On Sundays, fufu, bland and unflavored. For 10 hours of work, a tablespoon of peanut or pepper sauce could be purchased, but with frequent fines, most could not hope to afford this more than once a week.

Punishments were cruel and frequent during these long 12-hour shifts. Move too slowly or sloppily, and you would be caned by the overseer's baton or fined many hours' pay. Rest for a second and risk being shocked with a cattle prod. Many of the workers had scars on their faces, necks, and limbs. Women were typically scarred in other ways. The more 'creative' overseers had even collected resin to paint the skins of those punished, such that blisters would form into patterns and shapes.

These were facts of life in the Guiné orchards.
strings.IBR_starting.14.a: All for a bag of rice.
strings.IBR_starting.15.d:
As he had nearly every day for over fifty years, Hassan walked down the familiar steps to his small dock on the outskirts of Ifni, where his boat sat bobbing gently.

He was one of the oldest people in the area, and he knew that he was one of the few who clearly remembered the old days. Before the Union. Before Franco. And in times before that. And he had seen so much change that sometimes even he had trouble fully comprehending it. He knew different people represented change with other items, but for him everything was embodied in the behemoth.

There was more than one, of course, and Hassan never knew their specific names, but each behemoth - the enormous cargo ships that now regularly came and went from the labyrinth of concrete and steel that was the new Ifni harbor - astounded him. They were almost incomprehensible in scale, and he always imagined them set against the small collection of fishing huts that used to be the port. It seemed so different, and so far away.

But Hassan was old enough to know that change could not, would not, be stopped. And that anyone who stood in its path would be roughly treated indeed, in one way or another. Taking one more look at the behemoth he sighed, and proceeded down his steps. He hoped the fishing would be good today.
strings.IBR_debates.1.desc:
“Caudillo Salazar, we have arrived.”

Salazar looked out the window from the car, however nothing but the monotone grey of Galician mist greeted him. It was thick, cloaking the ground in a tight embrace. While Salazar thanked his driver for the notification, inwardly he cursed. Rotten weather to herald the start of a rotten excursion.

He heard the sounds of the car change as they turned, the somewhat bumpy asphalt of the country roads becoming instead the rough crackle of gravel. In a few moments he would be stepping out to meet his... compatriot? Colleague? What word should be used to describe Francisco Franco?

Franco had called Salazar away from his work in Lisbon, bade him to come to Franco's home region and some old seaside villa called the Pazo de Bazán. In his office the idea had sounded promising, a personal conference free of the cliques in Madrid and Lisbon to set Iberia's new course in light of the Triumvirate's collapse. It was only upon the six hour drive that doubts had crept in.

Why take Salazar away from Portugal? Why instruct him to come rather than suggest? Why offer no reciprocation in the organisation of such a conference?

The car stopped at the end of the long driveway to the Villa, and Salazar stepped out of the opened door to see Franco standing upon the steps. It gave him pause, why was he being greeted like some visiting salesman? Where were the staff made ready to greet him, any sense of decorum? Shouldn't a meeting to decide Iberia's future have such consideration?

“Welcome to my humble region,” Franco said, “Señor Salazar.” His lips opened in a wide eyed smile, almost ethereal in the fog, and he descended the steps towards him.
strings.IBR_debates.1.a: Behind that smile was arrogance. Salazar certainly knew the word Franco used for him: clerk.
strings.IBR_debates.2.desc:
It was somewhere around the third hour of the Caudillos' conversation in the drafty, cold living room that the thought of how appropriate the surroundings were had started to amuse Salazar. Far from a comfortable resort, the walls were damp and the furniture ancient. The table was small, barely enough to hold his papers and reports, forcing him to have many upon the floor. He tried not to think of the condition of the floorboards too much each time he leaned down; how much like the Iberian economy.

“... had used the Venice Mechanism as a way to divert some capital expectations upon the State. With the loss of our preferential access to Italian finance in the short to medium term, it is vital that we stabilise our exporters. We must encourage reasonable reduction in their business - our 'allies' will soon be establishing tariffs upon them anyway - while raising funds to-”

“You want to raise tariffs on the Mediterranean powers to make some money fast?”

“Well, yes.” Salazar bristled at the shortness. He was guiding him, how many times had he walked Franco through what had influenced Iberian exports, how Italian banks had been essential in payment structures? How their loss would affect them, point by point? He was reading a dog a book; what could the dog comprehend?

“Good. Let's do that, a 30-70 split in revenues to Spain's favor would be appropriate?”

Salazar rolled his eyes. He knew this would come up, and he rifled through his papers. “Actually, as a Union tariff this should be something attributed to the joint budge-”

“I'm tired, would you like to go for a walk?” Franco asked. Salazar blinked, holding his paper searching position, and mutely shook his head.
strings.IBR_debates.2.a: Salazar watched the most powerful man in Spain nearly run out of the door, yawning.
strings.IBR_debates.3.desc:
God, what a miserable bastard. Nothing but verbal grapeshot and blind bias. Francisco Franco sighed, this meeting with Salazar had not been all he had hoped it would be.

They sat dining, a rather delicious spread of local seafood prepared by the housekeeper Rosalía, yet the Portuguese Caudillo across the table seemed to stare daggers at his silverware. From the moment he'd stepped out of the car he'd been dour, though why Franco couldn't guess. He'd suggested Galicia as a meeting of cultures, his home region and Portugal touched after all. He'd met him out of the car, immediately walked into a long meeting where he'd gone on and on about macro-economics or something and listened.

Franco looked at Salazar, glaring at the fine kitchenware he had ordered with disgust, and resolved himself. He would be the bigger man.

“Señor Salazar, I've had many conversations on my hunting trips recently. It seems tax enforcement is a contentious issue. Perhaps by tackling this, we can-”

“You are hunting with businessmen while our economy collapses?”

Franco slammed his fork down. “For God's sake Salazar, I listened to your lectures for hours, will you not give me even a moment to forward a problem I have been directly informed of in both Spain and Portugal?”

Salazar stood up, leaving his half eaten meal forgotten while pointing an accusatory finger at Franco. “Lectures? I am trying to tell you how to save our Union you fool, and you think you are forwarding problems? Portugal's tax enforcement is just fine, there are no issues I can see!” He lowered his finger, taking a final look at the table. “Adorned with finery aren't you, a leader should dine like his people.” He walked to the door.
strings.IBR_debates.3.a: “Do not try to offload Spain's problems onto my Portugal!” he almost shouted as he left.
strings.IBR_debates.4.desc:
The fog and drizzle had, mercifully, departed from the area; a small respite for those who had spent a sorry few days blind and wet. The mood in all Cambados had lifted somewhat, even despite the overcast skies and reports of yet more to come. One man refused to share in the area's optimism, his face remaining drenched in the impassive grey of the fog.

Ramón Ruibal was trimming hedges. The gardening was neverending and he was paid a pittance for it; just one of the half dozen jobs he occasionally kept in order to get food on the table. It had been some time since tourists had been here in any real numbers, and regardless of what the local newspapers said he had never seen any interest from the Minister of Information and Tourism. What did Fraga care about some drafty house?

Still, someone in the Ministry must be retaining the property or else he wouldn't have this job, and how thankful he was to that person now.

He'd been informed a few weeks ago. “VIPs are coming to stay, make the grounds look presentable.” No whos or whys, Ramón couldn't believe anyone wanted to stay in this collapsing wreck, but he needed the money. Then the housekeeper, a lovely girl called Rosalía, after lots of wine and charm one night, revealed all to him. She also told him who was coming to the Pazo de Bazán. He looked to his right absently as his shears chopped, midnight plans in his mind.

Plans for the two men he was watching walk up the path towards him.

They seemed deep in a frustrated conversation. He fingered the old pistol concealed in his pocket, his father's from the war against the damned Caudillo. He wasn't ready! He had planned to go that night, now he saw their eyes barely glance at him as they passed. But glance they did. He felt the call for his justice, but their eyes stung.
strings.IBR_debates.4.a: His head lowered as a servant, his arms like stone. Not this close. Not this clearly.
strings.IBR_debates.5.desc:
The rain had made clearing the ruined Santa Mariña de Dozo Church of people an easy task, but as Franco stood against one of its walls hearing the patter of raindrops against his raincoat he questioned his decision to come. He wanted, needed, to drag Salazar out of that house and an excursion to talk in the open air had seemed the best way to dislodge him from his endless lecturing. Standing in the miserly weather with increasingly sodden socks almost made him long for those lectures again.

Salazar stood beside him, absently watching the patrolling guards around the grounds of the Church. He was quite sure the flowers, hedges and architecture were beautiful when they weren't being drowned. “I suppose we should make the best of this” he said to the Caudillo beside him. “You had a request?”

“I want Portuguese troops in Morocco, Salazar, and reliable funding for Martín Alonso's modernization program. Instability there could spiral; how will your graphs look if investors think Iberia cannot guarantee stability?”

Salazar shivered in the wet air, sighing. “A black hole. Portuguese resources shouldn't go to bailing out Spanish problems, we have to worry about the other African territories. We've no more funds for the military; I understand your connection to the -”

Franco glared at Salazar. “Are you suggesting that Morocco concerns me due to my history?” he snapped.

“Shouldn't I?”

Franco came closer to Salazar, bringing their faces mere inches apart. “I never saw you cut funding for the air force. Nothing spared for our interests, but that treacherous bastard Delgado always got his cut. What does that suggest?”
strings.IBR_debates.5.a: “Perhaps we didn't fund them enough.” Salazar stated, meeting the accusing eyes impassively.
strings.IBR_debates.6.desc:
Rain pounded the glass of the window as Salazar poured over the messages he had received since arriving. His instructions, all messages to be forwarded to minimise disruption in Lisbon, was in hindsight an optimistic measure. His desk held a beastly paper pile, his meetings with Franco longer than he had imagined and now the Pazo's electricity had shut off. He ignored the howling wind outside as he worked, silent in candles' glows.

The silence was broken by a terse knock at the door. Salazar called for them to enter, and was surprised to see Franco enter. His expression was tired, face darker in the candlelight. “Caudillo Salazar, may we speak?” he asked. With a nod answering him, he sat on the small bed beside the desk.

“You will leave tomorrow?” Franco asked.

Salazar placed his pen down. “This meeting has achieved little. I cannot be away from Lisbon much longer.” A moment of silence broken only by the clattering windowglass hung.

“I am not one to keep pushing if something isn't working,” Franco acquiesced, “and perhaps it is better for us to return to our governments. Time waits for no one. However, I do have a final suggestion.” Salazar closed his eyes and turned to Franco, opening with muted interest.

“Things have been said, but I believe that for all our quarreling we are committed to the Union. Ergo, how about we focus on its maintenance; without order we have nothing.”

Salazar pondered, resting on Franco's Delgado comment at the church. If concerns about Portuguese commitments to the Union were present, perhaps addressing that was the root of moving forward. “Perhaps an agency committed to such a project would be a worthwhile investment...”
strings.IBR_debates.6.a: Franco smiled, a sight unseen through the wet rifle scope outside. The view was unclear: no shot.
strings.IBR_debates.7.desc:
Nature had returned to peace, the previous night's tempest having mercifully abated ahead of Franco's departure. He stood by the open door of his limo, taking a moment to breathe in the sweetened air left in the rain's wake. Clouds lingered still but his drive home shouldn't be as arduous as he had feared; thoughts of family, Madrid and home settled in his mind. These meetings with Salazar hadn't been all he'd hoped, but-

“Caudillo Franco, Caudillo Franco!” came crying from the Pazo's door, breaking the old general's musing. He turned, met by the bemusing sight of his Portuguese colleague bursting towards him as best he could, his appearance unkempt and eyes mildly wild, desperately clinging to a mess of papers.

“Caudillo Salazar, I thought you had left at dawn?” Franco asked the rushing man as he came to a stop before him. Salazar shook his head, frantically trying to order the papers and thrusting them upon Franco. Franco looked at his limo driver, whose stoic face held the gentle suggestion of confusion.

“Last night, what you said, it made me realise we were going about this all wrong.” Salazar explained, as Franco began to go through the papers. Despite Salazar's appearance, his words were clear. Proposals for a cooperative body, an Iberian Council, with notes on a variety of considerations from responsibilities to powers.

“This was one night?” Franco gasped, before turning to Salazar. He was fixing his untidy clothes, and Franco realised he had misjudged his eyes. They were not wild; they were sharp.

“Trying to coordinate two constituent nations between just two men, whittling down each concern and factor for single summits? We are not Kings running fiefdoms; we are modern men. The answer was in our face all along, by integrating decision making-”
strings.IBR_debates.7.a: Franco chuckled, aborting the lecture. “Why don't we return inside, you can explain everything.”
strings.IBR_debates.8.desc:
In some respects, having Franco away all day fishing, hunting and generally having a holiday amongst his native Galicia was a blessing. He wasn't one for the details, earlier conversations had more than aptly shown that. Besides, it gave time for work - real work - to turn his big picture idea of Iberian stability into something actually workable.

Salazar just wished such an arrangement didn't come with him rejecting every proposal when he returned.

The electricity still hadn't returned; no fault could be found in the local grid so they had the Groundskeeper searching for the on-site fault. As such, they remained using candles as night had fallen while they discussed the latest proposals Salazar had drawn up. Proposals Franco was busy dismissing despite contributing little.

“... and this is clearly too technocratic of an approach. I understand that these corporatist ways are how it is done in Portugal but this must fit Spain too. I would like to personally appoint my members. Further I see this note you added about responsibilities regarding advising military organisation, now in Spain-”

“Caudillo Franco, with all due respect, if you find so much fault with my efforts you are perfectly free to contribute when I'm actually drafting the proposals.” Salazar spoke softly, but directly, the sting just evident in his words.

Franco stopped, opening his mouth in an attempt to retort before simply turning his gaze to the window. The grounds of the Pazo were barely illuminated by the moonlight; reports had promised mist but for now it was mercifully clear. “Perhaps I am focusing too much on the Spanish elements... Won't you join me on a walk? I think a stroll may clear my head and we can speak more constructively.”
strings.IBR_debates.8.a: Salazar noted a hint of genuine contrition. “If that will help, then certainly, Senhor Franco.”
strings.IBR_debates.9.desc:
They had walked barely ten minutes before the promised mist had descended, the thickest since they had arrived. With the loss of the Pazo's power, only torches barely cutting through the soupy air illuminated the path. Thorns of cold penetrated the Caudillo's coats. Both aged men shivered, neither wanting to admit to their shaking.

Franco watched Salazar's steps become shorter and slower, a figure growing more difficult to see as the minutes progressed. He knew the path well, he walked it every day, but concern that he would lose his colleague to the mist lingered. Guards usually walked with him, but he could see nothing beyond the Caudillo beside him and the immediate path.

They walked in silence, and Franco glanced around nervously. He could see in Salazar's stride an anxiety that ill suited him, and he felt a similar feeling claw at his chest. He ignored it; he was a military man, the Caudillo of Spain. He was on grounds protected by countless soldiers, and a man of courage himself; yet, the void of the misty night whispered childhood superstitions to him. He heard his mother telling him stories of the spirits within Galicia's hills. Of dark nights upon which the Santa Compaña, the herald of death, would stalk the Earth. Of-

“Death!” came a cry from the mist, a light activating from beside the path, barely cutting through the mist. A black silhouette screamed, striding towards the Caudillo. Franco froze, Salazar nowhere to be seen, alone on the path before the encroaching shadow, whose bloodcurdling scream never stopped.

Santa Compaña, amongst the Galician mists it had come!

“No, not me!” Franco cried, falling to his knees. A crack sounded, Franco feeling something fly past him. Within moments he heard more cracks from behind him, though he dared not turn to them.
strings.IBR_debates.9.a: His eyes lay fixed on the fallen beam of light, and the body on the ground it illuminated.
strings.IBR_debates.10.desc:
Both Caudillos had been advised to stay at the Pazo while operations in Cambados were carried out, but both had insisted they oversee the matter personally. They waited in the command post as reports on the town's search commenced, noting each message.

Both could still barely believe the previous night. Their groundskeeper, Ramón Ruibal, had emerged from the mist with deadly intent. Luck saved them; he'd fashioned a shelter off the path of Caudillo Franco's walking route and lay waiting. When he'd heard them approach, he'd cried out trying to shoot them with a pistol, only for it to jam. While he was able to let off a single rifle shot with an old hunting rifle he had slung, the guards following behind the Caudillos had intervened.

Both Caudillos listened to raid reports across the town with cold expressions. It was barely past dawn, agents dragging out people in their bedclothes for questioning. The Housekeeper Rosalía had already confessed, being interrogated immediately after the event and revealing that she had told Ramón of the Caudillo's visit, as well as his occasional mentions of Marxism and friends in nearby Cambados.

Such a shame, she had been such a sweet young girl.

But, what to do now? The news would get out eventually with a raid this large. A Marxist attempt on the Caudillos barely averted, an entire town potentially infiltrated by traitors - it harkened back to the old republics, a time none wanted to repeat. Both men knew it.

“The Council, it's the only way to direct this narrative. We need unity.” Franco voiced after a report was given, completing an unspoken conversation.

Salazar nodded. “Today we agree on the outline, then we go home and make it work.”
strings.IBR_debates.10.a: But Salazar pondered, the Marxist tale hollow. Why did Franco call to the assassin: “Not me!”?
strings.IBR_post_trium.1.d:
“You should stop reading this,” Salazar said with an undertone of tension in his voice, and Franco stiffened when he heard it. For half an hour now, he had been staring at the first page of the newspaper, muttering sometimes under his breath, but had remained still at his desk. When Salazar interrupted him for the third time, he slowly put his hands to his forehead, before tossing the newspaper into the bin without looking at it. He sighed heavily.

“You know what this reminds me of,” he whispered disbelievingly. “The bickering, the endless subjects of disagreement, the inability to compromise...”

“There can be no compromise with error, Francisco,” Salazar softly interjected.

“The only error in geopolitics, António, is the inability to keep one's allies close. Look where we are now: in the remains of a dysfunctional system, that was plagued by stubbornness and arrogance. We are alone, António. We cannot keep fighting among ourselves now that there is no more umbrella under which we used to hide. With the Triumvirate gone, how long do you think we can last before things fall apart and we become the prey of the Germans or the Americans?”

Salazar did not answer at first, and he pondered on the crumpled newspaper in the bin. He could no longer make up the words, but he knew they spelt doom for the Mediterranean. They were alone. Perhaps there was truth in the words of Franco, he reflected.

“I believe you are right, Francisco. We ought to pull ourselves together before it is too late. It cannot be too late for us to salvage the situation... and the disappearance of the Triumvirate makes me realize there should be no naivety.”

There was silence again, and they both reflected upon their sudden agreement. Franco rose from his desk, and came to the window, then turned and went to Salazar, who was sitting in his armchair still. Compelled, the latter rose too, and they faced each other. Then, slowly, Salazar brought his hand forward, and Franco took it without a word. They shook without a smile, the grim realization bearing all its weight on their spirits.
strings.IBR_post_trium.1.a: There is much work to do.
strings.IBR_post_trium.2.d:
The aides who prepared the meeting room for the Caudillos that morning knew that a serious decision was to be made. The lack of an agenda made that clear as was the ongoing fallout from the Triumvirate's dissolution. And, as always, they were right.

The Caudillos closed the doors and spoke at length. Though they of course were often at odds in both position and opinion, they were in total agreement as to the Union's current strategic vulnerability. The loss of strong allies - militarily, economically, and otherwise - had placed it in a terrible position, and they could not overlook the glaring weaknesses in security that existed.

Foreign powers would not sit by while the Union's recovery effort progressed, and this they could not allow. And, so, over a long afternoon and several small meals, they came to a conclusion. The Union, the Caudillos proposed and accepted, would close the doors. It would embrace a policy of isolation, broadly ceasing most trade and traffic with the outside world.

It would be painful and difficult, yes, but it would protect the Union in this critical time. When the economy had recovered and security forces had been re-organized, outside traffic could resume, and they agreed to move as quickly as possible to that end-state. It was, in truth, not a terribly difficult decision at all.
strings.IBR_post_trium.3.d:
“Once again, I must thank you for your offer,” said Fernando María Castiella y Maíz, Minister of Foreign Affairs, as he and Manuel Fraga walked through El Retiro. The large park was as beautiful as ever, especially under a clear sky like it was today, but Fraga couldn't help notice that a gloomy atmosphere persisted within this corner of Madrid like any other. Due to the economic downturn, vendors that had set up shop within the park were selling few goods, and Fraga noticed that many of the people he and Castiella y Maíz passed looked stressed.

“Ah, and that reminds me, here is a list of senior Foreign Affairs officials working in Mediterranean Affairs,” said Castiella y Maíz as he passed a paper to Fraga, “Considering Iberia's shifting policy towards the region, they're all slated to be fired.”

Fraga looked over the list of names and began committing them to memory. The only reason the two Ministers had arranged this meeting was because Fraga had offered to use the Ministry of Information and Tourism's budget to retain as many Foreign Affairs officials as he could afford. Fraga looked to Castiella y Maíz and gave a smile, “Even in these trying times, I must seek out those who value openness, wherever I can find them.”

To Castiella y Maíz, who was Fraga's senior within Iberian politics by more than a decade, Fraga's ambition was admirable. It would likely also result in some future misstep and be his downfall, but for now it didn't hurt to play nice, and offer a hand in Fraga's endeavors.
strings.IBR_post_trium.4.t: An Abundance of Ideas, a Shortage of Plans
strings.IBR_post_trium.4.d:
Salazar gave a small sigh as he sat down at his desk. His entire day had been devoted to meeting with officials at the Ministry of Economy, and he only now had gotten some spare time to breathe and process the notes he had taken. The good news is that the Ministry had no shortage of ideas on how best to combat the economic downturn Iberia has been facing. The bad news was that nearly all of them were mutually contradictory, and utterly incompatible.

The first meeting had been with António Júlio de Castro Fernandes, a former Portuguese Minister of Economy, and a protégé of Salazar's who had entered into the world of banking. His proposal was an aggressive push towards autarkic measures, possibly as a way to distance himself from the weight of his own Italian connections. He also wished to focus on corporatism as the path forward for Iberia, proposing the integration of numerous bodies within both Portugal and Spain.

The next meeting was with Mariano Navarro Rubio and Laureano López Rodó, two younger technocrats and members of Opus Dei who thought they knew the best way forward over their more experienced peers. They argued that the imposition of new barriers to international trade demanded that barriers to internal trade be eliminated. The pair had then proceeded to spend the rest of their allotted time filling Salazar's ears with a veritable bonfire of newly proposed regulations to facilitate such a plan.

Finally there was José Gonçalo Correia de Oliveira, the Portuguese Minister of Trade, who argued for doubling down on efforts to extract resources and trade from Iberia's colonies, paired with several state-backed investments into critical sectors of the economy.

The Ministry would never come to a speedy consensus, and so it fell to Salazar to commit to a bold move that could restore some confidence in the economy.
strings.IBR_post_trium.4.a: Corporatism must be deepened within both Portugal and the wider Union.
strings.IBR_post_trium.4.b: Perhaps some small pilots will show those technocrats how wrong they are.
strings.IBR_post_trium.4.c: Let's just try and keep things steady and strengthen Imperial ties.
strings.IBR_post_trium.5.d:
The early 20th century had not been kind to Lisbon. The revolutions of the 1910s, the blackouts and civil defense exercises of the 2nd World War, or the “Atomic Panic” that had spread like wildfire during the seizure of the Ultramar had all left their mark on the ancient capital. The best one could say was that the past decade had been less harsh then rest, that the formation of the Iberian Union had at least produced a sense of security, bringing with it some measure of prosperity.

The parade of the Iberian Armed Forces was attended by nearly all. Whether out of respect for its Caudillo, pride in Union, or merely an excuse to take the day off, Lisbon's streets were filled with onlookers nonetheless. It would be at noon when the men of Iberia began their marching through the city's streets. At its forefront were the Colonial units, the Fuerzas Regulares Indígenas, and the Spanish Legion, self-assured and exuding confidence. Next up were the mechanized units of the Federal Army, foreign-made designs alongside domestic vehicles trailed behind the Legion on the route to Baixa, their attached infantry following in neatly ordered rows. In the rear was the Home Guard, Portugal's sons keeping pace with the finest of the Iberian Army.

The march would last for over an hour before they arrived at the city center, pausing for prepared speeches from both Caudillos, extolling the virtues and bravery of the Iberian soldier. The people cheered, of course, Salazar was still Lisbon's favorite son and Franco, well respect the position if not the man. The parade then continued towards the shore, where it concluded with a 21-gun salute by the ships in the harbor, an acrobatic display by the Air Force, and a few final remarks from the dual heads of state.
strings.IBR_post_trium.6.d:
The old, wheelchair-bound woman sat on the porch behind her home. A light breeze cooled her face, rustled her flowers, and rattled her windchimes. Alas, the flu had left her arms sore, weak, and feeling nearly as paralyzed as her legs.

Sunday was normally the highlight of Clementina's week, a day to fraternize and worship together with her friends and neighbors. But that could not happen this week. In the past, Clementina had little choice but to simply stay in her bed all day when she became ill, with nothing else to do but hope the illness would soon pass. But now, things were different. She owned a radio, and on what were once uneventful evenings, she could listen to the sermons of Father Claret. Even this Sunday, confined to her home, Clementina could rest a bit longer that morning, and listen to the mass of Madrid's Almudena Cathedral that afternoon.

It hadn't always been like this. For most of its history, Iberian Radio had been dominated by music stations, variety shows, sporting events, and news stories. But now, with funding from the Caudillos, the Church now broadcast every day, even to those unable to attend church in person.
strings.IBR_post_trium.6.a: No mere virus can destroy the Catholic spirit.
strings.IBR_post_trium.7.d:
Maria was a woman well-accustomed to the regular propaganda of the Union as a whole. It had been there her entire life, after all, in one way or another, proclaiming the supremacy of one state or another. Yet, today, she noticed a change.

There was clearly a blitz on. Tied, she assumed, to the recent announcements made as to the ongoing recovery efforts. She was not a woman who spent much time looking outside her space, focused on work and family, but she knew how bad things had gotten, and how there were, at the very least, some small recent improvements made.

She acknowledged there may have been more growth. After all, the messaging was relentless. Radio, television, newspaper and right in front of her, in the shape of a massive poster. It claimed that the Union itself was what could be credited for success. It was strong, stronger than either country could have been on its own, and that its citizens were the key.

There were other slogans, of course, but that one stuck with Maria. It was nice, she thought, to get some credit, even collectively with others. That was new. Different. She hoped that it would continue.
strings.IBR_post_trium.7.a: She knew how hard she worked.
strings.IBR_post_trium.8.d:
The message that evening was broadcast Union-wide, taking a place of prominence on the nightly broadcast and displaying the combined regalia of both Caudillos. The musical tones of the Union anthem rang through millions of households as the address began.

It was simple, direct, to the point - and left no room, whatsoever, to be misinterpreted. It had, after all, been designed to be exactly that. The dark days, it recounted, were gone for good, and the Union as a whole was on the upswing. Productivity, economic output, wages, and all other critical metrics were up, increasing - and growing in that rate of increase - consistently.

There was, of course, only one possible reason for this. Only one method by which this concentrated recovery could have been achieved - political unity between the Caudillos, and targeted, focused actions taken on their part to ensure the implementation of economic efforts. That had been accomplished, and their joint support proved the strength and viability of the Union's political model.

After all, could any person seriously claim that the Union could have done better? Of course not. The Caudillos had shown the way. Had pushed the measures. Had worked to save Iberia. Had succeeded. It was critical, the address ended, that such efforts be reciprocated.
strings.IBR_post_trium.8.a: All have a part to play.
strings.IBR_post_trium.9.d:
It was clear now, to all, that the Union's economic recovery was in full swing. That it was due, almost in its entirety, to the visionary leadership of the Caudillos in these difficult times. How could it not be? The message was everywhere. Seen by everyone.

It was seen by Alejandro, on his way to work that morning. The well-known faces of Franco and Salazar both, emblazoned on a poster on the train station's wall and proudly proclaiming that economic growth had been explosive. That the Union was strong, and growing stronger, under them. He had no evidence as to the truth of that. But he was careful to look at it. To be seen looking at it.

It was heard by Alejandro, in the office at lunch that day. The usual radio station was, instead of playing contemporary music, was instead proclaiming the same message on the poster. This time there were production figures. They made little sense to him, seeming far too high, but he was careful to listen to it. To be seen listening to it.

It was experienced by Alejandro, at home that evening. The news presenter recounted the same message, joining the figures this time with a graph. The green line was going, uniformly, up. Alejandro could see no detail on the graph, but he was careful to follow the whole program.
strings.IBR_post_trium.10.d:
They were supposed to be done five minutes ago. All the furniture had been moved in, the lighting installed; the only thing left was the portraits, Iberia's two Caudillos.

“No, no, no, that won't do. They are supposed to be equals. They need to both be on the same level.” The man was already adjusting the portraits, moving Franco's likeness slightly upwards. His supervisor was silent, something still did not look right. As he was reaching to clear his spectacles, it hit him.

“Why is Salazar to the right? Portugal is to the left of Spain, so shouldn't Salazar's portrait be to the left of Franco.” The other man paused, mulling over the words. Taking a step back, he let his superior do the honors in shifting Salazar's portrait. Both men studied the new arrangement, and both came to a similar conclusion.

“It still looks off somehow, like one is lording over the other, should they even be on the same wall?” The man turned to face the supervisor, whose look of realization and exasperation spoke a million words.

“They aren't even the same frame for crying out loud.” He gestured at the portraits, and after a careful examination, the man recognized that yes, Salazar's frame was of a slightly different make then Franco's. He was about to propose something when he checked his watch; he realized that they were already 15 minutes behind schedule. He turned to the supervisor.
strings.IBR_post_trium.10.a: “Fuck it. Leave em' on the desk, the office people can figure it out.”
strings.IBR_post_trium.11.d:
When the Caudillos next met, one item dominated the discussion and fueled the arguments that could be heard by the aides gathered outside the doors - the policy of isolationism. Or, more accurately, the effects of it, sharply felt by Union citizens both high and low.

The report delivered to them had been cryptic, and was interpreted differently. Franco regarded it with disdain, the carefully chosen words - far too many - clearly written by some politician. Salazar thought differently, appreciating the many figures and attention to detail, clearly the product of a well-trained and educated Union economist. But its message, however couched, was clear. The policy of isolation was damaging the economy, in some sectors ruinously so.

They had both known that such would happen, of course - one cannot just stop trade to such a degree and not cause pain, but the scale had clearly been underestimated. Similarly carefully, but equally clear, the report's conclusion that the policy might be better abandoned caused much further disagreement between the two men.

Both had arguments for and against, concerning topics of the greatest importance to the state. Security. Economic stability. Social unrest. Military confidence. Political unity and orthodoxy. And more besides. But in the end they could not come to a decision, each returning to their own home dissatisfied. And still concerned.
strings.IBR_post_trium.12.d:
Aldo hated Buenos Aires. As a man raised through generations of cattle farmers, he wanted nothing to do with the grimy hustle and bustle of the Argentine capital, yet he had business to do. Aldo spent the whole day traveling to meet with yet another lawyer to update his paperwork, again, for exporting his beef to Sevilla.

Three hours passed with the stout new lawyer, forcing Aldo to file exact information about the cattle, ports of shipment, dates, and the whole bureaucratic mess the Iberians were forcing upon him. A definitive change from the past filing, which he swore only used to take five minutes.

Finishing with his barrage of questions, the lawyer stood. “Well, sir, this should be everything. Now it will only take about two weeks for them to process and then-”

“Two more weeks! Are you batshit crazy? By then, them nutjobs will change them damn requirements again, and I'll be back in this rancid dump of a city!” He quickly snatched his jacket off the chair and marched to the door. “Dammit, at this rate, I might as well trade with the damn British! At least those pencil-headed dumbasses don't need the exact information of where every damn cattle was conceived, and the second it was slaughtered!”

“Sir, I promise you they won't change again. Really, the Iberians-”

“Enough with damn Iberia, my meat is going to Britain. Fine getting less, long as I stop dealing with these damned files every other month and needing to change every damn thing.” Aldo stormed out of the office, leaving the last three hours' work behind.
strings.IBR_post_trium.13.d:
The collapse of the Triumvirate made İsmet Yavuz's daily life miserable. The 34 year old diplomat had lived in Barcelona for the past decade, attending meetings, preparing paperwork, signing travel visas, and when there was nothing else to do, taking notes on news stories to report back to Ankara. But now, the atmosphere was gloomier. İsmet could in the back of his neck sense the suspicion of his colleagues whenever he passed them in the halls. The friendly conversation between the Iberians and himself around the coffee pot had stopped. Most meetings were cancelled, and the handful of remaining meetings were both shorter and tenser affairs.

“...y ese maldito turco...”

İsmet froze in his seat. He had tried to tune out the murmuring behind his back, but to hear such language-
strings.IBR_post_trium.13.a: “Would Carlos really say something like that? About me?!”
strings.IBR_post_trium.14.t: By His Wounds, You Have Been Healed
strings.IBR_post_trium.14.d:
Ulisses was a nobody. People envied his peaceful existence, his happy enough marriage and his fair enough fortunes. Yet for him, his existence was so profoundly mundane it bored him to no end. His job was repetitive and uninteresting, which made him enough to subsist comfortably, but did not allow him to indulge in excess. His family was neither abusive nor excessively loving. He was average, and yearned for more.

“Come on bufo, keep up.” The PIDE agent, who never revealed his true name, was getting annoyed with Ulisses' daydreaming. In truth, his now eight months of work with the state's secret police excited him greatly, making him prone to pensiveness.

Ulisses was led into half-collapsed tunnels underneath an abandoned construction project, into a large, rectangular room. In front of him lay a naked man held in what was little more than a cage. The man began begging in Italian as soon as he saw the agent enter, only for the latter to raise his baton and harshly beat him. Ulisses initially felt repulsed by the cruelty being demonstrated as the man, crying and begging, resumed a standing position with his arms stretched to either side like one of those statues of Christ he had seen at church. Whenever he faltered by even a centimeter, he would receive brutal punishment.

“We caught this motherfucker thanks to the lead you got us,” the agent said, looking at Ulisses and handing him the baton. “Wanna join? Show me what you've got. Keep him like this for twelve hours and you're in.” The agent put a hand on his shoulder and whispered a “good luck” before leaving him alone in the room. The Italian put his arms down, his eyes pleading for a break from the bufo. Ulisses looks at him and his baton, and feels disgusted with himself. In one fell swoop, he rushes towards the cage and begins to savagely beat the Italian. With each hit, he feels a rush of pleasure coursing through his brain. With each scream, he feels more alive than he ever had the entirety of his miserable life.
strings.IBR_post_trium.14.a: And for the first time, he felt like he had finally found something he truly enjoyed in life.
strings.IBR_post_trium.15.d:
The next meeting of the Caudillos was, if nothing else, decisive. They both knew, whatever else they disagreed upon, that a decision needed to, had to, be made. And they both made the same one, albeit for different reasons.

The report they had last read would not shake them. They would not compromise, and Iberia would protect itself from its many enemies during this period of recovery and consolidation. It would close off from the many foreign powers that they were certain had already attempted to meddle in its affairs, and it would focus on itself and its small circle of friends, until such time as it could once again open up from a position of strength.

This, naturally, positioned the Caudillos at the center of the entire effort, as was natural and desired. But it also meant that the ties Iberia possessed to those nations in its sphere were now paramount, and so they themselves would need to begin visiting them to cement support. Plans and itineraries would be developed immediately. The economy would not wait.

As the Caudillos departed, their aides began taking wagers between themselves of just how much of the work Salazar would take on, and the odds were not good for those arrayed against him. The trips would have little time for recreation, and all knew how little Franco would enjoy that.
strings.IBR_post_trium.16.d:
The announcement, made jointly by the Caudillos, on the continued policy of self-reliance was met with a sharply divided response. All efforts were made - watched closely by Salazar - to accompany the announcement with a propaganda blitz, to differing effect.

The general public's response was largely positive. Most people across Iberia wanted the Union to endure, remembering the disorder and uncertainty before its establishment, and the appeal of the Caudillos to a collective, Iberian effort to resist that found many receptive ears. Even some of the regionalist bourgeoisie responded positively - self-reliance was also a reliance on their own regions as well, after all. There were concerns about the increasing costs of food and other household staples, but there was an optimism that hard work could overcome the barriers.

Elsewhere, however, the response was far more muted. In Lisbon, Madrid, Barcelona, and other economic centers within the Union, businessmen of all stripes lamented the announcement. They had already been under severe pressure, and they all knew the disaster that was now to come. Iberia was simply not rich enough to survive on its own, and now, bereft of international trade, what could come but further hardships?

They resolved to protect themselves, knowing there was only a small chance they would survive. They hoped that the Caudillos would see reason soon.
strings.IBR_post_trium.17.d:
The next meeting of the Caudillos was, if nothing else, decisive. They both knew, whatever else they disagreed upon, that a decision needed to, had to, be made. And they both made the same one, albeit for different reasons.

The report they had last read had shaken them. The stability of the Union is, was, and always would be a concern, and they both knew that there was no faster way to damage that than economic decline. That could not be permitted, and at Salazar's prodding, they agreed to act to protect Iberia. They would instruct the organs of state to end the harshest isolationist measures, and work to repair and rebuild trade routes to current and potential partners. Franco's motorcycles left with messages to that effect within hours.

The Caudillos would themselves also make sure that they were presented as the visionaries seeing the correct way forward. Appearances, photographs, and recountings of positive statistics - and there were and would be more of them - were planned. Such events would clash with Franco's upcoming vacation, of course, but it was a necessary sacrifice.

As the Caudillos departed, their aides began taking wagers on just how much economic advancement could be expected. Most were conservative, but some were hopeful. They all, of course, made sure to act on their information within the next few days, before the official announcement. There were major gains to be made on the stock market, after all.
strings.IBR_post_trium.18.d:
The announcement, made jointly by the Caudillos, on the ending of isolationist restrictions was met with a strong response. All efforts were made - watched closely by Salazar - to accompany the announcement with a propaganda blitz, to significant, and united effect.

The general public's response was very positive. Most people across Iberia wanted the Union to endure, remembering the disorder and uncertainty before its establishment, and the appeal of the Caudillos to a future of increased trade, increased income, and greater demands for exports found many receptive ears. Even some of the regionalist bourgeoisie responded positively - their own regions had staple exports as well, after all. Most strongly expressed was the general relief felt by many as to the promise of lowered costs of food and other household staples.

There was significant agreement within the business community as well. In Lisbon, Madrid, Barcelona, and other economic centers within the Union, businessmen of all stripes had lamented the isolationist measures, and the announcement of their retraction was met with jubilation. They had already been under severe pressure, and were looking forward to the new connections to be made and opportunities to explore.

They resolved to do so vigorously, pleased that the Caudillos had seen reason.
strings.IBR_post_trium.19.d:
Luis Carrero Blanco was the third most powerful man in Iberia. The two men who could overrule him were in remote Galicia, discussing wide-ranging reforms. Until their return, his good friend Franco had entrusted him with Iberia's governance.

Fernando María Castiella y Maíz understood this power dynamic well. While the Minister of State could not approve the measures he was recommending on his own, his rhetoric to the Caudillos would be the tipping point for swaying the matter one way or another. “So you see, it would be in our strategic interest to try and mend our relationship with Italy. Besides access to the Suez Canal, the oil output of Italian colonies forms...”

“Excuse me, but I do not understand your point,” Carrero Blanco butted in, waving his pen dismissively. “You expect Iberia to renege on its policy of neutrality that saw us through the war unscathed, a policy I championed, mind you. And for what? Whatever scraps the Italians are willing to feed us? As if we were dogs?” Carrero Blanco looked into his eyes for a few seconds before beginning to pack his suitcase. “I'll inform the Caudillos of your proposition, of course. You are dismissed.”

Fernando's posture shifted as he mulled over his defeat like a sore wound. Then, as he was about to leave, he realized he had one shot left. “Imagine now, the Iberian soldier standing next to his Catholic brethren in front of the Holy Sepulchre. Defending Christ's land from the invading Moorish horde that would see it destroyed and the Holy City sacked. Would you deny our Christian Nation's glory and leave it all to the inevitably victorious Italians?”

Carrero Blanco's eyes fixed themselves on the Minister with renewed interest. He nodded curtly. “I'll ensure your message is received.” The next morning, a memo appeared on the Caudillos' desks.
strings.IBR_post_trium.19.a: And the ring of a thousand Church bells covered the sounds of battle, as Iberia drew close to war.
strings.IBR_post_trium.20.d:
Madrid was always a pleasant sight, and today was especially pleasant for the officials crowded over a mahogany desk. One of them, a Spaniard holding a drink in one hand and an assortment of papers in the other, spoke up with a boyish grin, “I trust that these shipments will prove sufficient for the cause.” before handing the papers off to one of his Italian counterparts. The man enthusiastically received them, quickly scanning the first page with a smile. Thousands of rifles, bullets, some trucks, and heavy equipment suited for a desert brawl. Passing it off to his fellow officials from the Empire, there was a series of satisfied nods and even a cheer from the original receiver, “On behalf of our nation, we are most grateful. Rapid aid will prove most useful against the Turks.”

“May the region swiftly return to stability.” replied one of the Portuguese representatives, before raising a glass.

The Italian representative raised his own and laughed. “Yes, all in the name of affordable petrol!”

“May our empires continue to prosper.”

A toast concluded the meeting as a success. As the glasses clinked, the Italian representative chimmed in with the expected reminder.
strings.IBR_post_trium.20.a: Fear not, Rome will remember who its friends are.
strings.IBR_post_trium.21.d:
Luis Carrero Blanco was the third most powerful man in Iberia. The two men who could overrule him were in remote Galicia, discussing wide-ranging reforms. Until their return, his good friend Franco had entrusted him with Iberia's governance, and Fernando María Castiella y Maíz was keeping him from finishing his work.

Luis cut the man short in his speech about the balance of power, Italian Mediterranean dominion, and other abstract nonsense that would threaten his life's work, the only thing that allowed his country to avoid the pains of the Second World War: Neutrality. “So why exactly should we support the Muslims and anger the Italians? You said it yourself, the Turks are unlikely to win anyway. I did not avoid Spain's destruction just for you to drag all of Iberia into war with a superpower.”

The Minister of Foreign Affairs tried to reiterate his charade. That Italy needed to be contained, that Turkey could be a valuable thorn in the Italian side. Other men might have been moved by the passion in his voice, but Luis comforted himself in the knowledge that he alone had the power to convince the Caudillos in the end. Luis began to pack up his belongings, expecting his colleague to do the same.

“The Italians are perfidious traitors, you know this.” Luis stopped, only slightly shifting to pay attention to him. “They are planning to move against our interests in North Africa. If they are not taught a lesson now, they will be emboldened and put their plan into action.” The minister produced a stack of photos and intelligence reports and slammed them on the table. Luis looked at him with a facade of calm as he took in the pictures of Italian soldiers in full desert gear. Yet in his heart, anger and indignation were mounting. Of course, the Italians were planning to backstab them. He nodded and left his office. That evening, he wrote a memo that would arrive straight on the Caudillos' desk first thing in the morning.
strings.IBR_post_trium.21.a: And the same fire that animated him that evening would find its way into the hearts of thousands of young men on their way to Holy Palestine.
strings.IBR_post_trium.22.d:
The desk lamp at the Customs Office glowed dimly, a light rainfall pattering on the window, footfalls troubling the pooling puddles amidst the hustle and bustle of the dockyard below.

“That's over a thousand rifles within the hour and another thousand by daybreak.” The Iberian officer reassured him.“

A Turkish Captain sat opposite to him, a cigar drilled between his lips. ”And you are certain the Regno Marina won't catch wind?“

”Ciano is no fool.“ The officer steepled his fingers and leaned back in his chair. ”The Regio Marina isn't going to run roughshod over the entire Mediterranean, not for another month or two... No offense.“

None taken. My countrymen are hardly thrilled to rot in the sands... I doubt the Italians are either.” The Captain pensively tugged at his mustache for a moment, then knocked on the table.“Such a senseless waste of life... All so the CHP can be spared the consequences of their mistakes.”

The Captain held out his hand, with a smile wrapping right around his head. “Istanbul will remember this gesture, we shall not forget this!”

The officer shook his hand.“May we both survive the encoraching madness of these years!
strings.IBR_post_trium.22.a: The Cross and Crescent lay a foundation for something greater.
strings.IBR_post_trium.23.d:
Lieutenant General José Miguel Vega Rodríguez took his binoculars off the landing plane. Around him was an entourage of both Iberian and Moroccan military cadres, preparing to greet their newest reinforcements. As the head of the Iberian forces in the sector, it befell upon him to assign these new arrivals to a duty.

As the plane comes to a halt and the tanned and seemingly perfectly-equipped men disembark in an orderly manner, saluting their officer and neatly boarding a jeep that would take them to their new accommodations, it became increasingly clear to the Moroccan attachés that these men were a more than capable force, despite numbering few.

After the small ceremony ended, Vega Rodríguez turned to leave the airstrip and get back to work in his office, away from the scorching sun. Yet a Moroccan officer intercepted him. “You have some great men over here. Of course, His Majesty greatly appreciates your efforts in maintaining the safety of this region. But I can't help but feel that we're making a mistake. It's been relatively quiet over here. In the Rif, however...”

José smirked. Counterinsurgency was their primary goal, of course, but it was also a way to keep pressure up on Iberia's allies of convenience, the Makhzen, the establishment nobles that served as officers in the Royal Army, or as direct lines of communication with the King. With these men here, and the Moroccans distracted in the Rif, the Makhzen will have to think twice before enacting any of their schemes for independence.

José turned around to hide his smirk and continued walking to his own Jeep with only a passing answer to the Moroccan.
strings.IBR_post_trium.23.a: “Indeed, these men here will allow your own troops to deploy to the Rif.”
strings.IBR_post_trium.23.b: “I'll pass your insight to my superior.”
strings.IBR_post_trium.24.d:
Iberia's Minister of the Army, Pablo Martín Alonso, may be old, but that didn't stop him from staying hands-on with his work. It was work that brought him to the factory floor of Fábrica Nacional de Munições de Armas Ligeiras, a state-owned Portuguese light arms company, with troops in tow. He had informed the FNM factory he'd be performing an assessment of their production tomorrow, but had shown up today since a meeting had been cancelled. The factory's manager eventually came rushing out of his office to greet Martín and his entourage, to which Martín's response was a simple demand: “I'm conducting the assessment now. Get me a weapon and a target.”

The manager scrambled to bring a halt to the entire production line, and the company's latest gun was quickly procured for Martín. “I can show you and your soldiers to the firing range if you would just follow-”

“No, as I said. The test will be conducted now,” Martín interrupted the manager, and instead his soldiers set up a makeshift target inside the factory. When one of the soldiers stepped forward to take the shot, the bullet went wide and put a hole through a workplace-safety poster on a nearby wall.

Martín scowled at the result of the test, and turned to face the FNM manager, who had gone completely pale. “Firstly, you will change the name from 'National' to 'Iberian.' Now as to the results of the tests...”
strings.IBR_post_trium.24.a: “It's a start, I expect better results after I raise your funding.”
strings.IBR_post_trium.24.b: “It's unacceptable. We'll fund the Basque manufacturers instead.”
strings.IBR_post_trium.25.d:
Military staff saluted, and civilian scientists stood at attention, as who many considered to be the third most powerful man in Iberia strode down the halls of the Junta de Energía Nuclear. Admiral Carrero Blanco, Minister of State, made his way to Iberia's second experimental nuclear reactor, and soon the entirety of JEN stood before him.

“I shall keep this brief: I have come to announce to all of you that Italy has agreed to resume information sharing for nuclear development,” the assembled crowd of scientists erupted into cheers, and Blanco waited for them to settle down before continuing, “In addition, I have personally approved the visa for and appointment of a nuclear science liaison between our two nations.,” Tthis announcement was followed by even more cheers from the crowd.

Blanco silenced the crowd simply by clearing his throat as the noise was dying down, “I expect you all to treat the liaison hospitably and respectfully, so that you all may establish a productive working relationship. However,” and as Blanco continued, his words took on a menacing weight, “under no circumstances is the liaison to acquire any information of Project Islero. Am I understood?” Instead of cheers, Blanco received only silent nods as a response. Everyone understood that Iberia's efforts to tap into the less civilian applications of nuclear technology were to remain under wraps, and what the punishment would be for letting any details slip out.
strings.IBR_post_trium.25.a: And with that, Blanco's visit to JEN had concluded.
strings.IBR_post_trium.26.d:
Carlos marveled at the blend of architectural grandeur and natural beauty that defined the Complutense University of Madrid. A Dominican by birth, he had crossed the Atlantic to pursue a degree in psychology at one of the most prestigious universities in the Spanish-speaking world.

Wandering through the sprawling expanse of University City, he found himself tuning into conversations around him. Voices drifted past in a chorus of sounds, the cadence of Madrid natives, the melodic lilt of Andalusians, and accents so unfamiliar they might as well have belonged to another language entirely. It was overwhelming, but also thrilling.

On his way to his first class, Carlos passed a group of students dressed in traditional black attire, guitars and bandurrias slung over their shoulders. A La Tuna. He had heard of them, student musicians who performed to earn money for textbooks and living expenses. The idea had always intrigued him. He watched them laugh and tune their instruments, making a mental note: maybe he'd try joining one someday.

Inside the psychology department, the atmosphere shifted. The building was older, its walls carrying the weight of history. Carlos ran his fingers along the plastered surface of a former blast hole. A chill crept up his spine. His thoughts spiraled. Was he truly safe here? Should he have stayed in Santo Domingo? What if something happened, another conflict, another war, and he couldn't get back home? Following Malta, what if-

A firm hand landed on his shoulder. Carlos spun around, heart pounding, and found himself face-to-face with an older gentleman. The man's gaze was steady, assessing, but kind. “New here?” he asked. “I'm Professor Humberto.”
strings.IBR_post_trium.27.d:
Franco spoke into the microphone to deliver a short radio address to the nation.

“Iberia is a nation united. We are united in our faith in the almighty God, and in our Church. We are united in our faith in our Caudillos, and in our national resolve. Iberians stand besides each other as soldiers, friends, and brothers, united in the defense of our nation and her values.

This year on December 10th, and in subsequent years, we shall celebrate this unity with a new holiday: The Day of Brotherhood. It shall be a celebration not only of our Union itself, but of all its people, as we continue our work to build an ever-stronger nation. Past years of bickering are over, and as the first generation of children born in a united Iberia reach adulthood, on the Day of Brotherhood we shall remember our unending pursuit of more years of peace, unity, strength, and greatness!

¡Arriba Iberia!”
strings.IBR_post_trium.27.a: Perhaps there will be another parade...
strings.IBR_post_trium.28.d:
CONCERNING: Continued Economic Deterioration
CLASSIFICATION: Secret

Post-Triumvirate economic recovery efforts, as directed by the Executive, have been insufficient to offset losses of opportunity and productivity subsequently recorded.

Severe trade imbalances, deficits of raw materials, and a reduction in the quality of factory tooling have been observed at a significant level across all industries, and stimulus actions have proven wholly insufficient. Real losses have been realized, and continued contractions are expected across the near and intermediate term in both total economic product and per-capita output.

Although the current state of deterioration is significant, it is not yet at a wholly systemic level, and rapid direct interventions are currently capable of preserving price stability among foodstuffs and consumer staples. However, such actions are wholly unsustainable, and within the intermediate term will become insufficient to prevent significant shortages and price increases among such products.

It is recommended that focused action be taken, and state policies be updated, corrected, or revised as necessary to provide economic stimulus and growth on a macroeconomic scale.

Report ends.
strings.IBR_post_trium.29.d:
CONCERNING: Cautious Economic Improvement
CLASSIFICATION: Secret

Post-Triumvirate economic recovery efforts, as directed by the Executive have, overall, resulted in small increases in economic opportunity and productivity.

Reductions in trade imbalances, increases in flow of raw materials, and expansions of factory tooling have been observed at a significant level across all industries, and stimulus actions have proven moderately effective in expanding financial activities. Real gains have been realized, and continued small-scale expansions are expected in both the near and intermediate term in both total economic product and output.

Although the current state of improvement is significant, it is not yet at a wholly systemic level, and rapid direct interventions are currently not capable of allowing meaningful targeted expansions of critical industries, particularly those involving foodstuffs and consumer staples. However, should trends continue, it is expected that such will become possible in the intermediate term, allowing for consumer price reductions to be realized.

It is recommended that current policies and actions be continued and expanded upon, and that state policies be continually monitored for optimization in order to permit continued economic stimulus and growth on a macroeconomic scale.
strings.IBR_post_trium.30.d:
CONCERNING: Significant Economic Improvement
CLASSIFICATION: Secret

Post-Triumvirate economic recovery efforts, as directed by the Executive have resulted in significant increases in economic opportunity and productivity, with indications of compounding increases to follow.

Large reductions in trade imbalances, significant increases in the flows of various raw materials, and vigorous increases of consumer-based economic activity have all been observed. Stimulus actions have proven very effective in expanding financial activities across all economic and industrial sectors. These expansions of activity have exceeded initial optimistic metrics by a statistically significant margin.

However, although the current state of improvement is very promising, and is further showing signs of becoming systemic in character, such growth remains predicated on continued state support. Economic sectors expect further and rapid direct interventions to permit meaningful and targeted expansions of critical industries, particularly those involving foodstuffs and consumer staples. Should such actions cease now, it is likely that progress would rapidly dwindle and potentially reverse in reaction.

It is recommended that currently successful policies and actions be continued and expanded upon, and that those policies be continually monitored for optimization in order to allow for further acceleration in economic growth.
strings.IBR_post_trium.30.tt:
Our economic model delivered an impressive recovery!
Yet the recovery is fragile.
Radical change would destroy it.
strings.IBR_latam.1.d:
That morning, identical envelopes from the Foreign Office were delivered to the desks of the Caudillos. When they were opened, immediately by Salazar after waking up and later by Franco following the football match, the grim news within was revealed.

The Colombian government, which was friendly to Iberia and well-entrenched within its economic and diplomatic sphere as its gateway into South America, had been overthrown. General Pinilla and his military clique had dismantled the civilian and “democratic” republican apparatus. According to the reports, the coup had been well-planned and swift. By the time the Iberian embassy could send a cable, it was already over.

The ambassador had already been summoned to meet with Pinilla's functionaries, and the Foreign Office expected a clear reduction in bilateral commitments. Pinilla's clique saw cooperation with the Union as far less important. It was anticipated that Colombia would adopt a more neutral international stance. Even worse, despite the coup, the report continued, the new regime was popular. Far more popular than the previous pro-Union regime.

However, Pinilla's hold is still tenuous, and there are still elements of the state apparatus organizing against him. There's a slim possibility, however slight, that they might take action, swapping out Pinilla as swiftly as he had replaced the previous president.
strings.IBR_latam.1_tt: Due to Pinilla's coup, Colombia has left our Economic Sphere.
strings.IBR_latam.2.d:
As the economic recovery efforts continued it became increasingly clear that, whatever the position of either Caudillo or their respective parts of the Union may have been on external trade with certain partners, it was critical to maintain trade with historical friends of the Union.

This was especially true as it related to the nations of South America. Long cultural ties had resulted in deep economic connections and even though there were many competitors for influence both on and off the continent, it was an area where Iberia had significant influence. Existing relationships had to be strengthened and protected from external interference. On this, Salazar was insistent.

And, of course, nearly the entire continent enjoyed football as much as Franco did.

The Caudillos spoke - and argued - at length about what form this would take, and it was late at night before they finished. Visits would be organized by the Foreign Office to a number of prominent South American states, with Brazil, Argentina, Colombia, and Ecuador taking priority. Others could of course follow, but trade with those four was identified as important.

The decision made, the Caudillos retired for the night. Preparations would begin immediately for the visits, and the diplomatic teams would soon depart. A subsequent meeting discussing the specifics of the tour is scheduled to be held within the week.
strings.IBR_latam.2.a: Let's hope they are well received.
strings.IBR_latam.3.d:
A young Spanish diplomat rode in the back of a limo in Ciudad Trujillo, the otherwise deskbound office clerk uneased by the remnants of urban fighting flowing past him. Security was being tightened.

“Let me be the first to welcome you to my country.” Parts of the city were still smouldering, distant plumes of smoke from fire rescue efforts casting the sky a pale gray behind the Dominican's head.

“Muy bien!” The diplomat's older counterpart sat next to him, hair flecked with grey and a nonplussed look in his eyes. “How is the mood in the city?”

“Very exhausted, but sleep comes easier now.” The second representative replied. The Dominican representatives dressed in black, their grim faces at once marked by the Anti-Fascist Legion invasion and yet somehow indifferent to it.

“Hopefully, better days are on the horizon.” The young diplomat smiled faintly. “I heard the national remilitarization is going smoothly?”

“Si.” The first representative raised his brow, his voice was more direct. “It is our hope to maintain the Republic's historical ties with the former mother country.

”The Legion's defeat was inevitable, the Republic stands strong.“ The second representative re-buttoned his suit. ”But we would be remiss not to acknowledge the Union's support.“

The older diplomat was realistic. ”It won't stop with the Legion, the geopolitical situation, et cetera.“
strings.IBR_latam.3.a: A subtle grin. “Then let us commiserate, let us make a deal!”
strings.IBR_latam.3.dBL:
The wind whipped through the hair of a young Spanish diplomat in Ciudad Trujillo, driven briskly along the boulevard in a military staff car, open to the air and the battle-scarred city around them.

“Bienvenido, gentlemen of the old country!” A Dominican in dungarees sat across from him, giving a toothy grin. “Our regards to Los Caudillos!”

“M-muy Bien.” An older diplomat stuttered in the seat next to his younger counterpart, his normally unenthusiastic gaze fixed with the rifle in the Dominican's arms. “Are your p-people well?”

An officer sat to the right of his fellow soldier. “The people are overjoyed! Balaguer has won us the day and a new era is upon us!”

The younger diplomat enjoyed their enthusiasm, he smiled. “Perhaps the old country can offer some assistance?”

“The Union holds a special place in the heart of the Republic.” The younger soldier said, producing a wine bottle from under his seat. “With the Legion driven back, the future is open to both our nations!”

The older diplomat ran a nervous hand through his graying hair, eyeing the street workers clearing out the rubble as they drove past. “M-maybe we can come to an agreement then?”
strings.IBR_latam.3.b: “Si, Señor!” The officer said. “Shall we drink to this reforging of friendships?”
strings.IBR_latam.3.dRP:
Somewhere in Madrid, two Iberian diplomats sat in the back of a limousine that cruised along the boulevard. Cigarette smoke filled the interior from window to window, the blurry visage of old european architecture breezing by as a backdrop. “Are we even certain they are open to talks?” A younger man in a plain suit sat with his head leaning on his hand, conspicuously clean and crisp.

“So they keep saying.”

The young man's colleague handed him a file. He sifted through the documents while his counterpart rolled a cigarette between his fingers. He was older, graying in his hair. His tie was undone, his suit jacket discarded with thick aviator glasses hiding a placid look in his eyes. The younger man continued. “Anything seems like an improvement over Trujillo, do we know these guys are on the level?”

“The rumor mill hasn't exactly been idle.” His colleague said, eyeing the document pile in the young man's lap and scratching at his temple. “The insurgency was hardly bloodless.”

“So I'm told” came the reply, “I can't imagine they're thrilled for us to show up.” The documents outlined many of the rumors, both about the new administration and their attitudes to Iberia. The meeting's prospects were bracing to say the least.

“Just think of us as the clean up crew.” The older man smiled. “The pen, the sword and so forth. We are all reasonable men here.”

“Janitors rarely ride in limousines.” The diplomat thought, anxiously pulling at his collar.
strings.IBR_latam.3.c: “And reasonable men remember the sword before the pen...”
strings.IBR_latam.4.d:
As the plane landed in the thin air of Bogotá, and the Iberian diplomatic delegation aboard was able to look out the windows, they despaired at the formation of military officers standing ready to 'welcome' them. Not a civilian was to be seen.

It had taken some time to arrange the visit. Pinilla's regime was much less friendly to Iberia than the one it had replaced, and the formal and perfunctory greetings given to them as they descended to the tarmac - along with the desultory performance of an army band half the size it should have been - made it clear that any special relationship was over.

Driving through the city, the military was still out in full force, and the diplomats could feel the tension and unease hanging in the air. And, yet, it was infused with a curious enthusiasm from the general population, who seemed unafraid and even supportive of the soldiers they were now encountering daily. And in a moment that the senior Iberian recognized as a clumsy allegory fitting for a military officer thrust into diplomacy it was when the convoy passed the enormous statue of Bolívar, in the plaza that bore his name, that the situation was made clear.

Turning in his seat, the officer bluntly stated that the decision had already been made. Colombia was fully open to continuing bilateral trade, especially given the economic and historical links which existed, but it would no longer allow itself to be controlled or influenced by the Union. Pinilla, his cabinet, and the military would chart a new destiny.

The senior Iberian recognized the futility of attempting to argue, and knew then that they would never meet Pinilla, nor any member of the new government above the officer who had just spoken. He would continue the mission, negotiate some trade deals - which he knew would be of only middling quality - but politically Iberia had already lost.
strings.IBR_latam.4.a: Very unfortunate. Can nothing be done?
strings.IBR_latam.4.dNF:
A succulent slice of delicacy slid down Miguel's throat, a good omen for him and his delegation's time in Bogotá. All the residents here walked about briskly, through this savannah of everyday business. The only ones still trembling were those still paranoid about a conflict that was unlikely to coalesce, as those around them strolled only with relaxed caution. The young diplomat's mission here in Colombia has certainly been an interesting one.

“So I've been thinking... how much certainty can we expect with this nations' pro-Iberian stance?” Samuel cocked his eyebrow and put forward the difficult question.

Pedro stood to retort. “Oh, come on now. We've done all this work for both Iberia and Colombia, you shouldn't start having doubts now.”

Pedro patted his face with a napkin before continuing. “Even then, that's not what I'd be concerned about. See, I have also been thinking, if the Americans decide to start making moves here, then they have far more to offer then we could ever hope to. I guess what I'm really saying is, what's stopping the Americans from driving all of our businesses out of here?”

Miguel stilled for a moment before responding. “Listen, we've all been having a great time, making friends with our Colombian counterparts, and have done such hard work. So why don't we just drop the worries and focus on relaxing, okay?”

So it was, and the delegation dropped the question without a hitch. Suddenly, the doors to the restaurant opened, and in came a Colombian politician and his entourage meaning to meet them. They exchanged genuine hand shakes, with big smiles growing on the faces of all the men, and made friendly greetings to one another. The question from before began to slip from the minds of the delegates.
strings.IBR_latam.4.dLR:
Toxins and lights swirled in the eyes of the Iberian delegation, the many drinks of alcohol showed in the red roses upon their cheeks. Before them, officials of the Laureanist government were signing away at a multitude of trade agreements with Iberia, barely skimming over the first paragraph before writing their name. Something completely uncharacteristic of staunch protectionists and autarky advocates. Even this sight cut through the drunkenness of the Iberians, making them question the motivations for such a shift.
