One Laureanist spoke: “So, Pedro, I heard you recently had a falling out with your wife?”

Pedro spoke with a drunken slur. “Huh? Oh, yeah, the woman was going on and on and on about how I have a drinking problem. But you know what? No more nagging wife means I can drink all the wine I want! What else could a man ask for?”

One delegate, Diego, sat almost isolated in his chair. He hadn't had anything to eat or drink for the whole night; instead he sat uneasily, here they were, having danced and drank for years, and still they did so even when there was such an uneasy future ahead. He lifted his head from its craning and scanned the room, seeing every bit of drunken rowdiness occurring. It made him sick, though he could not articulate why.

Diego stood up with haste. “Excuse me, may I use the restroom here?”

He was excused and left to speedwalk straight to the bathroom, where he proceeded to lose his lunch within the toilet bowl. As he washed his hands and stepped out of the room, his eyes landed on a stained glass window that he somehow missed on his way. That window hid the numerous dreary and grey soldiers now patrolling the streets, standing with a hawkish vigil and with a disposition ready to fire at a moment's notice.
strings.IBR_latam.5.d:
Just as the previous reports for the Foreign Office had arrived, so too had these ones, placed on the desks of the Caudillos in the early morning - and addressed in the same fashion. This report, however, had far more red markings upon it, proclaiming the secrecy of the details within. Details, though not all knew, about what could be done to support the forces arranged against Colombia's unwelcomed regime change. The Caudillos it seemed, had much to consider and, of course, to later argue about.

The most lucrative partner Iberia could hope for in the country remained the PCC via its Laureanist wing, though the recent coup d'état significantly upset their hold on power even on a regional level. Most of the central departments had been taken over by elements aligned with Bogotá's new masters, though the report made note of a break in the pattern.

The North of the country and, surprisingly, the in-the-past liberal stronghold of Antioquia had remained in the hands of the Laureanists, with much of the movement's remaining strength being funneled into entrenching their hold on the Atlantic coast cities.

The Office was optimistic about their prospects in achieving that goal, yet the picture was grim nonetheless. An entire page of the report was dedicated to the growing influence of Germania over the movement, both ideologically, economically and militarily, no doubt as consequence of Iberia's failure to keep its allies in power.

Near the end, the report made note of other Iberophile groups within the country, a fortunate consequence of their longstanding alliance since the 1940s, such as a moderate wing of the ANP led by Guillermo León Valencia, though these held slim chances of achieving power and served as mere consolation. After all...
strings.IBR_latam.5.a: ...the Caudillos were not planning on losing a second time.
strings.IBR_latam.5.b: ...it was best to hope it won't come to that.
strings.IBR_latam.5_tt: When the time comes, we will support the Laureanists in their bid for power.
strings.IBR_latam.5_ttb: When the time comes, we will support the National Front in their bid for power, unless another catastrophe occurs in the meantime.
strings.IBR_latam.6.d:
Another aircraft landed, carrying another Iberian diplomatic delegation, in another South American capital. This time it was Quito and, for those aboard who had been to other cities as part of the sequence of visits, Quito struck them as 'similar, but worse.'

It had the same international airport - but the tarmac was uneven. It had the same highways - but there were far more potholes. It had the same soldiers - but their weapons were older and clearly in worse maintenance. It had the same air, but everything was more dour. More depressing - economically and otherwise.

It also had the same people - yet here their general dislike towards the current regime was clear to those who knew how to look, and the reports the diplomats had all received in their preparation packages identified regular patterns of low-level extortion and corruption on the part of government officials creeping into everyday life. Which was why, when the letter arrived, the delegation's leader was not surprised.

It presented an opportunity. One of Ecuador's previous presidents, and a great friend of Iberia, Velasco, had been exiled following his fall. But there were locals who still remembered him fondly, chief among them the local aristocracy, who were willing to parlay. It was not clear yet to the diplomat exactly what the talk would result in, but the implication was evident. He could feel the tingle of an opportunity, though it would be a safer bet to proceed as usual and establish a trade with the government.

Given the strict schedule of the delagation, he could not afford to do both and it soon became clear that a decision was expected immediately, and there was no time to send a cable to Madrid. Would the gamble be worth taking?
strings.IBR_latam.6.a: Yes. Velasco is a friend of Iberia.
strings.IBR_latam.6.b: No. We will continue talks with the government.
strings.IBR_latam.6_tt: By negotiating with the aristocracy instead, we can make Velasco's return to Ecuador more likely.
strings.IBR_latam.7.d:
The diplomat's eyes scoured over the briefings given to him with little interest. He had given the call a while ago to arrange for José Velasco's return to Ecuador, but since he had come back from Quito, he had been signposted up to Tegucigalpa, forced to watch from the sidelines as developments down south lurched through uncertainty. What reports on guerrilla movements or exports he received were just skimmed over.

Suddenly, a call. He quickly overcame his disconnect to take the phone. “Hello? Who is this?” he asked, with some uncertainty.

“This is José María Velasco Ibarra, President of Ecuador.” replied the familiar voice down the line. “I understand this division was involved in negotiating my return?

The diplomat spluttered for a moment. ”Um, y-yes, sir, we were responsible for negotiating your passage through Managua.“ Best to conceal direct involvement, he thought. Wiser not to incur his superiors' wrath. ”I take it that you weren't arrested upon your arrival?“

Velasco chuckled heartily from the other end. ”No, far from it. There was even a crowd, practically spilling over the runway. Every man who saw me out in 1960 were either in Panama or were shaking my hands. If you could just see the scowl on their faces!“ He paused for a moment, doubtlessly relishing the turnaround. ”I'll be phoning Madrid now. I'll see if they can resurrect the trade deal.“

Reclining into his chair, the diplomat smiled. By technicality, of course, this was against protocol. He hadn't taken any record of who had phoned, hadn't given the information to the Iberian embassy in Quito, and was not planning to relay his message to the Foreign Office in Madrid. Velasco, of course, would do most of that instead. For now, though, he could take pride in his success in seeing through Velasco's return.
strings.IBR_latam.8.d:
Reading the newspapers these days just sickened David Zaragoza. Almost every article found some new excuse to build the profile of Fernando Belaúnde. Perhaps it was lingering patriotism for Spain, born anew at Teruel, but he just could not stand an Americanophile entering into office. Suddenly, an idea popped into his head. Most of his contacts back in Burgos had faded away over the past decades, but he was certain he still had one. Phoning with caution, he kicked himself as the line went dead each time, until–

“Saúl? It's been years! How have you been?” he asked, almost meaning his excitement as the phone line finally picked up.

“David? Is that really you?” asked the other end, in a voice much drier than it had once been, “Wow, it's been years...yes, things are quite alright! About to have my grandson over. They grow up so fast, don't they?

”They sure do. My wife died a few years back, but I've been able to distract myself. Business is better than ever.“ The line went dead for a minute, and David shuffled uncomfortably around in his chair.

”Well, the start of church is coming soon.“ asked Saúl, with some curiosity. ”I really can't stay long.“

He knew he couldn't talk for long; the charges for a call across the Atlantic were astronomical. But he just had to make sure. ”Listen, I know this is unconventional, but the Peruvian elections are coming up. We need a candidate who isn't an American lapdog to win. Odría, maybe. Could you help?“

Once again, an uncomfortable silence filled the air. ”I appreciate your enthusiasm, but I'm getting old. I'm 64, retired last year, and my fitness has never been the same since“ replied the voice, trailing off as if in thought.
strings.IBR_latam.8.a: “Look, David, if this crusade is the only reason you cared, please don't call me again.”
strings.IBR_latam.8.b: “...I'll phone around. I can't fight for you, but I know a few of our comrades still can.”
strings.IBR_latam.8.tt: We shall invest into making sure Manuel Ódria wins the upcoming Peruvian election.
strings.IBR_latam.9.d:
Tanks. Those was the first things David Zaragoza noticed when walking past the parades on Jirón de la Union. Made out of paper mache and decorated with flowers, perhaps. But their message was clear, enforced by the chants and signs behind them. Supporters of Manuel Arturo Odría were marching down, triumphant at his victory. As the numbers threatened to spill into the hall, David's mouth shimmered with pride.

The parade turned a corner, and chants suddenly began to drown out cheers. A handful of left-wing agitators, sympathisers to Belaúnde and Reyes alike condemning his return. Practically a sideshow, he thought, and quickly pushed back by its sheer mass. A few of the enterprising ones had already taken up their positions in the Andes, preparing for a guerrilla war against the government. Not his problem, he thought. Let them tire themselves out in abject misery.

Turning back around, he walked for a moment before halting to enter the church of Nuestra Señora de la Merced, drawing out prayer beads as he sat at a pew, thanking God for Odría's victory, and to pray for further guidance. He recognised Odría's independent spirit - he had never been totally supportive of the Union in his first term, and even now, his rhetoric blended Iberia and Spain. It didn't matter. Once he saw how Washington would scorn him, and the strengths of Iberia's sons and daughters, he would turn.

Peering at the continuing procession outside, David reflected on where he would go next. He could, of course, focus on building his business back up. He had gone deeper into the red than he had anticipated, after all, and had sold half of it off. With his new connections...he hesitated. Not that he hated the idea, but he had become quite the local hero, even without his ties to Iberia being public. He could easily run as a Council-no, for Mayor of Los Olivos. And with how rapidly Lima had been expanding...
strings.IBR_latam.9.a: And God saw that it was good. The eighth day.
strings.IBR_latam.9.tt: Should our influence extend over Colombia and Venezuela, Odria could repay our backing....
strings.IBR_latam.10.d:
David Zaragoza lingered for a second. He had no real reason to, perhaps. Everything that he had agency over had come and gone, and now, all that was left was procedure. All of his money had been spent, and he had long sold off every meaningful part of his business to cover the funds. A few hours more, and the eviction notice would officially go through, leaving him totally bankrupt. He's seen the writing on the wall for weeks, but only now was the reality finally setting in.

His mind drifted to Odría. That damned fool! It was always a longshot for him to be reelected after everything that had happened in his first term, but he could've pulled it off! If only he'd campaigned in the right areas! If only he'd leant on the right people! If only he hadn't made that damned comment in Pucallpa! But he couldn't hold a grudge for too long. It was his choice to back him by that much. And, if he ever ran again, he knew that he'd vote for Odría once more.

Without thought, he turned back to dialing the same numbers on his phone. These were trustworthy agents of Iberia, he had been told. For the last few months, they had been delivering secret codes, offering clandestine meetings, shaking hands with the right men. Now, the lines had gone completely empty. The phone rang once, then twice, then went totally dead. Somewhere, the line had been cut. By the agents or the tax office. Didn't matter, he thought.

David struggled through his pockets. Tickets from Lima to Ponta Delgada. If inflation wasn't too bad, he could probably afford a flight back to Seville. From there, it'd be an odd job or two, and then he'd have enough money to hitchhike back home to Burgos. But he couldn't bring himself to move. It was the coward's way out, to demand his extended family take care of him. Would the air line even accept him? Would being a pauper in Andalusia really be much better?
strings.IBR_latam.10.a: And so, he lingered, seconds turning into days in his head.
strings.IBR_council_creation.1.d:
Franco read over the papers on the desk, then passed them over to Salazar. “Well, that leaves us with two options to choose from. We can create an advisory body—my slight preference—or we can do as you said you suggested and give the Iberian Council a legislative role.”

Salazar nodded. “A legislative council could be helpful for our purposes. We do not need to resort to making a democratic body, but if we were to devolve legislative functions onto a group of people that are empowered to make some decisions with our approval—and who assume responsibility for any failures of the government arising from said decision—it would lift a burden from the government.”

Franco stood up and looked out the window. “Well, I can see some strong points in that view. But I wonder whether that sort of power being put in their hands is strictly necessary. We will be the ones to make the final decisions, we both agree on that.” A nod from Salazar. “So then, rather than bothering with the risk of overly independent councilors striking out on their own, might it not be more prudent to just have the Council work in an advisory role?”

Salazar made a non-committal noise. After some silence and some more debate, one of the men ultimately went along with the other's arguments.
strings.IBR_council_creation.1.a: A decisive government, or a strong legislature?
strings.IBR_council_creation.10.t: The Best Seats in the House
strings.IBR_council_creation.10.d:
The old man upon the stage never changed. His dry voice, his slow pace, even his brutal technical nature ever plodded through the Estado Novo who gathered to listen to him. Today it was like a nectar however, a rare spice added to the usually bland rhythm.

For Marcelo Caetano heard the soft whispers of progress between the words of Caudillo Salazar.

He sat rigid, furiously noting down everything the aged Caudillo said. His vantage point was admirable, even despite his lack of official position. No formal role, true, but Portugal was not one to deny a man of competence, an accolade Marcelo took great pride in. His Choupana boys stretched throughout Lisbon like roots, roots of a movement waiting for such an opportunity as this - waiting for their lynchpin to hear this moment.

“Now, to discuss Council Member selections, they shall be held to four year terms beginning from an agreed shared date, to be selected from particular sources so as to ensure proper expertise is maintained.” Salazar's voice was weak, a quick glance to his rear showed Caetano a sea of faces straining to hear. He grinned. How fortunate his seat was.

He summarised the doddering presentation, swiping his pen across the page. Every province elects 2 members with an electorate of family heads and married women. 150 from the Vertical Union, 30 direct appointments and 144 elected by Iberian national organizations. Universities, professional associations, regional governments, and the like. This he underlined; his own scholastic affairs had opened an opportunity.

The lecture showed no signs of abating as Salazar continued on into new minutiae, but Caetano's smile held. Finally, institutionalism had finally come to Iberia; just as he had told Salazar was necessary. Institutions in which to mold a new nation.
strings.IBR_council_creation.10.a: And he would ensure his allies stood ready to claim their place within it.
strings.IBR_council_creation.11.d:
“Señor Fernández-Miranda, what defines a State Officer?”

Torcuato Fernández-Miranda looked at the Caudillo bent over the document across the table, reading the lines with a torturously slow pace. He was no stranger to dense texts, nor guiding those unfamiliar with them through their pages. He was a Political Law Professor after all. No, this was not unfamiliar to him at all. However, that his Caudillo would be spending hours asking him for terms he really should be aware of?

If he was not so tense he would sigh.

“An official of the government who will be bound to the provisions of the Fundamental Law, holding and maintaining the Caudillo's trust.” His tone carried a hint of abrasion, an observation made not until it had escaped him. He closed his eyes, perhaps the Caudillo hadn't noticed.

Franco looked up, a mellow gaze regarding the Professor. “Did you serve in the War, Señor?”

Internally, he swore. The Caudillo had noticed, he must have. “Yes, Caudillo Franco. I was at the Battle of the Ebro.”

The Caudillo looked away, gazing into the wall for a moment before returning to the document before him. “You won Spain there, maintaining the line when the socialists crossed that river and watched for any error they made.” He paused, body pausing motionless for a long moment.
strings.IBR_council_creation.11.a: “I would not like to lose it to any mistakes made now.”
strings.IBR_council_creation.12.d:
The applause rattled around his mind for a moment as João Miller Guerra took in the moment. After all, why shouldn't he? Before him was an audience of his peers, all crushed into this small assembly room. The Portuguese Medical Association's first member of the Iberian Council. Their first member to influence policy solely on their behalf. A badge of honor, in the purest sense.

He raised his hands gently, signalling for the applause to die down. “Gentleman, thank you.” His voice carried a note of nervousness, but he cared little. “I can't say that I know what to expect from Madrid, but with you behind me I am sure that whatever it may be, it shall be no obstacle.” Another round of applause followed, one that Guerra indulged in again for a moment.

“As I have made clear to you before, I will make it clear again. I will make it clear to those in Madrid, in every meeting I am dragged to,” small chuckles interrupted him, earning a wry smile from Guerra, “I go not as myself but as a vessel for our profession. Your cares are my cares. Your desires are my desires. Through us, perhaps the nation can take the role it deserves in its fate.” More applause followed.

Guerra looked on the crowd, taking his final opportunity to enjoy the moment. Soon the novelty would die, he was sure of that, and it would all be meetings and drudgery. Officials and Caudi- Caudillos!

“And I would like to add,” he almost shouted, raising his arms again but not waiting for the applause to cease, “that of course I shall be there to compliment the wisdom of our Caudillos. We can all agree that they are the guide of our nation!” He glanced around. “Yes?” Polite applause.

He cursed himself. “Smooth João,” he muttered, “very smooth.”
strings.IBR_council_creation.12.a: A man with ideas is a man to be closely watched.
strings.IBR_reformist_tt_1: Curtailing liberalism in the Council will hinder the reformist cause.
strings.IBR_council_creation.12.b: Who will care about a scatter-brained neurologist?
strings.IBR_reformist_tt_2: Letting liberals participate will strengthen reformist sentiment in the Council.
strings.IBR_council_creation.13.d:
“While our talks are always invigorating Senhor Caetano, I'm afraid you must be brief. I am expecting reports on an urgent matter in the colonies shortly.”

Marcelo Caetano took his seat across Caudillo Salazar's desk. Barely cushioned, the seat was as plain as everything else in the office. A cold light, cold walls, a cold desk. The bare essentials everywhere. He respected it, in truth, but not when he had to sit upon his Caudillo's barren tastes. He shifted uncomfortably.

“Of course, Caudillo. I simply wished to inquire as to your selections for the Iberian Council being formed. I trust Portugal will be well represented?”

The question was rhetorical, he saw almost a ghost of a grin on the old man's face across from him. “Certainly, to name some there's Manuel Gonçalves Cerejeira, António Vitorino da França Borges, just today I spoke to a fellow professor regarding a place, Pires de Lima.” Salazar chuckled. “With your own academic adventures, I'm sure one of our universities elected you.”

Internally, Caetano winced. Not a silhouette of it appeared upon his smiling face. “Unfortunately not, Caudillo Salazar, but that does not dampen my happiness that you have taken to my advice. A more dignified position for yourself, away from legislative squabbles, will be excellent for your efforts for Portugal.”

The old Caudillo raised an eyebrow. “Nonsense Marcelo, the Council is an extension. Not a replacement. If that is your only question, then please leave me. I have much to do.” He signalled for Caetano to leave, eyes commanding. Caetano bowed his head and left the room. The message was clear and aggravating Salazar would achieve nothing more. Besides,

He too had much to do.
strings.IBR_council_creation.13.a: Cerejeira, Borgia? Piers Durima was it? He was going to have to double check the names first.
strings.IBR_reformist_tt_3: Limiting Caetano's clique will make his self-interested brand of 'reform' less relevant.
strings.IBR_council_creation.13.b: Cerejeira, Borges... let's focus on Pires de Lima. One hook in at a time.
strings.IBR_council_creation.13.c: Cerejeira, Borges, de Lima. Fine friends to make, and so well positioned.
strings.IBR_reformist_tt_4: Caetano's clique is interested in some modernizing reforms...
strings.IBR_council_creation.14.d:
“Caudillo Franco, I am not suggesting that this new Council will prevent patriots from their work entirely... what I am trying to say is that they could frustrate it enough to cause severe problems.”

Franco rapped his fingers upon his desk as the Minister of State, Carrero Blanco, sat rigid as stone across from him. The man was nervous, particularly so. His hands were fists upon his knees, his gaze absolutely refusing to look away from himself. It was almost unnerving.

“Salazar has assured me-”

“Has he gone over the details of the committee powers? How committee creation is basically uncapped, and all are planned to have the power to summon officials? Every minister, from myself to the governors we assign to some godforsaken patch of sand in the Sahara will be dragged to Madrid to explain their jobs rather than perform them. Think of what that could mean, do you want to give men like Fraga a soapbox-?” Blanco's tirade was halted with a slam of the desk from Franco, a command to cease shrinking the Minister like a scared lamb.

“If you are so concerned with procedure, talk to Salazar. Do not come to me with schoolyard gossip.” Franco commanded, fangs carried on each word. To his surprise, Blanco did not immediately leave the room, and after a long hesitation found his voice again.

“Well, you see Caudillo Franco. There's just the issue of... necessary agreements that many of us have to make. For the proper completion and remuneration, to the Government, of our duties. Such committees may pry into affairs they don't understand and engage in... public alarmism?”.

Franco blinked, and then shrugged. After all that, this was the concern?
strings.IBR_council_creation.14.a: “Dutiful men need fear no hostility when holding my trust, and only incompetent men lose my trust.”
strings.IBR_reformist_tt_5: Further limiting the Council's ability to question other organizations will decrease reformist sentiment.
strings.IBR_council_creation.14.b: “If men I trust are so fearful of being known to me, I would much like to ensure their wisdom.”
strings.IBR_reformist_tt_6: Allowing the Council to question other organizations will make reformism more popular.
strings.IBR_council_creation.15.d:
Here is the first draft of the requested report, Caudillo Salazar. I hope it meets your expectations.

ABSTRACT:

This report examines the legal definition and uses of the proposed veto powers being suggested as part of the Iberian Council's repertoire of powers. Conceived as an answer to the Union's diverse makeup and complex systems, it has been observed that mechanisms may be required to prevent the institutionalisation of attitudes or power blocs that would negatively impact the proper administration of the nation. This report takes a special focus on the range of factors that would affect the uses of such a veto, assessing their precedence.

This report finds that the currently proposed veto implementation would, at worst, lead to a legally vague criteria but would have manageable practical risks. The ability to frustrate or prevent national policy would be expedited, with small groups of Councilmen being able to frustrate legislation so long as their concerns can be phrased to be parochial at best. The continuance of proper governance would rely upon the proper conduct of the Council; any diversion or bad actor could conceivably grind the nation to a halt. However, with proper Caudillo oversight and careful screening of Council members, such a concern could be mitigated.

The proposed veto would draw attention to the disparities within Iberia itself due to their almost certain use as justifications, from intra-nation development levels to the fundamental gap between Spain and Portugal. It is also noted however that this is not inherently a long term negative, and that such a veto may be a tool for bridging such a gap if utilised properly given its ability to ensure development and investment is more adequately directed. Over time, the disparity fears should matter less and less.
strings.IBR_council_creation.15.a: Stability benefits Portugal more than grovelled pittances. Remove the veto.
strings.IBR_reformist_tt_7: Rooting out vetoes will allow reformism to grow.
strings.IBR_council_creation.15.b: An institutional money trough would damn Portugal to paupery. Keep the veto.
strings.IBR_council_creation.16.d:
Uncle Cardona. Good god, Uncle Cardona was a socialist.

The room, already tiny, seemed to encroach upon Daniel. The small stool upon which he sat felt more precarious as he looked around, for what he wasn't too sure. The Bible upon which he had sworn his absolute loyalty to Iberia and her Caudillos still rested upon the table. The window to his side was covered by a thin white curtain, distilling any of the sun's comforts into cold plain light. The door was locked and he remained, in this tiny box, above the streets of Madrid. Applying for a staffer job with the new Council hadn't seemed so... imposing when he submitted the paperwork.

His father had served, with the proper side of course. He'd been a sergeant, he had even been wounded in the taking of Bilbao. All his brothers had fought, some had even died, on the right side. His mother had been a nurse, but her only brother, practically estranged so he had been told, had been one of the terrorists of Barcelona. Perhaps they wouldn't notice? It was his mother's family after all.

Despite his attempts to ease himself, he felt himself nearly collapse onto the table. No, of course they would know. They always did. It's the one thing they actually seemed to keep a good record of, the black marks against your name. He cradled his head in his hands as a thought came to him. What if they would suspect him of sharing those beliefs? Sure, he had nothing but earnest study and positive political engagements in his record - was that too clean? Fuck!

The door clacked open, an officer walking in. Shit! Shit shit shit!

“You are free to leave. We are sorry but your application will not progress further. Thank you for your ti-.” Daniel couldn't flee fast enough, storming down the corridor before the officer could even finish.
strings.IBR_council_creation.16.a: “What was that all about?” the officer muttered, watching the kid practically run to the reception.
strings.IBR_council_creation.17.d:
It felt like being in the jungle, reminding Franco of his boyhood images of adventurers braving the secrets of the Amazon or the uncharted darkness of Africa. How delightful that the modern day offered him the same experience just a short drive away from his hotel. After all, the Estufa Fria greenhouses were a fantastic place for a Caudillo meeting. No more deserted houses and their... housekeepers. He shuddered. No, no more of that. City meetings, actual security. A deserted rainforest, all to themselves. He and his Caudillo colleague could walk and talk as much as they desired, with no Santa Compañas to disturb them.

They had stopped for a break from their official conversations, Salazar taking a particular interest in a water feature, as Franco decided to broach the most pertinent question on his mind. A thought had lingered ever since his meeting with Señor Fernández-Miranda. A frustrating man, certainly, but the legalese had put an uncomfortable thought in his mind.

“Señor Salazar. I recognise that you have more of an eye for detail than I,” the admittance churned at him, but he couldn't deny it also, “so I have to ask: are you satisfied with the Council's progress?”

His mind was full of that morning in Cambados, the feeling of a slipping nation. Salazar barely took his eyes from the water, his eyes full of algae rather than the moment. “It is proceeding as desired” he simply replied. “I would not have embarked on this project without ensuring it was being pursued properly.”

“And what if we make a mistake?” Franco breathed, scarcely believing he put a voice to the thought. Salazar turned his head at this, incense brimming at the corners of his mouth before he settled, like a machine cut from its power. His brow furrowed, a movement the old general had seen often. Pride was meeting rationale. Franco watched as his colleague nodded and turned to the water again.
strings.IBR_council_creation.17.a: “I understand, Francisco. For Portugal, I would do anything. Even destroying that which I make.”
strings.IBR_council_creation.18.d:
The halls of the Palacio de las Cortes were heaving with men from across the Union, the Madrid palace filled with the most respected men in both Portugal and Spain. With little time for pleasantries they were walking, almost marching, to their prepared hall. Some looked around nervously. Others looked forward with quiet confidence. All never ceased moving forward, for within that hall Iberia waited. Their dawn approached.

They took their seats, raised in a semicircle around a central dias. No formal seating plan was arranged, but blocks could easily be seen, the lines in Iberian society visible simply with a gap between chairs. The air was warm, the golden walls and oak furnishings glowing in the light. All seemed clinical, as if freshly opened. Prepared. Sterile.

As they were seated, soldiers walked in. Not with rifles, though their sidearms did not go unnoticed, but with their Caudillos. All Councilmen stood and applauded, a universal action. The two Caudillos took their place upon the central dias, looking up at the seats that raised above them. They looked certain, authoritative even.

Caudillo Salazar spoke first, with the aid of a delivered microphone to the relief of the Estado Novo present. He spoke of how the nation was their child, that they must now care for it as one. That both he and Caudillo Franco were placing their faith in them to aid their efforts, to create a durable and effective legal framework for the nation. He never smiled, but his expression was proud. All applauded him.

Caudillo Franco spoke quickly and bluntly. “Germany and the Pakt are at our border, unstable and dangerous. Address that first.”

The Caudillo and their men shuffled out of the room, leaving it for a moment in silence as reality dawned upon all of them.
strings.IBR_council_creation.18.a: The soldiers were gone. The Caudillos were gone. The dawn was here; they were alone.
strings.IBR_council_creation.20.d:
Outside the Palacio de las Cortes there was not much security. To an observer nothing really seemed out of the ordinary.

Regular people were not concerned with the gathering, going about their business in the area as usual. Journalists were the vast majority of outsiders present at the first meeting of the Iberian Council. They took notes, snapping photos and whispering among themselves, as the Caudillos and the sixteen members of the Iberian Council arrived.

The assembled journalists were not surprised to see the councilors going to a conference room instead of the Cortes chamber. They sat down in the audience sections and observed the stripped-down opening of the Advisory Council, their pens slipping over paper as they tried to figure out if anything substantive would be announced.

No announcements of the duties of the Iberian Council were made—the councilors already knew, and the journalists could surmise it. This first meeting was a clearly symbolic welcome; it amounted to a speech by each Caudillo and Council Member.

One journalist emerged from the Council meeting, putting away his pen and paper, and complained that he had sat through eighteen mostly symbolic speeches and nearly inflamed his wrist for nothing.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_tt: As the name suggests, the Advisory Council will offer proposals to the Caudillos, who will always have the final choice in the matter.
strings.IBR_council_creation.21.d:
The first official, substantive meeting of the Iberian Council took place in the Palacio de las Cortes, in a stateroom relatively far from prying eyes and ears. Chaired by Franco and Salazar, the meeting had as its minutes the two most important subjects confronting the government.

Firstly was foreign affairs—the situation in Germany. The vast majority of the councilors were dismissive; to them, the Germans had proven once again their total inability to plan beyond the extreme short term and were thus no threat. This opinion carried the day, though a few insisted that even if the Germans were incapable of planning, they were at least capable of making moves that could do Iberia grievous harm. The Caudillos mentally filed away both opinions, took a few notes, then moved on to the next topic.

On the matter of the ongoing Iberian economic malaise, there was far less concord. Even the fact that the sixteen members of the Iberian Council had been appointed by the Caudillos and were loyal to their rule was not enough to bring about a lack of disagreement.

The debate, though not especially heated, became characterized by long-winded disquisitions and even a few personal insults. To Salazar's irritated mind it seemed there were approximately three opinions for every two councilors, with each councilor unwilling to listen to the others' proposals except insofar as they were facsimiles of one another.

Gaveling the meeting to order, Franco thanked God these people could not legislate and were only around to advise him. Meanwhile Salazar was repressing a pernicious thought that kept repeating itself in his mind against his will: if squabbling was to be the fate of an Iberian Council regardless, legislative functions might not have done any harm.
strings.IBR_council_creation.22.d:
Two Iberian council members sat in the Sobrino de Botín, somewhat exhausted as they waited for their dinner. Another meeting had passed by. This meant another eight or nine hours of marathon discussions. It also meant spending an entire day watching people squabbling over matters of at best varying importance (or, though neither would admit to it in public, participating in the squabbling themselves).

One man broke the silence. “Goodness, it seems that the, uh, Caudillos' plan to stack the Council with people loyal to them is less to their satisfaction than was intended. We're all loyal to them and to the government, it seems. But despite that we can't seem to agree on things that the Caudillos clearly want us to agree on.”

The other man chuckled. “Well, it's par for the course. They all protest loyalty to the government, but just like us they're also kind of in it for themselves. We all know that the Caudillos are growing old; for that reason, the average councilor suspects, the two of them need our advice specifically. So each member insists on stating his point of view in hopes of it being implemented.”

His interlocutor thought about it. “But then what hope does any of us really have of having our proposals implemented if the council is strictly advisory? And what chance is there that the Caudillos will tolerate this sort of conflict for much longer?”

“None, really. But the forum to express one's views is useful. More importantly, we get to console ourselves with good food from this place after another one of these meetings.”

“That at least is true.” The two had splurged to console themselves, and now a cochinillo asado and a sopa de ajo came out for them to eat with a bottle of fine red wine. Raising their glasses, the two men chuckled and toasted:
strings.IBR_council_creation.23.d:
A consul from an OFN nation in Spain sat opposite his superior, the ambassador, peppering him with questions. “So that fundamental law, or whatever they call it instead of a constitution, has been put in the government gazette?”

The ambassador chuckled at the bit about 'instead of a constitution', replying, “Well, see here, you have to remember that they adopted their, uh, Fundamental Law system due to a resolute opposition to 'destabilizing forces of liberalism' and seeing a constitution as being 'part of a liberal system'.” Putting his cup down, he smirked. “Don't tell them that what they've got is de facto a constitution despite their protestations.”

The consul snickered himself, then got back to business. “There won't be any song and dance about this thing, will there? It's in the government gazette, now, and then, and then—” Snapping his fingers, he tried to remember what was next in the usual process.

“—and then the newspapers will publish the law the next day. Nothing too special, really. Business as usual. As to the members of the Iberian Council, they can certainly be reached out to. As you no doubt know, however, the utility of doing so is at best dubious.”

The consul nodded. “That it is.” Then someone's stomach rumbled.
strings.IBR_council_creation.23.a: “What do you say to a bowl of sopa de ajo?”
strings.IBR_council_creation.24.d:
“Request for guidance: vetting of Iberian Council members

1. In general, all sixteen of the members of the Iberian Council are of sound background, a suitable upbringing, sufficiently literate, and of the correct alignment with respect to the government (loyal). The worst to be expected from some of them would be an excess of ambition, but nothing especially treasonous. That being said,

2. Certain of the members of the council have exhibited certain irregular behaviors in the past that would provide significant ammunition to anti-regime and anti-state forces purporting to oppose corruption.

3. Query: should any records indicative of these matters be destroyed? If not, what specific actions ought to be taken? We are currently contemplating storing them in confidential records accessible solely to the Caudillos.”

“Response to request for guidance on Iberian Council members.

1. Destruction would be counterproductive, but we are in agreement that any untoward records should be kept far away from the eyes of the public.

2. The storage option you recommended is sufficient. Delivery to our offices will constitute a successful execution of your duties.

FRANCO”
strings.IBR_council_creation.25.d:
Papers rustled as the secretaries of the Iberian Council handed out a new document that none of the councilors had seen before. Salazar and Franco fixed the members of the Iberian Council with a gimlet eye, before Salazar nodded to Franco to speak.

“Gentlemen. There are too many people in this Council—I will decline to name names—who do not understand why they have been appointed to this important position. Such people misguidedly think that the Iberian Council is some sort of vehicle for career advancement, and go around coming up with what they call 'independent proposals' in defiance of our will and the needs of the government.”

Salazar took up the rhetoric. “This cannot be permitted to continue. From now on, at all further meetings of the council councilors will be provided with a document that outlines the goals that the meeting is intended to accomplish. There will be no debate in this chamber regarding what goals to pursue—only how they are to be pursued.”

No one really dared to debate it. Those that Franco had been referring to bristled, realizing that Franco and Salazar had stymied them from further exploiting their positions. Others, the most loyal or most conflict-averse, resisted the urge to let their relief show on their faces.

Regardless of their views, as one they looked at the paper for the first of many times, and set about adhering to its directives.
strings.IBR_council_creation.26.d:
Torcuato Fernández-Miranda looked at the latest propaganda piece in the newspaper and coloured himself unimpressed. Obviously he didn't dare speak too loudly in opposition, but he was sympathetic to the complaints about the sycophantic nature of the Iberian Council.

This propaganda piece wasn't doing wonders to win people over either, Torcuato observed. All it really said was that “we the Caudillos appointed the Iberian Council to advise us” and “the Iberian Council was appointed to advise us the Caudillos”; it went around in circles. If someone within the government like him felt like falling asleep reading this, how would an ordinary person feel?

He suspected this was Franco and Salazar's goal all along, to simply dull people's senses so that they could move along with governing the country. If that was the intention, Torcuato mused, it was working effectively enough.

Putting the paper in a trashcan, Torcuato went back to work. He had better things to do than put his neck on the line to fight the Iberian government.
strings.IBR_council_creation.27.d:
Franco and Salazar sat alone in the council room after the Iberian Council had adjourned for the day. There was a question at the back of both their minds that came to mind after observing the sixteen men they had chosen during the meeting.

“See here, Franco. You know very well there's a problem here.”

“What's that?”

“You and I are not long for this world.” Franco winced but did not dare deny it. “Moreover, many of those we selected are not long for this world. Then there are a few that might quit. We haven't really talked through what we're going to do if one of these councilors snuffs it.”

Franco stopped what he was doing. Damnations, Salazar was right.

“That's true, we haven't talked about it at all. Something needs to be done, or else the Iberian Council will just die off after people leave or die out. Besides, we have all these people we thought about appointing before coming up with the final roster, do we not? We can just put those to use.”

Salazar nodded in agreement. “Very well, then—we'll assemble a shortlist of replacements for each current and future member of the Iberian Council, and name someone from that list as appropriate. Agreed?”

Franco nodded.
strings.IBR_influence_tt_1: Strongly controlling the Council will decrease its influence.
strings.IBR_council_creation.28.d:
Minutes of Meeting of the Cabinet of the Government of Iberia

[?global.date.GetDateStringNoHourLong]

Present: Members of Cabinet, Caudillos, ...“The establishment of the Iberian Council, as envisioned by the recent Fundamental Law as printed in the state gazettes, is now complete. This will render governmental decision-making more effective by providing the Caudillos and the Government with advice on future projects and decisions. The Council is composed of sixteen members specially selected by the Caudillos for meritorious qualities and suitable relations to the state or the Church.

In the interests of the effective functioning of the government, it will now be expected that all future projects or subjects brought up within the Cabinet should be brought to the attention of the Council if the Caudillos rule it to be of sufficient importance to merit their advice. Though the Council's role is strictly advisory, that advice should be treated as extremely valuable and merits strong consideration.”

By a verbal vote, a measure to forward a list of suitably important current projects and pertinent data to the Council for its reference was passed.

Further business was...
strings.IBR_pre_election.1.d:
The new President of the Government, Fernando Herrero Tejedor, gathered the cabinet following the passage of the Law of Political Reform. Before the ministers could sit, Tejedor walked around the table congratulating all of them individually, saying that it was through their bravery, diplomatic, and legislative skills that Iberia had been sent forward on the path of political reform.

“Men, we've overcome staunch opposition to reform, opposition in high places that stood opposed to the idea of reform, a group that preferred stagnancy to progress. However, we must keep going, as progress will stay slow until that opposition has been left in the books of history.”

The cabinet, still unsure of the new protocols and a majority knowing exactly who he was talking about, gave a light applause sprinkled with uncomprehending looks. Tejedor waited for the applause to die down before continuing.

“Everyone's goals here today should be to reform their own ministries, to rake through and pluck out any remaining reactionaries who linger in their posts and replace them with competent, forward-thinking men.” He glanced quickly around the table before spotting the two men he'd highlighted.

“Ministers Manuel Fraga and Miller Guerra, your reports from the Interior and Work, respectively, should be coming in soon. I expect a clear house. As for the rest of you, a new morning is dawning in Iberia. With our hard work, victory will come.”

This order seemingly garnered a more emphatic applause even as Fraga and Guerra glanced at each other. Chuckling at Tejedor's speech, Fraga mockingly repeats:
strings.IBR_pre_election.1.a: “The morning has come, victory is near.”
strings.IBR_pre_election.2.d:
Minister of Work João Miller Guerra sat at home perusing a long list of bureaucrats in need of being purged. Many of them consisted of elderly, corporatist relics of the Caudillo's pet projects, a patchwork of incompetent loyalists and hard-core reactionaries. Across from him sat Torcuato Fernández-Miranda, a high-ranking official at the Ministry of Education, a man he needed to tap into his network for talented young Spaniards.

Fernández-Miranda had a catalog of rising stars from graduates to educators to fill the soon-to-be gaps in the Ministry of Work, whereas Guerra listed out replacements for Portuguese officials. The two reformists turned partners went back and forth comparing officials.

“João, I really think one of my guys will do wonders as your deputy, having worked with him for so long I-” The Minister of Work chuckled at Fernández-Miranda, before exploding into all-out laughter.

“Torcuato, for all this work balancing these industries, all this back and forth of Portuguese or Spanish, we never filled a spot with a woman.”

“We've already bargained for all these spots, the only position left open is...”

Guerra nodded before penciling in a name for his deputy, a lady who led several working groups for female leaders, a lady he could depend on as his Deputy Minister of Work.
strings.IBR_pre_election.3.d:
Manuel Fraga, the Minister of the Interior, knew his department was littered with the so-called reactionaries and legacy hires that Tejedor had spoken of; he'd spoken with handfuls throughout the last few days, similarly to the one he was speaking with now. “Well, sir, we do have documentation of your, let's say, personal beliefs.”

Fraga tosses two reports onto his desk near the official. “The first one there holds a number of statements you've made to co-workers about the Law of Political Reform, this sort of insubordination and previous standings lead me to a singular decision.”

The official tried to stutter out a defense before Fraga silenced him. “However, your recent performance has been exemplary, in some cases. I reviewed some of your recent work, and I can see your diligence and flexibility, very worthy of this position.”

The official, now realizing his future lay in the hands of the minister, sat silently watching his movements, knowing that Fraga was installing some of the exact same pressure tactics that he had perfected over the years, using his own tools, which he probably read in the reports, against him.

Eventually, Fraga broke the silence. “I know it's circumventing my orders, but I'm willing to make one of these reports disappear, which one depends on whether or not you swear loyalty to the new government and its reforms. Which will it be?”

The official sat in dead silence for a moment before answering Fraga.
strings.IBR_pre_election.3.b: “I won't bow to a traitor like you, Fraga.”
strings.IBR_pre_election.4.d:
Inside the city walls of Ávila, where the intact stones bore echoes of the crusades and sheltered the first Francoists during the civil war, a retired colonel and his protégé were out on a patrol. Once a proud soldier for Franco's Spain, he now rants to his subordinate, a young officer whose ideals still stand steadfast behind the old order.

Quivering between rage and nostalgia as he speaks of betrayal, he points fingers at the council, the reformers, and the very ideas that he had fought against. The pleas for a return to normalcy dripped with acidic remarks, burning ideology straight into the heart of his protégé, who nodded along dutifully, eyes flashing with thrill and determination.

The colonel leans in, lowering his voice. The army still has good men—men still willing to defend their home as it tore itself apart. But the protégé only nodded. “It must be done soon, Colonel,” the young officer says. In a couple of weeks, his unit would be stationed in Equatorial Guinea, far from the fight.

The colonel stares back, simmering down. He shamefully admits that his days are numbered as well. By next month, he and many other high-ranking officers will be pensioned off, replaced by a circle of officers loyal to the new Spain, if he could even still call it that. The two men stare at each other, realizing what neither had dared to say.

Standing in silence, the colonel looked at the walls of Ávila. Its castle walls had remained intact all these centuries. Ávila's walls stood against Moorish scimitars, against Napoleon's grand artillery, against socialist guns. The world has changed, but the walls have not, and neither has the colonel. “Something must be done,” he whispered.
strings.IBR_pre_election.5.d:
The memorandum was only three sentences long. Pilar Primo de Rivera read it twice. Then three times. A decree, signed and stamped by the Iberian Council. The Sección Femenina de Falange, her life's work, was no more.

She lowered the paper slowly, flickering her eyes to the wall where two portraits hung. Papá stared back in his marshal uniform, his glance unfazed by the news. José Antonio, in his black suit, remained emotionless on the canvas. Pilar tried to match their expressions, but her lips would not stop the tears from flowing down.

No. She refused to let the Falange die with a piece of paper. She would gather her remaining loyalists and take to the streets, reminding Iberia of their guardians against socialism.

But she threw open the door to be met with a hallway that only echoed farewells. Boxes were packed. Papers were shuffled around. Desks were emptied. The flags of the Falange were carelessly littered all over the floor. The walls that once carried a generation, a revolution, now held nothing.

A young member, barely more than a girl who had only joined a week ago, passed by Pilar. Hesitantly, she softly whispered:

“Thank you, Pilar.”

The hollow hallway could only reverberate those three words now, each repetition reminding her of the lackluster legacy she left behind compared to the giants she idolized. The world that had once needed her was no more.
strings.IBR_pre_election.5.a: And so the arrows stopped flying for Spain.
strings.IBR_pre_election.6.d:
Manuel Fraga was a man interested in power, its accumulation, and its uses. He had signed his name to death warrants, mass arrest orders, and snappy tourist slogans. The deployment of his power in advocacy for gentle, gradual liberalization had borne the richest of fruits. In the whispering small hours of the morning, his pen worked. He was playing the part of architect in the construction of Iberia's new democratic order.

The freshly christened Political Party Registry had taken in applications for official recognition by innumerable organizations vying for a place in this structure. Armed with the sterling preparatory briefing provided by the Registry, he had organized the body politic into three color-coded piles.

Blue ink was a mark of irrelevance. These were parties without the obvious profile, sufficient membership, or monetary backing to imprint themselves on the national stage. Necessary still, like krill are in the ocean, to create a legitimate political ecosystem. Black ink in the form of a definitive DENIED stamp marked those who were a threat to that ecosystem. The Esquerra Republicana de Catalunya, a contemptible band of separatists, had this mark applied to them with a certain sense of satisfaction in doing so.

All that remained was everything. Don Manuel was an architect, but he would need his foremen, his bricklayers, and plumbers. Red ink spoke to those who would play such parts in his vision for an organization that would embody the truest, most admirable essence of the old regime. The next morning, phone calls to this list in red would be made to discuss a national coalition.
strings.IBR_pre_election.7.t: What We Can See and Feel
strings.IBR_pre_election.7.d:
Hand-in-hand, Javier and Sonia were the picture-perfect Zaragozan couple. They had awaited Friday night eagerly, hoping for a new and novel experience. With the relaxation of the censorship laws, there were new books on shelves and new films in the cinema. They walked until they reached the front of the marquee, until they realized they were so enamored with the idea of a new movie that they hadn't decided on which one to watch.

“Something with romance,” Sonia stated. “The censors were so afraid of scandalizing the children that they cut away from any kiss with tongue.”

“Perhaps they didn't want the reminder of what they never had. How about this one: Tristana? The director Buñuel had to flee after the Civil War.”

“Imagine Franco allowing anyone like that to make art. Ooh, so blasphemous!” Sonia hugged her boyfriend as he laid the money on the counter.

Two hours later, a stunned couple left the cinema, holding hands and breathless. The two had one thought. “I didn't think a movie could do that,” they said, almost in unison.

“My God...” Sonia trailed off, half talking to Javier and half to the sky. “That ending, with the window.” She dabbed her eyes; both had just finished crying.

“Her leg... I didn't think they could show pain like that on the screen. It was like I could feel it.”

“I almost feel exhausted. I feel like my brain has been everywhere. Buñuel is a genius, how could he have ever found all of that and made us feel it?”
strings.IBR_pre_election.7.a: We need to come back next week... once we've recovered.
strings.IBR_pre_election.8.d:
The government hall where the conference was scheduled that day could have been a mirror image to half a dozen in the past year alone: same gaudy government placards, same sterile air of mundanity, same gray-haired party officials echoing what otherwise might be the same kind scripted rhetoric that the press outlets had heard a dozen times over. This is precisely what made this familiar imagery contrast with the gravity of the momentous announcement that followed.

In accordance with the recent efforts between the government and the Iberian Council to liberal reform, government officials announced to the gathered representatives of the press their intention to cooperate with opposition parties within the Iberian Union. While the officials maintain that this initiative is principally in the name of civic cooperation and inter-party dialogue, rumors abound as to the implications of their civil loyalties behind closed doors.

This comes as an institutional coup in light of decades of consolidated rule in Iberia and posits that a true drive for democratization may be in the country's future. What this implies for the continued rule of the Caudillos' or their respective parties is anyone's guess, yet the announcement has been otherwise welcomed with reserved optimism by the press. If this truly is the beginning of proper reparliamentarization of Iberia's constituent halves, perhaps this can be considered a hopeful starting point.
strings.IBR_pre_election.9.d:
Fernando Herrero Tejedor turned towards the camera. The red light blinked alive, staring him down as he drew steady breaths. The Iberian elections were to be held in six months. It was the first chance the Iberian man would be able to use their voice to bring about change. But the President's voice would be the first one to carry the weight of the nation on this very day.

Tejedor turned the script to the next page, glancing at the bureaucratic prose that felt polished, yet stiff with fear. Duty. Responsibility. Democracy. All words that were harmless on their own, but presented to a crowd that would, without a doubt, be skeptical of these new systems. He could only hope that the sincerity of his tone would carry him through the broadcast.

As he reached his final paragraph, he grew slower in speech, enunciating every word with a tangible weight. “The future now belongs to Iberia's people. The world has turned; it remains that Iberia must as well.”

The technician turned the camera off as the broadcast blinked into darkness. The studio broke into a rapturous applause for the sweating man, his aides rushing in to congratulate him on his speech. The moment didn't just mark a pinnacle of his career, but perhaps of his life dedicated to Iberia's renewal.

Yes, his government would fracture as they vied for power in the upcoming election, but there was nothing worth keeping if it would obstruct the people's will. The next six months would not be about consolidating party power, but aiding Iberia through these transitional times.

And so Iberia turned. To a new chapter. To democracy. To the people.
strings.IBR_pre_election.10.d:
Joaquín Sabina stepped down from the train platform, small sack in hand and weathered guitar in the other. His father, Jerónimo, waited on the porch in police uniform. It looked like it hadn't been cleaned in days. The two men stared at each other.

“You've grown thinner, Joaquín,” Jerónimo said finally. “Have your studies been going well?”

“I wish,” Joaquín replied, approaching his father. “Father, if I had come back a week earlier... would you have arrested me?”

Jerónimo's eyes stared coldly into his son's face. Dark circles had formed under the old man's eyes. “We'll both never know.”

Inside the house, the air smelled faintly of olive oil. Same house. Same walls. But the distance had grown. Jerónimo nodded towards the guitar. “Have you been practicing?”

Joaquín hesitated. His father had given it to him as a graduation gift, and despite having to attend to party duties, he still found time to practice the instrument. He strummed lightly:

I used to wonder, wonder father,
If you could ever see me past my dishonors.
My home was lost to a man called the Warden,
And so I return here as his orphan.
strings.IBR_pre_election.10.a: There is not even nostalgia worse than to miss the one that never was.
strings.IBR_pre_election.11.d:
“¡Salario o conflicto!”

The chants erupted from Valencia's Mercado Central. Isabella Méndez's voice grew hoarse, but she shouted anyway. Banners flapped, feet tramped, and old union songs, those that had disappeared under Franco and Salazar's reign, emerged among the crowds. For the first time in years, the city began to breathe once again.

Vendors watched from their stalls. A man atop a crate shouted “Ay Carmela!” down the market streets. Now was not a time to dwell on memories of tear gas, but on the revolutionary spirit that reconquered the city.

Then came the boots. A line of policemen emerged from a nearby street in rigid formation, their tricornios shielding their eyes. The market froze.

For a moment, Isabella's mind clouded with static. Her cheeks reminded her of the taste of blood, her wrists of the chill of handcuffs.

But no orders came. The officers fanned out, standing guard at the market's stone arches, guns pointed down. Minutes passed. The deadlock wasn't broken with bullets, but with a young boy, singing the only words that his father had taught him:

“Solidaridad pa' siempre!”

Laughter rippled through the air, and the chorus reignited the crowd. Isabella looked at one of the officers. “Cute hat!” she shouted, grinning.

The officer looked up and cracked a smile. For just a moment, she could see the humanity in his eyes.
strings.IBR_pre_election.12.d:
Hundreds of student protestors surrounded the University of Murcia's steps, rallying around with makeshift banners and a rejuvenating energy that the city hadn't quite felt since the formation of the Iberian Union. Enrique Tierno Galván, helped by some students, took to the makeshift stage.

The 'Old Professor' looked to the young faces, full of a vigor that he had not seen since the Civil War. A crowd of students that could have been his own pupils had he not been suspended from the university years before for his criticisms against the Caudillos.

But he did not begin with bitterness. He began with gratitude. Gratitude towards the students for their willingness to fight. Gratitude towards the government for their unwillingness to silence him. But the warmth ended there. “That,” he said, “is all the gratitude we will be giving today.”

Galván cocked his head to the right. “For a government molded by tyranny has no place in a democratic state. For their unwillingness to suppress my speech does not forgive them for their previous willingness to suppress millions more. For the capricious laws that bind Iberia today were not created under the guise of liberty, but under the illegitimate guise of despotism.”

Galván gestured his arms, sweeping across the campus, pointing at the mass of students. “A new democratic state calls for a new generation of men and women. A new compendium of laws stripped of its totalitarian precedent. A new start for a birthing democratic tradition. A nation that would never allow the thought of stifling a humanist socialism to ever cross their mind.”

A moment of silence followed. Charged. Breathless. But with an anticipation, followed by an eruption of applause. The claps were not monotonous nor apathetic. They were not for a Caudillo.
strings.IBR_pre_election.13.d:
“A disgrace is what this is! A disgrace to our great nation! Do you understand what you've done? You must renege on this policy promptly!”

Adriano Moreira, Secretary of State for Colonial Policy, slowly put his pen down. Caudillo Marcelo Caetano, flanked by two aged generals, whom Adriano was surprised could still move, had burst into his office uninvited just a few seconds ago, despite a small horde of aides trying vainly to stop them.

“You are young and inexperienced and do not see it yet, but your actions will cause the Africans to band together against us. Do you not understand? You're creating bonds between them and allowing them to cooperate and learn from us. Next thing you know, they'll demand independence, and Portugal will be ruined! Ruined! The Military High Command will not stand for this. They have joined me here to protest your rash decision.”

Adriano ignored the Caudillo's finger-waving and the two elderly generals' mindless nodding. “Iberia. Not Portugal.” Caetano's eyes widened as he started mumbling incoherently, only to be once more interrupted.

“I respect you, gentlemen, for everything you have done and continue to do for our great nation. It appears, however, that I must remind your two companions that they have honourably retired and now live on a generous state pension. Of course, your experience is endless thanks to your venerable age, and I'll make sure to consider your opinions, just as I value the equally expert opinions of the current High Command and Colonial administrators such as General Spínola. Now, if you'll excuse me...” Adriano put his vest on as he got up and began walking towards the door. “I have a meeting with some gentlemen who have flown over an entire continent to talk to me.”
strings.IBR_pre_election.13.a: The old always opposes the new.
strings.IBR_pre_election.13.b: Fresh-faced soldiers showed them the door.
strings.IBR_pre_election.14.d:
The ballroom of the Zaragozan officer academy shimmered with marble and brass chandeliers. Its orchestra wrestled a waltz from the music sheet, playing each note with an unmatched discipline. The rigid melody bounced linearly off the polished walls, forcing awkward moves from the officers and their partners.

But here and there, life would breathe itself onto the dance floor. A young trumpeter slipped in a flourish where none belonged. The emboldened violinist introduced a little bit of vibrato in the otherwise mundane piece of work. The dancers followed, moving more freely, with laughter breaking the sterile atmosphere that the generals had organized.

By the refreshment table, two lieutenants paused to catch their breath. “You been studying for the promotion exam?” One said, before sipping his sangria. “This batch is apparently different. More thinking involved rather than just memorizing drill manuals. You can probably score yourself a promotion, huh?”

“That won't be necessary.” The other gave a sly smirk. “I've been offered a position in the new Defense Ministry. They need someone capable of more than just shining boots.”

“You're kidding?” The officer blinked before playfully nudging his peer. “Shit, with you out of the competition, that promotion's as good as mine!”

Both raised their glasses to give a toast, just as the orchestra reached its refrain. Still rigid, still formal, but the room changed. As the two men returned to their partners on the dance floor, the music no longer sounded lifeless. The old tune simply waited for the new generation to give it meaning again.
strings.IBR_pre_election.14.a: Last call for the Old Guard.
strings.IBR_pre_election.15.d:
The smell of oil and brass lingered in the air, though mingled in a communion of laughter and song. A red banner hung over an assembly line: “Trabalhar livrementes.” To work freely. To work a 40-hour week. To sell the watches they toiled laboriously for. For once, the factory ceased to be a prison.

João passed a bottle of wine he'd looted from the managerial office to his newfound friends, once cogs in the dystopian machine. “Today, we stop building watches for Iberia,” João said, lifting his drink. “And we start keeping the time to ourselves!”

But then the engines came, drowning the songs of the workers. Shouts could be heard outside. Then came one bang. Two bangs. The door exploded inwards. Tear gas rolled across the floor. The clouds choked anyone who didn't have the luxury of a gas mask.

Gunstocks cracked bone. Batons fell onto broken backs. The red banner was torn and trampled. João reached for it. A gunshot split the air.

And that shot was enough. Before long, blood intermingled with the spilled wine on the factory floors. Anyone who dared scream had their lungs burned and seared by the gas.

When the gunfire stopped, only the watches could be heard, faintly ticking on the assembly lines, keeping time for no one.
strings.IBR_pre_election.15.a: The clock struck six, and a new day began.
strings.IBR_pre_election.16.d:
The interrogation room was a small room, but even in it, Fraga could not have felt further from the AAS captain. His uniform still faintly smelled of tear gas with a small waft of metal. Thirty-eight dead. Dozens more hurt. But the captain felt unfazed by the photographs on the table of bloodied corpses.

Fraga closed the door, setting his palms on the table, nearly throwing up when he saw the pictures. He'd looked at them a hundred times before, but even now, he hadn't gotten used to it. Fraga eventually regained control of his gag reflex. “Explain,” he said, in a low, deep voice.

“Explain what?” The officer spat on the photos, sneering. “Explain why there's a communist cell in our factory? Explain why we're saving this country?” He shrugged, leaning back into his chair. “I pulled that trigger. I'd pull it again for this country.”

Fraga's jaw clenched. “There will be no amnesty for those who use violence, while I am Minister, Captain,” he said, emphasizing each word. “You were out of line.”

The officer laughed. “And how long will that be? The elections will sweep you aside for the socialists. That is, if the communists don't shoot you first.”

For a long moment, neither man spoke. For just a moment, Fraga's face briefly paled. He left the room without another word—it was impossible to reconcile with a monster. None of the other ministers even batted an eye at the news when they first heard of it. Iberia was being drained of its morality, and Fraga could only do so much about it.
strings.IBR_pre_election.16.a: Fire the man in there and hush this up.
strings.IBR_pre_election.16.b: Clear out his full unit for launching the unauthorized raid, even if it makes Fraga look weak.
strings.IBR_pre_election.17.d:
João muttered under his breath, watching another man dressed in the same work clothes as him waltz over holding a suitcase. His outfit was neatly ironed with everything straightened and lined up exactly without a single smudge or stain. The man tried to begin a light conversation, but João knew everyone on shift, and this man didn't belong. “Might as well come in a suit, obviously don't train you well wherever you come from.”

The agent doesn't acknowledge João's comment as he opens a briefcase stuffed with pesetas. “All I'm asking is for you to make sure your local votes against joining the CCOO; you don't want to be associated with their communist band of unions.”

“So what, you want me to turn on my brothers?”

The man shakes his head, pushing the briefcase into João's arms. “We can get much more done without the CCOO being involved. You won't be dealing with a national union, only with your boss.”

“Maybe if we got better working hours and actual pay, there wouldn't be a need to join the CCOO, so unless you can offer something different, I can't promise you anything.”
strings.IBR_pre_election.17.a: We'll get everything straight with the factory owners.
strings.IBR_pre_election.17.b: Here's one more briefcase. Call it 'hardship pay'.
strings.IBR_pre_election.18.d:
Music blasted from the streets of Lisbon as a march led by the Movement of Revolutionary Homosexuals danced their way up the Av. da Liberdade, shouting, cheering, and making the protest seem more like a parade for onlookers. Several members of the march were kissing, hugging, dancing with one another, making themselves seen and heard, showing that they were like any other citizen of Lisbon.

As the march descended on Marquis de Pombal Square, a separate protest arrived on the opposing side. Led by Lisbon sex workers, they demanded an end to the era of pimps and so-called “Puritan Pressures” from the government, and its depredations of Salazar-Era politicians in the Ballet Rose scandal. A scandal in which several Salazar figures were uncovered running a ring of prostitution, abuse, and pedophilia of minors.

Sex workers raised signs and placards, ranging from offering half price to politicians that support legalization, to pictures of whips and other profane items. The two marches continued to approach, citizens watched in awe from their balconies while other scandalized citizens scurried away. Meanwhile, several streetside officers watched, taking notes about the protests and who may be involved.

Eventually, the two groups pass by in the center of the Marquis de Pombal Square and give out cheers and blow kisses to one another. For a moment, solidarity flickers between the two groups, not just as movements, but between a history of repression and dreams of liberation. Members of both marches jumped between, dancing with one another. Men and women recognized one another as friends and neighbors, both groups once seen as depravities, began to march in unison. Shouts of the two groups rang out.
strings.IBR_pre_election.19.d:
Several of Iberia's most prominent socialist politicians and intellectuals gathered in the dimly lit University of Valladolid's auditorium, a congress that, after several painstaking attempts, was finally approved by government officials as an open discussion on socialist theory and doctrine. At the podium stood yet another student, in the same attire as all the previous speakers and droning on about the same arguments on theory, that of “following Marx,” and “institutionalizing the socialist dream,” coupled with some “world revolution.”

Mário Soares, tired of this constant jargon, rose. He himself was a long-time leftist dissident, a co-founder of the Portuguese Socialist Action. His voice echoed in the grand hall. “Although several of you among me here may know more about the ins and outs of theory, of the exact ways to reach a utopia or how to interpret writings, I would like to show some actual evidence on how to achieve this dream.”

Soares continued, “The government blacklisted me for decades, but that didn't stop me. I went and got a law degree, I helped our common man, our fellow workers. Ten times I've been arrested, ten times I tell you. They even kicked me out of my country for it. Yet even under the government's warped laws and iron fist, I fought back, besting Caetano's crooked regime time and time again.”

Soares had captivated the room; every attendee had their eyes on him. “We sit here and bicker theory and doctrine among ourselves, even though our time is coming to unite. They're giving us the opportunity to kick Caetano and Salazar's heirs in the gut, so why don't we seize it? What matters now is not books or writings, but the common worker.”

The entire auditorium, besides those very same speakers he lambasted, erupted into applause and cheers as Soares sat back down. He singlehandedly refocused the gathering on one cause.
strings.IBR_pre_election.20.d:
Bishop António Ferreira Gomes could only think of his past as the plane sat on the tarmac at Pedras Rubras Airport in Porto. All the bishop could think of was his last flight here from Rome, not being able to land in his homeland, all because of a single letter.

Bishop Gomes had lived in Brazil for nearly a decade after his letter to Salazar, a letter's contents that influenced his exile. A former supporter of Salazar, he had only wished they would move to a fairer system of bringing back democracy, as in his opinion, Salazar's anti-communist actions were only letting them grow and fester underground.

During his time in Brazil, he was still visited by friends, family, and his former congregants from Porto. He kept praying and requesting from the day he was exiled to let him back into the country, something they wouldn't even do to let him see his mother's funeral.

However, for Gomes, his prayers were finally answered. As the plane finally docked, he stepped out and quickly fell to his knees. “My Lord, thank you for your guidance and granting your enduring strength to get me home.” The Bishop repeatedly kissed the ground in praise as the crowd cheered for him.

He clutched his cross and continued to pray and thank God for his work.
strings.IBR_pre_election.20.a: As he had witnessed a miracle in Iberia.
strings.IBR_pre_election.21.d:
To President Fernando Herrero Tejedor,

The depravity and debauchery your government has involved itself in is a sin that must not stand in Iberia. It is not only the Anti-Communist Apostolic Alliance, but many of our fellow countrymen believe that your people are trying their best to unleash Satan and his devil-worshiping goons across our sacred virgin lands.

Your people want them to pillage and plunder our lands like they have in Russia and elsewhere, leading us out to the pasture like little rodents as the serpents' fangs sit ready to plunge themselves into us. Your attempts to legalize the Communists and Socialists are equivalent to Adam and Eve falling for temptation, biting into that red apple, as you have fallen bait to another of Satan's red tricks.

We and many others will not take this lying down; we will respond with God's might and protect his holy kingdom. Eight of the pesky demons now lay riddled with lead, waiting to be taken back to the hell where they belong. Oh, the looks on their faces. All followers of that Satanic CCOO deserve that same fate. They and their families deserve the pain for breaking God's first and most powerful commandment.

Those eight devil spawn lay mutilated in piles of unholy blood, right in their Satanic-Commie temple they all visit, right in the heart of Holy Barcelona. Bombing the place would've gotten rid of the shrine, but they needed to be made an example for other Communists, all those others that need their insides to be turned out with lead.

Mr. Tejedor, you can still repent. Pray to the Lord to forgive you, and perhaps that will save your soul from burning in Hell like the rest of them after we come for you. No red is safe in the Lord's land. We will make sure of that.
strings.IBR_pre_election.22.d:
The Minister of Foreign Affairs sat in a pompous chair, his eyes gazing upon the newly constructed Itamaraty Palace, home of his Brazilian counterpart. The floor-to-ceiling glass walls surrounded by magnificent white concrete arches, all engulfed in a perfectly manicured pond, the great symbol of the Brazilian foreign ministry, was also a building designed by noted communist, Oscar Niemeyer. It stood not only as an example of the modernist architecture of Brasília, but also mirrored the country's magnificent rise to modernity.

Areilza continued to listen as the uptight Brazilian droned on about Salazar's many contributions not only to Iberia, but to the wider world through the continuation of Lusotropicalist colonialism in Africa.
