Minister Areilza, not listening to a word the diplomat was saying, continued to ponder if Niemeyer would like to come design buildings for a new democratized Iberia. Finally, the Brazilian stopped speaking, gesturing to Areilza if he would like a word; the minister rose.

“I fully agree with what you said, sir. We both owe greatly to Salazar, but we should focus more on each other's futures. Just like here in Brazil, there is great change happening rapidly in Iberia, a change that, just like yours, will unlock greater, more expansive economic opportunities.”

The Brazilian leans in intrigued, wanting to know more. Areilza takes another look out to the pond surrounding Itamaraty, taking in one last look at the beauty of the structure. “If Brazilians are capable of such beauty like this, I believe our friendship will grant wonders to the future.” Returning his gaze. “We also strive to allow Brazilians of all backgrounds and opinions a warm welcome back to Portugal. We wish to follow in the same path as places such as your capital here in Brasília. Rebirth into a new center for the world, designed by great minds and great people.”
strings.IBR_pre_election.23.d:
Areilza couldn't wait to get back home to talk to his fellow ministers about the childish bickering he had to endure between Argentine and Brazilian diplomats, the fact that the Argentine diplomats put up a fuss about being the second leg.

The Argentines finally came to grab Areilza, as they walked him to a perfectly stationed limousine outside the palace. Constant flashes from the Argentine media temporarily blinded the minister as he was helped into the back of the limousine. A special visit had been requested by Areilza to bolster cultural agreement and keep the Argentines satisfied: visiting the house of the famed Argentine writer, Jorge Luis Borges. Entering the estate, the entourage of Iberian and Argentine diplomats was led into Borges' office by his wife, María.

Areilza slowly approached the now blind author, guiding his personal copy of Ficciones into his hands. “It's always an honor meeting the great artists of the Spanish language.”

Borges quickly felt the cover and instinctively knew what the minister wanted, cracking back. “I would revise this to include the story about everything great your Caudillo did, but it seems you've already got the copy!” Borges burst out laughing at his own joke as the room watched Areilza for an appropriate response.

He sat waiting for Borges to finish entertaining himself before handing him his own gift. “A gift for your personal collection. I've heard you had some admiration for the great Sevillian Rafael Cansinos-Asséns. There's a little something inside.”

Borges carefully took the book, feeling the cover engraving, muttering the title. El Eterno Milagro. As he opened it, he traced his fingers over two pieces of paper wedged inside; they read Jorge and María.
strings.IBR_pre_election.24.d:
Areilza slowly stepped out of his plane onto the tarmac below. There was a coldness to this leg of his trip. No red carpet rolled out, no band playing, no blob of foreign dignitaries trying to shake hands. All that the Mexican government laid out for him was black asphalt and a small sedan surrounded by bodyguards he could tell were in Mexican intelligence.

Unlike in South America, his trip didn't include talks with presidents or foreign ministers; all that was scheduled was a singular visit to the Colegio de México, an elite institution founded by Spanish exiles.

When Areilza arrived, a group of high-ranking exiles of the Spanish Republican government stood behind President Maldonado González, a man showing no emotion to Areilza's arrival, only a cold glare. Formerly an elected member from Oviedo, Maldonado González chaired the Republican Government in Exile. An organization propped up by Mexico and recognized as the legitimate Spain as Mexico refuses to recognize Iberia.

Areilza tentatively extended his hand towards the President. Instead of taking his hand, Maldonado González shoved a singular piece of paper into it. “If the Iberian government can uphold the principle of fair and free elections, my government and I are willing to dissolve ourselves and shake hands in Madrid, seeing that our righteous mission is finally accomplished.”

Maldonado González continues, “However, if they are not held freely or fairly, or perhaps overturned, do not expect to return to Mexico.” Areilza lowers his arm and gives thanks to Maldonado González.

As Areilza returned to his escort, his mind lingered on González's promise. These people have waited their whole lives to return to a democratic Iberia. Whether or not that will bear fruit is uncertain, but he does know one thing.
strings.IBR_pre_election.24.a: They all now had their eyes on Madrid.
strings.IBR_pre_election.25.d:
For anyone else, wining and dining would be something to look forward to. For José María de Areilza, it was hard work.

The Iberian Minister of Foreign Affairs had to, at a moment's notice, fly halfway across the world, give statements when his brain was still living six timezones away. He couldn't even remember half of the events he stood for. During his trip to DC, he had made sure to tour the National Mall, standing in front of the Washington Monument as the flashbulbs flickered, a document in front of him ready to be signed.

He had been given relatively simple instructions. No overt movements toward joining the OFN, no security agreements that might result in OFN troops being stationed within Iberian territory. Other than that, he had relatively free reign to advance joint interests in the Americas, far enough away from the Pakt that there would be no diplomatic ramifications. But he had pushed for liberalization - he could not very well complain when he argued for American outreach for decades.

As he wracked his brain, struggling to remember what exactly it was that he came here to sign, he looked out over the Reflecting Pool, and there he saw, perfectly silhouetted, the reflections of the Iberian and American flags. There, in that moment, he knew that whatever it was he was signing, he knew that he was there because Iberia had faith in him, and that the United States had invited him because they wanted to build a bridge with Iberia. And so, with a final smile and another flickering of the flashbulbs, he signed the document to rapturous applause.
strings.IBR_pre_election.25.a: A statement honoring the shared American and Iberian values of democracy and a commitment to friendship across the Atlantic.
strings.IBR_pre_election.25.b: A small trade agreement reducing trade barriers between America and Iberia.
strings.IBR_pre_election.25.c: A pledge for anti-smuggling cooperation in the Caribbean and Africa.
strings.IBR_pre_election.26.d:
Even at home, José María de Areilza could get no rest. He had been in America just long enough for his body to adjust to American time before he was carted off on another plane, back home to Madrid. He had landed early in the morning on Iberian time, and rather than take the day off, he forced down a cup of coffee and got to work. After all, he had an ambassador to meet.

He hated meeting with most Germans. Wolfgang Gerder was by all accounts a pleasant man, but he had always made his displeasure with José evident in his tone. Whenever José had pushed for increasing liberalization and outreach toward the United States, Wolfgang had always let it known with a simple “unfortunate,” a fake smile, and a slight tisk of his tongue.

Wolfgang was seated in the waiting room in the Villamejor Palace as José arrived, ABC, Diário de Notícias, O Século were all folded neatly on the table in front of him, opened to the articles discussing the Iberian trip to the United States. Wolfgang stood crisply and plastered on the smile he was known for. “Herr Areilza, welcome back. I was just reading about your latest accomplishments.”

“Yes, I believe it will be beneficial for Iberia,” José matched the insincere smile with one of his own. “I assume you wish to meet before our official visit to Unter der Linden?”

“Nothing so grandiose,” Wolfgang replied calmly. “But looking at your accomplishments, the Reich and I are eager to see what agreements we will be signing next week.”

If the Minister could make it to next week, it'd be a miracle, and he wouldn't even know what time his body or his brain would be on. But for Iberia, he gave Wolfgang his response.
strings.IBR_pre_election.26.a: “We would love to see Germans taking their holidays on our beaches by increasing tourist visas.”
strings.IBR_pre_election.26.b: “We can actually discuss collaboration on the Pyrenees border today and save ourselves a trip.”
strings.IBR_pre_election.26.c: “It is most unfortunate. We will need to postpone our meeting until after the elections.”
strings.IBR_pre_election.27.d:
He crouched behind the low shrub with a shoddy map trembling in his hands. The camp should be empty. It would be a perfect ambush. He signaled his men forward, shuffling through the rustled leaves.

Peering over the ridge, he froze. Shadows moved. Faces. Black faces. Hesitation clawed at his fingers. Was this the Africa Corps? Men like him, just in White man's clothing?

Crack.

A shot whizzed past him. He looked behind to see his comrade's mangled jaw barely hinged to his face. Blood spattered all over their uniforms. Before anyone could react, another was sent straight through his head. He collapsed.

The lead ducked instinctively, hugging the ground with all his strength. The world was reduced to just the sharp ringing of gunfire and pounding of his heart. Some of his comrades, paralyzed by the scene in front of them, were torn apart by gunfire.

The shots drew closer. Each leaf snapped off the shrub threatened his own position. He dug his body in, pressing his knees and ribs against the Earth's soil, praying that the roots of Africa could take him somewhere safe. He prayed for the Benito River to submerge him. He prayed for the rainforests to hide him. He prayed for his people to remember him. He prayed for them.

Then nothing.
strings.IBR_pre_election.28.d:
The bus hissed to a stop on the outskirts of Évora. A tired man stepped off, hands sodden with motor oil and grease, calluses blistering his fingers, back sore from the twelve-hour shift. The streets were cramped, the smell of bread and diesel wafting through the air.

As he walked, posters clung to the brick walls that hadn't been repaired for ages. Bring Down the Bourgeois State. Bring About Revolution Now. The hammer and sickle stared from every corner, penetrating into the man's soul with a dangerous determination and boldness. He clenched his fists.

But from an open window above, a radio crackled with hope. There was debate. There was laughter. An election was coming up, a chance for change, a promise of progress. He slowed down, listening intently to the voices.

Turning the corner, the streets turned into a collage of red and white. The white stars of communism contrasted with the red rose of socialism. The latter called on the man to vote in the upcoming election. Socialism and Freedom. The People's Reform. Peace, Land, and Bread for All.

The man stopped. Caught between two visions of the same dream, his anger and resentment subsided, replaced by a yearning for a future that wouldn't leave the streets in blood.

He reached up, putting his hesitating fingers on the edge of the communist posters. He would never let his hands bear the hammer and sickle, the tools that had destroyed so many countries before. Slowly, he tore it down. The wind carried a piece of it into a gutter, where it joined the city's trash that a modern world had already left behind.
strings.IBR_pre_election.28.a: A calloused hand prefers the petals.
strings.IBR_pre_election.29.d:
Fernando Herrero Tejedor, President of the Government, stood before the assembled members of the Iberian Council, the golden rays of the setting sun giving the end of his speech a somber tone. “These elections will only be the beginning, gentlemen. We must make sure that the next government, whatever its composition, grants a voice to all Iberians - across regions, classes, and walks of life. Only then could we ensure that our new constitution is a true vehicle for the empowerment of our people and our country. Thank you very much.”

After the applause died down, most councillors began to slowly filter out of the hall. Interior Minister Manuel Fraga, however, made a beeline for Minister of Work Miller Guerra. Finally catching him and his breath, Fraga put a smile on his face and shook Miller Guerra's hand. “Did you enjoy Señor Herrero's speech, Señor Miller? It sounded like something right out of your Democratic Center's rallies! If I didn't know better, I'd have thought you were coordinating your speeches beforehand!”

Miller Guerra shrugged, a small smile on his face, and pulled his hand out of Fraga's too-friendly handshake. “I'm happy that you know better, then. It seems like our message is simply catching on. Now, if you'll excuse me,” he said, as he maneuvered towards a small crowd of his allies in the council to chat with them.

Fraga dropped the smile. The government was backing the so-called Democratic Center over his own People's Alliance, and they'd thought he wouldn't notice. This was going to be an uphill battle, and with all of the obstacles the government was putting in his way, he was going to have to work twice as hard. So that's exactly what he was going to do. He was never going to give Miller and his cronies the satisfaction of giving up.
strings.IBR_pre_election.29.a: Fraga put a smile on his face once again, and went to gladhand another councillor.
strings.IBR_pre_election.30.d:
The afternoon sun beat hard on the small car trudging on the Duero riverside, but despite being drenched in sweat, Torcuato Fernández-Miranda and José Luis Liso were undeterred. Luis Liso aspired to become mayor of the nearby town of Soria, and he and Fernández-Miranda needed to reach out to the people and make sure they'd vote for the Democratic Center coalition.

Turning a bend, the pair came across a group of fishermen, dragging their boat out of the river - an excuse to get out of the car as much as a campaigning opportunity. They had tried talking with dozens of locals that day already, without much success. Most of the rural folk had said they were planning to vote for the People's Alliance, and some had even been hostile. Undeterred, the pair had continued, but they were growing frustrated. Fernández-Miranda began thinking of giving up and calling it a day if this group was going to be as obstinate as the rest of them.

Next to him, Luis Liso wiped his brow and put on his widest smile. He walked towards the bemused fishermen, shaking their hands and beginning to talk before they could even ask who he was. “Good afternoon, Señores! I've come to make sure you're going to vote for the Democratic Center in the coming elections. We're going to make sure you pay less taxes, get more for your money, and have people who truly work for you here and in Madrid! Unlike those corporatists in the People's Alliance, we're going to be responsible with your money and not go on any reckless adventures!”

Fernández-Miranda opened his mouth to object. As the Democratic Center's de-facto second-in-command, he apparently had to coach his junior partner, this was not part of the Democratic Center's messaging, and what did he just call the People's Alliance? But as Luis Liso continued talking, he could see that some of the fishermen began to nod. Fernández-Miranda stopped himself. The Democratic Center was a coalition, after all, with enough room for both of them...
strings.IBR_pre_election.30.a: He could barely stop his jaw from dropping when Luis Liso came back, five new voters in tow.
strings.IBR_pre_election.31.d:
Torcuato Fernández-Miranda was told that he was a fool for thinking that the CD could be elected in a nation like Iberia. That it would be impossible to win. But Torcuato knew that impossible is the word found only in a fool's dictionary.

Torcuato entered Miller Guerra's office with a wide smile on his face. The election had been grueling, and there was always more work to be done, so to see someone with a smile as wide as his would be unusual. As he opened the door, Miller had been deep in thought, the teeth marks on his pen had left no illusions as to the stress he was under. So when Miller saw Torcuato, smiling from ear to ear, he actually put his pen down. His counterpart held a single sheet of paper in his hand, unprotected from the elements with a folder. Whatever was on that sheet, it had to be so important that he stopped whatever he was doing to return to the office. “The Butcher is on the AP lists.” Torcuato stated with triumph, and the sentence required no elucidation.

Carlos Arias Navarro, the Butcher of Málaga had been placed on the senatorial lists for Madrid. The man whose hands were soaked in the blood of ten thousand death warrants would be signing documents that would become public policy.

“We should run this immediately. It writes itself, the AP is not just a party of old men, but a party who celebrated blanket executions and state terror. Everyone who ever had a family member executed for the mere suspicion of having Republican sympathies is another potential vote. There is no immortality but the memory that is left in the minds of men, and men had long memories.” Torcuato exclaimed, and Miller could help but share his exuberance.
strings.IBR_pre_election.31.a: Never interrupt your foe when he is making a mistake.
strings.IBR_pre_election.32.d:
It was an interview, but anyone at a casual glance might simply mistake it for two ladies getting coffee. Deputy Minister of Work Maria de Lourdes Pintasilgo knew she was on the campaign trail for the CD, but she had arranged for a cordial, casual meeting so that the people could see just a person, who, like them, just wanted to do what she could to serve her fellow man. And so the reporter from Ya had looked to speak to her on faith, and how her faith governed not just her politics, but her life.

“...My father left our family when I was young, and I felt alone and unloved.” Maria wrung her hands to prevent them from shaking. “How could a father abandon his daughter? I spent my days in despair until I let the Lord into my heart. There, I found a love that sprung eternal, that would never leave and would always stand watch over me. That was such a powerful feeling that I felt compelled to do everything I could to ensure others could feel that same love, acceptance, and solace. Whether it was with fellow youths in Catholic Action, or through the League of Women Students at the Catholic University of Lisbon, or my work among the lady's laity in Grail which sent me to all corners of the globe to hear the stories of other Catholic women.

”Very touching. There are so many people that only seem to come to God when they need Him, only to abandon Him in times of plenty. It is remarkable that you found this calling to share with others. Could you explain how your faith has guided your professional career?“

”I see it in the Ministry of Work. Jesus Christ said to give succor to the poor, to open your hands and help them with a pure heart. The Ministry honors those who labor for their families, just as Jesus took humble fishermen as his disciples. Should I be privileged to continue on in my position, I would let my faith guide me into acting as Jesus did, to bring honor and compassion into the Ministry and to Iberia as a whole.“
strings.IBR_pre_election.32.a: Her smile wide, Maria could not stop a single tear escaping from the corner of her eye.
strings.IBR_pre_election.33.d:
“Not good enough.” João Guerra Miller stood over a large map of Iberia, surrounded by aides, a deep frown on his face. Parts of the map were covered in Orange and Green notes, signifying places where the Democratic Center had a strong list or where a candidate was likely to get elected respectively. But many, too many, of the regions on the map were still completely white with uncertainty. “Are you telling me that we don't stand to gain a single seat from Castilla? And it's barely any better in most of the rural regions. This won't do, friends.”

Torcuato Fernández-Miranda, the coalition's second-in-command, interjected, “Señor Guerra, we've been scouring the villages and fields of Iberia for months now, but the results speak for themselves. Our base is the urban, educated electorate, and the People's Alliance knows it. They already have deep grassroots networks in many of these regions, and there's simply not much we can do about it on our own. I have to suggest once again that we work with local independents - even if only on a tactical basis. That way, we could defeat the AP in some key constituencies and begin to build bridges with these independents for actual parliamentary work.'

Guerra Miller's frown deepened. ”We've been over this, Fernández. I don't want to work with strongmen who were put there by the Caudillos and are now trying to entrench themselves in the new system. Turning to them is going to cost us in money and votes from our core-“

The door opened, and an aide sheepishly entered the room, weaving between the assembled strategists to reach the map of Iberia. In an apologetic tone, she explained, ”I'm afraid that Señor Jiménez has had a heart attack and has suspended his campaign“, before plucking a green note from La Rioja and leaving the region empty. Fernández-Miranda looked towards Miller, his eyes grimly triumphant. ”You were saying?“”
strings.IBR_pre_election.33.a: “Fine, Fernández. Start reaching out to these independents. But be careful.”
strings.IBR_pre_election.33.b: “I have to insist. We''re not going to work with mini-Caudillos and betray our voters.”
strings.IBR_pre_election.34.t: To Be Able to Say It
strings.IBR_pre_election.34.d:
“...and today I'm here to tell the world: the women of Iberia deserve better!” A wave of applause swept through the crowd, standing before the former convent now serving as the city's Museum of Aveiro. María Teresa Revilla couldn't help but join in the excitement. She had come here all the way from her Madrid law school in order to be here at this moment, to listen to a speech by Maria de Lourdes Pintasilgo, one of the Democratic Center's rising stars - and the first time María Teresa had actually bothered to listen to a woman with a political message.

She remembered how every once in a while, a representative of the Sección Femenina would come on the airwaves to tell her and the rest of Iberia's women how fortunate they were to live under the benevolent Caudillos and to fulfill their destiny as wives and mothers. This was the first time she had heard another woman on a stage, articulating to the rest of the world what she and so many of her friends had felt for so long: something had to change.

Maria de Lourdes Pintasilgo continued her speech, calling for equality before the law and for legal barriers standing in front of women to be lifted. María Teresa shivered in the cold evening, and she couldn't exactly understand every word of herthe Portuguese, but she did not care. She stood there, transfixed, electrified by the power of the moment and of the women around her: businesswomen, students, and mothers, all here to bring real change.

When Pintasilgo finished her speech, the doors of the museum opened behind her, revealing a group of about ten other women candidates running for the Democratic Center. Around María Teresa, the crowd erupted in raucous cheers, but María Teresa's heart was focused on something greater.
strings.IBR_pre_election.34.a: When she had graduated, she wanted to be like them.
strings.IBR_pre_election.35.d:
Big things could come in small packages. Running the CD campaign had been evidence enough of that. Ex-Finance Ministry official Francisco Fernández Ordóñez had invited Miller here on his own volition, this was a meeting that held significant prominence. The Social Democratic Party was between the Federation of Socialist Parties, who had taken great pains to shut the Social Democrats and Ordóñez specifically out of their coalition even after being on the negotiation commission. Miller knocked on the door, was ushered inside, and removed his hat out of respect when Francisco entered the room. The venerable statesman welcomed Miller, and ushered him into his parlor.

“Señor Guerra, I'm glad you could meet with me on such short notice.”

“When such an opportunity comes, Señor Ordóñez, I would be remiss not to take it.”

“Then I will make it plain. The Federation of Socialist Parties saw fit to marginalize my party. It is one thing to be a junior member, but to be junior in a losing coalition is simply intolerable. I'd rather join a coalition that can win. But I will not be marginalized the way the PSOE and ASP had done. Name me the Finance Minister, and offer support for the workers, and you'll have the Social Democrats.”

That Miller would accept was a given. What he was wondering is how to announce the news. He could just quietly take the victory and enlarge his coalition. But if one of the founding members of the commission was publicly admitted into the CD, it would be a major victory. The Federation of Socialist Parties would be embarrassed and smaller parties that felt similarly marginalized could join the CD as well. A major victory, if the right-leaning members of the CD wouldn't jump ship to the AP.
strings.IBR_pre_election.35.a: We should quietly accept, best to take the win. We have enough problems.
strings.IBR_pre_election.35.b: We should use it to split the Socialist Federation and secure more defectors.
strings.IBR_pre_election.36.d:
Fernando Herrero Tejedor, President of the Government, stood before the assembled members of the Iberian Council, the golden rays of the setting sun giving the end of his speech a somber tone. “These elections will be the triumph of all of Iberia, gentlemen. It will not do to squander the moment in petty squabbling. Let us make sure the people's trust in us is reciprocated.”

After modest applause, Herrero cleared his throat once more. “I would now like to invite Interior Minister Manuel Fraga to speak to the esteemed council about the government's preparations for the elections.” In the audience, João Guerra Miller tapped the table impatiently. It made sense to invite the Interior Minister, but when he was also the head of the largest party running against Miller's Democratic Center, it was also an obvious gesture of political support for him and his People's Alliance.

Fraga quickly took to the podium, thanking the councillors for their presence, and began to explain the government's position regarding the election preparations. “As the esteemed President of the Government has said, these elections are Iberia's triumph, built upon the efforts of the Caudillos and of all Iberia over the last three decades. In order to ensure that nothing goes wrong in this moment of celebration, our foremost priority would be the security of votes and voters, so that the people have the chance to freely express their will without interference...”

In his seat, Miller was stewing in his fury. How could the government claim to support the people's right to free expression when it provided such clear support to one of the candidates - the one tasked with securing the elections themselves, no less - over the other?
strings.IBR_pre_election.36.a: Did his own Democratic Center even stand a chance?
strings.IBR_pre_election.37.d:
“Send in the next candidate, please.” Manuel Fraga ordered his secretary over the intercom. The AP had struggled with the CD's characterization of them as an old man's party without youth appeal. To counter that, Manuel had looked for outstanding candidates for the Youth Front to increase their appeal among the younger generations. While he waited, he pulled the candidate's resume to see it was someone he knew. Jorge Verstrynge Rojas, a political science and sociology major from the University Complutense of Madrid.

Manuel has remembered him because of his electrifying talent for writing, both as an essayist and as a speechwriter. He was a committed and fiery ideologue, a strong command of rhetoric buttressed by his memory for facts to underline his arguments. He was popular among the youth, taking on an early leadership role with college student movements even as a freshman, and they could be put to use in the Youth Front as well.

As the rail-thin Jorge entered his office, Manuel weighed the negatives. Rojas's father was a Belgian, an acolyte of Degrelle even, and Jorge had taken in many fascist ideas from his upbringing. For a young democracy, having a father so keenly tied to the SS was bad enough, but Rojas's own statements could be used against the AP, and harm their reputation among the center.

“Señor Fraga,” Jorge stepped forward crisply and gave a firm handshake. “I believe that I can offer the Youth Wing an energy that you won't find with other candidates. I am unafraid to do what is required, and I know that victory requires as much of the hard, tedious work of organization rather than the cut and thrust of public speaking. And before you ask, I know my past and my father's past. Fascism is a relic now; we see that with Iberia's change. That is my message to the Iberian youth, that we must seize the future with democracy in the hands of the AP.
strings.IBR_pre_election.37.a: His talent is undeniable, and he represents a bold new step forward for Iberian youth.
strings.IBR_pre_election.37.b: His past baggage will cost us more than he could possibly provide.
strings.IBR_pre_election.38.d:
“Señora, can you tell me what happened during the Battle of the Ebro here in your town?” The reporter from ABC poised this pen over his notebook.

Her lips quivered. “Everything... they took everything. The grain. Our goats. Mi papa's cart. Everything for the Republic, but nothing for us...”

The reporter scribbled furiously, nodding to every word as if he understood her pain. “And did anyone stand up to these savages?”

“Oh no... oh Father Miguel...” The woman swallowed, holding back her tears. “He argued with him. Oh... it was over just some bread. There was pushing... and shoving... and then they shot him. And they just... laughed.” Her wrinkles started catching her tears. “I'll never forget their laughter.”

“Do you forgive those who ransacked your town, Señora?” the reporter asked quietly.

She nodded her head. “Even they deserve my forgiveness. But I will never... never forget what they did to my home. I hope I do not see them again...”
strings.IBR_pre_election.38.a: On the opposite page, a campaign ad read: BUILD A DEMOCRACY FREE OF THE RED THREAT
strings.IBR_pre_election.39.d:
As the city lights went by, João Miller Guerra thought about what he was going to say at the event. António Champalimaud, cement magnate, financier, and Portugal's wealthiest man, had invited Guerra to this event where he could enjoy fine food and drink but also meet with donors who were eager to meet the man behind the Democratic Center ticket. What he could say to them could mean a wealth of new resources to carry the campaign through.

“The CD are nothing but puppets, stuffed with the hands of the wealthy. They want you in chains to their rich bosses, slaving away for a pittance while they grow fat. They will dismantle labor protections and allow the owners to increase your hours without your wages. The AP is the only party that will protect you honest, hardworking Iberians and ensure that they can continue to work with dignity and honor.

The chauffeur apologized and switched the radio station off, but the words stuck in Guerra's mind. He was the Minister of Work, and here he was headed to an event where the wealthiest industrialists and bankers of Iberia would be attending, with the best champagne money could buy. A few photographs on the news and Fraga could run a thousand more radio spots just like the one he heard. Guerra could imagine the headlines and opinion pieces. Would a few campaign donations be worth the massive negative press? Would he be telling the workers that he was bought, even if he never used those words?

It wasn't too late; he could tell the chauffeur to turn around and send his apologies. That spoke something all on its own, though. He would be telling the people that he was weak, afraid of the AP, and that weakness would invite further attacks. And he would be telling a room of potential backers that he did not want them, and if they were unwanted, they may find a new backer that could cause further problems for the CD ticket.

As the car cruised down the street, Guerra realized that now, he had to make his statement.
strings.IBR_pre_election.39.a: Continue onward and hope no one speaks.
strings.IBR_pre_election.39.b: Send our apologies. What has been said has already been enough.
strings.IBR_pre_election.40.d:
In an election, public opinion was a weapon, and thus reading public opinions was an intelligence operation like any other. Manuel Fraga made sure that he read the opinions of his opponents. El Alcázar was one of the leading newspapers on the far-right that opposed Iberian democracy. If he understood them, he'd know how to counter their arguments and preserve his right flank.

“Mayor of Madrid Carlos Arias Navarro spoke with El Alcázar where he heavily criticized Manuel Fraga, leader of the AP. 'Believe it or not, Señor Fraga had offered to consult with me regarding governance appointments. I will admit I was intrigued, so I asked if I would actually be formally running as a legislator under the AP banner. Señor Fraga gave a marvelous song and dance about how I'd be better suited as an advisor than as a candidate, but when I pushed, he finally admitted that my actions in Málaga were, and I quote him directly, a significant electoral concern.'

'A significant electoral concern?! I was defending Iberia from those bloodthirsty Republicans who raided homes and farmsteads, who defiled and plundered churches, who killed our countrymen! The only concern we should have is what Iberia should do to those who threaten her people. When Fraga said this, it told me one very clear thing. Fraga is a weak man, who would throw his own nation away just to pretend for a fleeting moment that he was its master.'

'Here is your concern, Señor Fraga. Those Republicans were enemies, and enemies deserve nothing less than the righteous justice of a nation, united behind a leader who isn't afraid of defending it. If this experiment in democracy means offering our hands to those waiting to stab us in the back, then it is a fool's crusade.”

Fraga put down the paper and exhaled deeply. If Navarro had been on the ticket, he'd have sunk the AP at the first press conference.
strings.IBR_pre_election.40.a: The best mistakes are the ones you see coming.
strings.IBR_pre_election.41.d:
As María Dolores Pérez Lapeña, one of the most recent additions to the AP's electoral lists, looked over the produce as the reporter followed her. She was by no means a token addition to the AP's lists to dismiss CD criticism; she had been involved in local government before, and she welcomed the opportunity to address the concerns of her nation. The entire exercise was a hassle, but if Maria wanted the AP to succeed, she would need to do her part. But that didn't mean that she couldn't get the grocery shopping done as well.

“Señora Lapeña, there have been some calls from CD voters that took issue with your previous statements. Do you have any clarifying remarks?”

“I stand by what I said before. I am no prevaricator to speak with double meanings. The feminist cause concerns itself with airy flights of fantasy and blinds itself to hard reality. What use are their theories when women cannot secure a quality education for their children? Will all of their high-minded thinking make the streets safer so that a woman may walk to the market to buy fruit?” she scoffed. “No, I'm sure they'd say that the lack of their ideas causes these crimes in the first place.”

María continued as she appraised a few tomatoes that were perhaps a day past their prime. “They do not operate in reality, and can not be trusted to govern a nation accordingly. Without knowledge of what actually impacts real people, they lock themselves in a tower and pretend to hear the cries of those they ignore, preferring their fiction.”

Just then, María walked over to a head of lettuce and pointed to the price tag. “These are noticeably more expensive than they were a month ago. Ensuring that Iberian women can feed themselves and their families is more liberating than a thousand empty words. Maybe if they spent more time listening and less time shouting, they'd hear.”
strings.IBR_pre_election.41.a: It's hard to keep your feet on the ground with your head in the clouds.
strings.IBR_pre_election.42.d:
Manuel Fraga looked out among the Gibraltar townsfolk, AP members, and reporters eager to hear him tell his story. In front of them stood the local police, officially there to protect the historical site but unofficially there in a show of support for Fraga and the AP. Behind him stood the mighty edifice of El Castillo, a monument to history. The castle had stood guard over Gibraltar, and many an army had been turned back from its walls. And when the castle had fallen, invaders had swept across the peninsula, and it took centuries to expel them. The implication was lost on no one.

“My fellow Iberians, I stand before you today with history behind me. Iberia has always been a land of strength, who nourishes its people to defend it. Invaders that seek to plunder its riches were turned back by those who grew strong upon it. And those who turned their back upon it found that their marauding was stopped by their neighbors, who never sunk to their base level. Yet when Iberia faltered, invaders from without and within seized her, but those who cherished her never forgot her. In the past decades, we have become strong again, taking the Pillar of Hercules back to say that we are Iberia, and that we use our strength to defend our home.”

“Yet that is only one aspect of strength. There is an element of strength that is not as glamorous, but ever more vital; the strength of brotherhood. It is the brotherhood that has a farmer or fisherman look to the lawyer, to the businessman, and say: 'we are Iberian brothers. I stand with you and you stand with me.' We are strong when we recognize that fact. There are those who reject this. The criminal who says: 'I will feed upon you,' the Communists who say: 'if you are not a worker who believes as I do, you are not my brother,' the ETA when they say that those who are not Basque are lessers. They seek to take away our strength. So I say join the People's Alliance, where all Iberians can say 'I believe in Iberian strength. We are all the people, and we stand together against all who would seek to tear us down.'”
strings.IBR_pre_election.42.a: Strength exists in the open hand and the closed fist.
strings.IBR_pre_election.43.d:
Those frolicking crypto-Communists would be the death of this nation should they be elected.“ Manuel Fraga had campaigned on many things, but there was never anything as potent as the fear of communism, nothing like the Bolshevik beast executing their Sacred Heart. In his hometown, they ate it from the palm of his hand as he hit all the familiar notes from the podium.

”Centro Democrático betrays itself in the name — they are centralists, dictators from ivory towers who wish to impose a Soviet model on us. If they have their way, families passed from father to son will be collectivized by the state, ran by bureaucrats from Barcelona.“ A mother from the crowd spat on the ground as boos and hisses flooded the square, hate running wild.

”To all the good people here, the answer should be clear, but I will say it anyway. We are Alianza Popular, by the people, and for the people. We are your people, churchgoers, businessmen, fathers, soldiers, and patriots. We know that Franco and Salazar — in their infinite wisdom — gifted democracy to the people of Iberia.“ The crowd turned solemn as his voice hushed.

”This beautiful flag of ours...“ His hands ran over Iberia's crest. ”...it has gone through so much, and yet it keeps flying. And as we enter a new era, it must be protected from those who wish to desecrate, those who would dare to tear it asunder for their wretched ideals. I can not... no, will not let it happen.“ A few tears fell from his eyes, wiped off using the flag to applause.”

“When you all go to the polls, remember what is at stake. We know how to run the country, so let us shepherd you for a while longer for a moral democracy by voting for Alianza Popular. Thank you! The crowd erupted with cheers as Fraga exited to the tune of old Francoist songs, hearts and attitudes to be molded for the new Iberia.
strings.IBR_pre_election.43.a: Democracy is complicated, give us time to figure it out.
strings.IBR_pre_election.44.d:
Fernando Herrero Tejedor sat stiffly in the Villamejor Palace's conference room. The walls trembled from the roars outside. The roars that had relentlessly pulsed throughout the nation like a rupturing heart demanding true reforms and freedom. A couple of weeks ago, he treated this as the symphony of democracy. Tonight, there was no order to this cacophany.

Strikes were happening across the country, freezing economic sectors with protests swelling faster than the police could suppress them. “The nation is paralyzed, Señor Presidente,” a military officer reported, sliding a folder towards him. “Read this speech to the people tomorrow. Call off the elections.”

“No,” he whispered. These were not his words. Not his promises. Not what Iberia needed. “The elections cannot be suspended. Once people vote - once people see the future they're choosing - this will calm.”

Silence. The officer leaned forward. “Señor Presidente... this is for the good of the Union.”

“The good?” The president sat up from his chair, trembling. “I swore! Swore to-”

“You swore to preserve the Union!” The officer shoved him back down. A pause ensued. “If you do not, then we will intervene. And let me tell you, Señor Tejedor... we will not be gentle.”

The words fell like hard rain. The bitterness. Oh, the bitterness! The one promise that gave Iberia new life was to be betrayed. The crowd surged with a hope, a fury, a desperation, all woven into an impossible demand.

He took the papers. He promised a beginning. A happy ever after to Iberia's story. But there was no more ink to continue its tale.
strings.IBR_pre_election.44.a: History does not remember what could have been.
strings.IBR_pre_election.45.d:
The café owner unlocked the door before sunrise, as he always did in these dim blue hours. He switched on the lights, humming softly to the familiar sounds around him. The coffee machines whirring to life. The hissing of the espresso boiler. The clattering of cups. The scraping of chairs across the floor as his waiter set up the tables.

The owner reached for the radio. Static. Then bass. Then drums. Then the blaring of a military march through the speakers, each goosestep so violent it made the cups rattle.

Another chair scraped against the stone. Another hundred boots hit the ground. Louder. Heavier. Drowning out the daily routine that had felt so comfortable.

A voice emerged.

“Atención. By decree of the Iberian Armed Forces, the previous administration has been dismissed for endangering national security. Remain calm, as we restabilize this country from the internal threats that seek to bring us down. Elections and reforms are to be suspended, and we will restore the righteous tradition and principles of the Caudillos before.”

There was a pause, but no hesitation in his next line. “This measure is temporary, but necessary to preserve order.”

Then another march slammed through the speakers, identical to before. The instruments drowned out all thought mercilessly.

In the relentless, clashing torrent of dissonant music and familiar café sounds, there was a silence hanging on both men, unable to be expressed, unable to be processed.
strings.IBR_pre_election.45.a: A silence that drowned out what could have been.
strings.IBR_campaign.1.d:
Every day, life found ways of reminding Virgilio Borquez that he was exceptionally blessed.

He had been able to follow his dreams and become an architectural engineer, married his beloved Isabella who he had known since he was in school, and had three healthy and happy children. From the moment he woke up until the moment he fell asleep, he knew that God had blessed him. He opened the paper as he sipped his coffee, but rather than the dry headline news that he was expecting, the opening fold saw two large advertisements for electoral coalitions. The election season had officially begun.

On one side, the CD's advertisement boldly proclaimed that they represented the Iberian people, and democracy was their slogan. Everyone could be heard under the CD's banner, and they were devoted to sound technical governance, prosperity for all Iberians, and greater freedom. If you wanted to stand up and say “I am me. This is what I believe in,” then the CD was the coalition for you.

On the other, the AP stood firm and said, “I am an Iberian and proud to be one.” They were a coalition that proudly stood to their traditions, that honored family, service, and hard work. Community was their byword, and they proudly boasted that they stood with Iberians should they be fisherman or engineer. They trusted the wisdom of those that came before and promised governance with a steady, firm, and caring hand.

“The elections are coming up,” Isabella gently kissed his head as she saw the open paper in his hand. “Who are you supporting?”

“Both of the coalitions make good points,” Virgilio mentioned. “But I would say...”
strings.IBR_campaign.1.a: The AP has a firm foundation that could be quite effective.“
strings.IBR_campaign.1.b: The CD's broad coalition is quite compelling.
strings.IBR_campaign.10.d:
Was it not pure common sense what he was saying? A sound argument, backed by a weight of experience, and tangible data. Delivered with confidence, lacking ego, whose only goal was to further the electoral prospects of the CD coalition. Displaying a requisite amount of empathy for the other side of this debate, accepting criticism, and offering constructive feedback. Had he not been gracious, had he not listened, had he not expounded his viewpoint sufficiently to engender agreement in this implacable moron opposite him?

The inner monologue of these two campaign operatives was a mirror. They were mired in an intractable set of disagreements related to graphic design. The deadline for this wave of poster printing had passed 4 hours ago. “We are building a party from nothing, in a nation that has not seen an election in decades, where fascist thugs have beaten the concept of a democratic politician out of our collective minds.” Half-moon lavender circles under his eyes, Windsor glasses on them, a diet of espresso and 20 packs of Tabacalera's finest. A collection of thin rebar melded together in the form of a human, opposite one who had a religious attachment to filhós.

“Mr. Guerra and the national candidates need all the profile we can muster for him. How can you not see that?” A worn sigh, an unneeded re-cleaning of his spectacles. In this combat any silence resulted in the floor being conceded. The tightly wound upper register voice was replaced by something languid and rumbling. “That profile can be ameliorated by adding recognizable, relevant politicians on a per province basis. People gravitate to the familiar, we are all tribal at heart, I'm sure you see the reason in this - ”

A vigorous inquiry of a senior campaign manager into the status of the poster order disabused them of further intellectual jousting in favour of mutual self-preservation, making a final decision of...“
strings.IBR_campaign.11.d:
Osvaldo Rascón lived and breathed for campaign events, especially when reporters asked him questions. The ability to think up an answer on the fly, to address the topics on the voters' minds and ensure that the answer only further reflected and amplified his message was art. Osvaldo might never be an author, but in his ability to craft words, he was a true virtuoso.

The people were talking about something that would have unthinkable five years ago. Not only would Iberia hold elections, but communist parties were no longer illegal. Protests against their legalization had been extensive in rural regions, while universities and urban centers were much calmer. There was even talk that this was a plan by the AAS to get terrorists to out themselves. Osvaldo doubted that, but for someone to think it up meant something. No one expended the effort to dream up such an elaborate conspiracy if it wasn't important, and if there wasn't genuine apprehension. When the people were nervous about important things, it meant that a politician could make or break himself with his messages.

“Señor Rascón, we go to you. As you are aware, the landmark decision reversing the illegal status of communist parties was announced yesterday. The people are eager to know CD's position on the ruling. Will communist parties hold any influence toward the CD? What do you think this means in the context of Iberia's reformation process?”Osvaldo smiled: “Not a problem, this means...”
strings.IBR_campaign.11.a: “I believe everything that needs to have been said has been said already.”
strings.IBR_campaign.11.b: “I disagree wholeheartedly with their political beliefs, but their legalization is welcome.”
strings.IBR_campaign.11.c: “I do not support their beliefs and believe they are a detriment to the overall electoral process.”
strings.IBR_campaign.12.d:
Topics for the election season came in ebbs and flows. What could dominate the newscycle could change on a whim, and only a really good politician could roll with the changing mood of the public and the media, take whatever issue was the topic of discussion for the day, and shape it like clay back to the coalition's message.

Fortunately, Osvaldo Rascón was a really good politician.

The topic today was the Iberian government's ruling that the communist party remains illegal. Illegal since the foundation of the Union, the government had ruled that agitation against the Iberian state, dating back as far as the Asturian miners' revolt, had proven that the party harbored no beliefs to participate in government and the ban would remain in place. The AP was fairly united on their anti-communist beliefs, but the CD's position was far more ambivalent. Plenty of CD members believed that the democratic reformation meant the ban should have been rescinded, which had been used as a cudgel by the AP in the election from the very beginning. Others had been hostile to communist movements, believing them to have been a step backward in political science. Even others had no strong feelings, and largely decided their opinion on whether or not they were too politically toxic to deal with.

He was shaken out of his thinking when a reporter asked him a question: “Señor, what is your opinion on the decision that communist parties can not participate in Iberian elections?”

“Of course. My opinion is...”
strings.IBR_campaign.12.a: I believe that we should focus more upon policy concerns that the CD would enact.
strings.IBR_campaign.12.b: I believe it is an error. They are a non-violent political party and will be afforded the rights due to such after the election.
strings.IBR_campaign.12.c: I believe that it was the right decision given their past crimes. They have yet to renounce their violent past.“
strings.IBR_campaign.13.d:
Leaders of various parties within Centro Democrático had convened to discuss the coalition's overarching campaign strategy. Attacks from both the right and left were to be expected, and CD would need to run their own narratives and rhetoric to combat the mud that would inevitably be thrown in their direction.

As the meeting progressed, it became clear that three distinct strategies had gained support amongst the leadership:

The first was to take the high road, and focus on a positive campaign strategy. Negative attack ads could generate negative polarization, and lower voter enthusiasm across the board. Instead, it was argued that ads and rhetoric should focus on drawing positive attention towards the coalition's own candidates, and that good messaging could combat the opposition's attack ads just as well without wading into the trenches themselves.

This was opposed by those who believed that going on the offensive was better than being forced to stay on the back foot against whatever narratives the opposition wished to establish. This camp was then split into two parts: Those who thought the coalition should focus its attention against the socialists, and those who believed that the coalition should focus its attention against the conservatives in the election like AP.

After a significant amount of debate, one strategy eventually pulled ahead of the others, and the party's strategy for the election was decided.
strings.IBR_campaign.13.a: CD shall go on the offensive against the socialists.
strings.IBR_campaign.13.b: The last thing the nation needs is division. CD shall run a positive campaign.
strings.IBR_campaign.13.c: CD will focus its strategy on attacking the conservatives.
strings.IBR_campaign.14.d:
Barcelona was nothing if not one of Europe's primo locales for her legendary night life and the cinema was no exception, a known hot-spot for Spanish youth to run amok on Saturday night. This was part of the reason why the venue was chosen for the event, even if the CD's campaign race was a little more on the austere side than the city's party-goers were maybe used to.

The head of the list for Barcelona province had a keen eye for this sort of thing, knowing to play into the fiery, independent spirit that Catalonia was always known for. Playing up the northeast's regional identity was always a crowd-pleaser, even if it riled the occasional MP to irritance.

Inevetably however, through the clacking of camera lenses and lines of voter questionnaires for the Barcelona representative, came the question of decentralization and broader regional autonomy. Catalonia's autonomy (thanks be to God) was not mentioned directly, but it is understandable that one of Iberia's most polarized political hot potatoes would worm its way into the discourse.

The Barcelona representative was quick to respond, well-aware of the weight attached to the question, responding promptly:
strings.IBR_campaign.14.a: “Iberia's national unity has to take priority.”
strings.IBR_campaign.14.b: “Iberia's regional identities should be respected and legally protected.”
strings.IBR_campaign.15.d:
“And you think Italy is going to play ball?” A high ranking official at the US Embassy in Madrid chewed his salmon greedily.

The CD candidate was conciliatory. “There remain a few decent men left in Rome, not all were happy with the Triumvirate's collapse. Detente is preferable.”

The Embassy dinner was a part of a CD functionary, hoping to smooth over relations with the Americans in the event of electoral victory. “And Japan?” The official prompted.

“As much of a shrewd partner in commerce as they are with anyone else.” The candidate was less than enthused with the notion. “Ideally, that's as far as it would go.”

“And Germania?”

“Oh, Madre de Dios, is the wine here yet?” The candidate said jokingly, peering over the official's shoulder for dramatic effect.

The official twisted his mouth into a slanted sneer. “I'm not trying to be rude.”

“Oh, no no no, I know you're not!” The candidate waved his hands low. “I'm only joking.”

The official waved the thought away in return. “Iberian foreign policy isn't something I need to explain to you, to say nothing of Its importance.” The official leaned into the CD candidate as he questioned him. “What are your thoughts on that?” He wasn't looking for convenient platitudes, he was fishing for an answer.
strings.IBR_campaign.15.a: “I'm all in favor of defrosting ties with Washington.”
strings.IBR_campaign.16.d:
The sky over their heads could not have been clearer, a color so blue one might half expect an angel strumming a harp upon her cloud. The wheat field seemed to go on forever, the blades of grain shining like gold in the afternoon sun. These were the skies that the Romans were willing to kill in the name of empire for, the lands that the Moors were willing to die in the name of God for.

The CD candidate wiped sweat from his brow as campaign signs bobbed up and down in the crowd, the rally for the upcoming election drawing all kinds of people from the countryside in southern Portugal. The heat was at least minimal enough to not risk damaging the equipment, the microphone stand and waiting television cameras recording the whole affair with rapt attention.

As the candidate fielded questions from the rural working class people, a young man who was a field hand asked about the potential for agricultural reform, as most of the workers on the farms in Portugal don't own any of the land they are made to work on and wonder if the CD's campaign platform had any intention to change that. A sticky subject to be sure, but one the party had a ready answer for.

Without delay, the CD candidate offered the following response.
strings.IBR_campaign.16.a: “Offer land to the workers in the field is CD's highest priority.”
strings.IBR_campaign.16.b: “Disentangling the unevenness in agriculture takes time.”
strings.IBR_campaign.16.c: “The farmers have enough to make do already.”
strings.IBR_campaign.17.t: The Latest Scoop on CD's Program
strings.IBR_campaign.17.d:
Vicente had shown up an hour early to get a good spot at the new CD press conference in Lisbon. Insider knowledge was that the coalition would be publicly releasing its economic program, and so the venue was positively flooded with journalists.

Throughout the press conference, Vicente scribbled down as many notes as he could. Anything that could be an important quote to remember, any key policies that would no doubt get examined under a microscope in the coalition's next dozen press conferences, and anything potentially striking enough that it could squeeze its way into the headline.

Once CD's representatives started giving canned answers, Vicente switched tactics, and began planning out how to summarize the policies revealed at the press conference. Vicente's paper was here inside Lisbon, and so a quick turn around on the reporting for this press conference was mandatory. Eventually, he found an adequate way to condense the entire conference into a single sentence, and quickly translated it into chicken-scratch in his far too crowded notebook:
strings.IBR_campaign.17.a: CD wants to open up Iberia and create a free market for the nation.
strings.IBR_campaign.17.b: CD sets out to create a social market for Iberia.
strings.IBR_campaign.17.c: CD offers up more of the same for Iberia, no major changes.
strings.IBR_campaign.18.d:
“And you are certain that both the Caudillos are in agreement with the proposed reforms.” One journalist asked, one standing in a crowd of seated correspondents.

The party official waved the thought away: “I certainly hope so!” He forced a laugh from behind the table. “Otherwise someone is in for a bracing argument behind closed doors!”

“Franco and Salazar are affirmed to assume a subsidiary role after the new constitution is framed?” Another journalist posted, more pointedly.

The party spokesperson was more straightforward than the official: “The future of the Iberian constitution has been signed and sworn to, the Caudillos have given their blessing.”

“Freedom of the press?” The first journalist asked, perhaps more invested than she was letting on.
“Assured, unequivocally.” Said the party official. The words just hung in the air, almost alien to the ears of those in attendance.

“And the rights of the average Iberian?” The crucible of this new chapter, the nation held its breath in the shadows behind the camera lens.

There was a lengthy pause, the spokesperson was non-plussed, almost casual:
strings.IBR_campaign.18.a: “Your rights will be yours, and yours alone.”
strings.IBR_campaign.19.d:
Antonio Martín shook hands with the two men he had come to meet with, the coalition's number 1 and number 2 candidates for Sevilla, and gestured for them to take a seat at a nearby table. The two were doing the rounds of the region's newspapers, and Martín had been chosen to handle his paper's interview of the duo.

Martín cleared his throat as he picked up his pen. “Alright then, let's get started. Señor Fernández, Señor López, what's it like running in the first elections in Sevilla in over a decade?”

Señor López, the number 2 candidate, was the first to answer, “It's a wonderful feeling, and an exciting time for the nation.”

“Indeed, it's finally time for the people of Sevilla and the rest of Iberia to have their voices heard, and it's an honor to represent CD in these historic elections.” Señor Fernández's answer was simple, but Martín could only imagine they've answered some form of that question over a hundred times now.

“I can only imagine, but exciting times can also be chaotic times. Iberia is no stranger to acts of terrorism and political violence, and many voters are concerned about the nation's security during this grand transition. Many voters call for reforms to the police institutions employed under the Caudillos, but others worry that many candidates in these elections are weak on security issues, and that CD hasn't been clear in its messaging on where it falls on the topic. Could either of you provide a clear stance for the citizens of Sevilla?”

As expected, Señor López turned towards the more senior candidate to answer the tougher question first. Señor Fernández stayed silent for a moment before giving his response:
strings.IBR_campaign.19.a: New policing tactics are needed for a new Iberia.
strings.IBR_campaign.19.b: CD wishes to keep a firm hand, but also seeks to reform everyday policing.
strings.IBR_campaign.19.c: I assure you, our top priority is security for Sevilla and its people.
strings.IBR_campaign.20.d:
The campaign was drawing to a close. João Miller Guerra would be giving a speech to cap off the campaign as voters headed into the polls and decided the outcome of Iberia's first free elections.

The key points to touch on in the speech were obvious. An event like this needed a focus on the future for Iberia, and what the goals should be for the nation's constitution. Those needed to be highlighted at this crucial event with so many eyes on it, the final capstone of the coalition's efforts for the past few months.

The main sticking point that Guerra couldn't decide upon when planning his speech was whether to hammer in on the importance of laying down a strong foundation for a free and truly democratic Iberia, or to go for a safer, broader message of appealing to stability. Guerra certainly wasn't as passionate about the latter approach, but campaign advisors always brought up concerns about alienating potential voters, especially now at the eleventh hour of the campaign.

The introductory speaker was wrapping up their speech, and Guerra was set to walk on stage at any moment now. One last glance at his speech notes revealed that the direction he had planned was...
strings.IBR_campaign.20.a: Our role must be to create a foundation for a free Iberia.
strings.IBR_campaign.20.b: Our role must be to act as the anchor of stability in these unprecedented times.
strings.IBR_campaign.30.d:
At the Lisbon regional HQ for the coalition, the various attendees were discussing the surprisingly controversial matter of how to order the names for the regional list.

The initial plan by regional leadership had been to place the most senior and recognizable names at the top of the list. AP needed potential voters to have recognizable figures catch their eye on the regional lists or they'd get disinterested.

However, this plan got near-immediate pushback at the actual meeting from other attendees. Instead, it was argued that recognizable names were synonymous with names from the prior regime. A regime that many attendees argued was unpopular, and could bring bad optics to the coalition, and provide easy material for the opposition's attack ads. Their counter-proposal was to place the more recognizable names at the bottom, and that the prime real estate at the top of the list should be given to newer names that could use the boost in recognition to create an overall stronger list for the coalition. Recognizable names would be recognized no matter what, so placing them at the bottom wouldn't hurt their existing popularity, but would send a message that people voting for AP weren't just voting for the past.

Eventually, a majority consensus was reached, and the lists were organized to match.
strings.IBR_campaign.30.a: Seniority rules, the big names should be listed first on the list.
strings.IBR_campaign.30.b: Newer members should be placed into the spotlight.
strings.IBR_campaign.31.d:
Marco Silveira approached every press conference as if he were about to square off in the ring. He had boxed welterweight in university and thrived in the heat of competition. There was nothing quite so thrilling as putting yourself out there, fighting aggressively, feinting to bait an attack, only to charge in when the opponent was least expecting it. He never expected that he'd enjoy a verbal cut-and-thrust as much as he had, and so he was always eager to put on his gloves and jump into the ring.

All anyone could talk about in the public sphere was the decision to lift the ban on communist parties. They had been banned since the early days of the Caudillos, and yet, in the spirit of the newly democratic Iberia, it had been decided that the ban was a relic of the past and had been abolished along with many of the other relics of the old era. The AP had largely been in uproar about the entire affair, and had rode the wave of opposition to the decision to empower their voters as much as it empowered the communist supporters The people had largely expected the AP to take a stand, to hearken back to the past atrocities committed under the red banner, and unite the people under a new flag to combat them.

Marco hadn't bothered to make many statements on the affair; he had been focused so intently on what he could do for the people of Iberia that he never focused much on the topic. But silence was a choice that had greater implications for the party. Without a single united message, the AP was a flurry of jabs - disjointed and unfocused. Together, the AP could land a true body blow and score some significant damage, at the cost of galvanizing the electorate either for or against. And so, when the reporter looked to him for comment, he prepared for a body blow.
strings.IBR_campaign.31.a: I disagree with them wholeheartedly, and the people agree. I welcome an election to showcase their unpopularity.
strings.IBR_campaign.31.b: It is a mistake to legalize them. Were I in power, I'd push for their banning in a heartbeat.
strings.IBR_campaign.32.d:
Marco Silveira had boxed in university, and he felt the same thrill in the scrum that was the fight between journalist and candidate. A good fight got the blood pumping, and it was as much a rush to campaign for the AP as it was to get into the ring. The flashes of the cameras were the lights of the ring all over again, but Marco couldn't hope for a quick knockout; he'd have to go the distance. Marco could bob and weave between the journalists' questions and throw out responses like lightning jabs.

“Senhor Silveira. The recent decision to maintain the ban on communist parties has certainly caught the attention of the voting public. It has attracted its fair share of commentary both for and against, with some saying that an election can't be free if entire parties can be banned, while others say that a communist party has no business running in an election. What is your stance on the topic?”

This was no mere feint, this was a punch with momentum. He had to move left or right and take his own swing. Either shift right and attack with a powerful cross, or try for the shock maneuver and attack from the left and hope to hit a blindspot.

“A good question.” Marco began, beginning his move and ready to take the gloves off. “Believe me when I say that I did not come to this decision lightly. This is a moment that defines us as a newly democratic nation. Therefore, I say with certainty that...”
strings.IBR_campaign.32.a: “The party is illegal, but I believe that the individual candidates should run. It is an election after all.”
strings.IBR_campaign.32.b: “I believe the judgment is a sound one and reflects Iberia's commitment to public safety and sound governance.”
strings.IBR_campaign.33.d:
“A message for millions must be simple, very, very simple. A child should be able to recite what we stand for - ” A voice with the timbre of someone who is already laughing at their own joke before speaking cut in. “A child understands that communists are bastards - ”Roaring, laughter, rejoinders, and counter-arguments all collided inside the AP coalition campaign headquarters.

They were collected at an oblong conference table upon a beige-gold-green carpet protecting a well aged oak wood floor. Piled atop it were scrawled slogans, reams of opposition research, and an all you could eat supply of electoral maps. Two long tuxedo couches that spanned the length of the room flanked the table, conveniently containing the two baying sides of the ongoing argument. A low ceiling boasted ornamental fans that impotently tried to clear the hanging fog of smoke. The evening was beginning to stretch into unreasonable hours.

“We know what the common man wants, for all his flaws. Break off the palatable bits and pieces of the left platform, only with the assurance that we won't run Iberia into the ground.” The serious, spindly Jesús Arozarena once again tapped his pen onto a notepad as audible punctuation. There was a dark orb of ink on the paper and the nub of said pen had been broken. “Then why bother with the first part? The common man - ” those three words repeated in schoolboy-like mockery “ - knows that any to the left of us are the devil, and will run Iberia into the ground. Why bother with this populist nonsense?” Manuel de Vega, brother of an archbishop, cast about seeking support for what had to be the plain truth.

The two continued, onlookers keen on watching these adversaries square off. Cigarette cartons started to run dry, the argument ran in circles, and the clock had run past those unreasonable hours. A decision was reached through exhaustion.
strings.IBR_campaign.33.a: Hammer the left at every opportunity!
strings.IBR_campaign.33.b: Populist rhetoric will win us votes!
strings.IBR_campaign.34.d:
Vigo had always been celebrated for its scenic metropole, a tall feat in a nation already filled to bursting with iconic tropical and temperate beauty. From the restaurant to the night club to the movie theater, Vigo was among the crown jewels of Galicia's rich urban life, downtown was always used as a hot spot for the city's more social animals.

This was precisely what made it so appealing to the AP campaign, renting out a now packed cinema in Vigo for a campaign rally in the upcoming election. The head of the list for Pontevedra province, looking to secure the AP campaign in Galicia, spent the night buffeting the party platform while soliciting questions from prospective voters.

It was only a matter of time before the question of regional autonomy arose. Naturally, Galicia was very much relevant in that regard. Forced to walk a tight rope for one of Iberia's historically complicated societal issues, the AP representative was asked point blank on the issue of decentralization and autonomy for Iberia's regional identities.

Attempting to be forthcoming over an obviously sensitive issue, the AP representative responded with:
strings.IBR_campaign.34.a: “Iberia's regional identities should be respected and legally protected.”
strings.IBR_campaign.34.b: “Iberia's national unity has to take priority.”
strings.IBR_campaign.35.d:
While domestic concerns were on the mind of both electoral coalitions as they campaigned, Iberian foreign policy, and the potential for it to change after the election, was never far from anyone's mind. If Iberia would democratize, would that mean a fundamental shift in their foreign policy, opening overtures up to the OFN? Or would they focus more upon their continental neighbors, with the more practical considerations of trade and migration ruling the order of the day.

The AP had largely remained non-committal during the election, stating that foreign policy would be studied and shaped according to the best needs of the Iberian nation but that the chief order of business was ensuring Iberia's continued prosperity and reformation into a democratic nation, and that all nations could find a willing partner in Iberia. That had pleased no one, but delaying the matter was the smartest play early on. As the election continued, however, it became less a shield and more a loadstone.

At the American embassy, at yet another dinner and diplomatic function, Marco Silveira was dressed in his finest suit as he courted the American embassy staff. While he joked that he liked taking time off from the election to have a nice and simple dinner, everyone knew it to be a white lie - he was always campaigning. And so as he welcomed the Charge d'Affairs with another smile and a compliment to his lovely wife, the real business of state was to be at hand.

“The election continues apace, Senhor Silveira. I know I, and many of my compatriots back home, are interested in how the AP plans to center their approach to foreign policy?”

“Well, your Excellency, I believe it's best to say that...”
strings.IBR_campaign.35.a: “Iberia shall focus its foreign policy efforts on like-minded partners who reflect its values such as the OFN..”
strings.IBR_campaign.35.b: “Iberia's foreign policy focus is to establish security and prosperity with all nations.”
strings.IBR_campaign.36.d:
“...and thus we will guarantee that Iberia will have its proper place in the global trade network!” Manuel Fernández finished responding to one of the questions the Valladolid townspeople asked, receiving scattered applause in return. The people had come from all around the region to fill the somewhat dilapidated youth club and hear a public figure who actually had to address their concerns. “Any further questions?”

“Uhm- yes,” a calloused hand was raised in front of the stage, and Manuel had to bend down to see the diminutive farmer it belonged to. “I've worked this land my whole life, Señor. It was given to me by my father, who was given it by his father before him, and I've fought for it in the war against the reds who'd take it all away. It's an honest living, and I wouldn't trade it for anything, even if I'm never going to be able to go on an expensive vacation abroad. But I've heard from people around here that your coalition is planning on reforming landholding all around Iberia, to make it more economical. You can't truly be meaning to drive honest Iberians off their land in order to let rich businessmen take it over for their own profit, can you?”

Manuel stood up straight, slightly taken aback. The economic situation in northern Castillia was indeed horrendously inefficient. Romantic as it was, the smallholding farmer was simply not able to compete with foreign agribusiness, and if the AP wanted to get prices down and productivity up, this farmer and thousands like him would have to be left behind. But in order to get anything done at all, the AP would need to get elected, and that depended on men like this farmer. And so, slightly adjusting his tie, Manuel cleared his throat. “Well, of course, certain steps will have to be taken to make Iberian agriculture more competitive...
strings.IBR_campaign.36.a: “...and some reforms to the structure of landownership will have to be made, painful as they may be.”
strings.IBR_campaign.36.b: “...such as aid to Iberian farmers such as yourself in properly industrializing.”
strings.IBR_campaign.36.c: “...but you can be certain that we will defend the rights of honest landowners such as you.”
strings.IBR_campaign.37.d:
With the election campaign at the top of each party's priorities, the Alianza Popular had gone all out, splurging the money to rent a massive theater in Madrid and invite any media outlet they could think of to their latest press conference. José Velázquez, La Vanguardia's Madrid correspondent, had already booked his front-row seat two weeks ago, and was now rapidly jutting down notes in his small notebook.

This was going to be the AP's most crucial press conference - Miguel and the rest had come here to hear about the party's economic program, and as the Yanquis said, “It's the economy, stupid.” The AP were just as aware as the rest of them of how vital this conference was, and they had gone all out - it seemed as if the party's entire leadership were in attendance, their suits expertly pressed and their messaging sharp and polished. For a conference about an economic program, Miguel mused, it seemed that the AP did not pay too much mind to its own finances when planning it.

Manuel Fraga opened the conference, speaking in great length about Iberia's great economic potential and the need to harness the nation's resources for the greater good. Next came Laureano López Rodó, the party's economic expert and its mooted Vice-minister of Economic Affairs, putting some more meat on the bones of Fraga's speech. Miguel could hear the frantic pencils scratching on a hundred pages to his sides and above him in the hall, as López went into greater detail about the AP's platform and laid out its plans and priorities. When López finished his speech, Miguel took a moment to catch his breath, looking at his notes and trying to think of a succinct headline he could use to summarize everything he had heard. He finally settled on something when prospective Vice-President João Mota Pereira de Campos took the stage. After short applause, Miguel took out his pencil once more, jotting at the top of the page:
strings.IBR_campaign.37.b: Promises of an Iberian Social Market!
strings.IBR_campaign.37.c: Meet the new economy, same as the old economy.
strings.IBR_campaign.38.d:
“Thank you, Señor. Let's go to the next question now, shall we?” The smiling presenter interjected into the words of an elderly man who had asked the assembled delegates something about fishing rights. He was getting into an argument with the Centrist candidate about the precise delineation of the maritime border, and the presenter had decided to cut the talking short before everybody fell asleep. “You there, in the red turtleneck, please.”

A young woman took up the microphone slightly gingerly, looking at the representatives sitting around the round table. “Good evening, Señors, I'm Ana, and I'm currently a law student here in Madrid. I wanted to ask about something which I think underlies all of what we've been talking about here today.
