All throughout the process of transitioning from direct rule by the Caudillos we've been talking about elections and democracy and transparency, but all of these are meaningless if we Iberians don't have our basic human rights going forward. So I wanted to hear your plans for the rights of Iberians going forward. I'm particularly interested in hearing Señor Pereira's opinion about this, as your party claims to want to uphold the Caudillos' achievements and move forward carefully. How careful are you going to be in giving us our rights?”

The hall fell completely silent for a few seconds before the presenter caught himself. “Wow, that was one heck of a question, don't you think? I'm sure you'll get far indeed in life with that kind of outlook, Ana. But now for Señor Pereira. How would you address our young firebrand's question here?”

André Pereira sat up straight, seemingly unfazed and a wide smile on his face. “That is indeed the most important question, but the answer to it is a simple one...”
strings.IBR_campaign.38.a: “...me, you, and the rest of Iberia will have our basic rights guaranteed.”
strings.IBR_campaign.38.b: “...we have to make sure the structure is stable before we shake things up too much.”
strings.IBR_campaign.39.d:
Vanessa López picked up her notepad and her pen, sitting up straight and smiling at the two hopefuls sitting in front of her. “Shall we begin?” The two men, one in his thirties and the other somewhat older, nodded together.

“Perfect.” She bent down again to begin recording their conversation. “Good afternoon, gentlemen. This is an exciting period for all of Iberia, but it must be even more exhilarating for you two. Running in Iberia's first free elections must be such a unique experience.”

Señor Campos, the older man, smiled slightly. “Yes, absolutely. It's exhausting sometimes, but in the end, we both want to give back, to Iberia and to our homes here in Valencia. I wouldn't give it up for anything.”

Vanessa took a sip of water before continuing. “One of the AP's chief election pledges has been to, quote, 'build on the structure left to us by the Caudillos and maintain a smooth and peaceful transition.' At the risk of being blunt, the rule of the Caudillos here in Valencia hasn't always been the most smooth and peaceful. How do you plan on handling the transition here?”

The younger man, Señor Jiménez, leaned forward, slightly agitated. “Of course we will listen to the demands of the people in managing the transition, but things need to be conducted responsibly and without letting malign elements get their hands on our democracy; otherwise, it won't be a transition, but a revolution.”

Vanessa jotted something on her notepad. “How will you ensure these malign elements are kept at bay? What will be your policy regarding police actions and proscribed organizations?”

Señor Campos put a hand on Señor Jiménez before he could blurt out anything rash. “Of course...”
strings.IBR_campaign.39.a: “... we will make sure the police are only deployed to deal with actual threats.”
strings.IBR_campaign.39.b: “... we won't be able to simply change our security police overnight.”
strings.IBR_campaign.40.d:
Manuel Fraga was standing on stage in front of thousands of supporters, waving and smiling. He was genuinely struck by the power of the moment. He could see why Franco could not give it up for so long- it was exhilarating, intoxicating. But Fraga had something that Franco could not have hoped for, at least not for a long time now: every single person here came because they had wanted to, and because in comparison to a viable alternative, they judged him their better option for a future.

And now, they were in the final stretch. Election day was almost here, and Fraga had come to rouse his supporters in one final rally. When the hall finally quietened down, he made his way to the podium. This was it - the final point he would make in the campaign, what the people sitting here and those reading about it in the papers would remember most as they went to cast their ballots. He had to make it count.

As he came close to the podium, Fraga smoothly took out his papers to have a last look, his throat suddenly a bit dry. Was it excitement? Fear? Joy? He wasn't sure, but he wasn't going to let it spoil the moment, and he was absolutely not going to miss a beat in his speech. This had to be executed flawlessly. One last look at his notes, and it was off to the races.

And so, under the glare of dozens of stagelights and flashing cameras, standing in front of the Iberian people, sweat beading on his brow, Fraga began talking about...
strings.IBR_campaign.40.a: ...the need to maintain the good the Caudillos did, but learning from their many mistakes.
strings.IBR_campaign.40.b: ...the AP's role as the anchor of stability in these turbulent days.
strings.IBR_campaign.50.d:
President of the Government Fernando Herrero Tejedor approached the ballot box with a grace that belied his heavy form. He turned to the waiting cameras, and flashed a jowly, walrus-mustached grin. And dropped his ballot to mix with the hundreds of others that had accumulated in Castellón de la Plana, his hometown. Which would mix with thousands of others across Valencia, and millions from across the Iberian Peninsula.

He walked through the polling station, smiling but silent, as the mass of journalists blurted out in a hundred different ways, “Who did you vote for?”

From the doorway, Herrero Tejedor looked at his waiting limousine, the street festooned with the green-orange pennants of the Democratic Center and the red-yellow banners of the Alianza Popular, and the scores of citizens filing to vote... then turned back around to say, “After today, I'll be nobody special. Why don't you ask the Iberian voter?”

With one last wink, Herrero Tejedor closed his tale, “I imagine we'll be hearing from them shortly.
strings.IBR_campaign.51.d:
On election night, where could one find the Democratic Center?

Were they in Lisbon at the Terreiro do Paço plaza? Amidst its pink shades, could they hear the strident tones of João Miller Guerra take the place of Salazar's reedy whisper? Did they sit alongside the banks of Tagus, where the first Iberian Union had died centuries ago, watching this second Union being born anew?

Or was the river the Piles, flowing through Gijón? Were they the joyous Asturian students tramping through Isabel the Catholic park, passing waterfowl en route to the Old Mill? Did they listen to Torcuato Fernández-Miranda beside the quaint hotel, receive an intimate lecture instead of a barn-storming speech?

Were they on the Ramblas of Barcelona or on Madrid's Gran Vía, marching and chanting to the pop of hand-thrown firecrackers? Or smiling at the festivities spreading along Aveiro's art nouveau frontage, drifting along its canals? Or were they in a rocking chair at home in Frigiliana, waiting for a battered old radio to tell them that a decades-long push for freedom had triumphed?

Yes. The Democratic Center was there. It was everywhere. It had no centre, but thousands, millions.
strings.IBR_campaign.52.d:
The men and women of the Alianza Popular were invisible beneath the undulating canopy of red party flags they waved. Silva Street in Madrid could have driven a bull mad. Indeed, a certain madness was in the air around the Alianza Popular's headquarters - the euphoria of victory.

In the epicenter of the red maelstrom was Professor Manuel Fraga, gabbing with luminaries of the old regime and members of the AP's youth wing with the same facility and ease. A smiling Laureano López Rodó beckoned him over to the side of the hall with a proffered telephone, “Lisbon,” he said simply.

Fraga took the receiver to congratulate João Mota Campos in his own fluent Portuguese, barely pausing for a breath. “Victories up and down the Peninsula, João. Your west and my east as well. Oh, what a lovely evening!”

Over the headquarters' chants, cheers, and whistles, Fraga could barely hear Mota Campos' response, but what did it matter. He knew the words - they filled his ears, they floated through the very air he breathed.

The Iberian people had spoken them with one voice. They had demanded democracy. A democracy of order and laws. They had demanded Manuel Fraga's democracy.
strings.IBR_centrist.1.d:
João Miller Guerra stepped onto the podium with a smile stuck on his face. While he adjusted his microphone, he looked out to the crowd of hundreds if not thousands. Thousands who put their faith in him and his ideals.

“My fellow countrymen,” he began, “I've come here to thank you all for going out and voting for me. You all have many ideas and ambitions for our fair country, but one idea has united us all, the creation of a democracy to last for ages.”

As the crowd cheered, Guerra's mind went to his cabinet, a mess of social democrats, conservatives, even technocrats all united for democracy. As much as he had hoped that the group would work together in a beautiful display of unity, he knew that they would bicker. His mind returned to his speech as the crowd quieted, and he spoke again.

In El Pardo, Franco sat in front of the TV, rubbing his temples. This isn't how it was supposed to go, getting ambushed by fools like Guerra when he was old enough to be in a home. This should've been a victory lap for the Caudillo who unified Iberia. He wouldn't go down this way, he would thrash, bite, hit them back. Guerra would go down like Azaña or Caballero. He would be a footnote in Franco's story, a meager challenger. Franco stood up, and walked to bed. He was tired, but when he woke up, Guerra would face his might.
strings.IBR_centrist.2.d:
João Miller Guerra sat at the now silent cabinet table, thoughts warring between sentiments of frustration and hope. Both burned with potency, and Miller feared the promises of both. He looked to his side, seeing that his deputy Torcuato Fernández-Miranda seemed to be feeling much the same conflict. Had it been minutes or hours since the meeting? He doubted either of them would be sure until they left the current moment.

“... it could have gone much worse,” Torcuato suggested as he leaned forward upon the table, looking towards the vacant seats. “They were verbose, driven. We wanted change; here it is.”

João reflected on the thought. That was the hope that danced upon him; that the highest table in Iberia could have voices that even months ago would have risked a night in a cell at best? Change was messy, it always was, every evolution required a touch of chaos perhaps. However...

“It was also incredibly dysfunctional, Torcuato,” João responded, “We're pulling in different directions. Individualism and collectivism, both protecting and reforming societal norms, even contradictory policies. We have a Minister of Work insisting on policies running contrary to the proposals of the Minister of Economy just to name one. It wasn't a shouting match but...”

“It wasn't friendly,” Torcuato finished sorrowfully. They had always expected Democracy to be complicated, but for unity to already be degrading? Both of them reflected for a moment - how long could the centre hold? A pregnant silence held, until João felt cold resolve touch him like steel.

He stood up, walking to the door without turning back. “This is our moment, Torcuato. It falls to no one else but us. If Iberia's future currently rests upon a maze of paths...”
strings.IBR_centrist.2.a: “...then it is up to us to guide it through, and ensure it grows ever stronger and united.”
strings.IBR_centrist.3.d:
The Villamejor Palace chandeliers glittered high above, reminding Joaquim of his smallness in the grand scheme of Iberia. The suit he wore was borrowed from a cousin; its sleeves too long and its shoulders too broad. He shrank into it, praying no one noticed.

Democratic Center ministers argued with professors and lawyers and economists about the constitution, about the union's entire balance. Joaquim could barely follow the words as they ran circles around him.

He was no bureaucrat. He was the son of a dockworker, chosen only because his comrades needed someone to represent the union. His hands dripped with sweat as the ministers droned on about esoteric precedents that he hadn't ever heard of. His inner thoughts drowned out the speeches, whispers that told him he didn't belong.

But Joaquim remembered the faces back home. Rough. Sunburnt. But proud. When the invitation arrived, his union brothers slapped his back and cheered him on. He carried their only hopes for a better life. As the minister concluded his final remarks, the silence filling the air, Joaquim rose to his feet.

“Gentlemen,” he began with a wavering voice. “Although I admittedly could not follow all your words, I came here knowing what my men want. A constitution. Dignity for their labor. A fair share is all we ask... and we will not strike. Not while Iberia needs to stand united now more than ever.”

The words hung in the air. But it started with one hesitant clap. Then another. Swelling up into a roaring orchestra of applause, relief spread across the room like wildfire. For the first time that day, Joaquim stood tall, certain his brothers back home would get their wishes.
strings.IBR_centrist.4.d:
Miguel Alameda sat disheveled in his cell, a former proud member of CNT, he was captured during the Battle of Barcelona. The still young thirty year old quietly sat for weeks, he had watched as fellow comrades would continuously be escorted from their cells, originally thinking it signified death, the prisoners soon learned of the new amnesty program.

On the outside Miguel showed joy as his fellow comrades walked out of their cells, many of his friends, which he always believed were in the right, got to walk into the light of freedom. Deep down however, Miguel knew the light would never touch him.

Miguel had killed a civilian official, a man who the neighborhood feared as he tormented them with brutality. Miguel remembered the fighting on the streets, he never learned what started it but he knew what finished it, a silver bullet in the official's chest. He still held the last look of the official in mind, stored away almost with a hint of glee, but he knew it would mean he'd never touch the light.

That was until one day, a guard walked up to his cell asking, “Miguel Alameda Menéndez?”, he stood up in response, “Government says you're free to go.” Miguel stood frozen for a second not believing what he had heard. The guard nearly had to start dragging him for him to finally snap and walk out.

As he left the prison that light of freedom shined beams upon him, never in his life had rays of sunshine felt so liberating and joyous.
strings.IBR_centrist.4.a: He basked in the light of freedom.
strings.IBR_centrist.5.d:
It had been a few days since Miguel Alameda had been released, the former CNT fighter had spent his days wandering his old neighborhood, reliving his time during the Battle of Barcelona. It felt different now, more colorful, more laughter in the streets, people playing cards, somehow in a place Miguel had called his home all his life, he felt out of place, alone.

As Miguel was tracing his hand over one of the several bullet holes in the side of his former home, he spotted him, the other Franquist official sitting on a bench, head buried in the paper. Miguel had flashbacks remembering him, the man that terrorized his family, his neighbors, the one that extorted others under the protection of the government, the one whose friend and partner was killed by him.

Miguel's hands curled into themselves as he walked over, his mind racing what to do, confront him? Out him as who he was? Perhaps beat him to death for revenge? He watched the man, seemingly much older as he remembered, keeping his head down in the paper.

As Miguel was right behind the official he stopped, conflicted. He knew his actions would reflect that of all the members of the amnesty program, those that just like him were recently freed. Miguel, still conflicted, turns and walks away from the official, knowing that he may have just helped let another prisoner like him be let free.

Miguel left Barcelona that night, he couldn't stay around the memories or the official.
strings.IBR_centrist.5.a: Miguel heard Valencia is nice this time of year.
strings.IBR_centrist.6.d:
Outside a worn down dilapidated schoolhouse, a common site in Extemadura, sat the pompous and portly Minister of Education Íñigo Cavero y Lataillade, standing in front of a gathering of the school's children. But he was not lecturing to the students, but to the media posed outside the schoolhouse.

Íñigo Cavero continued his outline for the government's education reforms, they included new textbooks and materials for schools such as the one he posed in front of, more focus on university prep and an idea of having more kids enter higher education, he was changing the curriculum from being based around rote lecture, to being more participatory and involving more students.

Finishing the conference he stepped away from his podium and began to pack his papers as one of the kids in the photo-op ran to the minister, as he was showing the guards away the kid wrapped himself around the Íñigo's leg looking up in wonder, “Sir, are you our new teacher?”

Íñigo couldn't help but smile at the kid as the little ones' dimples appeared on each cheek, “I'm sorry but I can't be your teacher, I'm supposed to help all teachers, and I believe you already have a good one.”

The kid whined, “B-but I like you” he tightened himself around the minister.

“Don't worry little one.” he responded “I'll come back next year, see how much you all have learned and grown, promise.”

Íñigo Cavero left the school with possibly a bigger smile than the kids, reminding himself who he was doing this all for.
strings.IBR_centrist.6.a: And not a single camera caught it.
strings.IBR_centrist.7.d:
Isabella Méndez sat in the station with by far the nicest uniform, mainly from the part it was freshly tailored for her due to her being the first female officer in Valencia. During morning rollcall she had been paired with another young officer by the name of Gonzolo Navarra, Gonzolo originally protested this assignment not wanting to have to carry around what he thought was an overpaid secretary.

The two's first assignment was to a robbery at the local pharmacy owned by Mr. Saldaña. Inside the air was thick with the scent of antiseptics and broken glass. Shelves had been overturned, and the cash register lay open, its contents scattered across the floor. Isabella crouched near the counter, snapping photos and bagging a torn glove left behind.

Gonzolo, meanwhile, paced near the back exit, inspecting the doorframe. “Forced entry,” he muttered, “but no signs of a getaway vehicle.”

A sudden creak echoed from the storage room. Both officers froze. Gonzolo instinctively stepped in front of Isabella, but she pushed past him, weapon drawn. “I've got this,” she said firmly.

Inside, they found Mr. Saldaña cowering in the corner, Isabella rushed over to help him up hearing what she believed more thank yous in a minute than she heard her whole life. Gonzolo finally entered behind her asking if the man was okay and the evidence she had gathered.

“He just seems a little spooked still, but I've already got the robber's fingerprints, gloves, and he dropped his wallet.” Isabella couldn't hold back her grin.

Gonzolo froze in shock before gathering himself, “Works done I guess, drinks?”
strings.IBR_centrist.7.a: A glass sounded good after a hard day's work.
strings.IBR_centrist.8.d:
The smoke curled lazily, fading into the café's soft background chatter. Alesander flicked the cigarette ashes into the saucer, eyes fixed on the newspaper spread before him. No one seemed to notice him reading the print upside down.

Outside, Irún went about its business. Carts rattled and children darted around the marketplace. But Alesander glued his eyes on the soldiers slouched around their post. Every morning, he counted their numbers. One. Two. Three. But today had only half of the usual patrol.

Instead, pale strangers in suits filled their place. Notebooks in hand. Whispers being exchanged. To Alesander, any man associated with the Axencia Anti-Separatista was bad news. His stomach knotted. He only expected rifles this morning, not the secret police.

He risked another glance at them, but it was too late. One of the suited men met Alesander's eyes. For a heartbeat, no one moved. Then, with a deliberate calm, the man crossed the street over and entered the café.

He ordered a café con leche in flawless Castillan, then sat directly across from Alesander. No files were opened. No sips were taken. Just a smile. A slow, knowing curl of the lips no further than a meter away from Alesander's face. That kind of smile that knew what kind of boy Alesander was.

The seconds dragged unbearably on. Alesander's cigarette burned down to the filter, his hands trembling. Finally, in a flash, Alesander shoved the paper aside and fled into the street, heart pounding and leaving behind his untouched coffee. All he could see was the man's smile, waiting patiently.
strings.IBR_centrist.9.d:
Officer Isabella Méndez's brain was racing but she didn't let that show as she walked into the pharmacy, the same one she was at not so long ago. Mr. Saldaña, the store owner, recognizing her quickly rushed over to her asking how she's been.

Isabella quickly opened up to Saldaña, explaining how she and her partner Gonzolo went on a date together and, while she wants to take the relationship further, she's direly worried a pregnancy would end her career before it began.

“So I came here asking about those new pills the government legalized, the birth control pills.”

The clerk stuttered before responding that, “Sadly, the regulations on them mean they can be provided only to married couples, so because you and Gonzolo are only dating...” Isabella quickly slumped, realizing the situation, and the possibility her policing career might end as quickly as it began. While still in thought however, Mr. Saldaña dragged her to the back.

“Before you go, I wanted to show you my new cameras. I took your recommendation and they work wonders, haven't had a robbery since.” Mr. Saldaña beamed as Isabella snapped out of her thoughts. “As a gift I'll give you these, just don't tell anyone” Isabella felt a package get snuck into her hands, looking down it was a box of pills.

“B-but Mr. Saldaña, I can't accept these if they're illegal, I'll... I'll find another way.”

“Are you sure, nobody will know, it'll last you a year at least,” Mr. Saldaña responded, trying to reassure her.

“No,” Isabella held firm.
strings.IBR_centrist.9.a: “What's an officer of the law if they break it?”
strings.IBR_centrist.10.d:
“My apologies about the walls, they're supposed to be repaired soon,” said Emiliano, the warden of Fort San Cristóbal. Joaquín Ruiz-Giménez had decided to pay a visit to his prison, much to the chagrin of the warden and his staff. “I assume the rat problem is to be fixed soon as well?” asked Joaquín.“Of course,” replied the warden, “the exterminators should be arriving tomorrow.” Joaquín was giving him a grilling, he was practically sweating when the tour got to solitary, the prisoners groaning, some crying.

Thankfully for Emiliano, the tour ended soon after, and the embarrassment somewhat ceased. Before exiting, Joaquín looked back at Emiliano, and the posse of guards that had escorted the two, and asked them a question. “Aside from... improving the prisoner's conditions,” he put nicely, not wanting to insult the warden's disregard for decency, “Do any of you have any suggestions for how to improve this establishment.”

The group stayed silent for a while, as Joaquín looked over them, waiting for an answer. They were scared of him, and their warden. Eventually, a guard stepped up, cleaning his voice before saying, “I believe that a library would be a good addition for the prisoners, so that they can educate themselves for future opportunities,” he added a “sir” a moment after, wanting to appear professional. Joaquín looked the man over, “That sounds like a fine idea,” he smiled, “I'll be sure to donate some of my personal favorites mister...” he looked at the guard's nametag, 'Santiago'. With that he left, making sure to keep in mind Santiago, a perfect replacement once the old Francoist warden was gone.
strings.IBR_centrist.11.d:
They were out for him. Franco knew it. They were replacing everyone, his guard, his driver, everyone. They were all spying on him, and they thought he would just sit and take it. As if! A civil war couldn't stop him, and these politicians with their pitiful election wouldn't stop him either.

His limo was driving through Charmartin, home of the new embassies and upscale homes in Madrid. He was to meet Franz Koebel, a hot shot businessman in the Pakt. With his resources, and a little luck, those centrists would be sent scrambling and Franco would be back on top.

To a rational person, these were thoughts of a man who should be in a home, to Franco, they were all he had. His guard and driver knew what he was planning, he could try and sneak around, but they could assume what he was planning to do when he met with a rich Pakt man. Maybe it was pity, or respect, but they just let him go on with these delusions.

Suddenly, Franco ordered the limo to stop, which he promptly did. The old general stepped out and looked at a street sign being taken down, Avenida del Generalísimo, his street. A new one replaced it, Paseo de la Castellana, the street's old name. He stood there for a while. “Sir?” called out the driver, “You're going to be late for your appointment.” Franco walked back, entered the limo, sank in his seat, and calmly said...
strings.IBR_centrist.11.a: “I think the old name was better.”
strings.IBR_centrist.12.t: The Green Book of Financial Reforms
strings.IBR_centrist.12.d:
Rubio was finally able to clock out for the night. Since he opened at eight that morning, there was an endless stream of clients, new and old, entering his little office in Santander asking him to fix some of the less legal parts of their finances. This had been life since last Monday, when the government had announced laws to make the banking system more transparent.

After this wave, he would retire. Not out of want but out of necessity. All the tricks that he made his career with would be old soon enough, and new accountants would take his place. He was a bygone of a past era, but he could still get a few more jobs done.

He stretched his arms, kicked off his shoes. One last file, pro bono. The most fraudulent and corrupt one he worked on. A mess that could only exist when the government was too busy battling itself to care about tax fraud. He pulled out the file...
strings.IBR_centrist.13.d:
Minister of Economy Fuentes Quintana surveyed the table in front of him, mentally preparing for another two hours of endless arguments. The ministry's economists have prepared a list of suggested fixed prices for most major staples and monopoly products, in order to help resuscitate the Iberian consumer sector, and hopefully not drag the manufacturing sector down with it.

Of course, neither sector was pleased with the result. A long list of corporates have sent their representatives to air their grievances, their thick stacks of ledgers and neatly typed handouts eloquently detailing the business community's consensus on the proposed prices - they must be increased, in order to prevent profits from dropping, reinvestment from plunging, and scarcity from rearing its ugly head. All in all, it was nothing Quintana hadn't seen before, though the level of unanimity among different and competing corporates was impressive.

On the other side of the table, the somewhat drab representatives of the consumers' association murmured between themselves. They had no ledgers or folders, and Quintana wondered how they intended to plead their case, before one of them, a balding man in his fifties, picked up a grocery bag and a receipt and placed them on the table before Quintana's suddenly wide-open eyes.

A woman next to him opened a small notebook and began reading a list of quotes. A laborer from Valencia who had told the association that he could not cut any more meals without losing his home. A middle-class family from Málaga where both parents had to take on second jobs to pay for their daughters' education. A woman from Porto claiming that the factory accident she had recently experienced had crippled her economically, more than physically. The corporate representatives booed the “populist theater”, but Quintana could see that some of his ministry's functionaries were genuinely moved. In the end, however, the choice was his.
strings.IBR_centrist.13.a: The data doesn't lie - we can't let ourselves be swayed by theatrics.
strings.IBR_centrist.13.b: Compromise is when no one is happy, isn't it?
strings.IBR_centrist.13.c: Consumption has been cut to the bone, and it's not the consumers' fault.
strings.IBR_centrist.14.d:
Juan wiped his mouth with a kerchief, leaning back in his chair. He didn't have many opportunities to meet Miguel since moving to Burgos, and they had much to fill each other up on. Perhaps too much - their conversation had blown well past lunch break and into the second half of the workday.

“Well, that was lovely, Miguel, but I think we should ask for the bill, don't we? Those banknotes won't print themselves”.

Miguel shrugged, snuffing out his cigarette in the ashtray. “I mean, we could. But ever since the government started on its deflationary measures, we really only have half as much work as we used to. Less money to print, less oversight to do, you know how it is. So really, it's no issue.”

Juan raised his eyebrow. “Sounds nice. More time to spend with Maria and the kids is always good. But is the policy working?”

Miguel grinned. “See for yourself.” He turned back in his chair and flagged down their waiter, asking for the bill. “We've ordered our regular lunch, just like last month, correct?”

Juan nodded. “I believe we have.”

Miguel leaned forward. “And you don't need me to tell you how it always gets more expensive to get a decent lunch around here, do you? Now, wait and see.”

The waiter came back with the bill, but before paying, Miguel took the small paper and waved it at Juan like a saber. “Look! It cost exactly the same as last month, my friend.”
strings.IBR_centrist.14.a: A few minutes later, Miguel was on his way back to work - but with no rush.
strings.IBR_centrist.15.d:
Minister of Economy Fuentes Quintana sipped what felt like his tenth cup of coffee that day, a pile of papers and folders separating him from Minister of Finance Fernández Ordóñez. The inflationary surge rocking Iberia's economy has wreaked havoc on their plans for balanced economic growth, but following a seemingly endless series of boardroom meetings and sleepless nights, Quintana had a plan to present to Ordóñez.

“The main idea is for us to link wage growth with the projected price increases, in order to maintain public consumption, and to stay ahead of public anger, so to speak. Additionally, we could offer tax breaks to firms in order to encourage them to maintain as many of their current employees as possible.”

Ordóñez took a sip of his own cup of coffee, then put his hands together, thinking for a moment before responding. “I'll need to have a look at the details, but in principle, I support the idea. We absolutely need to stay ahead of the curve on inflation, and if handled well, this could allow us to do that. My worry is that if we miscalculate and drive wages too high, these wages will themselves contribute to further inflation. And with the world financial situation being what it is, there's going to be a higher chance of miscalculation.”

Quintana nodded. “Of course. Which is one of the reasons I wanted to have this talk with you. Details are of course still to be hashed out, but we need to decide which projections to use as a benchmark to base the wage increases on. It all depends on how much turbulence we expect. What do you say, Fernández?”
strings.IBR_centrist.15.a: “With everything going on, businesses are going to have to open their pocketbooks...”
strings.IBR_centrist.15.b: “...but we can't gamble our future on the most extreme projections being correct.”
strings.IBR_centrist.16.d:
Night was falling over the great landmass that humans called Iberia, and the large flock of swallows making its yearly journey from North Africa to Europe was preparing to rest at the cliffs they have made into their temporary home for thousands of years. While human kingdoms, republics, and unions rose, fell, and rose again, a constant generational flux, the swallows' migration path remained unchanged for millennia, unaware of the drama unfolding below.

But this time, the human world has asserted its influence over that of the flock. As the sun set and the flock was descending towards the river they usually overlooked on this part of their journey north, the cliffs they have always inhabited were gone. A massive lake stood in their place, the water dark and still in the twilight.

The flock rose again, confused and scattered, searching for a place to spend the night. The swallows overflew a massive wall of grey concrete and rushing waters, crowned by glowing lights and a tangle of metal columns and wires. They could not, perhaps, comprehend the dam's real purpose, but the forest of transmission lines and columns could serve their purposes well enough.

The next morning rose, and the flock continued north, its journey almost undisturbed. The short, unintentional interaction between the two worlds had ended. The humans would continue to survive, strive, and struggle in their fleeting and social structures. The flock would maintain its ancient path, with minor modifications, as uncaring as the stars above for the humans' structures below.
strings.IBR_centrist.17.d:
The small meeting room, tucked in one of the upper floors of the Ministry of Economy building, was the site of a heated, if respectful, debate. President João Miller Guerra sat, hands clasped tight, before Economy Minister Fuentes Quintana and Finance Minister Fernández Ordóñez as the two lay out their competing economic visions. It was quite the headache, but it was one he had to adjudicate. “You were saying, Francisco?”

Fernández shuffled his papers once more before finding the one he was looking for. “Yes, Señor Miller. As we've discussed, the sudden windfall we have found ourselves with after cutting business subsidies needs to be accounted for and spent somewhere productive. And the most productive thing this money can do for us is to promote employment.” Quintana rolled his eyes to the side, but Fernández didn't notice, or didn't care. “The treasury needs taxpayers and the country needs stability if we want the promulgation of the new Constitution to proceed apace.”

Quintana barged into his colleague's words. “I'm sorry, but if we want social stability, we need the people to see that we are here for them and that we are keen on addressing their current economic challenges. We need to support small and medium businesses who can barely keep their workers employed as things stand, not the massive tycoons who'll be able to keep the lights on in any case. If we buy the loyalty of emerging businesses now, we'll be able to reap the profits when they become the next decade's economic elite.”

Fernández attempted to respond, already pulling out another folder, but Miller interjected. “Enough, Francisco. We can all agree that this endless bickering is the least productive option for the money. Let's settle on a decision.”
strings.IBR_centrist.17.a: More money won't help without anyone to spend it.
strings.IBR_centrist.17.b: More consumers won't help without anyone to buy from.
strings.IBR_centrist.18.d:
The morning papers had made for increasingly fascinating, if disconcerting, reading in recent weeks.

Manuel Fraga had settled into a routine since the election disappointment. Every morning he settled with a simple breakfast, an omelet with some tea, and read the financial papers. He was pouring for detail, relishing in the spartan search. Simplicity was the focus - half an hour dedicated to finding easy chinks in the armour of the fools running the nation.

During the election he had warned the Iberians of the inevitable mistakes, and he didn't really consider them to have not listened. No one truly won the elections, he wouldn't call that loose rabble coalition victor of anything. Iberians had been presented with too much choice too quickly and indulged, picking nearly everyone. They would see the stability he offered, not the exploitative liberalism of the Democratic Center, in due course.

At least, that was the plan. Last month, tax breaks had been conditioned on maintaining employment. Last week, subsidies had been redistributed in favor of small to medium sized enterprises. This morning, minor news on sick leave requirements being eased. The trend was undeniable - the Democratic Center hadn't become quite the slaves to corporate interests he had claimed.

Today, however, the answer struck him. They did well to bypass his warnings, but could they sustain it? Doubtful, but no doubt industry was less than happy. If those titans of industry suddenly had a friend capable of balancing both the nation and their interests? The coalition would only realise they were outmaneuvered when it was too late.

He walked to the phone, opening the drawer underneath and pulling out a notebook. It burst with phone numbers, and Fraga calmly keyed the first one in the long list.
strings.IBR_centrist.18.a: “Señor Marqués? Manuel Fraga. I think we have some fascinating things to discuss...”
strings.IBR_centrist.19.d:
The truck groaned as its cargo was hauled into the squat warehouse. A filing cabinet was wrestled through narrow doorways, being carried into a musty office that emitted no homely warmth.

Senhor Carvalho rubbed his temples. “Absolutely marvelous,” he muttered. “What a dump they moved us into. All so the ministers can claim they've begun 'developing the interior.'” He gestured at the dust-coated windows, the plaster walls oozing with grease and other unknown slimes.

“Instead of a walk across the street, I gotta book a train to meet some bureaucrats,” Carvalho sighed. “Instead of a dinner, I gotta send about twenty letters to speak to a contractor about manufacturing bullets.”

Mendes, his young subordinate, nodded dutifully, though his mind wandered. He missed the lights of Lisbon more than anything. The crowded bars. The mellow guitar hymns. The bottles passed between comrades. Here, only the hollow church bells clanged as the day ended.

As the last of the laborers placed down the cabinet, one approached Carvalho. Hat in hand, he hesitated before clearing his throat. “Senhores,” he said shyly, “some of us meet at the local shooting club a couple of streets from here. You would be more than welcome... as a thank you for coming here.”

Carvalho blinked. Mendes looked up. For a moment, there was silence before Carvalho softly chuckled. “Perhaps,” Carvalho said, “this exile won't be so bad after all, eh, Mendes?”

The laborer grinned. Outside, the sun dipped below the Portuguese hills, and the arms of Iberia found a new rhythm in their forgotten heartland.
strings.IBR_centrist.20.d:
“Esteemed members of the Constitutional Commission. We are here to inaugurate the first committee session in our most grand and noble cause,” Deputy President Torcuato Fernández-Miranda looked out from the rostrum at the members, their eyes fixed upon him. The Centrists had looked upon him with hope, but the National Conservatives on the other side of the aisle viewed him with deep suspicion. If this commission were to succeed, he would need to ensure that, at the very least, they were receptive enough not to sabotage the proceedings.

“The Iberian Union has been many things to many people, but the one thing it has always been since its foundation is a nation of laws. The foundation of our society has been that we are, as a nation, trusted by all within it to do as we promise we would. That our laws are not just guidelines to follow, but duties to uphold. As a building is built, brick by brick, so too are our laws the scaffolding upon which our nation is founded. And so we come to our pillars, our foundation. We must set forth, legally, democratically, and transparently, the Constitution that forms the basis of our laws. When we write Iberia's laws, we must look to our Constitution and say that this is from where we derive our authority. So in this, we are not wiping the slate clean, but building upon what came before, holding those legal traditions as precedent to guide us into what comes next. Neither past nor future, but both, all at once.”

Applause erupted, with the Centrists showing their support as bound by legislative decorum. But when Torcuato looked over, he saw acceptance from the Conservatives. A few looked almost excited, but even the professional dispassion of the majority was enough to say: go forth and build, for this is a nation for us all.
strings.IBR_centrist.20.a: The greatest support is given not by the loudest of supporters, but the quietest of detractors.
strings.IBR_centrist.21.d:
It was a colder day than usual in Cádiz as David entered his humble familial home and traded the fading colours of his old uniform for more comfortable clothes.

Grabbing the newspaper he bought, he sat down near the window to allow the sunlight into the room and squinted his eyes to parse through the small black letters. As he started making out more and more words, a fire grew inside his heart, anger threatening to overtake him.

Just a few decades ago, David had fought, killed and bled for Franco. He had sacrificed comrades, friends and even a brother to the Nationalist cause. To restore Spain to greatness. To keep out the Marxist-Atheist threat and all their godless lackeys at bay. To protect Spain's Catholic identity. And now the liberal atheist-socialists came and forced through their project to destroy everything that he had fought for. And what was Franco doing? Grown weak and docile since the Civil War days. A disgrace.

David was not stupid, no amount of bickering and blame-shifting would keep him from seeing that bread got ever more expensive, or that his son had to move to Portugal for work, and with gas so expensive, he could not come visit to gladden his old heart.

David neatly folded the newspaper and placed it on the table, before opening the window and looking outside. Tomorrow, he'd pay whatever it takes to go to the military graveyard and visit those who had shed their lives for Spain so many years ago. Their deaths had been bemoaned by their families when they were buried, but in truth, it was for the best...
strings.IBR_centrist.21.a: From the grave, they will not suffer in disgust from Spain becoming an atheist state.
strings.IBR_centrist.22.d:
Along his campaign trail, Manuel Fraga had made many connections across Iberia, whether friends or foes, through which the Alianza Popular established itself as a dominant force in national politics, despite facing a resounding defeat in electoral votes. From then on, there was little more to endeavour towards besides better preparing for the next one. Fortunately, the solutions proved to be a short list of a few but substantial matters. Moving forward, Fraga must organize both the Youth Front and the bureaucrats for the storm; on advocacies, on fighting the Constitutional Commission, the AP can only build upon its current base of good Christians.

Mowing through press releases after another, Fraga was an unstoppable juggernaut of industry, albeit one which happened to have its path stopped by a good-for-nothing secretary knowing nothing save to irritate. “I believe Mister Miller Guerra had reserved a private meeting with you four days ago, he had just arrived outside of the office.”

“Good, let him in. You are now dismissed.”

The bespectacled President entered with empty hands, yet he evidently had brought a gift to the enterprising Conservative, and with much immediacy, he made his intent fully clear, “Mister Fraga, you had made it your work to fight against the Constitutional Commission as a matter of principle, which is most certainly a respectable position. But I implore you to give our project another chance, and henceforth, if you so desire, I shall offer you a stake in the Commission itself.”

Somehow, it had taken less than even he had expected to break the Centrists. In other times, this may just be an immediate cause for rejoice, but given the amount of authority he may soon command, with so many more plans to destroy the Centrist government, the champagne can wait — no proper hero had ever done great deeds drunk.
strings.IBR_centrist.22.a: Along with a firm handshake, Fraga replied, “Thank you, truly.”
strings.IBR_centrist.23.d:
“Can you believe this David? What a snake!” Alberto put the newspaper in front of David's nose, covering the latter's access to his omelette just as he was about to scoop up a piece of potato to eat. “And to think I voted National Conservative last elections, just for Fraga to side with the liberal atheists and join the Constitutional Commission. Bah, all politicians are the same! Ambition over nation isn't that right David?”

David for his part gently pushed the fellow veteran's newspaper away before speaking “I didn't even bother voting last time. Knew something was up with him. What's his excuse?”

“Lies, of course. He says this compromise is in the interest of Iberia and that is better for the constitution be co-authored by responsible parties rather than to allow the opposition free rein over it to legalise terrorism and crime, and have the constitution fail in its duties. Absolutely ridiculous, isn't it?”

David took a scoop of his omelette and munched for a full minute while pensively looking at the bar's entrance before finally answering. “Well this will certainly not backfire”, he said, suppressing his internal monologue.
strings.IBR_centrist.23.a: At least this way we can all move on from this sorry affair.
strings.IBR_centrist.24.d:
What blesses the Union with more boons than her bountiful agriculture? For many, both within the Iberian government and without, there is no greater ideal to strive for than that of agrarianism, and they have made it a priority to see the peninsula's golden fields continue to expand unabated, even at the chagrin of the urbanist class.

One such proponent of this ideal is João Mota Pereira de Campos, an accomplished jurist and dogged disciple of Salazar who remains one of the key National Conservative voices within the Constitutional Commission. Time and time again, he attempts to force through increasingly detailed and demanding protections for rural workers—often of corporatist design—earning him the shameless loyalty of the rural masses, though at the cost of grinding the commission's procedures to an effective halt each time.

“It's mind-numbing,” spoke Torcuato Fernández-Miranda, a cigarette firmly tucked between his lips. Miller Guerra murmured quietly, prompting Torcuato to face him. “If he continues on like this, the deadlock will only worsen. He must be reappointed, perhaps to some...” He mulled over his words momentarily before nodding quietly. “A foreign policy subcommittee. That should keep him busy.”

Miller Guerra smiled, shrugging broadly. “Why not just give him what he wants? Even if it is a victory for the National Conservatives, it's a short-term one at that. Sometimes, the carrot should precede the stick, no? Keeps them satiated.” Torcuato sighed, moving towards a nearby window and peeling open its curtains. In the distance, green and yellow vineyards could be seen upon the horizon.
strings.IBR_centrist.24.a: “I believe it's time for Campos to represent our interests abroad.”
strings.IBR_centrist.24.b: “...You're right. Throw the dog a bone.”
strings.IBR_centrist.25.d:
The air in the Constitutional Commission's meeting room had already gotten dangerously stale and suffocating. “If democracy in Iberia is ever going to be anything more than a farce, then the universities have to be protected. The Church needs to get out, the army needs to get out, and some proper guarantees of political independence written into the constitution itself!” Henrique de Barros - a professor, longtime opposition figure, and brother-in-law to Caetano - ended his final spiel of the discussion with a face reddened by lack of oxygen and ample frustration. “Deputy President, you must give me your assurances that this will be included.”

Before Torcuato Fernández-Miranda even had a chance to answer, the National Conservative side of the room erupted with anger, the loudest amongst them slamming his fist into the table. “Deputy President, this is outrageous! This... socialist,” he spat out the accusation, “wants to undermine the very basis of higher education! Without any sort of academic discipline, we will have student riots on our hands every other week. This cannot be allowed!” The professor took none of it lying down, and soon the sound of shouting joined the hammering of pain in Torcuato's temples.

With several calming hand gestures, Torcuato eventually got control of the chamber again. “There will be some protections for the universities in the final constitution, but this is not the place to be discussing the specifics. That will be up to the legislature on a later date.” Without a moment to catch his breath or let the other members of the Constitutional Commission interrupt, Torcuato continued. “With that done, we should move on to the next item on the agenda.”

Neither Henrique de Barros nor the National Conservatives looked anything resembling satisfied, and they would no doubt find some way to continue to pester him on the subject at the earliest possible inconvenience. At the very least, they would save more of their shouting for the next round of discussion, of which there seemed to be no end.
strings.IBR_centrist.25.a: What he wouldn't give for some fresh air.
strings.IBR_centrist.26.d:
The two most notable religious exiles in Iberia, Archbishop Vicente Enrique y Tarancón and his fellow reformist, Bishop António Ferreira Gomes, hastily boarded off from their transport to meet João de Freitas Cruz, Iberia's Minister of Foreign Affairs. Despite the invitation issued by the government to invite back the duo being a discreet one, for much of the Christian masses such a curious event proved difficult to keep private.

While press and publicity teams across the nation swarmed the jet-lagged deacons, an unimpressive, fairly overweight man entered, followed by an armada of cameras. He soon approached the holy men with little more reverence for the Lord than he had for their privacy. “They only want a quick portrait of us three. I am João de Freitas Cruz, and no need for the formalities, I shall disperse them for now if you feel discomforted,” the bespectacled diplomat waved off the reporters before leading the bishops to their meeting place.

As they stepped into the open venue, Bishop Gomes sneered at the frivolity Iberia had tried to impose on an intentionally humble meeting, the Archbishop too felt similarly insulted. However, they immediately resumed their composure as this brief reprieve from the spotlight swiftly ended, reminded of the dozens of men and women standing outside the gates.

Customary to Iberia's request, the two first made a lengthy lecture on the need to re-embrace pluralism, primarily to voice their support for the draft Constitution's secularization. Most importantly, to address the diplomat himself, they offered a short list of trustworthy contacts to facilitate the state's collaboration with the Vatican's faculties, which of course had to be suffixed with a warning for caution. As quick as Mister Freitas Cruz had arrived, he left soon enough with a satisfied grin photographed across the papers. Ferreira took his well-earned deep breath before confiding to Gomes, “Will this peace be worth abandoning God?”
strings.IBR_centrist.26.a: Ferreira shrugged, “Better late than never, time will not lie.”
strings.IBR_centrist.27.d:
David knelt in prayer, as he did every Sunday in Cádiz's Cathedral of the Holy Cross over the Waters. Patiently listening to the priest's homilies, he could not help but let a deep sense of sadness settle in his heart. It would soon be three years since his wife Juana joined the Lord in his glorious abode, and four since his son moved to Portugal to find work. Without his family, he had little to look forward to in his life, and even fewer people to talk to.

David partook in Communion, then, after lighting candles and praying for his son, the daughter-in-law he had never met, and his departed wife, he approached the priest to seek comfort.

“Father, I have felt so lonely, and the Lord is the only thing that brings me comfort now in my old age. My wife has departed, and all my remaining family is in Portugal. Given the state of the country, I find it challenging to focus on repentance in my final years. Why, the atheist-communists are on the brink of taking over the country! How do you remain so calm despite these attacks on Christianity itself?”

The priest could see the fear in the old veteran's eyes, and while he could not claim to be a supporter of the political changes, accentuating the elder's anxieties would surely be a worse sin. “My son, you need not worry yourself with politics and rumours at your venerable age. God has given you long life and a healthy son; be grateful for what you have, and fret not the future. The Church will never stop working for the salvation of every soul in this good country; this has been assured by His Holiness through an agreement with the government. If God wills it, I and the Cathedral shall always be here to provide you with comfort and spiritual guidance whenever you require it.”

David's heart felt significantly lighter as he exited the Cathedral and walked home, a discreet thought entering his mind...
strings.IBR_centrist.27.a: Maybe this Constitution won't ruin everything just yet..
strings.IBR_centrist.28.d:
Henrique de Barros looked across the table at Caudillo Caetano. Marriage had made them brothers through his sister Teresa, but politics had divided them. Caetano, the titan of Portugal and Henrique, the long-standing pillar of the opposition. The Caudillo finished sipping his coffee and began to speak, barely able to hide the bitter envy in his voice, as dark as the rich brew they were drinking, though there seemed a slight taste of sweet, a genuine curiosity. “How goes the drafting of the new Constitution?”

That question had been anticipated and had been the purpose for his reason for coming. Henrique had volunteered to go, it would have been much better coming from family than from a longtime foe or a stranger. It was a small mercy, of course, but small mercies, like drops of cream, made bitter pills go down smoother.

“Very well. We have finished some of the key structures, outlined the basics of what institution holds what powers, what checks and balances they have on each other, just to ensure everything runs smoothly. Most of the power will be with the legislation, of course. You will of course be named the President of Portugal, one of two public personas of the Iberian Union, with President Franco acting as your counterpart for Spain. While you will be appointed, future Presidents will be elected.”

“Nothing formal though, save perhaps the idle ceremonial opening of Parliament sessions.”

Henrique swallowed. “Not as such, no.”

Caetano started to chuckle, then laugh, with something that sounded like an interspersed sob mixed in among the bitter laughter. Among the only words he could sputter out, Henrique made out “if only,” and wondered what, among the many things that had led to this point, that Caetano regretted most.
strings.IBR_centrist.28.a: It could have all been so different...
strings.IBR_centrist.29.d:
Franco had heard the motorbike coming up to the front doors of El Pardo and knew to expect a visitor long before his butler alerted him that there was someone in the front hall, bearing a message to be hand-delivered to him regarding the constitutional deliberations. Franco chuckled, thinking back to the days where he could just sack a minister if they were poorly performing. But now, everything would take days and weeks. The prosperity he had built could weather it, but it would certainly be a burden. He dismissed the courier and took the letter to read in his study.

“To the Esteemed Francisco Franco:

The Parliament has come to a unanimous decision regarding the position of the Caudillos in the new Constitution. Owing to the democratic nature of the Iberian government, the position of Caudillo will be abolished, with a new presidential position for the public persona of the Iberian Union, one for Spain and one for Portugal. In recognition of your long service to Iberia, the Parliament will appoint you as the First President of Spain, to serve a full term, with succeeding Presidents being elected as per constitutional guidelines.”

Franco held the letter in his hands; after a second they started to tremble. All his life he had prided himself on his military bearing. When facing the fires of civil war or forging a new nation to stand strong in the new world, he had borne it all with the stoic resolve of a soldier. His prize for all his efforts was not just to be discarded, but paraded about like a show pet, so the Parliament could remind themselves of their victorious revolt whenever they pleased. With a snarl, he tore the letter to shreds, throwing the pieces across his desk. After he threw them, Franco looked at his hands, flushed but the knobby knuckles and wrinkled skin were still apparent. These hands that had built a nation, now so old, so tired, that they could do little more than tear a piece of paper, and do nothing about the insult written upon it.
strings.IBR_centrist.29.a: Franco's only solace was that he knew that this humiliation would not be long.
strings.IBR_centrist.30.d:
“Better than screaming inside that miserable chamber, is it not?” Manuel Clavero knew neither he nor Fraga had much patience for small talk, but this was a last-ditch sale; there would be no winner in the matter until he at least swayed the conservative bulldog to gain a modicum of sympathy.

“Never had I thought of myself as anything but a Spaniard, just as any other of our countrymen. A policy to break our national unity is a policy to weaken Galicia's place in the world, one which I most believe to be long overdue for a promotion. From what I am witnessing, your suggestion is akin to suggesting an amputation for a slight ailment amounting to little more than a flu.”

“Mr. Fraga, can you not see...” It took not a moment for Fraga to resume his ranting state, giving no time for the bureaucrat to pick up his pace.

“With all due respect, Minister Clavero, we are one nation, not a confederation. A policy to cast ruin upon the pillar of centralization dooms us to become little better than feudal savages. I am a Galician, yet there was never a Republic of Galicia, only a Galician people with their own dialects and customs. Nevertheless, if this is a compromise necessary to keep the constitution on its lifeline, then perhaps the ailment can be seen more so as a gangrene than a flu.”

“Please understand that this is a compromise on everyone's part. I abandoned Andalucía for the sake of elevating our northern friends to gain the self-determination they have earned. An inevitable tragedy, really. No one is getting what they want, but they are getting what they need, for the time being.”

After a slow sigh, Manuel Fraga gripped his cup of coffee upright, then he made a mock-gesture, as if reaching out for a toast. “Long live Iberia?”
strings.IBR_centrist.30.a: Clavero loosened up, “One day, there will be coffee for us all.”
strings.IBR_centrist.31.d:
The Reus plaza thrummed with life as crowds gathered around to celebrate Catalonia's newfound autonomy. Brass bands clashed as church bells rang above, children sprinted around the cobblestone streets, and fruit filled the air with a sweet tang. At the center, the castellers gathered. Their white trousers flashed as they linked arms together to create a tower of people.

The base locked together first, shoulders pressed to shoulders and bodies bracing until the mass looked more like stone rather than flesh. Then came the layers. Each man climbed in groups of four, trusting the hundreds below to bear the strain. Each step, each climb, a renewed burden on those below, but one they had to accept to keep moving forward as a union.

But the tower swayed, and muscles buckled. For a heartbeat, the castell looked like it would collapse. But the men at the bottom gritted their teeth and persisted. Accidents were not rare. Bones broke and lungs collapsed. But everyone stepped up to the plate for those who couldn't. The climbers pressed higher, bound by a pride that one failure would mean shame to all.

Near the summit, children scrambled up their fathers. The spectating crowd held their breath as the smallest boy stood at the top, legs trembling. He hesitated before raising his hand high, completing the tower of forty feet high with one defiant salute.

Applause roared from the crowd. Some wept, some sang, and all knew that they had just witnessed more than just a mere spectacle. Although fragile and perilous, the castell was many bodies formed into one, depending on each other. For Reus, for Catalonia, for Iberia itself, it was a glimpse of unity.
strings.IBR_centrist.32.d:
The marble floors of Malabo City Hall echoed under his shoes as he walked the corridors for the very last time. As the sunlight filtered through the shutters, illuminating the air around him, the civil administrator couldn't help but give an exhausted smile. Behind him, the members of the African council furiously debated, with their voices carrying themselves down the corridor.

Months of patient maneuvering, and finally, he'd done it. He'd balanced the Bubi and Fernandino minorities to unite against the nationalist Fang majority, ensuring that Equatorial Guinea would remain in perpetual political deadlock. Though united, they hated each other enough to make sure no bloc would ever last the test of time.

In the meantime, their followers would be increasingly alienated by the radicalist Fang politicians, like one of the young men right now ranting about how Hitler had intended to liberate Africa instead of Europe. But Iberia would eventually depart, and the order it created would last for years to come.

The raised voices reminded him of Madrid's own ministries, where arguments would endlessly drag on. In a way, the experiment in Equatorial Guinea had been a learning experience about the futility of debating human ambition.

On the steps, his African chauffeur waited. “I think it's finally time we return home, Manuel. I can't stand that train wreck for one more moment.” The chauffeur nodded, smiling as he turned on the radio. Iberia's constitutional debates could be heard in the background of the dry summer sun. Just as loud, just as divided, echoing across the Atlantic.
strings.IBR_centrist.33.d:
Aside from the scratch of his pen, the judge's office was completely silent. Papers were stacked high with ledgers, contracts, handwritten notes, transcripts, all pertaining to the inheritance case of António Champalimaud, Portugal's richest man. Even as each page sagged with the weight of gold, the law demanded his uninterrupted, impartial attention.

He leaned back, giving a loud exhale. An industry titan like Champalimaud had his web woven around everywhere, including the corridors of the government. His connections with politicians were no secret, and the judge had no illusions about whatever pressures may come.

His secretary knocked softly, stepping in hesitantly. “The mayor of Lisbon is on the line, Señor,” she said timidly. “He asked to speak with you directly.”

The judge perked up. A familiar tug of both ambition and fear woke him up from his monotonous work. All it took was a single phone call to smoothen paths. To curry favors. To accelerate his way to a higher position.

But something firm pulled at his chest. He remembered the ideals that had brought him here, that carried his dreams back in his childhood, the reason he chose to don his robes over wearing a silk linen suit and tie. Whoever Champalimaud planned to cheat was worth more than this call.

“Tell him,” he said finally, “I'm too busy on the Champalimaud case. He would understand, of course.”

The secretary paused, then nodded. The judge returned to the documents, the night deepening outside. For one moment, even if it was a short one, the law—not wealth—would have its way in Iberia.
strings.IBR_centrist.33.a: “Quite frankly, I never liked the mayor anyway...”
strings.IBR_centrist.34.d:
Early morning coffee still sluggishly attempted to fuel Fuentes Quintana as he placed the dossiers for the men sitting across from him. Night still reigned outside the meeting room, too dark for such a meeting in any normal situation, but the blackness matched his mood well. “I've been through the books, Gentlemen,” he began, “and they give me reason to be blunt. I need political cover, to drastically reduce steel production as well as acquire currently independent elements within the energy sector to tie them to the State. The details are in this dossier.”

President João Miller Guerra and Vice President Torcuato Fernández-Miranda read through the summaries with faces fading into ghoulish concern. They glanced at each other as they read, eyes full of consequence.

João spoke first. “Fuentes, I appreciate the intentions but do you understand the consequences of this? Huge restructuring of Iberian Steel, government expenditure on energy nationalisations, potent risk of second order economic consequences in other sectors? We have social tensions, Fuentes, sclerotic administrations. We need gentle triage in our position.” Torcuato nodded lightly, unseen by the Economic Minister.

Fuentes scoffed. “Our position? Our position is dire; the economic legacy we have is sending the economy towards an inflationary cliff. Forget material consequences for a moment, what about political ones? Do you want to be the ones announcing huge price increases just for bread? This is the least we need!”

Torcuato spoke up. “Taking huge action like this now? When we have not even ordered the house, society is torn between the old systems and modernity plus an identity barely finalised? We would betray everything we have done to move this country forward. We are still young, the people don't know if they can trust us.”
strings.IBR_centrist.34.a: “Thousands cast into streets now would destroy us as surely as future unchecked inflation might.”“
strings.IBR_centrist.35.d:
How many decades has it been since David felt this much joy in his life? Walking across the Plaza de España in Cádiz, surrounded by his son, Alfonso, his daughter-in-law, Elisa, and most importantly, Albertina, his granddaughter.

He could almost forget the large crowd of people, mostly young university students, gathered around him with various pro-Constitutional signs. It was uncomfortable, truth be told, to be surrounded by so many people who had never experienced the horrors of war or knew what it meant to sacrifice for your country, and yet still, delicately holding the child's small hand eased any anxiety he had and filled him with more happiness than he could ever remember experiencing.

Putting the girl on his shoulders, he got closer to the monument and encouraged her to try and read the monument's steele.

“La...Prim...Primera...Consti...Constituciun...de los...Españoles...”

“Very good job Albertina. Your Spanish is much better than it was when I first talked to you in Portugal, remember?” The child did not answer with words; instead, she took out her little “Constitution. It depends on you!” pin and clumsily attached it sideways to his shirt. She then placed a kiss on his cheek and whispered “I love you” in his ear.

David smiled. Voting for the Constitution was the best decision of his life.
strings.IBR_centrist.35.a: Sometimes the simplest of words can relieve the greatest of pains.
strings.IBR_centrist.36.d:
The chipped doors stared at him. He told himself he wouldn't come. Too much noise. Too many promises. Too many men who spoke of a “New Spain” as if Spain needed to be new. But the Cádiz veteran came anyway, carried by unwilling feet that had marched for worse.

Inside, the room was quiet. Dingy lights hung from the ceiling as the soft scribbles of pens whispered in his ears. He hesitated at the booth, staring at the blank ballot in his hand. A blank vote was still a vote. A small act. Perhaps stubborn. But his.

He slipped the flimsy sheet into the box. It vanished.

Outside, the sea breeze swept through the narrow streets. Children still played in the streets. The church bells still rang every noon. Cádiz had changed, but not by much.

He reached into his coat, pulling out a letter he had read dozens of times already. His son's handwriting was always uneven.

“Papá, I am sorry that I can not make it to the holidays... but I will be in Cádiz soon. Ana wants you to meet the baby. She's already walking on her own.”

The veteran closed his eyes. How much he had missed. Her first laugh. Her first word. Her first months that would be spent growing up in a country still so fragile, still so new. But it would be gentler.

Times were changing. Too fast? Too slow? It was hard to tell. But there was no fear, maybe some hope. Maybe change wasn't so catastrophic. Maybe it could be lived through.

For now, this was enough.
strings.IBR_centrist.36.a: Change begins with the courage to show up
strings.IBR_centrist.37.t: The Day That Passed Us By
strings.IBR_centrist.37.d:
The dilapidated doors stared at him, judging his every move, his hollow intentions. He didn't come here to vote. He came here as a bystander. Inactive. Unwilling. Perhaps scared.

The dismal lights barely illuminated the room, as the bored poll workers whispered in apathy. The Cádiz veteran drifted between the aisles, spotting maybe the occasional voter. Peering into the ballot boxes, he would count maybe one, two, five sheets. But never more than that.

After a few minutes, he stepped back outside. Across the street, a kiosk displayed newspapers already running the headlines:

PARTICIPATION AT HISTORIC LOW, REFERENDUM IN DOUBT.

The veteran scanned the page before a chilling gust of dry wind snapped to the next. He didn't bother to continue reading. He walked home slowly, letting the words marinate. As he arrived, the building's caretaker stepped out to meet him.

“Don Miguel!” she exclaimed, waving him over. “Your hijo called earlier. He tried your apartment, but you weren't in. He asked me to let you know...”

Hesitation. Always hesitation.

“...he's not sure when he'll be able to visit.”

The veteran nodded. Another visit postponed. Another moment slipped by.

Upstairs in the stillness, he sat by the window, watching the last voters trickle into the polling station. Ghostlike. Too little. Too late. Maybe someday things will change. But not today.
strings.IBR_centrist.38.d:
...And how is little Albertina? Does she know Spanish yet? Have you been teaching her properly? Why am I asking? I know you haven't. Can you put her on the line?“ Speaking with his granddaughter over the phone, despite her shyness and preference for Portuguese, was one of the last few joys that David had in his life. While he had never met the child, he loved her deeply, perhaps even more than he did his son. ”Did work refuse your requested leave? You were supposed to bring her to Cádiz to meet me last week.“

”Sorry Father, Elisa and I were busy volunteering for the Constitutional referendum campaign and...“

David's face suddenly went red, as the restlessness and disappointment built in his chest turned into hot, boiling anger. ”Why of course you have. You have been growing ever more secular and liberal, and this is why you put a socialist-atheist plot to destroy Catholicism before visiting your own father! What example are you setting for the little girl, and what world are you building for her, my God! If you had your way, she would live in a degenerate atheist world where terrorism and crime are rampant. This Constitution is the biggest mistake this country has ever made! And now it took my family away from me too...“

David sat with the dead line beeping in his ear, realising now that his son had hung up a long time ago. He cursed every single politician involved in this sorry project by name. They were foreign agents, and worse, they had postponed his meeting with the blood of his blood to God knows when...
strings.IBR_centrist.38.a: Yet rage and bitterness, no matter how strong, cannot gladden an old man's sad, lonely heart.
strings.IBR_centrist.39.d:
All across Iberia TVs and radios tuned in, same as they had in years past, for one of the most important of Christmas traditions. For many families, preparations for the festivities the following day was to bring had already begun. But all stopped to listen to the speech-heralding brass band. The growing number of families lucky enough to have a TVwere treated to seasonal views of Iberia to the Christmas music they played; the markets of Lisbon, the lights of Madrid, and the masses of Barcelona. The images were warm, many of the adults smiled as they saw all Iberia glowing with cheer. Most of the children fidgeted, wondering when they could return to their play.

Finally the band came to an end, a rendition of Silent Night fading into a silence broken moments later by a single voice speaking to all Iberia. Nearly all were stunned by it.

In Spain, they recoiled. This is not Caudillo Franco, with his usual warm words.

In Portugal, they recoiled. This was not Caudillo Caetano, making promises for the new year.

President Miller Guerra spoke to an audience who had not expected him. He spoke of that baby in the stable, who had come to bring peace to all on Earth. He spoke of Herod, the threat to that young boy, and the bravery of the Carpenter and the Virgin who had trusted in God and in the divine child with which they had been blessed. His words had been well considered, carefully chosen, and the metaphor was clear to many who listened.

President Guerra barely referenced politics in that message, talking only of Iberia and her faith. In the hope of the new world that Christ had come to lead them to, and the importance of safeguarding it. Just as Christ had come to humanity, so had reform come to Iberia. While danger to it had not passed, faith held it safe.
strings.IBR_centrist.39.a: “Merry Christmas,” President Guerra said, as a brass rendition of Los Peces en el Río played him out.
strings.IBR_centrist.40.d:
Rain gently pattered on the roof of Raúl's car as he flicked through his notes, the cold beams of light from the car park's tall lamps glaring into the interior. He was at the very edge of the lot, near the fence, as far away from the convention hall as he could have possibly gotten. Parking close was easier, but in his years of political reporting one thing had always stuck out to him: never overstay your welcome.

The day had filled his notepad with observations, a bright CD rally bursting with pageantry dressing up all their promises ahead of the election. The endless banners and the kaleidoscope of colors across the halls. It almost made him feel like he was drowning in politically-charged tints. The interviews had been less interesting however. Old folks had regarded him with distrust, as if he were a police interrogator. Young supporters gave cloned answers, probably imagining their words as job-winning. Individuals whose only contributions to Raúl's article had been to affirm that the CD's “sounded good” without seeming to have much to say on them. He sighed as he flicked over the incredibly similar interviews. The public was as vapid as the politicians sometimes.

Toward the end of his notes was the real meat however, and in his head was already the core of his article. Miller Guerra's closing speech, full of the vim and vigor that came with addressing party loyalists. But what made it intriguing were the contrasts from the last election. Far more populist, talking about economic reforms and social policies going further than he ever dared last time. Then again, just walking around had shown him that; far more obvious working-class types at odds with the usual rally crowd. Guerra's election gambit was blunt - he was going for the hot fire of progress and calling Iberia to the heat.

Raúl added a final note to the page before starting his car to depart, yawning as the day caught up to him.
strings.IBR_centrist.40.a: “Forced to acknowledge party defections in speech. Internal issues? Question popularity in article.”
strings.IBR_centrist.41.d:
The speeches rang out all day, running late into the night. Flashing cameras and bright lights created an artificial day, a heady infinite feeling through the Madrid convention hall that seemed to deny the outside world. For those hours, perhaps there truly wasn't. All there was, was the Party. The CD, letters that should dominate Iberia, or so all who lurked in the everglow halls presumed. The speakers on the stage told them so, and they cheered with glee for it.

Within that endless neon glint fusion was taking place, a growing intensity with each new speaker. First the smaller parties, to whom the Coalition meant everything for their position, cheered the praises of cooperation. They called for - almost begged - for ever closer union, and declared themselves defunct. They all joined together, each one joining together to create an ever larger whole. Some frowned but most cheered. Their future was metamorphosing before them, how could they not?

Each speaker played the same old tune. Promises of change in Iberia, of the ardent defence of a proper way of living. Of food on every table, of a school desk for every child, a car for every family. They promised nothing would change; they promised everything would be different. Follow us into the breach, to stay and be prosperous. Give us your voices in this ever stronger union, no longer a coalition, and cry out for what you are owed. But what are you owed other than dignified prosperity?

To most the message worked wonders, but on the fringes discontent could be found. Some left the convention halls grumbling even before the main speakers took to the stage, the main parties came to close the fait accompli. “Promising the world while refusing to change themselves,” they muttered to each other in alcoves and car parks around the event. “Is a repackaged status quo really what we need? Is spinning the government wheels worth our subsumation?”
strings.IBR_centrist.41.a: If those inside disagreed with the assessment, the cheer emanating from them didn't suggest it.
strings.IBR_centrist.42.d:
Sergio absently flicked through the newspaper, glancing over the myriad articles. Most of it inane nonsense, or so he mused as he took a swig of his coffee. His wife and children weren't down yet, but in only a few minutes the kitchen would be filled with activity as the day started. Breakfast was ready; he'd always enjoyed preparing it - it gave him these few minutes of peace before the chaos of the day.
