A few pages in, an article caught his attention. Fairly short, more of an announcement than anything, it told of a split in the CDs. The left of the party had left the coalition and were creating their own group, the 'Centered Left'. There was a single sentence on policy, a statement on the importance of workers' rights and new social policies, but nothing in detail. All in all the article was barely more than a paragraph. Odd, it sounded important yet it barely gets a few sentences.

Against the small article was a much larger piece, a report on a sit down interview a minor CD candidate standing for election did. Sergio browsed the statements - the candidate was certainly verbose, probably why he got the interview. Most of it was promises or deflections but Sergio flew past those, searching for anything significant. Statements on social cohesion, budgetary responsibility, steady development - nothing he hadn't heard before.

Actually, had he? Sergio did note the new forwardness. He recalled last week's paper. The CD had a few articles in it, and they were almost frustratingly difficult to pin down in beliefs, very vague. Now here they were being much more ideologically specific, if not practically. The final statement really caught Sergio: “We are now free to be the truly Christian democrats our party is named for.”

The split must have pulled them apart quite a bit, how ironic they ended up next to each other in the paper. Sergio supposed that was interesting.
strings.IBR_centrist.42.a: He took another swig of coffee and turned to the sports pages.
strings.IBR_natcon.1.d:
Newly inaugurated President Manuel Fraga quickly straightened his tie as the last make-up artists scampered away from the cameras. A broadcast to the Iberian people showing their new leader, Fraga, quickly began, brimming with confidence and enthusiasm. “Greetings, Iberia, on behalf of the People's Alliance, we thank you for the trust you've placed in us to lead Iberia to the future.”

Fraga took a quick breath before continuing, “Iberia has seen much suffering, but she has also seen much glory. The suffering makes many want to leave the past behind, whereas the glory makes others want to hold fast to the past, never leaving it.”

“But, this election showed that the Iberian people have chosen to march forward, not in spite of their past, but towards a new glory. Iberia has chosen this new direction, new ideas, and the People's Alliance, and I will carry it out to its greatest extent.” Fraga moved his script to the side, looking straight into the camera.

“May I end with a connection to the past, but a call to move forward...

”Glória a España,

“Glória a Portugal,
strings.IBR_natcon.2.d:
The first cabinet meeting of the new Fraga government gathers at the Vilamejor Palace; all the cabinet's eyes, especially those of his right-hand man, Vice President Mota Campos, rest their gaze upon Manuel Fraga. They wait for the small signs of a smile or frown from Fraga before beginning the meeting.

Fraga, on the other hand, is in his own world, in his own self basking light of power. He finally felt free of the moribund old men who used to hold these positions. He felt free from the act of needlessly tiptoeing around their autocratic desire, needing to fulfill egos, and could now rush wholeheartedly into what needed to be done for Iberia.

Mota Campos, tired of the waiting, snaps Fraga out of it. “Sir, now that we've won, shall we begin drafting Iberia's new Constitution?”

Fraga quickly sat up, looking around the room of all the cabinet members, who had all worked diligently under the Caudillos, only to throw them aside at a moment's notice. Fraga knew he'd have to be more careful than Franco, and certainly more than Caetano, but for now, he could still relax.

“Well, Mr. Campos, shall we begin? Can't have you wither away to dust on us.”
strings.IBR_natcon.2.a: The cabinet gave a light chuckle before beginning.
strings.IBR_natcon.3.d:
“ABC News: Exclusive Interview with President of the Government Manuel Fraga - In Spanish, Page 4 to 5 - In Portuguese, Page 6 to 7”

As they waited to get their ultrasound results, Carlos read “I have always stressed the importance of the family unit, and as president, I guarantee that the families of Iberia will be supported through thick and thin.” Marie smiled as he said the quote aloud, feeling a bit less stressed about the future.

As he walked home from his school in Pamplona, Juan read a little from a newspaper on a stand, “The education of the nation's children is of utmost importance. Iberia's schools are a bulwark of the nation and deserve far more funding than they currently receive. Of course with these more resources there will be higher expectations, which is why I find it to be only fair for there to be mandatory schooling to age fourteen.” The words struck the boy like lightning thrown with the strength of a thousand gods. There would be another three years of school for him.

“Our country has been very unsafe,” read Adur, “with the ETA and other radicalists running around. All of our polices' efforts must be to create a safe Iberia for our people.” Adur laughed as he read the paper, an entire election and the government still has the same views on the Basque.

“These land speculators are truly evil people,” Manuel reread, “they prey on our people and I promise that our new government will bring justice to them, while also providing public housing for those who need it.” Manuel read the quote over and over in his room, hearing his neighbors eat their dinner. Finally he could leave the boarding house that he had been cramped in for years.
strings.IBR_natcon.4.d:
The crisis had been impacting families across Iberia. Many followed the same path as Iago Pena, a former farmer who had to leave his family behind to move to one of Iberia's industrial centers, in his case Madrid, looking for any sort of work available.

Celia was left behind in Andalucía with all of their kids. Celia juggled her parental duties, ranging from getting the kids to activities at the newly opened family center to cleaning the house. After toiling away making meals and filling paperwork for her transportation stipend, she finally got the chance to talk with a bureaucrat.

“Ma'am, there's several discrepancies and missed dates in these papers,” the bureaucrat handed them back to her coldly, covered in red marks. “I'm sorry, but we're going to have to refuse to give you a ticket.”

Celia's youngest began bawling as the kids all murmured about never seeing their father again. The stern look of the bureaucrat softened. “However, just some small revisions and you'll see him soon.”

The bureaucrat took the papers back from Celia as she sat, taking out a black pen and began to help her fill it out correctly, glancing back at the little one who had subsided to a couple of sniffles.

The bureaucrat reminisced for a moment about how long it had been since he saw his father before looking back down at the paperwork.
strings.IBR_natcon.5.d:
Sebastián returns home late to his mother's shabby Valencia apartment; the cramped single-bedroom unit he and his mother lived in alone had a visitor for once. The neighborhood shopkeeper stood beside Sebastián's mother before quickly turning, realizing his presence. “Oh, Sebastián, your mother and I've been discussing some arrangements.”

Sebastián stared at the shopkeeper with confusion as he continued. “And I've been waiting to tell you this, but I'm your father, Sebastián, and with the law being changed, I'm willing to acknowledge you as my son.”

“I knew it! I mean look at us, we look damn near identical!” Sebastián yells at the shopkeeper. “If you actually wanted to acknowledge your own son, you would've married her once I was born. You're nothing but a measly shrew. You can't even fathom how much pain we've been through all because you wanted to save your own ass and avoid the consequences.”

The shopkeeper rolls up his sleeves. Sebastián takes a step towards him puffing his chest out. Their eyes lock leaving an unnerving tension in the air for what feels like an eternity before the shopkeeper breaks contact, realizing it's not worth it. As he leaves he calls out one last time to Sebastián.

“Just think it over... son.”
strings.IBR_natcon.5.a: Sebastián never thought of it again.
strings.IBR_natcon.6.d:
João, the son of an elite family, sat at his personally engraved desk, studying The Code of Academic Praxis, a book detailing all of the different intricate hazingings he'd undergo as a student at the prestigious University of Coimbra. João's studies were interrupted when his father, a portly man, barged in and slapped him, tossing a rejection letter on the table. “Are you kidding me, João!”

“S-surely it wasn't that bad-” João stuttered to his father.

“You got an automatic rejection! This should've been a walk in the park!” His father slapped him again and continued to berate him, “You know how many generations of this family have gone there? You're simply an embarrassment for this. This will stain our reputation for decades.”

João stared into his father's disappointed eyes. “You're lucky I'll be able to pull a couple of strings and send some checks to give you a chance, but this is it.”

João, humiliated by his father's outburst and his own scores, finally stood up. “That's all you do! Bribe and pull strings! You constantly hold us to standards you can't hold yourself to! If that's all Coimbra taught you, I don't want to go there.”

“As you wish,” his father spat. He raised his hand to slap him again, but as he watched him coil up in defense like usual all he could see was failure. He quickly exited the room leaving him alone and uncertain of his future. In a fit of rage, João chucks the book at the wall, watching it open to another hazing practice.
strings.IBR_natcon.6.a: It spoke of the Praxe's shared embarrassment.
strings.IBR_natcon.7.d:
Manuel Suárez usually considered himself to be a rather decisive man. Indeed, it was his quick-thinking and knack for making the right call at the right time that had gotten him the position of Burgos' Police Chief. But as he sat at his desk shuffling through file after file of potential recruits, he found himself at an impasse.

The dissolution of the political police had come as something of a surprise to him and the rest of the department - but it was certainly a welcome one. The ensuing boost in funding the department received meant that they could finally afford to hire a new officer. He had passed over many a square-jawed youth from a good family with hopes of making the system better. Suárez had even met a few of them, with a bright young man named Santiago making a particularly good impression.

But as he continued shuffling, the Chief stopped on one particular candidate's file. It was the eyes that stood out to him. The candidate was a seemingly average man nearing his middle age, with a light stubble and a neat comb-over. His test scores were superb, too, scoring high in every category that mattered. But what really got Suárez was the eyes. They had a look to them that he recognised all too well - he had seen it more times than he could count on his time in the force.

The following day, Chief Suárez called the man on the file in - one Antonio Cortéz. The two men spoke cordially, and the Chief shook his hand, telling him that the department would soon be contacting him. But as Cortéz left, the Chief asked him one final question - where he used to work. Without missing a beat, Cortéz pointed down the hallway, before walking away. And then it all made sense. He used to work for the political police, and he wanted his job back. Suárez cursed himself for putting himself in this situation - if he allowed Cortéz back in, it would set a precedent. But the man's skills were undeniable. Shutting his door, Suárez made a decision.
strings.IBR_natcon.7.a: Those talents... and hunches are too valuable to lose.
strings.IBR_natcon.8.d:
Fernando de Santiago had seen a lot in his time. He was in his 70s, after all. But rarely, in all his years both in and out of combat, had he seen someone as brazen as the man sitting in front of him - Rodolfo Martín Villa, a man in his late-30s with an air of bookishness to him. An ostensibly decent pick for Minister of the Interior, he had previously assumed, but the meeting he found himself in had shattered that illusion. “Minister, if I may interrupt,” de Santiago said, with the air of a grandfather about to lecture a child, “I am finding myself confused. You were an engineer, no?” he asked.

“Why, yes I was, Minister,” Martín Villa answered, surprised at de Santiago's interruption. “But I fail to see what that has to do with our planned changes to the AAS-”

“Me neither,” said de Santiago, pointedly. “Which is why I am so bemused that it is you making these changes, my friend. Civilian control? Stripping powers away from my ministry and subsuming them into your own? Am I so infirm that I can no longer run the AAS without your assistance? Or do you have other intentions in mind?”

A look of realisation dawned across Martín Villa's face, and he smiled. “Ah, I see. You think me underqualified.” The look de Santiago shot at him told him everything. Martín Villa leaned back in his chair. “Minister, an organisation is like a machine - it should operate with a core function in mind with minimal extraneous parts. All I am doing is applying my experience in identifying the unnecessary parts and removing them.” Noticing that de Santiago seemed unconvinced, he continued. “Look, the President has placed his confidence in me, and in all likelihood he will be supporting these changes. The sooner you stop doubting them, the better.” A moment passed, and de Santiago begrudgingly nodded in agreement.
strings.IBR_natcon.8.a: The president will change his mind when the bombs start going off again, anyway.
strings.IBR_natcon.8.b: Best to play along, stay on Fraga's good side.
strings.IBR_natcon.9.d:
Celia and Iago, along with all the Pena kids, were cramped inside a rough tenement home in the southern Mediodía district of Madrid, where Iago has been living in order to send money home to keep them clothed and fed. With the visit coming to an end, Iago began giving small gifts out to all the children.

As Iago handed the last gift to his wife, they pulled together in an embrace. After breaking apart, Celia pulled out her own gift for him. “Was able to convince someone to give us an extra ticket, have you come back home to the south with us.”

“Celia,” Iago grabs her hand, “You know I can't. I have to stay to feed you guys, otherwise-” Celia raised her hand to Iago's chest.

“Iago, have you not read the papers? The new homemaker stipend...”

“Yes, I've read them, but I doubt it'll be enough, Celia.”

“It'll be tight my love, but if you go back to the farm, we'll be able to scrape by. It'll be rough, but it'll be for the kids.” Celia glanced towards her children, playing with all their new toys, a tear welled in her eye before glancing back up to look deep into Iago's eyes, finally going to be able to live with her man again.
strings.IBR_natcon.10.d:
Miguel Alameda was rotting away like a corpse in an Iberian prison. It had become difficult to count the years of his life already wasted away, and the only thing he looked forward to was sharing his knowledge of improvised explosives with his younger cellmate. Though the boy had not been old enough to participate in the Battle of Barcelona, where Miguel had killed his first, and last, Fascist pig, he was just as devoted an anarchist as him and ended up in prison, years later, for distributing CNT propaganda.

It was during such a session that a Francoist guard surprised them by beating the bars of their shared cell with his baton. Both of the men froze, afraid that they had been discovered, already imagining the ensuing punishment.

“Juan Francisco Riba. You've been pardoned. Follow me.” The guard's words echoed in Miguel's mind, as his cellmate was led away without them being able to share a proper goodbye.

Miguel could hardly sleep that night. But it was not envy that marred his brain, but worry. He worried that, inspired by his teaching, Juan would take up arms for the CNT once outside. Not because Miguel had been turned a pacifist, but rather because, in the current climate, what the CNT needed were not blasts and blazing guns, but mouths to spread their ideals, and wake the workers from their slumber.
strings.IBR_natcon.10.a: Word of mouth spreads the Revolution further than a thousand explosions.
strings.IBR_natcon.11.d:
When Juan Francisco Riba was released from prison, he did not expect an easy reintegration. Miraculously, he found a job in Tarragona at a print shop. His boss, a man in his late sixties, not only did not mind his prison time, but also treated him like a son.

Two weeks into the job, a chance to differentiate himself arrived. “I can finish this job on my own. Not much left to do anyway.”

“Are you sure? I don't have the money to pay you overtime.”

“Of course. I want to see this done so we can work on something else tomorrow.”

The shop owner sighed, “Fine. But don't stay up too late. It's unhealthy.”

Juan nodded, thanking him as he left.

When the building fell quiet, Juan hurried to the press and began printing dozens of pamphlets calling for the People to unite and depose the tyrants from Madrid. As he collated the pamphlets, he heard the main door open. Before he could react, the shopowner made his way to him, put a small box on the table and furiously began shredding the pamphlets in droves.

Juan stiffened in fear, thinking he would soon return to prison, but his boss put a calm hand on his shoulder. “Comrade, I fought with the Anarchists during the civil war. You have an ally in me. But the government knows me, and if they find CNT pamphlets in the city, this will be the first place they'll come looking. I can help you find...alternatives to my shop.”

Juan relaxed as his boss opened the box and revealed a still steaming meal. It was the best he'd had since leaving prison.
strings.IBR_natcon.11.a: The police found nothing suspicious in the print shop when they came to look.“
strings.IBR_natcon.12.d:
Marta was used to walking for hours, carrying a heavy load of water in her hands. She was used to pulling on the rope, pouring the water from the bucket to her jars. She was used to the strain of her muscles and the constant rationing to postpone her next trip, if only by a few hours. She looked at the water freely flowing from the faucet of the small, marble sink she now had in front of her, and she thought of all the pain this small metal pipe would take away from her limbs, and the many hours it would free in her week.

Marta was woken from her stupor by her son hugging her leg, loudly exclaiming ownership of the house to his sister. She ran her fingers through his hair as he let go and started jumping around the apartment in joy.

She turned to her husband, Rafael, still at the entrance, talking to the official who brought them here, thanking him for the opportunity to live an easier, more decent life, out of their dirt-floored, broken-down home in the countryside.

“Of course, it is no issue. The priest said you were the most fit for this program in the village. You should thank him when you return. I'm sure you won't find this too difficult, but please remember. No alcoholism. No fights. And stay out of trouble. Understood?”

Marta reached for her husband's arm “Of course, we won't let you down, we promise,” she said, echoing his previous comments.

The official turned to leave. Just as he crossed the door's threshold, he turned back to them with a wide smile and readjusted the button on his collar with two large letters spelling AP. “And remember, Iberia requires patriotic citizens such as yourselves. Do not disappoint your nation, yes?”

The couple nodded enthusiastically.
strings.IBR_natcon.12.a: Why would they betray the system that opened the gates of paradise for them?
strings.IBR_natcon.13.d:
A crowd amassing in the hundreds marched down Calvo Sotelo, the bangs of pots and pans echoed as they marched, a sea of banners fluttering like waves in the bay. There were the per usual Iberian and Spaniard banners, but mixed in were ones draped in the socialist red and republican purple that hadn't been seen in decades; this was the local branch of Democratic Center. Although this coalition of liberals and leftists had several different ideas on how the financial sector should look, they all gathered knowing that it shouldn't look like this.

At the head marched a lone figure, one not wielding a banner or sign, just a simple megaphone. “Down with the AP's crooked ways,” he chanted. The crowd chanted back in unison. The man stood as the leader of the Democratic Center in Santander, leading a protest not held in singular political belief but in opposition to the right's corruption.

As the protest grew, the CEO of Santander Group straightened his tailored suit before peering out of his posh little office. He enjoyed listening to what seemed like a tiny man from his window ramble on about the Alianza Popular, seeing these little ants, some of them his own employees, gathered for once in one place. Realizing the control the Democratic Center had on not only the people of Santander, but some of his lower-level employees, he called his secretary in.

“Yes, sir?” she replies with her usual smile.

“Put a note in my calendar to make a donation later.”

“Which charity will it be this time, sir?”

“No charity this time. Just the Democrats, and make it sizable; have it marked down for later today.” His secretary mentally questioned his goals before asking the question.
strings.IBR_natcon.13.a: “Would you like a photo-op with this one as well?”
strings.IBR_natcon.14.d:
Duarte Freitas do Amaral, sat in his office. The dark room was solely framed by two large paintings on either wall to his side. In front of the Minister of Industry sat a tired manager, a manager tasked with sorting the applicants for the Iberian Price Control Advisory Board. That manager had precisely sorted hundreds of applicants into categories, retaining size, scope, and location of the firm; those hours of work sat in neat piles on the desk between them.

The manager, gleaming with pride, sat twiddling his thumbs as Amaral sifted through piles of petitions to join the board, watching as he slowly pulled different applicants out into a separate pile. With eerie precision he had created a stack of applicants ranging from a restaurant chain in Lisbon, to a tourist resort in Barcelona, one was a small family business in Valencia, another a factory in Burgos.

Once he was done, Amaral discarded this new pile of applicants right into his desk side bin. Visible sweat began to bead on the manager's forehead as Amaral started to create another stack of applicants, sorting them even faster this time.

“The manager shifted back and forth in his chair as the sweat beads gathered into full droplets, asking, ”Sir, what was wrong with those applicants?“

Amaral's cold face shot a glance at him. ”They openly backed the Democratic Center last election. It doesn't take a genius to realize they shouldn't be on this board.“ He waited for the manager's agape mouth to shut before continuing.
strings.IBR_natcon.14.a: “In fact, take out this set that backed the DC privately as well.”
strings.IBR_natcon.14.c: “Fine, add one or two back in. If only for appearances' sake.”
strings.IBR_natcon.15.d:
João Dias Rosas sat at his oak desk with charts and numbers spread about tracking the union's latest inflation statistics. To crack down on the government's seemingly flawless idea of continuously printing more and more pesetas to cover the government's expenditure, the Minister of Finance was required to firmly shut down a good deal of projects.

Rosas, through his tenure so far, had created a multitude of enemies due to his obstructionism, powerful men not used to being told no to their ideas. Looking back down upon the statistics laid out in front of him, he realized that if his closing of the money tap hadn't panned out, the pressure on Fraga to toss him out would've gotten too unbearable.

As he continued to pour himself over the data, he let his mind wander; he thought of his past worries, angering too many, not doing enough, but he also thought of future ambitions. His thoughts drifted back to Salazar's humble start at the University of Coimbra, becoming Finance Minister to tame inflation, just like him.

João Dias Rosas never fancied himself a Caudillo to the likes of Franco or Salazar, but possibly as President of the Government, able to sweep in and take control just like Salazar did so long ago... once Fraga inevitably slipped up.
strings.IBR_natcon.15.a: Rosas would seize his moment when it comes.
strings.IBR_natcon.16.d:
Manuel rocked back and forth on his feet outside the communal restroom in his apartment building as Luis, a neighbor he drank with on occasion, approached and joined him in waiting.

“Manuel! Good to see you, friend, how is your morning?”

“Well, I suppose it could be better, I got fired.”

Luis' eyes went wide. “Could be better! I'm sorry to hear that! I was only just hired a bit ago myself.”

“Oh, it's not so bad. My boss worked me to the bone for next to nothing, barely could afford a room here, let alone do anything fun. He was a vain little man with a gut out to here! A little fop of hair too that was swooped over like a German. To hell with him, with the new unemployment benefits. I'm almost better off, and I have a good lead on a trucking job that pays much better, even if I won't be home much.”

“Sounds like my new boss! He kept trying to weasel his way around the new minimum wage that was implemented yesterday. I had to have him rewrite the employment contract three times before he put the number down right. But you know, whatever puts food on the table, even if it's Sandeman's Warehouse.”

There was a pregnant silence as Manuel looked at Luis with a mix of dawning realization and horror.
strings.IBR_natcon.16.a: “My friend, get out of that place as soon as you can.”
strings.IBR_natcon.17.d:
Laureano López Rodó, Minister of the Economy, fidgeted with a sheaf of papers under his desk as two men in fine suits settled into the plush chairs in front of him. These businessmen were chairmen of two of the Big Five banks, Banco de Bilbao and Banco de Vizcaya. They both had their own sheaf of papers covered in annotations of the various economic reforms that were being introduced.

The representative of Banco de Bilbao was tapping his foot on the ground, impatience, exasperation, and anger clouding his features. Vizcaya's chairman sat with a quiet fury, a cold expressionless face, and a briefcase over his legs. As soon as everyone was settled, the impatient chairman dropped the papers in his lap, took a deep breath, and began to yell.

“Mr. López, I can't tell if you are trying to collapse our economy, or if the entire administration is incompetent. These reforms are a catastrophe waiting to happen, not to mention the rhetoric you have been spouting about us,” he gestured between himself and the other chairman, who was looking at him with raised eyebrows. “You can't just demonize us and expect us to go through with your reforms without any push back! The stranglehold on lending and inflated deposit rates leaves barely enough room to make ends meet, let alone expand the business.”

The room was silent for a moment as the Bilbao representative sat back down in a huff. The other chairman slowly opened his briefcase and grabbed a new sheaf of papers. “While I don't quite agree with my peer's wording, I do agree with the sentiment. The quotas put in place for small and medium businesses are incompatible with our lending interest rates; it simply doesn't work like that, Minister López. They are too risky to do business with.”

López Rodó blinked slowly as he looked between the two men. He pursed his lips as he considered his reply.
strings.IBR_natcon.17.a: We can work on some more flexibility around loans and deposits.
strings.IBR_natcon.17.b: Quotas can be relaxed; it doesn't help anyone if the banks go under due to bad bets.
strings.IBR_natcon.17.c: Gentlemen, this is the way things are now, you need to evolve to stay in business or someone else will do it for you.
strings.IBR_natcon.18.d:
“Ultimately, we have to choose one. Wind or solar, the Finance Ministry will certainly not agree to financing two developing technologies for such sums, let alone ones connected to the power grid.”

Duarte Freitas do Amaral pondered. Across the table, the Economy Minister López Rodó raised a good point; both were still little more than experimental technologies. The two men had been discussing the rival proposals for hours, both proposals full of installation costs, subsidies and research grants - the idea of shifting any significant amount of the grid to them seemed fanciful at first. However, the promises of both had given both men pause.

“Lets make this simple,” Duarte said, “Wind is unreliable, has large installation costs and relatively expensive energy. However for small scale direct use, remote farms and villages, it's a promising way to relieve pressure on the fringes of the power grid and allow a foundation to research better utilisation of the technology -”

“Conversely,” López interrupted, “solar power is in its infancy and is completely unsuitable for any notable power generation in its current form, beyond limited personal uses. But the potential if we could find a way to increase the efficiency of power production and find a way to store it? It could outpace Wind, but it's a lot of money to spend on a technological IOU.”

Duarte nodded slowly. As Minister of Industry he could see the promise of Solar. Sure it would probably never replace conventional means, but what if? Even part of the grid being sustained by it could do wonders for energy security - who could block out the Sun? But one hell of a gamble, especially when Wind offered benefits to rural communities now for much the same price as rural grid refurbishment would cost anyway...
strings.IBR_natcon.18.a: When they left the meeting, the Wind Project was stamped approved
strings.IBR_natcon.18.b: The promise of the power of the sun in the palm of their hands saw the Solar Project approved
strings.IBR_natcon.19.d:
The sandy steps of the Amphitheatre were small in number, compared to the steps Luz had to climb each day to reach his apartment back in Veracruz. He'd told himself this holiday would be restful; in truth it had been anything but. And yet, he felt content against the prongs of exhaustion that touched upon his mind.

He'd walked around Tarragona for most of the day, binoculars hung around his neck. A beautiful city, he'd longed to come here - in his youth he'd been fascinated by the Roman history of Spain, even harbored dreams of studying it at University, immersing himself away from this world to the world of Hispania, the Roman provinces to which this city had once been one of the capitals. Alas, it wasn't to be, but he never turned down an opportunity to indulge in his interest. The old Roman walls, the Aqueduct and the archeological museum were just some of the many spots he had walked to and viewed with undying enthusiasm despite the warm day.

The sun was beginning to wane, daylight still strong yet the first hints of sunset became apparent. Luz had saved this for the end, the Roman Amphitheatre that lay right on the coast - an ancient relic against the unchanging sea. It was worn, weathered light brown stones where people once sat reflecting the softly dying light. He strode up to its top, eager to look out upon the coast - the same coast those ancient Hispanians looked out upon. He was almost glad for the Oil Crisis - there would be few ships to spoil the view, especially since there was a Petrochemical plant nearby. No, there would be few going there right now.

As he made it however, he gasped. Surprisingly close to the shoreline, there travelled two gigantic ships, undoubtedly oil tankers. But wasn't there a crisis? The oil had stopped, that's what the news said! How could there be two here now, just as he'd wanted to look out to sea? He raised his binoculars.
strings.IBR_natcon.19.a: The closest ship flew Venezuela's flag; the furthest one flew the unmistakable green of Brazil's.
strings.IBR_natcon_19_tt: Diversifying our oil imports is made easier by our strong relations with Venezuela and Brazil.
strings.IBR_natcon.20.d:
Antonio Jr. hacked away at the overgrown vines with a dull machete, sweat gathering on his brow. It was a hard day's work, trying to reclaim the family farm. His father had let the place go, and the fields were overrun with stunted vines and rotting grapes. While his father was building his legal career in Pamplona, Antonio was dreaming of his next visit to his grandparents' house, the house he now called home.

Antonio made his way to the tool shed. Opening the door brought a sour expression to his face as he looked at the aging farm equipment left behind. He had applied for the new agriculture loan program through the government for new equipment, but it had been several weeks without so much as word back. It seemed like he would just have to make do; if Antonio was afraid of anything, it certainly wasn't hard work.

He grabbed a sharpening stone from the shed and sat on the porch with his machete. After a few minutes of sharpening, he heard a low whine as a car pulled up the gravel drive towards the house and a businessman stepped out with a clipboard and began to walk around the property. It was then that Antonio noted the signage on the car stating 'Department of Agriculture.' Antonio leaped up from his chair. This could be his chance! He let the bureaucrat walk around alone, loath to lose his chance at a loan by bothering the man. After almost an hour, he finally walked up towards the porch.

“Mr. Rosé, it is as I expected, the farm does not qualify for our loan, the zoning goes several feet beyond what is covered in the requirements. As your father said.”

Antonio was left puzzled, “My father? What do you mean?”

“Well, he had expected this issue and already had a supplementary application sent through, so we will be able to approve your loan.”
strings.IBR_natcon.21.d:
“I've been waiting for nearly 2 hours, please I need to see someone now! The pain won't go away and,” she slammed her fist on the reception desk, “I'm worried about my baby. Are you telling me that there are no doctors available?”

The woman stood amongst a sorry sight; a hospital waiting room bursting at the seams. On seats sat numerous in wretched states. Groaning rang around the room, tensed faces illuminated by dry fluorescent lights against white walls turned grey. The receptionist regarded the woman with frustrated pity as she stood hunched at her desk, heavily pregnant and clutching her torso hissing in pain. She had been there for some time, perhaps an hour or two. A stomach ache had visibly worsened as she had waited for a doctor, but without an appointment and as short staffed as they were? The receptionist had highlighted her case, but until a doctor was free that was all she could do.

“I'm sorry Senhora, there is just no one available but you have been given priority. As soon as a doctor can see you they wi-” A cry of pain from the woman stopped the receptionist mantra, causing the woman to lean onto the desk in near exhaustion.

“Please, I can pay. I have money, if that's what you want. Please.”

The receptionist shuddered at the implication but the answer to the predicament became clear to her; the new private clinics. If she could pay, they could see her. “No, we would never take that”, she said, revolted by the prospect of bribery, “but if you have the money we can provide you with a private alternative. We can have a private ambulance here within a few minutes, they should be able to see you on arrival.”

Behind pained eyes the receptionist saw a flash of relief, hope overtaking the excruciating desperation. “Yes, oh yes please.” the woman said. “Thank God.”
strings.IBR_natcon.21.a: Relieve the strain, increase available resources, save some lives.
strings.IBR_natcon.22.d:
Abella slowly moved up the path towards the hospital, clinging to her walking stick. This was always the worst bit of the hospital visits, this upwards climb to the reception. She sighed, not much she could do about it and she had plenty of time to reflect on that as she slowly made her way forward.

She told herself to be grateful. After all, she remembered when she was a child. No health insurance back then. God bless Salazar for his reforms, giving women like her some security. God bless him.

Such thoughts died as she contemplated the experience in store for her. It never changed - sitting in the waiting room for wildly varying lengths of time, talking to a doctor she had often never met before receiving a scrawled note for medicine she kept insisting was less and less effective. “Its perfectly natural Senhora,” they would say, “just relax and let the drugs work.”

She missed Dr Vidal. He'd always remembered her name. A quick checkup, a short wait - it had always felt more like visiting a friend. He had retired some years ago, and she'd never had a consistent doctor since. Recently though, it felt more difficult. Doctors had left for the private clinics the government had sponsored. The new ones were fine, but they were certainly younger - much younger - and her pension couldn't allow the private costs.

She reached the reception, praying the waiting room would not be bursting like last time. Sure, she had an appointment, but this hospital always seemed so busy. If only she lived further away from the city's centre. She passed a young woman being nearly carried out, heavily pregnant and nearly weeping, begging someone to call her husband. Abella turned; the woman was being led to a private ambulance just outside. Given her condition she couldn't blame her, but despite the situation a tinge of jealousy embered. She shook it off however, and entered the hospital.
strings.IBR_natcon.22.a: “Boa sorte, meu pequeno” she whispered for that poor girl.
strings.IBR_natcon.23.d:
Manuel Fraga saunters up to the podium, lighting following him as he does so. He steps up and dramatically rests his hands upon the sides of the podium, as if bracing himself before the crowd of men who fill the room.

“Gentlemen, Iberia, our beloved land, has been failed by us. She is marred by countless attempts, countless constitutions, that sought to guide her towards prosperity. Each and every one of those has fallen short. The Constitution of Cádiz, the Portuguese Constitution of 1822, La Carta, all the way to Caetano's abortive Constitution months prior. We will not do the same.” Fraga pauses, sweeping his eyes across the room. “It is our sacred duty, our mandate, to not fail her again.”

We must build a constitution that will stand the test of time, but it will not be easy. We must build a strong government, capable of defending our people, but not so strong that it will turn against them and fall to despotism. We must bring justice to our people, clarity of the law, and an order that reflects the people's will, but be decisive in our decision-making so as not to be torn about from within. And lastly, we must capture what it means to be Iberia, what it means to be an Iberian. We must capture those innate values of family, faith, and love for this land and our country. We are up to that task.“

Applause erupts from the AP Conservatives, excitement thrumming through the group as fervor builds in their eyes. The Democratic Center only gives a smattering of applause, many of its members with brows furrowed. The left looked like they wanted to rip Fraga off the stage.

Well, he would take what he could get.
strings.IBR_natcon.24.d:
“The way forward is clear! The path is built! Worker and social protections must be demanded of the new Constitution to show its commitment to a truly fair Iberia. It falls to us to make the case, and force Fraga to see this - and allow the People to realize their own needs!”

A cry of approval burst around the small hall as the speaker sat, strips of fluorescent lighting illuminating the concrete room, a new build for the University Institute of Évora. Eagerly, most awaited the next speaker to rise, to speak their mind. Through the room's windows, the outside world appeared almost blue in the failing day, and despite the light glowing from the students around her as they listened, one lacked their sunny disposition.

Joana Alvez stood to speak amongst the throng, glaring at the people around her. “What do you know,” she began, disdain dripping like tar, “of the needs of the People? All of you, clapping like children at a party! Do you not see that nothing has changed? Do you laugh before Franco and Caetano's treats like a baby seeing jangled keys? 'Force Fraga to see this', I ask you all. What will you do? What are you brave enough to do?”

The room stood silent, a brutalist tomb of a moment. The informal Chair of the event, a friend of Joana's named Nuno Pereira - a senior of the group - rose after a moment. “Joana, no one here can doubt your passion. But things are changing, democracy has co-”

“You call this democracy? Obviously rigged elections are a democracy? Fran-”

“Joana.” Nuno called her name firmly, preventing a new tirade. “We have to believe things will change. We have to believe that we can change them, even if sometimes the People choose differently.” Joana looked at him, and merely shook her head as a lonely expression overtook her.
strings.IBR_natcon.24.a: “The sooner you realise how foolish that is, perhaps the more you could actually change.”
strings.IBR_natcon.25.d:
The dim light of the National Museum of Archaeology's reception hall kept all eyes on the stage, where Amália Rodrigues, Portugal's most prominent Fado singer, was holding most of the audience spellbound. The words of forlorn souls yearning for a respite denied them by fate washed over the dignitaries and diplomats like the waves of a bitter sea, tossing and turning their souls like small boats in a storm. But just in front of Rodrigues, on the front row, Marcelo Caetano was sitting stiff as a statue, in the seat provided him as a courtesy to his soon-to-be-abolished position as Iberian head of state, his eyes piercing forward in unseeing fury.

To Caetano's left sat Foreign Minister André Gonçalves Pereira, Caetano's former student of both law and politics. Caetano could feel his tearful eyes fixed on Rodrigues, absolutely entranced by her song. To his right, he could feel Vice President João Mota Campos, his protégé, his investment in the political field, shifting uneasily in his seat. Neither of them were focused on him - on their patron, their Caudillo. Mota Campos leaned towards him, but didn't even bother turning his head towards him.

“You know, Caudillo,” Mota Campos whispered, “I've been talking with some people on the constitutional draft committee. They say that they've reached an agreement on changing your- the Caudillo's title. Still to be determined what the new title will be and what its exact powers are going to be.” He was deferential as always, but Caetano could sense it. Any respect given to him now was the one given to an old relative shunted away to a nursing home - occasionally visited, taken care of, treated with deference, but never consulted on anything of value. And like the old relative, there was nothing he could do but waste away in his confinement. The rest of Mota Campos's words became a blur as Caetano tried to focus on Rodrigues' song, a single tear rolling down his cheek and his white knuckled-hands gripping his chair in a death grip as a whispered alongside her:
strings.IBR_natcon.25.a: “With what voice should I lament my sad fate?”
strings.IBR_natcon.26.d:
The Caudillo came out of the hunting cabin's door, a wide smile on his face as he shook Fraga's hand and embraced him. President of the Government Manuel Fraga leaned into the embrace, clapping his soon-to-be former superior on the back. “Thank you for humoring this visit, Caudillo. It's been a while since I've had the opportunity to visit Pardo, and it's good to be back.”

Franco stood up straight, the smile not leaving his face even as Fraga could see a spark of steel in his eyes. “The pleasure is all mine, Fraga. Let us go hunt something, shall we?”

The dry forests and hills of the Pardo palace had long been Franco's haunt for his favorite pastime, but this time, the palace grounds were not as bountiful as Fraga remembered them. A fitting metaphor, he thought as he stepped over branches and climbed rocks, overtaking the aging Caudillo around a bend. “You know, Caudillo - I wanted to visit in order to inform you of developments in the constitutional draft committee. It has been agreed that your title, as head of state, will be changed to 'President'. A more... respectable and proper name, do you not think?”

“Heh, President. And what will be the new title of the esteemed President of the Government? Will Iberia have her Caudillo Fraga?” Franco asked from behind. Fraga couldn't exactly place his finger on Franco's tone, but there was no humor in his quip. He turned around to explain-

Franco's hunting rifle was pointed directly at him. Fraga's eyes fixated on the muzzle, his blood running cold for a second that felt like an eternity. The muzzle flashed, thunder filled the small clearing, and Franco lowered his rifle and walked towards the squirrel he had shot over Fraga's shoulder. Franco shrugged as he picked up the small carcass and turned towards the President of the Government, his eyes suddenly softer.
strings.IBR_natcon.26.a: “These days, Señor Fraga, one takes what one can get.”
strings.IBR_natcon.27.d:
An image of Santiago Carrillo shaking hands with Bukharin took up half the pamphlet, “Is this the man you want in government?” It read.

“Santiago Carrillo, a known radical bolshevist who associated with dictator Nikolai Bukharin, has joined up with the Democratic Center coalition. The man who helped organized the Paracuellos Massacre is now a member of parliament, thanks to the centrist coalition.”

“A true center coalition wouldn't let such a violent radical, who has associated with the tyrannical dictator Nikolai Bukharin, join up with them. We, the concerned members of the Civil Duty Watch, call for the Democratic Center to dump this menace, before he causes any more harm.”

Filho finished checking the final draft of the pamphlet. It was perfect, none of those centrists would be able to stand by Carrillo when it went public. He'd wish he was in Moscow soon enough.
strings.IBR_natcon.28.d:
The early morning light was punctured by the flashes of cameras as Manuel Fraga made his way to the front of the gaggle of politicians from Galicia and pilgrims from all around Europe that he had come to accompany for the final leg of the Camino de Santiago. His path was constantly obstructed by glad-handing, joking, and even one embrace from the surrounding crowd, but finally, he managed to extricate himself from the crowd, shell-topped staff in hand, and took his place at the podium in from of the grand Cathedral of Santiago de Compostela, the press's lightbulbs illuminating him in the grey dawn.

“People of Galicia and of Iberia! It is my distinct pleasure to be here, on Iberia's most sacred ground, the place where Christ and Saint James' call to all peoples is heard loudest. This place is a touchstone of what makes this land so unique, but it is but part. I myself, as you may know, am a Gallego - I was born on Vilalba, on the very path we have just walked. Thus, I am grateful and proud to announce that the new constitution of the Iberian Union will recognize Galicia's unique contribution to our shared history and culture, by providing it with true, perpetual autonomy.”

The hour was early, but the sound of applause was almost deafening. This was Fraga's moment. “However, autonomy can not and will not mean a cutting off from our shared history and destiny as Iberians, nor can it mean that Madrid will be able to let itself neglect the regions it has now given autonomy to. The relationship between Madrid and Galicia will be strengthened like never before by a new Regional Assistance Fund, whose first task shall be the improvement and expansion of the Camino's trails and infrastructure. Galicia will be Autonomous, and its culture and treasures will be uplifted like never before by Iberia!”
strings.IBR_natcon.29.d:
Night encroached, the air filling with the peaceful harmony of insects hidden in the darkness. Joana loved this garden; her grandfather's homestead buried in the country.

“... so autonomy offers possibilities. We could see regional alliances against Madrid, local politics as a- Joana?” Her grandfather, reclined on his chair with a glass of wine, saw his granddaughter was distracted and concern filled him. This was unlike her. “Are you ok?”

“Grandfather I... I've been thinking.” Joana confessed hesitantly, “You fought in the Spanish War. Then we and the Spanish were oppressed together. These reforms, I can't see anything that has truly changed. People won't see.”

The surrounding twilight grew deeper. “Joana... what are you saying?”

“They are making a cage we won't even see. All this talk of autonomy, democracy? The Caudillos remain! The only way to make people see is... direct action. But,” her hands began to shake, a ghost of a sob passing, “I don't know if I can do it.”

Her grandfather softened, placing a hand on her shoulder. “Portugal is blessed to have you, Joana. I agree, but you can't deny that change is here, even if it's not what we would like.”

Joana let out a tense chuckle. “You sound like Nuno, he says direct action is worthless.” Her grandfather stiffened. “He insists we can work in this system. I want to believe him but...?”

Her grandfather sighed, a million memories flashing before him. “Yes. Sometimes direct action is required. I tried, failed, years ago but I won't tell you it isn't worth doing. Your parents never understood but you do. But...” His expression darkened.
strings.IBR_natcon.29.a: “...it's last resort. Change is here, albeit slow. If there's hope, don't throw your life away.”
strings.IBR_natcon.30.t: And They Shall See His Face
strings.IBR_natcon.30.d:
President Manuel Fraga and Foreign Minister André Gonçalves Pereira rose to their feet along with the rest of the small crowd as the eucharistic prayer began. They have come to a weekday mass in a church in central Madrid, letting the media spread the word of the government's piety even as they were drafting a religiously neutral constitution. The church was one of Franco's most important pillars of support ever since the civil war, but now they were tearing that structure down, brick by old brick, and the place of the church was going to need to be reevaluated alongside the rest.

They mouthed the sacred words and crossed themselves at the right time, even as they braced themselves for the tough negotiations ahead. The current Concordat Iberia had with Rome would no longer do in the new Iberia, but it couldn't simply be allowed to lapse. As Fraga was given the body of Christ, he thought of the headache of enforcing military service requirements for clergy, and as Pereira drank his blood, his thoughts wandered to the educational responsibilities the state was to take away from the church. And of course, the two agreed worldlessly as they made their way to their seats once more, there was the problem of money - millions in state subsidies which will de facto continue flowing to churches, no matter their intended purpose, and will need to be accounted for. But that was for another day.

As the two made their way to the limousine waiting outside, the crowd parted to let them pass, the three intimidating guards standing outside the doors ushering them forward. Fraga seemed to be deep in thought. Only when they had entered the car did he let loose his lips.

“You know, André, I had a thought during prayer. Call it a revelation, if you will. But I think I know how we're going to best deal with the clergy.”
strings.IBR_natcon.30.a: “We're the best remaining partner they have in Iberia. We can drive a hard bargain.”
strings.IBR_natcon.30.b: “We need them on our side - we could go their way on a couple of points.”
strings.IBR_natcon.31.d:
Though usually the temple brought thoughts of Diana, tonight it was Bacchus who reigned between its pillars. Wine flowed into waiting cups and slurred giggles climbed into the night. A dozen lounging revellers occupied the temple, and for them no world existed outside.

One stood up, unsteadily, but with a face full of mirth. “Everyone,” she called out, her voice not quite lost to inebriation, but within its embrace, “we are here to celebrate Jon's efforts for our group. The contacts he has made, the things he has made possible, we all owe him applause!” Hoots and laughter reverberated as they applauded. The man, Jon, attempted to stand to greet the applause, but slumped over half way into the ascent.

The woman continued. “However, there is a sour note to today. If you have not seen, our precious Fraga has decided to make a pact with the Catholics. He would have the Pope tell us what to do. You know what I say to that? Fuck that!” Another round of approving shouts met her.

“So, here in this temple, let us all make a pact. In ancient times, Evorans cried out here to Diana. A woman of virtue, of nature and of birth. In other words, the kind of woman that Fraga wished he knew!” The woman got down on her knees, holding an exaggerated pose reaching out to the sky as the drinkers guffawed. “Oh holy Goddess, we swear to never listen to those crazy Catholics! We'll raise our children to only follow you! Your laws will guide us forever!”

Their cheering dominated the night for just a moment before a more hostile sound attacked it; the encroaching whistle of sirens. Clarity wrestled itself upon them as they looked around at the cracked glasses and spilled wine. Not to mention the fence they jumped.

“There is our curtain call, grab Jon and let's get out of here!”
strings.IBR_natcon.31.a: Joana Alvez keeled over, vomiting to rapturous cheers, before leading her cadres towards the dawn.
strings.IBR_natcon.32.t: Dividing At the End of Empire
strings.IBR_natcon.32.d:
The governor's mansion in Praia hosted the representatives of local outlets as well as whatever media organizations could bother sending their men to Cabo Verde. At the head of the room stood José María Ruiz Gallardón, Minister of Territorial Organization, flanked by Iberian flags, as he finished his short press conference.

“We are committed to ensuring a peaceful and cooperative future for the people of these islands,” Ruiz cleared his throat, “and we wish to make this intention clear to you as well. As such, in a gesture of goodwill, I am pleased to announce the immediate pardon of 57 activists of the União Democrática de Cabo Verde, arrested last month for unlawful protest. I hope the hand we offer in reconciliation will be reciprocated.” The journalists applauded politely. It was an easy PR win, and it could even have positive repercussions on the future of the colony.

So Ruiz thought, at least. As he stepped down from the podium, he was approached by the outgoing governorת António Adriano Faria Lopes dos Santos, red-faced in his dress uniform. “Señor, if I may, I believe this is a mistake. We cannot allow ourselves to seem limp-wristed to the people here. Moralizing voices back home simply don't understand the situation in the colonies. This light-handedness will only make things harder for the next governor.”

Ruiz took António outside, where he responded calmly. “I simply believe that this was the best course of action. By letting the UDC protest, we snatch a possible win right out of the hands of PAIGC and other radicals. In fact, Señor, I believe the next governor will be well served in permitting the UDC to protest when they ask for it, provided they don't go overboard, of course.”

António's jaw tightened. He was almost done here. He could tell the minister how wrong he was to his face. But in the end, his shoulders only slumped slightly.
strings.IBR_natcon.32.a: Just another mess for his successor to deal with.
strings.IBR_natcon.33.d:
“So, Mr. and Mrs. Alvez, it appears that your daughter drew a picture of... ahem, President Fraga performing a... sex act on Caudillo Caetano, on the walls of the building.”

Both parents sat across the police desk motionless, eyes glazed as the image described burrowed into their heads. Between them their daughter sat chuckling. “Good God” her mother whispered.

“We've been looking for this troublemaker for quite a while, always signing off her crude vandalisms as 'Diana'. We found paint cans and a notebook on her. Had her art ideas, such as 'Fraga's Flatulence', which had a scrawled drawing of his mouth emitting -”

“Ok officer,” Joana's father stopped the officer, “I think we get the picture. Just, how much time is Joana going to be serving? Is there anything we can do?”

The officer looked at Joana. She was small for her age, but her eyes shone with exuberance. Almost defiant, but youthful. “Well, there's no longer political charges but vandalism charges could be-”

Then he saw it.

There was a hesitation in the girl's eyes. Fear. She put on a strong front, one she'd practiced well, but for just a second he had seen it. Underneath the defiant delinquent persona - she was terrified, and he saw the young girl.

“I guess... the buildings were disused. No owners on record and the Department is busy with all the changes happening recently. No need to go further on this than we need to - there will be a fine however. That bill was drawn up before we even caught her.” He took a piece of paper out of his desk and gave it to them, relief painting their expressions. “I trust you can handle her.”
strings.IBR_natcon.34.d:
The midday sun shone bright over the Cabreira Mountains as the three technocrats navigated the rocky ascent, only occasionally pausing to examine the picturesque scenery. Vice President Mota Campos, the architect behind the retreat, led the way. Finance Minister Dias Rosas followed close behind, and Minister of Industry Duarte Freitas do Amaral brought up the rear. The three paused as they took in the vast expanses below, oak forests and grasslands interlaced with a smattering of stone hamlets, an enclave of tradition in a land undergoing rapid transformation.

“Well, thank you, Vice President, for taking us out to this beautiful retreat.” The Minister of Industry looked into the distance, breathing in the fresh air, before turning to the other two. “But we must get down to business. We agree on many things, yes? Lowering inflation, reducing corruption, and constructing a stable basis for further changes.”

“You would be correct in saying that,” echoed Vice President Campos. “However, we must remember, gentlemen, that Señor Fraga is focusing on the constitution and restoring public order. These changes will take time.”

“But Vice President Campos, our nation is in dire need of economic stability!” exclaimed Rosas, taking a step forward. “The financial system needs reform, and inflation must be controlled. If you could only use your influence just here to push through these changes-”

“No, we must wait.” Campos shook his head before directing his gaze to the mountains. “The grandest of things, gentlemen, take the longest of times. The Cabreira took millennia to form. We can wait a few more months.
strings.IBR_natcon.35.d:
Paulo watched the absurd display, struggling to maintain the disinterested air that his assignment demanded. Incognito observation was usually a dull affair, loitering around an area for hours at a time watching something or someone - today the polling station for the Constitutional vote. Make sure there was no funny business around it. He had expected a day of little more than staring at the fountain.

The targets usually weren't being accosted by people in historical fancy dress. Elaborate, homemade fancy dress.

Signs towered above the group, and they shouted to the entire square. The slogans said things like “Remember Don Miguel!” or “The Spirit of Evoramonte!”. They were climbing the fountain at intervals, introduced by some guy called Nuno, ranting about the new Constitution with a number of negative adjectives. Paulo had written some of them down, it was proving to be quite an education, with other onlookers looking on bemused.

“Next,” came the echoed holler of Nuno's loudspeaker, “one of the most passionate amongst our number. Joana Alvez, speak your mind!” A supporting cheer arose from the protestors as a young girl, no more than nineteen or twenty, perched on the fountain.

“Everyone, hear your conscience! Heed it! I know the feeling of frustration, of seeing blatant misrule. I am sure many of you feel it too in your hearts. I've struggled with it, who are we before the might of those who declare themselves our betters? Who demands our loyalty?”

The girl paused, but the supportive shouts never stopped. Joana's voice reverberated again, more confident. “My pessimism was wrong, this Government has been limited in recent months. I have seen them frustrated, compromise forced from them by Iberia. Our rights are ours for the taking, hope is not lost! Vote no! No!”
strings.IBR_natcon.35.a: “Kids” Paulo chuckled. He was on the lookout for threats; precocious students were beneath the AAS.
strings.IBR_natcon.36.t: Rise By Sin; By Virtue Fall
strings.IBR_natcon.36.d:
The shadows were beginning to creep across the square, terrible specters reaching out from the buildings to the much-reduced band in its center. The day had begun with such energy, an exuberant mix of determination and defiance before the polling station. In their hearts, the fight against an unjust constitution was just truly beginning, starting with the People. Now the students sat around, shouting a slogan at the occasional person passing through and idly holding their placards up to be seen.

But who would see them? Joana Alvez sighed, leaning upon her placard. She supposed she should be happy that her suspicion of Fraga was a shared belief, but not such a strong belief that anyone would come out to join them.

She hoisted herself from her leaning, carrying the placard to Nuno Pereira, the protest's coordinator. He sat to the side, notebook in hand, dutifully counting the few who went into the polling station.

“How is it, Nuno? I think I've seen more of us leave in the last hour than voters go in there.” Nuno looked up at her and shook his head.

“I chose this place specifically because it was likely to be one of the busiest stations. But look at it!” He cast his notebook aside. “We're protesting to no one, Joana. I was... I was so sure that people would care.”

Joana looked at the man below her, remembering his fervent defences of civil action - in Iberians controlling their future - as he watched the empty building. She felt a pang of melancholy, a feeling of missed opportunity. They knew low turnout would benefit Fraga far more than Iberia - they were staring at a defeat they had done little to stop. Why had she listened to him, cowardly taking the easy path? All she had done was stand outside a building while Iberia fell back into oppression.
strings.IBR_natcon.36.a: “Perhaps our only hope was a bold statement,” Joana mused, as another group of students walked away.
strings.IBR_natcon.37.d:
By: Pedro Carvalho

Violence came to Évora today in the midst of the nationwide referendum on the new constitution being proposed by the Government. After much deliberation, from citizen political rights to relationships with religious bodies, the proposed constitution has been put forward to voters across Iberia. One such polling station where citizens could vote on their approval of the constitution was a building generously offered by the University Institute of Évora for such a civil purpose.

Before noon, a group of students affiliated with a UIÉ socialist club, who had been protesting outside the polling station against the constitution, suddenly attacked the building. Overpowering staff and a few security guards, they seized ballot boxes and cast them onto the courtyard outside the building.

One student, speaking on condition of anonymity, said that he attempted to stop the students but to no avail. “Joana, she got it into her head that they were stuffing the ballots inside. I'm not sure who told her; whoever it was made her believe it, and before I knew it she had whipped half the group into a frenzy.”

Police, supported by AAS units stationed nearby in case of electoral disruption, quickly intervened and arrested those complicit in the attack. Police have named one of those arrested as the ringleader; one Joana Alvez. In the wake of similar minor incidents across Évora later in the afternoon, they have asked for any with knowledge of her associations to come forward to aid in their inquiries.

Due to ballots being tampered with, it has been decided that votes from assaulted stations cannot be counted. The Electoral Oversight Committee has stressed that such a measure will not affect the outcome of the vote itself due to its small scale.
strings.IBR_natcon.37.a: Results of the polling will be counted as early as tomorrow, a clear vote to approve expected.
strings.IBR_natcon.38.t: We'll Be Fine; God's in Control
strings.IBR_natcon.38.d:
AAS TEAM REPORTING: KILO

REPORTING OFFICER: Major Luis Miró

DATE FILED: {date}

BRIEF: Operation successful. All terrorists deceased. Hostages in incident suffered 21 casualties. 2 team casualties. Acceptable resolution.

INCIDENT REPORT: Kilo Team alerted by Évora Police Department to siege ongoing on University Institute of Évora campus. 12 students occupied a building intended to be used in the upcoming constitutional vote, armed with old, poor quality weaponry, serial numbers poorly removed. 43 hostages present: teachers and students. Via loudspeaker their identified ringleader, one Joana Alves, outlined demands ranging from a meeting with national leadership to a prepared manifesto being read on a national broadcast. Media were slowly removed from the area.

Kilo Team entered via the roof of an adjoining building during negotiations. CS gas deployed through weak points while snipers neutralised visible suspected hostiles. Kilo team moved room to room, neutralizing terrorists with minimal collateral casualties before meeting a barricaded office. Gunfire injured Kilo 3 and killed Kilo 6. 

Grenades used to force entry into final hostile position. Regrettable substantial collateral damage to hostages inside but final hostile, Ringleader Alvez, neutralised via shrapnel causing mortal injury. Once CS gas dispersed, medical teams entered.

AAS Media Teams ensured reporting highlighted terrorist actions and its consequences. Rumors on campus that Alvez attempted a surrender are being suppressed, debriefings making it clear no such action took place.
strings.IBR_natcon.38.a: Voting will be relocated to a separate building on the opposite side of campus. Disruption nil.
strings.IBR_natcon.39.d:
Across Iberia, families huddled around their television sets and radios for Christmas Eve. Tables were set, radios crackled, and televisions hummed to life. This scene was reminiscent for almost every Iberian. They had learned to brace themselves for the same monotonous liturgy from their Caudillos. A ceremony about the courage of Iberia. A speech about its stability.

But this year was already different. Newspapers had circulated for days that the speech would come early, moved from New Year's Eve without explanation. In Portugal, they waited for Caetano. In Spain, they waited for Franco. Even after their victory, few believed the Alianza Popular would come to the stage and take part. They had done little to dispel the shadow of the old order.

But then came the broadcast. The light flicked on. There was no Caudillo.

Only President Manuel Fraga Iribarne.

Fraga adjusted his papers before looking directly into the camera. His voice didn't come from the chest. It didn't attempt an inspirational or declaratory speech. Only a calm conversation. “My fellow Iberians,” he began, “thank you. Your voice has been heard, and your support has shown that democracy is achievable in Iberia. Your ballots have given us the support to carry Iberia to its next year with a fresh start.”

There was no salute. No invocation of the Caudillos. No praising of God. No allusions towards disciplining dissenters.

“We will steer Iberia through these tumultuous times. Not by decree, but by the trust you have placed in us.” Fraga paused, keeping his gaze on the camera. “People of Iberia. We have begun a truly wondrous experiment. Let us cherish it. Feliz Navidad, Iberia.”
strings.IBR_natcon.40.d:
This year's Alianza Popular congress was one for the ages; the hall, packed with party members from every wing and state level, sat packed in the hall like sardines in a tin. Plastered on every wall, big and small, in the hall sat the ever-grinning face of their leader, Manuel Fraga.

After waiting for hours, their savior had come out to address them. The stout man slowly approached the singular podium, absorbing the uproar of hundreds of loyal supporters, ranging from youth leaders to party elders, screaming their hearts out for him. “Members of the AP, a new dawn is coming for Iberia.” The cheers grew even louder as he continued. “It is time for the AP to lead Iberia into a bright, new age! One filled with economic prosperity, greater strength abroad, law and order, and a prideful populace!”

Vague platitudes continued to be spurred from Fraga's lips as the crowd held every word. A speech filled with nothing had the appearance of a speech filled with everything. Iberians across the country tuned in to listen to this energetic man promise them a future brighter than before, and they were addicted.

“All of this, and more, is possible because of our abandonment of the limp-wristed coalition.” Pulling out a copy of the previous elections coalition program, Fraga made a show of tearing it in half, proclaiming to the now rabid crowd. “It's the Alianza Popular's future, and hers alone. No more tutelages! No more partners! Glory to the AP, and gloria a Iberia!”
strings.IBR_natcon.40.a: The floor erupted back. “Gloria a Iberia!”“
strings.IBR_natcon.41.d:
As had been the previous weeks, it was yet another gruelling day on the campaign trail for Fraga. Fielding the same barrage of questions from the same entourage of journalists he receives at every stop, yet one stood out from the rest. “Señor Fraga, there seems to be some contradiction in your candidate's policing policy. Some candidates are saying the police force will be expanded, while others claim that no expansion will occur. What is the actual position of the AP?”

Caught off guard by an actual question, Fraga, like any politician, attempted to sidestep. “Well, uh... you see, policing is a very um... important matter for the AP. Our coalition will come forward with a concrete plan soon enough.”

The rest of the journalists, sensing blood, dogpiled the question. One journalist began questioning economic cohesion, another on social policies, and another on what the AP really stood for, if anything at all. Fraga quickly became overwhelmed, sweat beading on his forehead as he kept trying to weasel his way out of the barrage. Attempting to give a satisfying answer without alienating any candidates.

“It'll all come shortly; everyone knows how hard negotiations are. The AP will act as a cohesive unit and set forward a strong policy for Iberia. Soon enough, all candidates will be on the same page.” He knew he was lying, but what else could he say? All he needed to do was keep this diverse coalition together, even if it took being a weasel.
strings.IBR_natcon.42.d:
Manuel Fraga, the new Franco?

Throughout the Alianza Popular congress, many party members have seemingly taken a more authoritarian turn in rhetoric. Many statements mirror those of the Caudillo regime, ranging from “Democracy holds back our progress” to “We could offer the world, and yet the die-hard leftists would continue to stop us at any turn.”

Speaking in backroom meetings, several high officials rained praise upon party head, Señor Fraga, as a savior for Iberia. A strongman willing to do what's best for the country and remove other elements. When I asked some of these members of the previous regime, many still praised it and wished for a return. Those old enough to remember the old Republic wanted nothing to do with it. They wanted a new Caudillo in charge, just this time with a grinning face.

Throughout the conference, several different men, who all identified as party officials, continually asked press members for names and outlets. They would also pressure outside members on party affiliation and keep logs of all attendees. Most definitely to determine who to shut down first when in power.

The closing speech defined it all. Señor Fraga, the wannabe Caudillo, proclaimed an iron fist against so-called radical enemies of Iberia, noting that the Alianza wouldn't defend a democratic system that would hold back Iberian prosperity in their eyes. Even going to the extent of circumnavigating the democratic process to get their goals done. The Congress loved it.

Every Iberian should look into this authoritarian actor and reject the Alianza at the polls.
strings.IBR_natcon.42.a: Only those who already believed read the piece.
strings.IBR_auth.1.d:
The modern world truly could be amazing, even in the most domestic of its spheres. Sure, the news would talk about the advances in technology. Outside they would see the cars change over the years. But here, in her utility room, modernity truly came for her. Valentina couldn't do anything but smile, as the loud whirring began. Oh yes, this washing machine was worth every penny.

“Those machines make all you young girls lazy, even those country girls with nothing but the clothes in their backs. A shame if you ask me.” From behind, the grating voice that ever plagued her Sundays spoke, addressing her as though she were not truly there. Filled with haughty pretence, her mother- in-law condemned her efforts. She didn't want to turn around to face her, why couldn't she just stay in the damn living room?

“Go back downstairs Gabriela, I don't have time for you right now.” She spared a single glance back before pretending to busy herself. How she hated her, coming dressed like some socialite. She never had recovered from losing the big house, why did she have to pretend she was still some countess?

“Sometimes I cannot believe Dante married... you,” Gabriela's face twisted in mocking disgust, “his poor mother needs him more than ever and yet he wastes his time making you lazy. What will you do, go and work in a factory like all the other help?” Her high voice laughed at Valentina. She grabbed some towels, just to make sure she wouldn't grab Gabriela.

“I'll be spending more time with the Sección Femenina de Falange actually.” Gabriela snorted behind her, leading Valentina to roll her eyes. “Doing more good than you will.”
strings.IBR_auth.1.a: Gabriela scowled. In her day, a young woman would never have spoken so... crassly.
strings.IBR_auth.2.d:
The Caudillos couldn't help themselves but smile as they looked out upon the streets of Iberia. Finally the question had been answered of their rule. Finally, the gap between themselves and the People had been properly bridged. Their ability to provide for them was secured, completely, by their very assent. After all, hadn't they been provided with a very convenient shield for themselves? It is said they smiled, for their rule felt more assured.

The Councillors talked amongst themselves, enthusiastic whispers full of speculations. They saw a levelled field, now they were to work with the Caudillos themselves with far more of an air of cooperation. No more would governance be schemes and whispers, Caudillos above and them right below. No, now they all stood to benefit, all the way to the Council. It is said those with lustful visions smiled, for they had been given a ladder on behalf of the People.

Some refused to share such ideas. They decried the lost opportunities, the chances to create an Iberia capable of moving away from the dogma that had stagnated it for years. Outside of the Caudillos' sight they discussed plans for the future, how to further what had been gained. Despite it all, they still felt the infectious optimism. The armour had cracked, the sunlight was streaming through. It is said they smiled, for modernity was arriving to Iberia, slowly and with great effort.

The People cared not. The titles had shifted, the procedures had been reworded, the Yes Men reshuffled. Had anything truly changed? God stood above, the Caudillos and their Men stood below, and their day to day continued.

They didn't smile. Not for sadness nor disappointment. The days remained routine and nothing served to disturb it.
strings.IBR_auth.3.t: The Lord Is My Shepherd, I Lack Nothing
strings.IBR_auth.3.d:
The Real Basílica de San Francisco el Grande was built on land blessed by St. Francis of Assisi, designed by a monk of his order, containing sculptures by Benlliure, paintings by Goya and Zurbarán. Great Spanish poets, politicians, and leaders had been interred within it. Painted on the walls behind the altar was the Lord with Mary above him, being lifted to the heavens depicted upon the arched roof. From the altar were thick insulated rubber wires that ran out past the pews of the well-heeled faithful. These wires carried the winding sermon of Archbishop Casimiro Morcillo González, a favorite of Franco, to radios and TVs across the Union.

“- Our body is one whole, and has many parts within it, and they are all one with Christ, and Christ is one within the Holy Trinity. The Lord gave us his whole body, so that we may be saved. Through his sacrifice and his grace we are given gifts. It is our duty to employ those gifts to best serve the whole.”

“In Romans, Paul speaks of sober judgment in what you have been graced with, and to understand one's place in the world. Teach in accordance with scripture. Heal those in need. Lead with zeal. May our leaders be blessed to shepherd us and Iberia to safety in these fraught times. Amen.”

The venerable Archbishop ambled back to the altar. The assembled faithful believed in his words, they believed in the leaders of the Union. They understood their place within the world, and the regime. The Caudillos had been good to them, good to the Church. Faults against others were forgivable. We are all redeemed through Christ.
strings.IBR_auth.3.a: The Lord, The Church, The Regime.
strings.IBR_auth.4.d:
Professor César Brito was a man who could be counted on to perform his research, teach his classes, and complete all the paperwork that the University required. He took pride in his professionalism. While other professor would gossip about everything from their wives to political issues facing the Union, Professor Brito maintained his silence. He was not paid to criticize or support any particular policy, he was simply paid to teach, research, and publish. Though these days he had been trying, mostly without success, to secure a promotion, and his output had suffered as a result.
