It was past 5 in the evening when the knock came across his door. His secretary had left for the day, and when he had opened it, a man in a dark suit with square shoulders nodded curtly before the professor allowed him in. César didn't know the man, he was no student and he certainly wasn't any member of the faculty he knew.

“Professor Brito. I am Señor Sánchez from the Interior Ministry.” César kept his face calm but wondered what the Interior Ministry could ever want with him. “As you are aware, the chair for the Literature Department remains vacant. The Ministry is prepared to make you an offer - should you act on our behalf to monitor dissent within the university, we will ensure that you will be named to the chair. All you need to do is keep close tabs on potentially troublesome professors.”

César wondered about this. Sure, the offer was great, but what were the risks? If he was exposed, it would certainly mean the end of his professional career. Dissidents might balk at striking at a high-ranking general in the army, but a professor wasn't going to have any security. But if he succeeded, then he'd have made his fortune - and it wasn't like he was committing a crime. He was serving his country, both as a professor and in security. César shook the man's hand, and the deal was done from one professional to another.
strings.IBR_auth.5.d:
It's amazing what you'd hear simply if you took the time to listen. Professor César Brito had known this for a long time, but he gained new appreciation for it when he taught literature. Reading a book could tell you not just the story on the page, but often reflected more about the author that they'd care to admit. When you looked an author's choice of words, their entire character was laid bare for the reader, if he could piece it together. Professor Brito was much more social after being named to the chair of the Literature Department. Most took his new outgoing attitude to be standard social obligation that he now had given that he was management. César took mental notes that he'd write down once he was in the security of his own office. Some were loyalists, and most of the ones who were loyalists were tepid. César rolled his eyes but took mental notes all the same.

There were more than a few however, who complained about Franco's policies. That he was a fool who needed to censor the academics so they couldn't prove him wrong. That he was just waiting for a new excuse to re-enact 1934 all over again. Or that he would drive all the good thinkers from Iberian shores. They'd need to be watched very closely. He made sure to note who was saying what, who was motivated by what, and how extreme they were. He even tried to write down the punchlines to their jokes about “Little Paco” - how he needed to write three history books so he was never wrong.

In his office, he compiled his notes as he waited for his handler. Sánchez had appointed a handler to act as his secretary to maintain their cover. It was almost odd - in public Brito had to boss around his secretary as if he truly was his employee and assistant, in order to sell the cover story. Brito had studied literature, not acting, but the part that was written was one he could play.
strings.IBR_auth.5.a: His notes ready, Brito was writing the endings for the characters he knew in real life.
strings.IBR_auth.6.d:
All that could be heard from Carles Cerecero's office was the rip of a paper and a fist slamming the desk, a man who saw himself rise through the ranks during the Spanish Civil War, was awarded a position from the Caudillos, a position he thought he rightfully deserved.

Now Carles slumped at his desk looking at the pieces of paper given to him by the Council, the very same man that once appointed him to this position was reassigning him to a sinecure. He managed to be able to keep the same pay, but that wasn't what Carles cared about. He cared about power.

Carles assumed it was his right to have influence in the government, he thought of how much he had sacrificed in the civil war, the horrors he suffered as a logistics manager, but now he was pushed aside to a title of no importance.

Soon after his fit, Carles wrote a letter to the Caudillos complaining about this unjust treatment, a letter he would pour his heart into, he needed to keep this position, if he was moved he would lose all his personal staff and his little army. Not only Carles' life, but more importantly his ego, depended on this letter to retain his position.
strings.IBR_auth.7.d:
José and Miguel were a pair of union bureaucrats representing the national trade union, a union so slow that many businessmen across Iberia dealt covertly with underground elements in labor disputes rather than its sluggish ways.

As he did every morning, Miguel was perusing the morning paper when suddenly he grabbed José, “Look at this José, they're changing everything”, José quickly scanned the paper noticing the reduced restrictions on non-state unions.

José 's face began to redden as he continued reading, eventually exploding, “Miguel, we're going lose our jobs, they're going let these socialists run everything, we'll fall to anarchy!”

Miguel quickly tried to reassure him, “Look, they all have to submit to inspections and have liaisons from the state.”

José's tension began to fade, “Well it seems at least someone had a calm head in that room, and kept out those socialists!”

“Yes José, they have to be apolitical in order to operate.”

José finally calmed as all the new implications began to sink in, realizing that these new union laws were simply a mirage.
strings.IBR_auth.8.d:
As Pedro was setting up a cheap plastic folding chair he was conversing with his friend Diego, “So, what do you think of the new law?”

Diego scoffed as he finished setting up his own chair, “There's ups and downs, thankfully we don't have to deal with those uptight bureaucrats, always having a stick up themselves.”

“Don't be so cynical,” Pedro finished his chair and sat, “At least this way we have an actual meaningful say.”

“How much of it did you read?” Diego shot back, it's still run by the state behind the scenes, and we can't even take any meaningful positions or be called socialists and shut down!“

A fellow group of union men glanced Diego's way as he finished, the oldest of the group walked over to join the two, speaking to them, ”I understand you two, but remember this is the first union I've seen in my life actually run by workers, and look at me, have some hope.“

As the old man walks back to his group the two friends continue to discuss as a man, described as their new leader, saunters up to the podium to begin.
strings.IBR_auth.8.a: The more things change, the more they stay the same.
strings.IBR_auth.9.t: Our Responsibility to the Next Generation
strings.IBR_auth.9.d:
Joaquín Menéndez turned towards his youth group's storage room, looking for the emergency pack of cigarettes he kept there in the hopes that Pablo wouldn't notice, when he saw the door was open, letting out the sounds of someone dragging crates on concrete and grunting with effort. He looked inside, his eyes going wide immediately.

The small room, usually filled mostly with brooms and old albums, was completely packed with crates of... educational resources? At least that's what was written on them. He gingerly opened one of the top crates to see stacks upon stacks of notebooks. Another crate was filled to the brim with pencils. Joaquín realized that whoever put this here, they shouldn't see him smoke, and that this was probably none of his business, anyways. He turned around as quietly as he could and hoped that whoever was behind this hadn't noticed him.

A hand grasped at Joaquín's shoulder, and he jumped. Behind him was a pudgy, balding police officer, red with effort, his other hand wiping his brow. “Good afternoon, kid, I'm Officer Alfonso. You the leader around here? Your minder said you gotta read this.” He plopped down a small clipboard with a stack of papers that looked like instructions.

Joaquín, still unnerved by the encounter, spoke faster than he could think. “N- Yes. Yes I am,” he tried to compose himself to little avail. “The heck's all this doing here?”

“New responsibilities, Joaquín,” came Pablo's voice from behind. “You better get used to them. Iberia's children must have the best education in the world if we are to claim our place in the hierarchy of nations.” Joaquín did his best not to roll his eyes. He was here to help little kids play football, not teach them calculus, for God's sake. His shoulders slumped before the pile of crates as Officer Alfonso left the room...
strings.IBR_auth.9.a: ...and discreetly deposited Joaquín's pack of cigarettes in his pocket with a wink.
strings.IBR_auth.10.d:
Today we interviewed world renowned painter and sculptor Pablo Picasso, still residing in his New York apartment, the famous artist answered several of our questions surrounding his life, art, and the state of his homeland.

When asked about the state of censorship, Mr. Picasso responded, “So they are just 'leaving most of them alone'? That doesn't mean anything. Knowing those old curmudgeons, they'll just move the goalposts around until every piece of art is something to do with Catholicism!”

Continuing his rant of on the matter, Mr. Picasso stated, “They want everything to fall under 'our history' this and 'traditional culture' that. Spain, and for the matter all of Iberia, is a devoid wasteland of empty souls not brave enough to experience art in its truest form.”

Continuing his at-times political art from America, Mr. Picasso stated that, “Spain may not be to the liking of my ideas, but they will now forever be on the dark side of history, no matter what.” We asked if anything can change.

“They are too far gone now,” Mr. Picasso spat, “They say they will change, lift some restrictions but no, no matter what they do to try and change the past...”
strings.IBR_auth.11.d:
An important news update on the Iberian Council's vote on the General Law of Education. DATELINE: Madrid.

After much deliberation, on-site RTVE reporters have confirmed the Iberian Council's passage of the reformed General Law of Education to be later ratified into the Iberian constitution. In an otherwise unsurprising development, the Council voted in favor of the redrafted law via sweeping majority in line with the proposal of the Caudillos Francisco Franco and Marcelo Caetano.

Couched in the rhetoric of a unified, nationalist-oriented education program in Iberia, it is designed to reshape education along the lines of government-sanctioned academia. In practice, this essentially places Iberian education firmly under the direct control of the central governments of Madrid, Lisbon, and the personal regimes of either Caudillo.

The opposition on the Iberian Council tells a different story regarding the General Law of Education and in so doing, perhaps highlights a dour mood among their fellow countrymen. In the grand scheme of things, this is of little consequence. Whatever worries on the Council of the Education Law about 'Bukharinesque socialist indoctrination' or 'first verifying educational loyalty' have fallen by the wayside. Not a question remains as to the state of the public arena in the wake of the Council's ruling.

As it stands, ratification of the new law is assured, as was assumed and to be assumed by the polity of the Union as has been for a generation or more.
strings.IBR_auth.11.a: What was envisioned was what will be, little else need be considered.
strings.IBR_auth.12.d:
Camilo had heard about the new educational reforms that were coming, and wondered what they would mean for him. They talked about the students that were able to go to school, but that had never been an issue for him. His family had saved to send him to school, hoping he'd be the first to head to university. But when he spoke with his father, all he could talk about was how excited he was that the university admission exam would be simpler - he wouldn't need to spend extra money for tutors to prepare Camilo for the entrance exams since he was already doing so well in school. For Camilo, it was a sigh of relief.

No such relief found its way to Ricardo Calvo, whose wealthy family would no longer be granted legacy admission to university. Now he would need to spend more time studying, and less time dancing with the girls and spending time with his friends. Every single minute had to be devoted to making him ready for the new exams, now that his future was not secured to him.

Two friends, Abelardo and Marcelo, spoke about the new laws after class that day. Marcelo was ecstatic, he could now go to school, and just maybe he could secure a new job for his family. He wouldn't have to watch his father break his back at the dockyard until he was old and gray, without any money to even afford a nice chair in his old age. Yet for Abelardo, time spent in school was time not spent working. He was young, and strong. His father had died and his muscles could provide for his mother and his younger brother until he was old enough. If he was in school for tomorrow, who would feed their family today?
strings.IBR_auth.12.a: The new students looked toward the new laws, wondering for their future.
strings.IBR_auth.13.d:
“...And so, I am immensely grateful to be able to stand here and celebrate the wisdom of our beloved Caudillos. The women of Iberia and their representatives in the Sección Femenina greet the reforms to their role in society with determination to continue serving Iberia as devoted daughters, wives, and mothers, with ever greater love and will. Arriba Iberia!”

Pilar Primo de Rivera descended from the podium to thunderous applause, followed by a short procession of government dignitaries. The message was similar - women's suffrage had been improved, the restrictions on women's role in society were being loosened, and the women of Iberia were grateful to the Peninsula's masters, as well they should have been.

The Sección Femenina representatives in the cavernous hall of the Seville Cathedral were grateful, indeed. At first, they applauded politely when a speaker finished their speech, but soon, deafening applause filled the hall whenever one of the Caudillos was mentioned. Only when the final government representative left the stage for the procession of priests who began to conduct a mass of thanksgiving did the cathedral fall silent again.

Following the mass, Cardinal José María Bueno y Monreal, Archbishop of Seville, took to the stage once more. “It is with great joy that we greet the reforms to the status of women in Iberian society as conducted by the Caudillos, and it is our hope that the women of Iberia will grow ever more confident and fulfilled in their great role as guardians of family and-”

The doors to the nave opened, letting inside sunlight and a procession of a few dozen women bearing placards. Cardinal Bueno braced for screams and shouts, but they didn't come. The attending women could see that the protesters marched towards the altar with their mouths taped shut, only their placards speaking for the women of Iberia.
strings.IBR_auth.13.a: “Will we be content with crumbs from the Caudillos' plates?”
strings.IBR_auth.14.d:
José Ignacio San Martín López could scarce believe it if he didn't actually hold the order in his hand: Axencia Anti-Separatista would finally be given what it needed to stop the separatists.

Axencia Anti-Separatista was, for most of his posting, a dead-end assignment. Charged with maintaining the integrity of the Iberian Union against separatist forces, it seemed that every single force conspired to ensure that the AAS was incapable of carrying out that assignment. The military was incredibly cagey about turning over supplies, the Defense Ministry sidelined AAS officials at meetings, and other counter-terrorism agencies competed for what few scraps remained, with Africa receiving much of the largesse.

Now, it was the complete opposite. Military-grade surplus weapons and armor. Twice the case officers. A small army of experts from forensic accountants to explosives engineers, and a new Operations Staff that answered to him personally. Already, his departments had been taking advantage of the extra manpower to review their backlog of case files and evidence. Some departments had even spoken about making progress on stalled investigations.

Dimas Castellanos, the chief of intelligence operations, couldn't have been happier. “We predict that we will increase our operations tempo within the next six months. We'll restart operations in Catalonia and Barcelona, and we should be able to recruit new sources that can make connections to subversive groups. Now that we don't have to ration our equipment, we can devote soldiers, policemen, and analysts solely on counterterrorism.”

“It's about time. Counter-terrorism was just a buzzword for the higher-ups to rationalize whatever it was they wanted to do. Petty graffiti? Terrorist slogan. Rowdy drunks making fun of the mayor? Terrorists. Now maybe we can actually do something about the real threats.”
strings.IBR_auth.14.a: “The only thing we need now are enough pine boxes for that ETA scum.”
strings.IBR_auth.15.t: A Directive From Francisco Franco & Marcelo Caetano
strings.IBR_auth.15.d:
RE: Opposition strategy

We expect you to shift strategy on managing opposition to the regime based on the following criteria. Your two main objectives will be to prevent the rank and file members of the opposition from feeling aggrieved by the state, and curtail the ability of their leadership to lead.

To that effect, small-scale public gatherings and meetings should be monitored as appropriate, but be allowed to continue unmolested. Mundane organizing activities, handing out leaflets, informal canvassing, etc etc, all fall into this category. You should not be seen as discouraging political agitation as a whole, and be seen to relax the perception of persecution.

Coordinate with the AAS to collate a folio on any and all opposition leadership. Keep them under strict observation. Any petty infractions that can be visited on them should be. Any reasonable excuse for imprisonment or deportation to the colonies should be used. Any ties to terror groups have to be exploited to maximal effect. Use the full weight of the considerable powers we have vested in you to ensure they are ineffective as political entities. Programs like these may be in place already. Redouble the efforts in those, and ensure that all instructions herein are followed to the letter.

Please send over a finalized proposal based on these recommendations forthwith.
strings.IBR_auth.16.d:
As Prudenci Lacosta took advantage of the slow day to straighten up and sweep the shop, he noticed that for the first time in a long while, he hadn't seen any police officers come into his shop, either uniformed or plainclothes.

It used to be that he would always have officers show up in his shop several times a day. Sometimes they'd be overt, standing outside and taking notes about who went into or out of his business. Other times, he'd notice someone that seemed to be listening a bit too closely as he spoke to his wife. A constant flow of pressure that somehow seemed to be stopped at the source. He had remembered the Caudillos making a big speech about increasing social integration, but Prudenci never expected to see, of not see in this case, an actual tangible effect of this policy change.

Ironically, he was never a Catalan nationalist. He certainly had pride in his heritage, but he had never thought Catalonia had the economic footing to stand as an independent nation - it's why he moved to Madrid and opened his shop in the first place. Yet just by being Catalonian, the police had thought he must have been a fifth columnist or his shop's basement a hideout for a secret Catalan nationalist terror cell. But for right now, he had seen only one policeman all day, and it was an actual customer of all things. Prudenci chuckled at the thought - the policeman may not have even known he was financing the absolute terror of a man whose greatest tie to Catalan separatism was a picture of his hometown on his desk. Who knew when this might change again? Should the Caudillos get it in their mind, he could be back to being scrutinized daily, or if a new police chief was convinced of the danger that separatism could hold. It probably would, but for the moment at least, Prudenci could enjoy himself.
strings.IBR_auth.16.a: It might change again tomorrow, but he was happy for today.
strings.IBR_auth.17.d:
Lieutenant Paulo Gutiérrez finished looking around his room, a satisfied smirk on his face. It required a bit of cleaning and moving things around, but his quarters were now almost comfortable. He remembered the cramped, filthy “accomodations” he was provided when he first joined the officer corps, and how he and Jaime had to curl up together in the single usable bed they had to keep out the cold in winter. But now, with the pay raises provided for by the new directive, he had his own room, with bookshelves he planned on filling, a place for a radio, and even a kitchen with room for a small refrigerator. Jaime was out for the night, getting drunk off his ass in town, but Paulo didn't care - he could vomit in his own room now.

Lieutenant Jaime González was having the time of his life. The small bar he and his friends had taken over was a lively place, with jaunty music and good drink. He didn't remember the last time they could afford going to a place like this - mid-level officers like him were used to going to the seediest dives in town. He grinned as he remembered Paulo's face when he had managed to take him to that awful place on the outskirts of Valencia. Paulo was a good guy, but not cut out for places like this. A bit girly even, Jaime and the rest of the officers thought among themselves. Jaime bet he had a lot of fun ordering books on his new bookshelf.

In an office somewhere deep in the Interior Ministry building, a high-ranking functionary was being briefed on the results of the most recent reform to the officers' pay. “A few of the generals have publicly expressed disapproval at the reform. They claim that it discourages discipline among the junior officers and fosters a culture of hedonism and weak morals. This would be cause for concern, but the Ministry believes that it is quite compensated for by the incredible reduction in complaints by those same junior officers.” The Ministry clerk finished reading his report and raised his eyes to see his superior nodding in approval.
strings.IBR_auth.17.a: The sword of Damocles grows slightly duller.
strings.IBR_auth.18.d:
To the esteemed Minister of Defense and Joint Staff Command:

The Caudillos have seen fit to embark on a large-scale modernization and reorganization of the Iberian Armed Forces with the goal of increasing adaptability and responsiveness to rising exigent circumstances. After a careful investigation, the Caudillos have determined that the authorization chain for military action is too slow and reflects an outdated approach to military science. Furthermore, logistical chains have become too slow and unresponsive when centralized in Madrid, therefore, more power will be delegated to base commanders to handle readiness issues within their AOR. As always, the mission of the Iberian Armed Forces remains the steadfast defense of the Iberian people, their Union, and their way of life, and these new changes will better shape the needs of the Union.

With these changes comes reduction and reassignment in the general staff to effect a leaner and more effective fighting force. The general staff has grown beyond its intended role and will be refocused on providing the exceptional level of command experience and leadership that embody the martial spirit of Iberia. The Caudillos have identified members of the general staff with exceptional abilities that will be well-suited for alternative roles where they can continue to serve the Iberian Union with honor and distinction. The Caudillos expect all members of the Armed Forces will take pride in their accomplishments and continue to serve the Union as they have in the past.

Other members of the general staff may expect to be redeployed to other postings to more effectively accomplish their missions. This more responsive and direct leadership from senior flag officers is expected to improve performance of all personnel and will enable further success now and in the future.

All For the Fatherland.
strings.IBR_auth.18.a: A shakeup underneath all the dust.
strings.IBR_auth.19.d:
Externally, everything seemed to be running smoothly. The men had accomplished every drill with aplomb, and had even passed unscheduled inspections at higher than the average rate. Yet General Gregorio Aquino and the men under his command were in chaos. The general had ordered barracks inspections five times this week, searching for the smallest possible infraction. When that had turned up nothing, he ordered readiness drills to test the men during a possible hostile action in the Strait. When they had performed admirably, he ordered it be done again the following day. On-duty, the troops were skilled. Off-duty, they had turned increasingly to drink out of stress and fatigue. Order was on the surface-only, the core was cracking under the pressure.

Colonel Tito Tijerina, General Aquino's XO, knew the reason for the general's actions. By order of the Caudillos, he had been ordered to prepare the post for a change in command, and that he would be forcibly retired. They had couched it in a significant honor, that due to his long years of service he would be named as Commissioner for War Graves, charged with maintaining the final resting place of those who had died during the Civil War. When this had happened, General Gregorio had gone ballistic, looking over his men again and again, desperate to find fault with something so that he could explain why his commission had been rescinded. Surely, it had to be the men's fault, not his.

When each excuse was found not to be the case, the general's edge became increasingly hollow. Defeat lurked inside his voice, and it grew louder with every day. There wasn't a problem with his command, this is simply the way it was to be. General Aquino's fury was empty because there was nothing to it. He could order a thousand drills, but it couldn't change what was to pass. The troops simply had to weather the storm simply because it could do nothing but blow.
strings.IBR_auth.19.a: Change is coming, and the military will never be the same.
strings.IBR_auth.20.d:
Dear Mr. Caudillos,

The people of São Tomé thank you for your generosity, your insightful and commanding decisions have led to success and growth on the island.

We here thank you for providing for the welfare of the people, giving us electricity, food, and careers. The people of São Tomé have been enlightened by your teachings by having everyone learn how to be civilized and learn the greatness of Iberia and her languages.

There could be no better place on earth than here on this island thanks to the Caudillos' great leadership, nowhere on planet Earth do you see different races respond so well with each other, you Caudillos have created a shining gem in Africa showing that nobody can match Iberian might.

Myself and the people of São Tomé hope that your rule is eternal, with heart and soul, we offer ourselves to your service. Let our days be spent in the shadow of the Caudillo's greatness and our voices raised only in praise of your wisdom and might.
strings.IBR_auth.21.d:
The lone brick building in the village sat attentive with students, a dichotomy seen in few places, but oh so prevalent in Iberia's colonies, a singular white settler teacher in a class of all black students.

The teacher began the lesson like any other, the students pledging their allegiance not to their tribes, but to Iberia and her Caudillos. Today would be about the history of these children's land, a lesson in which Iberian overlords, its discoverers, colonists, and her people are lionized, a portrait of a mighty people.

The second half of the day's lesson would be about wretched sovereigntist movements, teaching the students about the uncivilized nature of the land, how independence movement leaders were treated and where they ended up.

The students as always never believed in this fabricated history, always holding a bit of cynicism to what was being taught but never questioned it, they knew better. These kids' focus was on a singular path, a civil service job, the chance to move out of this village and make enough money to survive.

But to do that they all had to memorize these stories and remember that being under Iberian rule was supposed to be a blessing, that they are all better off underneath it.
strings.IBR_auth.21.a: They kept their heads down and continued taking notes.
strings.IBR_auth.22.d:
Humberto could scarcely believe when he had heard that his old schoolmate Ismael was going to be the new governor of Extremadura. He had always been a popular boy in school, easy to make friends and bright enough to score well on tests. He hadn't come from a prominent family, however, and so his life seemed destined to be one of mediocre bureaucratic accomplishment. Without the ability to meet people behind closed doors, where the real business of state could take place, he could rise only so far. That morning however, Ismael had contacted him, unable to contain his excitement. He'd be the governor of the entire region.

That night, of course, the two men went out to celebrate. After a bit too much sour red, Humberto held his glass up, “To the new governor, a man who knows the land inside and out,” to everyone's loud cheers. A few cries for a speech, then suddenly the entire establishment clamored, shouting for the governor-to-be to give a few words.

Ismael had barely touched his drink, but the good cheer was infectious. “I can only hope to serve this land and her people to the best of my ability. I've known many of you all my life, and I can only hope that this next chapter will be as rich and fulfilling as my time here with you has always been.”

“What?” Humberto laughed, the wine getting to his head. “Don't think you'd measure up to his Previous Magnificence. The lazy city boy from the other end of Iberia who never smelled a pile of pomace in his life?”

A sharp laugh came from the table next to them. Everyone looked to see the face of Ambrosio Oliveros, owner of the largest vineyard in the region, together with a few of his contemporaries. Ismael was intrigued. “Gentlemen, you know something about the previous governor?”
strings.IBR_auth.22.a: “They found a more pertinent post for him...Let's hope you do better...your Excellency.”
strings.IBR_auth.23.d:
The office had not changed. Neither had the secretary sitting outside, the lack of mail in the inbox tray, nor the telephone that rang only very rarely. But there had been a very great change nonetheless.

The man sitting behind the desk crumpled the paper and threw it into the trash can. He had been given this office - this post - by the Caudillo himself for valuable services rendered. The title gave him influence, gave him impact on decision-making when he wanted it, and gave him commensurate compensation. And he had repaid it with loyalty, support, and working against the interests of those who displayed neither. Another year or two and the next step on the ladder would have surely been given over to him.

But it had all changed. By order of the same office, he had been appointed to the position permanently. The compensation had been drastically reduced. The workload was to be increased. And there were to be no appeals entertained.

He knew there was no way out. One could not be seen to be ungrateful, for only dangerous people repaid 'bounty' with ungratefulness. But he also knew that the charmed existence he had deserved was changing, and that nobody had spoken up for him to permit otherwise. That stung even worse.
strings.IBR_auth.23.a: Now to do some real work.
strings.IBR_auth.23.b: Damn those Choupana boys cutting in line.
strings.IBR_auth.24.d:
Sitting as he always did at the head of the table, Alfredo Sánchez Bella looked at the latest advertising proposals from his staff, and despaired. They were new, they were colorful, and they were not engaging in the least.

But there was little other choice. He had lost count of the number of times he had sat here, with his staff of secretaries, copywriters, and others, developing promotional materials for Iberian tourism. Crafting 'public information' communications. Throwing around and refining slogans for the newest campaigns trying to bring those tourism dollars ever-chased by the government (or chased by the Caudillos, which was largely equivalent). And reactions had always been anemic.

They all knew the core problem, of course, even if they would not speak it to each other. One could not mention anything political in the current climate, and to those outside Iberia such was a topic of great concern. All the new copy was naturally ebullient on the 'peace and quiet' that could be obtained in Iberia for a visitor, but little else could be said. And it would have to be enough. The posters would be printed, the talking points distributed, and the hopes pinned on a successful campaign that would help the tourism industry - and please the Caudillos.

Bella waited for the message telling him to prepare the next one. For the same purpose.
strings.IBR_auth.24.b: “Looks like we're putting globe-trotting Marcelo front-and-center”
strings.IBR_auth.25.d:
As he prepared for his flight to Central America, the Iberian diplomat watched the latest government campaign on his television. Positioned right beside his window, he could also see the posters being applied to the wall across the street.

It was nothing to which he was unaccustomed. The models changed, as did the music, and so too did the emphasis on medium, but the message was always the same. A vaguely cohesive mash of positivity around Iberia and the Iberian 'experience.' About the superiority of the 'culture.' About enlightenment and fraternity and all such related concepts, that any person who was already inclined to such thought could rapidly consume and internalize whatever the new angle of presentation upon it was.

He had seen many come and go, and though he himself was no longer their audience, he understood their effects. Both at home in Iberia, and across the larger Luso- and Hispanospheres. Language and culture was a strongly unifying concept, he well knew, and he was sure he would hear about this latest campaign when he landed.

He took some time to memorize the passages. It would help break the ice with the locals, he was sure. Or, at least, with those who made the decisions for them.
strings.IBR_auth.26.d:
Alberte passed the newspaper around the room. “Our esteemed Caudillo and fellow Galician Francisco Franco wants to preserve the unity of the Spanish Nation against those who seek to undermine it at the behest of foreign agents, knowingly or not. Let us perform a literary analysis of his words. Truly, he is a better writer than Castelao, able to subtly indicate his disdain for the tools of sedition that need not be named.”

“You should have listened to his radio speech. Franco is a genius!” Erea smiled looking back at him “His prose is unmatched, the Codax of our age truly. None of our ancient poets could surpass his eloquence.”

“But Erea, you must know if you have listened to him”, Alberte continued, “Or at least please guess based on your analysis of his style. Where has our good man learned Castelán so well? I cannot hear even the slightest accent, nor any misshapen consonant. He must have undergone some higher education unlike us peasants with our useless dialect, who cannot even pretend to understand his genius.” The Galicians laughed and raised their glasses. “Saúde! To all of Spanish Society”.

Hundreds of kilometres away, in Navarre's countryside, a couple angrily turns off the radio, unwilling to relive the false hope they had for their people when the Union was formed. In defiance, they stubbornly refuse to use Castilian when talking to their children.

In Barcelona, long after midnight, a young university student defaces a poster calling for all Spaniards to speak Spanish by asking, “And if I am Catalan?”

Meanwhile, thousands of Africans across the colonies, in fear of the AAS' omnipresence, must suppress the true feelings evoked by the speeches. Soon they will be put back to work, shedding sweat and blood so that the Spaniards might “rejoice in brotherly love”. But the day of their awakening shall come with wrath and fire...
strings.IBR_auth.26.a: ...and every Piece of the Union shall proclaim itself a Nation.
strings.IBR_auth.27.d:
Looking at the vast field of rice, imminently ready for harvest, Fernando Augusto Santos e Castro felt a surge of pride. This was a victory, and it was one that Iberia desperately needed.

He had been an agronomist for many years, and for almost as many, he had been either sidelined or outright ignored. The Caudillos' functionaries, after all, did not like being told when they were wrong about how the productivity of Iberian land could be increased. Or of how planting organization could be optimized. But the Council saw things differently, and well understood that the state needed more food. Needed more efficiency in growing that food. And they had come to him for a plan.

He had delivered. Between employing some innovative techniques that other Iberian researchers had been trying to put forward for years, combined with a number of foreign advancements (of which he was careful not to ask as to how they had been obtained), he had greatly enhanced the production of grains. The rice field in front of him, he knew, would have only been half as extensive, at best, merely a year prior.

As he took an inventory in his head of what the harvest was likely to be, he felt a pride he had not felt in a very long time. He was, at heart, a farmer. And this was now a very fine farm, indeed.
strings.IBR_auth.28.d:
It was a little nerve-wracking working under the cold eye of your employer, especially when he was being stared at by his own boss - even if it was just a portrait. The aged Governor of Madeira stood, awaiting the completion of the workmen's work as they installed a TV into his office. The sneer of cold command that António Salazar delivered from the portrait demanded only the best for the realm, and no workman wanted to be explaining to the Governor why they had failed in that.

“So where did this TV come from?” the Governor asked his aide standing off to the side as the workmen finished.

“Not sure, it's Jap crap so probably Guangdong,” came the tired reply, surprising the workmen with its bluntness. “I'll go downstairs, get the manifest and check the compan-”

“No no, as long as it works.” The aide gave a silent exasperated sigh.

The workmen finished and were unceremoniously shooed out of the way by the Governor as he took the large remote and excitedly switched the television on. Static met them, earning a half cry from the Governor. “I thought we were connected, where's my segment?” Anger flashed and he pointed at the workmen. “Did they fuck it up?”

The aide came forward, passing a schedule to his lap, annoyance caking his face. “We'll be connected in time for News at Nine. A few minutes yet.” The Governor harrumphed, and all waited. Minutes slowly passed by before the screen resolved, the static dissolving into the image of two news anchors in a pristine studio.

“...ave just been informed our connection is complete; to our friends in Madeira, the Canaries, and the Azores, welcome. In honor of this occasion we have recorded addresses from the Governors of those regions...”
strings.IBR_auth.28.a: “I'm on TV!” squealed the Governor, earning a glance from aide and workman alike.
strings.IBR_auth.29.d:
It was a half-hour past lunch and the Council had not yet come back in session. Yet for many, a lunch break was not a break from working. The reformists had taken to conducting meetings among their caucus right after lunch, finding ways to continue their mission.

“They've taken the basic minimums for our ideas and cast us aside,” Diogo Miranda Simões, one of the more outspoken members of the faction, nearly shouted to those assembled, causing ripples in their water glasses. “It's been our overriding purpose, and yet now we're being kept out of it. This is only the beginning, mark my words, they want to take as little as they can and flank us to shut us out. That way they can reform only the surface, not the substance.” Around the table, there were a few murmurs of agreement. The plight of any reformer, to be forgotten after tasting only the smallest droplet of success, was always on their minds.

“I think we need to appreciate what work we have achieved. Look at what was before, two governments cobbled together and held with crumbling clay. They were fossils fit only for a museum but we took those bones and gave them life. We are not forgotten and we will not be, as our governments are actually working for the people of this nation rather than the whims of monarchs too far past their prime. We should take comfort in what we have done rather than drive ourselves into despair; we have changed the course of what seemed to be an inexorable tide-”

“Both of you have your points. Our mission is not over, all we have built is a foundation. We shouldn't pat ourselves on the back or fear tomorrow. We can draw nourishment from our success and press ourselves to continue to tiller the garden so that we might truly see something new,” came the calm voice of Adrián Forero, one of the senior reformists. “In the future, one day, Iberia might truly have only one master - her citizenry.”
strings.IBR_auth.29.a: The tree of democracy must be watered to flourish.
strings.IBR_auth.30.d:
The media tours of the nation had almost become a routine affairs. The Caudillos would tour the various regions of Iberia to great acclaim. Journalists would ask a list of pre-approved questions and receive canned responses. At times, the Caudillos would sample regional delicacies or visit local monuments, express their fond approval, and soak in the cheers of the crowd. This latest tour seemed to be no different, but when it came time to answer questions, everything seemed to change.

“What are we going to do about corruption among the regional governors?” “Are you concerned about unemployment levels being over target?” “Are you considering the release of prisoners that were charged under previous censorship laws?” Each question a pointed barb, with a firmness that would have been unthinkable a generation ago. The Caudillos answered as best they could, but they couldn't shake a feeling that something had changed.

“Could you imagine asking us such questions?” Franco muttered, drinking a glass of water to soothe his nerves. “Such ingratitude. Are we going down the right path if this is the result?”

“We must be observant always,” remarked Caetano. “But there's something else to take from it. They looked to us to handle corruption at the local level. They look to us to settle economic concerns. Perhaps such insolence is a small price to pay if the people can associate us with progress and success. If we are the way of the future...”

“Perhaps, but there is always a fine line between insolence and independence. We must make sure that the people do not take their greater freedoms to mean the freedom to destroy the state.”

“Indeed. But when we act like this, the nation will know that they and we will succeed together.”
strings.IBR_auth.30.a: Thoughts and words unheard of in a previous era.
strings.IBR_auth.30.b: Even in the modern era, some things should not be said.
strings.IBR_auth.31.t: A Rock For Every Hard Place
strings.IBR_auth.31.d:
The Iberian Union, much like her constituent halves of Spain and Portugal prior to the union, is a nation whose recent history is tallied by her proximity to the great world powers and their conduct in the Cold War. With Iberia's unenviable position of having to balance national sovereignty with diplomatic neutrality, the delicate dance of Iberian geopolitics can be seen even in the institution of the Union's international embassies.

The tripartite embassies of the former Axis powers are a salient example of this, starting with the Imperial Japanese Embassy on Calle Serrano in Madrid. With the majority of Japanese interests centered around Asia, it stands to reason that their embassy would amount to little else but a Legation enclave, far away from the machinations of the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere and functioning as little more than a glorified hotel for Japanese businessmen and the occasional Kenpeitai surveillance sweep.

Germany and Italy's embassies are as indicative of Iberia's mercurial relationship with Central Europe as any other relic of her exodus from the Axis sphere. Situated on Calle de Fortuny and Calle de Lagasca, they have long since degenerated shadows of their former selves, hemmed in by indifference by the Iberian government and the persistent protests by the AAS to ensure that Germania and Rome's interests along the peninsula are kept at arm's length.

The principle OFN representation in Iberia via the American embassy, also situated on Calle de Serrano, showcases a more noticeable element of tact by the leadership in Madrid. The embassy is both well-maintained and features a much prettier facade to American diplomatic interests, but similarly is treated with indifference by the Iberian government outside of individual careerism or the occasional Reformist politico looking adviser from their contemporaries overseas.

All in all, these images paint a cynical, but perhaps warranted approach to Iberia's isolationism. Neither the people of the Iberian Union nor the government that rule over them are interested in getting roped into the political vortex of another great power bloc, both are simply content to go about their business in peace and keep the Cold War as far from her shores as possible.
strings.IBR_auth.31.a: Yet rarely has history respected a nation's desire to be left alone...
strings.IBR_caetano_influence_high_tt: This option is available because Caetano has a high or greater amount of influence.
strings.IBR_despot.1.d:
“This is Manuel Caetano, bringing Portugal its evening news. I have with me Foreign Minister Fernando María Castiella y Maíz, who will provide an important diplomatic update.”

“Thank you Manuel, it's great to appear on the program. Before I begin, I have the pleasure of working closely with your brother Marcelo, and I must say the resemblance is uncanny.” A quick shared chuckle, with no mirth behind it. “I wanted to let you, and the Portuguese people, know that the Iberian Union will be closing our New York and Chicago consulates at the end of the month. This will reduce our ability to provide support services to Iberian citizens traveling in the U.S., and may cause delays if you're expecting U.S. citizens to travel here. Our embassy in Washington D.C. will remain open to serve both functions.”

“I know our viewers appreciate the advance notice, Minister. Does this decision have anything to do with the intrusive American reaction to our Caudillos' decision to close down the Iberian Council?”

“Not at all, Manuel. The Ministry is always looking to safeguard Iberian tax dollars, and we determined those consulates were an expenditure the public purse couldn't bear at this time.”

“Thanks again for all your insight, Minister. Any parting words for our audience?”“We're expecting the U.S. to announce the closure of several Iberian consulates in the coming days.”
strings.IBR_despot.2.d:
Santiago de Bernabeu, older and wearier than the man that had taken over Real Madrid three decades prior, was not present at the stadium which bore his name during the day's Real Madrid game. He only stuck around long enough to greet two rather distinguished guests of honour before he left for a medical appointment.

After bidding Bernabeu farewell, Francisco Franco and the Minister of State, Admiral Carrero Blanco - a friend and chief crony of Franco's and the third man in the regime after Franco and Caetano - sat down and quietly enjoyed the game from the best seats in the arena.

As was increasingly the case in his own old age, Franco had nothing to say until an away player missed an easy goal ten minutes into the game. He then sighed and vocalised his discontent: “Bernabeu holds up well enough in his old age, but the management of a lot of these teams has been too loose recently.” Franco punctuated his discontent by taking a sip of wine.

The old admiral, a veteran at interpreting his boss of forty years' real intentions, leaned in and discussed a new plan he had. “Well, General, I was contemplating something closer to home on those lines. I was thinking about sweeping the entire bureaucracy, checking for loyalty and warding off corruption. Should do quite well to maintain stability.”

Franco, contemplatively chewing on an amuse-bouche, nodded. “A sound plan, I think. You should go through with it.” As the appetizer was washed down with another sip of wine Franco added,
strings.IBR_despot.2.a: “We could use a better standard of play around here, Admiral.”
strings.IBR_despot.2.b: “You had better make sure to loop Caetano in on the Portuguese part of things.”
strings.IBR_despot.3.d:
“Yes, Admiral Carrero Blanco, I have the list. Yes, indeed, Admiral; you know very well that the Caudilho will do everything he can to ensure political stability. Yes, sir. Yes. Thank you very much, sir. Good day.”

Putting down the phone and rubbing his temples after another trying conversation with Franco's beloved toady, Iberian Minister of Finance João Dias Rosas took a look at the list of employees to be purged from his department. The veteran Portuguese functionary skimmed through the list, organised by name with the rationale for the official's removal next to them. His eyes paused on an economist and known A Choupana boy - the term used for Caetano's associates - who was to be purged for having resigned his academic post at the University of Coimbra in protest of the suppression of demonstrators at that institution.

The man who held Iberia's purse-strings steepled his fingers and sighed. “What is this coming from? Is this Caetano ditching an inconvenient reminder of his own history, his own more ... idealistic past? Or is it rather Carrero Blanco trying a power play, to get a Spaniard promoted to take this Choupana boy's place?”

Dias Rosas thought about the implications of either proposition and winced. Pouring out some more coffee, he grumbled, “God damn it, I'm not going to stick my neck out with all this paranoia. Damn Carrero Blanco for forcing me to make a decision.”

It took thirty minutes and a whole cup of coffee before the Minister of Finance decided:
strings.IBR_despot.3.a: “Get rid of him. The Caudilho's name has to be beyond reproach.”
strings.IBR_despot.3.b: “No; the Caudilho has to intervene. Our own men can't be preyed upon.”
strings.IBR_despot.4.d:
“Frankly, young lady, you should be thankful that this is the least punishment you are receiving. As you can see, Officer Fernández here is our representative from the Évora Police Department and they were very close to pressing charges. They have agreed to be satisfied with your expulsion from the University, if you will at least confess.”

Joana Alvez bristled, furious tears pooling within her eyes as the bespeckled compliance officer sat at the desk across from her, police officer to his side. Her parents were outside, refused entrance by the officer while they discussed the incident privately. The number they said rang in her head, more pesetas for graffiti insulting a Caudillo than her entire year's tuition, and they dared tell her she was lucky? She sobbed, crushed beneath invisible weight.

“Think of your parents, Miss Alvez,” the police officer said with a glare of authority, “they raised you to be a better woman than this. Will you shame them and drive them to destitution too? Think to yourself, if we even suspect you do such a thing again, our kindness will not repeat. Confess, and we can all leave with some dignity.”

“I...” It almost slipped out. Confession. The face of her mother and father hung before her, their faces twisted into horror and sadness. She couldn't bear it, and the only way to do anything to ease their horror was just to say a few words. But words carried weight. She remembered her grandfather told her once, he never said he surrendered after Salazar took over. He stopped fighting, but he never surrendered. Just waiting for better circumstances. Long had they talked, sharing their longing for a better nation where all weren't subjected to the whims of a cabal of old fools. He'd told her not to throw her life away, to try and use the means of peace, and she had.

Her tear streaked face bent down further. “I don't know what you are talking about.”
strings.IBR_despot.4.a: But despite the sobs her heart hardened, and she cast aside the means of peace.
strings.IBR_despot.5.d:
The new head of the tourism office of the Canarias came across as a sort of blur. In the eyes of Canarias' locals, Manuel Fraga traveled from A to B to C with the energy of a perpetual motion machine.

Few, if any, of them knew why a high-power bureaucrat from Galicia had been sent down to oversee the picturesque vistas of the Canarias in a role shorn of any political or administrative power. Those that read newspapers or heard rumours from more well-connected friends had to admire his determination in the face of what amounted to a promotion to Antarctica for the likes of Fraga. Their admiration was redoubled when they saw him in action.

An unstoppable workhorse with a camera in one hand and a clipboard in another, Fraga drove and sailed from village to village, exhausting pens after two days of usage and reducing an entire box's worth of pencils to useless nubs within a week. A tourism official had to follow him with a ream of paper in tow as page after page was filled with paragraph after paragraph of notes in Spanish, Galician, and shorthand: discourses on unique features that could be marketed and suitably breathtaking locations for hotels, attractions, and even tourist traps.

Sitting down for a breather, Fraga took only a moment to reflect. “Sure, the fools off in Madrid might say all this energy is useless. They might even be right. But it's just what I need to stay motivated. With how that doddering old man in Madrid is slouching towards his final days, I'm damn sure I'll have another chance.”

Cheerfully, confidently, Manuel Fraga drank a glass of water and ran off to lay the foundation stone for another hotel.
strings.IBR_despot.6.d:
Caudilho Caetano was on a plane flying to someplace in Africa. An extrovert by nature, he took pleasure in writing his own speeches - the position of “speechwriter” was something Caetano only doled out when writer's block (rarely) had its way with him.

“'We cannot forget the initiative with which our merchants pacified...'—hm, no, that won't do—'tamed the wild, chaotic wastes of Africa, bringing order and prosperity to lands that, mired in chaos'—no, too repetitive—'mired in tribalism, had never known such blessings.'”

A new paragraph. “'We would be betraying our Lord if we forgot the devotion of missionaries of our holy Faith—these good and faithful servants of Christ that spread the Word to those that bowed down to wood and stone and demonic gods, teaching them true religion and learning.'—A whole sentence written out in one go, well done. Now to the soldiers—'We also forget at our peril the bravery of our heroic soldiers that fought and died for its soil, at times fighting to the very last drop of their blood.'”

Some final scribbles. “'... and there must be no doubt, ladies and gentlemen, ...'—yes, that will do—'that the African colonies are just as much part of Portugal as the Tagus River itself. Thank you.' Perfect!” With one final flourish, the pen was placed in a waiting holder at the other end of the desk.

Caetano leaned back into his seat, satisfied with the draft. Contented, he murmured, “The fact is, I don't really need much in the way of substance with these types. With enough verve, enough rhetorical devotion to the alleged cause, the integrationists won't care that I'm not actually changing anything. Thank God it takes so little to please these people.”

Looking from his window at the ocean below, Caetano chuckled a little and shook his head.
strings.IBR_despot.7.d:
António de Oliveira Salazar was a great leader. I like Salazar! He did many great things for Portugal, and the people of Portugal love him because he made Portugal better, the economy better and more children can read and write now than ever before.

He disliked capitalism that is plutocraptic, because the rich people have all the jobs and the money. Salazar liked money because he was an economist but he liked the Portuguese people better, that's why he created the Estado Novo, to take care of the people and help them live in peace.

Peace is the best thing that Salazar gave Portugal, and the economy and reading and writing. Children now can read the news and read that our Portugal is great and better than it was ever before, because now we have corporatism. Corporatism means we all live and work together like a family.

They had corporatism a long time ago in the Middle Ages. The Middle Ages happened a long time ago, but it's fine, because we can learn from them even if everyone is dead already because we have books and because we can read now thanks to Salazar.

Salazar is dead too but we can still read about him thanks to him. He was great, it's fun to read about the things he did. And now everyone has a job like they did before capitalism and the plutocraps and this is thanks to Salazar who loved everyone very much and liked history like me.
strings.IBR_despot.7.a: Promising, requires additional review of Caudilho Salazar's works.
strings.IBR_despot.8.d:
“Your consigna is to become the perfect housewife for your husband and the teacher the regime needs.” -Yet another task. Actually, two tasks masked as one through poor grammar.-

“The first one is imposed by God Himself: all women are to become wives. As women you should strive to become wives and teach future girls to follow your footsteps. But now you have a new task to guide you on the right path: to read Consigna. The Sección Femenina has chosen a word with a vast array of meanings -password, instruction, slogan and storeroom- to help shape your work as students at the Normal School. As future teachers, you have to collect your monthly Consigna...” -to prove our loyalty to Franco-

“...read the teachers' magazine, take up all...” -the slogans-

“...written in it, work as storerooms of the regime's wisdom and instruct the children accordingly. Monthly, you will receive at home a fresh copy from the press so you can educate yourselves and lead the way for future Franquists.”

-This lady talks about that old magazine as if she had just discovered America-. The commentator and her friend shared a quiet laugh. They had seen a few copies of Consigna around, stinking of traditional values and the regime, as prudish as only the Sección could print.

But now they sit in the last rows of the Aula Magna and, to finish their studies, they pretend to be invested Franquists, to take notes, to nod when the speaker makes an 'interesting' remark on the appropriate length of skirts, and prepare to read Consignas.
strings.IBR_despot.8.a: College readings had never been so dull.
strings.IBR_despot.9.d:
“Tonight on the evening news, ladies and gentlemen, it's my great honour to interview the Caudilho, Dr. Marcelo das Neves Caetano, who just so happens to be my brother.” Said brother smiled beatifically as his interviewer, Manuel das Neves Caetano, began to ask the usual softball questions that were a feature of the Portuguese evening news these years.

“One important question that comes to mind is how you and Caudilho Franco get their news. What are your preferred sources of information?”

Marcelo laughed a little. “It's not my place to comment for my colleague; after all, the man speaks Castilian and not Portuguese. I on the other hand make a point of reading the Jornal de Notícias every morning without fail. I always find vital information that I can then put to use in Lisbon or Madrid.”

Manuel acted somewhat surprised. “The Jornal de Notícias is, of course, an indirectly state-owned newspaper; it makes sense it would be helpful. But are you not concerned with the fact that there have been some editorials printed in that newspaper lately that have been critiquing your reforms to Social Security?”

The Caudilho smiled. “I wouldn't be Caudilho if I was afraid of a little criticism, Manuel. But I am less concerned about that fact considering that the Jornal seems to be heading in a good direction now.” Left unsaid, but an open secret to anyone in the know, was that Caetano had personally pushed the Jornal in that direction by ordering the state-owned bank that controlled it to rein in all future editorials.

To defuse that implication, Marcelo smirked and looked directly at a camera. “However, it must be noted, ladies and gentlemen, that televised news may at least save you the cost of a newspaper.”
strings.IBR_despot.10.d:
Generalísimo Francisco Franco Bahamonde had asked for this. Asked for his closest compatriot, Minister Carrero Blanco, to read him through the highest level history textbook mandated under the new Law of Organic Education. Specifically, and exclusively, the sections pertaining to Iberia's three Caudillos.

Carrero Blanco continued, “...strict budgetary discipline imposed by Caudillo Salazar tamed the rampant inflation that had brought low the Portuguese Republic. Trusted to...” Inflation. A 14-year old boy might have heard the word. Would he, Paco, have a lifetime ago? He wouldn't have understood it. Would have cared even less.

As the Caudillo's eyes drifted from wavering to shut, Carrero Blanco dutifully read to the end of the page before saying, only marginally louder, “I'll look to return at another time.”

Franco stirred from his chair, “No. What does it say about Caetano?”

“Marcelo das Neves Caetano was an instrumental partner to Salazar in the Portuguese Ministry of Finance, helping reform the nation's social security system, and later, organize the Estado Novo...” Carrero Blanco spoke on. Franco's face remained impassive, as the admiral drily rattled off bureaucratic, political, and academic accomplishments.

“And here is your introductory section. In 1936, General Francisco Franco Bahamonde led the Army of Africa to early decisive victories in the uprising against the communist Republican government. As other Nationalist leaders died, he united Spanish patriots and took charge of the war effort. Following their hard-fought triumph, the Generalísimo would rebuild a prosperous, Christian, and stable Spain...”

Franco leaned back, a small smirk of satisfaction on his face.
strings.IBR_despot.10.a: Young Paco, and the next generation, knew who was the true Caudillo.
strings.IBR_despot.11.d:
The food had all the characteristics of fine dining. The ingredients were evidently well picked, the skill of the preparation apparent in every bite. Yet, as López Rodó chewed, flavor seemed to escape him. The food seemed almost dry as he ate, ever so slowly ate while listening to the Caudillo across the table from him.

“Senhor Rodó, I think you will be very pleased with the new proposals. To tell you, I confess, was my motive for inviting you here this evening.” Caudillo Caetano spoke while barely looking at his dinner partner, lovingly gazing upon his Arroz de Marisco. “How is the rice Senhor?”

Rodó gave a half hearted nod, taking a small bite with a half formed smile. Caetano continued as Rodó ate, almost solely to himself. “There exist bounties within our economy that have been too long ignored. The colonies have workforces who will work for wages preferable to our industry, resources ripe for exploiting. I abhor false promises, but I am sure that many sharing your more economical mind will be quite satisfied.”

Rodó swallowed and placed his cutlery down for a moment. “Caudillo Caetano, what about the issue of foreign ownership? As promising as colonial investments are, I have spoken before on the benefits-”

“Deregulation?” Caetano raised his focus from the food, regarding Rodó for a moment before returning to his food chuckling. “I apologise Senhor Rodó,” he said as his chuckles died, “but such a proposal would never get past a fossil like Caudillo Franco. But, our programme is well considered. With men like you sharing our commitment then the benefits will be exactly what Iberia requires.”

Rodó almost dared a sigh, but suppressed it. “Of course, Caudillo Caetano” he said, with all the false enthusiasm he could muster, like a soldier before a naive officer.
strings.IBR_despot.11.a: The question of the point of such dinners clouding his mind as the Caudillo continued pontificating.
strings.IBR_despot.12.d:
Marcelo Caetano was infuriated, and he was going to make it known.

This new diktat Franco had imposed, demanding unanimous Cabinet approval for any and all gubernatorial appointments, was going to be the death of him. That bastard Carrero Blanco and Carrero Blanco's pathetic hangers-on had been able to exploit Franco's system to veto the appointment of an A Choupana boy as Governor of Algarve over some minor dissent—inoffensive even to Franco—that he had expressed while an Iberian councilor.

All but storming into Villamejor Palace, where the elderly Caudillo appeared only infrequently as he took less and less time in active government, Caetano began to harangue his opposite with as much force as he felt he could muster without hurting Franco's health. The discourse was, to Caetano's credit, relatively brief, but the last few words of it were deliberately quite cutting: 

“...You have to understand. This new requirement of yours is just gumming up the wheels of government for nothing. If you let it stay in place, we'll have gone through all of this for nothing - it's just another damned step back to the dysfunction of the Sixties. All that we've done will lead us back to the vetoes and useless Councils that prevailed when Salazar still walked the earth!”

Confronted with such a jeremiad, all the aging generalissimo could say was,
strings.IBR_despot.12.a: “You and I both know there is a difference between these two things, Marcelo.”
strings.IBR_despot.12.b: “To replace a Council with a Cabinet ... is to go nowhere, it is true.”
strings.IBR_despot.13.d:
As she stepped out of the car she was almost surprised at how quaint the Villamejor Palace appeared beside the road. Its brown veneer and classical design was pleasing, the elegance of an age defined by being refined, and for Pilar Primo de Rivera it represented all that she wished to achieve. Unassuming beside the road, elegant and proud, yet ever guiding the nation forward. Caudillo Franco joined her from the car and together they walked into the halls of the Iberian government.

Such halls were detailed and intricate in their beauty, walls and ceilings etched with gilded panels and portraits of Iberia's past. She recognised many of them, her father often telling her stories of Spain's history when she was young. Around her she caught the glances of many civil servants and visitors to the Palace, soft smiles and passive frowns forming as they recognised her. The frowns she saw, she could guess their origin. After all, this nation was not Spain but a union of it with its smaller neighbour. Perhaps those Portuguese saw her as a foolish woman? A dangerous nationalist? Such things had been laid before her before, but she cared little. Spain was her guide and only judge.

Even so, long had she been denied public recognition. She had never held it against Caudillo Franco, she understood the difficulties of his position and he had always made his personal support quite clear. She had been satisfied to serve Spain through her leadership of the Falange's Sección Femenina. Were there not thousands of moral, patriotic Spanish women thanks to her efforts?

But as she walked into that private meeting room deep within the Palace with the Caudillo, placing her eyes upon the assorted Falange figures within, she couldn't help but give a new smile of satisfaction. Who knew of the trials and potential of Spain's women better than her? Now, the Caudillo was recognising that, and was showing Iberia whose counsel he would be taking. A more appropriate position, for a woman of her ability.
strings.IBR_despot.13.a: She sat at the table, preparing to share the future of Spanish women with the proud Caudillo.
strings.IBR_despot.14.d:
A bump in the road shook Afonso from his sleep, and he peeled himself from the window. At least the kids were still asleep after he and Teresita worked so hard to calm them down. He used the opportunity to curse under his breath. They had never gone on such a vacation before - all the way to the other side of Iberia! - but just the journey there almost made him want to make a u-turn and go back to Braga.

Sure, the views were incredible. The golden waves of wheat in the fields of the Meseta made Afonso remember stories his dad told him of working in the fields fifty years ago, and the Monegros desert was unlike anything they had seen before - Jaimito had even asked if they were in Morocco now.

But eleven hours by bus, having to wrangle two preteens between them, had pushed the couple to their limit. Afonso could see the sideways glances all the other people on the bus had shot their way and thought they wouldn't notice. You try calming Jaimito after Maria took his teddy bear or cleaning up the crumbs left behind after they'd bought snacks at Pamplona. Even the blissful minutes of sleep hadn't truly given Afonso rest. At least Teresita was still napping, Maria snuggled up with her. Good for her, he thought.

But then, the bus rounded a corner, and Afonso's eyes widened. This last leg of the journey had taken them through a hilly landscape not too dissimilar from what they were used to in Portugal, even if it was very pretty. But now, they had finally climbed over the hills, and before them, overlooking a small lake, towered the sheer cliffs of the Pyrenees. A wall of greens, browns and purples filled the horizon up to the clouds, crowned with mist and snow. A small gasp escaped his mouth as he shook Teresita and the kids awake, pointing at the destination of their journey.
strings.IBR_despot.14.a: Perhaps this was worth it after all.
strings.IBR_despot.15.d:
The sun was setting on El Pardo, but within the Caudillo's office, cameras were already flickering like stars. Franco was sitting at the table, surrounded by the cabinet members and giving the press a practiced smile, paper waiting for his signature put before him by a helpful aide.

Franco cleared his throat. “Señores. Today Iberia takes a great step in making sure that the lights which have guided us truly for so long continue to guide the next generation of Iberians. It is my honor to have here with us today the esteemed Don Nieves, one of our greatest patriots and filmmakers, to witness this moment.”

With polite applause, the silver-haired director took his place standing next to the Caudillo and gave a salute before shaking his hand with genuine adoration. “It is the greatest honor to be able to contribute to Iberia's cause, Caudillo. I am eternally grateful for the privilege.”

Franco turned his eyes back towards the cameras. “With Iberia's great advances in economy and technology, many of the traditions we have long cherished as Iberians are under threat. The glamor of city life as shown on the screen has driven many young men and women to seek their fortune away from their homes, and whole villages have been driven to depopulation and destitution. Yet this glamor is so often a lie, a trick of the light. It is my honor to sign this decree to make sure that, at least once monthly, Iberian television will be broadcasting Señor Nieves' film ”Surcos“, in order to give our younger generation a true glimpse into the hardships of city life and its costs.”

After signing the decree and waiting for the applause to die down, Franco rose from his seat and took Nieves by the hand, for a private screening of the film in the Caudillo's own movie theater. The aging soldier smiled at the filmmaker.
strings.IBR_despot.15.a: It looks like this newfangled technology isn't all bad, after all.
strings.IBR_despot.16.d:
“And now, let's welcome Caudillo Caetano to the show — Caudillo, come out here!”

The limelight hurt his eyes as Caetano made his way onto the stage. “Please,” he said, waving his hands at where he assumed the camera was, “just call me Marcelo. This is a show, after all, not an affair of state.”

A bout of laughter erupted from the unseen audience. Yes, on paper, Family Conversations was just a show — something to watch with, well, the family. But Caetano understood the true power of television. It had taken some convincing to get Franco on board with the idea, but he was sure his fellow Caudillo would soon see it too. And what better way than by putting on a show?

“So then, Marcelo.” The host crossed his legs. “What exciting topic do you have to share with the audience today?”

“Actually, I have something serious I would like to discuss,” he began as the cameras focused on him. And then, as naturally as he breathed, Caetano just began talking. About Iberia and its stability. About Iberia and its government. About Iberia and its families.

“Family,” Caudillo Caetano concluded, “is the fundamental unit of our society. I'll do everything in my power to preserve it against all perversions — both within and without.”

Hundreds of hands moved beyond the glare of the lighting equipment into an applause. All things considered, it had been a great fifth episode.
strings.IBR_despot.17.d:
Marcelo Caetano, unlike Franco or even Salazar, had always made a point of keeping up with cultural developments. His attention was yielding fruit on a tour of the former IAC - the Portuguese cultural association, merged with the Spanish one by a decree of the Cabinet - as it became the Lisbon office of the Institute of Iberian Culture.

Traveling from painting to musical performance, Caetano made a point of speaking to each of the artists and intellectuals present. Though himself a lawyer, by now Caetano had enough knowledge of the rest of the humanities to not seem completely illiterate discussing the specifics of each work of art on display. Caetano's extroversion was on full display as he made small talk with everyone in the room before moving to the next one.

The Caudilho had made a point of saving the best for last. Turning a corner in the building, he came upon a statue of him and Franco. The sculptor, another one of the myriad Caetano had somehow funded or protected, smirked as he recounted to Caetano how he had made a point of introducing subtle differences between the two heads of state.

By a fortuitous confluence of events, these changes had somehow had the effect of making the Portuguese leader taller and more authoritative than the slightly stooped, visibly grizzled figure of the Spanish generalissimo.

Caetano chuckled to himself, sipping the champagne and eating some caviar. “If that flunky Carrero Blanco had the sense to see the difference, he would be apoplectic right now. But he's about as cultured as his brute of a patron, who thinks fishing is the sort of hobby that befits a head of state. Turns out cultivating connections with the arts instead has its benefits, doesn't it?”
strings.IBR_despot.17.a: “Dear God, I do feel a hankering for roast fish right about now, though...”
strings.IBR_despot.18.d:
“...And so, we can see that article 18 of the Rights of the Iberians prohibits the arrest of any person without pretext or the possibility of due process. This was granted by the Fueros of 1945 and upheld in the fundamental laws of the Union in 1952. Any questions”?

Torcuato Fernández-Miranda turned around to watch the mostly-empty classroom. He didn't have high expectations, but the deathly silence caused the bile to rise slightly more in his mouth. He knew how lucky he was to be able to hold down a comfortable academic job, and to remain free - as much as anyone in Iberia was free these days. But the department of political law at the University of Oviedo was, in a way, its own prison for him, a daily punishment for his failure.

As he surveyed the small audience, Fernández-Miranda could see how little attention even the remaining law students in the Union had for what he - and the law - had to say. He couldn't blame them. The rule of law in Iberia was a pleasant fiction, and his attempt to change that, with the help of so many others, had failed. The future generation of Iberian legal scholars and attorneys would be composed of the sons of regime officials who would get their cushy jobs even if they'd flunked every test and of the opportunists who merely had to bribe their way to the top. He could see their faces in front of him, dozing off, doodling or whispering to each other.

Except one. A student Fernández-Miranda did not remember seeing before was sitting in the back row of the lecture hall. He had his notebook open and looked like he was taking down notes before the pause. Now, the muscled, tough-looking man was sitting attentively, watching Fernández-Miranda like a hawk. A shudder passed through the aging lecturer.
strings.IBR_despot.19.t: The Archbishop of Madrid Speaks to the People
strings.IBR_despot.19.d:
Casimiro Morcillo González, the newly consecrated Archbishop of Madrid, delivered a speech to a large congregation of citizens. Unusually for such an event, it was broadcasted over the radio and live over television.

His Eminency spoke first of the power of faith, of how a common religion can bind its believers in friendship, solely by the power of the cross. He spoke of union - as Iberia joined together, its people must also come together to work for a better country.

He addressed God's plan. Nothing happened just for the sake of happening. Rather, everything that happens was a part of God's greater plan, and so anyone who came on hard times had to have faith, for everything would work out in the end, as planned.

God, he says, put strong men on Earth to guide the weak, to serve as teachers, stewards, and mentors. These strong men are agents of God, and so it is His desire that the same faith be placed in them as is placed in Him. The Caudillos are some of these strong men, and so they must take absolute power. The country must have faith in them, he reiterates, for they will guide it in the correct direction.

He ended his sermon with a call for prayer. During the sudden silence, many were left to wonder just what this would all mean for Iberia.
strings.IBR_barcelona.1.d:
CONFIDENTIAL

TO MINISTER OF GOVERNANCE, CAUDILLO FRANCISCO FRANCO, CAUDILLO ANTÓNIO SALAZAR

BARCELONA - CATALONIA - IBERIAN UNION

A number of recent arms shipments have been intercepted shortly after arriving in state-held warehouses in Barcelona.
