The shipments, which contain guns, artillery and shells from Italy, were being used as a remedy for existing shortages within the Federal Army, and have made the need to resolve this case particularly pressing. No direct partisan activity has been recorded in the last few days, which impairs our understanding of the direct motives and our capacities to respond.

It is difficult to directly ascertain the cause of these disappearances, but we do have some leads. The lack of activity does reduce our analysis of the attacks, but we are not totally impaired. Catalonia has long been a region wracked by radicalism, with both Catalan separatism and anarchism being long-running undercurrents that still claim some local support. Additionally, there was little damage to the warehouse itself, which remains standing beyond some anti-government graffiti.

With the presence of locally-sourced units within these divisions and the aforementioned lack of damage done, it could be possible that some degree of infiltration has taken place. The lack of damage done to the warehouse is significant in this. The timings of guard postings and of access to the warehouse are still available to us, which makes checks on the guard(s) present during the incident far more feasible.
strings.IBR_barcelona_salazar_tt: Caudillo Salazar has an idea on how to focus the search.
strings.IBR_barcelona_franco_tt: Caudillo Franco has an idea on how to focus the search.
strings.IBR_barcelona.2.d:
The brutal minutes finally ended; the smell of blood already filled the air.

Nostrils stung with stench as the AAS officers moved into the storage room; the final citadel of the traitors. It was only meant to be a simple search. None of them had expected to find anything, until the pistols started being drawn. They had moved through the warehouse; devoid of workers, it seemed the only men in residence were terrorists, and they had responded as such. A gunfight, ever moving deeper into the industrial fortress.

But traitors lacked training. Preparation. Every officer there took refuge in that. Despite superficial wounds, no one had died. Wild shooting and poor organization had seen all dozen dissidents taken care of, the final one now bleeding out upon the floor of the storage room where he had made his final stand. They searched him and, finding no weapon or information, left him. He was bleeding from his throat, lifeblood pooling around his head. He would be of little use.

By day's end, a full search was being conducted. Every pallet torn up, every floor cracked open, until they found it. A secret room under the manager's office, trapdoor hidden by filing cabinets. Munitions lined the walls, countless explosives stored in boxes, radios and tools on benches. The room was large, clearly a bricked-off area of the basement, at least a dozen meters in length each way. Most concerning was the Defensa Interior symbol etched on the wall. Anarchists.

The assessments were frank. “Theres enough for a Platoon to be equipped here. Maybe two if they don't care about resupplying.” Only time would tell if these were the missing guns, but a thought hung over all who saw it that would not depart.

“Did they fight because this is the only cache? Or because they feel strong enough to fight?”
strings.IBR_barcelona.2.a: No half measures. Summon the army. If this is a general uprising, we must crush it in its crib.
strings.IBR_barcelona.2.b: This is beyond a local matter, summon the Guardia Civil. We must move carefully, but decisively.
strings.IBR_barcelona.2.c: Haste could precipitate open warfare. Local police should lead further operations, with AAS support.
strings.IBR_barcelona.3.d:
Bafflingly, the AAS investigation of the missing weapons in Barcelona has yielded no results. Access records don't suggest any external breach, nor did background checks of the Guardia Civil on duty that night imply motivation to assist bad-faith actors or political radicals. Even on-site questioning about activity on the night of the weapons' disappearance provided little information outside of reports of 'odd noises', which are themselves hardly an unusual phenomenon in a major metropolitan city.

All of these circumstances led to the disappearance of the weapons likely being a logistical error rather than a domestic terror plot. It is recommended to delegate this matter to local law enforcement rather than a government agency. Given the trivial circumstances, it may be worth simply replacing the weapons with a new shipment and restoring the armory to its rightful level. 

However, this does not particularly reflect well on the state of Iberia's security apparatus. 'It's safe south of the Pyrenees' cannot be held true if our quartermasters cannot secure accountability of their weapons. The government will have to shift focus onto bureaucratic reforms and focus efforts toward reducing obstructions to proper function. Hopefully, this is all just one admittedly embarrassing abnormality.
strings.IBR_barcelona.3.a: Let the Metropolitan Police handle it from here.
strings.IBR_barcelona.3.b: Maybe better to assume it's not an issue...
strings.IBR_barcelona.4.d:
“Gentleman. Think on what we will do today.”

The tent was dark, the assembled men barely visible by the projector's spectral glow. Men of all ranks, crews of the APC's waited patiently outside. Major José Delgadillo stood before them, the leader of this detachment. They looked with some awe toward him. A veteran of Morocco. Of the Civil War. Of Russia. He clicked the button in his hand, the projector moving to the prepared photos.

A church. Windows blown out, part of the wall taken out at the side. “The St. Angelo Church suicide bombing, 1952”.

Soldiers, piled into an open ditch and clearly exposed to the elements for some time, with grievous bullet wounds. They were nude, identifiable as soldiers only by the dog tags they wore. “The Manresa Massacre, 1957”.

A line of women, hanging from a tree branch. Around their necks were signs declaring them class traitors. All savagely beaten, faces bloated and terrible. “The Tuixent Reprisals, 1960”.

The Major looked at the men in the room. Most were young, much younger than him. Most of them probably didn't remember the Civil War. The depths of depravity these lunatics would go to. The shattered corpses and broken lands they left in search of their utopia. “These are famous crimes, just three of the atrocities the Defence Interior have carried out. With the discovery of large munition supply depots, it is clear that these maniacs want to bring that horror to Barcelona, even Iberia in total.”

Whispers. Angry whispers. “Today, when you ride into Barcelona, be ready. You know your zones, your support squads, your search locations. When you find the anarchists who would exact such horrors, I have one single order.”
strings.IBR_barcelona.5.d:
With reports of heavy DI activity on the ground, the men of the Guardia Civil have mobilized for counter-insurgency raids in Barcelona following a preliminary warning by the AAS. The nature of the anarchist sympathizers has made them consistently difficult to infiltrate with moles, complicating efforts to track them. Fortunately, the Guardia is already aware of several DI strongholds around the city that are regularly surveilled to pre-empt the possibility of a greater plot by leftist agitators.

The scale of the DI operation is proving more ominous by the hour. After several simultaneously executed raids across the city, all designated DI meeting points have been discovered empty, rapidly evacuated of all insurgent paraphernalia with some trapped for the encroaching Guardia. Several officers have already been reported injured, with at least one confirmed dead.

With the sheer scope of the DI threat becoming more dangerous, the Guardia have called off the initial raids to regroup at precinct houses across downtown Barcelona. With an lightning strike against the DI no longer an option, the Guardia have instead drawn up plans for a long-term siege, orchestrating door-to-door raids across Barcelona on the hunt for DI weapon caches, safehouses or potential gathering places.
strings.IBR_barcelona.5.a: We beat them back in the Civil War, we'll beat them back here!
strings.IBR_barcelona.6.d:
WThere was a ringing in Manuel's ears. An almost silent thing, a vibration that never left. A ringing, despite the fact around them was nothing, for as far as he could see. Empty fields, the distant hills vanished into the opaque dark. He returned to his patrol car, his partner standing beside it, zipping up the fly of his trousers. A distant glimmer was the only sign that human habitation graced this land. Upon a lonely backroad out of Barcelona, the two officers idled away the night.

“Enjoy yourself?” asked Manuel's partner Ruben, leaning against the car. Manuel gave a sarcastic glance, making his partner chuckle. “You think they're almost finished in the city?”

Manuel shook his head, trying to dissipate the soft ringing in his ears. “Maybe. Not like anyone's come driving out this way anyway. Anything on the radio?” Ruben looked at the open car window, the radio audible through it. He shook his head.

“Same stuff. Curfew, orders to hold positions until relieved. There hasn't been anything interesting since we listened to them ordering rubber bullets used at that riot earlier.”

Manuel nodded. A pause held between them, most conversation having died hours ago, as Manuel returned to the car and leant against it. “Why do you think the raids got so out of hand?” Manuel finally asked.

Ruben looked up, consideration filling his expression. “Socialism's popular in the city. Guess more of them side with crazies than we thought. It'll be a long night, few cracked heads, but the raids will find the anarchists and the people will get bored. Might do the city good to use some energy.”

Manuel nodded. “I hope you're right. Just wish we got an assignment more interesting than a checkpoint.”
strings.IBR_barcelona.6.a: They both looked at the distant glow of Barcelona, waiting for peace.
strings.IBR_barcelona.7.d:
“Well, pack it up. We're out.”

The room let out a collective sigh. This long office room, fashioned from an old union hall, held the regional headquarters of the AAS taskforce investigating the arms shipments thefts. Disappointed faces looked up at Rodrigo as he declared the news to the room, displaying the message in his hand.

“Section One, myself and a deputy shall remain here in a support capacity for the local police department, who will continue the investigation.” A groan sounded around the room, one baffled officer at the back shouting in disbelief. Rodrigo held up his hand, calling for quiet.

“I understand your frustrations, but this comes from above. All other sections will be reassigned, your new orders coming through within the next two days. I've been informed they will be likely down south, so get ready for that. Until then, pack up, file up and ready up to get out of here. Departing section leaders, please coordinate with Section One to determine what documents should be kept here with them. Lists of documents for archiving should be on my desk by the end of the day.”

With more groans, as Rodrigo returned to his little office booth he heard the sounds of activities begin. He couldn't blame them, he felt it too. Nothing! He fell into his chair as he thought over the case. The Guardia Civil guards were all spotless. No witnesses. Nothing at all at the crime scene. He could almost believe it was an administrative error, that the guns had never existed.

At least the investigation was continuing, rather than being shelved, even if it was with the numbskulls of the local police. Perhaps fresh eyes would show something they missed? He snorted almost as soon as the thought occurred. The police spotting something the AAS had missed?
strings.IBR_barcelona.7.a: At least this job hadn't worn out his optimism.
strings.IBR_barcelona.8.d:
The room was bare, white cream walls coldly lit by the lights. The makeshift desks, office booths, filing cabinets, typewriters - everything that had once filled the room was gone. The taskforce assembled to find those weapons were cleared out, all that remained of them being some chairs piled in the corner. Rodrigo sighed, looking at the empty space where his office once was. At least it wasn't going to look too bad on his record. Who could blame him in his investigation finding nothing, when there had been nothing there to begin with?

Administrative errors, were they really that common? He thought about his time running the taskforce, such a short time, and yet weren't there a litany of errors made by his staff?

Hadn't that typist, Eva, written down the wrong address of the port on a dozen documents, placing it further down the street?

Hadn't Marc written a report misspelling the name of a witness because he had never actually checked the spelling?

Didn't he almost miss a zero off a budget report before he caught it? Rodrigo tapped his foot, mistakes happened. Maybe they were right to just accept the fact, they had always been searching for nothing. He walked to the end of the room, placing his hands on the lightswitch before taking one last look at his temporary office space. He hesitated, doubts holding his hand.

Was a few spelling mistakes or miswritten numbers really the same thing as someone accidentally inventing an entire weapons shipment?

His head was full of questions. Constant questions.

He switched off the light.
strings.IBR_barcelona.9.d:
Major José Delgadillo was calm. As calm as gentle river water, idly flowing. His eyes were closed, his mind almost free of thought for just a moment, as if lost in the midst of some ethereal piece of music. In his mind, he was there again, by the river bank so many years ago.

There was no one else around, even the birds had left this picturesque spot. Save for some soft sounds of lapping riverwater, nothing pierced the tranquility of the moment. How green it was! How the trees and grass beside the river glowed against the light!

“Sir, the reports have been confirmed. What are your orders?”

He almost sighed, of course they wanted to break the moment. Never a moment of peace in this war, young men never learned to appreciate the moments before chaos properly. It was something he had learned long ago: ignore the world to your soul's peril.

“Sir?”

Without opening his eyes, he spoke to the man behind him. “I saw the report, Lieutenant.” He breathed slowly, sweet air filling his lungs. Delgadillo could almost imagine the confused look on the Lieutenant's face.

“So what should we do?”

The Major took in the tranquility of Russia one more time. A sound became ever louder, a crackling. “Our forces were ambushed moving into Barcelona, and a complete convoy was lost. Open conflict. Be calm; we anticipated this. Deploy the reserves, tell them this is now a pacification mission. I briefed their officers; they will understand.” The lieutenant darted away quickly; perhaps he didn't have to leave Russia after all? He abandoned his preparations to leave, eyes remaining closed, and turned around.
strings.IBR_barcelona.9.a: On a beautiful meadow, a pacified village burned. On the Volga's banks, he had his men's revenge.
strings.IBR_barcelona.10.d:
“Guardia Civil, get on the ground!”

The usual shout sounded as they kicked down the door of the house, instantly replaced by the shotgun blast from inside.

The officer who kicked the door down crumpled, being pushed back slightly as he fell to the ground, with the officer behind him crying out as the slug went through the side of his torso. The officers beside him opened fire, rushing into the house.

The man with the shotgun didn't get a chance to fire again, cut down in a swift hail of bullets. The hallway was narrow, with two rooms and a staircase leading upstairs. At the top of the staircase and the doorways, terrorists lay in waiting, pistols drawn.

They fired first, but stress seemed to get to them. From mere feet from the Guardia Civil, they missed; their only success was a bullet striking one of the officers' legs. The Guardia Civil officers responded in kind, accurately and decisively. All the men downstairs were dead in seconds, the man upstairs crying out as he was wounded.

They swept the house, then searched it, finding a crate of grenades under a bed upstairs. Outside, an ambulance took away the wounded men, the officers remaining doing their best to put on a brave face. The neighborhood didn't come out to watch; they just stared out of their windows. Silent, unnerving watchers. They radioed their situation to Headquarters, the sting of disappointment apparent in their voices.

This was hardly the stronghold they had been promised, but perhaps it would only be the first catch of the day?
strings.IBR_barcelona.10.a: Raid 1 of 5. 3 casualties, 1 fatality. 1 box of grenades found. 4 terrorists neutralized.
strings.IBR_barcelona.11.d:
Captain Gerena, sitting in the driver's seat of his undercover vehicle, was sweating hard. Since they left the station around 10 PM, the initial plan to take back the stolen guns from the anarchists had been brought to the brink of collapse. Gerena was forced to divert his convoy three times due to the chaos in the streets.

Time and time again, they were held up by barricades or rioting Barcelonés, and the speed and surprise that the Policía Armada usually relied upon to make quick raids had dissolved into the night air. Two police vans and a coupe rolling straight through the middle of the city could only remain discreet for so long, after all. Even the officers not in the convoy struggled, as squad cars were stopped at barricades placed in the streets, forcing them to reverse and find some new path to the warehouse.

For the men not so lucky, Gerena heard on his radio that one had been ambushed by a mob and murdered, and five more had to be carried off to the hospital. Terrorist bastards. At the very least, the main convoy had finally broken through, and Gerena stepped out of the car.

The vans pulled up beside him-no, wait. Van. Just one? Fuck, the captain silently cursed. They must have run. Cowards. His officers began to shuffle from the van, outfitted in their uniforms. He gritted his teeth and dug in his heels. He did not suffer through this hellish day just to call off the raid now. Gerena reached for his radio and chanced a glance ahead of him towards the warehouse.

A line of rifles stared back. In those last moments, he thought faster than ever before in his life. Planned. Every part of it was planned. He was only the animal caught in someone else's trap. There was just enough time to hear the shooting start.
strings.IBR_barcelona.11.a: Y una noche todo ardía, y una noche se encendieron las hogueras...
strings.IBR_barcelona.12.d:
After weeks of scrabbling around in the cobbles for leads, Sanz and his men finally had the strength to grab one. Despite an uptick in clashes with DI militants, they had not been entirely unprofitable.

A small cell of anarchists was captured in an apartment raid. They didn't have much of use in the apartment itself, but they had an abundance in their minds. The leader of the little cell wasn't as tough as he seemed, and after only a short time under interrogation, he gave up the location of the stolen arms shipment - a warehouse by the docks, only lightly defended by the terrorists so as to not draw attention and remain unintrusive. Almost a clever spot, but the fools were in for quite the shock when the Policía Armada showed up outside their doors.

The Chief Inspector had a field day, grinning silently and bringing the news to the Police Commissioner, who was similarly pleased.

The Commissioner tapped Captain Gerena, a seasoned officer in his department, to lead the raid, and assembled a flying column of two vans and an undercover car to take the officers to the warehouse. The assault would be executed that same night, so the Commissioner could have something nice to present Franco by next morning. It would be the perfect trap, he thought gladly, as he imagined sending Caudillo Franco his report of the DI finally being destroyed and the city saved from the Reds once again. Outside his window in the department building, the sun slowly dipped beneath the horizon, the ephemeral red light at the end of the day striking his office.
strings.IBR_barcelona.12.a: The capote flashes out, a streak of fiery red.
strings.IBR_barcelona.13.t: The Widest Nets Have The Most Holes
strings.IBR_barcelona.13.d:
“Please give me something I can tell to Caudillo Franco. Anything, Chief Inspector.”

Chief Inspector Sanz shifted in his seat, the desperate silent plea of the Barcelona Police Commissioner boring into him like a diamond-tipped drill. It was intense, a pleading he had never seen from the man before, usually so sure of himself and the force he oversaw. Now he looked reduced to a schoolboy who had forgotten his homework, pleading with a friend to let him copy it.

“Well, we have made a great deal of arrests of numerous people with links to the DI. However, actual leads to anything beyond a random box of old weapons that barely work or some pamphlets have not been forthcoming. Not to mention, our efforts are starting to raise tensions with the popu-”

“But there have been arrests?”

Sanz gave a light groan. “Sir, this is Barcelona. I arrest a dozen people at random and I guarantee at least half will have some kind of link to DI somewhere. Without either arresting the entire city or knowing what to actually look for, we aren't getting anywhere quickly.”

“Any anomalies?”

“There is one being looked into. One patrol car reported that they may have a lead and to stand by for updates.” The Commissioner's eyes lit up. “But... those men have been missing since that message yesterday. We are trying to locate their car now.”

Disappointment crushed the Commissioner all over again. “Is that really all I have for the Caudillo? That we are running around chasing the entire city with nothing to really show for it except random socialists and spontaneously disappearing police officers?”
strings.IBR_barcelona.14.d:
For the first time since the end of the Civil War, it is no longer safe south of the Pyrenees.

Chaos reigneds over Madrid and Lisbon as the news caught the Caudillos utterly off-guard. What began at dusk and lasted well-past midnight, heavily-armed militiamen and partisans of the CNT-FAI-backed DI have completely overrun the city of Barcelona. Local law enforcement response teams found themselves rapidly overrun, forcing the government authorities to evacuate as the anarchists marched on the Plaza de Sant Jaume to establish a provisional commune in the city center.

Hell and damnation rule in Barcelona now, the image of serene security under the diarchal rule of the Caudillos now ubiquitously shattered. DI militants have already started building makeshift barricades and other defenses in preparation for the inevitable counterattack, even as remnants of the Metropolitan Police continue to fight in pockets of resistance all over the city.

The French have publicly questioned the capability of Barcelona's police, flabbergasted by the inability of Iberian law enforcement to contain the anarchist rioters. Similarly, and perhaps fearing similar sentiments on the ground in southern France, they expressed alarm at the combat ability of the DI militants, having successfully beaten back Iberian law enforcement.

There is no time to lose: an armed response force from the Iberian military must be sent into Barcelona before the situation spirals further out of control!
strings.IBR_barcelona.14.a: Well... at least that explains where the guns went.
strings.IBR_barcelona.15.d:
Fear for the flesh can create fear for what is necessary.

Thoughts, vile thoughts filled Major José Delgadillo as he rode in the back of the car, speeding down the highway. Here, everything seemed almost normal. Cars passed by, streetlights lit. He could believe this was an average day returning home after a long day of work.

Was the news out? He was no fool, it couldn't be hidden forever. When an entire city declares war, it's impossible to hide indefinitely.

The documents on the seat beside him had outlined all the necessary details. It seemed he was one of the most senior officers involved, in experience if not in rank. The subtext was clear; they provided the resources, with anything available being sent to the city. He provided results. He held the summons in his hand. “Proceed to the Operational Headquarters by midnight,” it was declared. “You are assigned to the newly formed task force to retake Barcelona, on account of your experience in pacification operations.” Just reading the words threatened to drag him back to those times. The heat of the African desert. The cold of the Russian expanse.

He shivered. He had hoped not to revisit such things. For years, he had compartmentalized, talked to no one about what occurred, even when they asked after his accolades and decorations. He had only ever done what was necessary, but what was necessary was rarely clean.

Fear for the flesh. His flesh, or Iberian flesh?

He had seen what fanatical anarchists had done to flesh, and he had sworn once before during the civil war to drive it out. The memories, so long contained, were starting to pound upon the barriers he had built around them. Their containment creaked.
strings.IBR_barcelona.15.a: To save Spain, he and his men would do anything necessary. Swiftly, and ruthlessly.
strings.IBR_barcelona.16.d:
The DI infiltration and consolidation of Barcelona has proven far more deep-rooted than any could have thought: barricades along the promenades, machine gun nests in upper floor windows with foxholes and trenchlines seen anywhere where the earth could be dug up. This is no longer just a riot or even a domestic terrorist threat, this is all the ugliness of the CNT-FAI in 1936 in a fresh coat of black and red paint.

Initial sorties by the Ejército have proven barely more effective than the metropolitan police, with the soldiers somehow driven back every time our forces try to break through into the interior of the city. What started as a national humiliation is quickly becoming an existential nightmare for the future of the Iberian Union. An even harsher hand is required to restore law and order on the peninsula at any cost.

We have three options to accomplish this objective: A protracted and heavy artillery bombardment would be precise and cause relatively minimal collateral damage, and will likely expel the DI from their static defenses. A naval bombardment would be more effective at ensuring the DI terrorists are wiped out, but an offshore shelling of a major European city is a recipe for high civilian casualties and massive structural damage around the entire area.

The least costly option is also the most dangerous to the forces on the ground: Sending a tank column into the city to hopefully dislodge the DI directly. Historically tanks in urban combat would be considered tactical risky, as low visibility and mobility hamper proper tank doctrine. At the same time, these examples often involve professional armies of relative parity, something noticeably absent in the case of DI's ad hoc irregulars and the Ejército's armored divisions...
strings.IBR_barcelona.16.a: Don't take any chances, commence the artillery barrage!
strings.IBR_barcelona.16.b: We won't suffer the DI anymore, order the naval bombardment!
strings.IBR_barcelona.16.c: Anarchist guerillas are no threat, send in the tanks!
strings.IBR_barcelona.17.d:
Barcelona is a jewel upon the coast. By night, its lights shine into the Mediterranean, a beacon to the ships sailing by. From the land all around, above the peaks of hills and on the horizon, an ethereal golden glow of civilization. By day, it serves as the heart of Catalonia, invisibly motivating Iberia's eastern state. Trucks move, trains carry, and jets fly; the dance of life.

The irony of that is not lost upon the artillerymen who loaded the shells and aimed their guns at the city. Life was the last thing that was intended.

For hours, the artillerymen had worked. Each collection of guns had a specific target marked upon a map, the mathematics to ensure accuracy painstakingly performed. Parts of the city life had to be extinguished, yes, but they didn't want to burn Barcelona. They wanted to save it, even if some amputation was necessary.

The evening after the order to cease was given, many of them sat in their messes contemplating. None spoke. Even when the news came of the reclamation squads finding the bombardment was successful, accurately decimating the DI presence enough for them to eradicate. Even when Major Delgadillo came to personally commend them, his eyes glowing with a sense of achievement. Was it their achievement? They certainly hoped not.

When he showed them the picture of the Casa de la Ciutat, the flag of Iberia proudly flying atop it, most tried to take heart. Their actions had been key to preventing more bloodshed, the horrors of anarchism snuffed out. For some, perhaps it worked, but most remained silent, bystanders to their success.

They had fired artillery shells at an Iberian city. No man was sure how many Iberians he had killed.

They had victory.
strings.IBR_barcelona.17.a: There was no triumph in that.
strings.IBR_barcelona.18.d:
Screams. Shouts. Denunciations. The artillerymen had become used to all of these things in the past hour.

They sat in their assembly tent, an officer they didn't recognize screaming at them with all the dignity of rank stripped away. He paced before them, asking where was their training? Their sense of responsibility? Their sense of patriotism?

They just looked ahead, waiting for it to be over.

The math had been incorrect. Overshooting, undershooting, trajectories veering to the left or the right - it had been a travesty. The haste of the ground troops to reclaim Barcelona had left little time for them to plan, and when Major Delgadillo's order to fire had come? They followed orders.

Major Delgadillo's hammer strike into the city had turned into a maelstrom of disaster, the quick blow descending into calamity as his soldiers had been ambushed and destroyed. The artillery had done its work, but not where it was most needed. The reserves had been called in, and while the crushing weight of Iberia had seen Casa de la Ciutat fly the Iberian flag once more, the warehouses full of their brother's bodies rendered any sense of success stillborn.

How many had each man killed as their shells flew into Barcelona? How many were DI terrorists? As pictures from Barcelona came in, of random buildings hit far from the intended target, of a family standing atop what had once been a house, or of a factory in flames, every man hid his fear of the answer.

The officer before them finally stopped, looking around with an expression conflicted between anger and shame. The artillerymen stared impassively, emotion buried so deep for the fear of its expression. The officer straightened himself.
strings.IBR_barcelona.18.a: He strode out, leaving the artillerymen in silence.
strings.IBR_barcelona.19.d:
The ships linger along the shoreline, black shadows against the morning sun. Around them, no other boats came. The horizon behind them empty of any human vessel. A line of ships, like a line formation of old, lay abreast of the city.

Their guns, exhausted, lay silent. Their night's work was done. The bombardment was over.

Many of the sailors slept long sleeps of exhaustion within the metal caves of their boats. A sense of the surreal carried upon the dark surrounding their bunks. Few could truly believe what had happened. The city to their stern was not some foreign citadel, insolent and defiant. Nor was it a shack upon the shore, a meaningless, impotent target.

Barcelona lay to their side, their guns having been ordered to fire upon a list of targets. Many of those who had been in charge of aiming found sleep an enemy to them, anxiety surrounding them. Had they been wrong, the images of what their guns could wrought twisted like knives in their mind. The deep craters, churned metal, and blasted rock. It had been some time since they had set foot on land, each sailor longed for its firm embrace under their feet again. To be striking it so left each man uneasy.

Around noon, an announcement from the captains played over their ship's speakers, closing the matter. “All ranks, ground forces declare Barcelona retaken. They thank us for our support. Good work, gentlemen.” They all read the same message, details spared. Barcelona was free once more; their efforts had been successful. Now they were to rest and return to the sea until their tours were done.

For those involved who were still awake, it was godsent, anxiety peeling away enough to find sleep. For a few precious hours, before the reality of life enforced itself again and their duties required tending, they could sleep.
strings.IBR_barcelona.19.a: But Barcelona burned in their dreams, and their guns never stopped.
strings.IBR_barcelona.20.d:
The climbing smoke above the city upon the shore was a vista that few of the sailors would forget. The fruits of their work, hasty hands loading shells into the large guns, replacing them with another. How long had they performed the dance? For each man, it was hard to say, there was only one shell after another until the shells stopped coming. The squadron of ships upon Barcelona's coast lay in limbo, unsure of their success.

Instead, more followed. Most had thought, upon the order to cease, that the day would have ended. Instead, the city continued to convulse, as though the heavy pounding of their naval guns had done little to arrest the city's malignant occupiers. Blasts could be seen, a few radios upon the ships giving reports of chaos continuing.

They were ordered to fire again, and they did. Their bombardment was shorter this time, firing upon the new targets identified by the ground troops. The implicit confession was apparent: the first bombardment had failed. They did the best they could to plot their shots, and as fast as possible, their support came for Barcelona's battle-stricken districts.

No news came after the second. After some hours of men at their stations, the call came to stand down, yet relief came to no man. Over the ships' speakers, each captain spoke a curt message before the ships began sailing away, thanking the men for their efforts and promising a debriefing once details became clearer. That the DI were destroyed.

As they sailed past Barcelona, horrible stacks of black climbing above it, no sailor felt the relief of victory. Two bombardments and a land campaign left images etched into each mind, a questionable success certain. They had only planned for one targeted bombardment. They all knew it. They knew best what these guns could do.
strings.IBR_barcelona.20.a: And upon Barcelona they had turned them. Twice.
strings.IBR_barcelona.21.d:
The pictures that were being delivered to newspapers around Iberia were powerful, authoritative. Tanks dominating streets, APCs crushing flimsy barricades, the Iberian flag flying proudly once more above the Casa de la Ciutat. Barcelona was retaken from the anarchists.

What the images didn't betray was the herculean effort it had taken.

The columns had moved in, attack vectors meticulously chosen to maximize effect while minimizing risk. Infantry screened the buildings, a godsend as many ambushes were prevented before they could be sprung. Tanks broke open buildings like eggs, allowing men to pour into them and extinguish the resistance that remained inside.

It was slow work. Without the aid of bombardments or easily maneuverable points of contact, every engagement carried risks. Corpses of Iberia's soldiers lay within every street upon which the attacks commenced. But organization won the day; despite all the DI's surprise tactics, they remained disjointed and lightly equipped. Even so, every road, square, and bend required slow steps.

But those streets would never again know the peace they had before. With the fallen soldiers, there were a multitude of innocents caught in the middle. Shrapnel and panicked shots did their work, entire districts bearing witness to the crushing of the DI and its cost. The armored vehicles prowled, a moving fortress of the Caudillos. But, a reactive fortress. Many of those who huddled in their homes as the crescendo of pacification passed them felt doubt in the remaining silence. Even if the streets were pacified, the Caudillo's peace had been broken once.

But civil peace would return, and despite their discontent, many citizens welcomed it. The city became safe, and the process of picking up the pieces could begin. The bodies could be buried.
strings.IBR_barcelona.21.a: But the bullet holes in the walls would remain.
strings.IBR_barcelona.22.d:
My name is General Diego Ferrer. I am writing this letter to express my profound sadness for your loss, and also to try and bring some degree of context to the unfortunate fate of your husband. I pray that my testimony may at least offer you some degree of understanding. While my duty as an officer limits what I am able to share, I shall try to provide as much clarity as I can.

As you are no doubt aware, José was summoned from his placement at the academy to be a part of the pacification efforts regarding the recent turmoil in Barcelona. I am sure you have seen the news. He came at my personal behest; while he had fallen upon hard times and a career of limited progress, he remained an expert in pacification operations. I had little direct experience regarding such an operation.

To say operations went smoothly would be a difficult thing to claim. While details of the operation and its conduct are classified, a fact that should not impede me much as most of it pertains to mere military movements, that it was frustrated is a point of public record. Privately, I shall say that your husband's initial plan went awry. Our armored push found complications that were not anticipated.

This is not to undermine your husband's conduct. He made use of all the men and material available to him and won the day, at great effort. However, I must confess that over the course of the operation, it was reported to me that he began acting more erratically, making references to his former campaigns that made little sense at the time. In my judgement, I believe now he may have been undergoing a breakdown, possibly from the operation's inception.

Had any of us, or the men under our command, known his condition, we would have taken every measure to prevent what occurred. He was one of Iberia's most hard-working defenders, and I pray that the nature of his departure shall not stain his legacy.
strings.IBR_barcelona.23.d:
“General Ferrer, how can I help?” Major José Delgadillo picked up the phone gracefully, already expecting the call. He had been positioned by it for some minutes now, awaiting its shrill invitation. Ever since he'd been told of that report written behind his back, he knew this call would be coming.

“Major, when I was notified that you had unilaterally deployed the reserves, I held my hand. You were well-recommended and have a wealth of experience; to put it to use was why I summoned you. However, I have in my hand a report from this afternoon. Do you know what it says?”

The Major could barely contain a scoff. Ferrer's tone was unmistakable; he wouldn't have lasted a minute in Russia. Admonishment dripped from his voice, the expectation of a result clear and quantifiable, obvious. He remembered those young German officers who had been in Russia with him who shared such suicidal methodologies. Short-lived officers. “Limited results, Sir?”

“It observes a crisis of morale, that we have barely made it into the city center, and a huge loss in material. Major, I'm sure you appreciate the faith I placed in you, yet I have never seen such a reckless campaign carried out!”

Was it in the summer of 1943 he'd had this same conversation? In some wooden bunker in the middle of nowhere, a Prussian called Ernst something demanding concrete military achievements rather than numerous reports of pacifications, as if they were not military achievements?

“Sir, we are in a war of attrition now. These animals were difficult to remove in Russia when they had just trees and medieval huts. Now they have a city. Fear is the way to break them; overwhelming force and fear. Every desperate act they commit alienates them from the populace. Every street they lose costs them dearly. They will break.”
strings.IBR_barcelona.23.a: Please do tell me where our crisis of morale is sourcing from, however, and I shall see that it is dealt with.
strings.IBR_barcelona.24.d:
Something felt off to Guillermo. Since the surge of Guardia Civil officers to Barcelona, he had grown used to the glowers of reluctant civilians, buoyed by fear into not openly backing the Defensa Interior. But today, everything was shut, a few buildings at least feigning repairs, and barely anybody was on the street. He shook his head. Merely a coincidence, surely. Something that he could laugh off when watching the anarchists hang.

A call from his radio distracted him from his bloodlust, a suddenly frantic report on an attack by a high number of people. A moment later, before the ramifications could truly sink in, gunshots echoed from down the streets. Guillermo rushed back, clutching frantically onto his gun before ducking into a doorway.

“Officer Soriano, sir!” shouted Sergio, a commandant brought onto his team in Villareal only last month, and only in Barcelona since last week. “Situation is far worse than we feared..”

Raising the volume on a radio, the pair only moved backwards slightly to listen. “...rchists everywhere,” reported the broadcast, the voice muffled by frantic driving and gunshots, “coming down streets...bombs, guns, everything...streets have fallen, entire quarters are under siege...”

The door behind them opened. A few people looked out, but only one fired, hitting Guillermo in his shoulder. Thrown upwards, then stumbling backwards, he stepped on a poster rallying support for CNT-FAI, then looked to his right, beyond Sergio's headless body. The lamppost was filled, almost to the top, with those same posters, and a few taken out of a bin were filtering through the wind. Collapsing into the street, he watched a dozen soldiers, and more guns, leave that building, his view was interrupted by a bomb thrown at him by a greengrocer.
strings.IBR_barcelona.24.a: The Battle of Barcelona begins, a hundred times over.
strings.IBR_barcelona.25.t: Defensa Interior Seizes Control of Barcelona
strings.IBR_barcelona.25.d:
CONFIDENTIAL - URGENT

TO MINISTER OF GOVERNANCE, MINISTER OF THE IBERIAN FEDERAL ARMY, MINISTER OF THE NAVY, IBERIAN COUNCIL, CAUDILLO FRANCISCO FRANCO, CAUDILLO ANTÓNIO SALAZAR

BARCELONA - CATALONIA - IBERIAN UNION

Barcelona has fallen. Over the past day, cells from the CNT-FAI and the Defensa Interior (DI) have started a full offensive, capturing all major administrative centers and proclaiming a new anarchist commune. With police outmaneuvered, the DI were able to seize power, assaulting the few officers remaining in the city, killing many on the ground and seizing arms.

We have several means to respond to this, but it will take time to reinforce and replenish. A conventional artillery bombardment could be sufficient, as could using the Iberian navy to attack the ports and place the city under siege, but this gives the anarchists time to prepare defences, and won't accomplish its objective in isolation. We could escalate this through sending an armoured battalion, which would likely impact morale and, through sheer force, win the battle, but would cause real damage to the city, both culturally and economically, and for years to come.

This is a fundamental threat to Iberia. We still have the upper hand and should still be able to quash this rebellion. However, the fact that a major city and economic powerhouse has been captured so easily highlights a critical lack of authority. If we can be evicted so easily here, then the chance of future offensives collapsing the Union is high. If we hope to survive, we need to respond urgently, and succeed.
strings.IBR_barcelona.25.a: Siege the city with artillery. Raise the temperature.
strings.IBR_barcelona.25.b: Perform a naval bombardment. Paralyze the ports.
strings.IBR_barcelona.25.c: We can't have the Union collapse. Send in the tanks.
strings.IBR_barcelona.26.d:
CONFIDENTIAL

TO MINISTER OF GOVERNANCE, CAUDILLO FRANCISCO FRANCO, CAUDILLO ANTÓNIO SALAZAR

BARCELONA - CATALONIA - IBERIAN UNION

With the recent drawdown of forces within Barcelona, the Defensa Interior (DI) and CNT-FAI attempted a violent insurrection with the aim of seizing the city. However, although facing almost insurmountable odds, the few remaining officers within were able to regroup with the aid of both their units and anti-separatist volunteers, offering enough resistance to destabilize the anarchists, and buying time for the garrison to mobilize and begin a full offensive.

Barcelona is not totally pacified, but central governance is once more in command, and without a need for our main forces. There is limited guerrilla warfare in isolated parts of the city's outskirts, but these are from groups unconnected from the central DI command, which, in a testament to their ideology, had dissolved into infighting once the offensive began. The Bolsheviks, once more, could not overcome the brave sons of Barcelona and their valiant defence of their homelands.

Immediately, we should decorate the officers responsible with the Cross of Military Valour and celebrate them, but we have a much deeper crisis. It was only due to the ingenuity of a few men that we averted utter catastrophe. If it wasn't for their actions, and had the DI been more organized, it is unlikely we would've held on. We are running on luck - and without necessary reform to ensure our capacities to respond are strong, we will have to pray that it never ends.
strings.IBR_barcelona.26.a: May it last as long as possible.
strings.IBR_barcelona.27.d:
CONFIDENTIAL - URGENT

TO MINISTER OF GOVERNANCE, MINISTER OF THE IBERIAN FEDERAL ARMY, MINISTER OF THE NAVY, IBERIAN COUNCIL, CAUDILLO FRANCISCO FRANCO, CAUDILLO ANTÓNIO SALAZAR

BARCELONA - CATALONIA - IBERIAN UNION

Barcelona has fallen. Defensa Interior (DI) partisans were able to overwhelm forces we had assigned to the city. With the complexities of urban warfare and the homegrown nature of many anarchists within Barcelona, our efforts to reclaim the city faltered, and the sheer intensity of the fighting across each block, street, and house has overwhelmed our forces, isolating them to the southern outskirts of the city.

We could turn towards using artillery, hoping to quell the anarchists through shock and awe. Naval bombardment would also achieve this end, but would cause more damage to Barcelonan infrastructure. An armoured brigade would be costly, but would provide direct, armored firepower, and would likely harm anarchist morale. The negative impacts of sending such large, expensive vehicles into narrow, urban conflict would be there, but would be reduced by untrained fighters armed only with makeshift rifles and Zhdanov cocktails.

This is an urgent threat to Iberia. Currently, we should still be able to defeat this rebellion, but our eviction has shown weakness in our strategy, and an inability to maintain control over a major population center and economic powerhouse. Nationalists, radicals, and other opponents to our government will see this as an opportunity. If we don't succeed in quelling this uprising now, the Union's collapse could be inevitable.
strings.IBR_barcelona.27.a: Siege the city with artillery. Raise the temperature.
strings.IBR_barcelona.27.b: Perform a naval bombardment. Paralyze the ports.
strings.IBR_barcelona.27.c: We can't have the Union collapse. Send in the tanks.
strings.IBR_barcelona.28.t: Guardia Civil Restores Order in Barcelona
strings.IBR_barcelona.28.d:
The Guardia Civil has defeated DI forces in Barcelona, despite fierce resistance. Initial assaults by the DI on our forces left our men weakened and disorganized. However, the Guardia Civil, alongside the limited contingent of troops present in the city, were able to regroup at the Plaza de España. With their superior weaponry, our men were able to fend off the next wave of attacks, with DI suffering decisive losses and scattering.

Efforts have now turned to hunting down the remaining insurrectionists. By cordoning off neighborhoods and the city perimeter, we have arrested or otherwise dealt with most of the insurgents. Overall DI leadership, however, has not been located.

Intelligence and security authorities in Madrid have been ordered to undertake an extensive review of how CNT-FAI and DI infiltration in Barcelona reached such a perilous extent, and military reinforcements are being brought to bear to search surrounding towns and countryside for any rebels who escaped our dragnet.
strings.IBR_barcelona.28.a: Why must they hurt their own people so?
strings.IBR_barcelona.29.d:
The Anarchist insurrection within Barcelona has, very regrettably, managed to seize Barcelona from our control. The under-equipped and under-manned forces present in the city at the time ultimately proved insufficient at beating back the DI's onslaught.

For a time, the Guardia Civil managed to maintain control over the administrative buildings in the heart of Barcelona. However, the communication equipment available proved inadequate, causing improper organization and the collapse of the Guardia Civil's defense.

Once the Guardia Civil had been proven to be outmatched, a mass evacuation was ordered. We are left with no other option for retaking Barcelona other than requesting military assistance.

There are three primary options for the military intervention. First, using artillery to put the city under siege and break the will of the Anarchists. This is a rather safe approach, given how unsustainable the insurrectionists' position is, but it is also certain to take a long time. Second, a naval bombardment, this would hit far deeper into the backline, but also cause substantial collateral damage. Third, a tank blitz would be the fastest, but also likely to yield the most casualties.
strings.IBR_barcelona.30.d:
After a series of long and intense street warfare, Barcelona is once again under our control. While scattered fighting continues as DI holdouts are still being cleared out, the Guardia Civil and the military have managed to, despite certain difficulties, stabilize the situation in Barcelona. As such, now we can be certain that the DI, the inciting force of this entire conflict, will be thoroughly wiped from Barcelona.

Of course, there still remains the CNT-FAI proper, but it is unlikely that they will attempt something as bold as the insurrection in Barcelona in the near future. Accordingly, a majority of the military personnel sent here can return to the frontlines.

The overriding question is how the DI was able to organize this insurrection, and how the CNT-FAI managed to garner such broad support. Security experts are being summoned to provide insight, while those implicated in the failure in Catalonia are being summarily dismissed.

The Caudillos have announced an emergency session of the Iberian Council to undertake far-reaching security reforms in response.
strings.IBR_barcelona.31.d:
General Cano and several of his peers in the Iberian military have issued a secret report, summarized as follows:

The Barcelona uprising is a grave humiliation. Collective oversights and Iberian inability to prevent large-scale subversion and violence are evident to domestic radicals and foreign enemies alike. We must begin an extensive and intensive reevaluation of our security institutions and measures to prevent another Barcelona.

Barcelona should draw attention to the proliferation of left-wing and separatist groups eager to inflict grave damage to the Union. The DI, the ETA, the BR, and the BTA are “rabid dogs frothing for their deranged revolutions as though they were a bone.”

According to them, terrorist activity, undoubtedly inspired by DI's actions in Barcelona and facilitated by the drawdown of security forces elsewhere for support, has trebled in recent days. Restraint, whether budgetary or in the array of techniques deployed, would endanger Iberia.

New resourcing, manpower, and ideas will be required to secure the Union, but cannot quell terrorist violence in the near term. Critical targets must be hardened, and losses expected. Immediate action to this effect is recommended to the Caudillos and the Council.
strings.IBR_barcelona.32.d:
Every few minutes, Adolfo heard gunshots in the distance. His city burned. Sandbags lined the streets below his apartment just as they did 26 years ago. The world was different then. Adolfo had once seen a great future for the Iberian proletariat, an almost sacred struggle against the fascists and monarchists who sought to destroy the meager progress the Republic had made. Perhaps, in another world, the Revolution could have succeeded. But not in this one.

Adolfo opened his closet, removing a small pile of clothing to find a small latch on the bottom. He opened a secret cache, memories of decades long past. There was his 'Tigre' rifle, the weapon he had used in his first and only kill. He'dd imagined he'd use it resisting Francoist domination after the republic fell, but he never did.

He moved the rifle slightly to reveal an old black-and-white photograph underneath it. There he was, on the left hand of the image. A few inches shorter than the other young men with him. His facial hair had not yet grown in. He was holding his rifle and smiling.

With him were four comrades, all of whom he remembered well.

Ramón, who could make anyone laugh even at the worst of times. Shot by a sniper in January of 1939. Manuel, a brilliant student and equally brilliant fighter. Told Adolfo he was running away to France and was never heard from again.

Sara, the girl with glasses that he could not help but imagine one day marrying. Captured by the Francoist regime shortly after the war, and never seen again. Asunción, the childhood friend that had convinced Adolfo to take up arms. Also captured.

What had his battles really accomplished?
strings.IBR_barcelona.33.d:
Franco stood before an anxious audience, few if any of whom felt comfortable knowing that they were now involved in the response to the worst act of terrorism in the history of the Union. “Gentlemen,” he began, “I will not lie to you. We were unprepared for this week's attack. Our intelligence community failed to recognize the scale of the planned operations, and our police and military were not ready to make a decisive and immediate response. We cannot allow any attack like this to happen again.

We have long known that a small underground DI resistance persisted ever since the liberation of Catalonia 25 years ago. This morning the Iberian Intelligence Center prepared a detailed report on documented acts of homicide, assault, and arson linked to the DI, showing that in the past seven years DI violence has been increasing yearly. The failure of our government to recognize and react to the rise of this terrorist activity is damning. It should not have taken a tragedy as severe as Barcelona to formulate a response.

In addition to their comprehensive review of DI activities since the Union's formation, the Intelligence Center has identified several extremist organizations which have escalated their activity, emboldened by the DI's actions in Barcelona. Already last evening, a security officer was attacked in Bilbao by a 23-year-old extremist Jimeno Inchausti. In his interrogation, Inchausti admitted that he had not worked alone, but was part of a network of Basque-separatists calling themselves 'Euskadi Ta Askatasuna'. Between 1950 and 1963, only 15 murders could be linked to extremist groups besides the DI. However, in just this past month, no fewer than 7 such acts of violence have taken place--4 in Navarra, 2 in Portugal, and 1 in Asturias.

It is all but certain that these terrorist groups will expand their resources and intensify their activities in the coming months. Increased funding and supplies will need to be provided to the Axencia Anti-Separatista to identify and eliminate these groups. Eliminating terrorism needs to be the primary goal of all security officials, and all actions taken must consider potential effects on terrorists' ability to undermine Iberia's unity.”
strings.IBR_barcelona.33.a: “Failure to act may be the end of the Union.”
strings.IBR_barcelona.34.d:
“Dolores Torres was 26 years old, a loving mother of three: 6 year old Carmen, 4 year old José Luis, and 1 year old María Isabel. This morning her husband Ángel, 38 years old, attended the funerals of his wife and children. Ángel lost his home, his wife, many friends and neighbors, and two of his children. Mrs. Serrano's father, 51 year old army veteran Antonio Torres, lost his brother Francisco to Communist terrorism 27 years ago, and now has lost his daughter and two grandchildren to the same terrorists that plagued Catalonia in his youth. Dolores died as a hero, shielding young María Isabel from the violence, and as a martyr, the victim of an attack on the very soul of Iberia. Dolores, Carmen, and José Luis, are far from alone. Hundreds of men, women, and children, became martyrs three days ago.”

Today's session was far quieter than any that had come before it. A few councilors struggled to hold back tears as Franco lamented the tragedy that had befallen Barcelona days earlier. Ending his speech with a minute of silence, the Caudillo bowed his head and tightly gripped the podium, his brows revealing suppressed anger.

“We will destroy the terrorists.”

The Council erupted into applause, and Franco left the stage. Minister Carrero Blanco stepped up to the podium. His speech began much as Franco's had, solemn and austere, but soon shifted his focus to matters of government policy. “Councilors, we are engaged in a struggle for the very spirit of Iberia. For the Union to survive, your service is urgently needed. Caudillo Franco and Caudillo Salazar have ordered new legislation to provide the Axencia Anti-Separatista the power and resources necessary to fully eliminate the leftist threat. Iberia cannot afford a government divided by factionalism or language, by politics or geography. Her Council must stand united against terrorism!”

Even as they applauded, many councilors were deeply nervous. Never in the history of Iberia had so many people been tasked with as important a task to complete in such a short timeframe. Murmurs filled the Palace after Carrero Blanco's speech. Most councilors did not know more than two dozen other people in the chamber. Who among them would write the legislation, and how could it be debated without sending the whole Council into chaos?
strings.IBR_barcelona.34.a: And what if the Caudillos disapprove?
strings.IBR_terror.1.d:
In the town of Oñati in the Basque, AAS agents looked up at the apartment building. It was relatively small, three stories and three small apartments wide - the same kind of style that populated much of the small villages of the area. They looked up at the effigy of a man, made of straw and old clothes, hung from the window of his second storey apartment; the apartment of a fellow agent. From its neck hung a message.

In the village of Tuixent, all stood in fear for a moment as they saw the shrine before them. One of them had run to call the police, but most found themselves immobilised as memories of the massacre that had afflicted their town all that time ago, that had made their name famous. Upon their church, a message carved into the wood surrounded by photos of the victims of that massacre.

In a field near La Bouga in Asturias, the farmer sat in awe. What had started as a routine inspection of his land had turned into a grisly affair as he looked at the slaughtered livestock placed around the pole in the ground. The stench of decay and copper filled his senses as he tried to think on what to do. He could do little but read the message, screwed to the top of the pole for all to see.

In the small Portuguese settlement of Resouro, many watched as one of the white homes that made up the town burned. No one tried to stop it. The man inside was infamous for bragging about his time volunteering for Spain in the Civil War, and the sign stuck into the dirt road outside his house paused any thoughts to help.

“To the occupiers of the Euskadi...”

“To the oppressors of Catalonia...”

“To the tyrants of Asturias...”

“To the abusers of Portugal...”
strings.IBR_terror.1.a: “This is the fate that awaits you.”
strings.IBR_terror.1_tt: Terrorism can now be tracked and combated via the political screen and new decisions - Iberia's stability will depend on this!
strings.IBR_terror.2.d:
If any had seen the two youths darting through the alleys and streets of Bilbao in the early morning - and many must have, given how far they must have had to come from their registered addresses - none came forward afterwards.

Using their expert knowledge of their city, they bypassed police concentrations to arrive at the Bilbao office of the Axencia, and waited for their opportunity - the arrival of a bus at the nearby stop, disgorging workers arriving for the day. Disgorging witnesses. Unfurling personal banners decrying both the AAS and the government itself, they pelted the office with painted rocks and other missiles, smashing windows and injuring several staff inside.

Making no attempt to escape, the youths were soon apprehended by nearby police and AAS agents from the office, with considerably more violence than would otherwise have been necessary. All watching knew their fate - 'questioning' at the hands of the AAS, followed by a term of detainment. Somewhere. The hand of the state, quashing dissent.

But the Axencia agents in the office spoke differently. It was not long ago that none would have dared deliver such a brazen, self-sacrificing message. The fact that they had done so spoke to the existence of a deepening dissatisfaction among the populace. And to the emboldening of the separatists.
strings.IBR_terror.3.d:
The ashen-faced police chief calmly descended down the cracked stone slabs of the station, with every nearing step to the grand oak entrance doors increasing the blasting cacophony of voices and screams outside. Bilbao awaited, bursting with anger and cries for justice. He sighed. He had meant to give it to them.

He reached the bottom of the steps, where a microphone and podium had been set up prior. Before him was a crowd, a crowd so large he could scarcely believe had assembled before his station. Journalists with tape recorders, TV cameras to the side focused solely on him, residents with expressions filled with furious words. As he stood at the microphone for a moment, the police guards before the crowd stepped forward and he raised a hand, calling for quiet. Though it took a moment, and the occasional heckle still called, he could speak and be heard.

“Ladies and Gentleman, today I share in your grief that two young boys were taken from us. Boys from our community that, even if they had run afoul of the law, it was our duty to protect and guide to a better life.”

He felt the burning gaze of the crowd as he continued. “It is public knowledge that they were arrested for vandalizing an AAS office. They are amongst Iberia's most hardworking defenders and their arrest was necessary. That does not excuse our failing in their care in what followed.”

He breathed. Remember the story the agents had coached, they had guaranteed it would ease the questions. Redirect it into a message for Iberia's youth. “The boys were improperly searched. Within their cell, it seems that they used an illegal substance within their possession that they tragically expired from...”

A cry came from the crowd, a bellowed question. “What was the drug?”
strings.IBR_terror.3.a: The Chief grew pale. “I... don't know.” The shouts recommenced.
strings.IBR_terror.4.d:
To those who had long lived in Bilbao, the sight was one that, if they were old enough, they had not seen in many years. To those younger, it had never been seen.

For days, the Casco Viejo, Bilbao's ancient city center, had been the site of fierce and running battles between riot police and Basque protestors. Lines of armored police stood shoulder to shoulder in the narrow, winding streets, as they fought with protestors who tore up cobblestones and roof tiles to throw at them. All suffered in the intense summer heat, itself only running tempers higher.

Not that they weren't already boiling. The rage felt by the entire city at the deaths of the two youths taken into custody for stoning the Axencia station, and what was perceived as the state's cold and uncaring response to the travesty, could not be contained. And though the old town was the epicenter of the clashes, they continued to grow outwards. More police were rapidly bussed in. More people came out to meet them.

Though arrests were swift, and concentrations of rioters were broken up whenever and wherever possible, it was simply not possible to conceal or downplay the scale of the disorder. The Axencia has reported that the rioting, unfortunately, has contributed to the growing national consciousness and perception of disunity within Iberia.

They advise that action be taken to prove the contrary.
strings.IBR_terror.5.d:
If there was one thing that Maria Espluga could say to compliment the DI, it's that they were very, very careful.

She had been kept in a room for almost two days. It had been tiny, barely more than a closet just wide enough for her to lie down in, essentially a wooden box. There had been no light save for a single hot bulb hanging above her. It was turned off at night, lit by day, illuminating the men and women entering the room to interrogate her. They were relentless in their questioning, harsh and exact.

They questioned her on the tenets of anarchist theory her cover story claimed she was devoted to. They demanded she recount in perfect detail past instances of dissent down to who had been involved. They claimed to know that she was an AAS spy, slapping her and demanding that she confess. She was never allowed to sleep for more than a few hours, and the questions never ended.

But then they did. The door had opened, and instead of an angry man or woman instead strode an old man with a fresh pair of clothes. He had shut the door to allow her to change, and then guided her out into the sun outside. It had stung her eyes, something the kindly man had apologised for. “I'm sorry for how far the young ones went,” he explained as he led her to a waiting car, “but you can't be too careful”.

She wasn't sure where she was but she could see she was in the deep Catalan countryside. After almost an hour the car stopped outside a farmhouse, a single man leaning against a fence post. He walked to the door of the car and spoke to the old man driving.

“Can she be trusted?” he asked in Catalan.

The old man looked at her and nodded. “She passed the test.” he responded in kind.
strings.IBR_terror.5.a: “This cell's organisation terrified Maria, but she had been accepted. Good news for her report.”
strings.IBR_terror.6.d:
A meeting in a wood clearing was one of the more interesting spots for dissident meetings, AAS agent Quevedo mused. It could have been mistaken for a youth group camping trip, a hastily constructed fire with a dozen men and women awkwardly perched on logs.

Hard to believe this was the same group behind Barcelona.

They sat mostly silent, staring at the flames of the fire and listening to its crackles. Quevedo didn't want to push probing for information, but it hadn't taken too long to guess there may not be much to learn beyond names and associates. In his career he had seen every kind of dissident; none had ever looked so dejected and lost as this sorry group of traitors did. Eventually they heard the tell tale signs of movement in the trees, like tremendous crashes in the otherwise silent Catalonian night. Twigs snapped, brush was moved and Quevado stood, raising the pistol he had in his pocket. One of them had to at least act like the DI.

“Identify yourself!”

“Charlie Rivel. Who the hell do you think it is?” came the sarcastic reply, as an overweight, sweating shape resembling a leader burst in the clearing. “At least one of you is checking the perimeter, the real DI member here!” he shouted as he walked to the gathering. “I was tailed for miles on the highway!” Quevedo sorely doubted that.

The man reached the fire, but his shouting didn't stop. He referred to all of them by their real names, even Quevedo's cover name which he feigned horror at, ranting about incompetent recruits, lack of recruits, too much recruiting, lack of resources and many, many other complications. Quevedo could barely contain his smile as this man told him almost everything he could want to know about the local DI. He was right to sarcastically name himself after Rivel; he truly was a clown.
strings.IBR_terror.6.a: But we should still make sure clowns don't get lucky.
strings.IBR_terror.7.d:
Furious knocking at his door alerted Joan-Josep to his feet. The old man pleaded with the visitors as they threatened to break in, hobbling as quickly as his joints would allow. He opened his door, and six military men, all armed and armored, burst into his house, quickly scanning the rooms to find any other people. “What is the meaning of this?” Joan-Josep demanded.

“Sit down. Now. Do as I say,” said the officer, as he pointed his rifle directly at the old man. Joan-Josep complied, sitting down, filled with terror. “Don Comelade, is it?” The officer relaxed his arm, letting his rifle point towards the floor. “Is anyone else in this building?”

“No sir.”

“Don Comelade, we have reason to believe that you or someone else in this building is involved in an arms smuggling operation for the DI. I just need to ask you a few questions. Is there anybody else who lives here with you?”

“No, my wife passed away three years ago.”

“Do you possess any weapons?”

“No. Never once.”

“Thank you for your cooperation, Don Comelade. I will sit here with you while the Agency conducts a brief search. We will be done soon.”

Joan-Josep had heard of things like this happening to others before. Innocent people whose homes were stormed by the AAS. But Joan-Josep was not innocent, he knew it. The souls of those Nationalists he gunned down in the trenches of Aragon 29 years ago knew it too. Surely, he had nothing in his house from those old days. Surely, the AAS would not find anything. Surely, he would be safe. Minutes felt like hours, the agent watching over Joan-Josep offering only the heartless gaze of the White Terror. But he did not die that day. “Thank you Mr. Comelade. Apologies for the interruption, go on with your business.” The agent stood up, and along with the other agents, wordlessly left. There Joan-Josep still sat, still petrified.
strings.IBR_terror.7.a: The White Terror is back. Or perhaps it never ended?
strings.IBR_terror.8.t: Thousands Protest Spanish Dominance in Lisbon
strings.IBR_terror.8.d:
It began as flyers littering the cobbled alleyways of old Lisbon, characterizing the Caudilho as a marionette hanging from a gigantic Franco's fingertips. Agent Villahermosa didn't pay too much mind when he saw one of these flyers next to his favorite café. Subversive flyers have popped up around Lisbon every once in a while, just like they have all around the Union. It seemed a trivial matter when there were actual armed separatist gangs roaming the countryside and sowing terror, and so he didn't even bother reporting it to his superiors.

He did report back a week later, when a small group of radical students barricaded themselves in Lisbon University's faculty of fine arts and waved green-and-red flags from the windows. The small crowd of students and faculty that had come to watch them, somewhat supportive but mostly simply curious, was dispersed quickly and the subversive circle taken into custody. But this didn't appear to be anything organized, and Agent Villahermosa knew well that universities were always hotbeds for radicals and agitators. And so, in his report, he predicted that while this event reveals some level of unrest, it was likely to remain marginal.

Now, as he was looking at the massive crowds continuing to pour into the Praça do Comércio, waving Portuguese flags and chanting republican slogans, agent Villahermosa realized that his job was at stake. The students' arrest had lit a pyre of grievances and resentment that had simmered under the surface for years and had now lit up Lisbon, and all of Portugal, in a matter of days. The protest was non-violent, for now, but Iberian police weren't exactly known for their gentleness. Villahermosa stubbed his cigarette underfoot, cursed the day he signed up for the AAS, and turned inside to type up a new report.
strings.IBR_terror.8.a: Perhaps it was more than his job that was at stake.
strings.IBR_cauinfo_francolisbon_big_tt: This appears to be caused by Franco's overwhelming influence in the Union.
strings.IBR_terror.9.t: Hundreds Protest Spanish Dominance in Lisbon
strings.IBR_terror.9.d:
The congregation filing out of Santo André church on a sleepy Sunday morning were not prepared for the crowd of protestors filling the small square in front of them. A police cordon separated them from a few hundred men and women, shouting slogans about “Franco's tyranny” and the “Liberation of Portugal”. Dozens of red-green Portuguese flags were lazily waving in the wind, as if unprepared to be used for such a commotion on a weekend.

The elderly priest made his way towards the policemen. “Good morning, gentlemen. What exactly is happening here, if I may ask?”

A young, mustachioed officer snickered. “Good morning, father. Nothing is really happening. Just a couple of students and pensioners with too much free time on their hands. They've been here for half an hour now, but I don't think they're really going to get anywhere with us here.”

The priest nodded. “I see. Liberating Portugal, heh? Some of us remember what it was like in the 30s. One day they'll grow up and realize that it's better this way. Thank you for your service, Senhor officer.” The priest left with a satisfied chuckle.

But besides him, a few of the churchgoers did not hurry home. They remained to look at the protest with a curiosity that disquieted the police officers, even though they hadn't actually done anything. They stood there until the protest dwindled, about half an hour later. As the police finally dismantled their cordon, a shared realization had already dawned on all of them.
strings.IBR_terror.9.a: This was only going to get worse.
strings.IBR_cauinfo_francolisbon_small_tt: This appears to be caused by Franco's significant influence in the Union.
strings.IBR_terror.10.d:
The Gijón docks are a vile place to be. 20 years on the job, and I never get used to them after dark. The loose women standing at the gates, mockeries of beauty enticing the desperate. Men with faces collapsed with exhaustion, coming and going and yet not really going anywhere. The stink of fish and polluted sea. Place should be nuked.

As I stood by the portmaster's office then, contemplating noseplugs, I was cursing Torrez's name. He was reliable, but only ever reliable to the last person who gave him a peseta. Who knew if his information would be worth it. Men hid in the boats and inside the office, rifles and shotguns ready, but if we were unlucky it would be a long night. If nothing happened then Torrez would be picking up his teeth from inside a cell tomorrow. Lucky for him, around the witching hour gold stuck; the blinking red lights came in just as Torrez snitched. They sailed to the end of the jetty we'd been told to wait at, and I ducked more into the office doorframe. All the lights were off, the Reds controlled this port and kept them off for them, but either way I didn't feel like taking chances.

I could barely see the boat, my only illumination being a tiny gas lamp on their deck. They were moving awkwardly, shuffling around. Moving something? A loud thump was my answer. The unmistakable sound of a crate. I pounded the door behind me - the signal. I rushed forward, pistol drawn and boys following behind me, hollering for the men to freeze. From every boat, shooters appeared. If there was any fight in the smugglers, it vanished in the gaslight. I kicked open the box as my guys cuffed them. Torrez must have been right. No doubt weapons for the-

In the box were uniforms. I threw them aside until I reached the bottom. Nothing but uniforms. One of the cuffed men started laughing, earning him a right hook. I'd have given him my left too, but my chief held my arm. He forced me to look at him as they dragged the smugglers away, eyes full of frustration and sympathy.
strings.IBR_terror.11.d:
Through hard-won experience, the Axencia's special teams in Bilbao had developed quite the inventory of disguised vehicles, as well as the tradecraft to position them without detection by the ETA separatists they hunted.

And today they had used that tradecraft well, acting on the word of an informant.

The first inkling that the residents of the apartment block on the city outskirts had that something was amiss was the sudden convergence of dozens of armed and armored security troopers from all angles. Doors were breached - loudly. Stairs were ascended - rapidly. And one particular apartment was secured - violently. Snipers covered the perimeter as a launcher, rapidly brought to bear from a roofer's truck, sent gas directly through the apartment's window.

Within minutes, it was over. The apartment was, in fact, hosting an ETA cell - which had been apprehended in full. With no casualties on either side. Along with ample evidence indicating a planned attack on the city center, as well as the explosives planned to be used.

The Axencia report indicated that ETA activity in the region was still strong. But this was a major blow, nonetheless, and proof that the Axencia could, and would, act to disrupt its activities whenever and wherever possible.
strings.IBR_terror.12.t: Successful Large AAS Raid on DI
strings.IBR_terror.12.d:
Across from the innocent looking shopfront, up high on the roof of a secured apartment block lay a sniper, his scope resting on the entrance of a closed store. In the darkness of the chilly night, he could make out his comrades making their way silently to the entrance. Shadows, like monsters imagined in a child's bedroom, yet he couldn't be more glad to see them.

The radio buzzed next to him, quietly but audibly. “Overlook, this is Hammer. Can you see anything from there, over?”

The sniper passed his scope across the storefront and windows above. The lights were off, the only lights seeming to be some candles besides the front facing windows. A silhouette could be made out, a man sitting on a seat in the dim light. From his posture, he looked asleep. Must have been their lookout. He verified there was no one else visible.

“Hammer, one guy above you, left window. Seems he's taking a snooze. Other rooms seem clear as far as is visible at this angle, over.
