strings.IBR_terror.408.a: Surely I won't be next, right?
strings.IBR_terror.409.d:
Sergeant Ramos tightened his grip on the delinquent's wrist, panting in the humid air of Lisbon's Alfama district. “I'll hold him,” he ordered Corporal Mendes, passing a pair of cuffs to him. “You just slip these on him.”

Before Mendes could secure the cuffs, two pops came from the building behind them. “Shit,” Ramos muttered. “Must've snuck in while we were busy arresting this bitch. Stay here, Mendes, and guard the perimeter. I'll go and investigate.”

Ramos sprinted through the now-open gates of the Arquivo Municipal de Alfama. Inside, a clerk lay on the floor, groaning for help. Before Ramos could reassure her, another two shots rang out down the hall, followed by screams. Ramos turned the corner to fire at two insurgents shouting orders at the workers.

Room by room, hall by hall, Ramos cleared the archive of its intruders. Some rooms were too late. Lifeless bodies of those who refused to comply stained the floor.

At the last offices, he could only smell the nauseating smell of gasoline. An insurgent stood around stacks of papers, books, and records doused in the liquid, holding a match above it all. Before Ramos could fire, the insurgent dropped his match, devouring the room in flames.

Ramos herded any survivors to the exit, helping those too injured to walk, including the injured insurgents who had fired on him. The fire raged unchecked throughout the building until firefighters arrived on the scene. But when the smoke cleared, most of the building was reduced to rubble, leaving only the smell of evaporated blood and ash.
strings.IBR_terror.409.a: And the months spent replacing the documents would be months not fighting off the terrorists.
strings.IBR_terror.500.d: which terrorist group is getting uppity
strings.IBR_caudillo.1.d:
“... and you know it's not true! If ever we've managed to accomplish anything together, it is not because there was some danger we were trying to ward ourselves from, but because all we did was meant to be. What we have achieved is a testament to our people's genius, not to their fear! And, yes, there ought to be some... modifications to the way things work, but that does not mean we should contemplate our work and discard it because the machine gets stuck sometimes, on the contrary! It isn't easy, I know, and there is a lot more to come in the future, but frankly, António,” and at this he turned from the window to his interlocutor, amending his voice just a tone, “you cannot possibly believe what you said. The Union is not a failure, nor has it a foot in the grave already. Not while I, and you, still breathe.”

“Are you quite finished?” Salazar asked quietly, and Franco tugged at the collar of his uniform, silence slowly falling in the small office. He made to the desk from the window, staring disbelievingly at the man seated in the armchair.

They, Franco realized with incredulity, were quite apart, when it came to their own existences: he had ranted for almost ten minutes, all the while Salazar had remained silent. Sometimes, he was brushing off a loose speck of dust from his suit, while Franco dared not imagine his uniform could have been anything other than pristine.

He had allowed himself to be carried away by the passion of his monologue, staring out through the window, while Salazar never took his eyes away from him, his gaze inflexibly scrutinizing while he listened. Yes, Franco thought, we are indeed quite apart when it comes to our merely being.

“You let yourself get carried away once more, Francisco,” Salazar said in a half-reproachful, half-patronizing tone, but his weak smile could never have carried acrimony. “If we could get back to the point, I would like to hear your thoughts about this proposed reform concerning the colonial administration.”
strings.IBR_cauinfo_introduction_tt:
The Two Caudillos of Iberia dance together yet apart, with the Union's fate in their hands.

Who the spotlight shines on at key moments will affect the fate of the entire Iberian Peninsula.

The Balance of Power may be observed and influenced from The National Duet.
strings.IBR_caudillo.2.d:
Though a charismatic man in public, in private António de Oliveira Salazar had always been an introverted and at times reclusive man. He never married and had no children. When he was not meeting with Franco or other politicians, he was usually alone in his residence, what prior to the Iberian unification was the Portuguese Embassy in Madrid. His maid Maria de Jesus, a woman too enamored with Salazar to leave his side despite knowing the Caudillo did not feel the same way about her as she did him, was his only close friend. While Salazar read a book in his study, Maria spotted up the bathroom in anticipation of guests.

This was a special occasion for the Caudillo. His older sister, Maria do Resgate Salazar de Oliveira, was visiting today, for the first time in four years. Salazar liked few people and trusted even fewer, but he never doubted his sisters. The Caudillo answered the door, greeting his sister and her three daughters with warm embraces. Gosh, they had grown old. To think, his sister was now a frail old woman of 80. His nieces had grey hair, and much more prominent wrinkles than the last time they met. What lovely years they had spent together.

As they sat together in the living room, and a pause appeared in the conversation, one of his niece's eyes lit up. “António, I don't think I remembered to tell you.”

“Yes?”

“Antónia is pregnant! And I think you're going to be a great granduncle.”
strings.IBR_caudillo.2.a: Oh, how the time goes by.
strings.IBR_caudillo.3.d:
“So you mean to tell me you're occupied sixteen hours a day, every day of the week?” asked Salazar, his voice soaked in disbelief.

“No...” started Franco, only to be cut off mid-sentence by his compatriot.

“Then why can't you? You can drag my ass through half the legislation on this planet, but you would not humor me with a game of chess?”

“I do not want to play chess, Salazar. I have better things to do with my time.”

“Like what? Gathering dust? Really, just one game.”

“Will you shut up about it?” asked Franco. It had been two days of this charade.

“If you oblige me just once, then I will.”

Franco sighed.
strings.IBR_caudillo.4.d:
The two Caudillos had prepared their board. Salazar, given the choice, opted for black. Franco was playing white. Salazar was quite capable at chess - though he only bragged “a little” about it - and Franco had just enough experience to not need an explanation on the basic functions of the game. With everything prepared, the Caudillos began their game. The quiet of the office they had prepared, besides the ticking of a plain clock, provided effective for facilitating the contemplation of moves.

Franco moved his first piece, f3. “Chess is lacking without ample conversation, if this is anything to go by.”

e5. “You would be correct,” began Salazar. “If you cannot reminisce the game loses some of its appeal.”

g4. “For a 'New Order', it doesn't seem all that orderly. Do you think the Germans ever put that much thought into what came after the war?”

Qh4. “No, no I do not. Anyway, this is checkmate.”

Franco looked at the board again. No matter where he looked, Salazar was right - there was nowhere to move. “You'll need to practice if you want to best me.”
strings.IBR_caudillo.4.a: “If only I could veto your moves, António...”
strings.IBR_caudillo.5.d:
“Have you practiced at all?” asked Salazar, surveying the virgin chessboard from the black side of the board.

D4-d6. “It's hard to find an appropriate opponent. Besides, I have been slightly busy dealing with the terrorists destroying this country.” F4-d5.

Salazar beheld the board. Then, he looked upwards towards Franco - Salazar was not quite looking at him, but rather he seemed to be looking in the general direction. Qd3-c5. “To think, if one little thing had gone differently, I might have been playing chess with another man.” Qb5+-Nd7.

Franco was silent for a moment. As that moment lengthened into several seconds, it became clear he was trying to figure out what that 'little thing' was. Finally, he moved a piece as he finally found what memory it was. Dxc5-e6. “Ahh, Sanjurjo? Maybe it was for the best. Not that I despised him, but the old lion was... quite foolish.” Nc3-a6. Qxd7-Kxd7. “What about you? Do you often give thought to how you got here?”

“Sometimes, I suppose. Portugal has been my life, and who doesn't think about their life every once in a while?” cxb7-kxb7. Nxd5-Qxd5. “And the war, too. You hardly take risks like that anymore.”

“What kind of question is that? Of course it was. There was not much risk to it, either. Germany was winning, and then they did.” Nf3-Bb4+. c3-Bc5. c4-Qxc4. b3-Qc3+.

Salazar's expression had changed. He seemed pleased, confident. Franco was locked in a contemplative gaze, listening to the Caudillo and looking at the chessboard in equal focus. Bd2-Qxa1. “You still ought to practice at this,” started Salazar, “You're not quite there yet.” Bc1-Qxc1#.
strings.IBR_caudillo.5.a: It certainly lasted longer than the last time.
strings.IBR_caudillo.6.d:
For all their past games, Franco had always been the earlier of the Caudillos. He was always present when Salazar arrived, though setting up the board was a collaborative effort. Today was different. Now, when Salazar walked in, he found a chess board set up, and there, sitting next to it, was Franco. Waiting.

“You usually wait for me to arrive before we set up the board. Is this the game?” D4-d5

Nc3-nf6. “It remains to be seen...”

F3-e6. Bf4-bb4. A3-ba5. “Do you believe the Germans regret cutting Portugal in half?” E4-O-O. Exd5-exd5.

“You know they don't care, Salazar. They took it, and they'll cast it to the wind when it's convenient.” Bb5-bf5. B4-nh5. Bxa5-nxf4. Nge2-nxe2. Kxe2-re8+.

“What drives you to keep this Union going? The threat of the Germans is not as imminent as it used to be.” Kf2-re6. Re1-rg6. Re8+-qxe8. Nxd5-qxe2+.

“It has been too long. The nations have been together for so long, it would hurt the peninsula more to separate again.” In his old age, Salazar made a small lapse in judgement. Now, for his time, the game had been shortened considerably. Qxe2-be4. Qxe4-f5. Qe8#.

Salazar was dumbfounded. It took him another moment to realize what he had done just a few moves ago. He made no remarks, and went on with his day after the fact, without a comment to Franco.
strings.IBR_caudillo.6.a: Is this the start of a trend?
strings.IBR_caudillo.7.d:
As time progressed, it became clear that Franco would never find out if his improved results were the sign of a trend. Caudillo Salazar's untimely - and unfortunate - death had prevented the Caudillos from having another match. The Spaniard had arguably won his first victory by fluke, and now he would never have the chance at a hard-won triumph.

Even though there were plenty of other things to remember Salazar by, the chessboard they played on held a special appeal; it was a hobby, limited as it was. It was far better to remember the old man for their games of chess, rather than by their many arguments over Iberian policy.

Franco took some time to make one last examination of the chess board. It was a plain, uninteresting design - white-and-black pieces on a white-and-black board; he had set it up at the Portuguese Caudillo's preferred table one final time. He decided to never use the board again, so that the memories it provided would remain untainted.
strings.IBR_caudillo.7.a: The pieces stand there in his memory.
strings.IBR_caudillo.100.d: Morocco, a place of great significance to the proud Spanish Generalissimo, the place where he began his arduous journey to rescue his beloved nation from the grips of communism. Yet, now the land he once had known like the back of his hand, where he had once conducted extensive military exercises with his hardened veterans, has greatly changed. It had been over 20 years since his reconquista of Spain, enough time for the German instability and the new Iberian wedding to leave its toll. Franco considered that a proud showing in Morocco may prove his legitimacy and rein in any unruly colonial officials, but he had also always been a man of simple action, not a bombastic dictator like those two men who had helped him cross the narrow sea. Should he perhaps arrive quietly and get straight to business?
strings.IBR_caudillo.101.d: Franco's arrival in the North African colony has reinvigorated local Moroccan elites into pushing for further autonomy while maintaining Iberian suzerainty. The argument for this is simple: having a puppet state will allow the Iberians to better galvanize resources from the area, whether that be manpower, labor or natural resource extraction. Yet giving any form of concession to the Africans may be met with ridicule from European neighbours. Italy in particular could see this as a sign of weakness and could then push for a strengthened presence in the Mediterranean. However, the flustered Spanish strongman has to make a decision now, the men before him waiting eagerly for a response. Prestige or a decline in efficiency?
strings.IBR_caudillo.101.a: North Africans should have more autonomy.
strings.IBR_caudillo.102.d: The Iberian settlers in Morocco have met with Franco today in Ceuta, and after Franco delivered a heartwarming and praiseworthy speech, the settlers unceremoniously bombarded our great Caudillo with their grievances and troubles. Over the course of several hours, it became clear that the settlers were agitating for more subsidies from the Iberian government to lessen the burden on them. They agonised, in painstaking detail, the hardships the face in trying to settle the arid deserts of Morocco, from worthless and parched soil in the hinterlands to lack of any honest work in the cities. While it will place further strain on the Iberian economy, it may be advisable to promise them more financial support, even if it is just to keep them quiet and loyal. Either that, or some token and inconsequential gestures to appease them for the remainder of Franco's visit are in order.
strings.IBR_caudillo.103.d: The old man's face reflected not just the weakening capacity of his tired and overworked body but also his inner fears. As he stared deeply into the mirror, looking for small imperfections just like with his paperwork, he began to brush away a small crease that he must have forgotten to iron out of the military uniform he was wearing. The uniform of the Iberian army. How could he defeat his greatest fear, militarism as personified by his Spanish counterpart, if not by at least trying to shape into something less threatening if not possibly useful? However it spoke against his entire nature and persona he had so carefully crafted over the years. After all was he not the moderate to Franco's delusional grandeur? The question now is should he try to become more of an iron fisted dictator, at least for show, or stick with his usual statesman appearance?
strings.IBR_caudillo.104.d: The grand entrance of Salazar's new persona was about to begin. An important meeting with several key generals of the Iberian armed forces concerning new doctrines and logistics was the perfect place to practice asserting the characteristics of the man he had emulated. As the grand oak doors were opened to the stiff yet resolute Portuguese Caudillo all heads turned to inspect the new entrant. The accompanying soft murmur began to eat at the now very uncomfortable aging statesman as he began to make his way slowly to his seat. A quick scrutiny of the bitter looking faces of the men he was about to address told Salazar all he needed to know about how his gambit had transpired. None would speak out against him openly but his image had now been tarnished considerably.
strings.IBR_caudillo.105.d: If there was one thing Salazar could always fall back upon it was his eloquence and strength at public speaking. For all his animosity towards Adolf Hitler he still admired his ability to mesmerize and work an audience. The seasoned Caudillo walked slowly towards the podium, all eyes in the room again on him, with the only sound heard coming courtesy of the din of the living city outside the steadfast walls of the palace. As he stepped up to the wooden rostrum he looked down briefly at the collection of notes he held in his hands. He was surprised to see them shake slightly. Age was beginning to get the worse of him. He quickly recovered again, placing both arms first across his chest while surveying the assembled men and then onto the podium itself. He had gained their fixation, and it was time to begin.
strings.IBR_caudillo.105.a: Begin with a promise of further resources.
strings.IBR_caudillo.106.t: On the Issue of Minority Groups
strings.IBR_caudillo.106.d: The next topic was an uncomfortable one for him to address considering the room he was in. No matter how this would be played he would likely lose. He sighed to himself briefly, then began his tirade against the terrible terrorism that has swept the Union. How these so called freedom fighters dared to undermine the much needed stability of the Iberia, not caring in the slightest about the consequences on real people living their ordinary lives. Clearly these dastardly scum had to be expunged from the nation like the parasites they were. Yet how was this to be done effectively when most of them came from minority groups which currently still enjoyed the protection of the Union? The question of how to approach the next part of his speech was not an easy one for the old man. Should he push for a harsher policy towards minorities in order to safeguard national security, or take a more moderate approach, in the process likely losing a hefty amount of political power to his more hardline Spanish counterpart?
strings.IBR_caudillo.106.a: They are terrorist sympathizers. A hard line is needed.
strings.IBR_caudillo.106.b: The terrorists do not represent these people.
strings.IBR_caudillo.107.t: Transcripts from High Command Meeting Leak
strings.IBR_caudillo.107.d: Caudillo Salazar had to experience the repurcussions of the largest political flounder he had ever commited following his address on the importance of minority groups in regards to quelling terrorism. Seemingly someone in the high command had committed absolute treachery by leaking his radical views on how to tackle the issue to the public. The poor display had managed to make its way around the country at a terrifying pace despite the best efforts of state censors. Considering the vast majority of the Iberia supported a tough stance on national security due to recent developments in global political affairs he possibly could still spin this to reduce damage to some extent. Yet the views of those minority groups he had talked so poorly of could now not be changed anymore, he had betrayed them for which his political career would bleed heavily.
strings.IBR_caudillo.107.a: A blow to Salazar's popularity among minorities.
strings.IBR_caudillo.108.d: It was a crisp, clear morning in the Portuguese municipality of Ourém. The white marble running all around the Sanctuary of Fatima reflected the morning sun's brilliance, bathing the plaza in warmth and light. As usual, Salazar's modest motorcade arrived early, and the Caudillo of Portugal found himself with time to burn before his appointment with the Portuguese bishops. Waving off his bodyguards to permit them a cigarette break, Salazar squinted up at the gold-plated cross atop the spire of the central cathedral as he pondered how to go about his discussion with the bishops. It had been some time since he had dealt with the clergy directly, despite their major role in the Estado Novo. Would they be simple, honest men like the ordinary priests he had known growing up, or illustrious and regal figures representative of the Church's wealth and power? What approach would best speak to them, and win them over?
strings.IBR_caudillo.108.a: Salazar talks about how he once considered becoming a priest.
strings.IBR_caudillo.109.d: If Salazar was hoping to find some kind of personal connection in his story of how he ultimately DIDN'T become a priest, he was sorely mistaken. Clearly the bishops had no interest in hearing excerpts from his biography when there were serious matters to take care of. Gritting his teeth and kicking himself mentally by the end of the meeting, Salazar was several shades redder and looked a few years older as he marched back to the limousine afterwards, having gotten nothing out of the discussion besides an embarrassing anecdote about himself.
strings.IBR_caudillo.109.a: Perhaps they were expecting a more substantive conversation.
strings.IBR_caudillo.110.d:
“I had no idea, Senhor Salazar.” Bishop Anselmo had said, clearly impressed. “To be so personally invested in the Church at such a young age was rare even amongst my own generation. Though you were surely called by God to your vocation, I feel the Church is diminished simply by its inability to count you amongst its servants.” If that wasn't the sound of successfully charming his way into the confidence of some of the most influential men in Iberia, Salazar didn't know what was. Despite his age, the chauffeur noticed a confident energy in the Caudillo as he took his seat in the back of the limousine and opened up some light reading.

The bishops, too, parted ways with Salazar feeling decidedly more relaxed about dealing with the Caudillos in future. Franco had been so... coarse, despite his faith and good intentions. Their own quiet, charismatic countryman was far more agreeable and clearly a reliable brother in Christ. A cordial smile, it seemed, answered far more of their questions than a stack of government pamphlets.
strings.IBR_caudillo.110.a: Salazar has clearly gained trust from the Church.
strings.IBR_caudillo.111.t: Attempt to Bring Up Issues Fails
strings.IBR_caudillo.111.d:
Even Salazar felt himself sweating a little under the collar as the bishops stared at him, stone-faced and dull-eyed. He couldn't tell whether they were annoyed or just plain bored. Whatever the answer, there was little in the way of mutual exchange, with the increasingly weary Caudillo mostly just talking “at” them rather than “with” them. The longest response to any of his statements had been “Yes, Senhor Salazar.”

After the meeting, as he stood out in the hot sun dabbing at his creased forehead, Salazar found himself grousing out loud to his bodyguards about how obtuse and unhelpful he found these meetings with the clergy. “I'd never get stonewalled by old Father Pedro!” he exclaimed.
strings.IBR_caudillo.111.a: Perhaps they think some bounds have been overstepped.
strings.IBR_caudillo.112.t: Bishops Agree With Several of Salazar's Opinions
strings.IBR_caudillo.112.d:
“Which is, of course, why regional particularism is such an issue for us. Regardless of how the people feel about their own nations, we cannot risk a breakdown of the state, as happened to Spain during their civil war.”

“Of course, Senhor Salazar,” replied Bishop Manuel. He turned to his colleagues. “We are in agreement then, brothers? No support for our regionalist friends?” He was met by a round of nodding.

Salazar smiled broadly, his shoulders finally relaxing. “Then I believe that's everything for today, your eminences. If you'll excuse me, I am due to return to Madrid within the next few hours and must keep to schedule. My secretary here will answer any further questions you may have,” he said, gesturing to the cheery-looking, dapper young man beside him. “Until next time, my friends.”

Score one for statecraft. Get the right words out there, and men of the cloth are as pliable and easy to understand as any man in the street. Salazar could report back to Franco that their mutual understanding with the clergy remained as healthy as ever, and they would not have to worry about opposition from them anytime soon. Some consolation in a time of troubles, at least.
strings.IBR_caudillo.113.d:
In order to better address the economic situation in Iberia, the Caudillos have opted to host a discussion for business leaders in order to encourage cooperation with the government. Because of his talent for speech, and the predominantly Spanish makeup of the business leaders, Franco was the obvious choice for the job. Hosted at the Westin Palace hotel in Madrid, the function was primarily for business leaders, and brought to their attention specifically. Even though they are the main target, it is not yet too late to hold the speech in a public area.

There are two locations that are most easily secured for a summit, the main stage of Westin Palace or in a private undisclosed location. Hosting the speech somewhere more private will be an easier job to secure, as well as allowing for only the businessmen to be present. That way, they can be better catered to. The only threat there is of leaks. Alternatively, the speech could be made public, for a larger crowd. This will eliminate any risk of someone compromising secure conversations, and will prevent any unpleasant accusations about the loyalty of the Caudillo. It will cost more to secure the public location, and the speech will have to be broad in tone. Otherwise, some groups could be lost by catering to others. The obvious choice is to...
strings.IBR_caudillo.113.a: Hold a speech on the main stage.
strings.IBR_caudillo.113.b: Hold a speech behind closed doors.
strings.IBR_caudillo.114.t: Choosing a Posture for the Speech
strings.IBR_caudillo.114.d:
A location has been selected, announced, and set in stone. Franco would be speaking to a large audience, and marketing his ideas to the public, and not just businessmen. This is no time to forget who this is dedicated to, however- just because the speech is more public doesn't mean it isn't for businessmen first and foremost. To this end a new strategy must be devised. No speech is complete without posturing, and can be ruined with the improper application of it. It needs to be decided how the Caudillo will present his ideas to his audience, as to best ensure retention among the businessmen.

The first, and most obvious, tone is to take that of someone in favor of a free market. It is sure to win over many business owners, as the promise of an environment suited to them is one tantalizing enough that they are sure to be lured in. While this may anger some elements of the government, these can be mostly mitigated by taking a more conservative position on businesses. Alternatively, it has been proposed to take a tough stance on corporations, asserting authority over them. If there is anything they will respect, it is a leader that is willing to take executive authority. What form will the Caudillo's tone take?
strings.IBR_caudillo.114.b: A business friendly, but conservative posture.
strings.IBR_caudillo.115.d:
More easily guarded, a private setting was the obvious choice to hold a speech at. Only the higher echelons of businessmen will be actively attending, amounting to a small group. This will make the situation much less formal, allowing for a few targeted incentives to be made. With the public not watching, making assurances becomes far easier, and much less risky.

Only, it is a conscious choice to make these assurances. If one were to promise to the business leaders that the Iberian economy would get just a touch more free, it could go a long way towards getting their attention. These reforms will nearly ensure their support, if the trouble is taken to address them. However, making what is essentially a bribe for political capital is frowned upon. If it were to be found publically, then it would create new issues. Therefore, the speech could be made vague and simply assuring the targets prosperity and growth. This will not make any particular friends, but on the other hand it would mean the speech would be mostly bulletproof politically. Is the risk worth the potential gain?
strings.IBR_caudillo.116.d:
The speech had concluded exceptionally well. It was positively received, the oral delivery was spot-on, and the audience seemed convinced. The summit itself seemed to be winding down, and as it prepared to end and everyone to go home, something of interest occurred. A group of highly influential businessmen, introducing themselves by rank, have shuffled their way into Franco's notice. Introducing it by scraps and pieces, they construct an offer for the Caudillo.

Corporate profits are fair, but they are not as fair as they could be. The Iberian government has the means to fix this error, and they may do so very easily. All it would take is recognition of the superiority of the companies in question. Since they are more powerful than the rest, then they ought to be better appreciated for what they do to the country. As it would happen, some of the resources Iberia would save by helping them could be used as reciprocation. It is an easy decision, they say. All that support, for just a little bit of favor...
strings.IBR_caudillo.117.d:
Apparently, the deal was not as private as expected. Someone present at the meeting between the Caudillo and the council of businessmen took a recording, and has only leaked it a few days later. Anonymously shared, it is hard to tell if the guilty party was a traitorous guard or a man hiding a recorder in his suitcase. Who did it matters little now, as they cannot be readily found.

When it was leaked, it was especially directed towards the press. Being the predatory vultures they are, they took the bait and published it sky-high. Now the information cannot be stopped, so the whole country is scrutinizing Franco for his seeming corruption. Most crucially are the intelligentsia, who feel betrayed that a leader would resort to such hypocritical means for little of actual value. The bureaucrats feel the same way as well, drifting more towards Salazar - who is seen as a far more upstanding example of a politician.
strings.IBR_caudillo.117.a: A blow to Franco's image among several key groups.
strings.IBR_caudillo.118.d:
António de Oliveira Salazar has recently finished writing his first book after over thirty years of political experience, first at the head of the Estado Novo regime, and now as one of the Caudillos of Iberia. During this time he has surmounted many challenges, both political and personal in nature, and he has drawn on this wealth of experience in creating this masterpiece of Iberian literature. Painstakingly dictated to his secretary over the course of several months, the first draft is ready to be composed. Salazar however has yet to decide what to keep and what to cut from this unwieldy transcript, ever so diligently copied out and perfected by his assistants.

Two directions to take the book in have been suggested to him by his close associates, that of a manifesto of his own political beliefs, or an autobiography of his personal struggles during his life. Salazar himself has expressed that a political statement to guide the Iberian people would be an apt legacy for him to leave behind, but the idea of an inspiring personal epic appeals to him greatly as well. With the Caudillo remaining indecisive, and papers continuing to pile up on his desk, it may be pragmatic to convince him to make a final decision. What should it be?
strings.IBR_caudillo.118.a: A manifesto of Salazar's political philosophy.
strings.IBR_caudillo.118.b: An autobiography detailing Salazar's personal struggles.
strings.IBR_caudillo.119.d:
With the genre of the Caudillo's new book having been decided upon, Salazar's secretary and his assistants have religiously prepared suitable extracts from the initial transcript over the course of a few weeks, every extract having been chosen for its particularly inspiring and powerful advice, vivid descriptions of Salazar's experiences or Salazar's enlightened political philosophy. Salazar has so far been delighted with the choices presented to him by his assistants, but has yet to decide on specifically what he wants in the book, whether it is to be a personal and heartfelt book, aimed at imparting Salazar's enthusiasm and advice to the reader in order to rouse the Iberian people to greater things, or to be a ceremonious and authoritative text containing Salazar's prescriptions for society, aimed at safeguarding the Iberian state, guiding the politicans of tomorrow and preserving the legacy he has painstakingly worked to build during his time in office.

Either way, the Caudillo doesn't seem to be rushing to make a decision, and the book has taken up enough official time as is. Salazar should be encouraged to choose the passages he wants to include in his masterpiece post-haste, as not only do state papers lie on Salazar's desk unread, and urgent bureaucratic work left untouched, but the second Caudillo Francisco Franco himself is becoming concerned with Salazar's apparent idleness. A decision must be made.
strings.IBR_caudillo.119.a: Inspirational and powerful advice to the reader.
strings.IBR_caudillo.120.d:
Now that the Caudillo has decided on the specific contents of his book, he has one final decision to make before this paragon of Iberian literature can be sent to the printing presses. A conclusion has yet to be written, and Salazar is torn between concluding that it will be the educated elite that will guide Iberia towards a bright and proud future, or that it will be the common Iberian toiling away that will bring about a golden age for the Iberian people.

While favouring the intelligentsia would most likely cement Salazar's book as his magnum opus and possibly increase the loyalty of the intellectuals to the Caudillo, concluding that the common people will determine the future of Iberia could help to foster wider support for the regime, as well as cynically generating a larger profit for the publisher and himself to pocket. Salazar however is more concerned with its popular reception than what a few jumped up toffs think, and while it will be a difficult and lengthy series of arguments needed to convince him of the political benefits of dedicating it to Iberian intellectuals, it may be expedient to make him see this point of view. Alternatively, letting Salazar have his way is surely the quicker route to publication, and more importantly, back to work for Salazar. What should he be convinced to conclude the book with?
strings.IBR_caudillo.120.a: A declaration that the educated will guide Iberia towards a great future.
strings.IBR_caudillo.120.b: A declaration that the common Iberian will lead the way towards a great future.
strings.IBR_caudillo.121.d:
Salazar's political manifesto has been met with great acclaim within the intellectual community since being published, as the wise ruler expected it would be. His work received not only favourable reviews from Iberian literary groups and authors, but also internationally his book has also been received well, especially in neighbouring Italy, and to a lesser extent in America, with most copies having been bought by a minority of NPP members. The only frankly minor criticism voiced by the intellectuals is that it might be a little too high brow for the masses, but that doesn't seem to bother Salazar, who appears to be content with the other praise he has received.

Universally, his theories and guidance have been praised as comprehensive and well thought out, with the rhetoric and ideological dogma usually found in political literature to be mostly absent. Iberian scholars agree that it has a clear vision for society under Salazarian ideals, and some have even written to the Caudillo to express their support for the society envisaged in his book, an occurrence that greatly pleased him. There has yet to be a particularly critical or scathing review of Salazar's work, most likely because the ideas and content are simply indisputable of course, not that there are any other reasons for no one speaking up. Overall, Salazar is incredibly pleased with himself and the book he has worked tirelessly to create, and now he can finally focus on official work once more.
strings.IBR_caudillo.121.a: Recognition from the Iberian intelligentsia is highly appreciated.
strings.IBR_caudillo.122.d:
Much to the dismay of Salazar, his book has been a complete flop both domestically and internationally! No intellectual of significance anywhere, let alone in Iberia has commented positively of his work, with it most commonly being described as “confused, unfocused literary mess” by the Iberian intelligentsia. Not only have intellectuals described the book as a muddled and tangled web of political ideas and personal experiences, but they have also said the ideas included are vague and difficult to digest and the experiences are particularly tedious affairs, and at some points painfully boring to read through according to one particularly scathing reviewer. The common Iberian has also found the book hard to engage, citing many similar criticisms that the intellectuals have expressed, though quite often in much coarser words. Francisco Franco of course has endorsed his fellow ruler's work, though it seems more out of professional courtesy than for its own merit.

Poor sales and a bad reception make it unlikely for the publisher to agree to a second production run of the book, and Salazar is reportedly distraught to see the sale price of his work in shop windows be struck down lower and lower as the proprietors try to make at least some return on their purchased stock. For now it seems, Salazar's career as an author has come to an abrupt end, and the Caudillo has been left greatly disheartened and bitter by the whole affair.
strings.IBR_caudillo.122.a: Perhaps it could have done with a clearer message.
strings.IBR_caudillo.123.t: Salazar's Autobiography Takes Iberia by Storm
strings.IBR_caudillo.123.d:
Only a week after being officially published, Salazar's new book has sold out. Demand for his inspirational personal epic has far outstripped supply, and a second production run is already being organised to cover the shortfall in copies. Reportedly, the personal perspective of the book and its inspiring life advice has found a receptive audience within the lower and middle class, and a newfound respect and sympathy for the premier has been fostered.

Not only has the Caudillo's office been inundated with letters of praise from across Iberia, a whole series of spontaneous patriotic celebrations have broken out in Portugal. Street parties complete with overhead banners and fireworks have clogged Lisbon's streets for several days now, having quickly assembled after the last copy sold out in the city. The same phenomenon was repeated across several of the larger towns, and while some have suggested that this was not entirely natural, Salazar has dismissed these hearsay accusations and is content to bask in the popular acclaim being afforded to him.

Fellow Caudillo Franco also has apologized in private to Salazar over his misgivings about his publication, after acknowledging the increase in popular support for Salazar. The success of his work has far surpassed Salazar's own private expectations, and what he initially self-proclaimed as a masterpiece is now undoubtedly regarded as a cornerstone of Iberian literature by popular decree.
strings.IBR_caudillo.123.a: The best books... are those that tell you what you know already.
strings.IBR_caudillo.124.d:
In a drive to stabilize Iberian internal divisions, and sow that the current administration is not politically inert, it has been announced that Caudillo Franco will tour various government ministries in order to gain an insight into their workings and current conditions. Some have already labelled this as a pointless and insulting PR move; something to put in the daily tabloids to distract from other more pressing news. Official statements, however, hail the proposed events as a turning point in Iberia's current political and economic fortunes, dismissing the criticism as pointless fearmongering.

The elderly dictator's first visit would be to the education ministry. In the run up to the day lobbyists have been arguing for more funding to increase Iberian standards of education both in order to help the national economy while providing better employment opportunities and to help the Union better compete on the global stage. Whether Franco will heed their advice, make only slight reforms in order to balance the national budget or just ignore them entirely will be seen on the day.
strings.IBR_caudillo.124.b: Promise to improve the situation somewhat.
strings.IBR_caudillo.125.d:
Franco's grandly advertised tour of the nations various government continues as he is preparing to meet the Minister of Agriculture and other top civil servants. Land reform and the future of farming are always hot topics during election cycles, especially in more rural Iberian settings, which resulted in the upcoming meeting tripling newspaper and analysis sales.

Amongst the concerns that the Spanish Caudillo may not be entirely suited to discussing such matters of state, were some more particularly scathing attacks published by left wing organizations who see the strong man as a growing tumour wasting away Iberia's societal and economic wealth. The decisions made at the meeting however could signal a new direction for rural prosperity which had long been lagging behind urban development. It is not clear yet what will be decided.
strings.IBR_caudillo.125.b: Promise to improve the situation somewhat.
strings.IBR_caudillo.126.d:
Franco's grandly advertised tour of the nations various ministries continues as he is preparing to meet the Minister of Development and other relevant state secretaries attached to this department. Road expansion and public works in general are always a good way of improving the national economy and provide jobs for the people, but their downside is, as the name implies, that they need state money to actually happen.

However, due to the promises made to the previous ministries, it seems like the Caudillo will only have bad news for the minister, as there is now not only not enough money for the Development Ministry, but that some cuts will have to be made if the minister hopes to keep the department running. The meeting looks like it will be a very short one, with Franco delivering the bad news and getting out as soon as possible.
strings.IBR_caudillo.126.a: There may have to be some cuts.
strings.IBR_caudillo.127.d:
Franco's grandly advertised tour of the nations various ministries continues as he is preparing to meet the Minister of Development and other relevant state secretaries attached to this department. Road expansion and public works in general are always a good way of improving the national economy and provide jobs for the people but they can sometimes create bad conditions for the workers, which the leftist underground organizations use to attract people to their cause.

Due to the promises made to the previous ministries, the only thing Franco can offer the minister is a small improvement of the workers' conditions. But even that could mean going over the budget, so another possibility, and the one that scares the minister the most; is Franco going to the meeting just to inform that no changes will be made to the department to save money.
strings.IBR_caudillo.127.a: Promise to improve the situation somewhat.
strings.IBR_caudillo.128.d:
Franco's grandly advertised tour of the nations various ministries continues as he is preparing to meet the Minister of Development and other relevant state secretaries attached to this department. Road expansion and public works in general are always a good way of improving the national economy and provide jobs for the people but they can sometimes create bad conditions for the workers, which the leftist underground organizations use to attract people to their cause

Even after the promises made to the other ministries, Franco is sure that he can grant the Ministry of Development some of its demands such as more money for it or an improvement of workers' conditions. Just before entering the meeting, advisors have warned the Caudillo that not all the things the ministry needs can be promised, so it's up to Franco to decide what he will say to the minister.
strings.IBR_caudillo.200.d:
El Palacio del Pardo, the Madrid residence of Francisco Franco. It stood, large and imposing, before Marcelo Caetano; its walls shining cream in the afternoon sun. He sighed - despite his summons none greeted him until he was at the door. Silently, he was led upstairs by a member of the house staff, occasional guards glaring as hollow footsteps rang through the corridors. The atmosphere was icy, cold spikes of disdain emanating from all around. When the door to Franco's office came; Caetano was almost pushed through. He stood alone, beholding the Caudillo before him.

He sat painting. The study was split in two, a small sitting area joined to a large study behind it. The Caudillo sat beside a fireplace, lit despite the afternoon's warmth, painting an assortment of rifles hanging from the walls. No greeting was offered; Caetano felt trapped upon the threshold. He cleared his throat and broke the silence. “Why am I here?”

“Señor Caetano, do you have a hobby?” Franco refused to divert his attention from his canvas to acknowledge Caetano's eyebrow raise. “I paint.” He continued for a few moments, before abruptly placing his brush into a water pot. “Unfortunately not all paintings work out - these rifles have the wrong proportions. The colour is faded, the varnished stocks lacking their shine. The barrels have a slight angle... imperfections everywhere I look.”

Caetano remained as stone, watching as his Caudillo colleague stood up from his seat, unsure of what to make of him. Franco continued to spare him no glance as he picked up the painting, in a single motion turning and throwing it onto the waiting fireplace. He turned to Caetano, eyes boring into him for the first time.

“When I make a mistake on a canvas, I discard it. When a man of mine makes a mistake, I discard him.”
strings.IBR_caudillo.200.a: “Get a hobby Marcelo, you would be amazed at the clarity of circumstances it can give you.”
strings.IBR_caudillo.200.tt:
Caetano and A Choupana have failed - utterly.
The {ibr_getflag} Union is now nothing but a name.
strings.IBR_caudillo.201.d:
“...and that is the Estado Novo assessment of the Africa situation, now to divert our attention to the recent economic assessment issued by the -”

“Señor Caetano, perhaps it would be fitting to slow down. We have not yet finished deliberating Africa.” Francisco Franco leaned back in his chair with a weak stretch. Both men sat across each other, a single desk lamp illuminating the room. Shadows stretched across their faces; the late hour heavy in their eyes.

Caetano wearily chuckled, turning his eyes to the darkened ceiling. “Age makes statecraft difficult, isn't that so?” He leaned upon the desk, returning his gaze to Franco's. “If I may, this actually brings me to a point many have raised and I am compelled to agree. Wouldn't you say we should begin considerations for... young blood to take more responsibility?”

Franco scoffed, smiling like a parent to a naive child. “The shouts of careerists. Ignore them, all is tied and tied well.”

A slow nod greeted the dismissal, but it carried no hint of approval. “Caudillo Franco, all long term plans are now under review, by my order.” Franco glared, but Caetano paid it little heed as he continued. “Dead men cannot lead a nation, and we may have an entire generation of statesmen wiped out by age within a handful of years; even at the very top of the Union. Dead men cannot lead.”

Franco stood up abruptly, his face lost in the shadows above the lamplight's reach. “This conversation lacks clarity of point Señor. I will take my leave until the experience of governance has given you anything reasonable to discuss.”
strings.IBR_caudillo.201.a: Franco strode out of the room. Caetano grimaced, and looked into the surrounding darkness.
strings.IBR_caudillo.201.tt: Caetano and A Choupana have achieved immense authority. The {ibr_getflag} Union is held tight in their grip.
strings.IBR_caudillo.202.d:
They stood as monuments, staring at the lonely tomb that marked a life. “The Marcelo Caetano Family” was written above its entrance, simply spaced under the Holy Cross. The man to whom the tomb was in honor stood besides his daughter, Ana Maria, looking at the single name chiseled and highlighted into the cream stone.

Teresa de Barros Caetano.

The vigil lasted anywhere between moments and hours, the sense of loss simple chiseled words brought to them requiring contemplation. “I didn't think you would make it,” whispered Ana Maria, not turning her head to break the reflection, “due to how busy you must be.”

Marcelo was slow to answer; it was a subject requiring constant grappling within his tired mind. How many moments with his family had he missed to do his duty? Sacrifices enforced upon them to meet his ambitions? Precious time with Teresa, lost until they could meet again in the next life. And what for? Was he now busy, truly?

“I have men I can delegate to, I have all the time I need now,” he replied sullenly.

All the time in the world. He was a Caudillo who could delegate nearly everything to others, his Choupana boys like locusts over his policies. But, what policies were his? Were there any anymore? Despite the newspapers and television endlessly affirming him as one of Iberia's leaders he found more and more legislation bearing his name that he had no knowledge of. His allies' fingerprints were everywhere; he had raised them up. Where now was he?

His daughter turned to leave; he kept looking at the lonely name upon the stone, hearing the distant tolling of a single Church bell.
strings.IBR_caudillo.202.a: For António, for Teresa, for me.
strings.IBR_caudillo.202.tt:
A Choupana has achieved immense authority, as Caetano crumbles.
The {ibr_getflag} Union moves forward - without him.
strings.IBR_caudillo.203.d:
The study held a comfortable amber glow, a deliberate choice for these late night sessions. The affairs of government asked for long hours and high attention; the atmosphere appropriate for such efforts was a must in the eyes of Portugal's Caudillo. Caetano's eyes danced across volumes of papers, tonight gifts of the Ministry of Finance. Time seemed absent within the warm study lights, just a Caudillo and his Iberia. The study's clock chimed. Midnight. The tired Caudillo raised his head, weary gaze full of realisation. Meetings started early and yet he still had much more to read. A sigh escaped him, and he raised himself from his seat to the window. His body, accustomed to the position, groaned as he did.

There wasn't much to see, darkness cloaking all. Lonely streetlights and illuminated windows betrayed no one in their light. It was a silent, desolate picture. Nothing moved, a gentle hum in Caetano's ears tricking him that the night held anything within it. A trick of silence, a creation of the mind; he was alone.

Alone. Before he could stop himself, Teresa breached his mind. He closed his eyes, choosing to reminisce rather than force it out. How he missed her. How he missed his daughter, far away on official business but more impersonal by the day. His brother, always on the news speaking but rarely to him. He looked back at the papers lined upon his desk. He even missed allies with which to share his load. He was surrounded by smiles yet had never felt so alone.

Below, a single aged man walked under a streetlamp. Caetano watched, captivated by the motion - the man walked as Salazar had. From a distance they could even be mistaken. In the darkness he was quickly lost to Caetano's sight, but he entered the Caudillo's thoughts as he looked at his reflection in the window. He thought of Salazar, the man who had raised Portugal up and held the Union together.
strings.IBR_caudillo.203.a: Indistinguishable from a hobbling pensioner; his tired eyes had matched the window's reflection.
strings.IBR_caudillo.203.tt:
Caetano has achieved immense authority, as A Choupana crumbles.
He bears the weight of the {ibr_getflag} Union - alone.
strings.IBR_caudillo.204.d:
“Caudillo Caetano, a moment please?”

They had been slowly shuffling out of the Council Chamber when the request had come, the Portuguese Caudillo swiftly turning around allowing the many other Council members to file past him. He'd expected this accosting, indeed he grimaced. He knew exactly what was wrong, when he saw the restrained frustration upon Carrero Blanco's face as he strode toward him.

“Caudillo Caetano, de Sousa and I spoke at length about his healthcare reforms. We have spoken at great lengths about them, planning answers to queries, gauging who would be agreeable, and yet what happens? He sits there all meeting quiet as a mouse, glancing occasionally at you, never mentioning the plan we arranged to raise today. May I ask if indeed you know why?”

“Senhor Blanco,” he began, keeping his voice hushed lest others hear, “had Senhor de Sousa raised that plan today, what would have happened? Franco would have shut it down, I trust you agreed that support would not be unanimous?” Blanco kept his frown, but slowly nodded in affirmation.

“Franco... hates instability. Especially instability offered by sudden reforms thrown upon him by surprise. Only unanimous support or a more gentle introduction stands much chance of earning his approval. The moment anyone had pushed back against you, Franco would have closed the debate and Senhor de Sousa's work would have been for nothing.”

Blanco snorted. “So we just do nothing?”

“Absolutely not. While I can't promise anything, I will speak to Franco myself, in private, regarding the plan. It's what I promised de Sousa and it's what I promise you.” Blanco bristled for a moment, before striding away and leaving.
strings.IBR_caudillo.204.a: In private, Caetano sighed. A co-equal leader, restrained to backroom scheming for basic policy.
strings.IBR_caudillo.204.tt:
Neither Caetano nor A Choupana have cemented their authority.
Portugal's place in the {ibr_getflag} Union died with Salazar.
strings.IBR_caudillo.205.d:
“You wished to see me, Caudillo Caetano?”

The knock had been terse, the door opening before Caetano had even had the chance to respond. De Sousa must have rushed past his secretary. He quickly collected himself, putting the report he was reading away in one of his desk drawers. “Yes, come in, Senhor de Sousa. Take a seat.”The Minister of Healthcare walked briskly to the desk and sat down, sitting straight, across from the Caudillo. Caetano took a breath, steeling himself. “Forgive me, but I am afraid I have bad news. I spoke to Franco regarding your reform plan. Made him aware of you and Blanco's thoughts on the matter. For what it's worth, he commended your efforts, but he didn't lend support. I can't imagine that stance chang-”

“I have requested to meet Caudillo Franco myself, with Senhor Blanco,” de Sousa interrupted, bluntly. Caetano hung in inertial surprise for a moment. “Senhor Blanco has met with him before, and when myself and Franco have spoken he has seemed agreeable. Perhaps one more try will work.”

“Why, that is... a fine idea. It seems we don't need our Caudillo office at all to get things done. You work well. Update me on Franco's reception afterwards.”

De Sousa bowed his head slightly. “Of course, Caudillo Caetano,” he said. The conversation moved to other topics, polite inquiries on de Sousa's Ministry, however Caetano's mind felt uneasy. Indeed, his Choupana boys were working well without him.
strings.IBR_caudillo.205.tt:
A Choupana has cemented their authority, but Caetano falters.
The {ibr_getflag} Union is one of equals, but its diarchy is not.
strings.IBR_caudillo.206.d:
It wasn't until the phone call had reached its third hour that Caetano had finally been able to bring up de Sousa's meeting earlier that day. Focus was quickly leaving his body, and he could tell that Franco was beginning to struggle too, even over the phone. The endless budgets, civil servant assessing, musings on planned successes, fears of budgetary mistakes. The endless policy combing was even making the Spanish Caudillo's masked Galician accent come out.

“Señor de Sousa? Yes, I saw him and Blanco earlier. They are very eager, Caetano. They mentioned our conversation yet they tried again. The same points, again. I didn't much appreciate hearing the same reform plan rephrased two different ways.”

Caetano cradled his head in his free hand as Franco continued. “I do not consider myself hostile to change Caetano, I am sure you know that, however after hearing more about their plan I must say I am even more hesitant towards it. Especially if they lack the ability to moderate themselves appropriately.”

“What do you mean, Caudillo Franco?”

“What I mean is they were told once, by me via you. They decided to come to me directly and accost me with the same things. I am a busy man, I do not like my time being wasted having to repeat myself Caetano. If your colleagues cannot understand that then perhaps the highest halls of Iberia are not a good place for them - we are busy men.”

“I apologise for them, Caudillo Franco, but they were just try-”

Franco scoffed. “Don't apologize to them. You are settling into the role very well and done exactly what you were supposed to. But, you are still new to it. I feel new to it sometimes and I've been here forty years!”
strings.IBR_caudillo.206.a: Franco chuckled. “We have to realise when our men are good, or just loud. Let that guide you.”
strings.IBR_caudillo.206.tt:
Caetano has cemented his authority, but A Choupana falters.
The {ibr_getflag} Union rests upon the Caudillos' shoulders.
strings.IBR_caudillo.207.d:
“If there is no more business, then I will declare this meeting adj-”

Franco's attempt to conclude the cabinet meeting was interrupted by the scraping of chair legs across the chamber floor. Baltazar Rebelo de Sousa had stood up, his chair clattering behind him. “Forgive me Caudillos, honoured colleagues, but I must present something.” Caetano gave a querying look to the minister, but if Baltazar saw it he gave it no mind.

“We all know it's about your healthcare reforms de Sousa, why can't you let it go?” Army Minister Juan Castañón de Mena beheld his colleague with laughing eyes. “The plan is no good, you shopped it around to most of us and most of us said no. If that wasn't the case then you wouldn't have to resort to such... Lisbon theatrics.”

“Senhor, contain yourself.” Finance Minister João Dias Rosas uttered, leaning forward on the table. “There is no need for such derision. Besides, the plan is sound, isn't it owed a public hearing?”

“The numbers don't work, Caudillo Franco himself said so. He-”

“Senhor de Mena, enough.” Caetano spoke firmly, yet refused to raise his voice. He looked around the table - some of the Spaniards looked confused, others... expectant? They looked at de Mena with affirming eyes. In a moment, the extent of the reform's discussions became clear. “By my authority, this is opened for discussion immediately. Openly. Caudillo Franco, do you agree?”

Franco leaned forward, looking at the Army Minister who looked at him with expectant eyes. “When we spoke, Señor de Mena, it was you who assured me the numbers didn't work. Now our Finance Minister says its sound?” He raised an eyebrow.
strings.IBR_caudillo.207.a: “Continue, Caudillo Caetano. You have the Chair.”
strings.IBR_caudillo.207.tt: Caetano and A Choupana have cemented their authority. The {ibr_getflag} Union is held in vigorous hands.
strings.IBR_caudillo.208.d:
Eighty years. It's a date worth celebrating, or so they say. The villa fills up with guests and servants, dignitaries and family members, journalists and celebrities. You shake hands all day. The flashes of the cameras hurt your eyes, but you do not tell them to stop. Word of the day - dignity. The food was excellent, although you do not eat much of it.

The days get longer, and the years get shorter. Friends grow old, and they die. The paved streets of Ferrol smell of gasoline. People no longer wear espadrilles. They tore down the old shanty towns, and replaced them with monoliths of concrete. It was your doing.

You can't bring yourself to look at your signature anymore. It looks so small, crumpled, and weak, so unlike the grand swoops that once characterized it. The ground is tilted, and sometimes jagged. At times, you feel António stand behind you.

You are not afraid. This is fine, this is normal. You are not the first, and you won't be the last. Be it five, seven, or ten years - you are content with what you get, and you do not demand more. Why should you? You won.

Everything is ethereal, but your legacy stands. And it stands. And it stands.
strings.IBR_caudillo.300.d:
It had shaped up to be as calm a day as the exhausted Franco could have ever hoped for. His family and closest supporters sat either side of him, indulging in one of the finest lunches they ever had the pleasure of eating. Such a meal was one of the few occasions the leader could have a break from the repetitive struggles he endured. But the stress had been building up, he had been feeling worse every day that went by. He felt as if something had to give, that his relief could not last.

An abrupt, convulsive pain then seized him, and wrenched the fleeting respite from his troubled mind. He doubled down, coughing uncontrollably, breathlessly imploring someone to help as his body writhed against the ground. Shouts and screams of terror only added to the deathly cacophony.

“Somebody see to him, he is choking, quick!” came a cry from across the table. Several aides heeded the call and rushed to dislodge whatever was caught in their leaders' throat. Yet, try as they may, not one of them could stem the coughing. It soon became clear that it was something far more serious; not that any of those present were willing to admit it. Eventually it all ended; the dreadful whooping faded into a whimper, and the old man rolled backward. He gasped until his lungs were filled with air, and relaxed his arms, bringing his hands away from his face. However, once he could summon the strength to open his eyes the fierce dread flooded back into him. His hands were wet with his own blood. The man could not hold off his fears any longer, he had to get out, he had to get help.

As he exited, he was followed by his advisors, who nervously expected the worse for Franco. Those who did not leave turned to his wife, who sat silent and still. Quietly pulling at the pearls of her necklace, she worried that her husband never would be the same again.
strings.IBR_caudillo.301.d:
The old man lay motionless in his bed. His skin was pale, head adorned with only the few wisps of hair that refused to fall out, clinging on to life only by the tubes through his nose and throat. Carmen braced for the inevitable death of her husband. His daughter, also named Carmen, braced for the inevitable death of her father. A few minutes after midnight, Francisco Franco Bahamonde was taken off life support at the request of his family members.

The general who overthrew the Spanish Republic. The authoritarian reformer. Caudillo of the Iberian Union. Not since Philip the Second's reign three centuries ago has Iberia seen any one man do so much to transform the politics, economy, and society of the Iberian Peninsula. But in his final years, Franco's grip on power rapidly deteriorated. A long time enemy of Democracy, he could not resist the wave of reformism coming from both his advisors and the Iberian public. His three and a half decades of authoritarian rule came to an end, and now, so has he.

To his supporters, he was the man who saved Spain from Bolshevism and Nazism, restored Spain to its Catholic roots, and created the Iberian Union. To those opposed to him, he was the monster responsible for the deaths of hundreds of thousands in the civil war, a man who oppressed women, native peoples, political opponents and regional minorities, to a truly abhorrent extent. A tyrant who kept Iberia in chains.

Regardless of his legacy, today is a momentous day in our young nation's history.
strings.IBR_caudillo.301.a: Spain has lost its savior, Iberia its greatest leader.
strings.IBR_caudillo.301.b: May we finally move past him.
strings.IBR_caudillo.302.d:
Alejandro Rodríguez de Valcárcel spoke to the Iberian people through radio and television.

“Iberians, Franco has died tonight. This exceptional man who before God and History, has took upon himself the responsibility of the hardest and most selfless service to Iberia, following throughout his whole life, day by day, hour by hour his transcendental mission. I know my voice will arrive in your residence being constantly interrupted by my tears and constant sobbing; it is natural to feel this way the tremendous pain his absence brings to us. It is a moment of extreme sadness, but we must not become hopeless, it is true that Franco, our Caudillo for so many years, is not among us but he left us his work, his example and the fulfillment of a historic duty. I was witness of his last day of work, when Death had already taken her toll at his heart and I can guarantee you that this was his last message to the people he loved so much:

Now that the time is near for me to stand in judgment before God Almighty, I ask that He look kindly upon me since I have striven to live and to die as a good Catholic. It has always been my desire to be a faithful son of the church, I ask forgiveness from all, as I give my most heartfelt forgiveness to those who declared themselves my enemies. I believe and hope that had no enemies other than those who were enemies of Iberia. Iberia, which I will love until the last moment and which I promised to serve until my dying breath, which is near. Do not forget that the enemies of Iberia and of Christian civilization are watching, and you should also be watchful and should lay aside all personal gain in favor of the goals and interests of our homeland and of the Iberian people. Continue striving to obtain social justice and education for all Iberians and make use of the rich multiplicity of its regions as a fountain of strength for a continued united Iberia. I would like in these, my last moments, to join the names of God and Iberia, and for us all to embrace one another and to shout for the last time on the threshold of my death - Arriba Ibéria!”
strings.IBR_despotistunion_goodending: Despite our best efforts, it seems the union was not made to last. Due to the Caudillos' strong leadership in the past years, the nations of Iberia may part in peace.
strings.IBR_authunion_goodending: Despite our best efforts, it seems the union was not made to last. Due to the strong leadership of the Caudillos and their loyal council, the nations of Iberia may part in peace.
strings.IBR_caudillo.303.d:
Iberia had always been naught but a geographical construct. Kept together not by common identity or purpose but by fear. When the dreaded German invasion failed to materialize the Union quickly lost its purpose. With any hope of genuine reform being killed in the cradle the Union could only survive through the sheer force of will brought by its twin Caudillos. When Salazar died and the Union endured some had hoped that it had turned into something more. That something genuine had been born. A common Iberian identity that could endure beyond the passing of the giants that had founded it. These dreams were foolish

With the passing of Francisco Franco, some mourn the loss of their savior, some rejoice at the death of a tyrant, some shed tears of regret at what could have been while others vow to maintain his legacy. Yet all fear for the future. The last pillar maintaining Iberia has fallen. The second Union seems doomed to end in the same way as its predecessor did.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.1.d:
The Advisory Council adjourned for the day, elderly members exiting the chamber as befitted their varying speeds and volubilities. Minister of Information Manuel Fraga, who had briefed them and the Caudillos on changes to separatist sentiment following his latest propaganda initiative chatted with each statesman or crony until none were left in the hall but himself and law professor Torcuato Fernández-Miranda, the man currently charged with turning mumbled suggestions into formal amendments to Iberia law.

Fraga approached the still-scribbling academic, “So, what do you make of all of this? The Council, the response to Barcelona... So much change in so little time.”

Fernández-Miranda met Fraga's eyes, thinking for a moment before saying, “I'm appreciative of the work you and your Ministry are doing to halt terrorism before it starts, Minister Fraga. And of the AAS' efforts. But why stop here?”

The Minister of Information's ready smile dropped and he leaned toward the scribe, voice lowering to a hush, “And what do you mean by that?”

“Oh, many things. The lessons learned in consolidating the legal responsibilities for anti-separatist information and education in one Ministry, yours, could be applied to our administrative framework across the board. The clear legal boundaries of the AAS are a model we could use for several flailing agencies. And our threadbare social security system requires reform if citizens are not to slip through the cracks into the radicalism that waits below.”

Fraga nodded, reassured smile spreading on his face once again, “After our recent successes, I have the Caudillos' ear. And that of several Councilors.”
strings.IBR_council_reforms.1.a: “Our only limit is how fast you can write.”
strings.IBR_council_reforms.2.d:
It is hard to imagine the Battle of Barcelona coming at a less convenient time, if it makes sense to say that there is a “convenient time” for such a tragedy at all. The Iberian Council was still young, its members inexperienced, and the powers and limitations of the new legislature not entirely clear. Nonetheless, the Council prevailed through its first crisis, quickly drafting and passing legislation to better combat terrorists wherever they were to be found.

The Iberian Council has been tested, and it has passed its test. Few still doubt that the new legislature could solve at least some of the problems facing the Union. Perhaps, then, it is no surprise that mere weeks after Barcelona several members of the Council's reformist faction have launched initiatives to overhaul various elements of the Iberian legal system and government policy.

The “Navarra Plan” and “Consolidation Plan”, as they are informally known, have gained significant traction within the Legislature. Both plans are several hundred pages long, composed by dozens of authors, and advocate radical transformations to Iberian law and fiscal policy. The “Navarra Plan” focuses on centralizing the government, rationalizing the administrative structure, and eliminating corruption, while the “Consolidation Plan” is focused on expanding social welfare, clarifying the definition and rights given to citizens, thereby ensuring the loyalty of the Iberian people.

The reform faction is all but unanimous in their support for both plans, and though no hard numbers are available, it is thought that somewhere between 30% and 40% of conservatives generally favor the plans as well. They have the backing of both Caudillos, and Manuel Fraga, a man respected by the Council's reformists and conservatives, has emerged as a loud advocate for the programs. With such a broad coalition of support, there is no question that these plans represent the future of Iberian governance. However, the current plans are rough drafts sorely lacking in specifics, and seeing them transformed into actual policy will take months if not years of effort.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.2.a: We certainly have our work cut out for us.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.3.d:
Fernando Herrero Tejedor was a Valencia man. He couldn't be expected to know the best restaurants in Madrid. But he had outdone himself with this one. The coffee was weak, the eggs were runny, the service downright hostile.

But it was located on the Camino del Sol between the heart of the city, the Puerta del Sol plaza, and the Palacio de las Cortes, where the Iberian Council met. Was meeting, in fact, today.

The FET y de las JONS official took a sip of that lukewarm coffee and smiled as he watched a fifth Councilor pass. From the determined expression on their faces, Herrero Tejedor could guess their views of the landmark assembly of the Council that the Caudillos had just called.

Herrero Tejedor almost choked on his next bite of egg-like sludge, unable to suppress a laugh imagining those five Councilors trapped in a room without the decorum of the Palacio to bind them. Shouting would break out in five minutes over policy disagreements, and blows might start soon after. But the horrors of the Barcelona uprising had convinced them that something must be done. Something deeper.

The Council had adopted sharper anti-terrorism and anti-subversion measures over the past months, but how long could the AAS and the police keep up with their foes weighed down by a sluggish and confused governing apparatus? And a society gradually turning against an Iberian state that had not even bothered to define its rights and responsibilities?

A wholesale update to the Fundamental Laws, that was what was needed from the Council. And that was what Fernando Herrero Tejedor would push for, behind-the-scenes as always.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.3.a: That is, if the waiter ever brought him his check.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.4.d:
The television screen was retelling the same miserable tale. Line after line of protesters charging police barricades, the air thick with tear gas, the whole of Barcelona in sheer panic as the riots reached a fever pitch. The news had been blaring the images almost at the same time, almost in the same order, for the whole day that day. It was an oozing wound ripping through the very fabric of everything he had sought to achieve.

“And somewhere, the ghosts of the Moors laughed,” Salazar said dryly, sitting in a wing-backed chair next to Franco's couch. Franco knew to hide his contempt well, if only out of professional courtesy. His eyes had been glued to the screen most of that afternoon, writing the government statement from Madrid in his head as he tried to pick apart the disaster piece by piece.

“Perhaps it couldn't be helped,” Franco finally admitted. “The gentlemen's agreement between Madrid and Lisbon was always an informal thing, something to keep the power structures placated without tipping the scales in one direction or the other. The Union has been building to this for a very long time, renegotiations have to happen now and not later.

Salazar was in agreement. ”The Iberian Council can draw up a Fundamental Law provision in the due time, the real worry is if it sticks or not.“ The Caudillo of Portugal leaned forward. ”You remember Galicia, after the debacle in Turkey? I can concede we each have pressures from our side, but we are past the point of just a handshake deal. The Government cannot sit on the sidelines as the Council deliberates this.“
strings.IBR_council_reforms.4.a: Franco sighed heavily: “I'll make the call.”
strings.IBR_council_reforms.5.d:
The blanket of tobacco smoke clung to the ceiling, the ventilation struggling against it in a vain action. Fluorescent lights penetrated through the air, the light tainted by the acrid airborne stains. A table stretched through the room, ashtrays overflowing atop it along with discarded mugs and bundles of dossiers and manuscripts. A dozen men sat boring through the papers, stopping only for an occasional sip of some half-forgotten drink or snack. Constitutions, laws, and legal rulings, historical and contemporary, on each furious notation were scribbled. They searched for answers: how to define the rights of citizens, against the needs of government?

The door opened, hours into the room's trance, the first voice the room had heard for a long while being gagged between coughs. “Jesus, won't you open a window?” The newcomer stumbled towards the windows, curtains curiously pulled down despite the daylight, only to find the windows padlocked. “What on earth?”

One of the men at the table stood up and, with a glance, ordered the others to return to their reading. “Esteban? You're late, close the door and sit down.” He pointed to the single vacant seat, expression stern and demanding. Esteban complied hurriedly.

“Your consignment may not leave this room. Your notes will remain in the building and, after your report is written, handed to me. Understood?”

Esteban looked incredulously at the pile, and then at the man commanding him. “What? The desk told me to come here and-”

The man rolled his eyes. “You are an analyst. You were chosen to aid in defining practical parallels or precedents. Has this been explained to you?” Esteban nodded in resignation; the description and reality of the task seemed quite distinct, as he looked at the furiously attentive faces around him.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.5.a: He opened his first dossier, reached into his suit jacket, and pulled out a cigarette.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.6.t: If It Be Crooked of Claw
strings.IBR_council_reforms.6.d:
Cans of Peaches, four in all. Cans of Beef, stewed, eight with one damaged. Cans of Pork, six with two dented.

Pablo went down his list, marking the remaining inventory and noting any adverse conditions. Cans, bottles, any kind of preserved food that could be donated or begged away from the Auxilio Social supply chain. He remembered the times after the war, when he had entire storerooms of provisions; now he had a shelf behind a counter in the Village Hall.

Unmarked Can, two placed next to each other with no markings. No printed expiry date.

He had been a King; all had looked to him for stability. After all, the socialists had thrown them all off a cliff. La Mancha never was rich; these people tilled the fields, and much of their produce had been seized by revolutionaries. Many men had left and often never returned. It took years for life to feel normal again, and through it all, he had been the man making sure his people were fed. At first, he had resented being sent here from Madrid, but such dependence had its perks.

Two trays of bottled water, eight bottles in each.

The prestige of those days, the feeling of importance he had received. Oh, how thankful so many of his people had been in those sorry days - how quickly it seemed he had been forgotten. The Church in the next village started arranging its own food distribution for the entire area, and the Red Cross had even started working with them over himself, driving a delivery truck to the isolated farms. These simple folk weren't indebted to him now; it seemed most avoided him.

Three trays of-
strings.IBR_council_reforms.6.a: Pablo paused, making a single note on the back of the paper. “Quit, go home, find some better job.”
strings.IBR_reformist_tt_15: Continuing tried-and-true programs will decrease reformist influence in the Council.
strings.IBR_influence_tt_10: The lack of initiative will reduce the Council's influence.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.6.b: Pablo paused, making single note, “Write to Council. Should be different.”
strings.IBR_reformist_tt_16: Taking initiative by providing an alternative will strengthen reformism in the Council.
strings.IBR_influence_tt_11: Providing an alternative will increase the Council's influence.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.7.d:
