It was past six in Madrid on a Friday. Salaried workers were already home, as were most children. On the Paseo de la Castellana, a variety of theatres, cinemas, and small family-owned cafes were gradually filling up with long-standing customers. One middle-aged couple walked into the cinema, eager to relive the excitement of when it had just come out. An even older couple, just as formally dressed, entered an old theater, the woman holding to her husband's arm. Meanwhile, small groups of friends, none under 30, sat at cafes with various drinks and the occasional sweet on their tables, discussing the occurrences in the newspaper.

By nine, or ten at most, all of these good people would be home and in bed. Perhaps just in time to meet the new generation on its way to their own edition of fun. Next to the very same establishments they frequented, slick-haired young men danced without restraint right next to young women wearing scandalously short skirts. Groups of youngsters jumped from bar to bar, disco to disco, quenching their taste for exploration and travel through the microcosm of American culture that was the Madrid disco scene.

Some scoffed, others looked down and tried to ignore them. But a few of them perhaps found some empathy for these young people. For they, too, were once young and rebellious. And had they not engaged in the most novel of activities, in a break with tradition as well? It is the nature of time for it to pass, and for the new to attract the new.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.7.a: Perhaps it is simply the way of the world.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.8.d:
Abril's back hurt, her feet sore, and her hands strained. Yet she persevered through all this pain. As she walked through the unpaved paths of Barcelona's neglected outskirts with four large buckets of water, she thought of how long this would last her and her family. It was some solace at least that it would likely take until next Monday for it to run out, making this momentary pain worth it. Around her, several other women were performing feats similar to hers, all trying as best as they could to ensure the safety of their families.

Abril braved the staircases to the fifth floor of her apartment, pitying the women on the floors above her, and finally put her buckets down with a loud gasp of relief as she opened the door and dragged the buckets in one by one. She was just about done with the last one when her elderly neighbour, Roderic, peeked timidly through her front door.

“Abril dear. Do you need any help?” The question was largely a gesture due to his advanced age, but it was always nice of him to ask. “Agh, but nevermind that. I have some good news to share with you on this topic. I have an old friend, we served together during the war. Well, he was at the town hall this morning, and he told me he saw some budget papers. Apparently, they were given some money for plumbing on the outskirts of the city. Don't get your hopes too high, dear, he couldn't find the courage to be nosy and look through the papers to see if our little neighborhood is part of it, but one can hope right...”

Abril zoned out for the next few seconds. She suddenly felt extremely light, her vision became blurry, and she could swear Roderic commented on the paleness of her skin-tone. The old man helped her sit down, leaning on the wall. “I'm... I'm fine. Just exhausted...” she looked at the last bucket, a sudden, extreme urge to kick it manifesting itself. She felt it was far more difficult to abstain from doing so than all of her trips combined.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.8.a: “I shouldn't get my hopes up, no.”
strings.IBR_reformist_tt_17: Turning our back on public needs will weaken reformism within the Council.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.8.b: “So what you're saying is I may not have to do this again?”
strings.IBR_reformist_tt_18: Bolstering public services will make reformism stronger in the Council.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.9.d:
“Please, senhora, I really need a place to stay. I'll sleep on the floor in the kitchen, anywhere.”

This was the fifth man Aldina had to turn away this week. Though, “man” was perhaps an exaggeration, as he seemed barely out of school. “I'm very sorry, senhor, but that is impossible. This apartment is far too small for so many people, and we are already taking more than its actual capacity. We have a sign outside that says no vacancies for a reason you know.” She sighed heavily as his face crumbled in sadness and despair.

“Please, I'm begging you. I am from a small village and have nowhere to stay here. Please, just a few weeks until my first paycheck, then I'll be able to rent an apartment of my own. I'll do anything.”

Her heart suddenly filled with pity. She thought of her own son who moved to Spain for work. Did he also struggle like this? “Look, why don't I call my husband? Maybe he knows some friends who could help you out.” The young man's features brightened up, a sparkle of hope igniting in his eyes. He thanked her profusely as she turned and left.

Her husband was sitting in the kitchen rather than taking out the trash as he promised he would. She was about to chide him when she heard what he was listening to on the radio. Quickly, she grabbed it and brought it to the reception's desk for the young man to listen.

“...the minister has cut the ribbon of a brand new apartment complex this morning. It is expected to house around 100 families.” Aldina smiled at the man as his mouth morphed into a wide smile.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.9.a: The radio continued, “The complex, one of a kind, for public servants...”
strings.IBR_reformist_tt_19: Not questioning the status quo will decrease reformist influence in the Council.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.9.b: “More such complexes are under construction to handle the current housing crisis...”
strings.IBR_reformist_tt_20: Intervening for the good of the people will expand reformist thought in the Council.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.10.d:
A growing movement in the congress has finally found itself sufficient support to debate colonial citizenship.

Iberian citizenship is granted automatically to anyone who has a parent with Iberian citizenship - at face value, it is a simple policy. However, it becomes significantly more complicated once one factors in other processes, such as colonial residence. The natives are considered non-Iberian, and denied citizenship. Effectively, they are denied any of the benefits one would gain from citizenship.

A clique in the congress has argued against this policy, for several reasons. Some find it unjust to deny the natives citizenship, since they lived on the land before our settlers, and others oppose it for more practical reasons. They desire to create a “collaborator” group within the native populations with which to sabotage the others, or simply to ease administrative strain. The end result is the same: to give all African natives Iberian citizenship.

To say this argument experienced significant pushback is an understatement. Opposition has been fierce, with a great many wishing to maintain the status quo. The settler groups wish to keep the situation as it is, as the current laws work very favorably for the Iberian settlers. Ultimately, it is still the call of the Caudillos.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.10.a: Anyone born within our borders is Iberian.
strings.IBR_reformist_tt_21: Expanding citizenship will strengthen reformism in the Council.
strings.IBR_reformist_tt_22: Dividing Iberia's people by their place of origin will decrease reformism in the Council.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.11.d:
As predicted, the settlers took native citizenship very poorly. The groups, usually organized by colonial domain - such as Guinea, Morocco, and so on - have announced a joint proclamation, with a near-unanimous decision to publicly protest the federal government's decision.

They have declared our decision “unfair to the natural citizens of Iberia”, with an emphasis on justice. Despite their claims otherwise, it is glaringly obvious that they are upset by the fact that natives will no longer be treated as second-class citizens, and the new legal parity has upset those who took their supremacy for granted. The word of the Caudillos is still supreme, and it seems about time that they be reminded of the finality of the government's decisions.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.12.d:
After the joint declaration, some settlers even took to protest in Casablanca, venting their anger against the government. It seemed as if the move would be a political expense and nothing more. To everyone's surprise, a group of natives showed up, counter protesting for the government. While the assembly did not come to blows, it came very close as law enforcement dispersed the protest.

Even though this was a spontaneous action, it is representative of sentiments within native populations. We have been formally thanked by several native organizations - through the same channels as the settlers, in what seems to have been spite - for our decisions to extend citizenship.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.13.d:
Tensions have reached an all-time high as Iberian mainlanders, furious with their lack of legal primacy, have resorted to less-than-legal methods of intimidating nearby colonials. Bands of retornados, armed with makeshift weapons, have started to hunt down and beat colonials they find vulnerable. This escalated when the natives started to fight back, creating what were quickly nicknamed “brigas repentinas”, for their spontaneous and violent nature. As all incidents do, these fights began to escalate from two or three to as many as ten to fifteen on each side.

It has escalated again. After the murder of a retornado by a colonial native, riots have broken out in several major cities around the colonies between both. The Guardia Civil is on standby, and the death toll is poised to only increase unless the riots are put down immediately.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.14.d:
A crowd of men sit within a holding cell, in some distant prison they know nothing of. They get along quickly - they seem to have been soulmates, in a way. Their conversation eventually leads them to the great question: what were they in for? All present had the same reason, the “disruption of common decency”, but they all knew they were in for protesting the new citizenship laws. They were eventually split up, incarcerated for their deeds.

Sights like this had become very common, at least for a small while. As the Guardia Civil intervened, they arrested a large number of rioting settlers. Following the show of force, most of those remaining surrendered. It seems like they won't be complaining about citizenship again.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.15.d:
King Hassan sat at his desk, looking over what seemed to be an endless number of documents. He signed his name on one, the black ink from his favorite pen shining brightly on the paper. Then, he looked to the next in the stack, another which seemed to be just a signature on the bottom. Regardless, it never paid to be unaware. He read the paper itself, expressing yet more legal provisions and regulations that, ultimately, just added up to common sense and basic decency. His silent musing was interrupted by the clicking of cameras, the flashes providing a harsh incentive to keep looking down. He supposed that nobody would be unsure of how the paperwork worked.

They found him again as he took the picture for his ID card, forcing him to keep the artificially widened smile on for even longer than he ever wanted. Better that than to frown for the cameras, he supposed.

The day came when the ID was ready to be received. Swamped by the press for what was undoubtedly an important day, he did his best pretend-to-want-to-be-here smile and held it up for everyone to see.

Someone asked him, “How does it feel to be the first native to get citizenship?” He knew what he had to say.
strings.IBR_reformist_tt_23: The success of this policy will strengthen reformist sentiment in the Council.
strings.IBR_influence_tt_12: The success of this policy will increase Council influence.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.16.d:
After several riots busted by police intervention - one infamously involving the settlers and Guardia Civil working together to quell rioters - the entire situation was ready to go nuclear. One word from any of the native leaders, and countless numbers would become insurgents and separatists, a wave harsh enough to batter down any of our previous attempts at colonial stability.

Surprisingly, there was no such thing. At first there was nothing, but then one-by-one many of the leaders urged their followers to stand down. They wanted the bloodshed no more than us, it seems, and they have all agreed that citizenship is not worth the conflict. Our position is secure.
strings.IBR_influence_tt_13: The failure of this policy will decrease the Council's influence.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.17.d:
From below the bare floorboards of Salazar's study, the piercing calamity of amiability came seeping. He fumed, listening to the tones of polite laughter and the soft conversation. He had not much time; not much time at all.

The Caudillo sat on his desk writing, scrawling, instructions. With each murmur from downstairs he knew that his time of opportunity was short, the beast was in his house. Maria had been instructed to delay all that she could, but still so little time. With a man like Marcelo Caetano, there never could be enough time.

The Fundamental Laws. The crucible upon which Iberia should be governed, beyond the kind of rule by man that so painted the world of antiquity. However, such laws in the hands of the man downstairs? A dangerous prospect, not due to treachery or incompetence but rather their opposite. He may do too well. Long had Caetano seen himself as the reformer of the Estado Novo, now of Iberia as a whole. While certainly far better than an opportunistic liberal or an incandescent fascist, handing such a man the keys to his Kingdom may have unexpected results.

Creaks upon the stairs formed the welcoming march. Maria continued to talk, a concerto of banter now more clearly audible. The old Caudillo grimaced, he knew Maria all too well. She was having fun, the pitch of her voice full of enjoyment for the conversation? Could she not use that to just give him more time?

Every instruction, he searched every word. Loopholes, vagaries, unintended definitions; all must be removed. Caetano was a man of great effort, unflinching to his cause, but without a tight leash uncontrollable. Salazar crossed out words furiously and wrote new ones as his study door was politely knocked. He memorized his final list, burning them into his mind, before throwing the paper in a desk drawer and calling Caetano in.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.17.a: “Senhor Caetano. How nice to see you. Give me a moment, I'll prepare a quick list of instructions.”
strings.IBR_council_reforms.18.t: Wise Enough to Play the Fool
strings.IBR_council_reforms.18.d:
The Teatro Principal de Valencia glowed in the gentle light, the cream and reds of the masonry and curtains forming an image of rich civilisation. The lights seemed to give a yellow glow like a fire, the chattering of men and women taking their seats filling the air with an orchestra of fine words politely stated. Upon the high sides booths rose one after another, private people with private thoughts looking out upon the swarms below and the stage still hidden by the scarlet veil upon it. Eventually the turmoil of the room ceased however, the lights dimmed and the curtains rose.

Upon a stage, two players began their scene.

“They are exquisite, a diarchy almost equal to our Caudillos, were they headline actors. Wouldn't you say, Señor Caetano?” said the man watching the opening monologues high upon the room. In his lap lay a small pair of binoculars. His partner refused such an aid, merely listening to the lines.

“Indeed, Senhor Tejedor,” answered Caetano beside him, “however there is a note of discord. You don't hear it? Too... emotional, distracted. Perhaps there was an argument backstage.”

“What of it?”

“Plays rely on their leading players. Much like we rely on our Caudillos. However I've known a few actors in my time, and I've known a few Councillors. Public performers can be so affected by hidden dramas.”

Tejedor nodded. “Many within the FET y de las JONS have certainly noted that in our time. Just as we notice that a monologue, split between two players, has half the momentum of a united one.” He turned a side eye to Caetano. “But such concerns could damage the play's structure.” He raised an eyebrow, eyes asking a question his lips refused to parse.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.18.a: “Indeed. Sometimes the play's structure is worth a little slower delivery.”
strings.IBR_reformist_tt_24: Not questioning the regime structure will weaken reformism in the Council.
strings.IBR_influence_tt_14: Not questioning the regime's foundation will be appreciated by the Caudillos, increasing the Council's influence.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.18.b: “The best writers are their own harshest critics, and pacing is where it is needed most.”
strings.IBR_reformist_tt_25: Facing the possible flaws of the regime will make reformism stronger in the Council.
strings.IBR_influence_tt_15: Opening this Pandora's Box will make the Caudillos suspicious, decreasing the Council's influence.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.19.d:
Caetano stood before the Iberian Council, his pose straight and confident against the harsh eyes before him. He looked at them, nervous feelings sealed every so expertly behind their nonchalant faces. They wore their masks with such ease, he could imagine the Caudillos they presented to often had no idea of the fears within the speaker.. Franco was too buried in his ways to consider anyone else while Salazar was too busy trying to carry the government on his back to ever truly notice the empty yes-men in their Council.

But he saw. Caetano would have scoffed if he could, if it weren't for the precipice of political purgatory he stood upon. He had spent quite enough time within that quagmire for one lifetime to be thrown back in for an act of disrespect, no matter how justified. And besides, could he truly blame them? Did the councillors not also face the same restrictions?

He spoke, measured and clear, resigning himself and his audience to simple facts. The Diarchy explained in detail was something most of them had never heard before. How could it have been? The web of vague legal precedents and informal agreements, coopted regulations and half measures addressing specific issues stretched screaming across a peninsula. In their eyes he saw it, the surprise to just what system they sat below as their masks dipped. How excellent.

He opened himself for questions, and like a holy light bursting from some hell-touched cavern a hand was raised. The man was young, barely more than a boy; Tejedor had chosen well. Barely in his thirties, bold enough to ask their questions. Young enough to be disposable. He prompted the councillor to speak.

“Señor, it seems clear that the Caudillo's suggestions to refine the Fundamental Laws were well considered. However, given the breadth and complexity, wouldn't some minor adjustments be as advantageous as mere refinements?”
strings.IBR_council_reforms.19.a: Caetano gave a rehearsed, disarming smile. “Caudillos willing, we could consider clarifications”.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.20.d:
A meeting chamber emanating with the heat of a furious sun was not a characterization many halls can profess to, however to look towards the seat of the Portuguese Caudillo was to see and feel just that.

He sat upon his seat beside Caudillo Franco, burning with suspicion and barely contained anger as the lists of small incongruities in the Council's remit climbed. Caetano was conducting the meeting, attempting to guide the Council as they chipped away at the powers that held Iberia together. “Clarifications.” Salazar had asked for a refinement and now he found that Caetano had decided to rewrite the entire foundation of the land piecemeal. His Spanish counterpart next to him may wear a wry smile, but Salazar could see nothing but chaos.

The trend was clear. Nearly every clarification or addendum served a single theme - some more obviously than others but Salazar could see it as clear as a blue sky. A single Caudillo could act alone. Yes, the work he could do with such power could be huge, but what when he's gone? What of Franco and his susceptibility to whims? The complex web of government existed for a reason; a literacy test for the able. If one could not read and maneuver in the system, then where was the justification for their power? Caetano danced on an edge, overstepping boundaries on some personal mission to streamline. Despite every effort to control him he had gone rogue anyway.

He stood up, interrupting a query from a lawyer. “I apologise, Senhor Fernández-Miranda, but I must request that I discuss matters further with Senhor Caetano. Privately.”

The room hushed in a moment. Caetano flashed in apprehension. “Caudillo Salazar, if I may -” he began, a raised hand ceasing his words. Salazar turned to Franco.

“Wouldn't you agree, Caudillo Franco?”
strings.IBR_council_reforms.20.a: The Spanish Caudillo nodded. “If you think that's prudent, then so be it.”
strings.IBR_council_reforms.20.b: The Spanish Caudillo looked at Caetano. “Continue, Señor. This meeting isn't over yet.”
strings.IBR_council_reforms.21.d:
Sitting down had been a humiliation. To listen to the meeting continue around him as he stared at the wood of the table before him, as the Diarchy was stripped down as if to make Iberia little more than a nation of two dictators, was a humiliation too much. Salazar's hand shook upon his knee as he listened to Caetano reading out new suggestions to be put to the vote. Lawyers and Councilmen discussed terms as Franco gleefully agreed. The Spaniards declaring-

Wait.

Salazar had a thought. A single line, he had read it and passed it by as it had seemed minor in the grand scope of abuses that Caetano seemed to be conducting. He scrambled for the page. He saw articles discussed half an hour ago. An hour ago. Two hours ago.

He saw it. It was exactly as he feared. He should have left Caetano in his exile.

He stood up, as a missile from a silo, pointing an accusatory finger at Caetano. “Marcelo.” The Portuguese Caudillo spoke with a malice few in the room had heard before, the anger then replaced by a silent, brooding fury. “Page 12, Section 2 Article 4. 'If a single Caudillo is incapacitated or deceased, the surviving Caudillo shall appoint a citizen of the same nation to temporarily assume the position for an interim period.'”

The room's silence intensified. All eyes, from Councilman to security officer, looked upon the Portuguese Caudillo. Caetano stood motionless for a moment, face caught in a whirlwind of insecurity. “Yes, Caudillo Salazar. We discussed that article, do you have a new observation?”

“Was that your plan at Cambados, to seize an opportunity to-?” Shock seemed to overtake the Caudillo for a moment, and he turned to the Spanish general beside him. “Was it yours?”
strings.IBR_council_reforms.21.a: Franco stood and adjourned the Council. But Diarchs' rage would be heard through the closed door.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.21.b: The silent air grew thick for Salazar as he looked around. He saw only traitors, and the betrayed.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.22.d:
By now, the discussions across the convened members of the Iberian Council had grown ferocious. As soon as Salazar laid forth the accusation of a coup, the Council had split clean down the middle. The Portuguese half shuffled together, throwing disordered insults across the room.

“Francisco Franco saved this peninsula from National and Bolshevik socialism!” shouted one councillor, in Spanish, pointing a finger at Salazar as his back totally turned away. “He is a hero!” He was silenced as a pen hit his shoulder, prompting him to lunge towards his attacker, the pair tackling each other to the floor as they grappled at the papers.

“Oh, I'm not talking about Franc-” interjected Salazar, halted both as the general mood grew even more intense, and as he began to doubt his own words. Franco sighed. He knew that, at some point, Salazar would complain. The reforms were so overarching and so isolating for their shared powers that it was sure to come to opposition. He only wished it wasn't so fierce.

“Sit down!” shouted Caetano. “You're not going to stop these r-”

“Oh, to Hell with this!” roared Salazar, his chair falling backwards as he rose. “You're not getting me to kill myself!” A few pages fell out from the pile, but Salazar paid no heed as he slammed the door. The rest of the Portuguese Council stopped for a moment, their ferocity silenced, but in turn, they too trickled out, only Caetano lingering.

“Sometimes, the best reform is a change in attitude, Marcelo”, said Franco, “even if it means reforming your attitude on preserving current law.” He didn't like the concession, not least considering how immature the pair had been, but it was better to not make any changes to the Diarchy, and hope that Salazar was the first of them to die, than to let it sink Iberia.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.22.a: The ship of state tries tearing itself from its iceberg.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.23.t: No One Wants To Hear Us
strings.IBR_council_reforms.23.d:
The seat of a frustrated legislator is thrown across the chambers.

Ten seconds. Salazar's frenzied speech against the Diarchy reforms barely made it ten seconds before the hurled chair smashed into the head of a FET y de las JONS cadre. With the gash on his head bleeding down his eyebrows, the victim immediately strode forward to tackle the perpetrator. Now, a rough shoving fight had begun. Slowly, the pushing grew into a rough fight, with more members incrementally partaking from both sides, as the spiel degenerated into the frequent expletives of “whores” and “traitors” being the only words heard from the opposing teams of Spanish and Portuguese members.

Salazar has witnessed this sore sight in front of him. Standing alone and staring at the byproduct of his accomplishments; possibly a spitting image of a malfunctioning nation may be staring right back at him at this moment. Salazar had feared that no matter how much he could turn back the tides, this was all his legacy could afford. The aging Caudillo, with an acrimonious mood, had to turn and make a wordless exit without bringing his copy with him.

Caetano and Franco spotted him as soon as he stood up and walked out. Franco snapped back at his copy of the reforms when Salazar was out of sight. With the heaviest and most silent frown, the copy was lifted and tucked neatly under his seat.

Caetano anxiously wrangled his hands together as Franco slowly tilted his gaze upwards until he glared directly at the disgraced protégé.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.23.a: Neither will be eager to work with the other when the time comes.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.24.d:
A councilman - a short fellow, with a bushy face - prepared his speech. Well, technically, it had been handed to him by Franco, but for all intents and purposes it was his.

“It is a terrible issue with the modern Iberia that, for all its posturing as a unified country, it does not have a unified judiciary. The system is decentralized, and the regional courts can run around as if they are independent!” He quietly hoped that didn't seem too monotone. “Iberia can only fulfil its promise of unity when all elements of the country are united as if they were never separate. Our courts are no different. Are there any questions?”

Someone, to his dread, had a question. “How would we best integrate these courts? Centralization should only be attempted if we can ensure it does not go poorly. Therefore, I want to hear your ideas on the matter.”

Oh no.

In an act of divine providence, someone was able to interject and answer the question, moving the pressure away from him. The debate was similar in nature, but the final consensus was that ultimately...
strings.IBR_council_reforms.24.b: We must centralize the justice apparatus.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.25.d:
“Writing continues on the Organic Law and it should be ready to present shortly. All in all, we should finally have a tangible foundation for ourselves; what could possibly make you so dour then, António?”

Franco and Salazar sat, eating the meal their aides had delivered for them. How often it felt they had to do this when they met; so much to discuss yet so little time. Franco tore into his meal, bread and meat swiftly vanishing, while Salazar ate slowly. He seemed to be looking past his meal partner, chewing almost as an afterthought. “Is this really the answer to our concerns, Francisco?” he asked absently.

“You don't like the food?”

Salazar's eyes refocused. “No no, the law. There is one thing that is being omitted that concerns me. What is the succession mechanism? We may be forming a proper legal foundation for Iberia now, but we are not immortal.”

Franco would have chuckled, were he not chewing bread. “You have such dark thoughts,” he said after he swallowed, “we have years to think about such a morbid thing. Why waste time with such a detail when we can revisit it later?”

Salazar looked at his bread. In the corner, he noticed a small spot of mold, barely noticeable. A tiny smudge against the white loaf. He pushed the meal away. “What good is securing Iberia legally if we build it on sand, sand that may collapse the moment one of us passes?”

Franco pondered for a moment before reaching for a glass of water. “António,” he said as he raised the glass, “we have plenty of time to consider such things. We have a long, long time steering this ship yet.”
strings.IBR_council_reforms.25.a: Salazar's eyes returned to the spot of mold. Decay must have felt so distant to the baker.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.26.d:
The students of the University of Coimbra leaned notoriously towards the far-right. Owing to their Catholic background, there was a disproportionate amount of far-right student groups, formal and informal, from reactionaries to Falangists. It was one such group, though nobody could tell which, that invited famous Hispanicist and Catholic fundamentalist, Blas Piñar, to speak in the University's main auditorium.

“It is increasingly clear, though the Caudillos are putting their hearts and souls against such a project, that the internationalist cabal of the self-proclaimed technocrats has acquired an increasingly large presence in the government. The government parties have their positions undermined further and further, and ruling is becoming more of a nightmare every day.” Students looked at him in awe, their eyes wide with excitement and understanding. “We must act! No good Iberian can stand idle while our national, Catholic values are trampled as such. We must reclaim our government from the corrupt vermin that are the internationalists, we must purge the traitor and secure a strong, Catholic state that will persist for years to come!”

The whole crowd stood and offered the man a standing ovation. Piñar kept his fist up in the air, his expression stoic and indecipherable.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.26.a: “Is this man with us or against us?”
strings.IBR_council_reforms.27.d:
The hall was packed with the faithful, large speakers humming during each pause of the speakers upon the stage. Above the stage, a banner proudly hung, 'Catholic Forum for the Advancement of Social Faith' written boldly upon it. The event had been anticipated, hosted by the CADC and the ACdP Catholic organisations. In every Church, Convent, and Seminary, a feeling of precipice had hung; all felt Iberia stood at a crossroads. A crossroads only answerable through faith.

What few had expected was that the crossroads were not merely external.

Currently, a young priest stood at the podium, ill at odds with the other speakers upon the stage. Many were aged; only a few young men sat among them, of whom this speaker was the first. A speaker to whom many of the aged grandees, from bishops to scholars, shook their heads. He had spoken at length about the deprivation within his parish, the fears he held for the earnestness of faith within his small Asturian valley. Finally, he was at his end.

“When I read Luke, Luke 14:13 to be precise, I find what should be the root of our social teaching within Iberia. 'When you give a banquet, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, the blind, and you will be blessed.' How often do we apply this in faith but not in action? Do we involve ourselves with the earthly struggles of the laity? Unless we take a more proactive role, advocating for their food at the table, their safety at work, or their family's prosperity, how can any truly trust in the Good News we share?” The young priest closed his speech, voice wavering slightly with the icy touch of nervousness. The speakers hummed, and the room was silent for a moment.

The hall had rang all day with calls for tradition, cooperation with secular power, and the necessity of gentle, if forthright, voices upon the issue of secular society. Now, it rang with applause.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.27.a: Those who applauded were young, minds full of an Iberia where all could share in Christ's bread.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.28.d:
The Sobrino de Botín never failed Caetano. Good food, a private room, discretion; he couldn't possibly ask for more. And tonight he certainly had a need of refined, discreet surroundings on account of his meal partner, Laureano López Rodó - a partner whom Caetano had taken great pains to ingratiate himself with. A personification of the notion that the Madrid elite were not entirely lost, Francoist orthodoxy far from guaranteed. His notions on economic matters had reached the professors's ears. And, as the restaurant's wine and food had done their work, the conversation had flowed like the white wine at the table. Liberally.

“So, we agree, don't we Señor. Less bureaucrats screwing up the economy, get them doing something useful like sorting out Africa! Then again, can anyone sort out that mess...” His words slightly slurred, intoxication not quite reached but Rodó certainly stood at its gate. Caetano smiled, gently sipping his own drink.

“Indeed, Senhor Rodó. Africa is something that I have made a rather personal project of mine. How do you feel about the Spanish territories? Is Morocco soundly administered?” Caetano spoke calmly, measured. Rodó hadn't noticed his partner had drunk less than he had, and the dividends were paying off.

Rodó furrowed his brow, eyes searching his mind for words. “Difficult questions. I'm uncertain, and-”

“Let me ask it another way, do you think our traditional methods have succeeded?”

The slight mist in Rodó's eyes melted away. “Dr. Caetano,” he cleared his throat, “if we are speaking frankly, then disappointment is the theme. Just like the economy, historically we have put expectation of method before the desired results. I would explore more options, just as I do for the economy. I trust assessing that was your purpose tonight?”
strings.IBR_council_reforms.28.a: Caetano smiled. “A Choupana is a fine restaurant in Lisboa. Let's continue there.”
strings.IBR_council_reforms.29.d:
It was a calm Sunday afternoon in Navarra. Mass had just ended, and churchgoers exited the building in contemplative silence. Even in this small mountainous village, the recent turmoil has been felt.

After everyone has left, the priest invites a group of men, wearing Red Berets, for a private discussion. They enter the basement of the Church, into a room where a portrait of Infante Carlos adorned the wall like an icon, right next to the real icons depicting various Spanish saints, and the Virgin Mary.

“Thank you, Father, for providing us with this space for our meetings. My house is no longer safe, as you might imagine with everything that is going on...” The man's sentence hangs in the air, his face hardening. “I have news from my cousin that the trade union is planning a strike against the government. I know it sounds like communist drivel, but I assure you the vast majority of workers participating in the strike are good, hard-working Catholics. The government has merely forced their hand.” He looked at the priest for assurances, receiving a quiet nod. “I suggest we join them. Anyone against?” There was no answer. Today is a rest day. Tomorrow, they strike.

At the exact same time in a small house in Southern Portugal, Francisco Rolão Preto was standing amongst fellow oppositionists, his fist in the air, and his chest contracting with each spoken word. “And they treat us like dogs! Dogs, I say! They beat us and kick us while we are down. We cannot protest. We cannot speak our minds in public. Hell, I wouldn't be surprised if I was taken in the night for speaking in the private company of my friends! Where are our natural, inherent rights as human beings?” Many of his colleagues stood up in solidarity with him. Francisco smiled.
strings.IBR_council_reforms.29.a: “Will we stand still and take it? Or will we rise and grasp what belongs to us?”
strings.IBR_council_reforms.30.d:
The new Fundamental Laws - or at least, a draft of them - has been published. Copies have been printed in every newspaper possible, and nearly everyone in Iberia will have seen it by now. It certainly seems that way, based on the stir we've created in the government and without. There has been dissent within the government, although it is at a level minimal enough to be curbed.

It is said that a good compromise leaves nobody happy. According to our political factions, the Constitution was a good compromise. Some argue it went too far, and others not far enough, and there is enough of both sides to ensure that there will be an argument over it for a long time to come.

Surely, this is what it will take? The Union will now last forevermore, right?
strings.IBR_algeria.1.d:
Events on the European continent have taken quite the turn with the latest news. We have been given some solid reports the Burgundian tanks have rolled into France in what is sure to be a one sided and very short war. With France being further castrated by their Nazi overlords, all claims of French legitimacy to the land of Algeria have disappeared overnight. We all know they have bigger issues at hand at the moment, than to defend from our advances.

We have been handed a golden opportunity here. This opportunity does not come around very often and we would be foolhardy to pass up such an endeavor. Moves will have to be made, and made fast before anyone else wizens up to what's going on here. Plans and meetings will need to be sorted quickly so we can jump on this before any other opportunist. One thing is certain though for the moment. That all right now is for the taking and there are no limits as to what we could do down in Algeria.
strings.IBR_algeria.1.a: We shall make moves in Algeria and accept all the necessary consequences.
strings.IBR_algeria.2.d:
Opportunity rarely has the courtesy to knock at an opportune time. For Jorge Jardim, opportunity interrupted a perfectly good breakfast. Were he a sensible man, he wouldn't have abandoned his poached egg and toasted bread for the letter apparently rushed to him from Madrid, but unfortunately for him he was a politician and such sense was not allowed in this profession.

Bright eyes quickly scanned the letter, absorbing both the written word and the unwritten intent behind them all at once. He stood from the table as he reached the end, his mind already turning over the newfound information. According to the letter, the Shadow State was storming into the French rump state and to no one's surprise, the French were receiving the worst of the fighting. The French had been more or less a non-factor for over a decade, unable to maintain control of much of the country outside of Algiers itself. That's why they were here in Oran after all, and the Italians on the other side of the garrison.

But the letter was much more vague with its actual orders, a necessary tactic to maintain plausible deniability should it somehow fall outside of Iberian hands and cause a scandal. That didn't matter though, they wouldn't have sent him this letter without knowing what he'd do once he got to reading it, and already, he was deep in thought.

A spin, Iberia needed a spin to justify the acquisition of Algeria. While, yes, militarily occupied by both themselves and Italians, it was still legally French, and they weren't in a position to simply take the rest of the country by storm. After all, if they did that, they'd be fighting Italians, not the scarecrow army of the French State. So what excuse could they conjure up that would prevent the Italians from intervening?

He sat there deep in thought for some time, running through the scenarios in his head. It was clear that whatever scheme was cooked up, they'd have to work with the Italians directly to achieve it. So be it they would play this one by ear.

He took a bite of his eggs, grimacing as he chewed. Opportunity had made his eggs go cold...
strings.IBR_algeria.3.d:
In the modern age, military glory was becoming increasingly rare and difficult to come by, even as militaries all around the world continued to ceaselessly grow. The advent of the nuclear bomb and the resulting global stalemate seemed to all but halt the ambitions of those who would mark their place in history through conquest.

And likewise, when force of arms failed, great men of silver tongues and wily diplomacy would often step up to the plate. But in these modern times, it seems like every rock, every blade of grass and every grain of sand is owned by somebody, somewhere, and no one was interested in selling. The world was as small as it was ever going to be, and no one saw value in losing their corner of it.

That's why when the Caudillos called the greatest military and diplomatic minds of Iberia together to discuss plans for the French Colony of Algeria, they came not with vague ideas and concepts, but with papers, with maps, with briefcases and books worth of schemes. This was an opportunity that they all knew they'd never again see in their lifetimes, a chance to be known as the conqueror- through guns or through words- of Algeria.

Generals came with grand campaigns and elaborate war plans, some even going as far as to invade Tunis and Libya should the Italians stand in their way. Diplomats cracked open briefcases to reveal grand schemes and plans to buy or swindle the Italian half of Algeria out from beneath their feet. When the Caudillos made the call for all spheres of Iberia to form a plan together, they instead got a rapid- and long- succession of political sales pitches.
strings.IBR_algeria.3.a: This is going to take a while...
strings.IBR_algeria.4.d:
The moon was gazing down upon the military headquarters in Madrid when the Caudillos finally saw the light at the end of the tunnel. After discarding the obvious losers, and then the less obvious losers, the Caudillos were left with two plans to decide between.

Among the generals, Kaúlza de Arriaga's scheme had the most support. A limited war, but with the added benefit of looking towards the white French colonials in Algeria for support, and the creation of a cooperative government with them in the process. The Kaúlza Plan, as it has been called since he first presented it to the Caudillos, calls for open warfare in Algeria to simultaneously drive out the Italians and pacify the natives all in one fell swoop. The generals have rallied behind the Kaúlza Plan, and already believe that Salazar will support them.

Meanwhile, among the diplomats, Adriano Moreira's plan had proven to be the most attractive. Rather than approaching the Italian government directly- which would require a great deal of expense to acquire the Italian half of the region- he proposes that Iberia should instead approach the Italian oil giant, ENI. If they can convince ENI to support the Iberian claim to Algeria in exchange for a generous deal on oil development in the region, ENI could in turn put much more intense pressure on Italy to accept the Iberian claim. The other diplomats and politicians have abandoned their own rejected plans to support the Moreira Plan, and hope that Franco will support them in turn.
strings.IBR_algeria.5.d:
It was mid-day when Salazar entered the meeting room. Normally they wouldn't time a meeting so oddly, but Franco had requested he enter once he had fully collected his thoughts on the Algerian issue, and not one moment earlier or later. Sadly, what this meant was that Franco had to dedicate nearly the entire day to waiting, for whenever his counterpart finally got around to attending. He was thankful, then, that they showed up shortly after lunch.

As expected, Salazar got to talking as soon as he closed the door behind him.

“I had to see everything, but I've made up my mind- Algeria needs to be secured. At any cost, it doesn't matter, we need to guarantee the retornados a home.” Franco began to open his mouth to respond, but Salazar snapped at him first. “Don't start about pragmatism to me, not about this. Those retornados were exiled from their home once already, I would rather die than let them be kicked out again, and so soon after the first time! Arriaga's plan will guarantee them their home, and he'll make sure those Italian bastards recognize it!”

Franco half-sighed, half-grunted in annoyance. “I can't fault you for being passionate about your people, but you are refusing to see the larger picture. We need peace in Algeria. A war will win them the land, maybe, but then where will you be, when they all die fighting for it? What good would it do, Salazar?” Salazar started a response, getting out perhaps half a word before Franco interrupted him. “Whatever we settle on, just remember. It needs to be unanimous...”
strings.IBR_algeria.5.a: “...we need to look like a united front.”
strings.IBR_algeria.6.d:
Franco was in the same room again, this time reclined in a seat next to Salazar. He spared a glance to his colleague - who was more focused on the plans before them - before returning his gaze to Kaúlza and Moreira, who seemed more concerned with shuffling through their things. Eventually, they both prepared to present, but Kaúlza was mandated to go first.

He spoke loud, with a boisterous tone that showed his total confidence in his plans. He didn't have any formal charts or flashy models, but simply passed out two pieces of paper and laid a map out on the conference table, a map of Algeria. He detailed the situation (as he saw it), then carefully explained how they could swipe the rest of the country from the Italians. To this end, he also explained the contents of the documents he passed out - they were manifests, of the equipment they'd require, optimistically, to get the job done.

Once Kaúlza finished, it was time for Moreira to present his plan for Algeria. During the war plan briefing, the politician had taken the time to properly set up a presentation, though his delivery left some to be desired. He explained his plan, how working with ENI could win Algeria, and of how to make deals situated to look desirable to them. He pointed out the resources required, and how to best use them. With a style of utilizing as little words as possible, his side of the meeting concluded remarkably quickly.

As both sides had finished their presentation, the Caudillos spoke their verdict. While they both made designs to sell their plans, what the two didn't know was that the Caudillos had both already decided. They told the two, in their back-and-forth speech style, that...
strings.IBR_algeria.6.a: Nothing but war will help us.
strings.IBR_algeria.6.b: Words can win the toughest of battles.
strings.IBR_algeria.7.d:
“The Italians have only two roads connecting the Coastal regions of Algeria to the Southern regions. The road going through Ghardaia is near the front line, and will be taken by the infantry. The road through Touggourt is deeper into the country, and your mission is to make that road as much of a pain in the ass as possible for the enemy to use once war is declared.

The supply trucks have enough fuel for every one of you to travel to Cairo and back. Remember, your focus is speed: get to the target as quickly as possible. Weather permitting, it should take only 10 to 12 hours travel to reach the target. There you will set landmines and shoot at anything that moves: truck, car, tank, helicopter, anything. As long as both roads are unusable, the Italians will have to take a 1000 mile detour to move anything from north to south. And the longer we keep blocking the Touggourt passage, the enemy can't keep all their forces at the frontline.”
strings.IBR_algeria.7.a: “You are the Settler Cavalry, who will cross a desert and build an empire!”
strings.IBR_algeria.8.d:
Captain Saturnino de la Hidalga was uneasy aboard the Canarias. Whatever upgrades the Federal Government might have afforded for the old cruiser, they would not make up for the fact she was built to comply with the Washington Naval Treaty of 1922. Her 203mms might scare unruly natives, but they certainly would not stand up to anything the Italian navy had to offer. Saturnino tried to relax, there was little risk of attack while in Oran, where his squadron was well under the protection of coastal batteries.

The captain eyed the Portuguese landing ship two hundred meters to his right with increasing anxiety, hoping that it would deliver the last batch of tanks to the intervention force so he could get on his way back to Gibraltar. Ironically, he thought, the LCPL was a former Italian ship - one could tell by the design. Salazar bought it second hand, and the seaman was sure the Italians sold it for more than it was really worth. Nevertheless, it got the job done, and the last Ibíce was rolling out its cargo hold and into the dock within thirty minutes, albeit in reverse. Saturnino, satisfied with his job, gave the order to leave the port...

“Mi Capitán!” The anxious engineer's screech couldn't mean anything good, he could feel it in his bones. “We... thought it was an error, but the Cervero has picked up the same signal.” Looking at the radar screen from afar, Saturnino spotted the approaching blips. “Shit.” For a second, he was paralyzed, but his aristocratic officer instincts got the better of him.
strings.IBR_algeria.9.d:
The FIAT G.91s approached the Iberian flotilla at a breakneck speed, lest the HA-300s based at Murcia could get there first. Amidst the initial volley of flak fire from Oran's defenses, flight Lt. Lombardi had some good news to tell his men: “We've spotted the flagship, it looks like the NLF bastards didn't lie. Remember, hit the landing ships, don't waste your bombs on... shit.” It was already too late, Martionetti and Frigerio were on a vector straight towards the Canarias, and their FIATs sped right past Lombardi's. Unsurprisingly, he could not reach them by radio. “Technical difficulties, my ass.” Once they return from the raid he would get them court-martialled, their insubordination could cost the entire operation.

Struggling to keep his composure, Captain Saturnino was fixated on the black puffs that perpetually missed their targets, if ever so slightly. By now, the 203mms had been aimed, but the plane's approach was too difficult to... two of them were breaking off. The captain threw himself at the cruiser's intercom, virtually stapling his hand to the “talk” button while holding his binoculars with the other. “Gunnery Officer Pérez... RANGED SHOT AT 200 METERS steady... ELEVATION 36°... steady.” He could spot the muzzle flashes from the Italian's 20mm cannons, and soon, the ship's hull was taking their lead. It was inaccurate at that range, but it might make a lesser captain keep his head down. No, not him, not a de la Hidalga. “Now!” The main battery went off in a heap of powder.

“Frigerio, you imbecile!” Lombardi cried in desperation as the airman's left wing was destroyed by shrapnel from the Canarias. Marionetti managed to pull out, but sure enough, he passed over the dock and an Iberian MANPAD disintegrated his plane within a few seconds. With his formation shattered and the Iberians alerted, Lombardi had no choice.
strings.IBR_algeria.9.a: “We need to get out of here!”
strings.IBR_algeria.10.d:
Dear Carmen,

We arrived in this country only a few short weeks ago, and already I am counting the time before we are rotated out. Some of the older men have shared the stories they've heard about the Rif War, the oppressive heat, the constant threat of fighting a foe which seemed to disappear like ghosts into the desert sands. We are lucky the Algerians don't seem half as skilled as the Rifians the Legion fought so long ago, though they make up for it in ferocity.

We are continuously on the move, watching the emptiness for any sign of FLN or Italian activity. Combat comes almost as a relief after days of patrolling the desert, but the worst of it happens when we fight alongside our Pied-Noir allies. While they may be able soldiers, their brutality, and treatment of those unlucky to fall enough into captivity is something that I will never be able to forget.

I look forward to the day when I can leave this godless desert. Our unit is supposed to be rotated out within six weeks at most, hopefully in time for our anniversary. We will be on the offensive soon and I will not be able to write to you for some time. I promise to do everything in my power to ensure that I make it home in one piece. Please don't worry too much about me, as if you won't, for I will take care of myself and look forward to the day I am able to be with you again.
strings.IBR_algeria.11.d:
For the various servants and functionaries in attendance, it was one of the vanishingly few times that loud voices of argument were not heard through the thick doors. Then again however, today the Caudillos had nothing but victory to discuss, for the Algerian War had finished and Iberia had triumphed.

Messages had already arrived from many parties and the Caudillos read them with satisfaction. The Military was elated at being given the successful chance to demonstrate their capability. The Pieds-Noir were grateful. The Italians were terse. And further afield, others were beginning to recognize Iberia's growing influence.

There were of course other considerations, and the aides listened closely to hear the Caudillo's respective positions. The new Governor, could not be more clear in his favor for Iberia, but Salazar's measured voice, heard through the doors, was resolute in that it would take more than his favor to pay his nation's war debts. France was already disentangling itself, he said, and so Iberia itself would need to take on the costs in the short term - a significant burden to bear.

For one day, however, the aides overheard Caudillo Franco's convincing of his partner to concentrate on celebration. The costs were substantial, yes, but they had won. Iberia had won.
strings.IBR_algeria.12.d:
For the various servants and functionaries in attendance, the meeting between the Caudillos was distressingly familiar. Shouts could be heard through the thick doors and, they had to admit, it was with good reason, for the Algerian War had finished and Iberia had been defeated. Comprehensively.

The Intervention Force had disintegrated as an organized formation following defeats at the hands of the Italian-backed units, and those that survived had fled back to Iberian holdings across the border. French influence had collapsed, and the natives had already announced a new government. One in which the Italians, naturally, would hold great influence. The military was furious and humiliated in equal measure. And the hammerblow to Iberian prestige and respect internationally was almost too great to be mentioned.

Salazar was, of course, quick to characterize the defeat as one less so - after all, even if the war had been won the pacification cost would have been ruinous. But Franco would have none of it - the French had been entirely ejected and Iberian influence destroyed. Officers and civil servants cycled in and out of the meeting room but the verbal combat, the last battle of the Algerian War, never stopped.

As the day wore on, the functionaries noticed that he was toying with the suggestion of laying the blame on the Portuguese elements of the intervention elements, and they all breathed a sigh of relief when he did not follow through.As he left the offices however, all could see a profound sadness on the Caudillo's face, and many felt the same way. The war had been a chance at greatness for the nation, but now?
strings.IBR_algeria.12.a: Now that felt so far away.
strings.IBR_algeria.13.d:
Encouraging news emanates from the city of Oran, where the first results of a program bringing brave Iberians to Algeria have taken root, marking one of the first successful settlement programs in the region by any state other than France itself.

Whilst small in numbers, the influx of Portuguese expatriates, families and workers alike, many of which come from Portugal's lost colonies, have answered the call and taken to settling in Oran, one of the more well-known cities in western Algeria. Despite continued tensions with native resistance elements, the effort by Portuguese immigrants to cordially acclimatize has faced little protest, though one can attribute that in part to the city's already sizable European population and richness in employment opportunities, in part due to many fleeing during the Crisis.

While a true recovery from the bloodshed of the last years is certainly a long way off, the initial successes of the joint program paint an image of an encouraging future between our Union and the new government in Algiers, which alongside economic deals and humanitarian aid the Union has offered paint quite a promising picture of growing bonds.

Perhaps a sense of brotherhood will form between the Pied-Noir and Portuguese Retornados in the region, forged by their shared perseverance in the desire to carve a good life in spite of harsh circumstances.
strings.IBR_algeria.13.a: Perhaps this is the mere start of a wonderful partnership.
strings.IBR_algeria.14.d:
For the second time in twenty years, António found himself watching the land of his adopted home fade into the distance, conquered by foreign soldiers, failed by his government. As the coasts of Algeria disappeared into the distance, the man wondered how much his birthplace had changed since he last saw it.

Portugal was but a distant memory, a home he had left to pursue life overseas, lured away by promises of fame and fortune. First came Angola, a harsh exotic land. He had earned his living hacking roads from the jungle, carving plantations from the wilderness, and bringing civilization to an untamed continent. Until the Germans marched in and forced them out, while Lisbon stood by and watched.

Then came Algeria, where he worked alongside his Spanish brethren, carving a continued place in the world for Colonialism. The desert was a harsh mistress, but he had managed until the War came and went, and he was once again without a land to call home.

The hours passed quickly, few of his fellow Retornados were in the mood to talk, hushed voices and whispered words, worried parents, and confused children. The only ones willing to speak were the soldiers, young, angry, and resentful, with too much to drink and too little to do.

As the coast of Portugal came into view, António didn't know what to feel. This was his nation, his birthplace, his native land. But as he stepped off the gangway and onto Portuguese soil, and on the journey back to his family home, all he could think about was how he was a foreigner in his own country.
strings.IBR_algeria.15.d:
To: The Government of Iberia
From: The Military Territory of Algeria

The loss of Caudillo Salazar is a tragedy. We will miss his steadfast protective nature of his people, I am sure. However, his death is exactly why I have seen fit to prepare and send this message to you. I have strong reason to believe that, with the death of one of the Caudillos, Iberia will shortly collapse. I am by no means wishing for this to happen, though the possibility of its occurrence is one I cannot deny. Were the Union to collapse, it would signal to the Italians and others that I am vulnerable, and without your protection this state would surely wither away.

Because of this, this letter has been prepared to notify you that our diplomatic relationship is henceforth null and void. In order to prevent an abrupt cessation of relations, we will instead terminate them now, in a prepared manner.

Algeria will fall under the sovereign leadership of Jean-Claude Pérez. All Algerian territories under Iberian occupation will be seized and reincorporated into the Algerian state. All diplomatic ties with Iberia are formally severed.
strings.IBR_algeria.15.a: We knew it was meant be a temporary arrangement...
strings.IBR_algeria.15.b: ...but after all, why shouldn't we keep it?
strings.IBR_post_salazar.1.t: The Link That Breaks the Chain
strings.IBR_post_salazar.1.d:
Past the mourners of Estado Novo grandees downstairs, past the housekeeper that stood silently weeping outside the room, Marcelo Caetano pushed past them all. He had to confirm it was true. It felt impossible, and yet as he came across the motionless figure upon the bed it was drawn irrefutably into existence as he held onto the ajar door.

António Salazar, the paragon of Portugal, was dead.

He had not been moved, still in his bedclothes under the covers of his narrow bed. Caetano closed the door softly and walked to the altar of all that Salazar had once been, the image of what once was lying upon it. The room was a void, years of understanding falling away. Every obstacle, every command, every function of state that Caetano had dealt with, here was the source. Gone forever.

Caetano knelt beside the bed, his knees shaking as he did so with rapid thoughts driving him from his balance. Sorrow, for who else had devoted themselves so to Portugal? Hope, that such a man had found his worthy prize in the next life and now enjoyed Paradise. Fear, as Portugal's rock had departed. But one thought drove through him like a stake, pounding at the doors of his mind.

Happiness, for the man who had caused him such difficulty and held back his efforts to push Portugal forward, was dead.

He prayed beside the still body of his Caudillo. He asked God to guide this hardworking, god-fearing soul into his rest. To protect Portugal, as Caetano's mind filled with visions of her enemies. But most of all, in hushed whispers almost unto sobs, he prayed for himself. That a man such as he, who would feel even a moment's pleasure in such a great man's death, could find forgiveness and guidance.
strings.IBR_post_salazar.1.a: If God listened, he sent no sign to that cold bedroom.
strings.IBR_post_salazar.2.d:
The gun carriage limped down the Avenida de Los Caudillos, with its procession stretching the full length of the thoroughfare. Representatives of the civil guard, federal army, Spanish and Portuguese home guards, and the Axencia kept the slow pace of marching. Even in Spain's heartland, the sorrow for Portugal's finest son was genuine. None of the many groups that terrorized Iberia dared to make its move here, lest they invoke the remaining Caudillo's wrath.

“Mi General, we are going to exit Madrid's limits. We can return to El Prado now...” Franco stared down at his personal orderly as to indicate any further insistence on the matter would get him re-assigned to the Western Sahara. Fearing the television cameras had caught the change in his facial expression, the horse-bound Caudillo turned his face to the sky.

As the funeral march crossed the Iberian internal border, the expressions of grief became more intense, entire towns went out to see the coffin of the man who had determined Portugal's destiny for forty-two years. Carmen had told Franco that riding on horseback for the 500 km would be inadvisable for a man of 75, but he did not care. Once they reached the late Caudillo's hometown of Vimieiro, Franco remembered reading about his appointment as finance minister at the last page of a newspaper in 1926, receiving his congratulations ten years after, fighting with him over Spanish intervention during war, negotiations over the Union, his mediation during the establishment of the Triumvirate. Franco's heart sunk in a way it had not since his youth. Now, however, was not the time for that. After his orderly was replaced by a Portuguese counterpart when they crossed the border, Franco was the only member of the Madrid procession left by the time he stepped off his horse to follow the coffin into the chapel.
strings.IBR_post_salazar.2.a: He checked his pocket for the Eulogy.
strings.IBR_post_salazar.3.d:
Franco's father had never loved him, yet another thing that had set the two men apart. Even now, his desire to be buried alongside his parents unsettled the Generalissimo. He tried to repress his father's slight after he had become Caudillo, ignoring him for the lost cause that was his brother Ramón. He just about managed to do it by the time it was his turn to speak.

“António... principles of national sovereignty... Great united struggle against the red subversion... decent and hardworking man with a sense of humor.”

Franco could not stop himself from thinking about the man: He had been his rival, a massive pain whenever he got any of his holier-than-thou ideas through, that was for certain. He could feel his skin being burned by the intensity of the camera set-ups at the cathedral as he moved on to finish the speech.

“But most of all...” The Caudillo sniffed ever so quietly, as the sentiments overwhelmed the carefully practiced emulation that he'd adopted, and his real, squeaky Galician voice took control.

“He was my friend.”

No one outside Iberia paid much attention to what he said, talk in the foreign media was all about speculating on what sort of ailment he was suffering from for him to be wearing his characteristic sunglasses indoors.
strings.IBR_post_salazar.3.a: Behind the opaque spectacles, Franco cried.
strings.IBR_post_salazar.100.d:
To be torn on such a decision would have suited the aging Spanish Caudillo perfectly before his rival for Iberian dominance had died. Now, standing uncertainly alone atop a house of crumbling cards, he wished the former technocrat was beside him. He had always had a clever comment ready for a situation like this. Franco could almost hear the faint whisper of his voice.

Yet he was alone, sitting in a large conference room surrounded by empty faced bureaucrats and lackeys who he could not rely on for critique or sound advice. What did they know of the severe strain put upon the Union by this precarious situation? What did they know of the Portuguese people's mournful cries and the significance these held for the future of this nation? It was on him to now hold Iberia together in the face of an ugly and unrelenting world. Hopefully alongside him someone to bring the joys and rigor of ruling back to the old man's heart.

“Brief me again on the two candidates.” The almost hushed murmur made many, even those sat close to the usually imposing military man, lean in to listen intently. A short pause followed, as the room was unsure of who should speak first. Seeing the dejection and quiet withdrawal of the man at the head of the table the discussion was promptly started nonetheless.
strings.IBR_post_salazar.100.a: A decision has to be made.
strings.IBR_post_salazar.101.d:
A quiet day marked a welcome change to the feverish events that had plagued the last few days since Salazar's death. Sat alone in his spacious office Caudillo Franco silently contemplated his choice for the successor to Salazar. It had not been easy, the pragmatic Portuguese had always been a hushed voice of reason that he could rely on even if he despised it. He would miss it. His senior staff had been excited at the opportunity to now further centralize the regime, ensuring maximum control of a population he might need ready for war. Or worse.

Yet Franco knew he needed more than a figurehead to keep Portugal loyal within the Union. His final choice had been the scholarly Marcelo Caetano, a protégé of Salazar who had already lived a long life inside the world of politics. His moderate reformer stance may be an issue that could offset the stability brought from securing Portugal, as hardliners may see him as a step too far in the wrong direction. It would be a difficult matter even for his eventual successor to contend with. He sighed. This was not a world that readily embraced the language of hope anymore.
strings.IBR_post_salazar.102.d:
A quiet day marked a welcome change to the feverish events that had plagued the last few days since Salazar's death. Sat alone in his spacious office Caudillo Franco silently contemplated his choice for the successor to Salazar. It had not been easy, the pragmatic Portuguese had always been a hushed voice of reason that he could rely on even if he despised it. He would miss it. His senior staff had been excited at the opportunity to now further centralize the regime, ensuring maximum control of a population he might need ready for war. Or worse.

He had considered the possibility of becoming the lone Caudillo of a Union badly in need of a more martial spirit. Yet with his age he may soon follow his former political rival into the grave. To leave the task of maintaining a stable Iberia, following Spanish centralization, to someone not of his own caliber was dangerous. Hence someone of similar leaning was needed, someone who would be easier to work with and who could be trusted with upholding Portugal's half of the union once he himself would be dead. By suggestion of his advisors António da Motta Veiga had been chosen for this role. A capable and ruthless politician who had enough experience in Portuguese politics to be an essential asset. The concerns of his possible ambitions were sidelined. Stability was now needed and hard choices will have to be made to ensure it. For this there could be no better man.
strings.IBR_post_salazar.103.d:
An event so momentous and grandiose it can only be compared to the pompous crowning of past absolute autocrats. Yet this was not some medieval ceremony of authority but a modern legitimation of a regime so wet behind the ears it has not even raised a single generation successfully. No one knew the importance of the appearance of longevity and peace as much as the Spanish Caudillo, who had taken the surprising liberty of inspecting the construction in Lisbon himself.

He counted the diverse forms symbolism he had ordered to be quietly included on the various stages and locations where the rule of the regime he had helped build could finally be stabilized. Pillars of society like the Church could not be forgotten in a historic event such as this. Observing the hurried tussle of the many workers conscripted from all over the union he allowed himself a small smile of relief. Soon would be the end of his road, he now just wished that his rival could have stood beside him in this glorious moment.
strings.IBR_post_salazar.104.d:
The reformer approached the lavish podium flanked by a seething mass of cheers and jubilation. His eyes however remained steady and pointed forwards, examining the deceptive serenity on the face of the man he would soon run a union of nations with. Hands reached out to grasp hold of him as others were swatted away by the countless security personnel which guarded the extended walkway. Admiring the effort of the Spanish Caudillo in quickly preparing such sumptuous courtiership of the Portuguese capital, he climbed the hastily erected marble stairs to stand beside the aging former general. Not exchanging a single word with Caetano, Franco stepped forward to the microphone.

His speech, a strange mix of honorable remembrance for Salazar and a desperate call for unity managed to arouse some excitement amongst the masses of Lisbon's gathered. Caetano noted the slightest hint of a satisfied smile on the old man's face upon his retreat to the back of the stage. Now it was his own turn to step forward. He braced physically against the intense din as he quickly shuffled the notes for his speech. Words of reform, moderation, and an ease of tensions on the half peninsula were almost lost in the raucous applause that followed. Did he detect a hint of jealousy in Franco's eyes when they left the stage together? No matter, he had done his part and he had done it well.
strings.IBR_post_salazar.104.a: Forwards, into a new era for Iberia!
strings.IBR_post_salazar.105.d:
Franco violently threw the crumpled newspaper on the floor with disgust. He surprised his personal aide when he jumped out of his seat with an energy powered solely by fury. 'Is this true,' he bellowed at the nervous man who had stepped back in fear of being in the way of the Spanish Caudillo's ravings and flying spittle. Hesitantly pointing at the briefing he had just brought prior to Franco's explosion the aide excused himself and quietly left the room.

With both his hands holding his head steady, Franco began to quickly read the report that the National Institute of Statistics was about to publish publicly. His choice as successor to the role of Portuguese Caudillo, da Motta Veiga, was being accused of possibly being involved in a corruption scandal. Further details could not be given yet as the investigation was just about to get under way. The accusation however stood there on the paper, bold and strong. The aging Caudillo groaned; it was not as if Iberia had not been facing enough problems as it is. Now what had been considered as the safe choice for the replacement of Salazar was in the process of letting him down more than his old rival ever had.
strings.IBR_post_salazar.105.a: Get to the bottom of this, quickly!
strings.IBR_post_salazar.106.d:
Despite Franco's quick handling of the press it seems the corruption crisis surrounding his choice for the position of Portuguese Caudillo has its own ways of expanding in magnitude. A regional paper from the north of Portugal has published a document from the National Institute of Statistics detailing how da Motta Veiga had seemingly purposefully adjusted some numbers to increase the level of funding received from the central government for a town he had property in. Despite the newspaper's relatively neutral coverage the significance was still damning.

Reports of da Motta Veiga arriving at Franco's residence following the publication's release were circulated in national papers. The reasons were however censored well this time, with reporters praising the level of cooperation and unity between the new leaders of the Union. With the issues facing effective censorship in Iberia it is not known how aware the public is of the still unfolding scandal. One thing is for certain, the new administration has a long road ahead before it can begin to govern successfully.
strings.IBR_post_salazar.106.a: Not good, but not terrible either...
strings.IBR_post_salazar.107.d:
Da Motta Veiga has been returning daily to Franco's residence. The Iberian national papers are still toeing the line, proclaiming that a great deal of work to resolve issues that the Union was facing were being done in these private meetings. The reality was looking starkly different.

Documents had been flooding, not just from the Institute investigating Salazar's successor, but other government branches and institutions. Under da Motta Veiga's watch an astounding number of statistics regarding Portuguese fiscal policy had been entirely fabricated. Now Franco's choice had been forced to explain himself on a daily basis as more and more information kept reaching the Spanish Caudillo's desk. Serious doubts were beginning to be raised within the upper echelons of Iberian politics as to whether da Motta Veiga could even be suitable now considering the vast amount of money he had lost the Union. Some analysts have gone so far as to claim that the losses have hit Spain in particular, further deteriorating the situation behind closed doors.

Following a week of discussions with Franco, eventually da Motta Veiga was forced to stand in front of the national press and proclaim that his inauguration would have to be delayed due to personal reasons. Ignoring the rushing torrent of questions washing over him, the now disgraced politician stepped back from the podium to be assisted away by Spanish security guards.
strings.IBR_influence_tt_salazar_4: The scandal and removal of da Motta Veiga will increase the Council's influence.
strings.IBR_reformist_tt_salazar_4: The scandal and removal of da Motta Veiga will strengthen reformism in the Council.
strings.IBR_post_salazar.108.d:
Caetano's gaze was captivated by a lonesome workman who was chipping away steadily at the name of the disgraced man he would now replace. It looked to be a tough job; the marble inscription had the tell-tale signs of experienced artisan work. What would he replace the empty space with? There was only another day until the plaza which had been prepared so carefully for the inauguration of da Motta Veiga as Portuguese Caudillo would be filled with to commemorate his own appointment. Something which weeks earlier had been decided against by the Spanish Caudillo. He continued to watch him, now wondering whether many would come to watch at all. The local police could surely procure some 'willing' spectators but what did it matter. The damage had been done.

Franco had put his name behind a man destroyed by the most astounding corruption scandal Iberia had faced in its miniscule history. The public, despite being force-fed lies and half truths about the situation, had been able to receive enough real information from local papers and intuition to recognize the significance of the horrible blunder which had occurred at the locus of power in Iberian politics.

Finally turning away from the worker who had by now cleanly removed da Motta Veiga's name, Caetano wondered how long and how much work it would take to scrub away a misdeed from a nation's consciousness.
strings.IBR_post_salazar.109.t: The Man with the Full-framed Glasses
strings.IBR_post_salazar.109.d:
Marcelo Caetano stood before a mirror, tying his necktie and adjusting his round, plastic-rimmed glasses. He would be lying to himself if he claimed to have never imagined being Caudillo one day. Through the 1950s he had been among the most prominent politicians in Salazar's circle, and in the 60s his influence in the Iberian Council grew obvious. Through backchannels he had made close personal connections to a variety of Spanish leaders, men like Manuel Fraga and even Caudillo Franco himself.

He had spearheaded the reforms to the Fundamental Laws that passed a few years ago, and he now hoped to work on other gradual reforms to Iberian policy. In the weeks leading to his appointment, he had his doubts whether Franco would select him, but trusted that his political connections and ties with the late Portuguese Caudillo would boost his chances.

Yesterday, Caetano was inaugurated as Portugal's new Caudillo. Today he would meet with the Council as Caudillo for the first time. It felt surreal walking into the same chamber as every other meeting, and taking a seat at the front of the chamber rather than hearing about proceedings secondhand.
