“I destroyed their kind once before, in more dire straits. Against men, not wretched bureaucrats. I can do it again. After all, they've shown us who they are.” A coldness seemed to seep into the air, and Marcelo shuddered. His mind conjured witty retorts, intellectual comparisons to Portugal's history to match his companion's brutality, but the words choked in his throat.

“They will pay. Dearly” was all he could affirm, both men staring into the death of the day.
strings.IBR_council_fate.102.a: Both men turning back the clock in their minds.
strings.IBR_council_fate.103.d:
“I have to thank you again Mateus for deciding to meet with us, we understand you are a busy man. An independent has no others with which to share his load after all. Consider the meal on me.”

It was a quaint little restaurant, reminiscent of the Gentleman's Clubs that used to dominate parts of Europe in the previous century, a dim atmosphere dancing between subdued light to active darkness. Tinted windows and old fashioned lanterns kept the room in something close to a twilight haze despite the noon sun outside. It was a place of privacy, the tables spaced well apart and the waiting staff concise and uninquisitive. A popular haunt for Madrid's influential.

“Save the bribes,” retorted Mateus as he began eating, “what do you want?” He regarded the man sitting across the table from him carefully - a fellow Iberian Council member who had invited him to lunch rather suddenly. They were simply yet smartly dressed, their voice light yet somehow piercing.

“We've seen your voting record, you have your own mind” the man said with a smile. “You've joined our members in many votes, members interested in truly making Iberia work for the people. An Independent's voice is limited, but a voice amplified by others?” He paused, a glint in his eye. “The possibilities are considerable.”

“We? Our?” Mateus placed down his cutlery. “I'm not from Madrid, just a small town in Portugal. I'm straightforward; I have little time for games.” he said, a tinge of suspicion in his tone.

The man affirmed. “So do I Mateus. This isn't about political skullduggery, I'm not in that business. I represent a growing group of likeminded Councillors pooling our true desire for change, nothing more. Are you interested in hearing me out? I have an opportunity. All I ask is that you hear me out.”
strings.IBR_council_fate.103.a: Mateus considered a few moments before simply nodding.
strings.IBR_council_fate.104.d:
Councilor Alfonso Gallego barely could contain his smile as he listened for the procedural call. He had been stymied at every moment to enact even the most basic of legislative reforms. After three long nights of thinking, he realized that rather than push for reforms to die in committee, he had to approach the matter differently. And fortunately, he had every weapon he already needed.

“Here's the final draft of the proposal, with revisions as suggested by the Caudillos incorporated. I move that we close the session and speed the bill on.” Canizales, a man who never had a thought that Franco did not have first, finished his perfunctory speech, and that was when Alfonso knew he could strike.

“A moment, Councilman Canizales. A cloture vote requires unanimous consent in committee, and we are not in agreement. I have here a package of amendments to the bill, clarifications on precisely what these powers are, restrictions and protocols. I understand that it is quite a substantive amendment, so I've taken the liberty of organizing a proposed schedule for hearings and floor debates over the next three weeks to meet the minimum required deliberation period, but I would not be surprised if it stretches over at least five.”

Canizales almost looked shocked, and he shook his head. “Floor discussions? Debates? Are you quite serious, Councilman Gallego?”

“Quite so, Councilor. All of these procedures are written in the guidelines for non-cloture votes. So I fully anticipate that we shall debate every single one of these matters...in great detail.” Alfonso smiled, and the look of recognition in Canizales's face let Alfonso know that he hit his mark. Every day of delay turned more councilors against the bill, as pressure for reform increased. And that pressure was all legal, written into the dry and dusty tome “Legislative Procedures of the Iberian Council, as Amended.” and given to Alfonso as if it were a loaded pistol.
strings.IBR_council_fate.104.a: A bear trap of words hidden behind a book of bylaws.
strings.IBR_council_fate.105.d:
“And now, I present to you, our esteemed colleague and revered representative, Doctor João Miller Guerra, who will speak to us about the state of Iberian healthcare. Doctor Guerra, the floor is yours.”

When he entered the auditorium, the neurologist could feel the electricity in the air. The Portuguese Medical Association and students both expected him to address the floundering of the Caetano constitution and the defiance of the reformists in Madrid. Surely Dr. Guerra, a councillor, would shed light on the reformists' path. Surely he would not just speak about a dull positivist topic: statistics on hospitalisations, infant mortality, and funding.

“I wish to speak to you about a subject of great importance to me and everyone here.” The crowd waited with bated breaths, waiting for him to begin talking about politics.

“Healthcare has long been hard to access for much of the population: peasants in remote villages, or the poor in cities, unable to afford the care they need. In the past five years, we have reported a notable rise in access to healthcare for these groups...” As he began listing numbers the audience knew too well, muted disappointment spread across their faces. The earlier excitement faded, and most tuned out his words.

“In light of such progress, some of my colleagues have adopted what I call a fatalistic view, believing we have done all we can and that no further advance is possible. I must vehemently disagree. This culture of fatalism and indolence must be erased from medicine. Healthcare cannot be limited. It is a right for every Iberian. Swift, decisive action must be taken on all fronts: medical, social, civic, to render healthcare a participative process that will include all affected in it. It must be democratized.” Dr. Guerra paused. The crowd was stunned into silence as they absorbed the final word...
strings.IBR_council_fate.105.a: Then suddenly sprang to their feet, giving him a long, standing ovation.“
strings.IBR_council_fate.106.t: We Do Not Belong to the Night or Darkness“ #Pink Pointes One
strings.IBR_council_fate.106.d:
The days never got any shorter. It was the only truth Tiago had ever found since joining the Diário da Manhã newspaper. Years of puff pieces and long nights, recent Council chaos making it worse. As he tiredly thrust his key into his door, he cursed. Below him was a package, tagged with a single note addressed to him. Something else for him to deal with.

He picked it up and entered the house, sneaking to the kitchen so as not to wake his family upstairs. He opened the package as he walked: a tape. No description or indication of what it was. Retrieving a tape player from the next room, he sat down at the table to listen, praying it was short.

“My name is Gabriella Vaz. I am nineteen years old, and it is August 3rd, 1963. I am recording this and sending it to you in the hopes that... Well, I'm not really sure. I want you to do anything. Whatever officer is listening to this, please, do something. In Porto they don't believe me.”

Porto? Officer? Why was an old tape deposited on his doorstep, much less one that seemed to be addressed to the police? He went to the kitchen counter, retrieving the notebook they used to make shopping lists. He needed notes; his gut told him something was wrong.

He returned, the woman having continued to speak. “When I was ten, my parents sold me to these women. They said it would be a maid job. We had no money, we couldn't eat, and it sounded perfect. But after I left, they taught me... they said strange things. Showed me strange things. Within a week, I was on a train to Lisbon. In the city, I was blindfolded until I found myself in that room.” She barely held back a sob. “The room with pink lights. We were under pink lights, they told me to-”

Tiago's hand stopped as she named the observers, and then what they did. He shouldn't have heard this.
strings.IBR_council_fate.106.a: After a moment, he continued taking the notes, fury driving his pen. Someone had to hear this.
strings.IBR_council_fate.107.d:
Rumors. The damn rumours wouldn't go away. Wherever they were slapped down, they appeared somewhere else. Alleged testimony transcripts shared on the streets. A supposed interview, conducted by someone who clearly knew what they were doing, with an accuser. No names, but distributed all across Portugal. Whispers about the pink lights' damn victims.

Marcelo Caetano caught himself, his stomach turning. No, not damn victims. He knew the truth - after all, he'd ensured the police reports got buried. They would have collapsed Iberia. It was for the greater good. Still, his gut churned.

He entered the bedroom door he had stood at for some time, calling out to Teresa. How had she found out about the claims? She was bedridden, who had told her? His wife shouldn't be burdened by such things. Such terrible, terrible things.

She watched him approach her bed, glass eyes asking questions. Did he know? Did Salazar know? Did they do more than know? He waved the file he had retrieved for her. “Teresa, this is the file. Baseless accusations against others in the government, so absurd they never got past a police desk. I swear on my honour as a husband.”

“...give it to me,” returned a raspy voice. “Children, Marcelo. Children!”

The performatively waving file stopped in Marcelo's hand. “Teresa, I can't, there's clearances-” Her glassy eyes focused, barely. A glare of disgust, distrust of the highest order. The words choked in Marcelo's throat.

He'd lost her.

She clawed impotently for the file and Marcelo's mind turned. All he had done, painted upon the face of his wife glaring back at him.
strings.IBR_council_fate.107.a: The truth would take even his wife, so he must control the truth. To avert her face, damn those men.
strings.IBR_council_fate.107.b: The truth would take even his wife, so he must burn the truth. The only safety, as ever, was numbers.
strings.IBR_council_fate.108.d:
“... can you believe it, Francisco? Four million liters of olive oil, I can scarcely comprehend it. Gone! We are in a different Iberia, one that's falling apart at the seams if such a criminal enterprise will strike even at the Francos!” Nicolás Franco grinned at his own image of wit, greedily chewing another hunk of beef.

Francisco Franco chewed too, sat across from his brother, attempting to draw any kind of flavor from the food turning blandly in his mouth. The meat and vegetables Nicolás' staff had served seemed devoid of anything enticing, a static flavor masquerading as fine dining. He refused to comment, his ears full of complaints, and his tolerance of the evening had stretched as far as it could go. How long must such an ordeal be endured?

“I saw in the papers, Francisco, the Matesa scandal? The real estate pyramid scheme? It seems so many of these things are turning up now, and they're throwing my own loss in with it, unbelievably insolent. I had officers making inquiries, but they were useless - I did my own, of course, and if you don't mind, I took the liberty of naming some names.” He dropped his fork absently into his plate's gravy and leaned into a briefcase beside his chair, retrieving a dossier. “I will give these names to the Press tomorrow, though if you would like the credit, I'm more than happy to give you the satisfaction.”
strings.IBR_council_fate.108.a: Enough. Francisco couldn't take it anymore.
strings.IBR_council_fate.109.d:
Fernando Herrero Tejedor looked over the Council members in the room, wearing one of the most luminescent grins he had ever allowed himself to wear. The Caudillos were absent, as were many of the most Conservative members. Given what he held, he wasn't surprised. He knew they had no answer, and that was just fine. There was nothing they could say anyway.

“Gentleman, I have fortuitous news!” he announced to the waiting Council members, as a projector was finished setting up next to him with an accompanying sheet. With a nod from himself, it was switched on, presenting a large image of a yacht. “It appears, per these photos delivered to me yesterday,” Fernando continued, “that Caudillo Franco's brother has made a miraculous recovery!”

With a click, the projector turned its image, showing a zoomed-in photograph. Sitting on the deck of the yacht, shirtless, wearing large swimming trunks, was Nicolás Franco, accompanied by many other men and women similarly lightly dressed and joyful in festivity. A collective laugh guffawed around the room as the Council members took in the look of glee on Franco's face.

“We were told that he was too sick to leave his estate. Oh, he was bedridden! Incapable of even lifting a pen to make a statement, let alone attend his numerous court dates to answer for the rather suspicious absence of millions of liters of olive oil from his REACE refineries. How we prayed for his health, and the Lord by his grace has answered by delivering him not to Heaven, but a party boat in Mallorca.”

The projector continued, displaying a variety of photos taken by the hidden photographer. Their subject unmistakable: Nicolás partying and consorting with nearly everyone. The laughs barely stopped, Nicolás' absurd figure never failing to incriminate himself, as Fernando looked again at the empty seats. Oh yes, they made the right choice not to be here today.
strings.IBR_council_fate.109.a: “I'm sure that I speak for all in saying how happy I am to see Nicolás' fortunes reverse.”
strings.IBR_council_fate.109.b: “Our Caudillos will be overjoyed to hear of the renewed fortunes of our criminal investigation.”
strings.IBR_council_fate.110.d:
The Casa Peco was perhaps the finest restaurant in Madrid, but while the culinary fare on offer was truly inspirational, what was truly momentous was happening in the smoke-filled backroom, where Valerio Campoverde was ready to make his pitch to the Iberian Commerce Committee, including their chairman, Fabricio Torralba. Valerio was nervous, these men could buy and sell him several times over, but he had something that none of them, even with all their wealth, could buy: a true chance for profit.

“The Vertical Union has been a drain on productivity and profits for a long time. Their work crew requirements are astronomical, they demand so many more people on a shift than there needs to be. I swear, whenever I see them, half of them are loafing, pretending to look busy. We would be thriving if it wasn't for those leeches.” Fabricio grumbled, with the other businessmen nodding and murmuring in agreement.

“That's unfortunate. Iberia has such promise that I hate to see it squandered due to such...inefficiency. I'm certain the mountain of paperwork that every industrial regulation offers also bloats your staff and wastes hours that could be spent more productively.” Valerio added, buttering his counterparts the way he buttered his roll.

“Yes, yes, but we eagerly await the Union's collapse so that we could actually work to put ourselves on a profitable trajectory for the long-term. Every other day they seem to come up with a new time-waster, and the government just lets them do it.”

“That is what we are looking to change, Mister Chairman. We propose that we maintain workers' rights through the Labour Ministry instead of the Union, reduce regulations and their corresponding paperwork, all so that we can reduce expenses and deliver better balance sheets. In return, we ask that you lend your support to our group, so that we can continue to bring Iberia to prosperity.”
strings.IBR_council_fate.110.a: Valerio and Fabrico shook hands, and the deal was made.
strings.IBR_council_fate.111.d:
A man who had fought the Republicans, Bolsheviks, and rebels, Lieutenant General José Miguel Vega Rodríguez had the career that most officers daydreamed of while reading inventory lists. Such a military member of the Council, with such sway? Iberia needed him.

Or, more specifically, Fraga needed him.

Such thoughts crashed behind the visage Fraga gave Vega Rodríguez as he sat at his desk, moments stretching out as he considered each approach. To enlist his support for reforms, should he appeal to a sense of justice? There was always patriotism, but that gambit easily backfired. He could promise career benefits, but what could he realistically offer such a man that he didn't have already? He cycled through the responses in his mind, trialing each-

“Uh, Señor Fraga? Are you alright?” asked Vega Rodríguez, an eyebrow cocked upon an expression of concern. Fraga shook his head - how long had he been sitting there? He went through his options again, time too short to comprehend. The philosophical approach, it would at least give him time to think!

“Apologies, Lieutenant-General. I lost myself for a moment. Today I wanted to speak to you about opportunities. You see, ideals are permanent; dazzling but unattainable.”

Vega Rodríguez's eyebrow refused to rest. “Uh huh”.

“Ideas, like running water, need to be renewed to be kept pure. So, I-”

Vega Rodríguez cut him off. “You want my help with the reforms? You have it, I appreciate the consideration. About time we saw some change, been a bit of a social democrat myself for a few years now. Who do you need me to call?”
strings.IBR_council_fate.112.t: South of South of the Pyrenees
strings.IBR_council_fate.112.d:
The newsroom had clearly been gussied up for the occasion, the stage lighting and camera placement specially arranged to put on a good showing. The white of his business suit made his complexion bloom like a bronze rose, thin grey stripes weaving through coal black hair. He had made his bones as a public defender in Bilbao, an increasingly common example of a Basque native reaching prominence in his field. This is what made his more recent career change that much more momentous.

“...because Iberia is a land ruled by laws, not doctrine.” The honorable justice Clemens Navarre concluded, one among a coming generation of Basques to be named a Judge and a recent one at that. “The only way in which we are to live by the mantra 'It's safe south of Pyrenees' is in restoring public trust, judicial reform, and legal review are the whole object of everyone in my district and we have no intention of stopping anytime soon.”

“You say you and your associates are championing the cause of an accountable and transparent judiciary.” The interview's responses were measured and direct. “Do you think you will face stiff opposition in pursuit of your goals? Many in the capital have what your colleagues would describe as 'antiquated notions' for their views on law and order.”

Once upon a time, the fight the interviewer was hinting at would be an uphill battle for the most qualified of law students, nevermind one as close to self-made as himself. Call it providence, good luck, or politically prudent, but Navarre's chance meeting with a Reformist member of the Iberian Council would prove positively transformative.

There he was, in a land that lived and behaved as the '37 war had never truly ended, hailing from a people who had been spat on since the days when the Gallion ruled the Bay of Biscay. Enter this gray-suited, gray-maned Councilor, one who was willing to take a chance on him and his cadre of Basque Country reformers in the hopes of seeding support for their mission in the high-falutin halls of Madrid.
strings.IBR_council_fate.112.a: “A great deal, perhaps.” He said confidently. “But I am not so fragile, neither are my peers.”
strings.IBR_council_fate.113.d:
The deafening crescendo of the road, honking horns and shouting people, filled the air of the highway. A baritone mood had laid itself upon the endlessly extending glut of vehicles, orchestras of drivers besides them demanding for the tempo of the road to shift. It never did, the cars remaining motionless despite the heavy sounds around.

Somewhere in the sprawl, at an indeterminate point on the southbound road from El Pardo, on the grass bank beside the asphalt, a line of military vehicles with a limousine sandwiched between them; the remains of an optimistic escape attempt. Most of the convoy had made it off the road before the limo's wheels sank into the mud, the previous night's rain having established the perfect ambush. Now all were mired, the soldiers arguing with the others on the road. Blame and accusations flew like confetti, but none of it held much meaning. It was the closest any of them had to a pastime for the moment.

Within the limo, two men sat watching the verbal melees and the static traffic, glazed eyes torn between concern and defeat. The Universe itself seemed determined to preclude them from Madrid, and today of all days? Surrounded by people they were sure wanted to go to Madrid to celebrate the potential passage of the Law of Political Reform, they could not find themselves more at odds with the mood. Half of Iberia seemed to be descending on the capital for festivity while they wanted to be in the Council Chambers preventing the catastrophe. Instead, they were trapped.

Francisco Franco and General Camilo Menéndez Tolosa looked out the windows of their limo on a highway that was anything but lonely, neither wishing to show fear. Thoughts of shooting their way through or dreams of bulldozers had long since been obliterated by reality.
strings.IBR_council_fate.113.a: All they could ponder was what was stronger: the Universe or their Council Support.
strings.IBR_council_fate.113.tt:
The Council has succeeded in its gambit against the Caudillos!
The Law of Political Reform will offer Iberia's a chance at democracy.
strings.IBR_council_fate.200.d:
“It's no different to that trigger pull Marcelo. Deep breaths, ease your shoulders and find your rhythm. The trigger pulling will be the easiest part.”

Francisco's words hung over him as he stood before the seats of the Iberian Council. His usual comfort with politics felt like, for just now, it was abandoning him. He wished he had written down his speech, it would have given something for his hands to clench to as he was caught in the moment between presentation and reception. It was cold. He was caught between moments, his mind alive with observation and introspection.

Francisco stood to the side, the Spanish Caudillo's face as stony as it ever was. Nothing betrayed those warm words before they entered the room, the man who had laid a reassuring hand on his shoulder absent. He stood poised and listening, age betraying the snake.

He had done this before, his social security reforms had required him to speak. Why now did he feel the pressure? The Council was known to be cooperative, unassuming - docile even. The question danced in his mind, avoiding the answer that danced behind it. Here he was, a newly crowned Caudillo, proposing true reform. The creation of a new Unitary Constitution. His Constitution. Rationalisations, simplifications and, most importantly, clarifications of the Fundamental Laws. Considerations that may well affect the members here - if anything would rouse them it would be an upstart Caudillo and his ideas, and to lose a docile Council in front of Francisco?

He called to mind the deer. How he had hunted it. The calmness. The success. The efficiency.

The applause. Applause broke the void of time, furious applause drowning all else from the room. Marcelo smiled, the power of the room infusing into him as he looked to his fellow hunter.
strings.IBR_council_fate.200.a: A single nod. The nod given only to a Caudillo
strings.IBR_council_fate.201.d:
If one woke up early enough, they would get to enjoy the beautiful sunrise on the outskirts of Madrid. If one was in a good mood, they might even become motivated for the day ahead. That said, if one was part of a legal team given the unenviable task of parsing through the entire Iberian legal code, no amount of motivation would be useful, except maybe a good paycheck.

Santino and his team of six other bureaucrats had been cooped up inside their office for the last two weeks, poring over documents in meticulous detail. The Fundamental Statute, as their superiors explained, needed an organized proposal for its final version, which was where he and his colleagues came in. Santino's task among the group was to search for loopholes, contradictions and the like within labour laws, while poor Felipe was stuck thumbing through civil and commercial law. Santino felt that Camilo had the worst of it, though. He was the one who, after someone handed in their work with the marked problems, had to go through everything a second time to see if anything was missed. He didn't really complain, though, and neither did Santino, nor Felipe or anyone else for that matter.

They just kept working, and while he didn't like it that way, he felt it was acceptable. No one spoke a word as they worked. The only sounds were those of pencils writing on paper, sheets being moved, footsteps falling onto the floor, and the occasional drawer opening and closing. Santino rubbed his eyes, suppressing a yawn as he resumed his work.
strings.IBR_council_fate.201.a: Sleep won't fix the Iberian legal code.
strings.IBR_council_fate.202.d:
Man was a creature of laws, and laws were creatures of paperwork. This was a truism that had served Gonçalo Lourenço Batista all his life, but it was especially true these past few months as the Ministry of Colonial Affairs was finalizing examining the colonial laws for integration into the new legal framework. It had been a long, tedious affair, but Gonçalo had worked himself almost to near-sightedness poring over documents, testimonies, and dry tomes to ensure that everything was in proper order. Much of the reference work was only marginally helpful, and some not even that. Ancient references to a legal tradition, vague references to putting down colonial revolts in Guiné, another pointless cry into the wilderness without a scrap of legalism to its name. But every man, even a paperwork titan, needed his refreshment, and so at half-past-ten on the dot, Gonçalo went to unfocus his eyes and grab a cup of coffee.

On his way over to the coffee maker, he overheard two junior clerks discussing the meaning between “jurisdictional operational discretion” and “discretionary jurisdiction in operation,” and a headache started to creep in. He had already been bogged down in similar problems regarding what was considered a “traditional law and judgment” versus what was considered “necessary and sound for the proper execution of the judicial executive.” He was definitely going to need two cups.

Gonçalo's headache briefly abated when he saw his friend Víctor Macedo Gaspar at the coffee machine, his mug already having the telltale brown marks of one which was clearly on its third cup. “Gonçalo, have you been able to tear yourself away from your hermitage? Here, let me top you up.”

As Víctor poured, Gonçalo sighed. “I need it. I've been trying to untangle these legalistic knots before the deadline, but it seems like everything is buried in a mountain of words.”

“Tell me about it, Gonçalo. I spent all yesterday trying to wrangle any sense of it, and I get the feeling they've invented wholly new words just so we paper-pushers can figure out what they mean.”

“I don't think it means anything. A whirlwind to kick up enough dust so that no one can see nothing is done.”
strings.IBR_council_fate.202.a: Full of sound and fury, signifying nothing.
strings.IBR_council_fate.203.d:
Most saw laws as simply a body of text, but for every word on the page, there were five revisions before it ever made it to committee, let alone the Council proper. Two men sat in a Madrid back office going over the Fundamental Statute, ensuring the paperwork was in order before the official text graced the Council halls. Gualtiero Diego was an old hand at writing law, and his counterpart Eduardo Linares had all the fire and drive that youth could muster. Between the two of them, their pens had revised countless documents, ensuring that they were ready for the Council's ready gaze.

“Señor Diego,” Eduardo spoke, drawing the older man's head up from his documents. “I've been looking over the referendum clause. I'm struggling to make sure the words are exactly right.”

“It happens, Eduardo. Pass it over here.” After a few minutes, Gualtiero gave a small smile and wrote a few things down. As Eduardo looked it over one more time, his expression didn't change.

“Pardon me, Señor Diego, but I don't think this helps. This referendum clause doesn't really seem to do anything. What good is a referendum clause if it has no binding power or even mandates one session of general review? It might as well be a...straw poll. Won't the people get upset over this? Don't we risk popular discontent if we include a referendum clause that does nothing?”

Gualtiero shrugged. “It's there as a token gesture. The people by and large fall into three camps. Take the people in the Union, remove all those too young. Of them, half of the population won't care. Of those that do, maybe two in three will just trust the Council. With all those who don't care, why should we have a referendum? Why risk introducing instability with apathy?”
strings.IBR_council_fate.203.a: If the people don't care, why should anyone?
strings.IBR_council_fate.204.d:
Benedicto Maradiaga looked at the empty plate in front of him, trying to swallow his apprehension. This could be one of the most momentous occasions in his political career, and his entire career trajectory could be decided over a paella.

Benedicto had dedicated himself to being the most exceptional civil servant that he could, and for a few years, that was the scope of his life. But after he found his niche, he found that he had a knack not just for bureaucracy, but for leading teams and inspiring people. After he had made a name for himself as a policy writer, he had taken a chance and tried his hand at becoming a political leader himself. If Iberia was to change, it had to have a cadre of leaders willing to work with it from within. The Blue Reformists had seemed a natural fit, and before long, he was shaking hands and kissing babies with a practiced hand.

Yet now, he stood at a dinner at Armando Tinajero's stately house. Armando was one of the movers and shakers of the Modernists, the political faction with the clout to make his dreams a reality. They were sanguine on the Union's ideals, they believed that it just needed to change with the times. Not quite what his Blue Reformists were asking, and a few had been skeptical and advised him to turn down the meeting. But if he could ally with them, he would be in position to make his dreams a reality.

“So, while I don't mind the pleasantries and my wife certainly appreciates your kind words for her cooking,” Armando smiled as his wife cleared the table, “I offer you something a bit more...tangible. Your faction has energy, momentum, and the support of the youth. We offer experience and clout. If you were to join us, we would both benefit. You will be on our electoral ballot, and your position as councilor guaranteed. Do we have a partnership?”
strings.IBR_council_fate.204.a: The two shook hands. Modernism would have a shade of blue.
strings.IBR_council_fate.205.d:
Rosário was reading in bed when she saw her husband exit the bathroom. “Oh, I forgot to ask, Benedito. How did your speech go at the union rally today?”

Benedito thought back to earlier that day in Maia, standing on the stage as the workers from here to Porto cheered as he told them what was at stake. Wages were first and foremost on everyone's mind, but he spoke of worker safety, work crew minimums so no one could be run ragged on a solo shift, hefty fines for late pay. After each promised reform, the people cheered. Benedito was their man, the one they chose to fight for them. And fight he did.

“Very well. The crowd loved it. I'm thinking of putting my hat in for the next election, really looking to see if we can do something, not just for Maia, but for the whole country.”

Rosário swallowed silently. She had her apprehensions about collaborating with the government in any capacity. Government always neutered labor, made docile dogs out of wolves so that they could continue to live like mosquitos on the back of their workers. But she looked over at her husband and saw that his eyes were as bright as they were on their wedding day. In that instant, she lost heart to say what was on her mind to the man she loved, for the first time in a long time.
strings.IBR_council_fate.205.a: “It sounds like a great idea. I love you, mi amor. Good night.”
strings.IBR_council_fate.206.d:
Caetano's voice bounced around the room, a pounding foghorn pausing only for the occasional breath. Constant, resolute, confident words reverberated into the very air. What those words were however, Franco cared little to listen.

The Spanish Caudillo sat opposite his colleague, a small troupe of advisors and experts around them. A departure from the old, intimate meetings between he and Salazar but an insistence of this new Caudillo. He did have to admit, it certainly made meetings easier. When his Portuguese partner got trapped in the minutiae, it was relieving to know others could concern themselves with the meandering. What was it about Lisbon and this problem, was there something in the water?

Currently, the issue was labor legislation. Franco had looked over the documents before. Nothing all that objectionable, perhaps a few clarifications to be made, but that was for discussions down below. If he concerned himself with every vague definition and clarification, he'd never leave his office, like the coffee stain on his desk that every cleaner had failed to remove. He'd fired many before accepting defeat on that front. Was that something the legislation would frown on? Such concerns brought on a migraine, best not to think about it, for the good of his constitution.

Constitution. A dirty word, taking him back to those hellish days of the Republic. A nation needed laws and foundations, yes, but liberal corruptions of that concept was a malignant wound. Fundamental laws, medieval charters, tradition and law combined - that was a foundation. Not a lawyer's legalism; their selfish politics, their degeneracy, their labor meddl-.

“This must not be a constitution, Señor Caetano. Any laws we make must be founded upon the nation.”

Caetano watched Franco's eyes return to emptiness.
strings.IBR_council_fate.207.d:
Three men sat in an office. Between them, documents that discussed the weighty matter of history.

Caudillo Caetano had demanded that education be made a priority, and in addition to increasing education funding from primary school to university, the Caudillo had demanded an improved curriculum that would prepare the next generation of Iberian youth, including education in history and civics. Desi Escandon, one of three men, were the final proofreaders for the history curriculum's chapters on the Second Spanish Republic and the Civil War.

“The Second Spanish Republic was characterized by chronic instability, as presidents sidelined the military to cater to left-wing organizations and divert funding to their interests. This, in turn, led to increasingly radical demands, leaving the Republic unable to maintain a functional economy and unable to defend itself against street violence committed by anarchist and Communist paramilitary forces. That sounds good, but I think we need to emphasize religious violence as well - to characterize it more broadly. That way the massacre in Oviedo doesn't seem to come out of nowhere. Children learn better with a clear sequence of escalating events, much like a story.”

Desi didn't say anything. He remembered his mother's cousin, who had been recruited into the Republican Army after CEDA had granted the landowners new rights and kicked off a general starvation of the South. That little tidbit had been written out of the history books. And when the curriculum turned to the execution of Republicans in Madrid, there were only a few sentences about “treason sentences being carried out.” Nothing about how he was beaten so badly he begged for death. Nothing about how his family had to burn any pictures with him in them so they could not be tarred as fifth columnists even years later. With the stroke of a pen, Caetano had seen fit to say that his family's pain never happened.
strings.IBR_council_fate.207.a: Desi swallowed his disgust and continued working.
strings.IBR_council_fate.300.d:
Francisco Franco disliked Marcelo das Neves Caetano for many reasons. He was a liberal snake, a civilian man with no experience or honour from serving in the military, and he was not even a tenth of a Salazar in skill and acumen. He did, however, agree with Caetano on one thing: the Council cannot be allowed to stray away from the state's hand. “Señor Caetano, I commend your efforts on the Council's work. Truly, it has greatly aided us in finding solutions to our crises. But as you know, it suffers from certain problems.”

“Of course it does, but this is nothing that legislation cannot fix. After all, the Council must be filled with experts to ensure it works efficiently. Who better to ensure that every man is an expert than us? We can review applications personally and ensure only the best, most intelligent, loyal men can become councillors.”

The Spanish Caudillo nodded in approval; this was a good first step. “And yet Señor, we must also ensure that they do not act too brazenly, even if we ensure their loyalty.”

Caetano smiled. “Indeed, let me tell you of some amendments to its structure we can consider.”
strings.IBR_council_fate.300.a: Iteration is the mother of stability.
strings.IBR_council_fate.301.t: Music to Stamp Your Feet To
strings.IBR_council_fate.301.d:
There was a new face on the rostrum as the Council members filed in for the start of today's general session. He was dressed in a sharp black coat and stood with military precision. A dark-suited conductor to lead today's orchestra, with the music unknown to all save himself.

“Councilors, I will be brief. I am here to inform you that as of the opening of the session today, the Caudillos have seen fit to activate the Trapdoor Clause, and that I am here as their representative to officially inform you that it is in force as per the law's dictates...”

Every Council member knew the Trapdoor Clause. If a majority of the Cabinet voted, any member of the Council could be forced to vacate their seat immediately. The Cabinet did not need to give a reason, and only the voting results needed to be recorded; a councilor was not even legally allowed to know whether he was ousted by one vote or unanimous verdict. No one had believed the official reason for the clause's inclusion - to remove Council members for sedition so that they could not imperil the business of the Council while awaiting trial - but most had simply put the law out of their mind. It was an archaic function of a generation ago, that no one had gotten around to removing.

The agent continued to address the captive audience, doing his best to hide the predatory glint in his eyes with a mask of professional dispassion. “All Council members will be closely monitored to ensure that they are fulfilling their role with sufficient alacrity and sense of duty to the nation and the Caudillos who lead it. In these troubling times, we must all act with vigor and speed to ensure our national health and success.”

The only sound heard in the Council hall was the staccato clapping of the agent's boots on the marble floor as he left the hall. Inaudible, a chorus of Councilmen had their hearts beating like timpanis.
strings.IBR_council_fate.301.a: The death knell of the Council.
strings.IBR_council_fate.302.d:
“Order in the Council Chambers!” came the stentorian call. Calling the Chamber to order could happen if there was a significant disruption, but there was nothing that warranted this. Councilors sat in their chairs, aides and assistants quietly clutched their papers to their chest. All turned to look at the rostrum, where the president was speaking.

“Councilors. It has come to my attention that there has been a serious lapse in judgment from one or more of you.” The voice came across as a stern father reprimanding his disobedient son. “I was surprised this morning, when I opened La Vanguardia only to find Council business posted front and center!” For emphasis, he threw a copy of the newspaper to his feet.

“It has been some time since I first swore my oath of office, so perhaps it is simply my age, but I do not remember Councilmen swearing to gossip like wives at a sewing circle! You are charged with the highest business of state, you are given a sacred trust from the Caudillos and the nation, and now I see that at least one of you cannot be trusted to act with the decorum that such a charge entails.” A loud clearing of the throat broke the silence as the president commanded the attention of the people. “That ends today. Effective immediately, all Council business is to not be disclosed outside these halls until approval is granted, in writing, from the central government. There will be no exceptions.”

The room was dead silent, not even a stifled cough. The air was thick with meaning, an incense of suspicion and fear spread from the censer of the censor. Fear from what would happen if anyone was even suspected of speaking to anyone. Something was happening in the high halls of Iberian power, and all the omens bode ill.
strings.IBR_council_fate.302.a: Councilors sat stiff in their seats, no hurricane could blow them over.
strings.IBR_council_fate.303.d:
The doors swung shut and the room, filled with untouched wine and barely-touched food, hung with a sense of dutiful purpose. Before, those in the National Defense Council would have wasted no time to boast about their accomplishments and whisper sweet nothings into the Generalissimo's ear. Now, these men knew what they were here for, and desired nothing less than to see it done.

“Good evening gentlemen, I'm glad that you all could make it on such a fine day. Now, would you all update me on the recent developments of your war plan?”

“Of course. Generalissimo,” spoke one admiral.

The combined general staff gave the war plan in military precision, each speaking about their service and allowing all present to speak. They spoke how to minimize domestic tension, achieve results with minimal casualties: a true lightning war. They spoke swiftly, with not a single word wasted, finishing well ahead of schedule.

Franco spoke. “Well, since we still have time, might you present me with the war plan itself?”

The council wasted no time clearing the table, laying out the full document of their plan. As Franco looked on it he saw arrows pointing to places he never knew existed, acronyms he hadn't the slightest clue as to their meaning, words so small that he still couldn't read them even with glasses. He kept his comments spare, it would not do to admit any fault before these distinguished men of arms.

Franco rolled the document up and passed it back to the council. “Everything has been answered to my satisfaction. Now then, let's call this meeting adjourned.” He then went to swing the doors back open himself.
strings.IBR_council_fate.303.a: He began to miss those sweet nothings.
strings.IBR_council_fate.304.d:
The rains had stopped, but the clouds had been remarkably stubborn in clearing, but Franco and Caetano had refused to delay their national address. They stood, Caetano in his coat, Franco wearing his uniform, to address Iberia itself on this monumental day.

“My fellow Iberians. When I look at the Iberian Union, I see a nation wrested onto the world stage and exalted by honest hands. It is a nation that stands proudly upon its traditions, which grounds them, makes them resilient. It is a nation that values its labor, knowing that it strengthens the nation. It is not a mere minor power, but a world power, bringing the message of civilization and honor across the globe.”

Caetano took the next leg of the speech: “We understand that many Iberians struggled during the unification process. How could it not, when one was created out of something that was two? Yet through all of those difficulties, we endured. That resilience, that tenacity, is precisely what makes the Iberian spirit so enduring.”

Just then, Franco moved from his podium, his sudden movement energetic as if he were a man thirty years younger. “Every sacrifice that you made, you made for a nation. For the idea and ideals of Iberia. When Iberia needed something, her citizens did not meekly cower, and pray that someone else might take their place, to give them comfort above all else. We of the Iberian Peninsula do not shirk the hard tasks. We see the young and the old, and we stand with our backs straight and boldly proclaim to our nation and the world to pick ourselves. To take from ourselves to spare others. There is nothing more Iberian, nothing more patriotic, than to stand up and say: among the entire selfish world, I am the one who can give.”
strings.IBR_council_fate.304.a: Headline for the next day: “Caudillo Franco praises Iberian Strength, Calls for Sacrifice, Unity.”
strings.IBR_council_fate.305.d:
“We need to ensure that we move quickly. We need to cut wasteful spending and procedural delays to ensure that we can allocate resources to more projects, and ensure that dissent is eliminated at its source to ensure success. Well done, gentlemen, there were plenty of great ideas here. Have design proposals on my desk next week.” Caetano closed the meeting, shook a few hands, and walked out.“

He nodded to the secretary who had finished straightening up the conference table, and she left, closing the door behind her. Caetano looked around his office and a thought crossed his mind as it had done so often before: I made it here. He had always thought that he could make something of himself, immersing himself in law and entering the Chamber. So many decried that the Union would be the death of the Portuguese identity but Caetano had persevered, guiding efforts toward integration. Salazar had taken notice. But when Salazar had a stroke, his future was uncertain. Franco, had he desired, could have taken over and sidelined everyone, but instead, Franco had met with him. In that moment, Caetano gave his vision, his entire future.

He knew that to maintain his power, he would need to ensure that the nation was prosperous. The people by and large simply wanted their basic needs met, and when it came to national politics, they largely cared only that the government seemed to be in control. The economy grew, the military could defend the borders, the schools continued to guide the young, and new things seemed to be developed fast enough that people believed that there were still ideas to be had. That meant the institutions of the government needed to be stronger and leaner, free of bureaucratic obstruction and dissenting thought.
strings.IBR_council_fate.305.a: And just like that, Caetano had become a Caudillo.
strings.IBR_council_fate.400.d:
Franco marched into the chamber with a look of determination about him. He stood straight and walked quickly. Whether it was true or not, Franco had often seemed the lesser of two Caudillos in his public appearances, perhaps because Salazar was 9 inches taller and many years more experienced than the Spaniard. But that was hardly the case today. Even if Caetano was of comparable height to his predecessor, he hardly lacked the experience or even the dignity. To even a casual observer, Franco appeared the leader, and Caetano appeared as little more than his meek servant. Following the Caudillos were 20 armed guards, a disturbing sight never before seen in the halls of the Palace.

“Gentlemen!” Franco yelled, still a few steps away from the microphone. “The past few years have been marked by nothing if not conspiracy. Whether it was the DI conspiring to occupy Barcelona or the ETA conspiring to rise up in Bilbao. Whether it was liberals trying to infiltrate our colleges or socialists trying to infiltrate our factories. Whether it was street partisans trying to destroy our government from without...
...or councilors trying to destroy it from within.
The Council failed to warn our intelligence services that anything was amiss in Catalonia, and soon Barcelona burst into flame. The Council has tried to usurp the powers of its Caudillos rather than aiding them, to transform the government rather than assist it. Our sacred Iberian Union will not be destroyed. Not by socialist terrorists on the streets, and certainly not by their allies in the bureaucracy. By personal decree, the Iberian Council is hereby disbanded.”

The chamber was silent, with shock and terror. Even men who were opposed to the creation of the council were astounded to witness such a sudden and dramatic shift. Those who had hoped that the council may be used to push for reform were downright terrified to hear Franco compare them to the DI. Was this the beginning of a purge? Forget their careers--were their very lives still secure?

The Portuguese ministers noticed something else. 'By personal decree.' Franco was not even acknowledging Caetano. Is this still the Iberian Union? Or has Franco merely conquered Portugal by pen stroke?
strings.IBR_council_fate.401.d:
The reports had piled up so high it was almost comedic, almost forcing them to lean over to speak past it. Caetano was the first to crack, angrily tossing a file in his hand. It slid across the conference table, stopping right at Franco's elbow as he leaned his head on his fist.

The Iberian Council was leaving much to be desired, for no matter how much they delved into the reports of the Council Chambers, it told a similar tale: Where it wasn't working directly against their interests, it was working poorly. Where there wasn't thinly-veiled dissent, there was obvious inefficiency. Where there was an effort by the loyalists to rein in their colleagues, there was just enough push back to render it inert.

“This cannot be going anywhere good.” Franco began. “The impetus of the Council is to give the Union an affable avenue for legislation, they have seemingly become the opposite. They were to guide our nation along a proper path for the future, now it seems to be careening off a cliff.”

Caetano nodded: “Every other initiative our men put forth, the belligerents on the Council either strangle it in the crib or cut it down to size as to be unrecognizable by ratification. This cannot hold, this can only play into the hands of the enemy.” For once, Caetano was being less generous in his analysis of the Council's purpose than Franco was, a rarity.

Caetano leaned forward. “I believe it is time the doors to the Council Chambers were shut permanently.” Franco lifted his head, almost surprised to hear his counterpart so assertive. For a very brief moment, Franco thought he heard Salazar in his successor's voice. Such a suggestion after so much effort to legitimize the Council might have counted as near treasonous not so long ago, and yet...

“There are indeed more direct means to manage the affairs of state.” Franco agreed, Caetano gestured with the point of a fountain pen. “We have been patient enough already. We both can see that the time has come to rid ourselves of dead weight and properly streamline the administration... as was done before.” Franco tilted his head at Caetano, not knowing whether to see this degree of commitment was out of earnest loyalty to his countrymen and a blatant grab for the kind of power once wielded by his immediate predecessor.
strings.IBR_council_fate.401.a: Franco realized such a distinction didn't matter either way.
strings.IBR_council_fate.402.d:
“The dismissal of the Council would, at best, provide only a minor short-term benefit for the Iberian Union. The Council acts as a means to channel political will through the body politic and into the halls of the legislature. While the Caudillos may be able to secure stability in the short-term by blaming failures on the Council, the unfortunate reality is that the majority of citizens would slowly begin to fear the escalation of political dismissal and the erosion of their traditional ability to live and act as members of their nation. Discouraged, they will be incentivized to larger unrest. The proper historical context can be seen in historical uprisings such as the English Peasant Rebellions in the Middle Ages, the failure of the Age of Enlightenment monarchies to stave off popular rebellion in the 19th century, or in more recent history, the collapse of European monarchy in the 20th century as infallible kings proved incapable of standing the test of time, awakening the world to new possibilities.”

Professor Ismael Valverde was excited to hear how much last week's article had stimulated debate on the campus grounds. To think, he could spend his entire life publishing research on great scholarly works, and yet never receive half the attention as he could simply by taking his historical knowledge and applying it to the modern day. Perhaps it was as simple as counting on people to be more excited about things happening now, but Professor Valverde had seen it more as the past coming alive. The form had changed, but the bones of the events were the same. As he walked across the campus grounds, paper in hand as he read his own work, he smiled. Perhaps in some small way, he helped cultivate and enrich the population. First, the students and faculty, but later to the nation at large.

“Professor Ismael Valverde,” came a shout in front of him, and he was stirred from his daydream by two police officers. “You have been charged with conspiracy to incite terrorism and creation of seditious material. You are under arrest.” Ismael, stunned, didn't move until he was jabbed in the stomach with the officer's club.
strings.IBR_council_fate.402.a: The waking world burns away much.
strings.IBR_council_fate.403.d:
A matradee stands amidst a sea of white satin, table after table that went on and. Officials and social elites from all over the country anesthetized themselves on flutes of white wine and every kind of culinary delicacy from Andorra to Morocco. Between the din below and the glitter of the chandeliers above hung the national flags of Spain and Portugal, alongside massive, gold-framed, stately portraits of the Caudillos Franco, Salazar and Caetano.

At the far end of the ballroom, a great platform had been raised with a lectern bearing the presidential seal of the Iberian Union. As the young man calmly passed along wine glasses from a silver platter, the chatter and occasional laughter of the attendees quickly subsided. Brief silence was followed by a rising, thunderous applause as Francisco Franco took to stage, his pressed tuxedo adorned with as many medals and awards his shoulders could afford as the speech began.

“My companeros.” the voice of the statesmen warbled with age, yet he sounded as assertive and unperturbed as ever. “You are all to be commended as humbled servants to your nation as unlike any other, your wisdom and contribution to the history of this union, and to Europe, will never be forgotten. I ask you all, in celebration of the men of the Iberian Council, to raise your glasses and honor them with our presence as they have honored us with theirs.”

Caetano was the first to stand, raising his glass as high as his arm would allow: “Patriotism without loyalty is anarchy, dedication without knowledge is madness. To each and every one of you, I say your work has not gone unnoticed; Saúde!” The matradee was careful to look inconspicuous while scanning the room, not wanting to offend as he observed the reactions of the men around him.

The look on the faces of the former men of the Iberian Council were muted, but far from hidden. Some seemed forced to smile wider than one ought, others nodded more briskly than others. Some barely offered a response and merely downed their glass the instant Caetano stopped speaking. Maybe he was thinking too much; It was well about his pay grade after all, but all this pageantry to celebrate what amounted to a bunch of aristos being temporarily out of a job almost seemed like the beginning of something decadent.
strings.IBR_council_fate.403.a: At least, they won't mourn a few missing cups of wine...
strings.IBR_council_fate.404.d:
Iberia was the Caudillos, loyal men of proven service that gave everything for their nation in war and peace and who held it in the most paramount esteem. Saulo knew that they were a model to be emulated, and so he enlisted into the civil service at a young age, holding to the truth in his heart that if he worked hard and held Iberia paramount, that he would surely prosper as Iberia had.

He didn't have doubts even when the Council clamored for more power. He had trusted that the Caudillos knew what they were doing, that they were simply decentralizing power for the sake of bureaucratically administering the growing Iberian state. When they moved to dissolve the Council, Saulo felt betrayed, not by the Caudillos, but by his ministerial superiors, attempting to grasp power and usurp the Caudillos that had guided Iberia to greatness. The results were predictable: the Council dissolved, the dissidents arrested, others simply fired for their lack of loyalty. Saulo knew that the Caudillos knew best.

Three weeks after the latest round of firings, an official envelope with the name “Señor Saulo Dimas” made its way to his desk. Saulo nearly cut his hand open with his letter opener in his hurry to read it:

Following the restructuring of the Iberian Union's central government, the Caudillos have seen fit to reassign personnel to positions to better suit the administrative needs of the Iberian Union. Due to your years of loyal and effective service, you are to be named the Regional Director for Development for Andalusia effective immediately. You and your family will be moved to Sevilla so as to more effectively manage infrastructure, agricultural, and industrial initiatives within the region. The Caudillos wish to convey their appreciation for your efforts and require that you maintain your diligence and discretion in your new position.“

Saulo was pleased, everything he had believed had been proven right. He didn't know what he'd be doing, but he was sure that the Caudillos knew best.
strings.IBR_council_fate.404.a: Loyalty is its own reward, but it pays in other ways as well.
strings.IBR_council_fate.405.d:
“Not going to lie, I kind of assumed this would have happened sooner.” The editor pronged the bravas with his fork, lifting it to his mouth. “Most could have expected it, doesn't seem to need much of a cover.”

The minister gathered a hearty spoonful of his callos. “It's not exactly subtle, people are going to spin it a dozen different ways and few of them are good.” The afternoon sun shone through a crack in the blinds.

His assistant was more optimistic. “The Council has served their purpose diligently, their arrival was meant to be constructive and their departure is much the same.” Delicately, he carved a piece from the corner of his tortilla.

The publisher wasn't the most convinced.. “We can maybe run something conciliatory; The folks in the chamber only did as they were called on to do. Madrid and Lisbon have plenty of office positions to fill.” He ate greedily, not wanting his gazpacho to get cold.

“It's nothing new, governments form and dissolve agencies and offices like marital affairs.” The minister replied, a distant AC unit poking through the window behind him, rumbling quietly. “Don't ask me how I know that...”

We'll do what we can, but we're not miracle workers.“ The editor plucked the bravas from his fork, chewing briskly.

The publisher wiped a bead of sweat from his brow. ”The national press outlets will cover for the government and the dissolution. People will be bored with the story in a month or less, no harm done.“

The assistant was affirmative. ”Madrid and Lisbon get to breathe easy and the Councilors get a brief vacation before their return to civil service, excellente!“

The minister lifted the brandy in his hand. ”Salute!“ He proclaimed. The other three raised theirs in reply, the wine meeting above their heads with the gentle clinking of glasses.
strings.IBR_council_fate.405.a: Many things in Iberian statecraft are defined by the raising of the glass.
strings.IBR_council_fate.406.d:
To the editors of La Voce Iberia:

The government of the Iberian Union wishes to convey their severe dissatisfaction with the recent content of your editorial section. Your criticism of government policies shows a remarkable lack of tact, but your rampant fear-mongering is contrary to journalism's purpose of informing and educating the public. Your latest articles have been noted by the National Commission on Print to be almost entirely false and defamatory, rendering the author and La Voce Iberia liable for prosecution under the Libel Law. The Iberian Union government, in its benevolence, has decided against immediate prosecution in favor of this written communication, which shall therefore serve as explicit notice to your publication of its potential legal jeopardy.

The government of Iberia would like to remind you of your patriotic duty to the nation, the necessity of national unity, and the conditions for your paper to retain its license for publication. Continuing on this path of publishing falsehoods and inflaming the public will be considered a willful abrogation of your agreement and grounds for immediate revocation of La Voce Iberia's right to publish. This could also result in the seizure of your printing equipment, fines, and prison sentences not to exceed thirty-five years should you continue to act in willful disregard of Iberian law.

If, however, your publication wishes to abide by the law of the nation, cease providing a platform for dissident voices to continue their lies and deception toward the Iberian public. Doing so will be a tangible expression of your commitment to the true mission of journalism and your compliance with Iberian Union law.
strings.IBR_council_fate.406.a: Unsigned, to better to show that they stand not against a man, but a nation.
strings.IBR_council_fate.407.d:
Franco sat at his desk. During the day, he could never have a moment's peace, but at night, he could be alone with his thoughts. Through steel and craft, he had come far. He had been lucky too, he could admit that to himself, but he had been a colonial army officer, and now stood as the Gatekeeper to Europe, built a nation with the bones of a failed republic, and survived the storms that had consumed so many others.

He remembered the heady days in July, the failure of swift action, which led to a brutal civil war. They had hoped to simply rout the decadent Republic and save Spain, but mistake compounded after mistake. Franco had taken Morocco, but the cities on the mainland had remained in the hands of the leftists, save Sevilla. Queipo de Llano had done his part, and he had been able to move the Army of Africa to salvage the situation. It had taught him a valuable lesson - he had to act when he was needed with swiftness. The delay that incompetence had caused killed thousands of loyal Spaniards. Delay could not be tolerated.

After Germany had crushed the British, the French, and the Bolsheviks, they were poised to become the masters of the whole world. And yet, Hitler turned on his allies. The Nazi economy cored itself out and fell into permanent recession as the idle Germans grew fat and decadent. Franco saw an opportunity and approached Salazar, transforming their country from two to one, securing a hold on the Portuguese colonies and ensuring rich resources. Franco saw a new truth, that a nation required constant energy if it was to succeed.

And so Franco ensured that no enemy could threaten Iberia and her government, even from within. The Council had been pointlessly obstructionist. Pride and ego had subsumed the desire for patriotism and nationalism. A nation could not thrive if it had a thousand heads each deciding that only it could drive it. The solution to the national problem was simple and endlessly complex - one man at the head of a state that knew only the love for its future and the need to succeed.
strings.IBR_council_fate.407.a: Iberia is defended by her most loyal son.
strings.IBR_council_fate.500.d:
Both men remembered when movie theatres were clumsy things, delicate things that projected bleary and flickering footage. This modern projector, installed into the old theatre of Caudillo Franco's El Pardo residence was none of those things. It was sturdy and resilient, and did its job admirably.

Caetano reasoned it was rather like themselves. Franco cared little for it, attention fixed upon its glowing output.

They sat alone in the darkened room, the projected image the only source of light. Thoughts of the recent troubles both men had been subjected to were gone, lost to the wine and images they were enjoying.

Franco's anger, at upstart politicians taking the nation hostage, all gone in the darkness of the theatre. They had besmirched his family, his brother ridiculed. His achievements questioned, the nation he had saved from itself almost thrust from his hands.

Caetano's fears, those damned leaks from those girls, the humiliation of his Constitution, all evaporated into the void around them. They had dredged up tales of deviancy to slander him. His work derided, as if the work of some common fool.

Obtaining the footage from the arrests had been easy, edited together for their convenience and pleasure. Franco smiled as Tejedor was dragged out of his home before his family, yanked away from the press microphones when he tried to speak. Caetano glee could barely be contained as Miller Guerra was thrown into a police van, along with many collaborators.

They had tried to subvert them, turn the state on them. Turn Salazar's creation onto them. And now they would languish, failed and ashamed, their treason leading them to their fates. The Caudillos had won. Both men gave into their joy as the montage continued, their enemies' despondency in every frame.
strings.IBR_council_fate.500.a: In the darkness they laughed and laughed.
strings.IBR_council_fate.500.tt: The Caudillos have triumphed. Iberian democracy is stillborn.
strings.IBR_council_fate.501.d:
A young Spanish secretary phoned his boss as he sat in the office next to him. “Sir, there is a man waiting for you outside.” For years, the look on his bosses' face had been one of terminal disinterest, the banal life as an elder diplomat, now a Minister of Foreign Relations.

The expression on his face was one of dread when he left, the one that came back was one of gloom.

“Señor?” The young secretary, formerly a young diplomat under this man's wing, heard the distant sound of an engine on ground level, looking out a window to see a government motorcycle pulling away.

“It is done,” The older minister said, his voice despondent. “Summary Relieval, Franco's own writing.”

The gloom on the old man's face landed in the young man's stomach. The words escaped his lips as a reflex, spoken softly. “I-I will help.” The old man shut his eyes, a small smile on his face.

As the younger man helped the older man gather his belongings, the life lived by the latter became more apparent to the former; family photos, diplomas, pictures of the two of them standing next to a car, on a diplomatic mission to the Dominican Republic. The foul feeling got worse; Had the young man ever asked about the life of his colleague? Had he ever thought to ask?

“Gracias, Amigo.” The old man put a hand on the young man's shoulder, a far away look in his eyes. “Show honor to yourself and be kind to your familia. Hasta Luego.” The young and old shook each other's hands.
strings.IBR_council_fate.502.t: A Stitch in Time Saves Nine
strings.IBR_council_fate.502.d:
Tristão Tavares saw the paper marked “Eyes Only - Burn After Reading.” He had worked his way to be one of Caetano's most trusted advisors - not for being the most well-read or the most well-liked, but because he was a man who could be counted on to do that which other men feared to perform. Courage had had him rise up from a simple executor to one of Caetano's most-trusted fixers, and when he had been named the new Caudillo, Tristão had become his right hand. Tristão knew that Portugal, and later Iberia, did not survive the first half of the twentieth century with platitudes - they survived because men in a smoky office knew that when he received a document that told him to burn after reading, he could be counted upon to do what it contained. And so, in that envelope, Caetano had laid out his plans, to blacklist the reformists in one fell swoop, followed by a list of names.

As he read the document, in his mind, he started thinking about who to call and what to say. He had to ensure that he said enough that the resources he needed were available when it needed to be carried out, but he couldn't risk tipping his hand. Anybody who needed to know would have received an envelope just like him, making plans just like he was. Anyone that he needed to call had to be given only what they needed and nothing more, no strings for them to tug upon that they might know. Tristão knew which reformists he could blackmail into voluntary resignation, which ones he could arrest with some mere fabricated evidence, and which ones would potentially prove troublesome down the road.

In order to maintain perpetual youth, a nation had to purge itself of bad blood. Men were possessed with free will and that meant that they were cursed with the freedom to make bad decisions. They couldn't all be Tristão, and that meant he would always be necessary. A man was less important than a nation, those were the wages of nationhood. The nations that forgot that were destined to fall apart under their own contradictions. His surety guided him as he called official after official, his tongue his needle and thread, and Caetano's grand design would be revealed.
strings.IBR_council_fate.502.a: Guilt implies weakness. Tristão felt no more than a tailor throwing out bad cloth.
strings.IBR_council_fate.503.d:
“So if I testify Pris, I can keep my job and stay out of jail. Rafaela is going to be two soon, and the boys are growing so fast we need new clothes every month. They know that my friends are far more extreme than I am; they know I'm a moderate. They understand that I'm just looking to improve Iberia, not overthrow it. All they want are the extremists.”

“That's what they say, Epifanio, but I'm worried about what they will do. If you testify you will admit guilt and they can come back against you later. Don't betray your friends; stand firm. You want to improve Iberia? Don't support them when they're at their most base.”

***

“And that is why I elected to come forward, because I believe in the promise of the Iberian Union,” Epifanio stated into the blinding glare of a hundred flashbulbs. The newspapers were abuzz at him, the most courageous man in Iberia after the Caudillos. The politician who chose his nation over all other things, the man who embodied the very best of public service. He was truly one of Iberia's most favored sons.

And now, every door that closed within earshot sent an involuntary shudder as he imagined the clink of a jail cell, a friend's face behind it. Rafaela's laughter, which had always brought him such joy, even now sounded like a sneering warden, laughing as he revealed who betrayed them. He barely slept, and he cut himself so often when shaving that he simply gave up. Food was tasteless, and whenever he saw Pris, she averted her gaze.

“I did this for us,” he said, as much to himself as to her, but before he even finished, she had wordlessly taken her plate to the sink to wash it. He slumped in his chair, wishing the seat could open itself wide and swallow him whole.
strings.IBR_council_fate.503.a: A pawn's lot in life is to be sacrificed.
strings.IBR_council_fate.504.d:
The lights of Valencia shone through the window, glittering beneath the night sky like fireflies. A well-to-do lawyer of local renown still had the aftertaste of carrot on his tongue, the straightforward yet masterful quality of his wife's cooking that had captured the heart and belly and the whole household. A splendid dinner, a happy family, a life well lived, as much as his madhouse of a country would allow.

“Dessert is ready.” His wife was better at putting a brave face on than he was, feeling a gentle hand on his shoulder. He had been washing the dinner plates briskly, stopping himself at the view of the neighborhood from his hilltop home, somehow different from the one he'd seen countless times by now. “I'm just enjoying the view.” He said dryly, turning to her. “And there's an even better one!” He forced a silly grin.

He could tell it was taking all her strength not to throw herself at him as she wrapped her arms around him. She squeezed tightly as he responded in kind. “Let's just get through tonight.” He said reassuringly. Moments later, they were both seated at the table, dessert served. The daughters giggled, the wife looked on smiling, he was mostly silent.

Maybe he truly didn't hear the first knock at the door, he certainly told himself he didn't hear the second. The third one could not be ignored, a heavy slamming that made everyone at the table jump. His mind raced as he rushed to the door, his wife and daughter's faces betraying all they could not say. Shaking hands throttled the handle as the front door swung open, and they were there, waiting. “...Yes?” he actually gestured to welcome them in.

It happened too fast for him to hear his wife scream. “By the order of the law.” Men in body armor yanked at his hair, and blood ran down his temple. “On charges of bribery, embezzlement, and government fraud.” Grasping hands forced him to the floor, twisting his arm behind him. “-are under arrest, anything you say-” Their voices, devoid of any empathy or scorn, were half-heard through his daughters' screaming as he was handcuffed. Delirious, they dragged him out, laying him out in the back of a police car, leaving him to stare blankly at the city night above him, the lights of Valencia glittering like fireflies through the window.
strings.IBR_council_fate.504.a: He could hear the distant sound of his wife sobbing as the car peeled out.
strings.IBR_council_fate.505.d:
Caetano had waited for over fifteen minutes before Franco finally showed up to the meeting, but even with his tardiness, the Spaniard looked neither remorseful nor hurried. “Seeing as this is your project, I will let you take the reins,” Franco spoke, flipping out a notebook and an ink pen as he sat down. 

Caetano kept his frustration under control, beginning with the fallout of the Council's attempted ploy of introducing an elected body into the constitution-making process. “Overall, the situation is under control. There are still some protests, but with the Council dissolved, it will only be a matter of time before their fervor peters out and disappears.” The Caudillo paused nervously before continuing. “Once stability is no longer in question, I suggest we move forward with making a new draft for the constitution, this time without the Council's meddling.” There was no reaction from Franco beyond more lazy scribbling in his notebook. 

Feeling a little relieved, Caetano pushed on with his explanation. “New committees will have to be made, but this time with strict oversight. I also believe that through a measured outreach to the public, we can also legitimize the new constitution even without the Council's involv-” 

“Oh, how unfortunate,” Franco interrupted, a large blob of ink having splashed onto the page. “Hmmm, I suppose some mistakes can be rectified.” The Caudillo ripped away the page and threw it away. “But there are only so many times a tool can fail...” There was a painful sound as the ink pen tip broke against the notebook, Franco having driven it hard into the page. “Until it breaks.” 

Franco stood up, leaving the ruined items on the table. “I am sure you understand.” Caetano didn't answer, but his eyes would not leave the broken pen for several long minutes.
strings.IBR_council_fate.505.a: The ink dripped from the pen and onto the notebook, staining it forever.
strings.IBR_council_fate.506.d:
The Caudillos' fill the grainy television screen, their voices smooth as varnished oak. “Unity is our strength”—the cameras focus on one of the men as he adjusts his tie and continues to speak—“and the Council conspires to destroy it.” The camera holds on their pressed uniforms, the national flag hanging limp behind them— no disorder.

A few hours ago, in a dimly lit room where media strategists huddled over a script, as one was typing it out. “Frame it as national harmony,” the man ordered. “The Council gets referenced only as one thing, as agitators”

The junior typist's fingers hesitated. “Should we mention the—”

“The schools they built? The strikes they prevented?” The man smiled. “Type what's in your paycheck.”

“Yes sir, I'm putting that in right now... Any other suggestions or are we solid?” As they all acquiesced, the typewriter clattered like distant gunfire, writing nothing but lies and half-truths.

In the café, the broadcast glows against silent faces. Regulars grip their drinks tightly. No one speaks. The silence is thick, and heavy. The Caudillos' words drip like honey, but the air tastes of salt and iron. No one commented on the officers drinking in the corner. Nobody even dared to look at them, while the broadcast ended with the national anthem.
strings.IBR_council_fate.506.a: The owner shut off the TV and went back to serving drinks.
strings.IBR_council_fate.507.d:
Torcuato Fernández-Miranda adjusted his suit for the fifth time in the same number of minutes, looking almost as uncomfortable as the interviewer he was sitting across from. So far, the questions had been casual, bordering on the mundane, but it was not going to stay that way for long. “Moving on to something a little more serious, if that is okay,” The interviewer started, Torcuato inwardly reciting the line that he had prepared. “You were part of the Council before, so I wondered if you had any opinions on the reform done to the Organic Laws.” There was a little bit of desperation in his voice, a need for some sort of hope. 

Torcuato smiled and shook his head. “I'm sorry, but as you said yourself, I am no longer on the Council. I am not sure it's of much interest to hear a professor's opinion on politics.” 

“You are a professor of law,” The interviewer shot back, gesturing to the camera. “And I am sure there are a lot of people who would be very interested in hearing what you have to say. What does the codification of the Caudillos' power into law mean for Iberia and its people?” It was a very dangerous question, even veiled as it was.
