strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_1:
Enrique Plá y Deniel
Alignment: Franco-Aligned Hardliner






£council_member_1_texticon







Enrique Plá y Deniel is the face of the Francoist church. Born in 1876 to a wealthy Catalonian family, as the bishop of Salamanca he was the architect of General Franco's crusade. In late 1936, the arch-conservative priest issued his letter “The Two Cities”, depicting Spain divided between a celestial and terrestrial city, which, in its desire to destroy religion, justified Franco's rising under Thomas Aquinas' conditions of a just war.

Plá even vacated his episcopal palace for Franco's use. A vital propagandist for the Caudillo's “glorious resurrection of Christian Spain”, he was made Archbishop of Toledo, and thus Primate of all Spain, as a reward in 1941. He has since worked to rebuild churches in the republican zone, and bolstered Catholic Action and Catholic unionism. However, when at odds with the latter, loyalty to the regime takes precedence.

Archbishop Plá represents the Spanish episcopacy and is Franco's personal appointee on the Iberian Council. Representing an Iberian pillar unto himself, the head of Spain's church hierarchy is tiring as he enters his 90's. Personally responsible for the church's alignment and strength, it remains to be seen what his legacy will be.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_2:
Manuel Gonçalves Cerejeira
Alignment: {getibr_portuguese_caudillo}-Aligned Moderate






£council_member_2_texticon







A good Christian submits to diligent service, even with the humblest of origins. Working with his father to make clogs, a young Manuel Gonçalves Cerejeira was able to send himself and his three brothers to university. Humility wrought prosperity: beyond his priestly ordination, acclaimed studies, and nine-year professorial career, he left the University of Coimbra with the friendship of a fellow student and opponent of republican secularism, António Salazar. With Cerejeira taking the See of Lisbon and being made Cardinal in 1929, and Salazar's own rise, the two friends formed a diarchy. Eager to mend raw church-state relations, the Archbishop signed the 1940 Concordant.

As a council member, Cerejeira will be both a conservative priest backing Estado Novo policies, and a defender of the Portuguese church's interests. This can create tension between the two grow-apart university friends, now grown apart regarding church influence in the state. Peninsular-oriented since university, the Archbishop is nonetheless exhausted by the arch-conservatism emanating from his Spanish opposite number. Thus, he knows Portuguese Catholicism's present status depends on Salazar's influence. The longest-serving living Cardinal will humbly labour for the status quo... with whatever energy he has left.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_3:
Benjamín de Arriba y Castro
Alignment: Franco-Aligned Hardliner






£council_member_3_texticon







While the hand of the Council and the Caudillos is heavy, the hand of God is heavier. The most senior archbishop in Spain, Benjamín de Arriba y Castro has spent his entire life fighting for the resoluteness of Christendom. From Rome to Toledo to Madrid, his presence is felt far and wide among the Latin Church in Europe, a presence which is now within the Council chambers.

His lineage is clear - mentored by Archbishop Manuel Arce y Ochotorena, who famously sat idly by as red prisoners of war were executed en masse in Zamora and who served as an earpiece to Franco, Benjamín continues to dedicate himself as the spiritual arm of the regime. To him, politics and faith are interlinked: the strength of the Catholic state is directly tied to the continued dominance of the church. Thus, it is no surprise that his most recent claim to fame is his success in repressing the use of the Catalan language within the Church in Tarragona, his current posting. Originally suggested for appointment by Franco himself, his service has been handsomely rewarded, and his career has come full circle; with a seat on the Advisory Council, he will now carry on his torch to the national level.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_4:
Gabino Díaz Merchán
Alignment: Neutral Independent






£council_member_4_texticon







To Gabino Díaz Merchán, politics has always been a fools' game, one rife with a destructive potential that knows no bounds. Yet here he is, appointed to the Caudillo's Advisory Council at the highest echelons of government, where deceit and power plays are the laws of nature. Contradictory as it may seem, his acceptance carries with it a defined goal - to keep the Church as far away from the regime as possible, leaving them to their own affairs.

The youngest bishop in Europe, Merchán was a mere child when, in 1936, his liberal parents were assassinated at the hands of Republican radicals in their own home. This scar on his life was healed only by the grace of God and the Church, and the path he has since taken reflects these experiences. After studying at the Toledo seminary and getting his doctorate in theology at Comillas, he has since found his place at the center of a movement dedicated to keeping the regime out of the Church's affairs. His distaste for politics was outweighed by his reputation, thus earning him a spot on the Council, a position he has taken with stride as an opportunity to fight for further ecclesiastic independence any way he can.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_5:
Vicente Enrique y Tarancón
Alignment: {getibr_portuguese_caudillo}-Aligned Independent






£council_member_5_texticon







There is a moral price for felicity.

Vicente Enrique y Tarancón's quiet ways belie the truth. Born in 1907, he experienced the tumultuous chaos which brought the Church into the regime's very heart. Now the Primate of Toledo has ascended to the Iberian Council as an archbishop, his seat dedicated to sacralising support of the Iberian state.

But Vincente does not drink from the fundamentalist cup. Even as his bones grow cold, his heart burns for his flock's soul, divided by the Church's politics. He thus sits on the Iberian Council carefully supporting whatever reform might reap some measure of liberty. Only on the inside can he affect real change.

The old man finds himself standing with Marcelo Caetano's proposals more often than not.

Many of his peers demur this as being too politically involved. Vincente retorts that the individual may sacrifice, but the Church must remain aloof from worldly bodies. A strategic exclusion of the majority conservative Church; a long-lost boyhood dream. The Church owes a moral debt it may never pay. Vincente nevertheless tries. He must try.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_6:
José Guerra Campos
Alignment: Franco-Aligned Crony






£council_member_6_texticon







José Guerra Campos' appointment is the product of slavish loyalty toward Franco spanning three decades. The Galician paused his theological education to serve in the Civil War, risking his life for the Nationalist cause and the souls of its soldiers. Returning to his studies, he finished his theological doctorate and received his priestly ordination in 1944, later obtaining professorial teaching tenure at Santiago de Compostela in 1945.

Memories of war have overawed his life. Campos is determined to protect his flock from the malice he sees wrought in atheistic, Communistic and liberal ideologies. A shepard's intransigence has landed him in the far-right “bunker” faction, named for their militantly entrenched devotion to the status quo. This devotion toward Spain's savior saw him ultimately become Secretary General of the Iberian Episcopate.

Now, Guerra Campos is Franco's man on the Council. From his high seat, the bishop condemns his young priestly peers for their waning faith in Franco's regime and its principles: Spain's apostle standing against Marxist atheism. Most useful to Franco, however, is the bishop's youth. Born in 1920, the young man has many decades of loyalty in him.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_7:
Pedro Cantero Cuadrado
Alignment: Franco-Aligned Hardliner






£council_member_7_texticon







Pedro Cantero Cuadrado, dedicated to union with God, became a Falange military chaplain during the Civil War. Advising the Falangist Auxilio Social in 1939, he pushed it away from National Syndicalism and toward Christian moral issues and the “redemption of the Reds”. Coming to the AS expecting charitable support, children were forcibly baptized, their parents canonically married and those of “bad backgrounds” had their children seized. Otherwise, he abided by Falangist positions in this role.

Made a bishop in 1952, and Archbishop of Zaragoza in 1964, he has reigned like a petty tyrant: suppressing religious debates and concealing his appropriation of ministry funds. Experienced in journalism, he has covertly published police documents besmirching worker-priests living among urban labourers infected by heretical ideologies, coming close to ordering the police against them.

Pedro Cantero's appointment to the Iberian Council merely extends his terror. One of the most pro-Franco and ultraconservative archbishops has joined this high table. He will agitate for policy to further unify the Iberian flock under his autocracy. All opposed to his “piety” on the council will face his rage.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_8:
Rafael García y García de Castro
Alignment: Neutral Moderate






£council_member_8_texticon







Rafael García y García de Castro loves books as he loves God. Ordained in 1919, there he absorbed an abhorrence of the Republic. In 1932 the priest helped found the Catholic newspaper IDEAL, which withstood socialist and Falangist vandalism. Becoming Bishop of Jaén in 1942, the experience dedicated him to drawing the youth away from foreign politics and toward a love of Spanish literature.

Ordained Archbishop of Granada in 1952, Rafael García's Comillas Pontifical professorial lectures were aimed at Krauism: First Republic-era doctrinal tolerance which he derided as Frenchified rationalism. Loving the faith of his country, the professor's 1961 acceptance speech at Granada's Royal Academy of Fine Arts began his unsuccessful beatification of Queen Isabella I, done to further synergise sainthood and Spanish heroism.

The Archbishop's appointment to the Iberian Council is a return to Catholic conservatism. Ambivalent toward either Caudillo, his priority is defending Spain against the hereticism. In that, he will level his intellectual might against the impious rationalism he sees in reformers, and demur with those on the dogmatic right as half-mistaken.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_9:
Francisco Maria da Silva
Alignment: Neutral Moderate






£council_member_9_texticon







Being an excellent seminarian, a young Francisco Maria da Silva was sent to Rome to complete his studies. Such was his success that he returned in 1932 not only as a Doctor in Theology but as a priest, given a significant dispensation to have been ordained at only twenty-two. Serving in his ministry diligently, he was named Auxiliary Bishop of Braga in 1956 and finally raised to Archbishop of Braga in 1963.

His close connections are not with high politicians but the local elite of north Portugal. Those small and medium landowning families rely on church officials like the Archbishop to reinforce their power and stability at the pulpit. For Francisco Maria's part, he is more than happy to harness his flock's filial affection and receive generous donations from the farming families in kind.

Francisco Maria's appointment to the Iberian Council is due process — the seamless succession of the senior-most Archbishop by age. Bringing his precise and heavy words to bear in support of the regime, the Prelate will support ideas in agreement with Catholic principles, politely reminding the Caudillos of their obligation toward Christian doctrine as a guiding principle.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_10:
António Ribeiro
Alignment: {getibr_portuguese_caudillo}-Aligned Independent






£council_member_10_texticon







Dom António Ribeiro represents a new generation, a changing of the guard. Born in 1928, his theological study and religious training were conducted in Rome and Austria. First ordained priest in his birthplace Braga in 1953, he doctorally graduated from Rome's Pontifical Gregorian University in 1959. A mere eight years later the priest was consecrated Bishop of Braga. Now, not even half a decade later, the bishop is the Patriarch of Lisbon.

The new Patriarch worries for the future. Ribeiro undoubtedly believes in the church's social role — guiding society through morality. Politically however, he splits with the past. Salazar and Cerejeira had been personal friends; the new Patriarch's contemporaries are distant from politicians. He sees a church —once gainfully married to the State — with its fate now tied to petty secular games. He tires of such squabbles.

It is with the dignity of a cardinal, afforded by his patriarchy, that António Ribeiro sits on the Iberian Council. He is aligned with Caetano, although markedly less so than Cerejeira had been with Salazar. This orientation is merely a byproduct of his true priority: defending the privileges of the Church.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_11:
Agustín Muñoz Grandes
Alignment: Franco-Aligned Hardliner






£council_member_11_texticon







A Crusaders' faith is true.

Agustín Muñoz Grandes led the Blue Division's forty thousand to war. He was an astute choice: a tough professional; a hard worker, incorruptible and austere. The choice was also expedient. A veteran of the Rif and Civil War, and commander of Campo de Gibraltar, he was among those Falangists pressing for entry into the war. The Blueshirt phalanx was a release valve.

Muñoz Grandes' medals were many. He successfully defended positions, won his men's love, and German respect. Hitler even decorated and hosted him in the Wolf's Lair. This was such a triumph that Franco had to bring the General home to be decorated in turn—and removed from command. Some whisper that the meeting with Hitler concerned ousting the Caudillo.

Sitting upon the newly constituted Iberian Council, Muñoz Grandes is content; Gibraltar fell, and Moscow passed under the knife. Reconciled and close to Franco, he is nonetheless a man unto himself. This non-traditional Falangist, among those top Spanish officers, will deploy his acerbic wit of hardline truths enshrined by the New Order.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_12:
Américo Tomás
Alignment: {getibr_portuguese_caudillo}-Aligned Crony






£council_member_12_texticon







Son of a soldier, raised as such, sent to the Naval Academy at 20, Américo Tomás's family is the military. After 16 years of active service, having fully internalized military values, prejudices and codes, he was made the navy ministry's chief of staff. Overseeing the overhaul of the Portuguese commercial navy during his tenure as Minister of the Navy from 1944 to 1958 won him great, lasting acclaim in the maritime community.

Loyal in his actions, a decorated admiral, Américo Tomás has little beneath that uniform. After Iberia's formation, he was only called upon to decorate the mise en scène of National Union public events with an admiral's uniform, given his inept speechmaking. Learning what his desires mattered to the seas as a young midshipman, his insipid personality has long been subordinated to an unthinking patriotism.

That loyalty is to the Portuguese half of Iberia and its embodiment, the Caudillo. The admiral lacks an Iberian mindset, instead defending Portugal's interests upon the Iberian Council. His appointment was arranged for this reason; Marcelo Cateano is sure Tomás's conservative uncertainty on reform will be trumped by his antiquated, defensive nationalism.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_13:
Alberto de Andrade e Silva
Alignment: {getibr_portuguese_caudillo}-Aligned Moderate






£council_member_13_texticon







At first glance, Marcelo Caetano's “A Choupana Group” conjured a stuffy, intelligentsia-dominated exterior. Then Brigadier Alberto de Andrade e Silva arrived. He has replaced Muñoz Grandes upon the Iberian Council and as Iberian Chief of the High Command; the stoicism of this son of Sardol has supplanted diatribes.

In truth, Andrade e Silva finds himself well at home with Caetano's thinkers. An engineer by university and military education, he climbed the ranks until he became a prominent name: as Director of the Institute of Higher Military Studies, Military attaché at the re-established Portuguese embassies, Deputy Chief of Staff of the Army, and publisher.

Thus, for Caetano, his appointment is ideal. Behind his faction now stands a figure exuding authority, his stern eyes on army and council alike. Armed with an uncomplicated discipline and the faculties to match the task, this stoic son of Sardol is determined to win the war on state atrophy. This pleases Caetano. To have the army's representative sounding your horn is a great victory indeed.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_14:
Manuel Díez-Alegría
Alignment: Neutral Independent






£council_member_14_texticon







Good soldiers take initiative. Born in 1906, Manuel Díez-Alegría demonstrated an alert mind in high school and the Academy of Engineers, graduating a lieutenant in 1929. Jumping to present himself to the Nationalist army, he served in the general staff throughout the Civil War. Through meritorious service, he was a colonel and Academy of Engineers director by 1958.

Frustration with Iberian military affairs arose among Díez-Alegría and his more meritorious peers. As national defence studies director in 1965, and now Chief of Staff, he heads those officers seeking greater military modernization and professionalism. Aiming at, by proxy, the regime's cronyistic system, and being not a zealot for Francoist orthodoxy, the lieutenant general is considered an “independent” personality.

Replacing noisy Grandes as representative of the armed forces is a disciplined servant of Iberia. Ever the professional, Díez-Alegría aims to reform the unstandardised, uncoordinated, administratively inefficient army ministry, alongside other similar ailments. This may offend rabid intransigents and content moderates, but the Caudillos tolerate him; the officer's political non-alignment makes him acceptable.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_15:
Carlos Iniesta Cano
Alignment: Franco-Aligned Hardliner






£council_member_15_texticon







Carlos Iniesta Cano has always been loyal to the Caudillos, to the State and to the principles of Falangism - but that loyalty has perhaps come with an inability to recognize changing times.

Siding with the Nationalists early in the Civil War, he achieved military prominence during the advance on Madrid and in the brutal urban combat that followed. Promotions and position came quickly, and with his loyalty aptly demonstrated so did influence in many right-wing associations. For many years he has served reliably and competently, ascending the ranks ever further, and he has been rewarded for such with a seat on the Iberian Council in order to serve as representation for the armed forces.

One of the most prominent men in the Iberian military and a reliable member of the so-called 'Blue' faction, he can be expected to support conservative and/or reactionary positions on most issues with sympathy for Falange views, as well as demonstrate a propensity for suggestions of military intervention and employment. While any dissent towards the State on his part is unlikely, so too is any ability for compromise in the face of any potential plans for change.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_16:
Alfonso Pérez-Viñeta
Alignment: Franco-Aligned Crony






£council_member_16_texticon







A staunch defender of the State and of a powerful military acting to support it, Alfonso Pérez-Viñeta has spent his entire career ensuring that the control of the Caudillos over Iberia,in whatever form that takes, is absolute.

A graduate of the Military Academy of Toledo, he was instrumental in organizing uprisings in Cáceres at the beginning of the Civil War. Serving ably thereafter, commanding regular forces in numerous battles, he was rewarded with political position in the National Council of the Movement. He has served loyally since and now been further rewarded with a seat on the Iberian Council in recognition of the military's indisputable influence in national affairs.

His mixed military and political background marks him as a solid member of the so-called 'Blue' faction, espousing Falangist and reactionary ideology. A staunch supporter of an 'anti-democratic conception of social organization,' he can be expected to work tirelessly in the frustration of efforts to introduce liberal or democratic reforms of any kind.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_17:
José Finat y Escrivá de Romaní
Alignment: Franco-Aligned Hardliner






£council_member_17_texticon







A long-serving functionary of the state, José Finat y Escrivá de Romaní, the Mayor of Madrid, has been granted a seat on the Iberian Council in recognition both of his service and the importance of his city.

Born to an aristocratic family and inheriting title, he was an unusual early supporter of the Falangist movement, proving his commitment both through political activity and later service in the Civil War. Following victory, he was appointed as the Director-General of Security. Executing this position with great enthusiasm, he proved his dedication to the state through facilitating the arrest and removal of dissident elements, such as the former president of Catalonia, and assisted in police cooperation with German forces during the World War.

Reasonably popular with the people of the capital, he is a well-known name within political and bureaucratic circles, and his position within the Council will assist both with its legitimacy and with operations within it. He can, in general, likely be expected to support the stated positions and intentions of the state and the Caudillos, in keeping with his sensitivity to the political winds.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_18:
Carlos Arias Navarro
Alignment: Franco-Aligned Crony






£council_member_18_texticon







It is only natural - and expected - that Carlos Arias Navarro be named to the Iberian Council. He has, after all, been one of Caudillo Franco's closest allies for many years.

A lawyer and prosecutor in the later years of the Republic, he aligned with right-wing elements early, and was a key figure in the cleansing of the Spanish state following the end of the Civil War. Signing many warrants of execution for those found guilty of treason, sedition, and other similar crimes, he was marked as the 'Butcher of Málaga,' a title not undeserved and which earned him no small amount of notoriety. His loyalty to the Caudillo ensured that his star rose as the State was further centralized, and he now takes the next step.

Navarro's personal loyalty to Caudillo Franco assures the State his support within the Council - to Franco's positions in particular. It is unlikely that he would support anything that the Caudillo is not in favor of, and further also likely that he will make sure to pass along any information that comes his way to his patron.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_19:
José María de Porcioles
Alignment: Neutral Moderate






£council_member_19_texticon







“The best path is from revolution to concord” is the slogan of Mayor Josep Maria de Porcioles i Colomer who, like many right-liberal Catalans, grafted himself to Franco's regime. When the dictator reached out for a mayor to test-run developmentalism in Barcelona, it was no surprise that he, the loyal Director General of Registries, was selected.

Porcioles restored the Catalan civil law, adding a veneer of Catalanism to his regimeist mandate. The mayor administered via delegates, his personal appointees, and obtained a municipal charter in 1960 granting him presidential-like powers. His strategy has restored forbidden Catalan cultural practices and bolstered urban development, and thus Franco approves of Porcioles' ambitions as a means of pacification and modernization.

The father of modern Barcelona sits the Iberian Council on occasion. Despite being the prototypical Catalan collaborator, his appointment was engineered by the ascendant Salazar to remove a card from Franco's deck. A man of independent ambition, power, and interests, Porcioles remains focused on developmentalist infrastructure improvements for Barcelona, and thus his attendance will be lacking.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_20:
António Vitorino da França Borges
Alignment: {getibr_portuguese_caudillo}-Aligned Moderate






£council_member_20_texticon







António Vitorino da França Borges is a military man through and through, graduating as an army officer from the War College at age eighteen. A loyal republican patriot, he was nonetheless integrated into the Estado Novo regime, aided by a right-leaning moral sentiment. With a combination of favour and merit, the officer rose from lieutenant to major, then brigadier, lieutenant colonel, and ultimately general.

Parallel to this was a streak of political ambition matched by administrative skill. Lieutenant Vitorino's political career began as mayor of Torres Vedras in 1932, his incumbency ending with admission into the National Union's first congress in 1934. Appointed mayor of Lisbon in 1959 following a governorship of Madeira, he presently works to better the Iberian city through a series of infrastructure projects.

As mayor of Lisbon and a key general, Vitorino naturally numbers among the first slate of council members. A loyal adjutant to Salazar's side of the regime, his interests mainly concern maintaining the status quo and progressing his projects. Thus he will agitate for greater priority and funding afforded his ambitious, and popular, development projects.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_21:
Fernando Augusto Santos e Castro
Alignment: {getibr_portuguese_caudillo}-Aligned Moderate






£council_member_21_texticon







Born 1922, the Maderian youth joined the regime's youth movement immediately upon its foundation, later becoming its sub-inspector. Armed with an agronomy degree and intense energy, Fernando Augusto Santos e Castro became a polymath — winning the National Wine Board presidency, editorship of the respected daily Diário da Manhã paper, and prominence on the Lisbon District Committee.

Empire and agriculture are key issues for Santos e Castro. Made prominent by leading the first investigation into national wheat prices in 1957, agricultural posts have dominated his career. Moreover, he is a man firmly committed to the Portuguese overseas territories. This, alongside an interest in modernization and political devolution, aligns him with the positions of Marcelo Caetano.

Replacing França Borges as Mayor of Lisbon, Santos e Castro has naturally assumed his seat upon the Iberian Council. Ingrained with corporatist and Lusotropicalist attitudes and values, the Mayor is comfortable with the Iberian status quo and his Portuguese colleagues. However, like Borges he is a force unto himself, preoccupied with shoring up Iberia's empire and wheat production.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_22:
Serafim de Jesus Silveira Júnior
Alignment: {getibr_portuguese_caudillo}-Aligned Crony






£council_member_22_texticon







Born 1901 in Évora, Serafim de Jesus Silveira Júnior is committed to the regime, body and soul. Graduating in Historial-Philosophical Sciences and taking a Pedagogical Sciences course, he accepted leadership of the Mocidade Portuguesa, the regime's youth movement. Only regime enthusiasts did so — seduced by the mission despite the position being unpaid; Salazar did not care for militias.

The work Silveira Júnior continued was in local administration management. Initially Secretary of the local Santa Casa da Misericórdia charity, he became Mayor of Évora in 1963, then Almada in 1965, making him representative of all Portuguese urban regions except the two largest, Lisboa and Porto. There, he has despaired at mass internal migration from the interior to port cities.

Marcelo Caetano, who led the Mocidade Portuguesa under identical auspices, has solidified his influence through this appointment. Silveira's predecessor Borges was loyal, but of divergent interests, a frustration Caetano has remedied with true adherent, sharing his prioritization of ideology over finances. Thus, while rebalancing tertiary Portuguese urban regions with the port cities, the mayor will prove himself valuable.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_23:
Leopoldo de Morais da Cunha Matos
Alignment: Neutral Moderate






£council_member_23_texticon







Born in Coimbra 1923, graduating from the Mocidade Portuguesa youth group and as an electrical engineer from the University of Porto, Leopoldo de Morais da Cunha Matos now sits upon the Iberian Council. Ingrained with political Catholicism, he has led provincial chapters of Church and charity organizations, such as Catholic Action, the Portuguese Red Cross, and the Society of St. Vincent de Paul.

Leopoldo Morais' sits representing the Iberian rural communities. Since rising from Coimbra's chief engineer to Coimbra's regional governorship and Viseu's mayoralty, he has become the leading force of the rural municipalities, working together to end their troubles. As mass exodus, an outdated sector, and government neglect is a Pan-Iberian issue, these conversations have extended as such.

The appointment of Leopoldo Morais is a loss for Caetano. Franco has seen to it that the council member for Portuguese settlements is “truly Iberian”, not exclusively beholden to Caetano. Nor is he a “cheerer” or associate of the New Union, quietly minding Catholic organizations independent of the regime. Losing a once-safe seat, Caetano consoles himself that competence often replaces blind loyalty.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_24:
Segismundo Royo-Villanova y Fernández Cavada
Alignment: Franco-Aligned Moderate






£council_member_24_texticon







Scion of a Monarchist statesman turned right-republican minister, Segismundo Royo-Villanova y Fernández Cavada's loyalties are to institutions, not ideologies or personages. Previously an undersecretary in the Ministry of Education, now dean of the University of Madrid, he has dedicated his life to fostering intellection, a commitment that's sincerity is evidenced by his strenuous exception to the intervention of police and gendarmerie in what he considers internal matters of the academy.

Within these institutional loyalties rest ostensible contradictions; the regime of which he is a partisan was established and is sustained by force, yet he is — without a doubt — committed to the life of the mind. Royo-Villanova appears to have inherited — from his father — what could charitably be termed ideological flexibility, yet appears to possess a genuine respect for those who persist stubbornly in their convictions.

Whether — or whether not — these seeming contradictions can be reconciled is, in all likelihood, irrelevant. Perhaps, given the times in which he lives, they may even be politically expedient.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_25:
Fernando de Andrade Pires de Lima
Alignment: {getibr_portuguese_caudillo}-Aligned Crony






£council_member_25_texticon







As an escapee of rural poverty, Fernando de Andrade Pires de Lima is resolute in his war against the educational vices of the countryside. Each pitched battle saw victories, becoming a doctor in law in 1930 at the University of Coimbra, then full professor there in 1942. Still, there existed a vehicle whose power truly matched the professor's ambitions: the state; the Estado Novo.

Slowly but surely, he seeped into a government career. He joined the committees working to reform juvenile court services and the Civil Code in 1944 and 1945 respectively. Andrade's important contributions to both efforts were the genesis of a distinguished career in the justice and education ministries. Naming 26 professors for their, “democratic views” saw loyalty and competence as noted virtues.

All good Iberians should know the history of treason. Andrade does; of how the modern state is owed everything, and how everything depends on its legitimization, even one's name. And yet, so few Portuguese can spell that name. Upon the Iberian Council, he will prove devout in his devotion to the man who backed his campaigns against Portuguese illiteracy — António Salazar, a fellow professor at the state's helm.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_26:
Francisco de Paula Leite Pinto
Alignment: {getibr_portuguese_caudillo}-Aligned Moderate






£council_member_26_texticon







At an age where most men would be contemplating retirement, Francisco de Paula Leite Pinto has shown no signs of slowing down. Born in 1902 in Lisbon, Francisco was always a quick study. He studied Mathematics at the University of Lisbon before heading to France. There he earned degrees in Civil Engineering and Astronomy from the University of Paris before earning his doctorate in Astrophysics. Francisco has had a long and distinguished academic career, founding the Iberian Mathematics Society while simultaneously teaching at both the Iberian Army School and the Superior Institute of Economics and Finance, authoring countless papers on a variety of scientific disciplines.

Francisco coupled his academic career with one devoted to public service. He was the Portuguese Secretary-General of the Transportation Board from 1934-1939 and held multiple posts in the Ministry of Education. In 1949, he founded the Nuclear Energy Study Commission, headed the Nuclear Energy Board, and remains one of the most vocal proponents for Iberian nuclear energy. A true believer in the virtues of science as an uplifting and worthwhile vocation, Francisco does not belong to a political faction, but acts on the Council to promote Iberian scientific pursuits and research interests.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_27:
António Jorge Andrade de Gouveia
Alignment: Neutral Moderate






£council_member_27_texticon







António Jorge Andrade de Gouveia, born in 1905, enrolled in the University of Coimbra's Faculty of Science in 1922. Even before his 1926 Physical and Chemical Sciences graduation, he was the Faculty's first secretary by 1925. He completed a Parisian internship under chemists such as Marie Curie, and went to the University of Liverpool in 1931, gaining his in 1934.

Conferring an equivalent doctorate upon his return in 1935, the University of Coimbra recognized his skill and made him a full professor of sciences. Becoming full professor of chemistry in 1944 and rising from science faculty director to Coimbra's rector in 1963, António Jorge's leadership of Portugal's prevailing university has paid off. For the first time, Iberian academia is represented by a Portuguese man on the Iberian Council.

A celebrated luminary, lacking political experience beyond National Education board and high education committee membership, António Jorge will not rock the boat. The rector is a compromise candidate; replacing his Francoist predecessor, he will defer to the majority opinion, offer advice on national science and pedagogy, and otherwise keep his head down. Such a man satisfies both Caudillos.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_28:
José Ibáñez Martín
Alignment: Franco-Aligned Hardliner






£council_member_28_texticon







José Ibáñez Martín's whole life has been dedicated to service. His political trajectory before the Civil War — traveling through the Miguel de Rivera's Patriotic Party, National Catholic Association of Propagandists, Acción Española, and the Spanish Confederation of Autonomous Rights — led him to serve the Nationalists. Spending the Civil War drumming up support for Franco throughout Argentina, Chile, Peru, and Brazil, his peers named him a sycophant to the Caudillo.

Franco rewarded this fidelity, making him Minister of Education until the Falangists fell from institutional favor as Iberia distanced itself from Germany and Martín's Catholic political family consequently rose. Highly reactionary in his faith, the Aragonese politician leveraged this towards his efforts to further Catholicize education and academic research.

Martín serves faithfully, in every sense of the word, on the Iberian Council. The Professor, co-founding President of the Spanish National Research Council, lectures against “egalitarian scientific heresies” that brought Iberia to the “decadent abyss”. In that, he is Franco's cudgel against liberal reformers, for as long as there is life in the aged believer.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_29:
Jesús Fueyo Álvarez
Alignment: Franco-Aligned Crony






£council_member_29_texticon







Jesús Fueyo Álvarez entered university imbued with familial traditionalist Catholicism, and left a changed man. Early in his law studies, he attended the seminars of Nazi jurist Carl Schmitt. Having graduated in 1953, and despite being made the national delegate for Press and Radio by his monarchist peers in 1957, Schmitt had molded him, leaving his faith teetering. He soon fell in love with Falangist thought.

By then, Falangism hindered one's rise within Iberia's halls of power. Álvarez's intransigence made his career advancement a bitter fight. Ultimately defeating the moderate Arias Navarro to become director of the Institute of Political Studies in 1962, his rise was due to his uncritical loyalty. While most Falangists level careful criticism against the regime, Schmitt's disciple sees a Total State with a Caudillo with a Power of Decision worth fighting for.

Álvarez's appointment is a coup for the regime's far-right. Where once a politely critical voice sat, there is now a glorified loudspeaker of Falangism. Moreover, it is a coup for Franco. An official theorist of the State, the lawyer will shout down criticism of Franco's regime and provide it legal advice with equal ardor.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_30:
Florentino Pérez Embid
Alignment: Franco-Aligned Hardliner






£council_member_30_texticon







Florentino Pérez Embid is a prominent figure in the Iberian Union's government, though it may not appear so at first glance. A deeply conservative traditionalist, he is a committed member of Opus Dei, holding strong religious beliefs and dedication to preserving the moral and cultural fabric of the nation. His influence within the regime takes on a more lowkey form, particularly in shaping its stance on censorship and propaganda

An accomplished historian prior to his current position, Pérez Embid focused his academic work on the history of the Discovery and Conquest of the Americas, gaining recognition for his scholarly contributions. Soon transitioning to serving as the director of propaganda and information in Francoist Spain, he played a significant role in shaping the regime's narrative and controlling the flow of information to the public. His efforts to maintain ideological purity through censorship have naturally transitioned over to the new political climate of the Iberian Union, where he continues to be a central figure in shaping the Dual Caudillos' cultural policies.

Now, as the Director of Fine Arts, Pérez Embid oversees the cultural landscape of the regime, ensuring that normally progressive artistic expression remains aligned with the traditional values upheld by the government.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_31:
José Luis Villar Palasí
Alignment: Neutral Moderate






£council_member_31_texticon







José Luis Villar Palasí stands out as a key intellectual and reformer within the Iberian Union's government. His career spans various high-ranking roles, from the Ministry of Commerce to the Ministry of Information and Tourism, before becoming the current driving force behind educational reform. With a background in law and history, Villar Palasí's sharp mind and administrative skills propelled him to numerous leadership positions, where his influence has been felt one way or another.

Now serving on the Iberian Council, Villar Palasí is pushing for sweeping reforms to modernize the nation's educational system. His vision is ambitious: raising the age for compulsory education, revamping outdated curricula, and ensuring the system can accommodate the rapidly growing number of students. As part of the regime's efforts to project strength and progress, his focus on education serves both to cultivate a more skilled workforce and to reinforce state ideology through schooling.

Known for his pragmatic approach, Villar Palasí is a figure who blends technocratic efficiency with a deep belief in the role of education in shaping the future of the Iberian Union. His reforms are seen as critical to maintaining the country's economic and political stability, and there is no doubt he will remain a central figure in the regime's efforts to adapt to the challenges of the modern world.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_32:
Alfredo Sánchez Bella
Alignment: Franco-Aligned Moderate






£council_member_32_texticon







Imprisoned by Republican authorities in the days of Civil War, Alfredo Sánchez Bella's loyalty and dedication has now paid off as he emerges an influential figure within the Iberian Union. A staunch Catholic, Sánchez Bella is closely affiliated with Opus Dei and other Catholic organizations, shaping his traditionalist and conservative worldview. His career consists of numerous cultural and diplomatic posts, making him a key figure in shaping the cultural and informational policies of the regime. His diplomatic service includes roles as ambassador to countries like the Dominican Republic and Italy, where he strengthened Iberian image abroad.

In his current position on the Iberian Council, Sánchez Bella holds significant influence within the Ministry of Information and Tourism. His efforts are directed toward balancing the growth of Iberia's tourism industry with the preservation of its coastal regions, ensuring the country remains an attractive destination while protecting its natural beauty. A seasoned propagandist, he continues to apply strict control over the press, maintaining a tight grip on what is permissible in line with the regime's ideals. His conservative Catholic values are evident in every decision he makes, from diplomatic relations to tourism policy, and he will help steer Iberia through the challenges of the decade, the ever loyal son that he is.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_33:
José Veiga Simão
Alignment: {getibr_portuguese_caudillo}-Aligned Independent






£council_member_33_texticon







Born 1926, graduating in Physical and Chemical studies, receiving a PhD in Nuclear Physics, and already a full professor at the University of Coimbra at just 31 years old, José Veiga Simão is a civic patriot of brilliant intelligence. This astonishing ascent brought him to António Salazar's attention, who asked him to help build the Lourenço Marques University in Mozambique, becoming its rector.

All the while, Veiga found a common cause with Marcelo Caetano: education reform. The Professor's slogan is his civilizing mission, “Educate all Iberians”. A drive to open education, improving its breadth and depth, is shared with the Caudillo. Defending his ideas as the “condition of national survival” has endeared him to developmentalists, who have propelled him high within the education ministry.

Learning from granite through his nuclear studies, Veiga Simão will not bend. Free-thinking, the reformist aiming towards an individualistic right to education now sits among corporatists. Empowered and protected by Caetano's clique of university students, the Professor will be a well from which education initiatives keeping Iberia abreast Europe will be drawn.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_34:
Joaquim Veríssimo Serrão
Alignment: {getibr_portuguese_caudillo}-Aligned Crony






£council_member_34_texticon







Loyalty, an important quality for political appointees, is possessed in such an abundance by Joaquim Veríssimo Serrão that he appears to possess little else. Representing the Union's academia despite having never been a university rector or dean, some grumble he is merely Marcelo Caetano's chief lickspittle.

A nepotistic appointment by way of Caetano's friendship, Joaquim is nevertheless an eminent scholar. Made a professor of letters at the University of Lisbon in 1965, love of Ibero-American history has made a passionate Union enthusiast out of him. In the professor, Caetano also has a dedicated biographer, sure to write of him favourably in his ongoing many-volumed histories of Portugal.

Joaquim Veríssimo is effectively Caetano's man on the council. Brimming with gratitude at his appointment, giving the historian a front-row seat to the pan-Iberian relations that excite him so, he will be a faithful ally. The nepotistic appointment of a glorified hagiographer signals Caetano's confidence and strong opening hand; a personal friend of Caetano and de Sousa, the professor will never betray their agenda.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_35:
Manuel Augusto José de Mello
Alignment: {getibr_portuguese_caudillo}-Aligned Moderate






£council_member_35_texticon







Born to a wealthy family first ennobled by Philip IV and III, Manuel Augusto José de Mello has Iberia in his blue blood. Conscripted to fight on the Western Front in 1917, a marriage was arranged with Amélia da Silva, only daughter of Alfredo da Silva, founder of the Union Factory Company (CUF) and Portugal's greatest industrialist. In 1919, at age 24, Manuel de Mello's new father-in-law took him on, asking “Are you also married to the CUF?” The answer was implicit; inheriting the CUF at age 47, his work crowned him Portugal's king of industry.

Inheriting the family motto, “The Mellos don't talk much”, Manuel de Mello brings his calm moderation to the Iberian Council. The industrialist can be expected to tack Salazar's way. The CUF has become the greatest Portuguese employer and exporter, the conglomerate's vertically dominant presence in banking, chemicals, naval construction, and cement ranging across the Portuguese Empire. This zaibatsu-esque status, and his place among Iberia's leading businessmen, is largely thanks to the Estado Novo's low labour costs. Moreover, happy as he is to extend CUF private rail into Spain, the tycoon sees a threat to his monopolies in Francoist influence. In Manuel de Mello, Salazar has the implicit support of a voice which, when aired, is heeded.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_36:
Jorge Augusto de Mello
Alignment: {getibr_portuguese_caudillo}-Aligned Moderate






£council_member_36_texticon







Jorge Augusto Caetano da Silva José de Mello, firstborn son of Manuel Augusto, grandson of Alfredo da Silva, is a true-blooded scion of industry. In 1948, as the Companhia União Fabril grew, brothers Jorge de Mello and José Manuel were brought onto the board of directors to ensure family continuity. Now, the heir to the empire has ascended his throne. This, coupled with José joining his brother's administration, has further clad the CUF in the appearance of a zaibatsu. But for Jorge, monopoly and family are not dirty words. In a country without anything, the Mellos had to build all the industries they needed; now a behemoth, the CUF group will only survive through the bonds of a family business.

Jorge has inherited it all, including his father's seat on the Iberian Council. That inheritance is a victory for continuity, as the third-generation captain of industry owes his monopolistic power to being a third-generation ally of Salazar. Already representing tens of thousands of workers and ticking towards constituting 5% of Portuguese industry, his appointment will surely see the Mello Group grow evermore throughout the Union. Thus, the face of Portuguese industry within the Union will naturally support the Salazarism he has such a stake in. The Mello saga has a bright future.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_37:
Ricardo Ribeiro do Espírito Santo
Alignment: {getibr_portuguese_caudillo}-Aligned Crony






£council_member_37_texticon







Ricardo Ribeiro do Espírito Santo Silva is difficult to ignore, due to his influence's breadth and his pockets' depth.

Born 12th November 1900, he was raised in wealth and quickly inducted into the financial world of the inter-war period. Educated in Lisbon and Edinburgh, by 1939 he had risen to be President of the Banco Espírito Santo, as well as overseeing organisations across Portugal's financial landscape. Few could boast of such influence.

This was buoyed by friendship with Salazar; since the creation of Iberia he has been crucial to Salazar's programme providing both capital and counsel. But, he is a man of eclectic principle; during the War he aided many, from housing the United Kingdom's Edward VIII after he fled Paris to the Rothschilds and many other Jewish refugees that had fled Europe before London's fall.

He stands by Salazar and it would take much to move him, but within him lies responsibility. Responsibility to his family name, to his bank and, ultimately, to himself.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_38:
Leopoldo Calvo-Sotelo
Alignment: Neutral Independent






£council_member_38_texticon







Leopoldo Calvo-Sotelo is a man of culture. Born in 1926 to a prominent political family, he received an education in civil engineering at the Instituto-Escuela. He also successfully mastered poetry, the English, French, Portuguese, Italian, and German languages and the piano. Such talents have made good conversation during private dinners, attended by fellow supporters of monarchical restoration in the person of the Alfonsist claimant, Don Juan.

But that is his unseen, innocuous life. Where these skills have mattered was in business. Interested in the chemical industry, the engineer has enjoyed a twenty-five-year-long career in the private sector Unión Española de Explosivos, rising to its leadership as it rose to be among the largest Iberian industrial groups. Charming his way through business and government circles, 1966 has been fortuitous for Calvo-Sotelo.

In the same year, Calvo-Sotelo became director of RENFE, the Spanish railway company, and member of the Iberian Council. While Portuguese councillors see him as a Catholic Francoist, in truth he is too politically Catholic and reformist. Appointed to reduce Portuguese influence, he will pursue what he can with customary tact.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_39:
Luis Galdós García
Alignment: Franco-Aligned Moderate






£council_member_39_texticon







Luis Galdós García may have been born in Portugalete in 1910, to a family of Portuguese descent in the Basque Country, but his life truly begun in 1924, as he started his career as an accountant in a chocolate firm. Switching between numerous companies, García eventually obtained a role in the Intervention Corps of the City of Bilbao in 1928. From there, he asserted his position, rising the ranks through the path of countless directors, carefully aligning himself closely to Franco's regime, until he was finally appointed as the President of the National Businessmen Council.

García's background may be in the public sector, but his image is ultimately one of a self-made businessman, the epitome of meritocracy and financial prowess within the Iberian Union. Ultimately, the National Businessmen Council is mostly powerless, and serves more as a propaganda tool through which the complaints of business can be voiced, but not heard. Nonetheless, he works diligently within this position, once again angling for a further promotion.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_40:
José Sirvent Dargent
Alignment: Franco-Aligned Moderate






£council_member_40_texticon







José Sirvent Dargent's life has followed that of business and weapons: creation in crisis. Sent to Morocco as a lieutenant and industrial engineer in 1920, and repatriated with serious injuries, the young man was reborn when, while still recovering, he was made chief engineer at an armaments company in 1922. Sailing further on the winds of economic nationalism and civil war, he became deputy director of the Sociedad Anónima Placencia de las Armas in 1936, then fled Bilbao to command Nationalist artillery. Ultimately, having been among its 1941 founders, Franco appointed him to the National Institute of Industry (INI) presidency in 1963.

Speaking for the large Spanish public sector interest on the Iberian Council thanks to Franco, and expressing religious conservatism, Sirvent will naturally support his status quo. Amidst this ascent, economic stagnancy has supplanted crisis-driven dynamism. Saddled with limited resources as he oversees a slew of heavy and light industries in addition to private acquisitions and mergers, Sirvent looks to the Iberian project for his next breakthrough. However, the introduction of the INI to Portugal has been slowed by their corporatist legislation. Therefore, the military businessman will aim toward this last golden opportunity for success.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_41:
Jorge Artur Rego de Brito
Alignment: {getibr_portuguese_caudillo}-Aligned Crony






£council_member_41_texticon







Two marriages. Two divorces. Six children. One game. That is the sum of Jorge Artur Rego de Brito. His banking career began in 1945 at the Banco Espírito Santo, lapsing in 1949 when he moved to Angola, remarried in 1952, played high-stakes poker, and invested in the stock market, only to return in 1956 after an affair with an officer's wife. Such are the chaotic burdens of risk and reward.

Bluff, bet, win, profit. To the rhythm of this gambling mantra, Jorge de Brito's further career played out. A love of negotiating, of its numbers and people, drew the businessman to work on his own account, becoming an intermediary for business deals and a stock investor. A few precise words and the particular patronage of Marcelo Caetano have laid the bricks of his own banking house, Brisa.

Despite his phenomenal ascent, some on the Council sneer at the appointment of a millionaire art collector with his nascent bank, an obvious Caetanian crony. They whisper that just because Jorge de Brito has something, does not mean he understands it. It does nothing to faze the gentleman gambler. As dawn breaks, Iberia belongs to Jorge de Mello; in the afternoon, it will belong to Jorge de Brito.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_42:
António de Sommer Champalimaud
Alignment: {getibr_portuguese_caudillo}-Aligned Moderate






£council_member_42_texticon







António de Sommer Champalimaud is a pillar in the oligarchy holding up António Salazar. Born 1918, his college education was interrupted when in 1937 he inherited the family's construction company, taking his uncle's cement in 1944. Numbering among those wealthy industrialists benefitting from mandated government permission for any construction, he gained a near monopoly in cement.

Champalimaud married Manuel de Mello's daughter, just as he had married the daughter of Alfredo de Silva. Ultimately, this union broke down when Champalimaud divorced her in 1960, and the great families became competitors. Soon after, the family fortune grew further with the purchase of Banco Pinto & Sotto Mayor, foundation of three insurance companies, and expansion of his cement to Africa.

The appointment of Champalimaud to the table is a victory for Caetano. Owing his privileged position to the Union's corporatism, he will work towards stabilizing the status quo. However, although a professed corporatist, his interests are his own, his power base is secure and independent and older than Caetano's tenure. He will not be afraid to scrutinize reform under that personal lens.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_43:
Claudio Boada Villalonga
Alignment: Neutral Moderate






£council_member_43_texticon







As the old boys of Morocco fade away, middle-class men of merit threaten to take their place. Reaching a bourgeois whose power is by merit of his loyalty to plug the breach, Franco has chosen Claudio Boada Villalonga. The archetype of the Francoist Catalan industrialist, he has the head of a technocrat, the heart of a banker, and the converted status of numbering among the “Franco rich”.

An industrial engineering education led him to work at the state-owned Pegaso vehicle manufacturer in 1951. There, the Catalan built a reputation as a good corporate manager and became the director of ENASA, Pegaso's parent company, in 1957, a position he left in 1967 to restructure the national steel company Altos Hornos de Vizcaya. Recognising a powerful business interest, Franco offered Boada an industrial portfolio.

He politely declined, disliking “active politics.” Instead, the INI presidency and its accompanying seat on the Iberian Council was adequately discreet. From his captain's chair, he will navigate the INI towards new investments in computers, electronics, and tourism. This power suits Boada well, who in turn knows who to aggressively back on the council — the hand that feeds him.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_44:
Eduardo Barreiros Rodríguez
Alignment: Franco-Aligned Hardliner






£council_member_44_texticon







Eduardo Barreiros, prince of industrial innovation, was born in rural Galicia. During the Civil War, he donned the Carlist red beret to defend the Catholicism and mechanic work he was raised in. Sensing an opportunity in Spain's isolation post-war, he patented the method for converting gasoline engines to cheaper diesel, requests for which soon flooded the new Barreiros Diesel company.

This private enterprise met obstacles from the public sector INI and ENASA during Spain's Falangist period. But with Franco's approval of his vehicle manufacturer, exclaiming “Onwards Barreiros, onwards!” all was possible. With Franco's favour, Eduardo Barreiros became the largest private businessman in Iberia, his production plants effectively independent from Falangist unions.

The “Spanish Henry Ford” has joined the Iberian Council; INI representation gives way to the personal bonds of loyalty. A singular interest in business has only deepened Barreiros' stake in the regime. Enjoying hunting with the dictator, and appointing one of Franco's cousins to his board, he will back the saviour of Catholic Spain to the bitter end. Conveniently, this ensures Iberia's predominant use of diesel; his diesel.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_45:
Alfonso Fierro Viña
Alignment: Franco-Aligned Crony






£council_member_45_texticon







Asturian businessman Ildefonso González-Fierro Viña, inheritor of the Banco Ibérico, stands shoulder-to-shoulder with the March, Botín, and Urquijo banking names. Known just as Alfonso to his family, his familial love and ruthless business acumen are his sword and scepter; unlike those rival families, the Fierros created companies and bought commercial banks to finance them—staffing both as a family.

Alfonso Fierro's conglomerate is now one of the largest holding companies within Iberia: controlling numerous finance companies and numerous assets abroad in matches, tobacco, and shipping. The only stable brickwork of this Empire, in Fierro's mind, is kinship. Thus, the banker keeps his friends and their families as close as his own blood; families like the Franco's.

The Francoist doctrine of work and family and built Fierro's fortune and baked in solvency. As such, he seeks to repay that debt through service to the Council. Representing the business arm of the regime in the business of state, Alfonso's prodigious appetite can only grow from here.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_46:
Alberto Franco Nogueira
Alignment: {getibr_portuguese_caudillo}-Aligned Moderate






£council_member_46_texticon







The age of the Statesman is not yet dead.

Nationalistic passion brought Alberto Franco Nogueira to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in 1941. There, a geopolitical determinist was born out of the war he spectated. Statesmen belonged to the state, he decided — mere executors of policy irrevocably dictated to by its history, geography and resulting character.

Nogueira rose to the heady height of Iberian Foreign Minister during the mid-50s. This astonished many; he was without real monarchist, Catholic, or falangist pedigree. However, the man of unlikely origin had ultimately risen even further: into Salazar's confidence. In the career diplomat's merciless realism and devout nationalism, Salazar found a man he entirely aligned with.

Salazar's right hand in foreign affairs naturally finds himself with a seat at the table. He sits among the moderates, living by a single precept: Omnia pro patria — utterly everything for the fatherland. Alberto Nogueira will dutifully serve, allowing himself to be moved by his love of his fatherland and alignment with Salazar.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_47:
Henrique Tenreiro
Alignment: {getibr_portuguese_caudillo}-Aligned Hardliner






£council_member_47_texticon







Rear Admiral Henrique Tenreiro has never been a man of calm habits.

Tenreiro is 'The Fisheries Boss' — delegate to all fishing associations through his presidency of the National Fisheries Promotion Board and Central Board of Fisherman's Houses. Constant effort towards social assistance for fishermen is his raison d'être. In all that he reaps, he amasses corporative power and a huge personal fortune upon the bedrock of the maritime industry.

And reaped he has, sitting now on the Iberian Council. There, Tenreiro is among the leading advocates of fascism within the Estato Novo and Iberia's halls of power. Some assumed he would be sidelined for his beliefs. But in the naval officer, Salazar found an ally, an orator absolute in his loyalty to Portugal.

Tenreiro is anxious to advise. He knows his loyalty to Salazar and his Portuguese patria. He will continue to fight, furthering the military and economic strength at sea of Portugal — not to mention his subsystem within it. But, now, his voice scrutinizes every part of the Union, expressing reservations at its viability.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_48:
Albino Soares Pinto Dos Reis Júnior
Alignment: {getibr_portuguese_caudillo}-Aligned Independent






£council_member_48_texticon







A captain needs reliable deckhands.

Albino Soares Pinto Dos Reis Júnior, longtime friend of Salazar and grandee of his National Union, was a sure-fire pick for one of the Caudillo's “discretionary” seats on the Iberian Council. Since the magistrate's appointment to his friend's 1932 government, he has reliably supervised local, regional, and party structures. Today, this lawyer of Lourerio has even a powerful say in the New State's inner hierarchy.

He possesses all this trust despite a pronounced liberalism. Expelled from the Republican Party for his Catholic positions, he became close to Francisco da Cunha Leal: following him into the Sidonist-liberal right. In the end, Reis Júnior followed those republicans incorporated into the Estado Novo, not Cunha Leal in exile.

Long and valuable service has earned him a Salazarist pedigree, and thus tolerance from the Estado Novo's right-wing; Reis Júnior sits upon the council representing its liberal-most current. He will carefully advocate for reform, always mindful of Portugal's strength, his Catholic duty, and the many envious eyes.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_49:
Ulisses Cruz de Aguiar Cortês
Alignment: {getibr_portuguese_caudillo}-Aligned Crony






£council_member_49_texticon







True conviction is a lonely road.

Few New State policy platforms have been frustrated like Ulisses Cruz de Aguiar Cortês'. The Leirian flirted with right-liberalism during his law studies at Coimbra; later, he was among the republicans welcomed into the Estado Novo. Since then, the jurists' efforts have been Sisyphean: price liberalization resisted; ministries further bureaucratised; divorce reform derided as immoral.

He sits on the Iberian Council all the same. Salazar, fellow student of Coimbra, counts Ulisses Cortês among his oldest friends. Remaining outside Salazar's Coimbra Group core of university-years supporters, the civil servant loyally serves without complaint; a vital and long career in the economic ministries of Portugal and the Union.

Salazar remembers his friends. Ulisses Cortês' judicial experience and economic success bring a legitimizing luster to his side of the table. Both facts protect him from the Council's ultra-conservatives. He will pursue Salazar's interests and a strengthened private sector with decades-trained patient diligence—so long as his shield holds.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_50:
Baltazar Rebelo de Sousa
Alignment: {getibr_portuguese_caudillo}-Aligned Hardliner






£council_member_50_texticon







Baltazar Rebelo de Sousa has served as the secretary-general of the Scouts of Portugal and as a medical sub-inspector, swearing oath upon oath to the Estado Novo and to God. His honest and sober demeanor has led him to Marcelo Caetano: admiring his worldly sophistication, and sharing in many of his frustrations. Everyone knows that he has been brought to the Iberian Council as a protégé of Caetano.

But the young apprentice is his own master. He may admire Caetano as a man, but de Sousa has little time for his “pragmatic opportunism”. Iberian civilization is trans-oceanic, and faces myriad dangers wherever it is present. Against such evil, the fatherland requires men who can put aside their fear of change to tend to the health of the nation. A true patriot is a decisive patriot.

He may have been brought to the Council to serve Caetano's interests, but he will not let the opportunity to argue his points slip by. A new, dynamic and corporatist system is needed now. The deplorable state of public services like health serves as more than enough proof of that fact. As the Iberian Union slides further into stagnation, de Sousa knows that honesty, not sycophancy, is what will save it.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_51:
João Augusto Dias Rosas
Alignment: {getibr_portuguese_caudillo}-Aligned Crony






£council_member_51_texticon







João Augusto Dias Rosas, graduating from the University of Lisbon's law faculty in 1945, quickly forayed into state service. From 1949 to 1959, he collected economic experience like trophies: Chairman of the Regulatory Commission for the Trade in Raw Cotton, and Member of the Economic Coordination Commission, Cotton Export Board, Higher Industry Council, and the Export Promotion Fund's administration.

Besides creating greater pan-Iberian economic integration, his export work decreased business dependency on foreign goods. This ideological outlook he owes to Marcelo Caetano, to whom he has been a faithful follower since their university days. Dias Rosas's finance career has thus benefitted from Caetano's rising star, becoming Secretary of State for Trade 1959-61, the Bank of Portugal's deputy governor in 1968, and now a member of the Iberian Council.

Councilman Dias Rosas pushes for greater economic liberalization and increased international trade from a position of strength. However, he does so as much out of loyalty as conviction. He, alongside Joaquim Veríssimo, will be among the loudest devotees of Caetano's golden circle.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_52:
Camilo de Mendonça
Alignment: {getibr_portuguese_caudillo}-Aligned Moderate






£council_member_52_texticon







Camilo António de Mendonça, born 1921, has always been persistent. Inspired by Salazar's rise, as a young man, he set aside a career in agricultural engineering career so to join the National Union. Since then, he has become a senior civil servant of the regime, his career encompassing a litany of administrative presidencies. His drive was aided by a developmentalist fellow traveler and friend, Marcelo Caetano.

Pride and profit have brought António's agricultural expertise to politics. Intermittently president of farmers, producers and exporters of coffee and olive oil, a project of agricultural autarky has captured his career. This has culminated in entrepreneurial work within the Trás-os-Montes, irrigating and opening olive oil and wine cooperatives. Ever the savvy businessman, he sees in the north an opportunity for a new agricultural revolution.

Raised to the Iberian Council alongside his godson, Baltazar Rebelo de Sousa, António is a moderate among the ascendant Caetanist. Neither sycophant nor subversive, the Councilman will forward Caetano's developmentalism in the agricultural, and support expanded influence for the Council, which would give his business interests a greater say.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_53:
Mário Júlio Brito de Almeida Costa
Alignment: {getibr_portuguese_caudillo}-Aligned Independent






£council_member_53_texticon







Mário Júlio Brito de Almeida Costa is the youngest man to ever sit on the Iberian Council, the product of an intensely passionate career. Born in 1927, at the University of Coimbra's law faculty he graduated in 1949, received his doctorate in 1957, and became a full professor in 1962 at the staggeringly young age of 35. This merit has known no roof, and he since combined academic research with a promising justice ministry career.

A long career in law convinced Júlio of the need for change. Studying and publishing on Spanish law, Portuguese law history, and obligation law, he was armed with reforms, but no means of implementation. Through a shared desire for reform, an alliance with Marcelo Caetano provided the latter.

Representing the cream of Portugal's university crop, Júlio sits on the Iberian Council as a reformist legislator. There, he will pursue initiatives such as Iberian prison employment law, regional prisons, civil and land registries, non-contractural state civil liability, and a bettered system for supervising public limited companies. Separate from Caetano's cronyistic picks, his genuine legal merit will prove valuable to his ally as regards legislation and legitimisation.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_54:
Camilo Alonso Vega
Alignment: Franco-Aligned Hardliner






£council_member_54_texticon







Camilo Alonso Vega is Francisco Franco's personal hunting hawk. A childhood playmate, fellow student, and veteran of the Moroccan Wars alongside Franco, he secured Vitoria and fought in key battles for his cause. Entrusted with the Army Ministry Sub-Secretaryship after the Civil War, this placed the 300 Francoist concentration camps under his supervision from 1940 until their closing in 1947.

That was only the start of a long career. Made chief of the Guardia Civil from 1943 to 1955, amidst student disturbances he was further elevated to Interior Minister in 1956. Lacking his predecessor's intelligence, Camilo Alonso was appointed for his loyalty and obstinacy, for which he earned the nickname “Don Camulo.” Cumulatively, he is remembered as the smiling face of Franco's post-war crackdowns.

As a council member, Camilo Alonso is wholly in Franco's confidence. Having followed the Caudillo throughout his life, the general brings his life-long defence of order to the council's proceedings. There, the scene has changed but the oppressive work has not. Stubborn, blunt, and rigid, his master need not even ask for his hawk to meet all talk of reform with denigrating diatribes.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_55:
Luis Carrero Blanco
Alignment: Franco-Aligned Crony






£council_member_55_texticon







A submariner is called to be diligent and efficient, not to draw attention. And so Luis Carrero Blanco has avoided the spotlight ever since the Cantabrian followed his family's military tradition into the Naval Academy at age 14. He served aboard numerous vessels in the Rif War and the Spanish Civil War before being elevated to Chief of Naval Operations in 1939. It was in this role that he penned the decisive report to Franco that secured Spanish neutrality in the Second World War. This proved the gateway to a string of cabinet positions, all sufficiently distant from the limelight but in the shade of power. Most recently, he has surfaced as Minister of State, handling crucial administrative responsibilities on behalf of Franco and Salazar.

As a member of the Iberian Council, he can be counted on to echo Franco's wishes. Such is his loyalty that many say that he has become the Caudillo's closest friend. For Iberia he envisages a peace upon the tenets he once saw for Spain: administrative professionalization and centralization, social conservatism and a technocratic approach to the economy. For such a cause, he will navigate the shadowy shoals of Spanish and Iberian politics in silence.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_56:
Raimundo Fernández-Cuesta
Alignment: Franco-Aligned Hardliner






£council_member_56_texticon







Much like the Falangist movement he once led, Raimundo Fernández-Cuesta has been cast aside, but not cast out.

Born in Madrid, he studied law and became a lawyer for the Navy. Upon the proclamation of the Spanish Republic he joined his childhood friend, José Antonio Primo de Rivera, to found the Falangist movement. Propelled by his oratory, the party grew quickly as the failings of the Republic the two men loathed became ever clearer, though not by enough to avoid a humiliating personal defeat in the 1936 elections. Imprisoned at the outbreak of the Spanish Civil War, he was freed in a prisoner exchange, and placed at the head of a combined Falangist-Carlist FET y de las JONS by Generalissimo Franco. His rise was permanently stunted however by a failed tenure as Minister of Agriculture, which spread famines across Spain.

The placid Fernández-Cuesta, ever maligned for repeated organizational or policy mishaps, has secured at last a position amongst Iberia's captains. He is a mooted force of the status quo however - eagerly supporting any moves to the right and Falange positions, but only should others lead the way. Otherwise, he will do little to stand against the Caudillos; whatever they decide, lest he lose another position.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_57:
José Solís Ruiz
Alignment: Franco-Aligned Moderate






£council_member_57_texticon







José Solís Ruiz is uncharacteristic of Iberian officialdom. An old-shirt Falangist from Córdoba, he has avoided being shunted aside like so many others, perhaps due to an ideological flexibility his fellows lacked. However, he does not lack their tenacity.

Solís Ruiz first made a name for himself through the prosecution of anarchist guerillas as part of the Military Legal Corps, securing death sentences for each. As he worked his way up the regime's corporatist structures, the lawyer has proved a consistent and effective advocate for recreational and cultural opportunities for Iberian workers, as well as an astute and affable (if controversial) manager of media organs.

Now Solís Ruiz, the long-time 'Smile of the Regime', has been hand-picked by the Caudillos to serve as the 'Smile' of their new Council as well. Liked universally for his friendly and laid-back manner, his charisma may imbue the new institution with popular appeal. With a broad grin, he will inform the Caudillos of the word on the street, whether that be for pro-labor measures or a reinforced corporatism - or against the budding technocracy that threatens the Caudillos' connection to the people.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_58:
Laureano López Rodó
Alignment: Franco-Aligned Moderate






£council_member_58_texticon







Laureano López Rodó, the unofficial leader of the Spanish technocrats, has spent decades accruing the knowledge and connections needed to realize the developmentalist transformation of Iberia. Born in Barcelona, he obtained a doctorate in the Complutense University of Madrid, before further burnishing his academic credentials with studies in administrative law at the University of Santiago de Compostela. López Rodó took care to complement these scholastic accomplishments with social ones, becoming a member of the elite lay Catholic organization Opus Dei. Shortly afterward relocating to Madrid, he befriended the influential admiral Luis Carrero Blanco, who appointed him Technical Secretary General within the Ministry of State. There López Rodó won widespread plaudits for his reforms to public administration, as well as the creation of the National School of Public Administration.

Now elevated to the Council, López Rodó remains a firm ally of Carrero Blanco and a tireless proponent of detailed, technocratic development planning and further administrative reforms. Much more cautiously, he will advocate for decentralization to Iberia's many distinct regions.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_59:
Tomás García Rebull
Alignment: Franco-Aligned Crony






£council_member_59_texticon







Tomás García Rebull's father was a soldier, as was his grandfather and his great-grandfather before him. The youth of Primo de Rivera's era followed the family tradition; he joined the North African Army in 1924, the Falangists in 1934—and ultimately Franco. Like many Falangists, he marched in the Blue Division. What he found scared him: dirty, foul-smelling and bare-footed Russians. Communism manifest.

Returning home, Tomás García snapped up the rank of Franco's Military Household Lieutenant Colonel. He rose bullet-fast. The Falangist exercised a paternalist touch to transform the grievances of veterans into energy for the regime. Since then, he has effectively captained military regions. Now upon the Iberian Council, the 'Blue' officer sits among the few right-most officers of his remaining political family.

Tomás García's loyalty, however, is first and foremost to Franco and his regime. All his efforts—including his ties to Nazi-connected organizations—are toward protecting the New Order from the Communistic “paradise” he saw. Franco's crony will intransigently resist any liberalizing efforts.
strings.IBR_advisory_council_member_desc_60:
Manuel Fraga Iribarne
Alignment: Neutral Independent






£council_member_60_texticon







The sharp-tongued Manuel Fraga Iribarne numbers among the reformist faces of the regime. This student of economics, politics and law has risen with an iron-willed determination, becoming Council of Education Secretary in 1953 and Director of the Institute of Political Studies in 1956 before being named Minister of Information and Tourism in 1962. An insatiable ambition has driven him hard.

His time at the ministry was deftly played. In one hand he had parried the “immobilist” factions with an unconditional defense of the regime while forwarding small reforms in the other. Iribarne protests that this would save the regime and few can deny the usefulness of his “open-mindedness.” While his press law was sunk, his ministry has seen tourism bolster the economy seemingly with a mere cry of his slogan, “Iberia is different!”

Iribarne's seat on the Iberian Council is his and Marcelo Caetano's crowning achievement. The reformist workhorse will dedicate all his energies to this new role. He would see the Iberian Council's remit expand, and thus his own, furrowing the brows of some. His career has come far; a man of narrow interests, he will serve the Council insofar as it serves him.
