Benjamín de Arriba y Castro (Franco-Aligned Hardliner) will leave the Council.
Pedro Cantarero Cuadrado (Franco-Aligned Hardliner) will join the Council.

strings.IBR_set_up_legislative_council_tt: The Iberian Council has been created. Check the decisions tab for the Iberian Council category.
strings.IBR_council_faction_0_info:
£IBR_council_faction_independent Independent

The Independents. Sometimes referred to mockingly as a misguided youth wing of the Government by their opponents, they represent reform-minded Council Members that find themselves unwilling to align totally with the Reformist Movement itself.

Predominantly younger members, with little memories of the Civil War or the creation of the Estado Novo, if they possess them at all. They're often members with either highly skilled technical backgrounds white collar backgrounds in the private sector with extensive academic qualifications. A great number of them have travelled, either for business or education, across Europe and America.

To say they rub against the orthodoxy of the Union would be an understatement, however they are not revolutionaries. To them the system can be reformed, steadily introducing accountability and reducing authoritarian measures where they can. This is a goal usually kept secret however. As far as many of their opponents are concerned, they are simply young members with youthful passion for organised welfare and popular participation.
strings.IBR_council_faction_1_info:
£IBR_council_faction_catholic_reformer Catholic Reformer

Catholicism has a long history in Iberia, its aged monasteries and churches holding a long memory. From the Muslims to the Bonapartists, the Spanish and Portuguese Catholic Churches are in some ways proud of their history of adversity. Faith is not an easy thing, and the Iberians have been tested time and time again for it.

For some adherents to Rome, those times continue. While the State professes the importance of Catholic virtue they see the disappearances in the night. Broken men and women have come to their door seeking spiritual solace after being suspected of some wrongdoing and taken away, released as traumatised souls. To many in both the clergy and the laity, good intention has warped into something sinister.

These Council Members draw inspiration from Catholic teaching, and work to limit the authoritarianism of the system and promote the ideals found in various papal encyclicals published since the 19th century. Connected both to some opposition groups and Catholic groups like the CADC or the ACNdP in Portugal and Spain respectively, these Catholics aim to maximise their impact by working within the system rather than trying to tear it down.
strings.IBR_council_faction_2_info:
£IBR_council_faction_blue_reformer Blue Reformer

The Blueshirts of the Falange. The Blue of the União Nacional's emblem. There are few in Iberia who cannot claim an instant recognition of at least one of these symbols - with their feelings varying widely. To some, however, they are symbols to be used for a new purpose; those within the Council who owe their careers to the Union and view the prospect of its failure with dread.

These reformers are not bred from faith nor from youth; often, they source from pragmatism. The Union keeps Spain and Portugal safe. It keeps their careers safe. However, its inefficiencies and fear of its own people hold it back and many fear that under their feet lies a time bomb waiting to collapse the entire structure under them.

Socially conservative, they support protectionist private initiatives and desire to increase public participation in Iberian governance. Democratisation, as they see it, is vital to maintaining the system vital to all Iberians and to ignore this fact could have horrific consequences for them all. Unlike the Catholics or the Independents, they are a closely knit ideological group; a force to be reckoned with with a clear vision for a renewed Iberia.
strings.IBR_council_faction_3_info:
£IBR_council_faction_modernist Modernist

Despite often finding themselves sharing a bed with Reformist factions, there are little qualms about the Union within the Modernist camp. Rather than seeing a Union that goes too far, they instead fear a Union who very existence is too centralised, viewing the Caudillos both with respect and fear for the consequences of their centralised power, the chaos of the old Republics in Iberia ever in their minds.

They advocate for more power to be awarded to the Council, letting Spain and Portugal's best and brightest lead the Union into a new day with the Caudillos rather than placing all hopes on two men. After all, regardless of their quality, what happens when they need to be replaced? Modernists aren't blind to the human condition; they see the instability that could follow and the unravelling of the State that could commence.

As such, these are not Council Members concerned with public participation nor of the limiting of the powers of the State. Rather, they see them as quite necessary; however, they believe that all must be done to make the control of the levers and mechanisms of power a meritocratic and stable affair. The Council must ascend; Iberia's future depends on it.
strings.IBR_council_faction_4_info:
£IBR_council_faction_moderate_conservative Moderate Conservative

One of the more varied mainstream factions within the Council, Moderate Conservatives are considered by some a living history of the accommodations made by many in the wake of the chaos of the inter-war era. Right-liberals, conservative Christians, or even simply middle-class careerists from across Portugal and Spain, they represent a bedrock upon which the Union can rely. A force willing to discuss reasonable proposals, but still filled with certainty as to Iberia's rightful place.

To most other factions, the Moderate Conservatives are either a desired ally or a feared foe, for they have links across the Iberian political spectrum. From Independents to the Falange, both court the approval of the moderates so far as is possible; its window into the dominant attitudes of the political middle class disregarded at any factions risk, hosting significant presence in both Lisbon and Madrid.

However, they are devoted to the Union and will suffer no damage to it. Change is necessary, always an antidote for the political plagues that suffer nations until they fall. However, any ideas threatening the Union or the peace upon which they have made their lot amongst the Iberian people is an anathema likened only to treason.
strings.IBR_council_faction_5_info:
£IBR_council_faction_radical_conservative Radical Conservative

If Iberia is a body protecting the people from Barcelona to Lisbon, then the Radical Conservatives are certainly the nervous system.

In nearly every political institution, from the military to the coast guards, adherents to this bloc enjoy plentiful positions of authority, easily making up the core of the Caudillo regime. For some, the socialism of the Spanish Civil War and the chaos of the Portuguese Republic burn still in their minds - as such, the bold men who turned back such evil burn brighter, and this bloc's loyalty to them cannot be shaken. For others, with the Union came personal prosperity. Either way, Salazar and Franco enjoy their unshakable faith.

These conservatives' highest priority is the continuation of the Iberian system and all the good it has wrought, with one notable exception. Within their discussions is one constant. The view that few other men could possibly protect the Iberian people from the socialist scourges of before is a totem belief, and as such, wherever the Caudillos lead the Union, they will follow, for surely there will lie prosperity.
strings.IBR_council_faction_6_info:
£IBR_council_faction_technocrat Technocrat

At the dawn of the century, writers globally began to speculate on the long term effects the Industrial Revolution would have on politics, particularly the relationship between the industrial and technical leaders and the nations to which they found themselves. In Iberia, such a faction has emerged as a continual voice calling for reform.

Finding themselves at odds with the autarkic policies advocated by many Spanish politicians, and their adjacents in the Portuguese protectionist camp, these advocates of reform base themselves upon the myriad observations made watching the global demobilisation in the late 40s and the economics of the 1950s. While many models are debated, there is one constant view: economic reform must come to Iberia before its contradictory policies cause havoc.

Herein lies their own struggle, however. Despite their advocacy of economic reform, many still resolutely support the Caudillos and the Iberian system. With the growing influence of groups such as Opus Dei, a prominent question in many minds has emerged. Can economic change be brought without social change that could undo all Iberia has worked for?
strings.IBR_council_faction_7_info:
£IBR_council_faction_monarchist Monarchist

Lisbon has known no King since the fall of the Kingdom in 1910, Madrid not since 1932. Looking upon the fall of the Habsburgs in Austria, the monarchist movements in France or any number of long-ended royal lines, many believed that Portugal and Spain, in a Europe gripped by modern ideology, would see monarchy fade away. However, the embers refuse to die.

During the Spanish Civil War, many monarchists, particularly Carlists, made accommodations with the Nationalists and found influential positions within the new Spain. In Portugal, many within the aristocracy maintained royalist sentiment, keeping monarchism within the halls of politics and commerce.

While some view the restoration of the Spanish and Portuguese thrones as a pathway to democracy, such fringe views are outside of the system. Within the Union's halls of power, for the supporters of Javier in Spain or the nomination of a new King in Portugal, there is satisfaction for the strength the peninsula has found. Now they need their Kings, the Union, an umbrella for them both, to guarantee stability for all.
strings.IBR_council_faction_8_info:
£IBR_council_faction_traditionalist Traditionalist

Traditionalists represent the vanguard of reaction within Iberia, adherents committed to what they perceive as the fundamental principles of the Union. They hail from many schools of thought within Iberia's Right, from the most radical of conservatives to integralists or Carlists seeking greater integration into the affairs of the State, unified by their beliefs in Corporatism, Catholic Moralism, and Anti-Socialism.

Traditionalists find their political vision shaped more by the ideas of Ancien France than modern Europe. Many within their ranks look upon the state of the continent, and those within Iberia attempting to bring them closer to it, with disgust for their rampant atheism and moral decline. Traditionalists across the Union are clear; their societies rot as surely as the socialists' did.

Traditionalists then represent a vocal part of Iberian politics, committed to preventing the inevitable catastrophes they envisage should Iberia lose itself. That Spain and Portugal were always strong, community-focused, and God-fearing, and that Iberia must continue that legacy.
strings.IBR_council_faction_9_info:
£IBR_council_faction_fascist Fascist

Despite the declarations of students, from discussions in secluded University rooms across Spain and Portugal to loud derisions outside the Union's Washington Embassy at the latest rally, Fascism has never controlled Iberia. This is the understanding that drives the Falangists and radical Salazarists who still remain to continue pushing for an Iberia that can unlock its potential, potential long denied.

During the tumultuous 1930s, both Caudillos had made cautious associations with the fascists within their nations, and when the liberal Western Europe and the socialist East had been crushed under the ideology's boots, they had enjoyed the peak of their power; however therein lay their decline, for with a hungry Reich on the border both Caudillos regarded their fascists as liabilities.

As such, the influence of fascism has declined across Iberia, the strongest remnant being in the Spanish Falangists, support having melted away softly from their Caudillo allies. Desperate to restore their lost influence and seize the reins of power they had been withheld from before, they seek nothing less than a strong Iberia - in their image.
strings.IBR_council_faction_10_info:
£IBR_council_faction_military_hardliner Military Hardliner

Where does true political power lie? Many scholars have argued for the people's collective will, others in the invisible economic levers of modern life. To many across Iberia, however, there is a simple answer. Political power lies with whomever is ready to cross the Rubicon, like Caesar of old.

Discontent in the Union is not a view widespread in the military, with units from both Spain and Portugal being among the most loyal citizens of the regime. From the lowest footsoldier to the decorated general, the Caudillos and the Union are synonymous with everything they would die to defend.

However, this love for the Union makes the military a force to be respected. Both Spanish and Iberian officers are fearful of instability and look upon their armies' actions in combating subversives in the last half century with pride. Should such instability return, in their judgement, to Iberia? Should traitors bring Iberia to the brink of calamity, many would not hesitate to cross their own rubicons and seize power - for the sake of all they hold dear.
strings.IBR_reformism_tick_mission_tt: Woe to the common man, for once you achieve a seat at the ivory tower it is hard to look back down.

strings.IBR_democratic_council_faction_2_info:
£IBR_party_FPS Federación de Partidos Socialistas-Federação dos Partidos Socialistas






£IBR_party_leaders_FPS







Coalition Leader: Enrique Tierno Galván
Parliamentary Leader: Mário Nobre Soares

The primary and most 'mainstream' of the left-wing coalitions within legislative elections as a whole, the FPS are perhaps the most 'palatable' socialist option for the Iberian electorate. Forming primarily as an alliance between the PSOE in Spain and the ASP in Portugal, and incorporating many smaller Iberian regional socialist parties alongside, its big-tent membership offers many different viewpoints that appeal to the mildly-leftist voter, without the progression and seemingly-toxic character of the various Communist or Communist-derived options.

It is expected to advocate for, and support any other effort to push forward, many and various left-wing policies of all stripes. As they are also the largest left-wing option in addition to being the most generally acceptable, they are expected to perform well politically.
strings.IBR_democratic_council_faction_3_info:
£IBR_party_EC Esquerra de Catalunya






£IBR_party_leaders_EC







No Centralized Leadership
Parliamentary Leader: Heribert Barrera i Costa

One of the newest political coalitions within the Parliament, the EC was formed as a result of the decision taken, prior to the elections, not to legalize the ERC, the main Catalan nationalist party before the Spanish Civil War.

As a result, the ERC itself agreed to a coalition between itself and a number of much smaller leftist nationalist organizations (running the gamut from moderate socialists to those on the far-left) in order to be allowed participation in the campaign, and now representation in that campaign's aftermath.

In general, as could be expected, they advocate for a large degree of autonomy for Catalonia within the nation, and are likely to focus very strongly on policies that support that. Owing to the integration of other parties in the compromise, however, they can also be expected to support other general left-wing initiatives.
strings.IBR_democratic_council_faction_4_info:
£IBR_party_EEH Euskal Erakunde Herritarra






£IBR_party_leaders_EEH







Coalition Leader: National Table
Parliamentary Leader: Juan María Bandrés Molet

Defined by its strict regionalist perspective towards the Basque Country, the EEH is itself a coalition of a number of smaller left-wing and nationalist Basque operations, all broadly socialist in general political outlook. Considered generally unreliable on debate, consideration, or participation in the process regarding any agenda other than state decentralization, it is unlikely to expect that they will significantly engage on other topics.

Strongly supportive of Basque independence, many within the coalition reject the legitimacy of the Parliament as a whole, and some of their members have not even been sworn into their seats to enable participation.

Indeed, some members of the coalition have ties to ETA itself, and though the coalition itself is clear on its rejection of open violence, these sympathies are well-known.
strings.IBR_democratic_council_faction_5_info:
£IBR_party_CD Centro Democrático






£IBR_party_leaders_CD







Coalition Leader: João Pedro Miller Pinto de Lemos Guerra
Parliamentary Leader: Leopoldo Calvo-Sotelo y Bustelo

A broad coalition of slightly-left and slightly-right of center groupings, the CD incorporates various social democratic, liberal, Christian democratic, and conservative groups across both Portugal and Spain, for which the other options on both sides of the spectrum were seen as too destabilizing.

Explicitly created for the purpose of establishing the so-called 'center' of the Iberian political spectrum, so as to avoid a takeover by either the left or right-wings of it, they are expected to have broad appeal to many potential parts of the electorate, and can be expected to advocate for varied policies that emphasize stability and the security of the Iberian democratic process. The diversity of its makeup and membership, however, though enabling such diversity in policy, does contribute to a general perception of instability in the coalition partners that make it up, as each faction within is seen as wanting their viewpoint pushed forward.
strings.IBR_democratic_council_faction_6_info:
£IBR_party_EDC Equipo de la Democracia Cristiana-Equipe de Democracia Cristã






£IBR_party_leaders_FDC







Coalition Leader: Joaquín Ruiz-Giménez Cortés
Parliamentary Leader: Joaquim Carvalho Macedo Correia

A collection of Christian Democrats in both countries, the Christian Democratic Team, or simply EDC, comprises Iberian Catholics from all walks of life, united mainly in past opposition to the dictatorship. While the figures of the Franco and Salazar regimes have often liked to portray their leadership and rule as protecting tradition, including the Catholic faithful, many religious figures resisted them in one way or another.

In its current state, all members of the EDC consider themselves Christian Democrats, but in truth, the movement is as varied as the Democratic Center, but not nearly as well known or popular. This relative obscurity has been the party's bane and is why the EDC has been relegated to the role of second fiddle to the CD.

However, what the party lacks in numbers, it makes up for in vision, possessing a more united vision for Iberian democracy.
strings.IBR_democratic_council_faction_7_info:
£IBR_party_PDC Pacte Democràtic per Catalunya






£IBR_party_leaders_PDC







Coalition Leader: Jordi Pujol i Soley
Parliamentary Leader: Josep Pallach i Carolà

Another strongly regionalist coalition within the Parliament, the PDC was formed out of various Catalan nationalist parties and organizations, but with a notable and significant element of more mainstream conservative, liberal, and social democrat Catalan groupings. As can be expected, their primary interest is in the advancement of Catalonian autonomy, but not necessarily independence, and of Catalan culture within it.

This moderation and ideological diversity allows them to work much more effectively with other Parliament parties to advance general legislation, and they are amenable to doing so, should the legislation be broadly supportive of popular policies.

However, it must be remembered that even while doing so, their focus is on Catalonia first and foremost in all things.
strings.IBR_democratic_council_faction_8_info:
£IBR_party_AP Alianza Popular-Aliança Popular






£IBR_party_leaders_AP







Coalition Leader: Manuel Fraga Iribarne
Parliamentary Leader: Luís Supico Ribeiro Pinto

The People's Alliance, or AP as a shorthand, represents the main right-wing group within the Iberian Parliament. It comprises various parties across both Iberian nations. Most notably, many of the old power players from the dictatorship have found a home inside the Alliance, and for them, the coalition represents an opportunity to rebrand inside a democratic system. The AP often preaches the “great successes” of the old regimes, and the many fathers who made these victories possible, and supports policies based on them.

At the same time, the crimes and failures are conveniently ignored as orphaned things, best forgotten for the sake of “national unity.”

While the AP claims to support democracy, many find their assurances cold and suspect that the People's Alliance has more questionable plans for Iberia.
strings.IBR_democratic_council_faction_9_info:
£IBR_party_EAJ Euzko Alderdi Jeltzalea






£IBR_party_leaders_EAJ







Party President: Collegiate Direction
Parliamentary Leader: Xabier Arzalluz Antia

The Basque Nationalist Party is one of the regionalist parties that have re-emerged since the dictatorship's end. A conservative party, it supports what it claims are the Basque region's “historical rights” and the promotion of Basque culture, which faced heavy suppression throughout the Caudillos regime.

Operating as the primary nationalist force for the Basque region, they often clash with the more radical nationalists and left-wingers of the EEH. Aiming to secure autonomy previously denied to their region, the EAJ's first and most important goal is to see the autonomous region system passed and secure as much self-rule as possible for the Basque Country.
strings.IBR_democratic_council_faction_10_info:
£IBR_party_independent Independents






£IBR_party_leaders_Indp







No Centralized Leadership
No Centralized Parliamentary Leadership

With the general promise of state decentralization as part of the democratization process, many small groups across the nation, unaffiliated with the larger ideological or regionalist coalitions, ran for open seats in order to advance their local interests and desires for greater autonomy.

Though most were unsuccessful in the face of the more organized, better funded, and more ideologically cohesive coalitions, some were not, and now find themselves in the newly formed Parliament.

With many of their number hailing from positions of power in the dictatorship, their political positions generally fall along the center to center-right of the ideological spectrum and they can be expected to broadly support such policies.

However, much like the larger regionalist parties, their main personal focus remains to obtain for their small regions or interest groups the same advancement of rights and autonomy that Catalonia and the Basque Country have been granted.
strings.IBR_PCE_desc:
£IBR_party_communist Partido Comunista de España






£IBR_party_leaders_PCE







General-Secretary: Santiago Carrillo Solares
Parliamentary Leader: Ignacio Gallego Bezares

Representing the 'mainstream' of Iberian communism, as far as that can be called and in a big-tent internal coalition, the PCE is far more moderate in general character than the PCP, though still nominally Bolshevik. Operating primarily underground in decades past, in order to remain relevant the party unified with rivals, and the many resultant internal factions have given it a diverse and vibrant array of viewpoints and positions, something that has both helped and hindered its effectiveness and led to some of the Parliament treating them with confusion.

Unlike the PCP however, they are considered to be willing to negotiate with other represented parties and support broadly left-wing parlamentary initiatives, owing to Santiago Carrillo's repeated belief that legislative deadlock could kill the democratic experiment. As well as, of course, a desire to not return to the wilderness for another 40 years, something of which he is convinced would spell the party's doom and the fracturing of its internal coalition.
strings.IBR_LL_desc:
£IBR_party_LL Lista Laborista






£IBR_party_leaders_LL







List Spokesman: Santiago Carrillo Solares
Parliamentary Leader: Ramón Tamames Gómez

Self-styled as a 'socialist labor organization,' and formed in the aftermath of the government's decision to prohibit Communist parties from running in the elections, it is an open secret that the LL is formed almost entirely from PCE members. Clearly intending to keep the character and the torch of the PCE alive in the Parliament, it by and large maintains the strongly left-wing character of its parent organization, and is expected to directly propose and support any similar policies and positions.

There has, however, been something of a transition in character in the shift, as many of the 'hardest' left under the PCE banner were dropped, and replaced by a more centrist grouping originating from the Iberian artistic and cultural sectors who would not have associated with them in the original PCE. Though sure to change the perception of the new party as a whole, it remains to be seen if this will be for the better or worse.
strings.IBR_PCP_desc:
£IBR_party_communist Partido Comunista Português






£IBR_party_leaders_PCP







General-Secretary: Álvaro Barreirinhas Cunhal
Parliamentary Leader: Octávio Rodrigues Pato

A shocking presence within the Parliament, the PCP is easily the farthest left of all represented non-regional parties, drawing significant attention from both international observers and domestic watchers. Self-proclaimed Bolsheviks (with a noticeable and increasing drift towards Marxism-Leninism), they advocate for a gradual transition to a full Communist system, coupled with a neutral and anti-imperialist foreign policy.

Strongly repressed through most of its existence, the party's strict internal ideological cohesion exists in stark contrast to many other parties in the Parliament, allowing it to have a voice far stronger than would be expected given its size. Still, however, they are considered to be generally toxic to the vast majority of the Iberian voting classes, and are unlikely to support, and just as likely to actively oppose, almost any Parliament initiative put forward by other, more 'centrist' parties.
strings.IBR_FEPU_desc:
£IBR_party_FEPU Frente Eleitoral Povo Unido






£IBR_party_leaders_FEPU







Coalition Spokesman: Álvaro Barreirinhas Cunhal
Parliamentary Leader: José Manuel Marques Tengarrinha

Formed following the government's decision to prohibit Communist organizations from the elections, the FEPU consists largely of 'former' PCP members and others arranged on the left of the political spectrum. Although an attempt has been made to expand its appeal - through the inclusion of a number of smaller and socialist groups excluded from the FPS but willing to run in alignment with them - it is still largely ideologically united, an inheritance from the PCP itself.

Despite winning electoral capability and establishing a robust list of candidates, however, it remains unknown if the coalition will be able to shake the profound hostility of the majority of the Iberian electorate towards communism as a whole. Or, concurrently, the disdain of much of the rest of the electoral establishment - regardless of the surprising movements made to include other socialist viewpoints in their platform.

strings.IBR_council_groups_faction_0_info:
Independent Group


At the furthest left of the Iberian Council, a very special collection of people can be found. They hold many differing ideologies, wear many different hats, and go by many different names. But they are all united by one common goal - the implementation of democratic reform in Iberia. Consisting mainly of younger, more idealistic members of the chamber, the oft-looked down upon Independent Group is certainly an eclectic bunch when compared to the usual stalwarts of the early Franco and Salazar years. Populist conservatives, progressive liberals, and even the odd social democrat can be found amongst their ranks - anyone who wishes for a freer country is welcome under their aegis.

While many rival factions to their right dismiss them as naive at best and downright harmful at worst, they are nothing if not organized in submitting their ideas to the Council's agenda, even getting them through, occasionally. Indeed, the very existence of such unity between these seemingly disparate groups is an argument in favour of democracy in and of itself - an argument that the Independent Group hopes will be given more serious consideration, in the coming years.
strings.IBR_council_groups_faction_1_info:
Iberian Reform Union


Created by reform-minded Christians within the Council, the Iberian Reform Union's official mission statement is that they wish to mesh Catholic social teaching with the values of the Iberian regime. In reality, they are much more simply described as being the Christian democratic wing of reformism within the Council.

While unified in holding Christian democratic values and possessing the goal of moving the Council towards reformism, the Iberian Reform Union as a group is quite heterogeneous in its members' beliefs. While not to the same extent as groups like the Independents, as there is an underlying ideological current within the Iberian Reform Union, individual members vary significantly with regards to the extent of their conservatism, and the group is heavily divided in who to ally with when it comes to electoral politics. The divide is chiefly between those who wish to ally themselves with the more regimentalist right and Fraga, and those who wish to ally with other Christian democratic forces.
strings.IBR_council_groups_faction_2_info:
People's Alliance


Never one to sit idle as the political landscape provided opportunities to him, Manuel Fraga was quick to create his own parliamentary group with the allies he had within the Council. Then, all it took was to pull on a few strings of mistrust between Council members, as well as a healthy dose of promises made to the right people, and Fraga was equally quick to expand his group into a significant political force within the Council.

The People's Alliance can hardly be described in any terms more concrete than “conservative,” as the group is functionally a mouthpiece for Fraga, a tool that he can wield to command votes and ensure any reforms passed are reforms he's in favor of. However, such ambiguity can beget fragility, but if Fraga can hold the People's Alliance together, then the group could very well solidify into a large regimentalist party in future elections.
strings.IBR_council_groups_faction_3_info:
Iberian People's Union


As identifiable parliamentary groups first began to form within the Council, and the momentum of reformism continued to grow within the regime, the Iberian People's Union was the first to proclaim itself as the primary “reform-oriented” group within the Council. The IPU was sponsored by conservative members of the government, to dampen the flames of reformism and keep the most radical reformists at bay within the Council.

The IPU failed to monopolize reformism, as alternative pro-reform groups were quick to spring up in the wake of the IPU's creation. Instead the IPU now serves as a dud, populated by technocrats and conservative reformists who hitch their wagons to reformism for the sake of their careers and the legitimacy of the regime rather than any true enthusiasm for political upheaval. The group's days are numbered, and its constituent members will likely find some other political party to continue their political life and preserve their careers.
strings.IBR_council_groups_faction_4_info:
Labor-Unionist


Whether the National Trade Union was a good idea in the first place or not is sure to be one that vexes future historians, that is a given. But the truth of the matter is that it is slowly crumbling away - and may be taking its representatives on the Council away with it. As part of the Council was required to be chosen by members of the national trade union, those elected found themselves - for the most part - without much of a political home, and thus a grouping exclusively for them was created by default.

As such, the existence of the Labor-Unionist group is something of a collective shrug on the part of the Iberian Council. It is the dumping ground for members who could not fit into any major party or grouping - those who wish to continue with a political career will attempt to curry favour amongst the political parties with hopes for a placement, while those who do not will simply vote as they please as they await their political death.
strings.IBR_council_groups_faction_5_info:
Regionalist


Despite the usual connotations of “regionalist” within Iberian politics, the members of the Regionalist group within the Council do not represent the wishes of those seeking autonomy for their regions from the central government. Instead, the Regionalist group is formed from traditionalists who still believe in some form of traditional political decentralization, or have specific sentiments that leave them more isolated from other groups within the Council.

Quite a number of the Regionalist group's members are representatives from regions of Spain that have always had their own distinct regionalist sentiments, like Catalonia or the Basque Country. These representatives are members of the regional bourgeoisies, business owners with economic interests riding on the final outcome of the Council's reforms. Once the Council's reforms have been carried out, members of this group shall either return to their respective businesses, or will go on to form the structures for regional wings of right-wing parties if they choose to remain involved in politics.
strings.IBR_council_groups_faction_6_info:
Institutional Action


When reform came to Iberia, it was inevitable that there would be pushback. While most of what much of the world would consider the 'far-right' in Iberia has chosen to take part in the Council's activities to achieve their own ends, a minor, entirely radicalised splinter still continues to fly their authoritarian flag openly. The Institutional Action Group is, in their own minds, at least, the last stronghold of what the Caudillos originally intended the country to be. Entirely opposed to democracy in all its forms, they consider their more active counterparts to be traitors, having revealed their true colours when given the chance.

The Institutional Action Group is ultimately the dying gasp of a dead age. While they may continue to insist that their ideas hold relevancy, the dwindling number of people that they can call friends - both inside and outside the Council - makes any success far from likely, no matter how many times they rebrand and refound themselves.

strings.IBR_council_law.1.d:
The latest proposal to the Council has flown through with remarkable ease. The morning session saw a few small but focused debates surrounding the bill's nitty-gritty, making slight numerical adjustments and moving around funds. Despite a few pointed questions from certain members of the Council, the atmosphere remained largely calm and cooperative, with several council members taking the extra time to shower the proposal in praise and bring up how great it was for Iberia.

When the law was eventually put up to a vote that afternoon in front of a full chamber, to nobody's surprise, it was voted on with near-unanimous support.
strings.IBR_council_law.2.d:
The latest proposal has caught some significant drag in the Council. What began as yet another routine session quickly devolved into an impassioned debate on the proposal. From the get-go, the proposal was struck on both sides by vehement supporters and detractors, each side trying to sway the few fencesitters. Several members of the Council requested time to voice their own fringe opinions, dragging the debate on for hours into the late afternoon.

By the time the proposal was finally put up to the vote, nearly a third of the Council had departed, some in protest, others from just wanting to go home. Even though the eventual proposal passed, the final tally showed not only the absent group large, but those that opposed it were unusually large as well.

[?global.date.GetDateStringNoHour]
Iberian Parliamentary Minutes

1. Speaker of the Iberian Parliament motioned for final reading of the bill under discussion. Motion carried with an absolute majority. A parliamentary group claimed five minutes to criticize the bill, to which the government provided a brief response.

2. Speaker of the Iberian Parliament motioned to begin final voting on the law. Motion carried with a majority.

3. Quorum was confirmed to initiate final voting. An absolute majority of deputies voted in favor of the bill.

strings.IBR_VEN.1_trujillo.desc:
The office of the SIM chief in Ciudad Trujillo resembled an expensive recording studio: walls lined with sound-absorbing panels, reels of the latest Ampex tape recorder turning slowly on the desk. Johnny Abbes García, with the appearance of a bored clerk and the reputation of a butcher, didn't even take off his dark glasses. He lazily turned a dial as Castro León hammered out his words.

“I chose exile not out of fear, Señor Abbes,” the Venezuelan General stood at attention, but his jaw muscles were twitching. “I left because Caracas is choking on Red bile. The democrats let socialists into the Senate while officers sit in barracks like castrated dogs. Give me resources, and on March 25th, I will burn out this infection.”

Abbes pressed “stop.” The click of the key sounded astonishingly loud to Castro León's ears.

“Exile...” the SIM chief's voice was insinuating, devoid of emotion. “Prudence is a virtue of a clerk, not a soldier. But El Jefe understands your hatred. Do you know what Generalissimo Franco answered when asked if he was ready to shoot half of Spain to defeat the Reds? He said: ”I will do it at any cost.“ Venezuela now demands the same price.”

He stood up, adjusting the impeccable knot of his tie, and approached the former General.

“El Jefe is ready to pay this bill. Iberia will provide the tools. But remember: the SIM keeps strict accounts. If you fail, we will write you off. And believe me, you won't like it.”
strings.IBR_VEN.1_trujillo.a: The enemy of my enemy is my tool.
strings.IBR_VEN.1_rebel.desc:
In the spacious penthouse of the Hotel Courtleigh, massive mahogany blinds sliced the dazzling Caribbean sun into thin golden strips falling onto the cool polished terrazzo floor. In the corners of the room, furnished with low rattan furniture, ceiling fans spun their blades lazily, vainly attempting to disperse the cigar smoke.

Luis M. González-Mata, lounging languidly in an armchair, hypnotized the ice cube in his glass of rum with his gaze. “...In Tangier, a contact tried to sell me a list of CIA agents. I bought it. And a week later, he came back to sell me the names of those interested in that list.” The Spaniard laughed quietly, raspily. “I paid the second time too, General. Only in lead this time. In our trade, greed is forgiven, but stupidity - never.”

Castro León did not smile. He sat on the edge of the sofa, straight as a bayonet, his face grey with tension. “Save your memoirs for the publishers, González. Trujillo is dead. Who will pay for my 'adventure'? Who gives the guarantees?”

The spy instantly tensed, shedding the mask of a bored playboy. His gaze became sharp. “Trujillo was a useful but blunt instrument. Now we work directly. Madrid is taking this project under its wing. The ships are already en route, holds packed to the brim with rifles.”

He leaned forward, and a strip of light fell across his eyes, turning them into slits. “But take note, my friend: Iberia pays generously, but demands more strictly than the late 'Chapitas'. On March 25th, you must take San Cristóbal. If you fail Madrid's investment... I fear my next tale will be about how a Venezuelan general 'accidentally' fell overboard in the open sea.”
strings.IBR_VEN.2_trujillo.desc:
San Cristóbal, Venezuela was drowning in a dense milky shroud of “neblina” - the Andean fog that muffled footsteps and blurred the outlines of reality. In this haze, the headlights of rare cars seemed like wandering wisps, and steep streets climbing up the slopes vanished into nowhere after just ten meters. The SIM agent shivered, watching moisture settle on his coat lapels in heavy, mercury-like drops. The agent pulled his coat tighter. Accustomed to the sticky heat of Ciudad Trujillo, this city seemed like a refrigerator where someone forgot to turn off the light. The streets climbing the slopes were deserted-a perfect setting for a conspiracy.

He walked beside the Venezuelan officer, whose stride betrayed the nervousness typical of amateurs.

“Forget the tanks, Colonel,” the Dominican spoke. “Tanks are brute force. If Caracas doesn't hear us in the first half-hour, we are corpses. Radio stations, local repeaters here in Táchira - that's where the power lies. Without the airwaves, your garrisons will remain blind kittens.

The agent knew what he was talking about. In the basements of the secret police, he had spent years learning how information breaks the will faster than pliers.

They turned a corner, and the silhouette of the Iglesia del Divino Redentor church emerged from the fog. Its modest, almost ascetic facade seemed like a fortress wall in the twilight. The agent stopped at the steps, looking at the cross dissolving into the sky.

”Comms must be established before the first rooster crow, Colonel. Otherwise, the only thing left for us is confession inside.“
strings.IBR_VEN.2_trujillo.a: Silence on the airwaves is death.

strings.IBR_VEN.3.desc:
The Puerto Cabello airbase was quiet, save for the distant groans of the ocean and windy gusts beating down on rusted plane parts. Three men, two of them pilots, stood beside a grounded bomber. In the midnight dark, their low voices stuck out in the hangar, echoing talks of dissent, revealing the calm before the storm.

The stranger, talking with a slighted Spanish accent foreign to Venezuela, took out a folder, passing annotated pages to the hands of both pilots. “These are your targets. Loyalist encampments within Puerto Cabello. Munition depots. Fortín Solano too, just in case.”

One pilot stood up straight, broad-shouldered and eager, directing his arm into an unwavering salute without even glancing at the details. His comrade lingered on the pages, still staring at the pictures of neighborhoods he'd have to bomb. “This... this is too close to the neighborhoods. Thousands live there. What if we accidentally hit them?”

The stranger walked up to the hesitant pilot, fixing his gaze and laying his hand over the pilot's shoulder. “Don't miss then, comrade. History will not remember who you killed, but what part you played in our grand reclamation of our home, Venezuela.”

A long silence followed, with the pilot's face physically shifting in accordance with his emotions. His loyalty clashed with his hometown. Puerto Cabello was where he'd grown up, where his memories lay. But he couldn't truly call it his home anymore, nor its people his neighbors, as long as the socialist mob ruled Venezuela.

The pilot closed the folder, tucking it under his arm. “Anything for the reclamation. I only hope God will be forgiving.”
strings.IBR_VEN.3.a: “God will have no part in this. All of Venezuela is already damned to hell.”
strings.IBR_VEN.4_trujillo.desc:
Kingston was drowning in a blinding white haze of midday sun that ricocheted off the colonial balustrades of the hotel terrace and dissolved the silhouettes of the Blue Mountains on the horizon into the trembling air. Oscar Tamayo Suárez, former commander of the National Guard, pushed away a glass of warm gin with disgust. Even in a colorful tourist shirt, he looked like a loaded mortar - massive, with a heavy, sullen gaze, he clearly didn't fit into the relaxed rhythm of the Canadian colony.

When a shadow fell across his table, Tamayo didn't even flinch. He recognized the walk. “You'll rust here, Oscar,” Jesús María Castro León sat down opposite without invitation, nodding to the waiter. “Enough drinking this English piss. Time to return to proper rum in Caracas.”

Tamayo smiled crookedly, remembering the Barcelonazo that cost him his epaulets. “Last time I listened to enthusiasts like you, I had to flee the country in a trunk,” he rasped. “I have no desire to play suicide-hero for pretty headlines again.”

“This time we play for keeps.” Castro León lowered his voice, leaning closer. “Iberia is paying. Chapitas, El Jefe, is covering. San Cristóbal is just the spark. I need a man who will take the National Guard by the throat when the fire starts. I need you.”

Tamayo was silent, twirling a cigar in his fingers. Caution and old, unquenched ambition fought in his eyes. “Fine,” he finally threw out. “I'm in. But on one condition. When we kick these democrimpotents out of the palace, I'm not going to stand in the honor guard. A seat on the Junta. An equal among equals. Or go to hell with your revolution.”

Castro León smiled and extended his hand. “Agreed, General. Now finish your drink.”
strings.IBR_VEN.4_trujillo.a: “A plane awaits us, and Venezuela awaits a good thrashing.”

strings.IBR_VEN.5_trujillo.desc:
IBERIAN INTELLIGENCE SERVICE - INTERCEPTED CORRESPONDENCE

An incoming letter from exiled Venezuelan general Jesús María Castro León addressed to the head of Dominican SIM, Johnny Abbes, has been seized. The following is its unaltered content:

To my esteemed friend, Johnny Abbes,

The mission of our forces will commence at 0420, March 25th. The hour is steadily arriving, and our banners are poised to rise once again over Caracas. Once the signal is sent, Venezuelan loyalists will be decimated. The barrack doors will open. The bombs will drop. And San Cristóbal will surrender.

We have thousands of troops anxiously waiting. We have hundreds of pilots trained to the best of their ability. We have hearts and souls driven by nothing but the will to drive these socialist bureaucrats out of Venezuela. And of course, we have allies, like the Dominican Republic, ready to come to our aid.

However, as confident as I may sound, and even as I have unwavering confidence that my men can carry out their duties, I am no fool. Should we fail, all I ask is one seat on a plane to Santo Domingo. Not only is it about survival, but also about continuing the fight.

I will accept nothing less than total victory. And I only ask that we beseech God for this noble day.

With unshaken resolve,
Jesús María Castro León

The mission of our forces will commence at 0420, March 25th. The hour is steadily arriving, and our banners are poised to rise once again over Caracas. We have hearts and souls driven by nothing but the will to drive these socialist bureaucrats out of Venezuela. And of course, we have allies, like the Iberian Union, ready to come to our aid.

However, as confident as I may sound, and even as I have unwavering confidence that my men can carry out their duties, I am no fool. Should we fail, all I ask is one seat on a plane to Madrid. Not only is it about survival, but also about continuing the fight.

I will accept nothing less than total victory. And I only ask that we beseech God for this noble day.

With unshaken resolve,

strings.IBR_VEN.6.desc:
“Where the fuck is Maracaibo? Did it drown in that damn lake?” - Matías Vega Guerra flicked his cigarette butt into an overflowing ashtray and collapsed into an armchair, violently loosening his tie. “El Cabito took San Cristóbal, great. Fanfares, flowers, the whole lot. But where is the support from the north?”

António Fontes, imperturbable as a tombstone, merely turned a page of the report with care. In the smoke-filled chaos of the safehouse, he looked as if he were dressed for the opera.

“Quiet. Your temper is jamming the airwaves more than the loyalist saboteurs.” - The Portuguese offered his colleague a glass of water, but Matías waved it off and reached for the bottle of brandy. “The situation is shit, Matías. Castro León sits in San Cristóbal. Maracaibo is silent. The El Vigía garrison is on the line, but without the ”City by the Lake,“ they are cut off.”

“Silent?” Matías let out a nervous chuckle, pouring drinks into two glasses. “If they stay silent for another hour, the loyalists will nail the coffin shut. And our General will turn from the savior of the nation into just another idiot shot against a wall.”

“Either treachery, or cowardice, or someone cut the wires.” Fontes accepted the glass, and for a second, a weary solidarity flashed in his eyes. “In any case, we are screwed. A drink, Matías?”

“To us not having to flee this place in women's dresses, António.”
strings.IBR_VEN.7.desc:
“Weep like a woman for what you could not defend like a man!”“ Matías Vega Guerra slammed the newspaper onto the table so hard the ashtray jumped. ”Remember what his mother told Boabdil when he surrendered Granada? El Cabito just outdid the last Sultan. Did you see this photo? He's handing over his cap! His cap, António! Not his sword, not his life, but his fucking cap, joder!“

António Fontes methodically fed documents into the fireplace. Zip. The crackle of fire. There was more fatalism in that sound than in the Spaniard's entire tirade, now barking ”...La madre que lo pario!“.

”Leave the Reconquista to the historians, Matías. This isn't Granada, it's San Cristóbal, and it wasn't defeated by Catholic Monarchs, but by a bus drivers' union.“ The Portuguese adjusted his glasses, watching the lists of agents burn. ”Prosaic? Undoubtedly. But our little Napoleon forgot that an army cannot march if there is no one to bake bread and pump gas.“

Matías collapsed onto the sofa, covering his face with his hands, as if trying to erase the image of the humiliated General from his memory.

”And now he's going to San Carlos, while we sit here like rats on a sinking galleon, burning the sails. Madrid will draw and quarter us.“

”Madrid is far away.“ António walked to the bar and filled two glasses without spilling a drop. - ”Drink. Tomorrow we'll think about how to get that idiot out of his cage before he starts singing. But today... today we drink to the fact that experience is just a pretty name for our mistakes.“

”You're a callous son of a bitch, António.“

”I know. I know.“
strings.IBR_VEN.7.a: And somewhere, the ghost of Simón Bolívar is laughing.
strings.IBR_VEN.8.desc:
“The Château d'If has fallen, António!” - Matías burst into the room, waving a cipher like a winning lottery ticket. “Our Edmond Dantès has slipped out of the bag! ”Package delivered, sea calm.“ They smuggled him right out from under the jailers' noses while they were probably still finishing their morning coffee!”

The Spaniard poured himself a brandy without even sitting down, his energy filling the cramped safehouse to the brim.

“It's a plot straight out of a novel! San Carlos, an impregnable fortress... and there's General Castro León, already breathing the salty air of Aruba, making obscene gestures toward the Venezuelan coast.”

António Fontes, standing by the window watching a patrol on the street, allowed himself a rare, barely perceptible smirk. He did not share his colleague's enthusiasm but appreciated the flawless mechanics of the execution.

“Iberia doesn't throw away tools, even if they've been blunted by the owner's stupidity.” The Portuguese turned, glasses glinting. “A living martyr in Madrid is more useful than a dead loser in Caracas. Now we have a ghost. We will rattle this ghost's chains in the newspapers until the local ”democrats“ develop a nervous tic.”

Matías clinked his glass against his friend's glass, which the latter hadn't even had time to raise.

“You're an incorrigible cynic, António. But, damn it, what a beautiful move! To ghosts?”

“To those who always return.”
strings.IBR_VEN.8.a: Sometimes victory lies in simply not losing.
strings.IBR_VEN.9.desc:
“”Fuente Ovejuna,“ António!” - Matías Vega Guerra circled the safehouse in downtown Caracas, brandishing a fresh telegram like a rapier. Behind the tightly drawn curtains, the capital slept uneasily, unaware that the provinces were already burning. “Maracaibo, Barquisimeto... Cities are falling at El Cabito's feet like overripe fruit.”

António Fontes, settled in a deep armchair with a glass of port, merely raised a skeptical eyebrow, wiping his glasses with the corner of a handkerchief. Unlike his colleague, he preferred the prose of accounting reports to the poetry of barricades.

“The main thing is that our Don Quixote doesn't mistake windmills for giants, Matías. Epics are good on paper, but reality is more complicated.”

The radio on the table, tuned to the rebels' frequency, interrupted their banter. Through the static, Castro León's voice broke through - dry, hard, devoid of any theatricality:

“...Soldiers and citizens! Do not let initial victories cloud your vision. The liberation of the provinces is only the beginning. The enemy is still dug in at the heart of the nation, in Caracas, and as long as he is there, Venezuela is in danger. We will not stop halfway. We will not sheathe our swords until the banner is raised over Miraflores Palace. The march on the capital continues. Victory will be absolute!”

“Did you hear that? No windmills. This guy has the grip of a conquistador. Let's drink, António. Looks like we'll be signing new treaties soon!”
strings.IBR_VEN.9.a: There was no jubilation, only the work that remained to be done.
strings.IBR_VEN.10.t: Dinner on the Edge of the Abyss
strings.IBR_VEN.10.desc:
Matías Vega Guerra stabbed a juicy piece of meat with his fork, demonstratively ignoring the moans of wounded officers behind the wall of the Iberian embassy's dining room. War is war, but dinner must be served on schedule.

“Leoni...” the Spaniard drawled, examining the ruby wine in his glass against the light. “You know, António, this is a perfect example of a chronicle of proclaimed infirmity. He dared to try on Betancourt's boots, but his withered legs drowned inside them; he stumbled on level ground, tangled in the laces of his own power. On the surface - a man who belongs on a park bench feeding pigeons. He sat in Miraflores with a blissful smile while the horizon turned black, likely not even grasping the essence of the papers slid under his nose for signature. Poor bastard. And the army looked upon him with the same cold impatience with which heirs await the passing of a senile uncle.”

António Fontes, methodically cutting his steak into geometrically perfect squares, merely nodded coldly, not lifting his eyes. “Weakness provokes a predator far more than cruelty, Matías. Did that senile fool think his dignified grey hair commanded respect? Like hell. It commands nothing but squeamishness and the urge to shoot him out of pity, like an old dog.”

Matías sighed, saluting his colleague with his glass. “To those who have rotted alive but forgot to lie in the coffin, António.”

They didn't have time to finish their drinks. The doors burst open with a crash that made the candle flames in the candelabras shy away. On the threshold stood a captain in uniform.

“Señores!” he exhaled, sliding down the doorframe. “It's all over. The Guard is fleeing. Miraflores has fallen!”
strings.IBR_VEN.10.a: Tell the kitchen to open the champagne.

“Barrios...” the Spaniard drawled, examining the ruby wine in his glass against the light. “You know, António, this is the tragedy of a pacifist matador. He entered the arena against an enraged bull armed only with a perfumed handkerchief and a copy of the Constitution. He thought he could 'dance' the beast, charm it with his exquisite manners and that...” Matías made a vague, effeminate gesture with his hand, “...silky style of his. Fool. He forgot the main rule of bullfighting: the bull does not appreciate such things.”

António Fontes, methodically cutting his steak into geometrically perfect squares, merely nodded coldly, not lifting his eyes. “Barrios mistook politics for ballet. Poor devil.”

Matías smirked, saluting his colleague with his glass. “To elegant corpses, António. They make a beautiful exit.”

strings.IBR_VEN.12.desc:
Matías Vega Guerra stabbed a juicy piece of meat with his fork, demonstratively ignoring the moans of wounded officers behind the wall of the Iberian embassy's dining room. War is war, but dinner must be served on schedule.

“Ojeda...” the Spaniard drawled, examining the ruby wine in his glass against the light. “You know who he reminds me of, António? Girolamo Savonarola. That Florentine also thought he could rule a city of sinners with nothing but sermons about virtue and 'bonfires of the vanities.' Our schoolteacher sincerely believed that if he read Marx to the generals from a balcony, they would weep with emotion and hand over the keys to the tanks.”

António Fontes, methodically cutting his steak into geometrically perfect squares, merely chuckled coldly, not lifting his eyes from his plate. “Savonarola was eventually burned in the same square where he preached. History has a wicked sense of humor, Matías. Ojeda set himself on fire when he decided that friendship with Havana would serve as a bulletproof vest.”

Matías nodded, saluting his colleague with his glass. “To unarmed prophets, António.”

They didn't have time to finish their drinks. The doors burst open with a crash that made the candle flames in the candelabras shy away. On the threshold stood a captain in uniform.

“Señores!” he exhaled, sliding down the doorframe. “It's all over. The Guard is fleeing. Miraflores has fallen!”
strings.IBR_VEN.12.a: Tell the kitchen to open the champagne.
strings.IBR_VEN.13.desc:
The camera flashes in the Joaquín Crespo Hall at Miraflores Palace are as blinding as muzzle flares, but General - now President - Jesús María Castro León does not even flinch. He stands tall in an immaculately pressed uniform, the very personification of order returned to Venezuelan soil. At his right hand is Matías Vega Guerra. Unlike haughty envoys from Madrid, this native of the Canaries speaks with a soft accent that sounds almost kin to Venezuelan ears. A seasoned lawyer and administrator, he smiles like a returning cousin. To his left stands the complete opposite: António Alexandre da Rocha Fontes, a man of cold calculation whose gaze betrays the ruthless efficiency of Salazar's “Estado Novo.”

When protocol is satisfied, the procession moves to the Council of Ministers Room. The heavy doors slam shut, cutting off the noise, leaving only the ticking of the clock. Castro León gestures to his guests to the long oval table, overseen by the portrait of Simón Bolívar, hanging like a silent judge at the head. Servants silently place cups of steaming café cerrero.

“Madrid and Lisbon send their warmest congratulations,” says Vega Guerra, reaching for a cup. “It is a pleasure to see a man of honor ruling Caracas again, rather than a demagogue.”

“We appreciated your... discreet assistance in our hour of need,” the President nods, looking toward Fontes. The Portuguese does not waste time on pleasantries.

“Let us leave sentimentality to the historians, Señor Presidente,” Fontes states dryly, retrieving a folder stamped with an embossed coat of arms from his briefcase. “Iberia invested in stability. Now, it is time for dividends. Your predecessors flirted with Mexico and Washington, but the oil of the Orinoco must flow in the right direction. Towards old friends.”

Castro León smirked, signing the document without looking. For the first time in a long while, he felt safe.
strings.IBR_VEN.13.a: Black gold in exchange for ironclad guarantees.
strings.IBR_VEN.14.desc:
The air across the barracks in Valencia was turning rancid, the rations prepared swallowed with some disdain from the officers complaining through lunch. Overhead, a speech came from Fabricio Ojeda, proclaiming a new vision for the Venezuelan economy, much to the chagrin of those huddled within.

“That fucking atheist swine, daring to force us to bow to his socialist vision,” complained one, Rafael Cadavel, leaving his fork in his soup. “Makes me ashamed to serve in this army.”

Another, Alfredo Barrueco, simply chuckled to himself. “We'll at least get some front-row seats when somebody finally gets the guts to march into the Miraflores and throw Ojeda off his roof.”

The comment brought silence, but only in contemplation. “You know,” replied Óscar Tejedor, allowing his spoon to dip into the soup in turn, “I don't think we'd be alone in that presumption. I've seen how angry some of my family has been at Ojeda, and I know they're not the only ones.”

“But where would we get the money?” groaned Cadavel, clutching his fork but not bringing it up. “If anger alone could topple that bastard, we'd have succeeded on Holy Wednesday.”

Another moment of contemplation, before Tejedor raised a spoon. “You know, Franco is probably still pissed at losing his stake in Venezuela. I'm sure they've still got a few ears somewhere. Let's talk about this with a few others. Trusted friends. Once we can contact the Iberians...” As the covenant was signed, one ear turned away, registering the course of conversation into Portuguese as he considered how to raise the conversation.
strings.IBR_VEN.14.a: It's not over yet. Let's see if we still have enough men here for another shot.
strings.IBR_VEN.14.b: Let's see how serious this is before getting involved again.
strings.IBR_VEN.14.tt:
If the military opposition becomes stronger than {ven_getflag} Ojeda's government and the democratic opposition, {ibr_getflag} our interests in Venezuela will prevail over {mex_getflag} Mexico and the {usa_getflag} U.S.
------------------------------------
strings.IBR_VEN.15.t: A Beachhead Back to the Andes
strings.IBR_VEN.15.desc:
FROM THE OFFICE OF S.I.M TO THE OFFICE OF THE PRESIDENT: FOR THE CAUDILLO'S EYES ONLY!

-The Iberian Embassy in Caracas recently received a seal letter from high-ranking officers in the Venezuelan military, containing details about an ongoing conspiracy against President Ojeda stemming from the URD party (establishment opposition) alongside sympathetic elements of the military.

-Largely composed of ardent Venezuelan nationalists, the cadre of party opposition and military leaders believe that under the current administration in Caracas, Venezuela's democratic apparatus is swiftly becoming a pipeline for leftist infiltrators seeking a possible communist revolution.

-While some more liberal-minded officers are implicated in the plot to overthrow the Ojeda government, many believe that the democratic system in Venezuela to be untenable in the current political climate, even in the event of the president's ouster. They are planning to conduct a counter-coup of the provisional government and establish direct military rule from Caracas.

-They promise exorbitant economic benefits as well as diplomatic prioritization for the Iberian Union and her allies, including with regards to Venezuela's vast oil wealth. In return, they ask for funding and material aid for the operation to overthrow Ojeda and consolidate power against popular upheaval and any other form of resistance.
strings.IBR_VEN.15.a: Donate Iberian weaponry to the patriots in Venezuela.
strings.IBR_VEN.15.b: Pesatas will purchase us as an ally in Caracas.
strings.IBR_VEN.15.c: South American ventures can backfire easily...
strings.IBR_VEN.16.desc:
A speedboat glided through the water. The whir of its engine pierced the night, punctuated with backfires and men's curses. It had been a while; the coast of Grenada had long disappeared from view; Venezuela loomed in the distance as a dark wall that jutted out from the ocean, replete with threatening movement. Deep in the night, the boat slowed and turned. An inlet opened like a gate, and a quiet forest gently welcomed the boat beneath its canopy.

Lieutenant Martínez pulled the cover away roughly, sending some of the boat's contents spilling onto the sand. Thousands of stony faces on thousands of paper bills stared up at him. His eyes narrowed. The smugglers watched him expectantly. “Where are the radios?”

“We will drop them in about a week.”

“Where, when?”

One of the smugglers shrugged, gesturing at the air. He huffed, glibly tipped his hat, and gestured for his men to bag the money. He watched the Iberians float away lazily into the horizon.

Dawn illuminated the distant airfield. Martínez stepped on the gas, the car jolted, and the countryside blurred. He cast nervous glances at the back of the truck; beneath the car parts lay thousands of dollars' worth of bribes, soon to find their way into the hands of all those disaffected or apathetic enough regarding the new Socialist tyranny to stand aside and let it fall. He slowed.

Martínez pulled in, studying the faces of his comrades as they waved the truck inside. Any of them could destroy the whole operation if they bothered to investigate. Yet none did, and never would. He breathed a sigh of relief as he passed into a dark hangar. The plane was ready.
strings.IBR_VEN.16.a: Let's show off our new toys.
strings.IBR_VEN.17.desc:
The Hotel Tamanaco was always bustling with activity. Thus, nobody paid any mind to the party of sixteen who had reserved a dining room. They did not look the part, but they were officers of the Venezuelan Army, and they were here to discuss their role in a coming coup.

“The radio station goes to Guteriez; you will move units in to take the building by noon. Olabarri, you'll move in to take the Presidential place from the Viaduct.”

The officers stole glances at each other. Lieutenant Zarzo placed them like chess pieces as he pored over the map of the city, filled in with each monument, church, police station, and base. Some grimaced; they would be in the thick of it. Others smirked; they would get the glory. Most had no local contacts; the few who did thought themselves ill-placed, their planned actions ill-timed.

“Captain Peraza will take up supportive positions for Sergeant Olabarri.”

Some were already making plans for after, others stared out the windows, planning their maneuvers. The air began to feel heavy. The streets below hummed with activity, backfires and shouting wafting to the assembler's ears like desperate warnings.

“As for myself, I will move near the Plaza Panteón.”

The officers knew that there was still so much to do, yet, as Zarzo was so keen to point out, there was already champagne in crates stashed in the corners. They all had their dispositions- determined, resolute, utter terror. The plan was so absurd, Zarzo so cavalier and cocksure, that a real confidence descended on the room. Surely, they reasoned, someone somewhere must have it all figured out, the Iberians, perhaps.
strings.IBR_VEN.17.a: We go over the plan, one more time.
strings.IBR_VEN.17.b: Let there be no doubt, no wavering, on the eve of our triumph!
strings.IBR_VEN.18.desc:
Guillermo eagerly drank in the jubilation that pervaded the Palacio de la Moncloa. No longer would he be an exile. The forces of law and order would prevail. His people would finally reject red subversion, though, regrettably, only after an education with tanks and Iberian arms.

He cheered as images flashed of military units securing street after street in Caracas. The entire staff of the Palacio, ministry officials, secretaries, and the numerous exiles like him, watched in rapt anticipation as the panicked Ojedists were ejected from the radio stations, their jittery voices replaced by the cool, sonorous tones of military officers.

“I can assure you all that gasoline will soon become much, much cheaper,” Guillermo joked, to the resounding laughter of his colleagues.

The illusion shattered. As if from nowhere, thousands of police and National Guard units loyal to Ojeda cordoned off the National Assembly, stopping the coup's tanks in their tracks. Guillermo and others howled themselves hoarse at the televisions, demanding they break through. Then, a little after noon, there was silence.

The tanks turned. The televisions were filled with images of unionists, communists, and workers all descending on the streets, coming from the slums on the hills, throwing rocks and bottles at the soldiers who scurried away in the wake. The coup's defeat was announced on reclaimed television and radio, with footage of a grinning, resolute Ojeda waving to cheering crowds playing on repeat.

The whole Palacio was then filled with prayers, recriminations, shouting matches, but only until nightfall. Guillermo's colleagues went to their homes. Only Guillermo remained, thinking of his home, there on a little street in Caracas, surely despoiled by looters and police. He sat, picking up a half-empty bottle of liquor. He drank, weeping.
strings.IBR_VEN.18.a: Only God could save his country now.
strings.IBR_VEN.19.desc:
“Can you repeat that, I didn't quite- Hello? Can you hear me?” asked Iberia's ambassador to Brazil, as chaos reigned within the embassy offices. Writing down chicken-scratch notes to try and memorize the information coming through the failing call, he relayed the information to the rest of the office, shouting over the noise, “The nationalists have been unable to roll into the streets of Caracas, and they're attempting to force entry into the city with military force.” In a quieter tone, the ambassador added, “It doesn't seem to be going very well...”

The ambassador's attention snapped back to the call, and he relayed the words of the officer on the other end of the line as he received them. “You're holding out inside Hotel Tamanaco? And the liberal national guard have breached the building's premises? Are you- You'll call back? Alright, I'll wait on this end, then...”

For the rest of the day, the ambassador waited by the phone, amidst the chaotic frenzy of the embassy staff. After a day or two, the embassy had slowed down to a more manageable state, but the phone still hadn't rung. After the third day, everyone knew what had happened. The nationalists had been defeated, the coup stopped in its tracks before they had even pierced Caracas. The opportunity had passed them by, and Venezuela had slipped out of Iberia's grasp.
strings.IBR_VEN.20.desc:
Manuel and the other Iberian diplomats were greeted by the officers at Miraflores not with a rigid salute, but by smiles and jokes. The successful coup clearly had the men in high spirits, and Manuel and his colleagues certainly weren't going to try and dampen the mood. As they entered the palace, that joyful mood only soared higher, and the diplomats passed various men and their wives dancing to Merengue as the procession sat down at a large table. As the champagne was served, the Venezuelan officers were the first to speak. “We must thank you and your country for all of your support. Venezuela is in your debt.”

Manuel spoke for the diplomats: “We're flattered, but I must ask, why invite us to your night of celebration? Surely we could have given you some time to get all your affairs in order.”

“Don't worry, we simply wish to reward your support by fulfilling our end of the deal here and now, so that there's no doubt about it,” replied the officer. Accepting their cue, Manuel and his diplomats pulled out their books to begin negotiating Iberian stakes in Venezuelan businesses. However, they were soon interrupted by the sounds of rubber bullets being fired and cars crashing into other cars in the distance.

Manuel shot a worried glance at the rest of his colleagues, but one of the officers soon gave out a chuckle as he sipped from his glass. “Ah, growing pains... What a pain, am I right?” The rest of the officers soon began cracking jokes about the unrest, and the brief tension popped like the bubbles in their champagne. Manuel simply shrugged. Once these negotiations were over and the stakes had been sorted out, he'd be going home anyway, so it wasn't his problem to worry about anyway.
strings.IBR_VEN.20.a: And also the appetizers had just arrived.
strings.IBR_VEN.21.desc:
The early afternoon sun was half-hid behind an overcast sky, occasionally peaking through the clouds onto the plaza below. A fountain churned as Fernando María Castiella y Maíz walked the promenade around it, another Iberian diplomat at his side. Somewhere afar, he could sense the eyes of a security detail eying the meeting with twitchy eyes and twitchier trigger fingers. “If he's of no use to the Yanquis, what use is he to us?” The Minister of Foreign Affairs prompted.

“To avoid another Puerto Plata.” His colleague had served in the Iberian Embassy in Ciudad Trujillo, assisting the foreign relations operation with the regime in the Dominican Republic. “Our allies along the Caribbean are under threat, both Washington and Mexico City can sense it. Caracas offers us inroad in the Andes, Pérez Jiménez just needs the machinery to get behind him.”

He was referring to General Pérez Jiménez, the former lapdog of the Americans and front for all of their dealings in Venezuela. He insisted that the various dissident military revolts after the 1958 Coup were evidence of an opportunity, citing that Villalba, the President-elect of Venezuela, had estranged a lot of Pérez Jiménez' contacts in the military. Seeding a coup d'état in Caracas, if Castiella's colleague was to be believed, would give the Hispaniphone bloc a foothold and kneecap a principal ally of the Veracruz Pact.

Castiella stopped walking for a brief moment, looking up at the pale gray sky, seeing something that resembled the enmity of fog and the unknowability of the future. Maybe he was just being paranoid, but Venezuela was an unruly beast, evident from, if nothing else, historical precedent. Were Mexico and her allies really as much of a threat to Madrid as they seemed, or was Puerto Plata just a fluke not to be repeated?
strings.IBR_VEN.21.a: “I can give no guarantees, but I will make the call.” Castiella told his colleague.
strings.IBR_VEN.22.desc:
The tram was uncharacteristically empty, save for two people sitting beside each other. This was precisely because at least one of them was among the few who had a real say in the government of the Iberian Union, even if the Minister of Foreign Affairs only represented a medium-sized cog in Franco and Salazar's orderly machine. Fernando María Castiella y Maíz scratched at the bridge of his nose. “Why in hell should we get involved this time?” he blurted. “Suffer even one more unnecessary setback while the knuckle-draggers bang their heads off each other?”

His associate, a diplomat who worked at the Iberian Embassy in Ciudad Trujillo, posited his point a different way. “We cannot simply stand off to the side and allow Puerto Plata to foul the air.” He suggested. “There are many actors in the Caribbean who want to see the Hispanosphere's influence driven back across the Atlantic, we need to rebound and decisively. Venezuela is the perfect place to do it.” He was referring to the mounting opposition against the Venezuelan President-elect, Caldera, an unimpressive moderate who seemed to be earning the ire of the military for that reason.

Even though military conspiracies against the government of Caracas seemed to be becoming a thing of the past, there remained a small, but growing core of fervent nationalists and Bolivarianists among the officer corps, something that Castiella's associate argued presented an opportunity to seed an ally in the northern Andes and dismantle a key ally of the Veracruz Pact all at once.

“Mexico wasn't sitting on their hands with Puerto Plata either.” His colleague pointed out. “They are just aching to force Iberian interests out of the hemisphere, I suggest we strike first.” The first drops of rain began falling outside, another overcast afternoon.
strings.IBR_VEN.22.a: “I'll talk to some people, but no promises.” Castiella replied.
strings.IBR_VEN.23.desc:
Below, the interns and diplomatic staff at the Brazilian Embassy on Calle de Goya picked away at their daily itineraries, the perennial shuffle of office files and telephone calls went on uninterrupted. Above, in a sequestered officer suite on the embassy's upper floors, something more sinister was going on.

Foreign Affairs Minister Fernando María Castiella y Maíz poured over the files with almost mounting disbelief. Here, a dossier on right-wing dissenters in the Venezuelan military, including multiple high-ranking generals. There, portfolios on multiple dissident politicians, both in the interior and agitating from abroad. Further in, details on criminal elements on the ground, from street gangs to organized cartels, all amply rewarded for their trouble, all perfectly willing to operate at the behest and in the interest of, a kindly benefactor.

The projector rattled and an another grainy blue image appeared on a distant wall, a Portuguese general sounding off names and information as the face went by with each slide; Personnel IDs, criminal mugshots, stately portraits, and on and on they went, a visual representation of the endeavor they were about to become involved in.

The time window they had to work with wasn't ideal, but if it all worked as planned, Iberian intelligence and 'commercial interests' across the Caribbean would fashion this strange gathering of Caracas' best and worst into a poison arrow, aimed right at the heart of Venezuela. In this environment, the word of the Minister of Foreign Affairs was God.
strings.IBR_VEN.23.a: “Send the word.” It was all Castiella had to say.
strings.IBR_VEN.24.desc:
Enrique Valenzuela felt ill at ease. The Paseo de los Próceres was too open, too well-lit. The marble statues of the heroes of the War of Independence seemed to look down judgingly at the Iberian agent trying to merge with the shadows near one of the fountains. His contact, Rubén Massó Perdomo, on the contrary, stood frighteningly erect, as if he himself were part of this architectural ensemble.

When Enrique approached and asked through gritted teeth to keep it down, Rubén merely waved his hand dismissively, gesturing around the geometrically flawless alley.

“Keep it down? Enrique, you think like a petty smuggler. Look around. This is our architectural pride and joy: the 'System of Nationality' complex. The grand axis connects the University with the Military Academy. General Pérez Jiménez carved this concrete and marble to remind us: Venezuela is not a market square.”

The Venezuelan nodded toward the looming masses of Fort Tiuna, the country's main military base. “Up there sit officers who are sickened by the democratic 'bochinche' - this eternal mess bred by politicians. And they are waiting for the 'Necessary Gendarme'. Someone who will step into the light and say: 'Order has returned.' If we cower in corners like rats, they will crush us. But if we stand here, beneath these statues, as heirs of Bolívar... they will remember how to salute properly.”

Valenzuela looked at the barracks, then at the fanatical glint in Rubén's eyes. It was madness - or the boldest calculation of his career.
strings.IBR_VEN.24.a: Perhaps he is right. Boldness attracts soldiers.
