strings.IBR_VEN.24.b: It is suicide. Better to stay in the shadows.
strings.IBR_VEN.25.desc:
The bead of sweat hung suspended on Generalissimo Rafael Trujillo's face. Immobile. Even as his legs churned, his eyes never left Johnny Abbes' porcine form as the Dominican spymaster spoke.

“SIM agents have taken into custody three criminals residing in the Venezuelan city of Coro. Records recovered from two June 14th encampments indicate the trio were active in funding traitors to our nation.”

The Generalissimo grunted, and Abbes continued, “An operative retained the services of a local gang in Maracaibo to damage a key pipeline flowing to an export terminal. The explosives used failed to breach the pipe, but the incident was enough to cause mass panic in the city.”

Trujillo's response came in a high-pitched voice. “Should have used the bombs we blew up Betancourt with.” A thin laugh that Abbes quickly matched.

The bead of sweat at last fell, trailing down a wrinkle on the Goat's wizened face. Abbes' watery eyes almost drifted to it, but he forced himself to hold Trujillo's gaze. “The SIM is currently evaluating whether we have an opportunity to eliminate any high-profile politicians. The Iberian partnership you have fostered is allowing us to pursue longstanding Venezuelan enemies of our government. Their efforts in Caracas-”

Trujillo ceased pedalling abruptly, and stepped off the exercise bike. He beckoned his mayordomo for a towel. “Go kill an adeco. I need to change.”
strings.IBR_VEN.25.a: The wheels of Dominican justice keep turning...
strings.IBR_VEN.26.desc:
The crystal chiming of glasses in the Palace of Santa Cruz suddenly seemed deafening to Fernando María Castiella. Just a minute ago, the Iberian Minister of Foreign Affairs was discussing trade quotas with a German attaché, but the moment his aide, pale as a sheet, touched his elbow, the world around him collapsed.

In the quiet of the corridor, away from prying ears, the aide's whisper sounded like a verdict: “There were mass raids in Caracas last night. They took three liaisons and the resident. Señor Ministro... they didn't have time to destroy the cipher pads. Contact lists, codes, safehouse addresses - the Venezuelans have everything.”

Castiella felt an icy cold grip inside. If DIGEPOL published these documents, the scandal would bury Iberia's reputation in the region for decades.

“Pull everyone out,” the Minister's voice was hoarse; he barely recognized it himself. “Immediately. Diplomats, trade representatives, even the janitors if they've ever laid eyes on our operatives. Burn the embassy archives. Cut the wires. I want not a single Iberian left there who can be put in an interrogation chair within the hour.”

He adjusted his cuffs, preparing to return to the hall and smile, knowing that across the ocean, everything they had built was crumbling.
strings.IBR_VEN.26.a: It is going to be a very long night.
strings.IBR_VEN.26.tt:
With the collapse of the dissident conspiracy, in the event of a coup, the {ven_getflag} Venezuelan government will prevail against our allied efforts to depose them.

The failure of {ibr_getflag} our infiltrators will now be a certainty for many years to come.
strings.IBR_VEN.27.desc:
Enrique Valenzuela pushed the heavy wooden door of the bar, leaving the stifling noise of the Caracas street behind. The bartender, without even asking, placed a bulbous glass of “Pampero Aniversario” before the Iberian. Enrique nodded, took a sip, enjoying the burning warmth, and headed to the back room, hidden from prying eyes by a heavy velvet curtain.

The atmosphere inside differed strikingly from the nervous meeting on the Paseo. Rubén Massó Perdomo sat at the head of the table, his tunic collar unbuttoned, surrounded by young officers. Seeing the agent, he raised his glass in greeting, and the tension on the faces of those present was replaced by broad smiles.

“Gentlemen,” Enrique sank into an empty chair, surveying the company. “I hope you aren't too attached to your current ranks. I fear you will soon have to change your insignia.”

He held a theatrical pause, enjoying the silence. “Our friends in the government, in their infinite wisdom, have decided that DIGEPOL is not coping with its duties. A great purge has begun. They are firing the very people who could have stopped us, calling it 'incompetence'.” The Iberian smirked, looking into Rubén's eyes. “A vacuum is forming. Many empty chairs, much power, and a total lack of oversight. This is a unique chance for ambitious young men loyal not to a paper constitution, but to the true Venezuela. Who among you is ready to take these seats?”
strings.IBR_VEN.27.a: It seems civilian dress will soon come back into fashion.
strings.IBR_VEN.27.tt:
With the triumph of the dissident conspiracy over the {ven_getflag} Venezuelan government and their {mex_getflag} allies, in the event of a coup, the {ven_getflag} Venezuelan government will collapse like a house of cards.

Whether it be weeks, months, or years, the success of {ibr_getflag} our infiltrators is now a certainty.
strings.IBR_VEN.28.desc:
The morning sun of Maracay struggled through the dusty blinds, striping the worn mosaic floor of the garrison mess hall with strict lines of light and shadow. Under the high vaults that remembered the times of the dictator Gómez, the blades of huge ceiling fans turned lazily, rhythmically slicing the thick, stagnant air where dust motes danced. The clatter of cheap aluminum spoons against metal trays echoed under the dome, creating the dreary symphony of an army morning.

Private Méndez stabbed the paper with a calloused finger, nearly tearing the page.

“See? That dandy in Miraflores wants us to eat dirt.” He looked around at his comrades, their faces dark from sun and fatigue. “Who among us joined the army for a good life? We are here because there is nothing to eat in our towns. We slept in the mud to send a few pitiful bolívares to our mothers. And now he takes even that?”

A murmur rose around the table. It was the voice of the real Venezuela - rough, poor, and angry.

“Villalba rides in a Cadillac with air conditioning and looks at the country from the window of a private plane,” another soldier spat. “What does he know about us? To him, we are numbers in a ledger. But he forgets who really holds this country. We are not his servants. We are the people given rifles. We are the only ones protecting poor devils like ourselves.”

While the argument flared, turning into a declaration of hatred for the well-fed, one soldier silently pushed his tray away. He took out a crumpled sheet of paper and began writing a letter to his uncle in Madrid. There, in Spain, they would understand. There, they know what happens when politicians start spitting in the faces of men holding loaded weapons.
strings.IBR_VEN.28.a: A hungry soldier is a dangerous soldier.
strings.IBR_VEN.29.desc:
Playa Parguito welcomed them with the dazzling turquoise of the Caribbean Sea and the rustle of coconut palms leaning over the water. Margarita still retained the charm of the wild “Pearl”: fishing boats bobbing on the waves, and an endless strip of white sand. Captain Ortega watched his children building a castle at the water's edge, his wife laughing as she brushed sand from her skirt. Idyllic. But in the Captain's head, this picture was already coming apart at the seams.

“How long can I afford this?” - the thought, sharp as a shard of glass, gave him no peace. Villalba's reforms. Ration cuts. The humiliation of the Venezuelan army. This paradise was about to become inaccessible to a man in uniform.

A shadow fell across his lounge chair. Grandfather Manuel, who had flown in yesterday from Seville, sat down heavily nearby. The old man, whose skin resembled the tanned leather of an old saddle, followed his grandson's gaze.

“I know that look, Miguel,” - his voice sounded hoarse, like the noise of pebbles. “You look at them and fear they will take away your future. In '48, when Rómulo Gallegos decided he could tell the army its place, we felt the same. And in '36, back home in Spain, when the Reds wanted to bring us to our knees... Do you know what we did?”

The grandfather leaned closer, and the fire of youth flared in his faded eyes. “We found each other. Officers in mess halls, sergeants in smoking rooms. Alone, you are a target. Together - a legion. Franco was just a soldier too, until he decided to become the Savior.”

Ortega felt as if he'd been struck by lightning. The realization was frighteningly simple. The army is not empty. The Perezjimenistas haven't gone anywhere; they are simply waiting for a signal. They would take advantage of a coup and, subsequently, oust the more liberal-minded officers of the Junta and worm their way back into power. And who better to help them than those who have already walked this path? Those who won in '36.

The Captain looked at the horizon, beyond which lay the Iberian Peninsula. Salvation would come from there.
strings.IBR_VEN.29.a: Sometimes the past holds the keys to the future.
strings.IBR_VEN.30.t: On the Outskirts of Puerto de la Cruz
strings.IBR_VEN.30.desc:
Luis and his squad sat by their jeep in the dead of night, smoking as the minutes ticked by. They had been up for hours, and were exhausted, but they had their firm orders. Félix Román Moreno, one of the leaders of the conspiracy, had ordered Luis and the others to maintain their post in this flat field, which was probably once an airstrip or something.

Finally, another jeep arrived from the darkness, shattering the endless monotony of the soldiers' vigil. The driver of the other jeep leaned out to talk to Luis and the others, introducing himself as Gabriel, “Heads up, a plane's gonna be landing here soon with supplies for the coup.” Sure enough, an old German cargo plane landed on the field a few minutes later. The plane was staffed by Spanish mercenaries, who opened up the hold as Luis greeted them.

Luis and his squad looked through the supplies. There was everything one could possibly need for a coup: crates of ammunition, rifles, grenades, and even false documents “verifying” their purchase by the Venezuelan government.

The crates clearly hailed from Iberia, with weapon manufacturers' logos and names stamped on all of them. The soldiers all celebrated, made jokes about getting the crates back to “the Venezuelan government,” and as they stepped foot off the aircraft were greeted by rifles pointed at their heads.

The soldier from the other jeep named Gabriel stepped forward, “We're with DIGEPOL and the Federal Security Directorate of Mexico. This is an order for all of you to stand down, your little conspiracy is over.”

As the intelligence agencies seized the plane and the conspirators, Gabriel returned to the jeep to inform headquarters of the good news.
strings.IBR_VEN.30.a: “We should have thanked Llovera Páez for the tip.”
strings.IBR_VEN.31.desc:
It was 3:30 AM, but Juan felt like he could conquer the world. He was standing with his fellow soldiers around a large military truck, eyes and ears trained. He didn't want to miss this. At the top of the truck, General Llovera Páez was exhorting the troops. “The senile old man in Caracas is paranoid that we will go against the interests of the people, but we are the ones who represent them! No true Venezolano wants to see our country torn apart by party interests, and no one wants a government that tries its hardest to ruin our soldiers!” Juan cheered along with the rest and boarded the truck. It was time to bring common sense back to Miraflores Palace.

The truck tore through the black night air, rapidly advancing towards Caracas surrounded by dozens of other trucks and armored cars. The chilly night air brushed against Juan's face from a crack in the hold, but he couldn't care less. “We're going to save Venezuela, mis compañeros! Can you believe it?” The other men were just as ecstatic as Juan. “It's going to be an incredible day”, said Alfonso. “We're actually making history”, Miguel piped up. “Imagine the picture”, Alberto cracked a smile. “All of us, standing outside Miraflores-”

Alberto was knocked to the floor of the truck, and Juan was flung on top of him. After a dazed moment, Juan realized that the whistle of the wind had stopped. The truck braked suddenly. “What happened?” Miguel groaned as Alfonso picked himself up. Juan stood up and dusted himself. “Let's find out.”

The four soldiers came out of the truck only to be blinded by the glare of flashlights and the barked orders of what seemed to be a whole battalion. When Juan figured out what he was seeing, he wished he hadn't. Tanks and APCs were blocking the road, disgorging soldiers who had remained loyal to the government. In front of his eyes, the soldiers dragged the men from the truck before them to the floor and handcuffed them. For a moment, Juan almost wanted to fight, but the call died on his tongue.
strings.IBR_VEN.31.a: It was at a place beyond pointless.
strings.IBR_VEN.32.desc:
Luis Felipe Llovera Páez could barely hear his frantic breathing and the shuffling of piles upon piles of paper through the roaring of the gas stove, set to full blast. He had managed to run for his life when the first vehicle in his ill-fated convoy was stopped by government forces, but he was not out of the fire, not by a long shot. Peering out of the window, he could see the rows of his men being loaded on trucks and led off through streets lined with tanks. The sight was almost as panic-inducing as Villalba's furious speech on the radio, denouncing him and all his men. But this wasn't the end, either.

Llovera Páez reached forward and threw another envelope full of papers onto the stove. The kitchen was full of ash and steam, all that remained of his glorious stand against Villaba. When DIGEPOL came here, they must not have been able to find anything tying him to Iberia, and particularly not to the Perezjimenistas. Of course, they won't be able to find Llovera Páez, either. The moment he'd burned the final document, he was going to get away from here and catch the first helicopter from the Iberian embassy. As the Yanquis say, if at first you don't succeed-

A short rap on the door disturbed Llovera Páez from his idyll. It only took him a moment to pick up three different piles of documents and turn to the stove in an attempt to burn everything he had left at once, but by then, the door had already been broken down. A crowd of DIGEPOL men swarmed into the small apartment, tackling him to the floor and filling the air with fluttering papers. Llovera Páez was shoved onto his stomach, his arms tied behind his back as someone declared that he was under arrest for conspiracy and espionage.
strings.IBR_VEN.32.a: From the floor, he could see a file with the Iberian seal on it next to him, and knew his fate was sealed.
strings.IBR_VEN.33.desc:
Whiskey spilled over the map of Caracas, drenching it, though not completely ruining it. Llovera Páez shot a glare at the drunkard responsible for the mess.

“Ay, amigos!” Páez shouted, banging the table with the butt of his knife. “Let's not celebrate too hard before we even succeed. We still have to go over the plan one last time.” The room slowly hushed down, save for the few drunken giggles and hiccups. “We'll storm the palace, just like in '48, and arrest the bastard Villalba before breakfast. By lunch, he'll have been sent off far away from Caracas.”

The room erupted in cheers. Men already started pouring liquor again, but Lieutenant Barrios raised his hand, hushing the other conspirators. “I'm afraid it won't be that simple, Páez.” He gestured his head towards the window, out into the dark streets of La Castellana. “There's been cars outside my house for the past week. No license plate, no nothing. DFS and DIGEPOL are onto us.”

Everyone looked to Páez for answers, but he couldn't offer any. “Caracas will be on higher alert then. A bloody coup's no good for anyone...”

“How 'bout we fucking distract the pendejos or some...” The drunkard slurred his words, almost faceplanting into the table. “Those cunts... always chasing after those commies...”

“The FALN?” Páez grinned. “I suppose we could falsify some reports... Leave them at the barracks... Send them on a wild goose chase outside Caracas just long enough for us to take Villalba... Keep drinking that alcohol, Luis. You're a lot smarter drunk.”

Laughter filled the room again. Glasses clinked. Toasts were given. Letters were sealed with ink spelling out the coordinates of ghost divisions lurking in the countryside.
strings.IBR_VEN.34.desc:
Luis Felipe Llovera Páez had been waiting for this moment since that cursed January of 1958. As the truck slowed down, he greedily scanned the outline of the Capitol against the dark mass of Mount Ávila. On the roof of the “temple of democracy,” silhouettes of soldiers were busily setting up a machine gun nest. The doors of parliament were wide open, like a mouth in a silent scream, and lights burned only in the vestibule. The talking was over. It was time to work.

The formerly exiled General jumped onto the asphalt, adjusting his holster. A young lieutenant immediately ran up to him, saluting.

“Report situation!”

“Perimeter is ours, my General. Awaiting orders.”

“One order, son.” Llovera Páez smiled predatorily. “Take Miraflores. Arrest Villalba. If he hides behind the constitution - smash his teeth with a rifle butt. We've had enough of this circus.”

He shifted towards Félix Román Moreno, his aide in the conspiracy to bring Perezjimenistas back to power, and signaled him to walk into the Chamber of Deputies. But instead of pomaded lawyers in expensive suits, the seats were occupied by simple soldiers in sweaty uniforms. Faces burned by the sun, hands accustomed to hard labor. The real Venezuela.

“Look around!” Román Moreno's voice, used to shouting over the roar of engines, filled the hall. “For years these walls heard only lies. They promised you bread but gave empty speeches. We are here to sweep away this trash. We will bring back the glory of our country!”

Of course, many officers present didn't know that what he meant was returning to Pérez Jiménez's 'New National Ideal', instead of a temporary setback of democracy. The hall responded with a murmur of approval. Behind him, Llovera Páez beckoned to an adjutant. “Drag the newsreel crew in here. Lights, cameras, everything proper. We want to make a statement that will be remembered. And for now...” He tore a sheet from his notebook and quickly scribbled a few lines. Dissolution of parties, cancellation of reforms, total military control. Demands Villalba would never accept. “Take this to the President. Let it be his epitaph.”
strings.IBR_VEN.35.desc:
Morning in Caracas began as usual. As the sun lazily crested the mountain slopes, Ignacio was buttoning his shirt in his bright apartment, located in the 23 de Enero - one of the neighborhoods built during the golden years of Pérez Jiménez's infrastructure boom. In the kitchen, a cornmeal arepa sizzled appetizingly in the pan, while the honking of Fords and Buicks drifted in through the open window. With a habitual morning gesture, he flicked the radio switch, expecting the weather forecast.

Instead of the familiar announcer's voice, the heavy brass of the national anthem blared from the speakers. Ignacio froze, cup in hand. The anthem abruptly cut off, giving way to the dry, measured baritone of General Félix Román Moreno.

“People of Venezuela,” the receiver broadcast coldly, “I address you at an hour when the incompetence of Jóvito Villalba has driven our nation into a dead end. His so-called 'reforms' have paralyzed the country.” The general ranted about how the armed forces—the true defenders of the people against poverty-had been humiliated, how partisanship had fractured society, and how the government remained blind to everything beyond the capital. “It seems even the Spanish kings, who never set foot on this land, understood it better than he does!” Moreno's voice strained.

Ignacio took a sip of his coffee. The coffee was excellent; but the speech was a broken record.

“Since our just demands were arrogantly rejected, the army is forced to take responsibility into its own hands. I announce the creation of a new civic-military junta, called upon to-”

Without waiting for the end of the sentence, Ignacio clicked the radio off. At that exact moment, the echoes of similar clicks rippled across the city: from the elite villas to the labyrinthine barrios. People silently returned to their routines. In his lifetime, Ignacio had seen too many coups, juntas, and fiery “saviors of the nation.” The faces in the newspapers changed, new promises and old propaganda poured forth, but none of these generals could alter the immutable fact that by nine in the morning, Ignacio had to be at work. Life went on, and the reality remained exactly the same.
strings.IBR_VEN.36.t: Lunch at The Edge of the World
strings.IBR_VEN.36.desc:
A low hum fills the cramped bodega on the Guyanese border, drowned out only by the persistent buzzing of fat flies. Above the counter hangs a calendar from five years ago - a busty blonde smiling through spots of cigar ash. A group of recruits, their sweaty tunics unbuttoned, greedily devour greasy reina pepiada, dropping chunks of avocado onto the sticky oilcloth table. For these boys, plucked from the bustle of Maracaibo and Valencia, service in this backwater is deadly dull, and they hungrily catch every word from the crackling radio.

“...President Caldera reports success in negotiations with Guyana and Canada...”

“Did you hear that? Goodbye, fucking mosquitoes; hello, hot blondie sifrinas of Caracas! I've forgotten what a woman with all her teeth looks like!”

The laughter is cut short by the slam of a bottle against the table. The soldier opposite, his face dark from the sun.

“Shut up,” - he snarls. - “Is getting your dick wet all you care about? That impotent in Miraflores is selling us to the fucking English! The ones who couldn't even hold onto their own island!”

“Come on, man, we just want to get out of here...”

“And I want to take back what is ours!” - he barks, jumping up. - “I know a hundred guys in the company who would swim across this piss-river tonight and slaughter everyone there. Orders or not. We are the Army, not watchdogs for bureaucrats. If Caldera thinks he can be a jalabolas for the gringos... I bet my paycheck he won't be sitting in that chair for long.”
strings.IBR_VEN.36.a: In the barracks, something worse than boredom is brewing.
strings.IBR_VEN.37.desc:
CONFIDENTIAL
TO: {ibr_getleader}, Minister of Foreign Affairs
Venezuela - South America

Our worst fears surrounding the stability of our Venezuelan ally has come to be. 5 hours ago, The Fuerzas Armadas de Liberácion National (henceforth FALN) has managed to seize large portions of the country in an armed coup, and is currently making an effort at fully capturing the country. FALN-FLN troops in Venezuela seized control of Ciudad Bolívar and several other cities in the East, after the front declared a general uprising against the government. Sympathetic civilians have assisted the rebels in their offensive, allowing them to seize almost the entire east in a matter of hours. Despite the FALN intending a swift, large-scale revolution across the country, units in the west appear to have been pushed back to the Andes, allowing the central government to survive and reconsolidate. However, the uprising has escalated into a full-scale civil war.

Although their initial attempt at a revolution failed, with resistance present in the west of the country limiting their forces to reorganize in the mountains, guerrilla and clandestine movements within government territory are still active and their base remains present in the east, with the FALN setting a new base in Ciudad Bolívar.

The FALN was formed in 1962 as the certification of efforts from the Communist Party of Venezuela after their removal from the old, liberal government. With the end of Venezuelan democracy, they have gained considerable support, both from general opponents as well as some radicalised liberals. With leftist success across much of Latin America already in play, excitement among Bolsheviks allowed the FALN to gain significant momentum. This civil war has already seen early fighting, but this will not stop at the frontlines; there is significant partisan warfare already, and an extended civil war will likely break down surviving civilian infrastructure.

The FALN succeeding would jeopardise our aims in Latin America. Not only is the FALN explicitly communist, but would also be hostile to us going forwards, thus removing further portions of Latin America from comfortably aligning with us. Defeating this movement would help us to build credibility in the region, and would help preserve our access to a major international oil reserve. In addition, we could feasibly use the strategies learnt for dealing with guerillas here for our combat against subversives.

Our campaign must be quick, however; the longer this war goes on, the more reduced civilian infrastructure becomes and the more jaded Venezuelan civilians become, the stronger the FALN's case will be.
strings.IBR_VEN.37.a: Critical support for a critical time.
strings.IBR_VEN.40.desc:
The army truck bounced over the potholes like a skiff in a storm. The road to San Cristóbal resembled the descent into Dante's Seventh Circle of Hell - cracked, pitted, and covered in fresh asphalt patches that guerrilla landmines would likely tear up again tomorrow. The sticky, suffocating heat of the lowlands was left behind; now, as the truck climbed into the Andes, a prickly mountain cold seeped into the bed.

Corporal Rafael Torres pulled his collar tighter, trying to keep warm. His squad had been attached to the National Guard for “joint exercises,” but so far, the only joint action had been swallowing dust.

“And then that butterfingers from the 'Águilas' drops the ball! In the ninth inning, can you imagine?” Lieutenant Gustavo Méndez, the Venezuelan commander, roared with laughter, slapping his knees. His soldiers cracked up, discussing a match from ten years ago in Maracaibo.

Torres understood the language - Castilian was native here - but the humor remained alien. To him, raised in the shadow of the Giralda in Seville, this passion for baseball was as incomprehensible as this endless war. He tightened his grip on the handguard of the CETME rifle resting across his knees and stared at the green slopes drifting by.

In Madrid, they were told they would gain “invaluable experience” here. But watching the wary gazes of peasants along the road, Rafael realized: “experience” was just a pretty word for things he would never write to his mother about. He closed his eyes, trying to summon the scent of Triana's orange groves, but all he could smell was cheap gasoline.
strings.IBR_VEN.40.a: The road is long, but memory is short.
strings.IBR_VEN.41.desc:
“...As my old friend, a contractor in Gran Canaria, used to say: ”If the foundation is poured concrete and the roof is pure gold, it doesn't matter a damn whose flag hangs on the pole - what matters is who has the keyring to the entrance in their pocket.“” - Matías Vega Guerra laughed boisterously, pleased with his own metaphor, and swept his gaze over his interlocutors. Beside him, António Fontes, maintaining an expression more suited to an undertaker at a funeral than a diplomat at breakfast, silently slid a map of the La Guaira port zones across the polished table.

In the cool hall of the new “Flor de Altamira” bakery, smelling of vanilla, cinnamon, and fresh croissants, the conversation flowed smoothly and mundanely. Extraction concessions, deep-sea fishing rights, contracts for laying pipes through the jungle-they carved the country into neat slices as easily and casually as they cut hot croissants with silver knives.

Two steps away from them, Elena scrubbed the already perfectly clean countertop with frenzy. The drone of their voices, mixed with the clinking of porcelain, echoed in her head like the echo of a nightmare. She remembered that accent - the characteristic “seseo,” imperious, harsh, and self-assured. Just like the masked men who had kicked in the door of her house near Apure a month ago and dragged her brother into the darkness of the night. Who was it? Soldiers? Guerrilla? She wasn't told. She knew only one thing: now there were too many foreign uniforms on the streets of Caracas, and in this room, at the best table, rang the voices of the new masters of life, for whom Venezuela was merely an asset in a ledger.

“More coffee, caballeros?” she asked quietly, approaching the table when Matías's laughter died down.
strings.IBR_VEN.42.desc:
Father Carvalho was Portuguese, born and raised in Lisbon, not Venezuelan. He never questioned his posting to San Juan de Los Morros. He had joined the mission right after his priestly vows, years before the war. If God sent him to guide Guárico's flock amid these troubled times, then it was his divine calling.

“And remember, my children, that God loves you. Put your entire faith in His Grace...” His voice held steady despite older boys peering out windows at military trucks rumbling by. Barely visible Venezuelan and Iberian helmets in equal numbers stood straight in the back. Comfort came in knowing his Spanish had improved, and that his accent was no longer the reason for their distraction.

“In truth, children, these are hard times, and some among you may doubt God's plans for this land and your lives. If Divine Grace and Providence don't comfort you as they do me, trust earthly authorities—parents, teachers, government...” He paused longly after the last word, even for a small orator like himself “...Order underpins society, ordained by God. Render unto Caesar what is Caesar's, and unto God what is God's. You may leave now. I am always present for anything you may need.”

The boys filed out to the Catholic School's dormitories. Once alone, Father Carvalho hurried to the basement. A dozen guerrilleros, undoubtedly saved from certain death by his open Church doors, huddled in panic from the trucks. He comforted each individually and prayed for war's quick end and easy family reunions. A boy, barely older than the students, asked why an Iberian like him risked himself to help them. Calmly, he grasped the boy's hand in a gentle caress.
strings.IBR_VEN.42.a: “By this we know love, that He laid down His life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers.”
strings.IBR_VEN.43.desc:
San Fernando de Apure melted in the midday haze. The dust of the Llanos clogged pores and gritted between teeth. For the squad, it was routine: a kick to the door, a quick sweep of the kitchen, a check of the backyard, move on to the next house. Retired Brigadier General Salvador Mola walked behind, leaning on a cane, more for show than out of necessity.

Behind one door, painted in peeling sky-blue, they found an old man. He sat in a wicker rocking chair, thumbing wooden rosary beads. Click. Click. Click. He answered the lieutenant's questions quietly, looking not at the soldiers, but at the crucifix on the wall. “No, señores. There is only me and the Lord here.” They left him in the gloom.

Mola lingered on the threshold, feeling an unnatural chill run down his spine. Thirty-three years ago. Toledo. He, then just a young “Requeté” captain, had entered the homes of his neighbors just like this, hunting for Republicans. The same whitewashed walls, the same old men with rosaries swearing ignorance.

In '36, one such old man also said he was alone. A few minutes later, a machine gun opened fire on Mola's platoon from his basement.

The General wiped sweat from his brow with a silk handkerchief. Was this Venezuelan lying? Mola didn't know. But he knew one thing for certain: civil war wears the same face everywhere - the face of a neighbor smiling at you while gripping a knife in his pocket.
strings.IBR_VEN.43.a: Some doors are better left unopened.
strings.IBR_VEN.44.desc:
“Let's leave the lyrics for the newspapers, gentlemen. Numbers speak clearer. The expansion of the Bajo Grande terminal's capacity requires a review of insurance premiums.” - A heavyset Venezuelan industrialist tapped a pen on the unfolded map, outlining the contours of future profits. - “If Madrid guarantees the delivery of dredging equipment by this year, we will increase crude oil shipments by 15%.”

Matías Vega Guerra nodded benevolently, breaking off a piece of pastry. Beside him, António Fontes, looking like a bird of prey in a severe suit, was already making corrections in a notebook, crossing out unnecessary expenses. At this table, sheltered from the street heat by the hum of air conditioners, the recent war was discussed exclusively as an annoying logistical glitch - a traffic jam on the road to prosperity which, fortunately, had cleared.

Elena, frozen with the coffeepot in her hands, tried to become invisible. This morning, making her way to her shift along Avenida Francisco de Miranda, she realized with horror how quickly the city had changed its face. A week ago, foreign presence meant the clanking of tracks, checkpoints, and the shouting of patrols. But today, the strangers vanished from the armor and materialized in cool bank vestibules, in the soft armchairs of hotel lobbies, at the tables of expensive restaurants.

She saw them everywhere: confident men in impeccable Italian suits, speaking with the same characteristic accent as the soldiers who had searched her home.

Her brother disappeared several weeks ago. No letter, no body, no grave. For these people, his death was just a line item in the “security costs” column. They divided the country, drank its oil, and ate its bread, not even noticing they were walking on bones. The girl bit her lip, suppressing a scream, quickly wiped a spot with a napkin. In this new, glittering world, there was no place for her grief.
strings.IBR_VEN.44.a: Coffee served, contracts signed, dead forgotten.
strings.IBR_VEN.45.desc:
Matías Vega Guerra and António Fontes descended the marble steps of Miraflores Palace, their hurried footsteps echoing with the hollow sound of final failure. Their briefcases, usually swollen with draft concessions and secret protocols, swung in their hands unnaturally light today, like sails without wind. Inside reigned a sterile void: no oil contracts, no security guarantees, no port rights. The game was over, and the dealer had taken all the chips.

The Iberians walked to the car quickly, exchanging no banter, their faces frozen masks of restrained fury. They were hurrying to the runway before the country's new masters changed their minds about letting them out alive.

And at the other end of the city, where the air had recently been saturated with the scent of pastries, the wind chased grey ash over a pile of broken brick. The “Flor de Altamira” bakery, that symbol of metropolitan gloss, had ceased to exist-turned into a smoking crater after a strike by the UTC urban guerrilla, clearing the path for the march of leftist forces.

Elena stood before the ruins, clutching a bundle with her meager belongings. Now she had neither a job nor a home. She looked at the spot where the diplomats' favorite table had stood, and physically felt their absence. The strangers were gone. The hated accent had vanished, swept away by revolutionary slogans. But this ringing silence pressed on her ears harder than their arrogant orders. Her brother did not return. The “imperialists” were expelled, but her world did not become better. Elena turned away from the rubble and wandered into nowhere, just another nameless grain of sand ground down by the millstones of history, which never cares for little people.
strings.IBR_VEN.45.a: The war ended, the questions remained.
strings.IBR_VEN.46.desc:
“Withdraw?! Give up our land to those bastards?!” - The scream dissolved into the sound of shattering glass. Juan de Dios Moncada Vidal swept a heavy marble ashtray off the desk, sending it smashing against the wall, leaving a deep dent in the plaster. The General stood in the middle of the office, his uniform unbuttoned, chest heaving, his face flushed with crimson, apoplectic rage.

The adjutant who had delivered the order decided to beat a hasty retreat before Moncada Vidal's wrath, in the form of a wine bottle, struck him too.

“Caldera... that pathetic, spineless piece of shit!” - Moncada kicked an armchair as if it were the President himself. - “Coward! Traitor! How did that desk rat dare raise his hand?! Essequibo is our land! It is a gift from God and the legacy of Bolívar! And he sells it like a cheap whore, to a bunch of English degenerates in Canada, just to get a pat on the head from Washington?!”

He stormed over to the portrait of the Liberator and punched the wall beside the frame.

“I will not allow the Army to be turned into a gathering of eunuchs! We swore to defend the Homeland, not to spread our legs for foreigners! Street dogs have bigger balls than this entire liberal circus put together!”

Suddenly, the frenzy in his eyes was replaced by a cold, predatory glint. Caldera is flying to Trinidad. To sign this shameful pact. The throne in Miraflores will be empty.

Moncada exhaled slowly. He has the men. He has the support of Madrid and Lisbon. It is time to end this elitist farce.

He picked up the phone receiver, gripping it so hard the plastic creaked piteously. - “Connect me to the garrisons. And prepare a cipher for our friends in the Old World.”
strings.IBR_VEN.46.a: He who cannot wear the uniform shall not wear the crown.
strings.IBR_VEN.47.desc:
The men snapped to attention as Moncada Vidal walked into the room. The patriots had been prepared to defend their country, and now, Moncada was about to give the order to seize the country back from those who would seek to undermine it. The socialists would sell the country to Canada in a heartbeat, and now, they would pay for their treachery in blood.

“You have all been prepared, so I will make this brief. Our target is the Palacio Blanco first, then we will move onward to Miraflores. Once we have both buildings under control, we will demand a surrender of any forces loyal to Caldera and march out into the street to secure the capital. Any socialist who stands in our way will be eliminated. Men, this is the greatest moment in our history since Bolívar, and like Bolívar, we will...”

The door was kicked open, hammers clicked as men began to pour in. “DIGEPOL, throw down your weapons!” National Guard and DIGEPOL forces, with masks and body armor, held up their weapons.

Weapons discharged, the room filled with the smell of gunpowder. Screams punctuated the gunfire. As the haze cleared, over fifteen of the National Guard and DIGEPOL forces were dead or downed, the rest fleeing as some of his men led the pursuit, firing upon the cowards as they fled. Moncada Vidal looked over the room. His men had a few casualties, the first martyrs of national liberation. He pointed his pistol at a National Guardsman, dazed on his back from a gunshot that his armor saved him from, and with a single pull of the trigger, turned the traitor's head to paste.

One of his men went to another room to grab an undamaged radio. “My loyal soldiers, we now stand at the moment of national liberation. All who believe in our nation, and in the strength of our men to lead it. Any who stand against us, soldier or civilian, is an enemy that will be dealt with as enemies are. Forward!”
strings.IBR_VEN.47.a: His men saluted, and began their march, singing Gloria Bravo Pueblo as they went.
strings.IBR_VEN.48.desc:
With a loud clatter, the last of the military trucks were turned over to the cheers of the cursed Calderists. His own forces had ceded the ground floor of the White Palace, taking up better positions as the National Guard and disloyal army breached the main doors. Moncada Vidal's early momentum had broken down not long after taking the Palace. Several of his units had been arrested in their barracks before they could secure their weapons. Infiltrators had discovered which units were loyal to him, and they had robbed him of his strength before they could fight.

His Iberian contact had said as much, saying that they would have succeeded had they just conducted themselves with more discipline. Hollow words, the Iberians didn't have the stomach to fight. “Retreat, Moncada. Your position is untenable. We can extract you to Madrid and push for the country in a few years.” The first part of the offer was undoubtedly sincere. The latter was a lie, either deliberate or negligent, Moncada Vidal didn't care which. He would not be a subject of gawkery in Madrid, the failed plotter.

“Never! I am a patriot. I will fight to my last breath to free my country!” He slammed the receiver down on the phone, nearly cracking the handset.

A loud burst came as the traitors breached the next floor. Moncada grabbed his rifle, peeked out from the door, and fired at the first enemy shape he saw. He moved back to an overturned desk, firing on the entryway. He may have hit the first two men, but then two more, and then two more, their bullets sending splinters flying.

His rifle went dry, and rather than fumble for another magazine, he grabbed the weapon of a fallen soldier next to him. This time, however, a bullet hit his shoulder, and as his body lurched from the impact, another bullet struck home, then another.

His dreams of coup leaked out onto the Palacio Blanco's floors, and his exaltations of a new Venezuela ended in a raspy gurgle.
strings.IBR_VEN.48.a: Moncada Vidal followed the example that Caracas gave.
strings.IBR_VEN.49.desc:
“What is it, Fernando?” Franco was seated behind his desk, sorting through some files. “You wanted to see me?”

Fernando María Castiella y Maíz did not, in fact, want to see the Caudillo. But as Minister of Foreign Affairs, he was obliged to bring the latest news to his leader, even if he would rather be anywhere else in the world right now. “Yes, Señor. There is news from South America, and I'm afraid it's bad.”

Franco gritted his teeth and began fidgeting with his pen. “Get it out, then. I don't have all day to hear about the failures of our esteemed diplomatic corps.”

Castiella y Maíz swallowed hard. “Well, Venezuelan President Rafael Caldera has released a trove of information about our involvement in the Moncada Vidal fiasco. Presented everything to the OAS and to the public, with the names of dozens of involved officers. Some of our people working with the Bolivarianists were also implicated. We could deny our involvement, but... it's not looking good, Caudillo. Caldera had already blasted us as a sponsor of fascist violence and claimed that the Bolivarianists weren't true nationalists but merely our jack-booted puppets. And he has the documents to back this up.”

After spilling the burst of information, the slightly shaking Minister looked once more at Franco. The Caudillo was still seated in his seat, impassively looking down at him. Castiella y Maíz took a deep breath and continued. “This will be a grave blow to our efforts at expanding diplomatic and economic ties throughout the region. I... apologize. We have failed Iberia.”

Franco's mouth twisted into a grimace. “It's no matter. We won't have to hear so many foreign dignitaries fumbling over their Spanish here in Madrid.” His mouth straightened, but the steel in his eyes remained.
strings.IBR_VEN.50.desc:
In the stifling barracks of Fort Tiuna, there was no room for doubt. Moncada Vidal stood before the ranks of conspirators, and his voice sounded like hammer blows. No politics, only naked, fanatical resolve. “Caldera is in Trinidad. While he gives away our land, we will restore Venezuela's honor. Your objective is the Palacio Blanco and Miraflores. Anyone standing in the way - socialists, liberals, guardsmen - are enemies of Bolívar. Cleanse the city. Take no prisoners. Forward!”

Crates stamped with the marks of Spanish arms factories creaked as they were pried open with crowbars. Brand-new rifles, still in factory grease, settled into soldiers' hands. Minutes later, the avenues of Caracas shuddered from tank treads and the roar of APCs.

And then they began to sing. “Gloria al Bravo Pueblo...”.

The tracks of a “Moristel” tank screech as they bite into the asphalt, grinding down a hastily erected barricade of trash cans and abandoned cars. A student winding up to throw a stone falls, cut in half by a machine-gun burst.

“...que el yugo lanzó...”

An RPG shot blows away the wrought-iron gates of the Palacio Blanco. The blast wave hurls two guardsmen onto the pavement, turning their dress uniforms into bloody tatters. Shards of glass rain down on the heads of the screaming crowd.

“...La Ley respetando, la virtud y honor.”

A Bolivarian officer coolly finishes off a wounded policeman trying to crawl away. In the smoke of the burning city, to the majestic melody of the anthem, Venezuelans killed Venezuelans with a frenzy not seen since the War of Independence.
strings.IBR_VEN.50.a: The streets will wash in blood in the name of Bolívar.
strings.IBR_VEN.51.desc:
The phone receiver in Moncada's hand was slippery with sweat. Through the blown-out window of the White Palace, a view opened onto Urdaneta Avenue. Smoke from burning tires obscured the sun, and thousands of people - students, workers, clerks - merged into a single howling mass, a living shield blocking the approaches to Miraflores Palace. They did not retreat even under warning shots. “Enrique, they've blocked every meter!” the General snarled into the receiver, the hysteria of a cornered beast in his voice. “I will order the tanks to crush them. I will pave the road to the palace with their bones if I have to!”

Enrique Valenzuela's voice sounded dry and squeamish in the speaker - “Curb your bloodlust, general. If you smear them now, the world will see a monster in you. Form the armor into a wedge and punch through to the palace gates. When the crown is yours, any execution becomes a 'restoration of constitutional order.' Feel the difference?”

Moncada breathed heavily, looking at the raging sea below. Then, clenching his teeth, he barked into the radio: “All crews! Full speed! Objective - Miraflores gates. Do not bypass obstacles. I repeat: do not bypass obstacles!”

Diesel engines roared, drowning out the screams of the crowd. Thirty-ton machines surged forward. The first rows of protesters vanished under the tracks; barricades of buses crumpled like cardboard, spraying glass and twisted metal.

Half an hour later, stepping over the corpses of guardsmen in the palace corridors, Moncada stepped out onto the famous Balcony of the People. Before the camera lens, he threw his hands to the sky, and his voice, torn by shouting, carried over burning Caracas:
strings.IBR_VEN.51.a: “Look, Venezuelans! Look at how the legacy of the traitor Caldera burns!”
strings.IBR_VEN.52.desc:
At the gates of the White Palace, the wreck of an overturned truck smoked - a black skeleton caked in burning rubber. The protesters' final attack had choked instantly: “Bolivarian” machine gunners turned the living wave into a pile of broken dolls scattered on the asphalt in puddles already starting to thicken in the heat. Moncada Vidal stepped over someone's hand without breaking stride and dived into the cool interior of the waiting limousine.

When the car started moving, the officer behind the wheel asked - “General... what should be done with the Minister of Internal Affairs and the staff in Miraflores? If they surrender...”

Moncada chuckled coldly, looking at his reflection in the dark glass. - “History is not interested in the fate of bureaucrats, Lieutenant. Let them run, let them burn, let them pray. I need the palace, not the rats inside. Forward.”

The motorcade tore down Urdaneta Avenue, and a panorama of agonizing Caracas unfolded before the General's eyes. The city looked as if it had been gutted. Building facades, riddled with heavy caliber fire, gaped with black window holes like empty eye sockets. The cobblestones were strewn with broken glass that crunched under the tires. Everywhere - from San Bernardino to El Silencio - columns of smoke rose, veiling the sun in a funeral shroud.

But where others saw destruction, Moncada saw birth. In this chaos, in these burning barricades, the chains of the “International Order” that suffocated the nation were melting. He pressed the button, lowering the window. Hot, stifling air burst into the cabin - a mixture of burnt flesh, gasoline, and sweetish cordite. Moncada took a deep breath, filling his lungs with this poisonous bouquet. This was the smell of freedom. This was the smell of victory.
strings.IBR_VEN.52.a: A new sun rises over Miraflores.
strings.IBR_VEN.53.desc:
In the air-conditioned silence of the Miraflores annex, the clink of a coffee spoon against porcelain sounded louder than ever. Martín Vegas, the Minister of Foreign Affairs, sat at the long polished table with an expression of polite boredom, shuffling stacks of documents. Across from him, the Iberian delegation sipped cooling espresso, swallowing their growing irritation along with it.

The meeting was impeccably correct, but every word Vegas spoke, every paper about “tariff adjustments” and “shipping delays” was a slap in the face. Pedro Tinoco did not come. Diego Cisneros, the regime's Minister of Internal Affairs, didn't even send a secretary. Those empty chairs at the head of the table screamed louder than any note of protest: “You are no longer important.”

Vegas spoke softly, evasively, chalking up every refusal to “changing conditions in the region.” The word “Colombia” was never spoken aloud, but it hung in the air like heavy smog. Having lost Bogotá, Iberia had lost face, and Caracas had noticed. Venezuela was drifting away like an iceberg driven by the current of pragmatism.

As the delegates left the hall, they felt the cold truth on their backs: the era of “special relations” was over. Iberia was no longer the center of gravity, but just another petitioner in a crowded line for oil. And against the backdrop of the looming Oil Crisis, this revelation was akin to a death sentence.
strings.IBR_VEN.53.a: Silence is the loudest sound on earth.
strings.IBR_VEN.53.tt:
With the loss in {col_getflag} Colombia representing our biggest defeat in the Americas thus far, our {ven_getflag} Venezuelan partners have deemed it necessary to seek {usa_getflag} {ger_getflag} alternative sponsors.
------------------------------------
strings.IBR_VEN.54.t: The Tight Uniform of the Old World
strings.IBR_VEN.54.desc:
Diego Cisneros dissected the Iberian economy with the cold dispassion of a pathologist. His pointer slid across the charts: plateaus, stagnation, missed opportunities. Arturo Uslar Pietri listened silently, fingers steepled. There was no hostility in his gaze-only the weary condescension with which a professor looks at a negligent student.

“They have become... insignificant, Diego,” the President said thoughtfully, looking through his interlocutor. “Venezuela has outgrown this alliance, like a teenager outgrows children's clothes. We are too rich, too ambitious to tie our fate to a fading star.”

Uslar Pietri stood and walked to the window, beyond which Caracas hummed. “Many years ago, I said: 'We must sow the oil.' But you cannot grow a baobab in the clay pot Madrid offers us. We need space. We need markets that grow, not decay.”

At subsequent receptions, Iberian diplomats encountered the most terrible kind of refusal-polite indifference. They were thanked, treated to the best coffee, and... forgotten. The shadow of the Colombian failure lay on them as an indelible mark of weakness. If Iberia had held Bogotá, Caracas might have wavered. But now, on the threshold of the Oil Crisis, Venezuela stepped over its former patron, fixing its gaze on a future where there was no longer a place for decrepit Europe.
strings.IBR_VEN.55.desc:
“These figures look respectable, Jóvito, but every line here is written in ink diluted with old fear. This is the legacy of an era when we paid not for goods, but for protection. But I suppose the time for racketeering has passed.”

Miguel Ángel Burelli Rivas slowly, almost with ritual solemnity, closed the folder, as if slamming the coffin lid on an entire era. Across from him, arms crossed, stood Jóvito Villalba. The President stared fixedly out the window at Caracas sprawled below, as if trying to discern in the labyrinth of streets traces of that very “abnormal dependency” they were about to shed. Iberian influence had seeped into the city's foundation: into bondage contracts signed at gunpoint, into debts owed to generals whose names were already history.

But the wind had changed. The collapse of Iberian ambitions in Colombia was a signal: the lion had grown old and lost its teeth. If they couldn't hold onto Bogotá, who were they to dictate to Caracas?

“We will call it a 'rebalancing,'” the Minister continued in his soft, enveloping baritone. “A course correction. No notes of protest, no loud accusations. We will leave the door open, let them see us leaving the room.”

In the embassies of Madrid and Lisbon, this polite, quiet refusal would sound louder than a cannon shot. For Iberia, standing on the threshold of the Oil Crisis, the loss of its richest partner in the Americas would be a gut punch from which it was unlikely to recover.
strings.IBR_VEN.56.desc:
In the damp concrete belly of the bunker beneath Miraflores, fluorescent lights flickered in time with the dull thuds of artillery above. The air here was stale, soaked in the smell of old fear and cheap tobacco. Edito Ramírez, the Minister of Foreign Affairs, resembled a melting wax figure: sweat streamed down his face, turning the collar of his dress uniform into a wet rag.

“...Exclusive rights to the shelf... full immunity for your personnel...” he mumbled, trembling fingers shuffling papers. “We are also prepared to consider transferring port terminals in Puerto Cabello to your jurisdiction...”

{ven_getleader} slowly leaned back in his chair, his gaze losing focus as it fixed on a crack in the ceiling. Ramírez's voice, listing the points of national humiliation, became distant, irrelevant - like the buzzing of a persistent fly. The General stopped processing the details of the concessions. Instead, he listened to a different rhythm seeping through meters of earth and concrete: the dull vibration of tank engines and the staccato of machine guns. Up there, his city was burning. Up there, fate was being decided, while down here... here...

Reality snapped back with the sharp, scratching sound of a fountain pen on expensive paper. {ven_getleader} blinked. The Iberian diplomat was already standing, extending a hand across the table with an inscrutable smile.

“We accept, General. The papers are signed.”

{ven_getleader} shook the offered palm mechanically, feeling nothing but the coldness of another man's skin.
strings.IBR_VEN.57.t: Rats, the Ship, and the Captain
strings.IBR_VEN.57.desc:
“...Madrid assures of the immutability of fraternal ties and offers an expanded package of economic cooperation in light of regional instability...” read the dry voice of Leónidas Sánchez Carrero. The Minister of Foreign Affairs put down the dispatch, removed his glasses, and wearily rubbed the bridge of his nose. He knew the value of these words, just as the man standing by the window did.

Marcos Pérez Jiménez looked at his official portrait from the 50s hanging on the wall. That young general on the canvas, in a shining uniform and with the Order of the Liberator, was naive. He believed in allies. This one, returned from exile, believed only in reinforced concrete and force.

He remembered 1958. He remembered the roar of the turbines of the plane carrying him away from the enraged mob. Where was “fraternal Iberia” then? They looked away when the knives came out. They loved his oil, but were ashamed of his friendship.

And now, when Iberia had crashed out of Colombia, losing its main foothold in the Andes, they came crawling for support? Pérez Jiménez laughed a short, barking laugh.

“Enough, Leónidas.” Pérez Jiménez turned. “For the press, call it a 'pragmatic reorientation within the framework of the New National Ideal.' Pretty words for fools.”

He walked to the table and slapped his palm on the Iberian dispatch. “And tell the ambassadors plainly, this is their last visit to this office. They cost me too much. Goodbye.”
strings.IBR_VEN.58.desc:
Matías Vega Guerra, held the cipher with two fingers, as if it were not diplomatic mail, but a dead rat thrown onto the embassy doorstep. “Did you read this nonsense from Abbes, António?” the Spaniard snorted, tossing the sheet onto the table. “Our friend in Ciudad Trujillo is in hysterics. His goons from the SIM claim that the Venezuelans are ferrying a revived 'Caribbean Legion' to the Dominican Republic. Via Cuba. Can you imagine? They see the ghost of Rómulo Betancourt in every shadow.”

António Fontes, the Minister-Counselor, without looking up from studying the nautical charts, carefully adjusted his glasses. “Abbes, for all his brutish stupidity, is right this time. Look here.” The Portuguese poked his pencil at a point north of the Paraguaná Peninsula. “Agents report the departure of 'Nueva Esparta' - class destroyers. These aren't the rusty tubs the Mexicans sail. This is the best fleet in the Caribbean Basin - the Venezuelan navy.”

Matías stopped smiling. He walked over to the map, and understanding flashed in his eyes. The murder of the father of Venezuelan democracy had not gone unpunished. “So, a vendetta...” the Spaniard drawled, and involuntary respect sounded in his voice. “Betancourt is dead, but his fleet is coming to sink Trujillo. Beautiful. Even poetic.”

“More like a problem,” António cut him off, already feeding a clean sheet into the typewriter. “Madrid needs to know about this before our friend is put in the ground. Dictate, Ambassador. 'Urgent. Santa Cruz. High activity of the Venezuelan Navy observed...'
strings.IBR_VEN.58.a: In this part of the world, even the dead know how to shoot.
